artigo.texto: Carlos Wizard amplia investimentos em Portugal com expansão da Help Battery Empresário aposta em modelo de hubs logísticos para serviço de atendimento automotivo 24 horas e prevê chegar a 80 unidades no mercado Português O empresário Carlos Wizard está ampliando seus investimentos na Europa com uma nova frente de atuação no setor de serviços em Portugal. No início deste ano, Wizard associou-se a um grupo de empresários brasileiros radicados no país para impulsionar a expansão da Help Battery, empresa que atua no atendimento automotivo emergencial. Com sede em Braga e operação há mais de seis anos, a Help Battery oferece atendimento 24 horas a motoristas que enfrentam problemas relacionados à bateria de seus veículos. A proposta é levar o serviço ao cliente de forma ágil, com uma estrutura operacional apoiada por hubs logísticos distribuídos em diferentes regiões. O modelo de expansão adotado para o negócio difere do sistema de franquias que marca a trajetória empresarial de Carlos Wizard. Na Help Battery, a operação central concentra atividades como estratégia comercial, expansão, marketing, atendimento ao cliente, cobrança e gestão da entrega dos produtos e serviços. O investidor, por sua vez, torna-se proprietário de um hub logístico responsável pelo armazenamento das baterias utilizadas na região atendida. Segundo a empresa, a estrutura foi concebida para operar sem a necessidade de uma equipe própria de funcionários no hub, já que a gestão operacional é centralizada pela matriz. Expansão em Portugal Com investimento inicial acessível a partir de 70 mil euros, o candidato interessado no projeto pode ter operações em cidades como Lisboa, Coimbra e Porto, além da expansão gradual para outras regiões de Portugal. A expectativa de Wizard é alcançar 80 hubs de atendimento no país e, posteriormente, avaliar a entrada da Help Battery em outros mercados europeus. Além da oportunidade de investimento, o projeto é apresentado como uma alternativa para brasileiros que consideram estabelecer negócios e residência no exterior. De acordo com Wizard, os investidores recebem suporte na preparação da documentação necessária para o processo de imigração, obtenção do visto adequado à condição de investidor e regularização comercial em Portugal. "Após as eleições, cresceu significativamente o número de famílias interessadas em imigrar para os Estados Unidos, Canadá e vários países da Europa. Essa é uma opção para quem busca diversificação em seus investimentos ou até mesmo a imigração para um novo país", afirma Carlos Wizard. Para o empresário, a entrada em novos mercados também faz parte de uma estratégia de diversificação e busca por oportunidades além dos segmentos em que tradicionalmente atua. "O sucesso do passado não garante o sucesso do futuro. De tempos em tempos, é necessário analisar e considerar novos modelos de negócios e novos mercados", conclui Wizard.

artigo.texto: Juniper Green Commissions 108.50 MWp Solar and 94.77 MWh BESS 23 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Juniper Green Energy has commissioned capacities across two renewable energy projects through its subsidiaries. Juniper Green ETA Five has completed the entire 108.50 MWp solar component of a 75 MW wind-solar hybrid power project, while Juniper Green Stellar has commissioned a 94.77 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). Both commissioning activities took place at their respective project sites on November 19, 2026. The solar component forms part of a project being developed under a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company (MSEDCL). Juniper Green ETA Five, a wholly owned subsidiary of Juniper Green Energy, undertook the commissioning. The company disclosed the development through a regulatory filing. Juniper Green Stellar, another wholly owned subsidiary, commissioned the 94.77 MWh BESS as merchant capacity. The storage facility will initially operate in the merchant market, although the subsidiary retains the option of transferring the capacity to a long-term PPA in the future. Earlier this year, Juniper Green Energy fully commissioned a 100 MWh merchant BESS project at Bikaner in Rajasthan through its subsidiary Juniper Green Cosmic. The project is among the first operational merchant BESS facilities in India. The company also completed a 150 MW wind-solar hybrid project awarded by Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam after commissioning its final 5 MW wind turbine. The 150 MW hybrid project was secured through the greenshoe option under a 500 MW tender issued by Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam. Juniper Green received the project at a tariff of Rs. 3.04/kWh, while KPI Green Energy secured a 50 MW project at Rs. 2.99/kWh. The latest commissioning adds to Juniper Green Energy’s operating renewable generation and storage portfolio. artigo.texto: Transmissoras de energia sinalizam que não vão participar dos leilões de baterias marcados para os próximos dias 2 e 4 de dezembro, a despeito de terem se engajado há anos em estudos e projetos pioneiros de baterias instaladas na Rede Básica. O motivo é a possibilidade de terem de compartilhar com os consumidores a receita proveniente dos sistemas de armazenamento, para fins de modicidade tarifária. A Taesa já anunciou que não vai participar do certame, mesmo após ter cadastrado diversos projetos para a disputa. A diretora Financeira da empresa, Catia Pereira, explicou à Coluna que o principal motivo da desistência é a insegurança regulatória e citou dúvidas relacionadas à “modicidade tarifária”. “Pensando em disciplina de capital, pensando em ter clareza sobre essa questão regulatória que vem para as baterias, dado que estamos em um setor regulado e muito previsível, temos um cuidado maior, então decidimos tirar o pé desse leilão e continuar estudando, continuar contribuindo com essa discussão regulatória, mas não participando”, afirmou. Já a Isa Energia, detentora do primeiro projeto de baterias do Brasil, instalado junto à subestação Registro, no Estado de São Paulo, afirmou, também no início do mês, que analisava a potencial participação no leilão de baterias “com cautela”. A diretora executiva de Finanças, Relações com Investidores e Desenvolvimento de Negócios da companhia, Silvia Wada, também justificou a prudência adotada pela existência de “incertezas” sobre o certame, incluindo a questão da modicidade tarifária e rateio do encargo que custeará os sistemas contratados no leilão. Pela lei em vigor, o custo será arcado exclusivamente pelas geradoras, em um formato ainda sujeito a regulamentação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). A regra desagradou as geradoras, que tentam alterar a norma no Congresso e entraram na Justiça para tentar suspender o leilão e tornar a regra inconstitucional. Durante videoconferência com analistas e investidores, Wada afirmou que o potencial compartilhamento de receita poderia reduzir a competição no certame, uma vez que inviabilizaria a participação das transmissoras. Regulação O tema do compartilhamento de receitas não consta no edital do leilão, mas chegou a ser comentado em reunião de diretoria da Aneel, durante a deliberação sobre esses documentos. O assunto veio à tona após a Taesa fazer uma consulta ao regulador sobre a necessidade de alteração do Estatuto Social da companhia caso viesse a participar do certame e obtivesse outorga independente na condição de armazenador. As áreas técnicas da agência indicaram que a transmissora poderia disputar o leilão e constituir uma Sociedade de Propósito Específico (SPE) sob controle direto, mas teria a captura de parte da receita para modicidade tarifária para os usuários conectados no segmento de transmissão. Durante a reunião da Aneel, um representante da Taesa criticou a orientação e defendeu que a participação da transmissora deveria ser em “igualdade de condições, em benefício da isonomia e da livre concorrência”, portanto sem a captura de receitas do novo segmento, mas como atividade segregada. “Aqui a transmissora não está prestando serviços de engenharia dentro de seu contrato de concessão, mas sim como empreendedor único e independente de armazenador de bateria, para participar desse leilão, com objetivo de ter uma outorga de armazenamento”, argumentou Rafael Janiques, advogado que falou em nome da empresa. Ele lembrou que já existe no mercado estrutura de modelo de negócios em que um mesmo CNPJ opera concessões de transmissão e separadamente usinas de geração ou concessões de distribuição, sem compartilhamento de receitas, e citou empresas como Axia, Copel e EDP. O procurador geral junto à Aneel, Eduardo Ramalho, explicou que a procuradoria qualificou a atividade de armazenamento como conexa aos contratos de concessão existentes, o que permitiria o compartilhamento de receitas. Já o diretor relator do processo sobre o edital do leilão, Gentil Nogueira, avaliou que o regulador não controla todas as formas possíveis de participação de uma transmissora no certame e em que medida algum ativo poderia ser compartilhado, por isso não poderia fazer uma análise genérica sobre o tema. Com isso, a questão ficou em aberto. Com a palavra Procurada pela reportagem, a Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (Abrate) disse entender que o compartilhamento para a modicidade tarifária só se justifica quando há aproveitamento de ativos já remunerados pelos consumidores via Receita Anual Permitida (RAP). “Esse pressuposto não se aplica a projetos de armazenamento estruturados de forma autônoma - com outorga própria, patrimônio, financiamento e contabilidade segregados, investimentos integralmente novos, riscos assumidos pelo investidor e sem uso de bens reversíveis ou recursos da RAP”, disse, por meio de nota. Diante da indefinição, a entidade apresentou uma carta à Aneel solicitando à Secretaria de Leilões e às áreas técnicas da agência uma manifestação conclusiva que sinalizasse para a não aplicação do mecanismo de captura de receitas para a modicidade tarifária nos casos de Sistemas de Armazenamento estruturados com outorga própria, patrimônio, financiamento e contabilidade segregados, sem utilização de bens reversíveis, recursos das concessionárias de transmissão ou custos imputados a essas concessões. No entanto, até o momento nenhuma comunicação oficial foi divulgada pelas autoridades setoriais. artigo.texto: Residents of Dade County gathered in Trenton, Georgia, Monday night, just one week after the county’s Industrial Development Authority withdrew a letter of intent with Masterworks Atlanta, LLC for a proposed data center. The pitch caught many off guard at the November 5th County Commission meeting where a potential 90-day moratorium on data centers was scheduled to be introduced. That announcement led to an uproar from the crowd and caused the commission to push the 90-day moratorium discussion to its next meeting on December 3rd. Still, protesters express their frustration with a lack of communication and transparency. “We're very uncomfortable with the data centers because of the non-disclosure agreement, all the smoke and mirrors that's going on behind the scenes. Yeah, the local authorities say they're going to put a moratorium, but there's a lot more going on,” said Rob Rush, a resident and former congressional candidate. Protest organizer Carter McCormick says they are also concerned by the existing lack of regulations. “Recently our IDA has rescinded their letter of intent to sell to Masterworks. So while that proposal has kind of been taken off the docket, we still remain as a county very vulnerable to hyperscale development, as we don't have any zoning laws here in the county. So as it stands now, there is absolutely nothing that can stop a hyperscale data center from coming in next door,” McCormick says. McCormick says their demonstration Monday night is a push to be a part of the conversation and for more transparency moving forward. “I think it's important for our community leaders to see that we are not divided on this issue. This isn't red, Blue; it's something that's bringing us together in this community, all across the political aisle, and we just want to be protected,” McCormick said. Commissioner Melissa Bradford, who introduced the moratorium, told Local 3 in a statement that she agrees that transparency is key. “I think transparency is the key to county government. I want to see work being done in open meetings. I would like to have ordinances and policy in place before these types of industry come in to our county! I am tried of back tracking and being on a limited schedule to protect the citizens of these type of business. I want to be proactive,” Bradford said in the statement.

artigo.texto: In a narrow decision, McHenry County officials have approved a pair of battery storage projects that will operate at solar farms – the first such projects the County Board has voted on since new state requirements went into place over the summer. The county cannot adopt stricter requirements than state law on battery storage projects, a provision that was outlined in a new state clean energy law that took effect in June. An earlier, similar state law that applied to solar farms sparked backlash from county officials who say it has forced them into the position of having to approve solar farms under legal pressure that they’d already rejected. The McHenry County Board approved the two battery storage plants in a pair of 10-8 votes at its November meeting, and board members voted the same way on both of them. Both battery storage plants are located in Coral Township in the southwestern part of the county and are near each other. They are proposed to be about 5 megawatts each. Battery storage plants store electricity from the grid and then release it when electricity is in high demand. While it may be the first direct vote the County Board has taken on battery storage plants in recent months, residents in Prairie Grove have been opposed to a proposed battery storage plant off Behan Road. Pivot Energy is the developer behind both of the Coral Township projects. Brittney Krebsbach, a representative with the company, told the board the company will continue to work with all parties involved and will uphold its commitments to safety and community accountability. She said the company is looking forward to working with current and incoming board members. Board member Terri Greeno, R-Crystal Lake, said she was voting no because local fire officials have raised concerns about the projects. County documents indicate Union Fire Protection District officials had raised concerns to the Zoning Board of Appeals about battery storage projects. After the votes, County Board member Mike Shorten, R-Crystal Lake, said in a statement the county kept battery storage out of solar developments before this year but state law has since overridden the county’s ability to decide that. “Springfield’s takeover of local zoning for solar, wind and industrial battery facilities is a massive overstep,” Shorten said in a statement. “State law has taken this decision away from the people who live here. That’s why I voted no on both battery projects.” Shorten said he also has concerns about fire safety at large lithium battery sites, as well as about flooding, saying one of the sites has about 30 acres in a 100-year floodplain. “Putting industrial batteries in a floodplain is exactly the kind of decision that should be made locally, not dictated by Springfield,” Shorten said. Shorten said state and federal authorities “should speed up small modular nuclear reactors and invest in fusion power, which can deliver safe, reliable, low-cost energy.” Greeno was unsuccessful in her reelection bid this fall and is among six County Board members who are leaving after their terms expire in December. Shorten, who is also the elected Nunda Township supervisor, is up for reelection to the County Board in 2028. The new board is due to be seated Dec. 7.

artigo.texto: Concerns have arisen that Native American artifacts or human remains could be found at the site selected for the University of Michigan’s planned data center in partnership with Los Alamos National Laboratory. The State Historic Preservation Office warned the University the $1.25 billion data center’s proposed location is “highly archaeologically sensitive” due to its proximity to the Huron River. The University chose a 144-acre site along Textile Road — a historic Native American trail — as the preferred location for the data center in August, citing its access to technical infrastructure and separation from residential areas. On Oct.16, the United Tribes of Michigan adopted a resolution opposing the data center development without proper consultation and safeguards. The University issued a statement on Oct. 30 in response, claiming a background search found “no evidence of archeological artifacts or culturally-sensitive materials.” In the resolution, UTM considered the historic Native American usage of the land and burial sites adjacent to the property. They further expressed concern over the project’s potential impacts on tribal cultural resources. “United Tribes of Michigan expresses its support of Ypsilanti Township as it seeks to guide this potential development including its demand that consultation with the Tribes be conducted prior to any development,” the resolution reads. In an interview with The Michigan Daily, Ypsilanti Township attorney Doug Winters said the township is unsatisfied with the University’s practices. Although the regents approved of a Community Investment Resolution, which calls on the University to implement a Community Partnership Program with Ypsilanti Township, Winters criticized it as an attempt to distract from environmental racism. “They picked this area in Washtenaw County because we have the largest percentage of Black and brown (people),” Winters said. “We have less access to healthcare and educational opportunities. We don’t have generational wealth, and there’s a reason why they chose this part of the township: because they did not expect to have this kind of a pushback.” Winters said he does not trust the University to conduct a careful archaeological assessment before beginning construction on the center. “They’re not going to do the right thing unless they’re forced to do it,” Winters said. “We intend to make sure they’re held accountable on that issue.” In an interview with The Daily, LSA senior Calvin Stineman, a former intern at the University’s Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act Office, said the data center’s scientific advancements should not come at the cost of disrespecting Native American culture. “These sorts of precedents — along with all other data centers being built in places around the country — undermine the community’s sentiments and show how we are moving backward as a university and a society in terms of our respect for human and environmental agency,” Stineman said. Winters said Ypsilanti Township is working to build partnerships with UTM to oppose the data center. Winters was invited to Traverse City by UTM to share Ypsilanti Township’s resolution against the data center. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act mandates federally-funded institutions consult with Tribal Nations about the repatriation of Native American cultural items and human remains. “They are required by federal and state law to do an archeological investigation whenever there’s evidence of Indigenous artifacts and burial grounds,” Winters said. “They have to consult with the Native American tribes before they go forward with any type of activity on that property.” In an interview with The Daily, University alum Vidhya Aravind, member of local advocacy group Stop the Data Center, criticized the University’s lack of transparent communication with the community regarding the data center. “While I do wish for a more open channel between the University and its impacted communities more broadly, here it seems unlikely that anything we would have said would have killed this project, which the community clearly and unanimously doesn’t want,” Aravind said. “They’re not communicating with us because they know it’s bad too.” Daily Staff Reporter Mercy Wisecup can be reached at wisecup@umich.edu.

artigo.texto: Utica Common Council discusses BESS legislation at committee meeting Alexis Manore | Staff writer | AManore@RNYmedia.com Alexis Manore Staff writer Author facebook Author linkedin Author twitter Author email Nov 24, 2026 5 hrs ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Utica City Hall Sentinel photo by John Clifford Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save UTICA — The Utica Common Council discussed proposed legislation to regulate battery energy storage systems (BESS) at a Monday, Nov. 23 Committee of the Whole meeting. The council currently has a moratorium on BESS in Utica, having passed several extensions, with the most recent extension set to expire Saturday, Dec. 5. The council’s next regular meeting is Wednesday, Dec. 2. At the Nov. 23 meeting, the councilors reviewed legislation that Assistant Corporation Counsel Stephanie DiGiorgio prepared. The legislation split BESS into three tiers: one for smaller systems that would be allowed, one for larger systems that would require site plan approval from the Planning Board, and the third for large-scale systems, which would only be allowed in industrial and mixed-use industrial zones, and would require a special use permit. After discussion, the councilors decided that large-scale systems should not be allowed at all, and talked about further regulating second-tier systems. The councilors decided to call for a special meeting on Monday, Nov. 30 to introduce its BESS legislation, before introducing it at its Dec. 2 meeting. Check back at ursentinel.com for more information. artigo.texto: It’s the Roaring 2020’s for the HPC-AI Data Center Industry, But It Comes with Costs Key Highlights - Overall HPC spending grew nearly 17% in 2025 to more than $70 billion, with cloud usage up nearly 30%. - The combined on-premises and cloud market for HPC and AI-for-science servers is projected to approach $140 billion by 2030. - GPU wait times can exceed 18 months, while rising HBM and DDR5 prices are pushing up system costs. - Dell overtook HPE for the top server market share, with 23.8% compared with HPE’s 20.9%. - Hyperion estimates the quantum computing market reached $1.4 billion in 2025, while 54% of respondents see a chance of a quantum winter. It has been, and will very likely continue to be, the “Roaring 2020's” for the HPC-AI data center industry. But similar to the generally healthy U.S. economy, affordability is a problem. Driven by demand for advanced computing technology, the HPC-AI data center infrastructure industry is generating tremendous growth, according to the latest market update figures released by industry analyst firm Hyperion Research. But with high demand come strains on supply chains that result in higher costs that restrain even higher growth. This is the picture presented this week by Hyperion at their annual breakfast at the SC26 Supercomputing Conference in Chicago. The customary large crowd turned out to hear Hyperion CEO Earl Joseph and colleagues discuss the state of the industry, some sectors of which are expanding at a clip Joseph said has never before been seen. “2025 was an extremely high growth year for the market…,” said Hyperion CEO Earl Joseph of on-premises servers for HPC, AI and data centers. “The first half of this year is growing at 20 percent… This is more than a doubling of historic growth. And then looking at the overall market in addition to servers, the storage, middleware, application services and spending for running HPC and AI for science workloads in the cloud…the market has just grown tremendously.” Among Hyperion’s key findings: - Overall HPC spending grew by just under 17 percent in 2025 reaching a total of more than $70 billion, including nearly 30 percent growth in cloud usage. - Worldwide sales of on-prem for HPC and AI-for-science servers reached $29.4 billion, an increase of nearly 15 percent, with the EMEA region growing by roughly 10 percent. - For the combination of HPC and AI-for-science on-prem servers plus cloud, the overall market is expected to double over the next five years, approaching $140 billion by 2030. - Growth in sales for on-prem servers during the first of this year was approximately 20 percent, and looking out to 2030, Hyperion projects sales to reach nearly $55 billion. Hyperion also disclosed that Dell has taken the top spot for servers from perennial leader HPE, with Dell capturing 23.8 percent market share versus HPE’s 20.9 percent share. HPC-AI Growth Runs Into Supply Chain Reality But these rosy growth figures generate pressure and unmet demands across the HPC-AI technology ecosystem, including processors, solid state drives (SSDs) and memory. For example, while more than 1 million GPUs were installed in 2025 – a roughly 25 percent growth rate over 2024 – there are reported wait times of 18 months or longer for new GPUs, which command higher prices. There also are the well-documented supply chain problems for memory. Hyperion Senior Vice President of Research Bob Sorensen said the rise in memory prices has added significantly to HPC systems pricing. A Hyperion study found that costs for high bandwidth memory (HBM) per gigabyte has increased since 2021 from between $9 and $11.50 to between $13 and $17 this year. Spread across the hundreds or thousands of nodes within a single system results in a powerful multiplier effect. Sorensen also cited prices for DDR5 SDRAM (Double Data Rate 5) synchronous dynamic random-access memory has jumped in price since 2021 by more than 300 percent. He compared pricing for an HPC system of around 600 petaflops ordered in 2023 compared to 2026 and found that system memory costs have increased from $35 million to more than $60 million, contributing to a complete system price of $125 million (up from $100 million four years ago) in which memory comprises 47 percent of total system cost. The AI boom means high demand and good times for memory vendors, but as Sorensen explained, memory is a volatile business. “Memory makers are loath to increase capacity,” he said. “They know the memory market is a boom bust sector…, they know that sooner or later demand is going to turn and they're going to be dealing with overcapacity or under capacity. So we don't see a real solution to this problem, at least for the next few years.” Cloud Adoption Accelerates as Quantum Computing Faces Uncertainty Hyperion also reported that cloud usage is increasing, with 80 percent of their survey respondents across industry, government and academia reporting utilizing cloud for some portion of their HPC and AI-for-science workloads. Hyperion Research Director Mark Nossokoff said industry sectors sites use cloud the most, according to Hyperion, compared with government organizations and academia. Leading factors favoring use of external clouds include the ability to dynamically add or remove resources, to access new hardware that is otherwise unavailable and to run jobs at scales not possible on-prem. Barriers to cloud adoption include concerns, “sometimes real, sometimes perceived,” Nossokoff said, that cloud is too expensive compared with on-prem. “There's also the difficulty in migrating existing applications to the cloud… We see that the government (sector) in particular identifies cost as being the highest issue and, interestingly, academia indicated that between costs and security, they didn't feel (cloud) met their requirements.” Sorensen also delivered an update on the quantum computing industry that included these highlights: - The global QC market in 2025 was estimated at $1.4 billion, wi

artigo.texto: A Netscout Systems, fornecedora de soluções de Observabilidade de rede, AIOps, Cibersegurança e proteção contra ataques DDoS, acaba de anunciar que sua estratégia de design sustentável proporciona aos usuários uma economia de 20% na eficiência energética dos produtos Netscout, diminuindo tanto os custos operacionais quanto o impacto ambiental. Esse resultado sustentável pode ser potencializado de acordo com a fonte de energia adotada. De acordo com uma pesquisa recente da BloombergNEF, a demanda global de eletricidade dos Data Centers quase quadruplicará até 2035, chegando a 2.354 terawatts-hora, o que representará 7% da demanda global de eletricidade. Materiais da Forrester destacam que a otimização de recursos se tornou responsabilidade de todos: “Os vencedores não vão debater ou se importar em rotular a resposta como ‘sustentabilidade’. Eles serão forçados a planejar IA, energia, água, terra, infraestrutura e impacto na comunidade de forma conjunta. Afinal, é isso que o crescimento resiliente exige atualmente.” Abordagem da Netscout na incorporação de sustentabilidade às suas soluções: Prioriza o design com eficiência de recursos tanto no nível dos componentes quanto da plataforma. Ajuda as organizações a mitigar os impactos ambientais e financeiros do rápido aumento no consumo de energia de Data Centers e IA. Permite a atualização de dispositivos mais antigos com um único equipamento (Appliance) para otimizar ainda mais a eficiência energética. Economia de Energia Comprovada Testes de desempenho em laboratório do equipamento InfiniStreamNG 3U compararam a plataforma M-series com a J-series. Os resultados mostraram redução no consumo de energia, gerando uma economia anual estimada de 1,3 MWh por dispositivo. Quando as perdas com refrigeração e distribuição de energia no Data Center são consideradas, a economia pode ser ainda maior. Resultados semelhantes foram observados em uma implantação real em ambiente de cliente. “A abordagem arquitetural de sustentabilidade desde a concepção da Netscout significa que priorizamos a eficiência energética no nível da plataforma e dos componentes”, disse Jillian James, diretora de sustentabilidade da Netscout. “Nós nos preocupamos com o impacto energético e de IA na Cadeia de uso de nossos clientes – e não apenas com as nossas próprias pegadas. Nosso objetivo é ajudar os clientes a tornar suas redes e análises melhores para o meio ambiente e mais eficientes no que diz respeito à preservação recursos.” Compromisso com a Sustentabilidade A plataforma M-series, com alta eficiência energética, reflete o compromisso corporativo mais amplo da Netscout com a responsabilidade ambiental. A Netscout está integrando ativamente a sustentabilidade em suas operações e ciclos de desenvolvimento de produtos para apoiar os princípios da economia circular. O menor consumo de energia proporcionado por esses produtos contribui para que a empresa avance em sua meta de reduzir a emissão de gases relacionados ao efeito estufa até 2030. Incorporando a eficiência energética ao design dos produtos, a Netscout ajuda os clientes a transformar a modernização da infraestrutura em valor duradouro para os negócios: custos operacionais mais baixos, menor impacto ambiental e maior capacidade para suportar as crescentes demandas digitais e de IA. A Plataforma M-series demonstra como o desempenho operacional e a sustentabilidade podem avançar juntos, ajudando as organizações a fazer um uso mais eficaz de energia, espaço e investimentos em infraestrutura. Essa abordagem amplia o valor da Netscout à medida que a eficiência de recursos se torna um fator cada vez mais importante nas decisões de compra de tecnologia. Serviço www.netscout.com

artigo.texto: Influential Women: Elizabeth 'Bess' Wildman, Builds People-First Leadership in Academic Healthcare Administration IL, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Vice Dean for Academic Administration and Finance in the Biological Sciences Division at the University of Chicago, She Pairs Financial Discipline With a Lifelong Commitment to Developing Leaders Elizabeth âBessâ Wildman is a seasoned academic healthcare administrator and financial leader who serves as Vice Dean for Academic Administration and Finance in the Biological Sciences Division at the University of Chicago. With more than three decades of experience in healthcare administration, she oversees a broad portfolio spanning finance, human resources, information technology, clinical operations, and grants administration. Her work helps advance the institutionâs missions of patient care, education, and research. Bess brings strategic and financial discipline to complex academic medical operations, along with a strong commitment to authenticity, collaboration, and organizational development. Bess began her career in banking operations before moving into healthcare after earning her MBA from the Wake Forest University School of Business. She also holds a BA from the University of Virginia. Since entering the field, she has held leadership positions at multiple academic medical centers. Along the way, she has built significant experience with faculty practice plans and complex healthcare operations. That combination of financial training and operational depth has shaped the steady, strategic approach she brings to her current role. Her early grounding in banking gave her a practical understanding of financial operations that continues to inform her leadership of a large and varied administrative portfolio. Bess attributes her success to people. She has always been committed to developing others, particularly administrative fellows, and to mentoring her teams so they grow into outstanding leaders. Investing in people, supporting their growth, and helping them reach their full potential has been central to everything she has achieved. She takes particular pride in watching members of her teams become confident, capable leaders in their own right. For Bess, the growth of the people around her is the clearest measure of her own achievement. Her advice to young women entering healthcare administration begins with a frank observation: being a woman leader often requires an additional level of balance. She encourages young women to remain authentic to who they are while recognizing and navigating the different ways society may view women. Bess urges them to challenge inequities without adopting a victim posture. Above all, she tells them to know their value and to refuse to be walked over or overlooked. Bess sees healthcare in a significant period of disruption. Policy changes, the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, public intolerance of rising healthcare costs, and workforce shortages are all reshaping the landscape. At the same time, she views these pressures as a source of important opportunity. Precision medicine, in-home care, AI-enabled healthcare delivery, alternative providers, and new approaches to system-wide learning and workforce development all have the potential to transform the field. People-first leadership stands at the center of her values. Bess places a strong emphasis on developing talent, mentoring others, and helping people become outstanding leaders. Outside of work, family and active engagement in her community matter just as much to her. Together, these priorities guide how she leads, how she supports those around her, and how she contributes to the communities she serves. Her community involvement includes the University of Chicagoâs South Side community engagement efforts. Bess is also actively engaged with professional and leadership organizations, including the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), the American College of Healthcare Executives (ACHE), Women of Impact, and CHIEF. These affiliations keep her connected to peers across academic medicine. She has also contributed to leadership networks focused on advancing women in healthcare. Across more than three decades, Bess has shown that sound financial stewardship and genuine investment in people can advance together. Her legacy is measured not only in the operations she oversees but in the leaders she has helped develop. For Elizabeth âBessâ Wildman, the lasting meaning of her work lies in a stronger, more equitable healthcare workforce prepared to meet a changing future. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Sérgio Leverdi – A desinformação tem custo: o que os mitos sobre data centers fazem com a economia brasileira Publicado 24/11/2026 • 21:48 | Atualizado há 10 horas Foto: Divulgação/Ascenty A nova geração de data centers combina eficiência, energia limpa e rigor regulatório. Debater o tema com fatos é condição para que o investimento chegue ao país. Por Sérgio Leverdi, CEO da LAWINFRA A história da indústria é, em boa medida, a história da busca por fazer mais com menos. Cada salto tecnológico trouxe consigo a pressão por economizar energia, usar a água com mais inteligência e reduzir o impacto sobre o meio ambiente: dos motores mais eficientes à iluminação que consome uma fração do que consumia, das fábricas que reaproveitam seus insumos às cidades que medem o que gastam. Não será diferente com os data centers e a inteligência artificial. A modernização, bem entendida, nunca foi inimiga do meio ambiente nem da qualidade de vida e é justamente o conceito que permite combinar produtividade, preservação e bem-estar. É dentro dessa lógica que nasce a nova geração de data centers. Desinformação não é apenas um problema de reputação. Ela encarece o capital, atrasa decisões e afasta investimentos que geram emprego, arrecadação e capacidade tecnológica. Quando um investidor lê que o Brasil vai repetir os problemas americanos ou que data centers consomem toda a água e a energia limpa, o risco percebido sobe, e o dinheiro vai para onde o debate é menos ruidoso. Um relatório recente, "Data centers no Brasil: mitos e fatos", reúne dezesseis dessas ideias equivocadas e as confronta com dados. Vale olhar para as mais frequentes. A comparação com os Estados Unidos ignora a escala. O mercado brasileiro soma cerca de 1 GW de capacidade; os americanos têm cerca de 60 GW em operação, com projeção de chegar a 150 GW em 2030, segundo a S&P Global. Lá, a demanda cresceu mais rápido que a rede e a geração, com filas de conexão e projetos que passaram a gerar a própria energia. Aqui, o acesso à rede é planejado e autorizado de forma centralizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e pela ANEEL, e há sobra de geração renovável, que hoje é cortada. Quanto ao carbono, a pegada de um data center depende da eletricidade que ele consome. Em 2025, 86,8% da eletricidade ofertada no Brasil veio de fontes renováveis, segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional da EPE. Os operadores ainda contratam energia renovável no mercado livre, por contratos de longo prazo e certificados de origem que permitem rastrear cada MWh. Processar dados aqui, e não em mercados de matriz fóssil, reduz as emissões associadas ao mesmo serviço digital. Esta é, talvez, a maior contribuição que o país pode dar ao debate global sobre data centers sustentáveis. Há ainda um benefício pouco discutido. No Nordeste, parte da geração eólica e solar é cortada por falta de demanda ou de capacidade de escoamento, o chamado curtailment. Um data center instalado perto desses parques transforma em processamento de dados uma energia limpa que hoje se perde, sem retirá-la de nenhum outro consumidor, e ajuda a viabilizar usinas renováveis existentes e futuras. A imagem do data center que "bebe" água vem de projetos antigos ou de resfriamento evaporativo. No Brasil, mais de 80% dos data centers operam com refrigeração em circuito fechado, e os novos projetos o adotam por eficiência, por compromisso ambiental e para atender ao regime especial do setor. A água entra na carga inicial e circula sem evaporar, como no radiador de um carro, com reposição apenas pontual em manutenção. Depois disso, o consumo equivale ao de um pequeno escritório. Os geradores a diesel, por sua vez, funcionam como seguro: só entram em operação se a rede falhar. Fora das emergências, são testados por cerca de 15 minutos por trimestre, um equipamento por vez, e os limites de emissão são fixados no licenciamento ambiental. Já a conta de luz não sobe por causa deles: o data center paga pela própria conexão, aporta garantias financeiras e recolhe as tarifas de uso da transmissão como qualquer usuário. Como sua carga é grande e constante, ele dilui custos fixos do sistema e tende a reduzir o custo por MWh para os demais. Nenhum data center de grande porte se conecta à Rede Básica sem estudos do ONS e autorização da ANEEL, e todos passam pelo licenciamento ambiental, em licenças sucessivas, com condicionantes e documentos públicos. O país tem regulação madura em zoneamento, setor elétrico e meio ambiente, construída ao longo de décadas de hidrelétricas, grandes plantas industriais e mineração. O risco existe e precisa ser planejado, inclusive diante do crescimento da demanda por inteligência artificial, mas o setor elétrico tem instrumentos para isso. Cada nova geração de equipamentos processa mais dados por unidade de energia, e os projetos novos são construídos com refrigeração e distribuição elétrica mais eficientes que os antigos. Dizer que data centers geram poucos empregos é medir uma estrada pelas vagas da praça de pedágio. Bancos, varejo, saúde, agronegócio, indústria e governo dependem de processamento de dados para operar e crescer. Hoje, boa parte do processamento consumido no Brasil acontece fora do país, o que significa importar serviços e deixar investimento, empregos e arrecadação em outros lugares. O regime especial – REDATA - desonera os equipamentos em troca de contrapartidas, como energia limpa, eficiência no uso da água e pesquisa e desenvolvimento local. Dados processados aqui ficam sob a jurisdição brasileira, com menor latência para pagamentos instantâneos, telemedicina e serviços públicos digitais, e menor dependência de infraestrutura estrangeira em situações de crise. O Brasil tem a vantagem do momento, com mercado ainda está em formação, cerca de 60 vezes menor que o americano, e as regras de rede, zoneamento e meio ambiente já existem antes de a escala chegar. artigo.texto: Loudoun’s Board of Supervisors wants more authority from the General Assembly this year, particularly relating to the data center industry. Each year, county supervisors adopt a legislative agenda that lists priorities and specific issues they want their representatives to support during the session. This year’s additions to that wish list include a focus on energy, data centers and transmission lines. One item requests authority to deny land use applications because of local power grid constraints. That was included in last year’s requests as well. During rezoning applications for data centers, supervisors are not allowed to consider the building’s impacts on the electric grid since the application is a land use request. This would change that. Another item requests authority to require that data centers provide a comprehensive list of their tenants at the request of the Commissioner of the Revenue. Supervisors also support legislation that would allow a locality to implement a pause on data center applications, although the board already approved a pause last week during its Nov. 17 meeting. Supervisor Koran T. Saines (D-Sterling) also earned support to add an item requesting permission for the county to restrict data centers’ use of generators. This comes as Saines has been working to reduce impacts from a turbine-powered data center in his district that has garnered public pushback. He earned support in July to have staff find ways to regulate generator use. Supervisor Laura A. TeKrony (D-Little River) also successfully moved to add support for legislation that would allow a jurisdiction to issue fines on data centers if they did not notify the locality of backup generator use during emergencies. “Loudoun County has 6,200 diesel generators,” she said. “If some, or all of these generators are used during an emergency, it will be a public health emergency, not just a grid emergency.” The longer the generators are used, the higher the impact, and residents deserve to know when that is happening, she said. Supervisors also opted to add support for legislation that would allow localities to increase fines against data centers for violations of noise ordinances. The request seeks authority to impose fines of $5,000 for first offenses, and $10,000 for subsequent violations. Currently, fines can be implemented at $250 and $500, Saines said. Supervisors are also looking for more of a say in where transmission lines are built, another issue garnering significant public input. Becker & Poliakoff Senior Government Relations Consultant Clarence Williams said the county’s lobbying team is working on a “smorgasbord” of policy options on that issue. “I’m looking for any and all ideas if we possibly can,” Supervisor Caleb A. Kershner (R-Catoctin) said. A proposal by County Chair Phyllis J. Randall (D-At Large) to support any legislation that would shift the cost of new energy transmission infrastructure to high energy rate classes, protect conservation easements and historic landmarks, protect landowners, increase transparency from utilities, make existing transmission corridors priorities for new lines, expand participation in load forecasting, establish pilot programs for underground transmission lines, and improve demand management. Randall said she’s contacted Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) about sponsoring legislation on those issues in response to concerns from residents in western Loudoun, particularly about the Valley Link transmission line. However, residents across the county would be impacted if this legislation passed, she said. Randall said large load transmission through conservation easements and the taking of private property owner’s land for the lines are especially concerning to her. “If you put your land in conservation easement, you do not expect to get a transmission line through your land. That’s the point of doing a conservation easement. … These are the things we’re trying to respond to,” she said. TeKrony also earned support during a Nov. 5 meeting to request legislation that would remove a utility’s obligation to provide power to high facilities using more than 100 megawatts of energy in Northern Virginia if the local power grid is constrained, a viable transmission line corridor or substation does not exist, or if there’s an energy service backlog of more than three years. “Loudoun County has a severely constrained grid,” she said. “The number of data centers in the queue and the duty to provide power to these extremely high load users is unsustainable.” Utilities may delay service to users if needed, but currently they have a legal obligation to eventually provide that power. This year’s agenda also includes support for a work group to study the health impacts of transmission lines, substations and generators. Changes to this year’s agenda also included language to continue supporting Oak Hill’s establishment as a state park; to extend the timelines for residents to appeal corrections to local tax assessments; to allow local oversight for animal releasing agencies, pet shops and boarding facilities; to extend absentee voting; to provide collective bargaining legislation that protects local government authority; to permit more housing regulations on landlords; to expand tax-setting authority; to support traffic calming and to make several environmental protection changes. The board adopted the full agenda during its Nov. 17 meeting. The 2027 General Assembly session is set to begin Jan. 13.

artigo.texto: Moradores de Atibaia (SP) querem barrar data center de R$ 3 bilhões por questões ambientais Ação na Justiça pede suspensão de licenças, enquanto abaixo-assinado aponta para problemas do projeto Um projeto de data center de R$ 3 bilhões em Atibaia (SP) enfrenta a resistência de moradores, que pedem a apuração de possíveis irregularidades no licenciamento ambiental da obra. Nesta segunda (23), uma ação popular apresentada na Justiça de Atibaia pediu a suspensão de qualquer licença, alvará ou autorização municipal que permita a construção do data center. O projeto pertence à DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON comandada por Luiz Fernando Ortega. O plano prevê investimento de R$ 3 bilhões no Data Center Alfa, um complexo com capacidade de 50 megawatts (MW) e conexão em 138 kV, que ocupará uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol no Bairro do Tanque. A operação está prevista para começar entre 2029 e 2030. O empreendimento faz parte de um pacote nacional da companhia que soma R$ 39 bilhões em oito projetos. Em agosto de 2025, ele obteve parecer de acesso do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que prevê a expansão de cerca de 15 km de linha e dois módulos de entrada em 138 kV, além de tratativas com a distribuidora Elektro. Embora o portfólio oficial da DataSpots apresente o projeto como "aprovado e estruturado", a ação popular afirma que a Prefeitura de Atibaia recebeu apenas "consultas preliminares, sem processo formal de licenciamento ambiental ou urbanístico". Por isso, a ação pede que o município entregue, em dez dias, cópias dos documentos relacionados ao projeto e identifique as empresas interessadas e os servidores responsáveis pelas decisões. Em nota, a prefeitura de Atibaia afirmou que não há, até o momento, "nenhum projeto de implantação de data center formalmente protocolado junto à Administração Municipal para fins de análise e aprovação". "Não existe qualquer processo em andamento ou análise técnica realizada pela Prefeitura relacionada à implantação desse tipo de empreendimento, tampouco qualquer processo de licenciamento ambiental neste particular", diz o documento. A prefeitura confirmou que houve uma reunião sobre o tema. Porém, afirma que o encontro "não representou qualquer compromisso ou tratativa formal, nem deu início a processos de análise ou autorização de empreendimentos, pois não houve qualquer protocolo para aprovação de projeto neste sentido". A reportagem procurou a Prefeitura de Atibaia e a DataSpots, mas não obteve resposta. Já o ONS confirmou que emitiu, em agosto de 2025, o Parecer de Acesso para o Data Center Alfa, com previsão de atendimento de carga de até 25 MW a partir de 2029 e de até 50 MW a partir de 2030, condicionado a reforços e ampliações previstos no sistema elétrico. Segundo o operador, a análise concluiu pela viabilidade do empreendimento, conforme os critérios e procedimentos vigentes para acesso às instalações de transmissão. Sobre outras questões, o operador declarou em nota: "O ONS ressalta que questões relacionadas ao licenciamento ambiental, estudos de impacto, uso e ocupação do solo e demais aspectos socioambientais são de competência dos órgãos responsáveis por essas análises e autorizações". Argumentos contra o projeto Antes da ação popular, o movimento Fora Data Center criou um abaixo-assinado que já reúne mais de 4 mil assinaturas pedindo a proibição desse tipo de estrutura na cidade. Entre os argumentos dos moradores contra o projeto estão os impactos ambientais, como o alto consumo de água e de energia elétrica, o ruído contínuo, a poluição luminosa, as bolhas de calor e o tráfego pesado nas rodovias. Eles também contestam a promessa de desenvolvimento econômico: apesar de o setor contar com incentivos federais bilionários, a operação, altamente automatizada, gera apenas de 50 a 200 empregos permanentes depois das obras (que mobilizam de 150 a 500 trabalhadores temporários), enquanto o ônus ambiental e viário fica com o município. "A implantação de complexos industriais que demandam água e energia em escala massiva, produzem poluição sonora perene e desfiguram o ordenamento territorial colide frontalmente com a vocação turística, ecológica e residencial que define o município", diz o abaixo-assinado. Em 27 de agosto, a Associação Salve Atibaia e o Movimento dos Atingidos por Subestação em Atibaia (MAS Atibaia) protocolaram representação na Promotoria de Justiça de Atibaia (MPSP) pedindo a apuração de irregularidades no licenciamento ambiental da infraestrutura elétrica associada ao data center: o Projeto Fernão Dias, da ISA Energia Brasil. Com investimento superior a R$ 300 milhões, 33 km de linha de transmissão e ampliação da Subestação Fernão Dias, o projeto obteve Licença Prévia em junho de 2025 e tinha energização prevista para o segundo semestre de 2026. Em julho de 2025, o diretor de Projetos da ISA Energia, Dayron Urrego, afirmou: "O Projeto Fernão Dias contribuirá para a transição energética no Brasil. O empreendimento é essencial para o crescimento econômico no Estado de São Paulo, em especial para data centers que contarão com o fornecimento energético ainda mais seguro e eficiente para avançar em suas operações". artigo.texto: The Lead In: Albert Lea water expansion, Olympic Torch Relay, Mitchell County data centers, moving forward in Winneshiek, and watching Twin Lakes ROCHESTER, Minn. (KTTC) – A massive expansion project. Bringing the Olympics to Freeborn County. Mitchell County talks data centers. Winneshiek County plans after mass resignations. And Twin Lakes prepares to learn its financial fate. Here is The Lead In, for Nov. 22-28. Albert Lea: Water and sewer extension City staff will present the council with a plan to extend water and sewer services to the area around Richway Drive/County Road 20 and Plaza Street in 2027. The $3.3 million project would improve failing septic systems and water pressure. It also would give industrial lots in the area access to city water. The city would pay for the project through sewer and water funds, state aid, property assessments and bonding. The project also would annex several properties into the city. The council meets at 7 p.m. Monday in the council chambers. Albert Lea: Olympic torch relay agreement The council will also vote on approving an agreement between Albert Lea and the Los Angeles Organizing Committee for the Olympic Games 2028 to participate in the Olympic torch run. The run for the 2028 Summer Games will cover all 50 states. The city is seeking consideration for the relay route. The agreement does not guarantee Albert Lea will be on the route. The process is in preliminary stages. City staff said the opportunity is too good to pass up. Again, the council meets at 7 p.m. Monday in the council chambers. Mitchell County: Data center moratorium The Mitchell County Board of Supervisors is scheduled to discuss a data center moratorium Tuesday. The item is listed on the board’s regular meeting agenda. In November 2025, the board issued a data center moratorium through Dec. 31, 2026. The vote was 4-1. It is unclear what action, if any, the board will take Tuesday, including whether it will extend or change the existing ordinance. The meeting begins at 8:30 a.m. Tuesday at the Mitchell County Courthouse in Osage. Winneshiek County: Discussing recent planning and zoning resignations The Winneshiek County Board of Supervisors is set to meet for the first time since every member of the county planning and zoning commission resigned in protest. The board’s Monday agenda indicates it will discuss the resignations. Former commissioners said they quit after supervisors declined to reappoint Mary Hoffman, who wants to keep serving after more than 15 years. They said tensions had built for years. They said supervisors, who have the final say on rezoning requests, did not give the commission’s recommendations enough consideration. Five former members said they will return if Hoffman is reinstated and Supervisor Mark Vick resigns by the end of the year. Former Chair Wendy Stevens said two new members have been appointed, but four are needed to conduct business. She said work on a proposed data center ordinance was about halfway done. The Board of Supervisors meets at 9:30 a.m. Monday in the Courthouse annex in Decorah. Twin Lakes: State aid on the line for the final time More than $40,000 in state aid is at stake in Twin Lakes, Minnesota. The city had until Friday to submit required financial reporting from 2025. KTTC reached out to the State Auditor’s Office for an update. The office said it will follow up Monday. KTTC also attempted to get a response from Twin Lakes City Clerk and Treasurer Keith Haskell. The reports were due in March. The state offered additional deadlines, which the city continued to miss. Haskell has previously said he was unable to submit the reports because of mismanagement issues by the former city clerk. Find stories like this and more, in our apps. Copyright 2026 KTTC. SpaceX sees the problem very clearly SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers. Image source: Getty Images. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. artigo.texto: UTICA — The Utica Common Council discussed proposed legislation to regulate battery energy storage systems (BESS) at a Monday, Nov. 23 Committee of the Whole meeting. The council currently has a moratorium on BESS in Utica, having passed several extensions, with the most recent extension set to expire Saturday, Dec. 5. The council’s next regular meeting is Wednesday, Dec. 2. At the Nov. 23 meeting, the councilors reviewed legislation that Assistant Corporation Counsel Stephanie DiGiorgio prepared. The legislation split BESS into three tiers: Tier 1 for systems at one to two-family dwellings that do not exceed 40 kilowatt-hours within utility closets and storage space, and 80 kWh in detached garages, exterior walls or outdoors on the ground, or those that have an aggregate energy capacity less than or equal to 80 kWh Tier 2 for systems that have a capacity of less than 300 kWh or comprise more than one battery storage technology in a room or enclosed area. Such systems would require site plan approval from the Planning Board. Tier 3 for systems that greater than or equal to 300 kWh or are composed of have more than one storage battery technology in a room or enclosed area. These systems could be built in industrial or mixed-use industrial zones, and would need a special use permit to be built. Tier 3 systems are large-scale battery energy storage systems. The councilors debated whether or not they’d like to allow Tier 3 systems with the regulations, or ban them altogether, with Councilor-at-Large Jack LoMedico arguing strongly in favor of prohibiting them, due to the lithium battery fires that have occurred at such installations. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lithium battery fires can be very hard to extinguish and could reignite, can release harmful gases, and require specialized procedures for cleanup and disposal. “I think we should ban it. I think let’s just get it by us,” he said. We don’t need battery storage areas in the city. I’ve seen what they’ve done and they’re a mess. Maybe 50 years from now or 20 years from now, if we want to take another look at it, but I don’t want to be responsible,” LoMedico said. “Have you ever seen one catch fire?” Sixth Ward Councilor Joseph Betrus, whose district includes many industrial and mixed-use industrial zoned areas, said that he is also not in favor of large-scale BESS, but expressed hesitance about closing the door entirely on such developments. “In my opinion, if that’s the case, we should go with the top two [tiers] and don’t do three right now, because I don’t think we know enough about it,” Betrus said. “But I don’t want to shut anybody off either down the road.” The council does have the ability to revisit the legislation after its passage, and could go through the process to amend the ordinance by adding in the section allowing Tier 3 systems if so desired. Betrus said he would be satisfied with this. First Ward Councilor Katie Aiello said that while she was hesitant about BESS at first, she’s since learned more about the world’s increasing reliance on electricity. BESS draw electricity from the grid during periods of low demand, and then stores it until it’s needed, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. These systems provide backup during power outages from severe weather or accidents, and stabilize the grid during peak demand times, like during the summer when everyone is running their air conditioners, according to NYSERDA. “It’s just the way the world is going. There’s pros and cons. We’re up front, we don’t know all the risks, and we’re setting ourselves up, some people are feeling through the dark on this one,” she said. “But there’s also, you get ahead of it, and we can position ourselves. There are things that I’d like that other cities have done, if they do it. … I just don’t want us to get short-sighted and not be prepared.” After discussion, the councilors decided that Tier 3 systems should not be allowed at all, and so DiGiorgio said she would remove it from the proposed ordinance, to prohibit them from the city. After a lengthy discussion about putting further limitations on the number of electric vehicle charging stations that can be placed outside buildings and facilities, they decided to exclude home and business charging stations from the legislation, so that the regulations would not apply. She said she would also amend the Tier 2 definition to reflect that it would be for accessory use to a building. The council scheduled a special meeting from 5 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 30 to introduce its BESS legislation.

artigo.texto: CHESAPEAKE, Va. — A new announcement about the future of the former Frank Williams Farm property in southern Chesapeake is renewing questions about whether data centers could eventually become part of the massive development. Praetorian Fund, the private investment firm behind the proposed 4,000-plus-acre Praetorian Park off Highway 17 near the North Carolina border, announced it has selected engineering and planning firm Kimley-Horn to help advance planning for the property. The announcement comes after News 3 Chesapeake reporter Erin Holly first reported in September on Praetorian's plans for the property and neighbors' concerns about its future, including questions about possible data center development. Watch previous coverage: Investment firm purchases Chesapeake's 4,000-acre Frank Williams Farm for multi-billion dollar hub Praetorian envisions the property as a multi-phase innovation hub that could include advanced manufacturing, defense technology, energy, sports, entertainment and what the company describes as "modern digital infrastructure." The company says Kimley-Horn will support design, infrastructure coordination, entitlements and planning, helping establish a framework for land uses, parcel configurations and connections between different development areas. Kimley-Horn has an established practice working on data centers and other "mission critical" facilities. The firm's website says its work in that field includes site planning, power and cooling infrastructure, utility coordination, zoning and permitting. News 3 also found recent examples of Kimley-Horn working on major proposed data center developments in Ohio and Texas. That experience does not establish that Kimley-Horn was selected to plan a data center in Chesapeake, or that one will ultimately be built at Praetorian Park. However, city records reviewed by News 3 show data centers have been contemplated as one possible use for a portion of the property since years before Praetorian Fund became involved. In November 2022, Chesapeake City Council approved the rezoning of approximately 1,420 acres of the larger property from agricultural land to a Planned Unit Development Industrial Park, or PUD-IP. The development criteria approved as part of that process specifically state that the proposed industrial park could accommodate several types of employment uses, including advanced manufacturing, corporate headquarters and offices, medical campuses and higher-learning centers. The document then states: "The PUD contemplates the inclusion of light fabrication and assembly ancillary to a research and development use, as well as data centers." Elsewhere in the document, data centers are described as an appropriate use alongside advanced manufacturing, research and development and other employment uses. The distinction is important: those documents apply to roughly 1,420 acres, not the entirety of the 4,000-plus-acre property, and they identify data centers as one of several possible uses. They do not establish that a data center is currently planned. The city has been laying the groundwork for large-scale development here for years. In 2016, City Council identified the Williams property as a target for economic development. In 2018, Council changed the city's long-term plan for part of the property, opening the door to industrial and other non-residential uses. The next major step came in 2022, when Council approved the Coastal Virginia Commerce Park rezoning. At the time of the 2022 rezoning, city staff described the project as a "mega site industrial park" designed for a small number of large users. During a presentation ahead of the rezoning, city staff said parcels within the park would have a minimum lot size of 100 acres and that individual users were expected to occupy even more land. City staff also acknowledged at the time that there was not yet a detailed master development plan because the eventual users and their needs would help determine the layout of the park. News 3's review found another connection between the old plans and the new Kimley-Horn involvement announcement. Kimley-Horn was already working on the Frank Williams Farm property years before Praetorian Fund's involvement. The 2022 PUD documents identify Kimley-Horn as the firm that prepared the Master Land Use Plan associated with the project and the property's traffic impact study. The firm also prepared a preliminary engineering report studying water and sewer service to the Williams Tract. Public utilities were a major issue during the 2022 planning process. City staff said the property's lack of public utilities had prevented its economic potential from being fully realized. The PUD documents describe extending public water and sewer to the commerce park as "critical," with the applicant or property owner responsible for continuing that infrastructure south from the Chesapeake Regional Airport area to the property. The criteria also contain environmental and military-related development requirements. The property lies within the Northwest River Watershed Protection District, which protects a drinking-water source for Chesapeake. The criteria require additional review related to runoff and development within that watershed. The site is also near Naval Support Activity Northwest Annex and within an area where development can potentially create electromagnetic interference with military equipment. The approved criteria call for future development plans to be provided to the Navy for review and recommendations on mitigating that interference. In announcing Kimley-Horn's newest role, Randy Royal, a principal with the firm who has previously worked on the property, said the firm's job will be to turn the larger vision into a workable plan. artigo.texto: Sodium vs. Lithium: New Economics Challenge Lithium-Ion's Proven Resilience in Next-Gen Energy Storage Markets Key Highlights - Wood Mackenzie reports more than 70 GWh of sodium-ion supply agreements across the U.S., China and Europe. - Sodium-ion cells could reach LFP-level production costs by the end of 2026, while grid-ready systems may not match LFP upfront pricing until after 2030. - Passive cooling, extreme-weather durability and fewer mid-project battery replacements are among potential SIB advantages. - Global markets are evaluating 21% lower total ownership costs over a 20-year SIB project lifespan, despite higher upfront cell costs than LFP. In the race for next-generation grid power, lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries (SIB) are increasingly competing in the global energy storage market. Amid this shifting landscape, SIB developers like Alsym Energy are advancing non-lithium-ion and advanced battery energy storage systems (BESS) across multiple use cases like mining. The safety performance of lithium-ion is significantly stronger in newer systems than in vintage BESS designs. As EnergyTech previously reported, the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) highlighted in an October white paper that BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. For years, however, lithium-ion batteries in legacy systems were prone to catastrophic fires. That same seven-year span includes separate fire events at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, and a 2019 thermal runaway event that severely injured eight firefighters in Surprise, Arizona. These incidents exposed critical safety risks in early-vintage BESS—just as large-scale energy users race to bring record capacity online for AI data centers and next-gen industrial electrification. That behind-the-meter and grid-scale surge has prompted the industry to look for safer alternatives. Beyond safety: The commercial surge of sodium-ion Although newer lithium-ion battery designs have largely addressed these safety concerns, sodium-ion batteries are still surging into commercial production for the global energy storage sector. This includes production of the TENER Sodium Energy Storage System from Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL), which debuted in Munich, Germany. The company claims it is a field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution. In early market deployments, sodium-ion batteries are demonstrating their potential viability for long-duration storage, weather resistance and safety in next-gen operations. Yet this momentum isn’t directly linked to thermal runaway in vintage lithium systems. According to a recent Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac) report, sodium-ion's improving economics stem from its 20-year lifecycle math, extreme-weather durability and broader shifts in global trade policy. In WoodMac’s November report, “Sodium-ion batteries: commercialisation begins, economics to follow,” the global research firm noted that sodium-ion batteries are now entering commercial production with over 70 GWh of supply agreements already secured across China, the U.S. and Europe. Tracking market trends in China, the U.S., Germany and India, the report found that sodium-ion is establishing itself as “the most cost-effective emerging alternative” to lithium-ion battery storage. Top manufacturers are on track to produce raw sodium-ion battery cells as cost-effectively as lithium iron phosphate (LFP) by the end of 2026. However, WoodMac noted that grid-ready sodium-ion BESS won't match the upfront pricing of comparable LFP systems until after 2030. “The 2030-2035 window is where the economics decisively shift,” said WoodMac senior research analyst Priya Shrivastava in a statement. “For projects being deployed today, LFP remains the bankable choice for two- to four-hour duration assets.” China, which dominates early manufacturing in this sector, is projected to achieve an 18% to 20% "learning rate" between 2026 and 2035. WoodMac explains that this means China will have the ability to drop its production costs by roughly one-fifth every time its cumulative sodium-ion output doubles. “While SIB offers manufacturers a valuable alternative, the chemistry still faces material challenges: scaling production, refining cell materials and establishing a track record of consistent performance,” added Shrivastava. Today, sodium-ion chemistries account for less than 1% of global battery production for EVs and energy storage, according to WoodMac, and still cost more overall than lithium-ion for an equivalent storage capacity. Yet sodium is the sixth-most common element available to miners, roughly 1,000 times more abundant than lithium. Shrivastava explained that the most probable outcome WoodMac views is a sodium-ion battery market served by different technologies, each optimized for distinct applications and duration profiles. Passive cooling and the 20-year lifecycle math LFP, a lithium-ion battery chemistry, uses iron phosphate as its cathode material and can store up to 205 watt-hours per kilogram in each cell. Major manufacturers like CATL have unveiled LFP architectures that meet this threshold to boost energy capacity for large-scale stationary storage. However, as WoodMac previously highlighted, LFP requires energy-intensive active cooling to maintain safe operating temperatures in standard energy storage tech built around its chemistry. U.S. companies like battery storage developer Peak Energy are developing passively cooled BESS tech to deploy next-gen sodium-ion battery cells, built for stationary grid storage applications. By eliminating active cooling systems, Peak Energy claims its sodium-ion BESS reduces lifecycle energy storage costs by 20% (compared to conventional systems) while delivering more than 99% uptime. artigo.texto: Ginlong Technologies invested 544 million yuan in the transition from photovoltaic power curtailment to energy storage investment, tearing up the old account books of photovoltaic power plants. Is energy storage the answer to everything? New energy capital flows between the photovoltaic and energy storage tracks following the revenue model. According to Energy Insight, on the evening of November 20, Ginlong Technologies announced that its board of directors has terminated the "Distributed Photovoltaic Power Station Project", which was originally planned to invest 354 million yuan, and not a single penny had been invested as of November 13; the company reallocated 189 million yuan from two inverter projects, pooling 544 million yuan to shift the investment to an annual 8GWh energy storage system production line. Prior to this, Zoomlion Energy also carried out similar capital reallocation, while other enterprises transferred the remaining funds from energy storage back to the photovoltaic sector. The back-and-forth flow of capital between the two tracks is far more complicated than just the rotation of industry trends: the electricity pricing mechanism, grid connection rules and revenue models have all been rewritten at the same time. The rooftop remains the same, but the checkout counter has adopted a completely new settlement method. The rooftop project accounts no longer add up at first When the Document No.136 was implemented on February 9, 2025, what was truly rewritten was not the subsidy figure, but the most valuable part of the revenue of new energy power stations — certainty. The National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration divided new energy projects into two categories: existing projects and new projects, based on the cutoff date of June 1 of that year. The former will follow the current policy for benchmark electricity prices, which will not be higher than the local coal-fired power benchmark price, while the latter will enter provincial bidding, and the electricity included in the mechanism will be adjusted up or down according to the difference between the market price and the benchmark mechanism price. The mechanism electricity price is not a fixed purchase price, but a contract for difference. In the past, the "electricity sales revenue" line in the calculation sheet was a fixed figure, but now it is split into two parts: electricity under the mechanism and market revenue outside the mechanism. The monthly rent-like certainty in the past has been broken down into hourly prices. The inflection point of the installed capacity curve appeared in the data earlier than in the announcements, and the statistics from the National Energy Administration clearly depict this trend. In 2024, China's new installed photovoltaic capacity reached 278 million kilowatts, which rose to 317 million kilowatts in 2025, while the figure for the first three quarters of 2026 was 110.33 million kilowatts, down 53.9% year on year. The new photovoltaic mechanism electricity price in Shanghai is 0.4155 yuan per kWh, 0.225 yuan per kWh in Shandong, and the 2026 figure in Xinjiang falls at the lower limit of 0.15 yuan per kWh, meaning different provinces no longer follow the same accounting standard. BloombergNEF estimates that the actual market electricity price for photovoltaic power is on average 0.127 yuan per kWh lower than the mechanism electricity price. In Shandong, the average spot trading price of photovoltaic power in February 2025 once dropped to only 0.057 yuan per kWh, and there were about 1330 hours of negative electricity prices in the spot market for the whole year, nearly half of which were concentrated in spring. The stronger the sun shines, the lower the price goes. The decline in yield is not an abstract curve in research reports, it soon fell on specific people and projects. According to media reports, the internal rate of return of distributed industrial and commercial projects was originally about 13% to 14%, which dropped to 8% to 9% after the issuance of Document No.136. A person in charge of a distributed photovoltaic project in Shandong said that he has suspended investing in new projects since May 31. The aforementioned project of Ginlong Technologies was originally planned to be connected to the grid by the end of 2026, which already belongs to the category of new projects. The zero investment does not mean capital shortage, but a halt after the accounts no longer add up. The suspended fundraising project is equivalent to the financial model casting a vote of no confidence first. With no mandatory supporting orders, the energy storage sector has to seek business on its own The fundraising change plan of Zoomlion Energy in February 2025 is most easily interpreted by the outside world as a simple track switching story. It reduced the fundraising for the distributed photovoltaic power station project from 700 million yuan to 450 million yuan, with 250 million yuan returned to the capital pool. In the same plan, the renamed and expanded energy storage project is proposed to invest 690 million yuan, which is even lower than the original 800 million yuan. The so-called "abandoning photovoltaic for energy storage" in most cases does not mean taking one yuan from the photovoltaic sector and putting it directly into the energy storage sector, but reordering the capital in the overall plate. The reason why capital shifts to the battery sector is not that the battery sector is better at telling stories, but that it has begun to have independent and accountable cash flow. Document No.136 clearly stipulates that allocating energy storage shall not be taken as a precondition for the approval and grid connection of new energy projects, so energy storage power stations that used to make a living by leasing capacity once had no buyers.
