artigo.texto: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 23. The State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) is exploring opportunities to introduce new energy storage technologies and improve the resilience of the country's power system, SOCAR Vice President Afgan Isayev said on Monday at the Azerbaijan-Italy Business Forum in Baku, Trend's correspondent reports. According to him, existing power grids cannot accommodate unlimited amounts of electricity from variable-output renewable energy sources, making grid modernization necessary. "In this regard, technologies such as sodium-ion and vanadium flow batteries are being considered. Energy storage systems play an important role in enabling the integration of renewable energy sources into power grids," he said. He also highlighted the development of sodium-ion batteries in China, noting that the technology could become more affordable due to the widespread availability of sodium and have a lower environmental impact than lithium batteries. According to SOCAR's vice president, the company is exploring opportunities to integrate such technologies into Azerbaijan's national power system in cooperation with AREA, the Ministry of Energy of Azerbaijan, and Azerenergy OJSC, the country's electricity transmission system operator. In addition, Isayev highlighted the potential of grid-forming inverters, which provide additional flexibility and help improve power grid stability. He also spoke about the possible use of microgrids in industrial parks being established across various regions of Azerbaijan, particularly in areas where connecting to the main power grid is challenging. According to Isayev, microgrids could represent the next stage in the development of energy infrastructure, ensuring energy independence for industrial zones and residential areas.

artigo.texto: GS Engineering & Construction said Monday it had partnered with LS Electric, LG Uplus and Honeywell Technologies to shorten data center construction timelines amid growing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The four companies signed a memorandum of understanding at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in southern Seoul to establish an integrated engineering framework covering four stages of development — procurement planning, design, system installation and integrated commissioning. The companies aim to agree on technical requirements early in each project to minimize design changes, duplicate work and delays between phases. That would help bring forward the ready-for-service date, when a data center can begin serving customers. GS E&C will coordinate technical work during system installation and provide engineering support for construction. LS Electric will review power systems and major equipment specifications and provide technical support for electrical infrastructure during integrated commissioning. Honeywell Technologies will contribute expertise in building automation, integrated controls, security and safety. The company plans to use its Forge industrial AI platform to help improve energy efficiency and operational reliability. Drawing on its experience operating large-scale data centers, LG Uplus will help define customer requirements and set criteria for operating and accepting completed facilities. It will also help validate operating procedures for emergencies such as power outages. The companies plan to hold regular working-level meetings to define responsibilities and work out how to apply the framework to future data center projects. The agreement follows GS E&C’s recent partnerships on data center power infrastructure, prefabricated modular data centers and immersion cooling technology. GS E&C said delivering projects quickly is becoming increasingly important as demand for AI data centers grows. yejinlim@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: Battery storage system could power 170,000 homes Plans to build a battery storage system capable of powering more than 170,000 homes have been recommended for approval. CONNECTID 2 Ltd has applied to install the infrastructure on land west of the A140 at Red House Farm in Yaxley, near Eye, Suffolk. However, the application has been opposed by Yaxley, Thrandeston and Mellis parish councils over concerns including flooding and fire safety. Mid Suffolk District Council will make its final decision at a planning meeting on 2 December. Blueprints showed the storage system would consist of 448 battery container units and be built on 10.4 hectares (25.7 acres) of mostly agricultural land. The facilities enable electricity from renewable sources, such as solar and wind, to be stored outside of national and local networks and then released into the grid when power is required. According to planning documents, the development would have 520MW of storage - enough energy to power 176,100 homes a day. If permission is granted, the site will be returned to agricultural use after 40 years or if it goes six months without operating. Similar proposals at land south of Eye Airfield Industrial Estate were approved by the council in July 2025. The local authority is run by a Green, independent and Liberal Democrat coalition. artigo.texto: Car battery gigafactory builder drops out - Published The company building the UK's biggest electric vehicle (EV) battery factory has said its opening remains "on track", despite a major contractor stepping away from the project for the second time in six months. The gigafactory near Bridgwater in Somerset, is being led by Agratas and built on the site of a former ordinance factory, creating around 4,600 jobs once open. Contractor TSL, which is building the factory's exterior, will step down, external once that work is complete, but the company has declined to say why and it is unclear if it had planned further involvement. Buckinghamshire-based TSL only joined the project in June after previous lead contractor Sir Robert McAlpine ended its involvement. Agratas, part of the Tata Group which owns Jaguar Land Rover, said it will not need to replace TSL as it is already working with another contractor - NG Bailey - who will carry out the remaining work fitting out the inside of the factory. More from Somerset - 'Stunning' sculpture could replace M5 Willow Man - Published20 hours ago - Hopes damaged tower could reopen to visitors - Published21 hours ago - Loss of farm school land to have 'massive impact' - Published1 day ago A spokesperson for Agratas said: "We are on track to meet our customer requirements. "The Somerset site is a large and complex industrialisation project, and all of our supplier partners are supporting us well as we prepare for the facility's launch phase." Construction of the factory on the 616 acre (249.2 hectare) brownfield location near Bridgwater was expected to take two years, with about 2,000 people working on site this year. Project leader Agratas said in the summer the original 2026 factory opening date had been pushed back to 2027, and has now confirmed it will be the end of that year. The company said 1,500 operational jobs would be created in 2027, with 4,600 jobs on offer once it expands across the whole site. artigo.texto: Data center surge powering questions of who pays electricity bills Q. Electricity demand has increased after years of little change. What is driving this? Average annual change in electricity consumption in the U.S was about 0.1 percent from 2005 through 2020—hardly any change whatsoever. The economy [had become] less energy intensive and more efficient. Manufacturing moved offshore and everyone knows light bulbs changed. Refrigerators and dishwashers and other sorts of heavy electrical, durable goods in the household became more energy efficient. Even though we were growing, the economy became less energy dependent. What's changed very recently? I would say two things. One is data centers. Second, we didn't have electric vehicles in large numbers 20 years ago. Now, we have millions of electric vehicles that are on the grid. Q. How big a contributor are data centers? Data centers aren't new. We've had data centers around as long as we've had the internet and computers. For example, Netflix’s streaming service has to store things on the cloud and make them available to access at any given time. But data centers for this were smaller, maybe 10 to 25 megawatts [each]. Now with the boom in artificial intelligence, we have to train these [computing] models in what's called inference. These AI models require significantly higher amounts of computation and hence, power. These types of data centers are a lot more energy intensive and can be upward of one gigawatt or multiple gigawatts. (One gigawatt equals 1,000 megawatts.) This is equivalent to a medium-sized U.S. city, about 250,000 households, which can use about one gigawatt of electricity at peak demand. Q. For context, what’s the maximum amount of electricity on a summer day that we can produce and consume in Texas? We just set records this year. We went over 90 gigawatts for the first time during a handful of days in the summer [of 2026]. Before that, the record was 85 gigawatts. That’s a 5 to 7 percent increase in the peak load just from one year to the next in the service area of ERCOT [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas]. We're going from 90 gigawatts as the peak load last summer and potentially adding 60 gigawatts of data centers on top of that within a handful of years. You can see how we would need to be building out a lot of electricity supply. Q. How is this new electricity demand likely to be met? Natural gas is far and away the answer in the moment as far as what we see in the pipeline of what is being built [for generation] over the next handful of years, as well as solar. There's been a conversation from the federal government about extending the life of coal plants that were supposed to be retired. That can bring some relief. The other piece is nuclear. I think there's been a resurgence in the role that nuclear can play on the grid, but it's a very long timeline for permitting and construction. Q. What about data center operators creating “behind-the-meter,” off-the-grid power supplies? I don't see that much behind-the-meter generation powering data centers. It's extremely difficult to run your own power grid. There's a lot that goes into also having a power supply onsite. It's also not as reliable [as grid power]. The grid offers reliability, and that partners well with what a data center requires. Data centers need to have “five nines” reliability. That means that their up-time is 99.999-plus percent of the time. They can only be offline for a single digit of hours throughout the year. When you run your own power plant, all that risk of making sure that your electricity grid does not fail is on you as the island behind the meter. If you lose your power plant and then can't guarantee reliability to your customers, that's a big problem. But also, because you want to guarantee this reliability, you have to either do many smaller power generation units or you need to build in redundancy called “N plus one.” You basically have to overbuild your power capacity. The estimate I see usually is around 30–40 percent more power built onsite than you'll consume, because you need to make sure that in case one of those goes down, you can continue. It's costly for companies to do this. What behind the meter offers is that you don't have to wait for the regulators. These grid interconnections can take a long time depending on where you're trying to locate. There's conversation about whether some data centers in the next number of years might start off as behind the meter while they're waiting for an interconnection. There's not too many data centers currently operating fully behind the meter. I think some estimates show that maybe 30 percent of what's in the pipeline over the next three to five years would be behind the meter. But it's unclear if that's going to materialize or pan out. Q. What's going to be the impact of all this extra electricity demand on prices? We have a good sense of how power plants work and the way that the grid operates. We have less visibility into how a data center is going to be operating from hour to hour or whether they're going to actually be constructed. Starting first off with what data centers have already cost so far, [we have] an average of about a 7 percent increase nationally in the wholesale [electricity] price compared with a world in which data centers don't exist. If you were just to strip out the demand from data centers and set the price at that point, cost increases [would] vary from month to month, from around 4 percent to 8 percent depending on the time of year. There's a lot that goes on with the price variability that…[can include power plant] fuel costs as they change over the year. Now, let's fast forward to 2028. A lot of data centers are coming online over the next couple of years. artigo.texto: As the midterm results rolled in a few weeks ago, making clear that Democrats were headed for a huge night, the world’s richest person, the largest individual midterm donor, and one of X’s most relentless posters was focused on his latest extraterrestrial scheme: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk wrote on the social media platform he owns. It was his first public reaction to the election results, which amounted to a harsh rebuke of the MAGA messaging he’d spent the past four years underwriting. A self-serving take? Absolutely. SpaceX aims to launch a huge amount of AI processing capacity into orbit, with the goal of eventually deploying 100 gigawatts of solar-powered computing satellites every year. But does Musk have a point? Maybe. As the midterms proved — and as Heatmap has long been tracking — anti-data center sentiment is exploding. Our most recent polling found that 71% of survey respondents would oppose a data center near where they live, which is actually down slightly from 75% a few months earlier. The overwhelming majority of congressional and gubernatorial candidates who won this year favored cracking down on these facilities through stronger regulations or even moratoria. That’s all to say that Musk is hardly the only entrepreneur betting the moment is ripe for AI infrastructure to reach far flung corners of the planet and beyond. So far, the middle of the ocean and low Earth orbit look like the leading frontiers. Wave energy startup Panthalassa, for instance, is building ocean-based data centers, while other space-based data center hopefuls such as Cowboy Space, Starcloud and Orbital are also jockeying for a share of the market alongside bigger players like Google and Blue Origin. “When we first embarked, there was probably more skepticism than there was conviction,” Joseph Yaffe, COO of data center startup Cowboy Space, told me. “Now I think the balance has changed, and there’s more conviction than there is skepticism.” Yaffe originally founded the startup with the goal of beaming solar power down to Earth, but pivoted to data centers this spring when the company raised a $275 million Series B at a $2 billion valuation. Unlike other startups in this industry, Cowboy Space doesn’t want to rely on SpaceX to get its satellites into orbit — it plans to build its own rockets. While taking on Musk’s nearly $2 trillion rocket-slash-AI company may sound like a fool’s errand, Yaffe sees this as the startup’s edge, in part because the midterms revealed the deep unpopularity of Musk’s priorities. “We’re operating in an industry that’s dominated by one single polarizing company, or really a company with a polarizing leader. His side lost,” Yaffe told me. “People who are thinking a lot about space as a new commercial frontier would like to have other ways to get access to space.” Cowboy Space’s rockets are purpose-built to house its 1-megawatt orbital data centers, with an upper section designed to detach and double as the GPU-packed satellite. By contrast, Starship, Musk’s next-generation rocket, still requires a separate satellite to house AI chips. And if an outside company wants to hitch a ride, they’ll have to pay SpaceX for the privilege; if Cowboy Space’s rocket design proves skyworthy, it avoids that. The company thinks these advantages will eventually make its computing as cheap as anything on Earth, if not cheaper in the long run. “But not 20 years — we think five years,” Yaffe told me. It’s targeting first launch by the end of 2028. No major customer has yet committed to buying compute from orbital data centers at scale, though some are testing the waters. Starcloud says its next satellite, slated to launch by year’s end, will run workloads for Crusoe, and it has partnerships with AWS and Google Cloud. But Yaffe expects to see more action within the next year. “People, understandably, are now in the place of, Well, do we wait and see if they can put a one-megawatt data center in orbit, or do we commit and try to at least have first dibs on the first 10 gigawatts in orbit now?” Orbital, a pre-seed space-based data center startup founded earlier this year, also sees the midterms as a gift of sorts. “I guess folks are going down the same research journey that I did like a year ago, and realizing that this is not at all that crazy of an idea,” Euwyn Poon, the company’s CEO, told me. Orbital is targeting its first launch for next summer, aboard a SpaceX rocket, with plans to begin scaling by the end of the decade. Neither Yaffe nor Poon, however, views community opposition as the primary constraint on the AI buildout. Both support building on land, they just don’t think terrestrial energy supply can keep pace. But they’re split on what comes next. Poon thinks orbit will become “the dominant way of capturing energy and running AI compute,” while Yaffe expects the majority of computing capacity to stay on Earth. In the broader context of the industry, however, this is a fairly minor point of disagreement. After all, plenty of investors still view the prospect of scrappy startups building orbital data centers as a wildly expensive and exceedingly unlikely proposition in the first place, including Mike Schroepfer, founder of Gigascale Capital and former Meta CTO. “It’s a trap. I’m just amused by how many people are falling for it,” Schroepfer told me. “Elon’s so good at this. He’s convincing everyone this is the thing, so everyone’s going to invest in it and build the supply chain. And he is best positioned to build space-based data centers, so I don’t know how anyone’s going to compete against SpaceX on this.” Schroepfer thinks Musk will put AI infrastructure in orbit, but that the economics of this approach will still look pretty poor compared with his favored alternative: deploying data centers in the open ocean. artigo.texto: New York Data Centers - Manhattan’s 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue (now Google-owned) are among the most interconnected buildings on Earth — critical nodes for global internet traffic. - ConEdison rates of 20–25¢/kWh make NYC the most expensive data center market in the country, while upstate utilities offer 6–8¢/kWh near Niagara Falls hydropower. - A 2022–2024 moratorium on fossil-fueled crypto mining reshaped the upstate pipeline without affecting traditional data centers. Manhattan Carrier Hotels to Hudson Valley Campuses New York’s data center geography reflects a stark economic divide. Lower Manhattan hosts iconic carrier hotels — 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue — where financial institutions pay premium rates for sub-millisecond latency to Wall Street. The Hudson Valley has emerged as a lower-cost alternative, with operators in Westchester and Orange counties building campuses that maintain fiber links to NYC at a fraction of Manhattan real estate costs. Upstate New York attracts operators seeking cheap hydroelectric power near Niagara Falls and Syracuse, though the 2022–2024 moratorium on fossil-fueled crypto mining reshuffled some of that pipeline. New York’s Data Center Counties 26 New York counties have tracked facilities, spanning from dense urban colocation in Manhattan to hyperscale builds along the I-87 corridor. The split mirrors the state’s broader economic geography: downstate pays for proximity and connectivity; upstate competes on cost and clean energy. Wall Street, Big Tech, and the Latency Premium New York’s operator mix is unlike any other market. Financial institutions drive demand in Manhattan and northern New Jersey, paying enormous premiums for microseconds of latency advantage. Equinix, Digital Realty, and Sabey Data Centers provide the colocation infrastructure. Google’s ownership of the iconic 111 Eighth Avenue symbolizes big tech’s presence, while the Hudson Valley attracts operators like EdgeConneX and Stack Infrastructure building for NYC-adjacent demand at lower cost. New York’s Highest-Capacity Facilities Genesee County tops the capacity ranking at 1,500 MW. The largest New York facilities are no longer in Manhattan — space and power constraints have pushed hyperscale capacity to the Hudson Valley and upstate, where land is available and utility rates can be one-fifth of ConEdison’s. Climate Mandates and a Bifurcated Pipeline New York’s pipeline reflects the state’s Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA), which requires 70% renewable electricity by 2030. Operators are shifting toward renewable energy procurement and behind-the-meter generation to comply. The pipeline is bifurcated: high-value, low-latency colocation in NYC proper, and hyperscale campuses in the Hudson Valley and upstate. The 13 facilities in development are weighted toward the latter. ConEdison vs. Upstate: A 4x Rate Differential No state has a wider electricity price gap within its borders. ConEdison in NYC charges commercial customers 20–25¢/kWh — the highest rates of any major data center market. Upstate utilities like National Grid and NYSEG charge closer to 6–8¢/kWh, and facilities near Niagara Falls access even cheaper hydroelectric power. This price gradient explains the ongoing migration of price-sensitive workloads upstate, while latency-critical financial applications remain tethered to Manhattan. The NYISO market allows large consumers to hedge costs through forward contracts. Compare current New York electricity rates across utility territories. Frequently Asked Questions Why is Manhattan a data center hub despite extreme costs? Manhattan’s data center market exists because of latency requirements. Financial institutions on Wall Street, media companies, and ad-tech firms need sub-millisecond connectivity to exchanges, content delivery networks, and each other. Carrier hotels like 60 Hudson Street and 111 Eighth Avenue are among the most interconnected buildings in the world. For these customers, the premium of 20–25¢/kWh electricity is justified by the value of proximity. What happened with New York's crypto mining moratorium? In November 2022, New York enacted a two-year moratorium on new fossil-fueled proof-of-work cryptocurrency mining operations (S6486D). The law, which expired in 2024, did not affect existing operations or renewable-powered mining. It did not apply to traditional data centers or cloud computing facilities. On July 14, 2026, Governor Hochul signed Executive Order 62, pausing state environmental permits for data centers over 50 MW until a generic environmental impact statement is completed. How expensive is electricity for New York data centers? Costs vary dramatically by location. ConEdison in NYC charges commercial customers 20–25¢/kWh, among the highest in the nation. Upstate utilities like National Grid and NYSEG charge closer to 6–8¢/kWh, and facilities near Niagara Falls can access even cheaper hydroelectric power. What submarine cables connect to New York? New York and New Jersey host multiple transatlantic submarine cable landing stations connecting to Europe. These cables land at stations in Long Island and northern New Jersey, with backhaul fiber running to Manhattan carrier hotels, making NYC a critical node for international internet traffic. How many data centers are in New York? New York has 199 tracked data center facilities across 26 counties. Facilities range from dense colocation hubs in Manhattan to hyperscale campuses in the Hudson Valley and upstate. Which companies operate the most data centers in New York? Major operators include Equinix, Digital Realty, DataBank, Sabey Data Centers, CyrusOne, and QTS. Google owns the iconic 111 Eighth Avenue building. In the Hudson Valley, EdgeConneX and Stack Infrastructure are building hyperscale campuses.

artigo.texto: As AI-driven demand pushes data center construction to record levels, communities and governors are responding. We track 583 active restrictions across 46 states. 583 restrictions are currently active across 46 states. New Jersey leads with 93 municipal bans, followed by Michigan (63), Ohio (59), and North Carolina (52). Open any state below to see where restrictions have passed. All 46 states with tracked data center restrictions, ranked by count New York became the first state to enact a statewide moratorium in July 2026, and governors in Virginia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Kentucky, Ohio, Texas, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Nebraska, and Louisiana have signed executive orders or directives. At the federal level, the Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417–3 in September. Below are the 115 actions we cover in detail, newest first. Search by place or bill, or narrow by level or state. Data center moratoriums and restrictions, newest first, with what each does, how long it lasts, and its status Where What it does Duration Status Details Emporia, KSLocal Approved 4,346–2,891 (60%) on Nov 3: bans large data centers.Applies to: Data centers drawing 10 MW or moreUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Emporia, KS Emporia voters approved Ballot Question 2, an ordinance prohibiting the construction and operation of “High Impact Data Centers,” defined as facilities drawing more than 10 MW at peak. The vote was 4,346 to 2,891 (60.1% yes), per Lyon County’s unofficial results. Wells, MELocal Approved 5,818–1,282 (82%) on Nov 3: retroactive moratorium.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Retroactive moratorium Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Wells, ME Wells voters approved Article 5, an ordinance establishing a retroactive moratorium on data centers, 5,818 to 1,282 (82% yes), per the town’s unofficial results. The Board of Selectmen (5–0) and Planning Board (7–0) had both recommended a yes vote. Wiscasset, MELocal Approved 1,363–712 (66%) on Nov 3: data center moratorium.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Moratorium Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Wiscasset, ME Wiscasset voters approved Question 2, adding a data center moratorium to the town ordinances (Article X, Section X-19), 1,363 to 712 (65.7% yes), per the town’s unofficial results. Grove City, OHLocal Approved 11,317–9,411 (55%) on Nov 3: data centers now need a public vote.Applies to: Any data center developmentUnofficial results Permanent (charter) Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Grove City, OH Grove City voters approved Issue 28, the Community Consent Amendment, 11,317 to 9,411 (54.6% yes), per Franklin County’s unofficial results. The charter amendment requires a public referendum, plus enforceable community impact standards, before the city can approve a data center. Hubbard, OHLocal Approved 2,622–802 (77%) on Nov 3: citizen-initiated ban.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Hubbard, OH Hubbard voters approved an initiated ordinance banning data centers in the city, 2,622 to 802 (76.6% yes), per Trumbull County’s unofficial results. Sunbury, OHLocal Approved 2,809–763 (79%) on Nov 3: charter limits on data centers.Applies to: Data center constructionUnofficial results Permanent (charter) Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Sunbury, OH Sunbury voters approved a charter amendment restricting the construction of data centers in the city, 2,809 to 763 (78.6% yes), per Delaware County’s unofficial results. Perry, OHLocal Approved 946–140 (87%) on Nov 3: required review of data center agreements.Applies to: Village agreements with a hyperscale data centerUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Perry, OH Perry voters approved Issue 16, a petition-initiated ordinance requiring the Village Fiscal Officer to review any village agreement with a hyperscale data center before signing it, 946 to 140 (87.1% yes), per Lake County’s unofficial results. Alhambra, CALocal Approved 12,496–2,772 (82%) on Nov 3: voters lock in the city’s ban.Applies to: All data centersUnofficial results Permanent Voter-approvedNov 3, 2026 Details for Alhambra, CA Alhambra voters approved Measure DB, affirming the city council’s data center ban, 12,496 to 2,772 (81.8% yes), per Los Angeles County’s unofficial results. Any future change to the ban now needs voter approval. Beaufort County, NCLocal One-year countywide pause on accepting or approving data-center applications.Applies to: All new applications 12 months EnactedOct 5, 2026 Details for Beaufort County, NC Beaufort County commissioners voted 6–1 on October 5 to stop accepting, processing, or approving data-center applications for one year. Commissioner Hood Richardson was the lone no vote. Residents testified about noise and electricity impacts. Staff will use the year to study those issues before writing permanent rules. Bangor, MELocal Council voted 8–0 to extend Bangor’s data-center freeze another 180 days.Applies to: New data-center developmentFirst confirmed active Maine local pause 180-day extension (through ~Apr 2027) ExtendedSep 29, 2026 Details for Bangor, ME Bangor first imposed a 180-day freeze on April 13 after a developer inquiry from Kratos AI. On September 29 the City Council voted 8–0 to extend the moratorium another 180 days so staff and consultants can finish zoning rules and public outreach. The original pause was due to expire in early October. The extension keeps an active local restriction in force in a state the tracker currently lists as having zero active moratoriums after Gov. Mills vetoed LD 307. artigo.texto: EU and UK Finalize Deal to Link Emissions Trading Systems, With Interchangeable Allowances From January 2028 Why It MattersLinking the two carbon markets shifts airline compliance toward one pooled allowance market with a single UK authority, while the EU's separate plan for long-haul flights keeps its external reach contested. What happened The European Union and the United Kingdom have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS), with the deal announced at the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Nov. 20, 2026. The UK ETS was created in 2021 following Brexit, and businesses called for it to be linked to the EU ETS from the outset. Negotiations began in late 2025. The European Commission's Directorate General for Climate Action said the agreement will ensure the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading applies in the EU and the UK. If ratified on both sides, the deal is expected to simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a "one-stop shop," so airlines deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, with any necessary legislation to be passed in 2027 and procedures to be enacted in January 2028. According to the UK government, from Jan. 1, 2028, UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline at which allowances from both systems will be accepted is Sept. 30, 2028, covering operators' obligations for the 2027 compliance year. The two systems will continue to operate separately, with "dynamic alignment," and the UK government said it will have an early "decision-shaping role" when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. The aviation scope dispute In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) range. The proposal drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who view it as extraterritorial and as undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization's program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with "elements" of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland's ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. Industry impact & what to watch For airlines and business-aviation operators flying between the UK and the EU, the practical change is administrative as much as financial. Two separate carbon regimes, each with its own regulator and allowance pool, are set to become one interchangeable pool with a single UK point of contact. Operators that today hold and track allowances separately for each scheme would be working from a common stock, and a larger linked market is expected to steady carbon pricing. The link also ties UK aviation policy more closely to Brussels. With dynamic alignment, the UK follows the EU's rule changes while keeping a separate system, and its early role in shaping new EU policy sits alongside its stated alignment with elements of the EU's aviation coverage. That makes the EU's July proposal on flights to non-EU countries within 5,000 km a live question for UK-linked operators, and it keeps the objections tied to Corsia in play. The next dated milestones are legislation in 2027, procedures in January 2028, and the Sept. 30, 2028 surrender deadline for the 2027 compliance year. Ratification on both sides is the condition on which the deal's benefits depend.

artigo.texto: Brasil mira boom de data centers até 2030 O Brasil se prepara para um crescimento expressivo no setor de data centers até 2030, conforme apontam projeções do mercado. O país busca converter sua matriz energética limpa e a crescente demanda digital em uma vantagem competitiva regional. O movimento ocorre em um contexto global de aceleração da digitalização e da necessidade de infraestrutura de processamento de dados. No interior paulista, o maior data center da América Latina já opera em Vinhedo, um modesto complexo de 61 megawatts (MW). A unidade serve como referência para o potencial de expansão do setor no território nacional. Empresários e gestores públicos observam com atenção os desdobramentos dessa tendência para a economia local. Infraestrutura silenciosa e operação contínua O monólito cinzento é silencioso por dentro. Máquinas zumbem, o ar frio circula e técnicos deslizam pelos corredores como fantasmas. A descrição, presente em relatos sobre a instalação de Vinhedo, ilustra o ambiente controlado e a rotina discreta desses centros de processamento. A operação exige precisão e monitoramento constante, características que demandam mão de obra qualificada. Do lado de fora do maior data center da América Latina, a estrutura aparenta simplicidade, mas abriga sistemas complexos de armazenamento e transmissão de dados. A fonte não detalhou os investimentos específicos em expansão, mas o setor projeta crescimento contínuo até o fim da década. Esse cenário tende a gerar oportunidades para fornecedores de serviços e equipamentos na região. Energia limpa como diferencial competitivo A região tenta converter energia limpa e demanda digital em vantagem competitiva. O Brasil possui uma das matrizes elétricas mais renováveis do mundo, o que atrai empresas globais de tecnologia que buscam reduzir emissões de carbono. Data centers consomem grandes volumes de energia, e a disponibilidade de fontes limpas é um fator decisivo para novos investimentos. Para o noroeste paulista, a expansão do setor pode gerar demanda por serviços de manutenção, segurança e logística. Pequenas e médias empresas de Araçatuba, Birigui e Penápolis podem se beneficiar indiretamente, fornecendo insumos ou mão de obra terceirizada. A fonte não detalhou projeções de empregos diretos, mas o histórico do setor indica efeito multiplicador na economia local. Impacto no comércio e na indústria regional O avanço dos data centers no estado de São Paulo tende a aquecer o mercado imobiliário industrial e o setor de construção civil. Cidades próximas a grandes centros de processamento podem atrair empresas de suporte técnico e logística. A instalação de Vinhedo, por exemplo, já movimenta a economia da região metropolitana de Campinas, com reflexos em municípios vizinhos. Comerciantes de Araçatuba e região devem observar as cadeias de suprimentos que se formam ao redor desses empreendimentos. Fornecedores de materiais elétricos, refrigeração e segurança patrimonial podem encontrar novas oportunidades de negócio. A fonte não detalhou valores de investimento, mas o crescimento projetado até 2030 sugere demanda consistente por serviços especializados. Perspectivas para a próxima década O Brasil mira boom de data centers até 2030, com potencial para se tornar um hub regional de processamento de dados. A combinação de energia renovável, estabilidade institucional e mercado consumidor amplo favorece a atração de capital estrangeiro. Especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem não forneceram números específicos, mas o tom é de otimismo moderado. Para o empresariado do interior paulista, a recomendação é acompanhar editais e licitações de infraestrutura digital. Entidades como ACSP, CDL e Sebrae podem oferecer capacitação para pequenos negócios que desejam se inserir nessa cadeia produtiva. A fonte não detalhou políticas públicas específicas, mas o setor privado já sinaliza interesse em expandir operações no estado. A transição para uma economia mais digital exige planejamento e adaptação por parte dos agentes locais. O exemplo de Vinhedo demonstra que mesmo estruturas aparentemente isoladas geram empregos e renda em seu entorno. Até 2030, o Brasil pode consolidar sua posição como destino estratégico para data centers na América Latina. artigo.texto: In Eatonville, Florida, America’s first all-Black municipality, the Hungerford School taught generations of Black students how to build a life in a country determined to limit their futures. The Florida boarding school for Black students built in 1897 paired academics with skilled trades, making it an engine of Black self-sufficiency. Now, 17 years after the school was shuttered, part of its former property holds a project that some residents and advocates argue could limit the futures of its Black children: a data center. The facility, which began construction in 2019, came with grand promises that have only shrunk as time goes on. In the early stages, HostDime, the developer, pledged to set up the town’s residents with free at-home Wi-Fi. As construction costs have nearly doubled and the open date keeps being delayed, the company’s CEO, Manny Vivar, said its original promise of free at-home wifi is “not sustainable.” The company also said it would provide scholarships, programs, and STEM training for Eatonville students and residents upon completion of the facility. It is not clear if that will move forward. HostDime has now said it will offer “public” Wi-Fi through an antenna atop the building. Without any binding agreements or clear enforcement from local officials, those commitments have faded. Meanwhile, residents are left without access to the land and the memory of their self-reliance, and now, potential pollution from the data center. “That’s just been the story of Eatonville,” said Julian Johnson, an Eatonville resident. “It’s almost like the norm to be on defense and fighting because of the valuable land.” The fight in Eatonville reaches far beyond the 5 acres where HostDime is building its data center. Across the country, the artificial intelligence race is raising questions about who makes the deals, controls the land, and must live with the demands for electricity and the threat of pollution. For many Black communities, it is also a question of whether land that sustained generations can remain a foundation for their futures. “We don’t have anybody to stand for us,” resident Chad McKendrick said at a recent town council meeting about the data center. The situation in Eatonville is “another example of data centers making these promises and offering community benefits, but then failing to deliver on those benefits,” said Shelby Green, the research and communications manager at the Energy and Policy Institute. In Eatonville, the average household income is less than $33,000. It is located in Orange County, where the average income is roughly 2.5 times higher than that at $80,000. Green said this disparity in wealth is seen in data center placement. “This data center expansion is almost replicating the failures of urban renewal back when the federal government through state governments was acquiring land from Black communities and building highways over them in service of white or wealthier communities,” she said. At a recent town council meeting, Vivar said that offering Wi-Fi to the community “came from a pure heart.” “Do I regret saying it the way I said?” he added, “Probably, because there was no technicality behind it.” A century-long fight over Black land At one point, the land in question was owned collectively by the town’s residents before being donated for the school through a trust. Nearly 50 years after the school was built, Orange County Public Schools acquired the property from the trust following a court battle. In its 1951 order, the Florida Supreme Court required the school board to only use the land to educate Black children. But over the next half century until the school was closed, the school district had regularly tried to sell the property, prompting continued backlash from Eatonville’s Black community. “You see, somebody is going to make money off Eatonville and that’s because Eatonville is such a precious commodity. The people of Eatonville are the ones who should be able to benefit and build a lasting legacy and lasting economic legacy,” said N.Y. Nathiri, the executive director of the Association to Preserve the Eatonville Community, or PEC. HostDime’s 5 acres are only one part of a broader dispute over the former school property, where residents are also contesting how the remaining 100-plus acres of land should be developed. For years, residents called on the city government to buy the land from the school district. Instead, former Mayor Angie Gardner supported selling land to the data center developer and to Sovereign Land Co., which attempted to build a shopping and entertainment district. Eatonville’s need for investment is urgent. The town has remained under a state financial-emergency designation for more than two decades and is at threat of running out of money because of a dwindling tax base. Residents and town council members understand this, but want more say in how to address the crisis. Some accused Gardner of advancing these projects without proper council approval and public input, raising concerns about a lack of transparency and oversight. Gardner “sat out there and essentially sold this town out,” said Councilman Tarus Mack. “I have always been saying give us the property or let us buy it back.” Gardner did not respond to Capital B’s request for comment before publication. Following the accusations made during a town council meeting, Gardner said there were several constituents and officials who supported the sale and development of the former school property, and others could have voiced concerns but did not. In 2023, PEC challenged the effort by Orange County Public Schools to sell roughly 100 acres to Sovereign Land Co. The lawsuit argued that the proposed sale violated restrictions intended to preserve the land’s educational purpose. Sovereign Land Co. subsequently withdrew from the deal. Now, PEC is suing again, challenging the process behind a new agreement to transfer the property to Dr. Phillips Charities. Plans by the charit

artigo.texto: Korean POSCO Group has strengthened its relationship with battery manufacturer CATL through a long-term lithium supply agreement covering the 2026-2028 period. The deal will see POSCO supply lithium for use in electric vehicle battery production, further deepening cooperation between the two companies as demand for battery raw materials continues to grow. Supporting Battery Production CATL is the world’s largest EV battery producer, accounting for around 40% of the global electric vehicle battery market. The company supplies batteries to major vehicle manufacturers in China and international markets. Under the agreement, POSCO Group will provide lithium required for CATL’s battery manufacturing operations between 2026 and 2028. The companies have also committed to strengthening their long-term partnership and cooperating to support a stable supply of battery raw materials. According to the announcement, deliveries under the contract have already begun. Expanding POSCO’s Lithium Business The agreement forms part of POSCO Group’s broader strategy to grow its lithium business, building on capabilities developed through its long-standing experience in securing and developing raw materials for its steel operations. The company has established a production base through the early acquisition of high-quality lithium resources and believes the CATL agreement will reinforce its sales position in China while enhancing its standing in the global lithium market. The deal also aligns with the strategic direction of POSCO Holdings Chief Executive Chang In Hwa, which focuses on securing high-quality resources and developing long-term relationships with leading global customers. Focus on Supply Chain Stability POSCO said it plans to continue improving the production stability and sales competitiveness of its lithium resources in an effort to strengthen profitability. The company also highlighted its role as a major Korean supplier of critical minerals, stating that it aims to contribute to greater stability across global supply chains for key battery materials. For the battery sector, the agreement underlines the importance of long-term raw material partnerships as manufacturers and suppliers seek to secure reliable lithium supplies to support continued growth in electric vehicle battery production.

artigo.texto: China's Arcfox Teams Up With CATL to Push Battery Swapping for the Masses: Can a $7,500-Class Swap Car Crack the Recharging Market? The battery-swap race heated up abruptly in the autumn of 2026. Geely and NIO took cross-shareholdings in each other, Huawei Yinwang and CATL connected the Qiankun intelligent-driving system with the Chocolate battery-swap network, BAIC signed a million-vehicle swap agreement with CATL, and Chery, GAC and Changan joined the ranks one after another. Against this backdrop, Arcfox Auto on Nov. 13 launched its "Arcfox + Era" mass-market battery-swap ecosystem strategy, announcing it would work with CATL to build a swap ecosystem network and push for unified swap standards, while simultaneously launching two new models: the Arcfox Beta S3 535ULTRA laser swap version and the Arcfox Beta T1 swap version. According to a report by 36Kr, the Beta S3 swap version measures more than 4.9 meters in length with a wheelbase exceeding 2.8 meters, approaching C-segment dimensions. Under a battery-vehicle separation and battery-rental plan, the bare-car price drops to just over 50,000 yuan (approximately $7,500). A 50,000-yuan budget previously covered only A0-segment small cars, and this pricing directly rewrites the segment's price anchor. Prices disclosed by Arcfox show the Beta S3 535ULTRA laser swap version starts at 78,800 yuan (approximately $12,000) under a battery-rental plan after a limited-time subsidy, while the Beta T1 swap version starts at 52,000 yuan (approximately $7,800) under a rental plan. The two cars stake out the B-segment spacious family market and the A0-segment entry-level commuter market respectively, contributing volume models to the Chocolate swap network. Two swap paths advance in parallel Battery swapping is not a new concept. Tesla demonstrated a 90-second swap in 2013 but abandoned it two years later. Its business logic relies heavily on network effects: station density, model supply and traffic volume reinforce one another. The industry currently has two representative paths. One is led by vehicle manufacturers that build their own networks and refine the experience around their own brands, with NIO as the exemplar. The other centers on cross-brand collaboration and standardized openness, pushing for unified standards in battery dimensions, interfaces and locking mechanisms so more brands can plug into the same network, with CATL providing support in battery standardization and network construction. The industry often compares the two to "Apple and Android." The focus of Arcfox's partnership this time is no longer simply supplying batteries for a single model, but jointly advancing ecosystem building around standardized batteries, the swap network and vehicle products. CATL's Chocolate swap system currently offers standard No. 20 and No. 25 swap blocks, has deployed more than 2,520 swap stations, and covers 31 provinces and 200 cities. The two sides plan to jointly build 30,000 swap stations in the future, strive to cover all cities nationwide within two years, form a 10-minute recharging circle in core areas, and leave room for more brands to join. On product strategy, the entire Arcfox lineup natively supports swapping, but the company is not going all-in on swapping; it advocates "chargeable and swappable," with its own charging network and CATL's swap network forming a "two networks in one"—charging where plugs exist, swapping where they don't. Swap versions account for 70% of orders Market data offers preliminary validation of the model. During the Beta S3 pre-sale period, swap-version orders accounted for 76%, and six months after launch they remain stable at around 70%. With charging and swap versions sold side by side, consumers have made their choice through orders. NIO's data offers a reference point. After adopting the BaaS battery-rental plan, the NIO ES8's entry threshold fell from 406,800 yuan (approximately $61,000) to 298,800 yuan (approximately $45,000), a one-time difference of 108,000 yuan (approximately $16,000); the model remains the sales leader in the 400,000-yuan-class large SUV market. The 2026 halved purchase-tax policy further amplifies the swap advantage, as swap models use the body price excluding the battery as the tax base. Recharging efficiency is another practical advantage. The Beta S3's standard swap time is 99 seconds, with users averaging 90 seconds in practice, and 99.9% of orders swap immediately upon arrival with zero queuing. NIO user surveys show swap satisfaction at 9.29 points with a 90.9% satisfaction rate, and 57.3% of owners say they will definitely choose a swappable model on their next purchase. A deeper shift lies in where battery-asset risk sits. Buying the battery outright means users bear the degradation and depreciation themselves, while renting transfers that uncertainty to the operator: each swap doubles as a battery health check, battery health is centrally managed by the platform, and selling the car no longer means absorbing a discount for an aging battery. According to estimates by the China Passenger Car Association, by the end of 2026 about 2.6 million new-energy vehicles will be more than eight years old, and by 2032 nearly 20 million NEVs will successively cross the battery warranty line—while cases of a battery replacement quote starting at 80,000 yuan (approximately $12,000) against a vehicle residual value of only 30,000 yuan (approximately $4,500) are not rare. Network density remains a hard constraint The appeal of swapping also has clear limits. China has built about 6,862 swap stations nationwide, while the total number of EV charging infrastructure connectors (guns) reaches 25.391 million—a stark gap in network density. Swap stations are heavy-asset investments, and a single station needs 60 to 70 swaps per day on average to break even; currently only about 20% of stations meet that bar, with most still relying on continued investment to stay afloat. artigo.texto: The tech industry is famous for moving fast. The power grid is famous for not. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Big Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032. The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it. That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too. The grid is years behind demand Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely. Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom. Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years. The industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building new infrastructure.” Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on. Voters are pushing back on power bills Public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults. Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C. A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%. Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill. Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.” “The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms. Big Tech is getting into the power business Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.” Some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations. President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the new-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding. On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S. SpaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune. It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment. The next tests come quickly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more. artigo.texto: China's EV battery market shifts: CATL's share slips quarter by quarter as second-tier makers rise The rankings in China's power battery market are being reshuffled below the leader. A Nov. 23 analysis of the October new-energy vehicle lithium battery market by Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Association, shows CATL still leads with a 44.0% share but has declined quarter by quarter, falling to 40.5% in the fourth quarter (through October); BYD edged up to 19.1%. Meanwhile, second-tier players such as Gotion High-tech (6.1%), EVE Energy (5.5%) and Geely Yaoning (2.5%) posted clear share gains, while tail-end companies have largely exited the competition. This is not an isolated event. Two years ago, in 2024, CATL and BYD together accounted for nearly 70% of China's power battery installations, forming a "two-strong" structure. According to statistics from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance, in the first 10 months of 2026 the two leaders' combined installation share had fallen to 62.3%, while the top 10 still held 94%; 41 companies achieved supporting installations, 10 fewer than a year earlier. The reordering of orders is mainly happening among companies with scale and customer bases, rather than a broad dispersion. Looking globally, the picture is the opposite of China's domestic market. According to SNE Research, global EV power battery installations reached 994.5GWh in January-September 2026, up 19.7% year on year, with September alone hitting a monthly record of 145.1GWh. CATL led with 389.2GWh and a 39.1% share, up 1.6 percentage points from a year earlier; BYD was second with 150.9GWh and 15.2%, putting the two at 54.3% combined. Seven of the top 10 are Chinese companies, with a combined 73.0% share, up another 3.5 percentage points in a year; the three South Korean majors (LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI) fell to 12.6% combined, down 4.1 percentage points. LFP batteries' share of global installations also rose to 57.7% from 52.5% a year earlier, in line with the LFP-led direction in China. Note: Panasonic Energy's share is calculated as installations divided by total global installations of 994.5GWh; the remaining top-10 spots are held by Chinese manufacturers including CALB and Gotion High-tech. In other words, China's domestic share is dispersing beyond the leaders while the global share is concentrating among Chinese manufacturers — and the two are not contradictory: second-tier players are grabbing domestic orders, while the leaders rely on overseas automaker customers and the cost advantage of LFP. For the Japanese supply chain, the direct effect of this reshuffle is share dilution — Panasonic Energy installed 35.6GWh in January-September, down 0.8% year on year, with supplies highly concentrated on Tesla; as global low-priced models keep shifting to LFP, suppliers tied to a single customer and the ternary route will see their share left behind by market growth. North America was the only major market to contract in the period (down 24.3% year on year), which is where the pressure on Japanese and South Korean battery makers comes from. Total installations are still expanding, but growth has clearly shifted gears. China's October power battery installations were 99GWh, up 18% year on year and approaching the 100GWh mark; January-October cumulative installations were 676GWh, up 17%. By contrast, output expansion has been more aggressive: October power battery output was 245.1GWh, up 44% year on year; January-October cumulative output was 2,078.1GWh, up 61%. With output growth far outpacing installations, the monthly installation-to-output ratio was just 41%, and the cumulative ratio fell to 33%, highlighting destocking pressure across the supply chain. Note: LFP accounted for 83% of January-October installations and 87% in October alone. Changes in demand structure give supply-chain adjustments a landing point. In October, LFP accounted for 86.9% of China's power battery installations, while monthly ternary lithium installations fell 22% year on year, leaving the market in a pattern of "absolute LFP dominance and continued ternary shrinkage." Companies with existing LFP expertise can participate in more model development around cost, fast charging and lifespan. Gotion High-tech also disclosed that its standardized battery packs have been supplied in batches to customers including SANY Heavy Truck and Geely Remote. Commercial vehicles focus more on charging efficiency, cycle life and whole-life costs, offering second-tier companies a niche in which to build scale. Second-tier expansion first benefits from changes in automakers' procurement strategies. When new-energy vehicles were rapidly scaling up, adding suppliers could ease supply-guarantee pressure; as price competition intensifies, automakers also want multiple suppliers to gain more room for cost negotiation and order allocation. Whether second suppliers can pass validation and achieve stable mass production determines whether this procurement choice is truly effective. This year, automakers' moves to bring in second suppliers have extended further into in-house development and capital cooperation. In September, Li Auto disclosed that the 5C fast-charging cells for its 2026 Li i6 are developed in-house by Li Auto and contract-manufactured by Sunwoda and CALB, with the battery pack produced by Li Auto. The same month, Sunwoda disclosed that Li Auto plans to invest 2.65 billion yuan (approximately $397.7 million) to increase capital in Sunwoda Power; at the end of October, it disclosed a 1.7 billion yuan (approximately $255.1 million) capital increase plan by Xiaomi's Hanxing Venture Capital. Automakers are beginning to participate more deeply in battery development and to strengthen cooperation with suppliers through equity ties. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is playing an increasingly strategic role within Spain's energy system. Its development will depend not only on technological advances, but also on factors such as regulation, revenue mechanisms and investor appetite. Arup's Energy, Business & Investor Advisory and Foresight teams analyse the current state of Spain's energy storage market and explore how it could evolve by 2036. Combining sector analysis, international market comparisons and strategic foresight, the report examines the key challenges, opportunities and business models that are likely to shape the sector's growth. Through four possible scenarios for 2036, we explore different futures for Spain's energy storage market, defined by who assumes investment risk and how value is distributed across the market. These range from Regulated Champions, where growth is driven primarily by regulated mechanisms and large operators, to The Algorithmic Bazaar, a more distributed market in which data-driven optimisation plays a central role. The report also considers Competition by Design, characterised by broader participation from independent developers, aggregators and industrial consumers, and Guardians of the Spread, where value is concentrated among players able to integrate generation, storage and energy retail activities. More than an assessment of current market conditions, the report offers a strategic perspective on the factors that will shape the future of energy storage in Spain. It helps developers, investors, energy companies and policymakers identify opportunities, anticipate risks and prepare for the decade ahead.

artigo.texto: By John Dobberstein, Editor The Broken Arrow City Council has extended a temporary moratorium on data center development while city officials continues to study zoning solutions and a variety of other connected scenarios for such projects. A data center was proposed earlier this year on the city’s east side, but the purchase agreement for the parcel fell through. The City Council unanimously approved Resolution No. 1783, extending the temporary moratorium on data center development in Broken Arrow’s city limits through June 30, 2027. The resolution reaffirms Ordinance No. 3929, originally adopted on June 15, 2026, which established a temporary moratorium on accepting, processing, approving, and issuing permits and development approvals for new data centers within the City. Before the Council passed Resolution No. 1783 on Nov. 16, the moratorium was set to expire Dec. 31. City Manager Michael Spurgeon said the moratorium lets the city develop a comprehensive and “defensible regulatory framework” should the City Council ever allow data centers in certain zones. He said it’s also essential to protect the city’s critical infrastructure and available resources, especially the city’s water supply. Spurgeon also wants the city to have a better grasp of the long-term economic and community impacts if data centers were allowed. Since the original moratorium was passed, Spurgeon said the city has received two inquiries or “pre-application requests” about potential data center development in or near the city, but city is not considering them. Since the moratorium was put in place, a Data Center Study Committee was formed in July and has met eight times. The city has been coordinating with Public Service Company of Oklahoma (PSO) regarding large-load service, interconnection, and infrastructure planning. The city has also reviewed data center regulations adopted or under consideration by other communities in Oklahoma and Kansas. Earlier this month, the City Council authorized spending $190,000 to hire Westwood Professional Services to complete a Data Center Regulatory Study and develop permanent zoning standards. Spurgeon said the study will examine the impacts of data centers, engage the public, review best practices from peer jurisdictions, and develop permanent zoning standards, “that protect public health, safety, and general welfare while managing this emerging land use. “The State Legislature passed a law on July 1 that said you can’t pass any costs for data centers on to customers. They must provide notice and pay all their own expenses, so some of the concerns from last spring no longer exist,” he added. “PSO has assured us they’ll make sure anyone who comes through their system complies with that state law, so we’ve got strong support from the state.” Spurgeon acknowledged the city is also considering its water capacity. Broken Arrow’s water system is currently sized to accommodate growth through 2040, with the projection primarily on residential use and knowing there will still be some large commercial areas. Utilities Director Timothy Robins his department are, “doing a model based on current zoning and the amount of water that will be used in those areas based on what we know about where we are capacity-wise.” The city is working with Mid-America Industrial Park to provide additional capacity. “Plus, at some point in 2040, we’ll need to upgrade our water plant to meet our needs. So that’s all being looked at to determine what we could support,” Spurgeon said. “Our biggest concern is if they decide to select a portion of the city that we do not serve, like Rural Water District #4, and that is something we’ll have to take under consideration.” The study will also provide the City Council with recommendations and requirements to consider for amending the City’s zoning ordinance regarding data center development.

artigo.texto: Eight EU countries join forces to defend carbon market against calls for delay The eight countries warn that further delays to the EU's expanded carbon market would undermine energy security, prolong dependence on fossil fuel imports and jeopardise investment in clean technologies. Eight European Union countries have joined forces to defend the bloc's expanded carbon market, warning against any further delays or changes to its implementation. In a letter to Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, seen by Euronews, the climate ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden argue that the EU's dependence on imported fossil fuels is a major economic and security vulnerability. They see the new Emissions Trading System (ETS2) as part of the solution, pushing governments and businesses to accelerate the shift to electrification. "By providing a cost-effective means to accelerate the decarbonisation of the road transport and building sectors, ETS2 strengthens Europe's energy security by reducing dependence on fossil fuel imports and promoting electrification," reads the letter dated 23 November. Related The intervention comes amid mounting political pressure from the four-nation Visegrad Group, Italy and Greece to soften or delay the system following the 15-16 October EU summit in Brussels. Resisting calls to scrap ETS2, EU leaders instead agreed to assess its impact ahead of its introduction in January 2028, after it was already delayed by a year. ETS2 will put a carbon price on fuels used for road transport and heating, with energy suppliers expected to pass the additional costs on to consumers through higher bills. The scheme has become increasingly politically sensitive as EU governments grapple with high energy costs and growing concerns about the impact of climate policies on households and businesses. Energy security before climate goals In their letter, the eight ministers invoke the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz to argue that reducing fossil fuel consumption is no longer simply a climate objective, but a matter of strategic autonomy. The EU imported €340 billion worth of fossil fuels in 2025, the ministers noted. Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, the additional cost of imports resulting from higher prices has reached €127 billion. The ministers warn that Europe's continued dependence on imported oil and gas leaves its economies exposed to geopolitical tensions, volatile prices and political pressure from suppliers. They argue that the ETS2 can help reduce that vulnerability by accelerating electrification in buildings and road transport, reducing fossil fuel imports and creating demand for clean technologies manufactured in the EU. Danish Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa said ETS2 was essential to the EU's electrification ambitions. "We need to accelerate the clean transition so the EU can reduce its dependence on expensive and unreliable fossil energy imports. That is crucial for lowering energy prices, strengthening our long-term competitiveness and stepping up our efforts to combat climate change," Nawa reacted. A warning against reopening the ETS2 The eight governments also warn against allowing the Commission's review of ETS2 to become an opportunity to reopen the legislation and water down its provisions. They argue that the system is part of a carefully balanced climate framework, combining emissions reductions with financial support for those most affected by the transition. Central to that balance is the Social Climate Fund, designed to cushion vulnerable households and businesses against higher heating and transport costs. Changing ETS2 in isolation, the ministers warn, risks undermining that broader agreement. They also insist that sticking to the agreed timetable would provide businesses with the regulatory certainty needed to invest in cleaner technologies, while generating revenues for national governments. Related "A strong implementation of ETS2 without further delays provides regulatory certainty and investment signals that are crucial to ensure the necessary investments towards decarbonisation and electrification," reads the letter. Czech Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlíček said the energy crisis, Russia's war in Ukraine and continued geopolitical tensions have let to "exceptionally high energy costs" for households and businesses across the EU. "Implementing ETS2 under these circumstances, when the system was designed and agreed upon under completely different geopolitical and economic conditions, simply does not seem reasonable to us," Havlíček told Euronews. "It will also be increasingly difficult to explain to our citizens across the EU why additional costs should be imposed at a time when many households are already struggling with high energy prices and the cost of living."
