artigo.texto: The Global AI Data Center Debate, Explained As countries race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence (AI), the electricity, water, and land that data centers demand are shaping who can compete. By experts and staff - Published - Emilyn LarsonIntern, Digital Content, Editorial Global construction of data centers is accelerating as the race to lead in AI development heats up. These facilities have the computational and physical infrastructure needed to train and run large-scale AI models, making them a critical part of countries’ efforts to drive AI expansion. However, while technology companies are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into building these facilities, countries’ approaches to their construction differ, shaped by energy supply, land availability, and economic capital. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, and communities have pushed back over concerns about rising power bills and strained resources. In response, some countries have restricted new construction, while others have taken action to fast-track projects with the goal of attracting investment. These differing approaches reflect broader uncertainty about AI proliferation. “It’s not really about energy or water so much as people’s concerns about AI,” David Hart, CFR senior fellow for climate and energy, said of the backlash to data center construction. “It’s very hard to tackle that directly because it’s a very abstract, amorphous thing, but if the data center is right there, then it’s a much easier target.” CFR unpacks what data centers are, the debate surrounding them, and how different countries and regions are approaching their development. What are data centers, what do they do, and how do they work? Data centers are large facilities filled with servers that store and process the data behind nearly everything people do online. Traditional data centers run mainly on central processing units and were built to supply roughly five to ten kilowatts of power per rack—the cabinet that holds a stack of servers. These centers use air cooling systems to prevent servers from overheating. AI data centers, however, rely mostly on graphics processing units (GPUs)—specialized processors that can run thousands of calculations simultaneously, making them well suited to building and running large-scale AI models. These systems require substantially more power: A single rack of Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72 system, for example, draws approximately 120 kilowatts per rack, equivalent to the average electricity demand of one hundred American homes. To manage the added heat, AI facilities primarily use liquid cooling systems that pipe coolant directly to the chips. AI’s growing power demands are driving a rapid consumption of electricity. Data centers consumed an estimated 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024—about 1.5 percent of all electricity consumed worldwide that year—and the International Energy Agency estimates that figure will more than double by 2030, primarily due to the increase in AI use. Much of that electricity demand is a result of how AI models are built and used. Before an AI model can be deployed, it needs to be trained, a process that involves feeding enormous amounts of data through many thousands of GPUs at once. Because these models run around the clock, AI data centers require a reliable, continuous power supply that renewables such as wind and solar alone cannot provide, causing developers to look increasingly to natural gas and nuclear energy. How many data centers are in the United States and globally? The United States has more data centers than any other country, with more than five thousand operational and planned facilities of varying sizes listed across the country, according to Data Center Map. Globally, more than 13,000 planned or operational data centers are listed across over 180 countries. Beyond the United States, these centers are clustered primarily in major European economic hubs, such as France and Germany, as well as large Asian markets such as China and India. Why do data centers use so much water? Data centers use water directly to cool their servers and indirectly through the power plants that generate their electricity. Many still rely on evaporative cooling, which requires a constant water supply because lost water cannot be immediately reused. In 2025, global data centers used almost 1.2 trillion gallons of water, according to a report [PDF] by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment, and Health—enough to meet the annual basic household water needs of more than six hundred million people in sub-Saharan Africa. AI expansion could drive water consumption much higher. By 2030, the UN report projects that AI-related water consumption could reach nearly 2.5 trillion gallons annually. Where data centers are built also matters: S&P Global estimates that 43 percent of data centers worldwide face high water stress, including 38 percent in the United States and roughly 60 percent in China. Why are data centers controversial? Concerns about AI infrastructure center on two major issues: Environmental. In addition to concerns over water usage, AI data center growth is driving up carbon emissions and increasing demand for coal and natural gas, which still power many facilities. AI-related carbon dioxide emissions could reach four hundred million tons annually by 2030—roughly what the entire United Kingdom emitted in 2025. AI’s expansion is also challenging tech companies’ climate goals. Microsoft, which has promised to become carbon negative by 2030, saw its emissions rise 25 percent in fiscal year 2025, largely because of data center development. Data centers can also pose health risks to nearby communities. artigo.texto: Transmission Corporation of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APTRANSCO) has issued a request for selection tender for setting up 1,000 MW/4,000 MWh standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) across selected substations in Andhra Pradesh on a build-own-operate basis for on-demand usage through tariff-based competitive bidding. The tender comprises two components of 500 MW/2,000 MWh each: one eligible for viability gap funding (VGF) of up to Rs 1.8 million per MWh through the Power System Development Fund and the other without VGF support. The bid submission deadline is December 14, 2026. According to the tender guidelines, the selected developers will be responsible for setting up, operating, and maintaining the BESS facilities, building dedicated 33 kV evacuation and interconnection infrastructure up to the designated APTRANSCO substations. The developer will also be responsible for installing necessary protection, control, metering, and communication systems within the BESS plant, obtaining all applicable approvals and clearances, and carrying out the operation and maintenance of all developed facilities. The tender is technologically agnostic. APTRANSCO will provide right-of-use land at an annual lease charge of Re 1 per acre per year and develop power evacuation infrastructure up to the 33 kV level. The project is required to be commissioned within 12 months of the effective date of the battery energy storage purchase agreement. Furthermore, the bidders are required to submit an earnest money deposit of Rs 800,000 per MW and a performance bank guarantee of Rs 1.6 million per MW. As per the financial eligibility criteria, the bidders must demonstrate a net worth of at least Rs 15 million per MW of quoted capacity as of the previous financial year, a positive net worth across the last three financial years and an annual turnover of at least Rs 15 million per MW in the last financial year. Under the technical criteria, the bidders must have commissioned projects over the past 10 years in any one of three categories: grid-connected BESS projects of at least 10 per cent of total quoted MW capacity, power generation projects of at least 20 per cent of total quoted MW capacity, or power transmission projects worth at least Rs 20 million per MW of total quoted capacity.

artigo.texto: [Exclusive] "Hyundai Motor-Invested" U.S. Battery Firm Sues Korean Battery Maker That Partnered With POSCO Over Patent SES AI Files Patent Infringement Lawsuit Against BEI in U.S. Court "Claims Infringement of Two Anode-Free Lithium-Metal Battery Patents" Technology Plates Lithium Metal Directly onto Current Collector Without An Anode Material... For Use in Drones a The complaint in a patent lawsuit filed by U.S. battery company SES AI against South Korean battery company BEI. View original image U.S.-based battery company SES AI has filed a lawsuit against South Korean battery company BEI, alleging that BEI infringed its patents for anode-free lithium-metal batteries. According to the battery industry on November 25, SES AI filed a patent infringement lawsuit against BEI under U.S. patent law in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on November 18. SES AI alleges that at least two products developed by BEI, including the "Maximus UL17B" and "Maximus UL20A," infringe its anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. The two patents SES AI claims were infringed are a patent on "the design and performance of a battery in which the anode capacity is lower than the cathode capacity" (U.S. Patent No. 9,887,415) and a patent on "a high-capacity battery in which a metal coating forms on the anode surface during initial charging" (U.S. Patent No. 10,727,483). Both concern anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. Images and specifications of BEI-developed batteries "MUL 17B" and "MUL 20A." Screenshot from BEI's website. View original image The patents were registered to Singapore-based Viking Power Systems Pte. Ltd., a wholly owned subsidiary of SES AI. The second patent is also registered with the Korean Intellectual Property Office as "Electrochemical Cell and Method for Manufacturing the Same" (Registration No. 1025884540000). Lithium-metal batteries, which use lithium metal instead of graphite for the anode, are lighter and have a higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, and are being developed primarily for aerial mobility applications such as drones. Anode-free lithium-metal batteries, which have recently attracted attention as a next-generation battery technology, are exactly what their name suggests: batteries without an anode material. During charging, lithium ions from the cathode combine with electrons and plate directly onto the current collector as lithium metal, thereby forming the anode. During discharge, the lithium metal loses electrons and moves back to the cathode in the form of lithium ions. The battery operates through an electrochemical process in which the anode forms and then disappears. Because anode-free lithium-metal batteries do not contain an anode material, they can have thinner cells and store more energy in the same volume. They can also simplify the manufacturing process and reduce costs. Since its establishment in 2020, BEI has manufactured batteries for drones, defense applications, and robots. In particular, the company is expanding its business, including through an MOU signed in March with POSCO Future M and Kumho Petrochemical to jointly develop anode-free lithium-metal battery technology. BEI is preparing for a KOSDAQ listing in 2028 and has selected Samsung Securities and Mirae Asset Securities as lead underwriters. Posco Future M signed an MOU with Kumho Petrochemical and BEI at the POSCO Center in Seoul on March 25 to jointly develop anode-free lithium metal battery technology. (From left) Ko Younghoon, head of Kumho Petrochemical’s Central Research Institute; Hong Youngjun, head of Posco Future M’s Technology Research Institute; and Bae Changdeuk, CEO of BEI. View original image SES AI has also recently been expanding its drone battery business. In 2021, SES AI established a lithium-metal battery production facility at its plant in Chungju, North Chungcheong Province, and is developing it into a key production base for drone batteries. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plant's annual production capacity from around 200,000 units to 1 million units by the end of 2026. In its complaint, SES AI alleged that "some of BEI's employees were former senior executives of SES AI" and that they would have been familiar with SES AI's patents. According to LinkedIn, at least four BEI employees previously worked at SES AI. SES AI's patent lawsuit appears to signal its determination to actively protect its intellectual property, as anode-free lithium-metal batteries have recently drawn attention as a next-generation battery technology. SES AI said, "SES AI has groundbreaking proprietary technology and patents that can enhance the competitiveness of military drones and drone batteries, and plans to strongly protect its intellectual property rights." It added, "If infringement is confirmed in the future, we will continue to take active steps to protect our intellectual property rights." BEI also said it would contest the matter through legal channels. BEI said, "We are currently reviewing the scope of the claims and the technical specifications of the patents in question," adding, "We are consulting with a U.S. law firm specializing in patent litigation on how to respond." artigo.texto: A Telebras, empresa estatal de telecomunicações, estima iniciar a operação de um novo data center voltado para o uso de inteligência artificial no fim de 2027. Com custo estimado de R$ 375 milhões, o projeto será financiado pela EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz. Mesmo com a liberação dos recursos, a Telebras ainda precisa definir como será mantida a operação do empreendimento. De acordo com Albuquerque, a estatal não concluiu um levantamento dos custos de manutenção, mas vem trabalhando na elaboração de um plano para que o data center comece a funcionar com geração de receita operacional. O local de construção do empreendimento também não foi definido ainda. Em entrevista ao Poder360, Albuquerque mencionou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. Fundada em 1972, a Telecomunicações Brasileiras (Telebras) é uma empresa estatal federal vinculada ao Ministério das Comunicações, sendo responsável por implementar as Políticas Públicas de Telecomunicações do Brasil. Em 2022, a Telebras registrou um receita líquida de R$ 491 milhões e um lucro líquido de R$ 140,5 milhões. Atualmente, a estatal conta com cinco data centers próprios, localizados em Brasília, Rio de Janeiro, Campo Grande, Salvador e Florianópolis.

artigo.texto: Consumo de energia – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) deve provocar um aumento de 70% nas emissões de carbono dos data centers até 2030. A projeção é da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), que relaciona o crescimento à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica para atender à demanda por processamento de dados, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na China. De acordo com o relatório anual da agência, o consumo de eletricidade dessas estruturas deve dobrar até o fim da década, em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial será responsável por aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento, devido à necessidade de maior capacidade computacional. LEIA: Jensen Huang retorna ao comando da Nvidia após suspeita de espionagem A estimativa da AIE é que os data centers voltados à IA consumam 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) adicionais de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume supera o consumo anual de energia do Reino Unido. O avanço acontece em um cenário de mudanças no setor energético mundial, que também enfrenta pressões sobre o abastecimento e precisa atender a outras necessidades, como climatização e crescimento populacional. Combustíveis fósseis devem abastecer data centers Mesmo com os investimentos de grandes empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por meio de combustíveis fósseis deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, a previsão é que aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida por essas instalações venha de usinas a carvão até 2030. A parcela restante será fornecida principalmente por fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural deve representar cerca de 60% da eletricidade destinada aos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, os projetos anunciados para novas usinas a gás vinculadas a essas estruturas somavam aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, número próximo ao de toda a geração a gás atualmente disponível na União Europeia. Infraestrutura mundial cresce com avanço da IA O levantamento da AIE também aponta uma rápida expansão da capacidade global de data centers. Nos últimos dois anos, o indicador aumentou dez vezes, chegando a 17 GW. Com os projetos que estão em construção, a expectativa é alcançar aproximadamente 50 GW. Atualmente, a capacidade instalada mundial é de 120 GW. Outros 120 GW devem ser acrescentados até 2030, sendo que três quartos dessa expansão serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial. Read More The European Union and the UK concluded negotiations on linking their emissions trading systems (ETS) at a summit in Brussels last Friday, taking a step toward closer cooperation more than 6 years after Brexit. While many actors in the European chemical industry see the pact as an opportunity, others, including the big UK chemical maker Ineos, fear it could add to their financial burdens. The two sides aim to apply the agreement on Jan. 1, 2028. Chemical industry associations on both sides of the English Channel welcome the prospect of shared ETS, which are market-based mechanisms that cap the total volume of greenhouse gas emissions and let companies buy and sell emission allowances. The goal is to create a financial incentive to lower emissions by investing in decarbonization.

artigo.texto: Moment Energy has unveiled Nova, a battery energy storage system (BESS) built using repurposed electric vehicle batteries and designed for commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications across North America. The company said Nova is the first BESS based on second-life EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. Production is already underway at Moment Energy’s Megafactory 1, with the system intended to help customers lower energy costs, improve reliability and integrate renewable energy into their operations. Second-Life Batteries for Energy Storage Nova has been developed around a flexible architecture capable of integrating batteries from multiple EV platforms. The system uses the company’s AI-powered battery management system (BMS), which continuously evaluates batteries in different states of health to optimise performance, efficiency and reliability throughout their operational life. Each Nova unit delivers 200kW of power and 500kWh of energy within a footprint measuring 2.94m by 1.80m. The scalable design is intended for space-constrained commercial sites while also supporting larger installations reaching tens of megawatt-hours. A key feature of the platform is its swappable battery architecture. Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age rather than requiring the entire energy storage system to be removed. Moment Energy said this approach can extend operational life beyond 20 years when combined with its capacity augmentation service. North American Supply Chain Focus The company said Nova is manufactured in North America and has been independently verified as compliant with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. Moment Energy has also been verified as a non-Prohibited Foreign Entity. According to the company, repurposing retired EV batteries creates a domestic battery supply chain while helping retain the value of batteries beyond their automotive use. The approach also supports circular economy objectives by extending battery lifetimes before recycling. Edward Chiang, Co-Founder and CEO of Moment Energy, said: “We see a future where reengineered EV batteries become essential infrastructure for powering businesses and onshoring manufacturing and supply chain. Nova brings that vision to life, combining safety, engineering and North American manufacturing to deploy what we believe are the safest and highest-performance batteries ever made: EV batteries to supercharge our aging grid.” Safety Certifications and Commercial Deployment Nova has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification and has also been tested to UL 9540A standards for thermal runaway fire propagation. Megafactory 1 is certified to UL 1974, covering the sorting, grading and repurposing of electric vehicle batteries. The system incorporates liquid cooling, smoke, heat and flammable gas detection, as well as an integrated deflagration prevention system. Additional features include a Type 3R enclosure, operation across temperatures from -25°C to 50°C, and compatibility with grid-tied, grid-forming and virtual synchronous generator operating modes. Moment Energy said first deliveries are planned for the first quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: City staff estimate a 50 megawatt data center would use as much electricity as 25,000 new homes. San Francisco’s moratorium on new data centers has been extended to next fall, Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office said Tuesday. In extending the moratorium, San Francisco — like Oakland and Seattle — is giving city staff more time to study data centers and their impacts. “We will continue listening to our communities and labor partners, collaborating across city government, and drawing on the best available data to develop a policy that keeps electricity rates low, protects the clean water and air our residents deserve, and supports the technology infrastructure our hospitals, universities, and government rely on,” Lurie said in a statement. The Board of Supervisors last week unanimously approved an extension to the zoning moratorium until September. Lurie signed the moratorium Monday, his office said. Although the Planning Department shared some of its findings with the public in a report two weeks ago, it was only an initial assessment identifying areas needing more research. That includes understanding how many data centers there are citywide — besides three “standalone” facilities — as well as how much water they use. The initial report did have some clarity, though. It found that San Francisco’s electricity transmission is near capacity and that data centers would be competing with other developments that also need electricity, including housing. The report estimated that a 50 megawatt data center in San Francisco would demand the same electricity as 25,000 new homes. Additionally, two of the three “standalone” data centers in San Francisco identified by city staff are in the Bayview, and one of them has “five active notices of violation” issued this year by the Bay Area Air District over diesel-powered generators out of compliance with permit conditions, operating with expired permits, and exceeding run-time limits of 35 hours. Southeast San Francisco, with its industrial zoning, has been identified as a part of the city that faces environmental burdens and elevated levels of air pollution. The initial 45-day moratorium, as well as the extension (opens in new tab), were proposed by Supervisor Shamann Walton. He terms out in January, making his efforts to curb and study data centers among his final actions as supervisor. He will be replaced on the board by Theo Ellington. While campaigning, Ellington endorsed the idea of a data center moratorium specifically for District 10, which stretches from Dogpatch and Potrero Hill to the Bayview and Visitacion Valley. Land in District 10 has been the subject of speculation. The lobbyist for a private equity firm known for developing data centers met with city officials in August about building and planning permits for a big plot of land in Dogpatch. The moratorium doesn’t allow for the city to process building or planning permits to establish new data centers. Right now, there are no such applications before the city’s Planning Department. “The absence of pending applications is not a reason to let the moratorium expire,” Walton said at a Nov. 16 committee meeting. “The city must proactively evaluate future development and its potential impacts.” More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: Rolling Meadows approves data center tax incentive for development over residents' objections The Rolling Meadows City Council approved support for the county to give a data center a tax incentive to develop land, despite passionate opposition from residents at their meeting Tuesday night. The meeting exemplified the different approaches Chicago suburbs are taking different to the data center dilemma, with one facing opposition to a project while another welcomes the developments. In Rolling Meadows, neighbors brought signs and packed city chambers as its city council weighed bringing in a data center. A former office space that sits on 40 acres off the tollway on Route 53 has been vacant for years, and that's where the Rolling Meadows data center would end up if approved. But residents raised many questions at Tuesday night's meeting, including the impact to nearby Bussey Woods and its wildlife. But the biggest concern is about nearby homes. "To also state the nearest home is 2,000 feet away is also a huge dismissal," one resident told the council at the meeting. "Two thousand feet isn't far." Residents are worried about the noise, environmental issues both known and unknown, and what a data center could do to the community. Most of the residents in attendance said they believed they should have a vote and a voice in whether the data center is built. While the vast majority wanted the Rolling Meadows City Council to vote against the project, some in the room showed support, saying they would bring jobs and economic benefits. Other communities are not willing to close the door completely to data centers. In Zion on the North Shore, Mayor Billy McKinney said nothing is off the table. He pointed out the village was approached previously about a data center but that deal lacked vision. "I want to make this point, being cautious does not mean that we are opposed to progress. That is the big key," he said. "The plan was so inconclusive, and it raised more questions." McKinney said he understands community concerns, but is not willing to implement a data center ban. "But also know that whatever decision we make, it has to protect our community and future generations," he said. In the end, the Rolling Meadows City Council voted four-two to approve their support for the county giving a tax incentive to develop the land with a data center.

artigo.texto: The growing demand for electric vehicles, renewable energy storage and reliable power backup solutions has increased the importance of battery manufacturing in India. From automotive batteries used in conventional vehicles to advanced lithium-ion systems powering electric scooters, cars and industrial equipment, battery manufacturers play an important role in the country’s energy and mobility ecosystem. As the country moves towards domestic battery manufacturing, companies are expanding their capabilities across battery cells, packs, energy storage systems and recycling. Here is a look at some of the leading battery manufacturing companies in India, their products and their presence across different battery segments. Top Battery Manufacturing Companies in India: Quick Overview These companies operate across different parts of the battery value chain. Their manufacturing capabilities, technology and target applications vary. 1. Exide Industries Founded in 1947, Exide Industries is one of India’s most established battery manufacturers. The company has a significant presence in automotive, industrial and stationary energy storage markets. Its product portfolio includes automotive batteries for two-wheelers and four-wheelers, industrial batteries, inverter batteries and energy storage solutions. Exide also operates multiple manufacturing facilities across India and serves both original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and replacement markets. The company is expanding into lithium-ion battery manufacturing through its wholly owned subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions Limited (EESL). Its planned lithium-ion manufacturing ecosystem includes a cell manufacturing facility in Bengaluru and battery module and pack manufacturing capabilities at Prantij, Gujarat. According to its FY2025-26 annual report, the Bengaluru cell facility progressed through installation, process validation and customer sampling activities. This investment reflects Exide’s strategy to expand beyond conventional lead-acid batteries and participate in India’s growing electric mobility and energy storage markets. 2. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is another major name among Indian battery manufacturers. The company operates under the Amara Raja Group and is widely recognised for its automotive battery brand, Amaron. Its business includes automotive batteries, industrial energy storage, UPS batteries and advanced lithium-ion battery solutions. The company’s lithium-ion expansion is being undertaken through its Giga Corridor project in Telangana. In July 2026, Amara Raja commissioned a Customer Qualification Plant for lithium-ion cells with an investment of approximately ₹500 crore. The facility supports the development and qualification of different cell formats and chemistries. The company has targeted commercial-scale cell production beginning in 2027. artigo.texto: Virginia data center deals face transparency tests BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - From Botetourt County to Northern Virginia, fights over how local governments approve data center projects are playing out in court. In Botetourt, one such challenge has brought construction on Google’s data center to a halt. The cases involve different projects and different alleged violations, but they raise a common question: Did local governments give the public the access and notice required by law before making decisions? Megan Rhyne, executive director of the Virginia Coalition for Open Government, said challenges to government decisions have focused on alleged Freedom of Information Act and public notice violations. “There already are lawsuits around the state that are trying to change this, change decisions based on either FOIA violations or public notice violations,” Rhyne said. “Most well known is up in Prince William County.” A public notice case in Northern Virginia In Prince William County, a court threw out rezonings for the Digital Gateway data center project after finding that the county had not properly advertised the public hearing. The Court of Appeals upheld that ruling, and the last developer pursuing an appeal later dropped it. Rhyne said transparency rules apply regardless of what a government decides. “These rules of transparency exist no matter what the decision is,” she said. “All decisions that the government made have to follow these procedures and these rules.” In Botetourt, a judge found that supervisors agreed to the Google data center deal behind closed doors and then failed to adequately identify it when they voted in public. Court records say the Board of Supervisors discussed a performance agreement with Google in closed session in June 2025, then returned to open session and approved what board members called “walk-on item number one.” Google’s announcement followed the vote. The judge voided the initial action on procedural grounds and ordered new construction to stop. Crews had begun grading the site and moving dirt in September. Rhyne said the violation affected the public’s ability to see its government make decisions. “This technical violation has resulted in undermining the very thing that FOIA is supposed to protect, which is their access, the public’s right to see their government making its decisions that impact them,” she said. On Tuesday, the Board of Supervisors took action to stop items related to Google’s investments, including a museum and library renovations, while the county evaluates its next steps. The agreement also included investments in first responder equipment and athletic infrastructure; some projects have already been completed. Questions about another project Tim Dooley, the attorney who represented the plaintiff in the Botetourt case, said the ruling raises questions about the process used for another data center project at Wood Haven in Roanoke County. “I think if you scrutinize the process the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority, the process they used, you’ll see some striking similarities between that and what happened in Botetourt,” Dooley said. Rhyne said the Botetourt ruling is not binding on other judges, although they could look to it for guidance in future cases. Botetourt County could appeal. The judge also said the board could hold a new public hearing that follows the law. Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Polarium Energy Solutions AB has been declared bankrupt by the Stockholm District Court The company more than halved operating expenses since 2024 but remained under financial pressure Chairman Harald Mix is exploring a potential acquisition by his private investment company Mounting financial pressures have forced Swedish battery energy storage company Polarium Energy Solutions AB into bankruptcy. The Stockholm District Court declared bankruptcy after the company concluded that it could not continue operating in its current form. The company attributed its bankruptcy to several factors, including sharply declining battery prices amid growing competition from Chinese suppliers, reduced investments by telecom operators and tower companies, and delays in some distributed BESS development projects. Overcapacity from the Chinese suppliers and a shift to cheaper battery chemistry is pushing down prices for every player in the supply chain leading to sharply lower gross margins. “Like the auto industry, several European battery and energy storage companies have been hit hard by the dramatic increase in competition from Chinese players, and a number of European manufacturers have been forced to file for bankruptcy or restructure financially,” said Harald Mix, Chairman of Polarium. Morrow Batteries and sonnen are some of the European battery companies to have walked the same path (see Germany’s sonnen GmbH Faces Insolvency As US Business Expands and Europe’s Morrow Batteries Files For Bankruptcy). Earlier another Swedish battery manufacturer Northvolt filed for bankruptcy. Its recycling patents were acquired by Refinyx (see Refinyx Acquires Northvolt’s 134 Battery Recycling Patents). These developments, explains Polarium, weakened its financial position despite efforts to reduce costs and restructure its operations. The company claims it had more than halved its operating expenses since 2024, but demand remains “too low relative to costs” leading to an unstainable financial situation. It also made changes to its strategy, business model and organizational structure in an effort to improve profitability. The company had explored options to secure its future, including finding a buyer for all or parts of the business and a court-supervised reorganization, but concluded that bankruptcy was the only remaining option. Polarium’s bankruptcy follows a strategic transformation initiated in 2025. In August 2026, Polarium announced a sharper focus on telecom power solutions and distributed energy storage, areas it identified as having stronger growth and profitability potential. The company also sought to reduce costs, improve margins, strengthen its presence in local markets and move closer to key suppliers. As part of the transformation, Polarium reported that its 2025 net sales declined to SEK 896 million from SEK 1.332 billion in 2024. However, gross profit improved to SEK 114 million from a loss of SEK 46 million, while its EBITDA loss narrowed to SEK 61 million from SEK 270 million. The decision to file for bankruptcy follows the October 1, 2026 appointment of company EVP and Head of the Residential and C&I business segments Pontus Winberg as Polarium’s new CEO. Winberg succeeded Leif Ottosson who retired after leading the transformation and strategic renewal of Polarium. Polarium Chairman Harald Mix said he intends to engage with the bankruptcy trustee to explore whether parts of the business can continue. He has also indicated that he is prepared to consider financing a potential acquisition by his private investment company. According to the company’s announcement, the bankruptcy trustee, Mikael Kubu of Ackordscentralen, has now taken over the company and will determine how its assets and business will be handled, including the possibility of a sale and continued operations.

artigo.texto: By Andrew Blakers, Australian National University The final cost estimate for Snowy 2.0 has been released. The conversion of the original Snowy hydroelectric scheme to a large pumped hydro energy storage scheme will cost A$22-25 billion and will be completed in late 2029. Much media coverage has focused on the major blowouts in cost and time. When the scheme was announced in 2017, then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull gave a rough costing of just $2 billion – extremely low for a project this size – and said it could be finished in four years. Engineering issues, stalled tunnelling machines and surging costs of construction all contributed to the blowouts. The project has endured a remarkable amount of negative press, including from renewable energy advocates. Some of it is warranted – early cost estimates were overly optimistic. Some is debatable, such as claims it won’t work as advertised. But let’s zoom out. Snowy 2.0 is about 80% done. It will likely be finished within three years. Once up and running, it will convert the original Snowy scheme into a giant rechargeable battery, able to back up solar and wind overnight and during calm and cloudy weather. It will arrive in time to allow ageing coal plants to retire. Once up and running, it will last 150 years. $22 billion sounds like a lot – but it translates to about $5 per Australian per year of operation. As more and more renewables enter Australia’s power grids, we will need much more energy storage. Building grid-scale batteries with the same energy storage as Snowy 2.0 would cost three times more than the final cost ($22 billion). But batteries last 20 years, while Snowy 2.0 will last for 150 years. Why do we need so much energy storage? Renewables currently provide about 50% of the power in the National Electricity Market, Australia’s largest power grid. The government’s target is 82% by 2030 (mostly solar and wind). Reaching this goal will require much more storage. That’s because over half the demand for electricity is overnight (defined as 4pm to 8am). During these hours, solar output is minimal or nonexistent. Wind provides some power, but not enough. Coal plants currently meet most of the overnight demand. But Australia’s coal fleet is ageing rapidly and will not be replaced. Almost all will close over the next ten years. How can we keep the lights on overnight as coal exits? We can use wind (which is intermittent), gas (expensive and responsible for high emissions), or store energy for use overnight and on cloudy days. Energy storage has shot to prominence in recent years, driven by rapid falls in battery costs. Home batteries and battery-electric vehicles are surging in popularity for consumers. In the grid, batteries are muscling in and taking a role once occupied by gas-powered plants to cover short spikes in demand. Because batteries can do this job more cheaply than gas, electricity costs are falling for everyone, not just the owners of batteries. So why do we need pumped hydro? Batteries are an increasingly cheap way to store energy short term, meaning minutes to hours. But they’re an expensive way to cover longer periods, such as overnight and during cloudy days. This is where pumped hydro can help. Pumped hydro turns a normal hydroelectric plant into a giant water battery. When power prices are low, water is pumped uphill to a high reservoir. When power prices rise, water is run downhill through turbines to produce power. These schemes excel at long-duration storage, as very large volumes of water can be kept in dams and released as needed. Every year, Australia’s science agency, CSIRO, releases GenCost, an update on changes to the costs for all components of the clean energy transition. The latest figures show pumped hydro can store and release power much more cheaply than batteries can. The cost advantage is highest now, but it will still be there in ten and 20 years time. That’s because the steep falls in battery costs are expected to taper off. Pumped hydro typically lasts five to ten times longer than batteries. Keeping water behind a rocky dam is an extremely cheap and durable way to store energy long term compared to extracting metals to make batteries. Pumped hydro also stimulates the local economy more, compared to imported batteries. Time to take a longer view Once up and running, Snowy 2.0 will roughly quadruple Australia’s total rechargeable electricity storage. Behind the 45-metre high wall of its upper reservoir, Tantangara, is up to 254 gigalitres of water. That’s about 50% of the water in Sydney Harbour (500GL). This enormous volume of water represents 350 gigawatt-hours of storage – the equivalent of the energy available in the batteries of seven million electric vehicles. To stop climate change from worsening, we have to stop burning fossil fuels. To do that, we have to triple or quadruple how much electricity we produce so that we can electrify transport, heating, industry and other sectors. Almost all of this new electricity will come from solar and wind. We will also need large-scale energy storage so renewable power can be released at night or as needed. Energy storage is becoming a solved problem. Batteries and pumped hydro can do the job of storing power over shorter and longer periods. As electrification gathers pace, Australia will need more pumped hydro projects – some as large as Snowy 2.0. The good news is that the technical issues and tunnelling problems Snowy 2.0 has faced have taught us a great deal about how to overcome them. The key challenge the engineers of Snowy 2.0 faced is the need for a 27-kilometre-long tunnel. Australia has hundreds of excellent options for off-river pumped hydro sites between Brisbane and Melbourne, located close to transmission lines and away from national parks and rivers. artigo.texto: As the data center boom draws intense backlash across Pennsylvania, the state’s consumer advocate wants to ensure existing customers aren’t saddled with higher costs and increased risk of outages. In a legal complaint filed with the Public Utility Commission in October, the consumer advocate argues that PPL Electric Utilities’ rules don’t adequately protect customers from the potential negative consequences of data centers connecting to the grid. There’s already broad agreement among government officials that data centers should pay for the extra costs they cause and bear the risk of reliability problems if the grid becomes overwhelmed, the complaint says. Major tech companies and utilities, including PPL, have publicly committed to following these principles. But the legally binding rules that cover how the company sets prices and delivers power don’t fully reflect those aims, the consumer advocate argues. “We just want to make sure these pledges and promises actually have teeth to them,” said Consumer Advocate Darryl Lawrence. “What we’re trying to do is get this enshrined in regulation.” PPL has forecast more demand from data centers than any other electric company in Pennsylvania, according to the complaint. “This is going to be the case that should pretty much set the guiding principles for everyone else,” Lawrence said. One indicator of the proceeding’s significance is that Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office has filed to intervene as a party in the case. It’s been at least 15 years since the governor has taken that step in a utility proceeding. Intervening in the case gives the Democratic governor another avenue to set the terms for data center development and its impact on residents. In August, Shapiro signed an executive order incentivizing data center developers to meet certain standards, including securing their own supply of electricity and paying the full cost of grid upgrades necessary to serve them. The case is progressing as state and federal officials weigh legislation and regulations. Regulators are grappling with the new challenges posed by data centers in the face of widespread public opposition. “There is a level of bipartisan consensus on the idea that Grandma should not be subsidizing Big Tech’s electricity bill that I don’t see in any other facet of American life,” said Abe Silverman, an energy researcher at Johns Hopkins University. Even with residents, elected officials and utilities agreeing on the wider issues cited in the consumer advocate’s complaint, disputes could still surface as details are hashed out. There are different ways to define the costs at issue, legal filings show. Anticipated demand from data centers has already driven up electricity bills across Pennsylvania, after record price spikes at the auctions where utilities secure their power supply. Going forward, the consumer advocate wants data centers to shoulder more of those costs. PPL agreed to some changes around data centers, including long-term contracts and exit fees, as part of a settlement in its most recent rate case that state regulators approved in June. More recently, the company also proposed a plan to insulate existing customers from transmission costs associated with data centers. The consumer advocate argues that neither effort goes far enough. In a statement, a PPL spokesperson said the company is “committed to protecting customers, maintaining reliability and ensuring that large-load customers pay the costs associated with their projects.” The case, which will include public hearings as well as extensive testimony, is still in its early stages. A final decision from the utility commission is not due until next July. A new paradigm Data centers need massive amounts of power, consuming as much as thousands or even millions of homes. To accommodate the extra demand, utilities must spend millions of dollars upgrading their networks. Data centers use so much electricity and want to connect to the grid so quickly that they upend old assumptions about how to share those costs fairly, experts told Spotlight PA. For instance, utilities typically spread the cost of upgrading transmission lines — which transport electricity across long distances — across all their customers, because everyone benefits from a more reliable system. In guidance issued in May, however, state regulators concluded that data centers require a different approach. If network upgrades would not have been necessary “but for” the interconnection of a data center, the utility commission concluded, the data center should pay for them — even if other customers also benefit. In some cases, it’s straightforward to determine which costs have been triggered by a data center; in others, it can quickly become complicated, said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. Even with a “but for” standard in place, “it will be up to the regulator to decide what that standard means,” he said. Most electric utilities haven’t yet indicated how or whether they will adopt the commission’s recommendations, which are not binding. PPL’s current rules — updated as part of a settlement negotiated before the guidelines were finalized — still allow other customers to share increased transmission costs caused by data centers, the consumer advocate says. The complaint cites a planned transmission line in Luzerne County that’s needed to serve a potential data center campus. The project drew national attention after the developer offered residents $10,000 payments if the data center were built. The planned transmission upgrades will cost about $178 million, legal filings show. PPL plans to recover only 12% of that from the data center itself — “the cost causer and the primary beneficiary of the network upgrades,” the consumer advocate’s complaint says. artigo.texto: Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. has said that there will be no data centers located at development sites associated with the Pax Silica initiative, which aims to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains for rare earth materials, semiconductors, and other AI infrastructure components. As reported by the state-run Philippine News Agency, President Marcos Jr. said that his government had yet to finalize any agreement under Pax Silica and that no specific provisions had been discussed or signed. “There will be no data centers in the place that we are going to put this development on AI. It’s AI-centered,” President Marcos Jr. said. “We have yet to discuss anything. We have not signed anything yet.” As w.media has previously reported, the Pax Silica hub planned for New Clark City would serve as an AI-focused investment zone that would support manufacturing and supply chains for semiconductors and other technologies. The president described the initiative as an opportunity for the Philippines to take part in the global discussion on artificial intelligence. However, critics and affected communities have raised concerns about what the development will mean for national sovereignty, the environment, community displacement, indigenous land rights, and human security. At least 24 anti-Pax Silica protests have broken out since April 22, 2026, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) project, which monitors political violence and protests worldwide. Protests came to a head last week when US President Donald Trump visited Manila to discuss artificial intelligence and more with President Marcos Jr. As many as 20,000 security personnel were deployed in response to the unrest, and access to several areas of the capital were restricted. “Hundreds were arrested after authorities had heated confrontations with demonstrators. Students, farmers, and Indigenous people in danger of being displaced by technological advances agreed under Pax Silica, tried to approach the main venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit at the Philippine International Convention Center in Manila,” said Tomas Buenaventura, Asia-Pacific analyst at ACLED. “Pax Silica spans over 20 countries, but the Philippines is slated to play a special role, with the project’s first industrial hub set to occupy a 1,600-hectare site in Tarlac province in Luzon, on the ancestral lands of the indigenous Ayta people,” Buenaventura explained. Last week, two AI-related defense deals worth a combined US$ 100 million were announced during President Trump’s visit. The Philippine Department of National Defense (DND) announced a US$ 37 million contract with a US firm to deliver AI-enabled mission support, expanding defense cooperation and interoperability between the two countries. The DND also committed to work with US providers on a US$ 63 million initiative to modernize its defense cloud infrastructure for AI use cases. The deals are not related to Pax Silica.

artigo.texto: AI has turned data centers into one of the fastest-growing electricity users on the planet. In its Energy and AI report, the IEA estimates that data centers used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of the world’s electricity. In its Base Case, this becomes about 945 TWh by 2030 and about 1,200 TWh by 2035. In the US, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory counted 176 TWh in 2023, 4.4% of the country’s electricity, and expects 325 to 580 TWh by 2028. That would be 6.7% to 12% of all US electricity. Every one of those kilowatt-hours goes through power supplies before it reaches a chip, usually more than one. So here is a question I keep asking: who checks how efficient those power supplies really are? The honest answer is the manufacturer itself, or a voluntary label it chose to apply for. As far as I can find, no law anywhere requires an independent lab to verify the efficiency of a data center PSU. Someone buying an 850 W PSU for a gaming PC has more independent efficiency data to choose from than an operator buying thousands of server modules that run 24/7. Before I go further, you should know where I stand. I run HWBusters and the Cybenetics lab, and Cybenetics would gain from what I propose here, because we test and certify power supplies for a living. Keep that in mind and check my sources. Every number below is linked. Where the power goes In a typical data center, electricity from the grid passes through a transformer, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), and power distribution units (PDUs). Then the server PSU, or a power shelf that feeds a whole rack, converts it to a low DC voltage, and converters on the board step it down again for the CPU or GPU. Every step loses a little. The server PSU is the one stage that every server has, and it never switches off. The diagram shows the uncomfortable part. Transformers have mandatory EU efficiency rules. The UPS has only voluntary programs. The server PSU has a minimum in the EU that the manufacturer declares itself, and nothing mandatory in the US. DC and high-voltage DC (HVDC) supplies, where the industry is heading, have no rules at all. What the rules already do Credit where it is due. The EU has had minimum efficiency rules for server PSUs since 2020, in Regulation (EU) 2019/424. Since 1 January 2023, a single-output server PSU must reach 90% efficiency at 10% load, 94% at 20%, 96% at 50% and 91% at 100%, with a power factor of at least 0.95 at half load. Multi-output units need 90%, 94% and 91% at 20%, 50% and 100% load. Those are demanding numbers. Three details matter, though. Compliance is self-declared under CE marking, so no independent lab has to confirm the numbers before a product goes on sale. The PSU limits exclude DC-powered servers. And the regulation exempts several server types, including servers with more than four processor sockets, large servers, fully fault-tolerant servers and network servers. The Commission was supposed to review the regulation by March 2022. More than four and a half years later, its own website still lists it as “under review”. In the US, I could not find any federal minimum for server power supplies. ENERGY STAR includes PSU efficiency and power factor tables in its Computer Servers v4.0 specification, and it requires independent certification: an EPA-recognized certification body accredited to ISO/IEC 17065 by an IAF MLA signatory, using data from an ISO/IEC 17025 lab. That is the right model. The catch is that it is voluntary, and it nearly disappeared. The administration’s FY2026 budget request zeroed the program, and Congress restored full funding in a law signed on 23 January 2026, with votes of 397-28 in the House and 82-15 in the Senate. In March 2026, EPA and DOE signed an agreement that makes DOE the lead agency. Then there is 80 PLUS, run by CLEAResult. It is voluntary too, but it has categories for 230 V, 277 V, 480 V, and 380 V DC redundant data center PSUs, and a new Ruby level that CLEAResult describes as ultimate efficiency for AI data centers. I found no 800 V DC category. Its test method comes from the EPRI/Ecova Generalized Internal Power Supply Efficiency Test Protocol, which checks a handful of fixed load points. China went another way. Its GB 43630-2023 standard sets mandatory efficiency limits and grades for tower and rack servers, and servers now need a China energy label. But it rates the whole server with a benchmark; it does not test the PSU on its own, and it covers general-purpose one- and two-socket machines. Blade, multi-node, full-cabinet and HPC systems are left out. Facility rules are moving faster. Germany’s Energy Efficiency Act requires new data centers that start operating from 1 July 2026 to reach a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.2 or better, with limits of 1.5 from July 2027 and 1.3 from July 2030 for existing sites, although an amendment that may relax them is being debated. In the EU, data centers with at least 500 kW of IT power already report their energy performance, and on 21 September 2026 the Commission adopted an A to G rating and label based on PUE, water use and other indicators. The first labels are expected in 2027. Three blind spots The first is the metric itself. PUE, defined in ISO/IEC 30134-2, divides the total energy of the facility by the energy of the IT equipment. The PSU is part of the IT equipment. So a watt wasted inside a server PSU counts as IT energy, exactly like a watt spent on computing. PUE tells you how efficient the building is. It cannot tell you how much your power supplies waste, and neither can a label based on it. The second is how efficiency is measured. The EU rule and 80 PLUS check a few fixed load points. That is fine as a minimum, but redundant PSUs share the load with a partner module, so they can spend long periods at light load, and nothing below 10% load is checked at all. In our redundant server PSU protocol, we apply more than 1,450 load combinations from 2% to 100% of the operating range in a hotbox

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT COUNTY, Va. – Construction on Google’s planned data center campus in Botetourt County has been halted following a circuit court judge’s ruling Monday evening, a decision that some residents are celebrating as a victory for transparency and government accountability. The ruling has drawn praise from residents who have opposed the project since its inception. “He (plaintiff Robert Dallas) basically gave Google a black eye. He hit a giant in the face and knocked him down. So that’s something important,” said Chad Bean, a Botetourt County resident. The decision comes after county resident Robert Dallas sued Botetourt County and a company associated with Google, arguing that county officials failed to adequately disclose that they were voting on the project’s performance agreement during a June 2025 meeting. Transparency has been a central concern among opponents of the project. “FOIA does matter. And we showed that. There is a desperate need for transparency with the county,” Bean said. The judge’s ruling halts construction, voids the performance agreement and rescinds all actions taken on the data center since the June 2025 meeting. The decision creates new complications for the county and Google, as construction has already begun and money has changed hands. Dr. Mac Scothorn, chair of the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors, provided an update on the project during a regularly scheduled board of supervisors meeting Tuesday. “The county is reviewing the ruling carefully with our legal counsel. Construction activities will be minimal for destabilization into the holidays to ensure this site is in compliance with the permits,” Scothorn said. Google also responded to the ruling Tuesday, saying their considering their options moving forward. “We are evaluating yesterday’s ruling by the court. We remain committed to working transparently with Botetourt County and the community in full compliance with all legal and regulatory requirements,” a company spokesperson wrote. While many celebrate, Botetourt County resident Danny Goad says this isn’t the end of the fight. “I think over the next three or four weeks, you’re going to see many things come out of the groups that oppose this. We want the people’s voice to be heard,” Goad said. The ruling does not necessarily mean the data center project is dead. The county could move forward by holding a public hearing and taking another vote on the performance agreement.

artigo.texto: Regulating carbon emissions is complex. Digital tools developed through Imperial Consultants will help Malaysia's policymakers decide how to establish the country's first emissions trading system. Malaysia is preparing to introduce a domestic carbon emissions trading system (ETS) as a way of persuading its companies to reduce the amount of greenhouse gases they produce. Researchers at Imperial College London, working through Imperial Consultants, are supporting that process with two digital tools that will help regulators and businesses see how the new scheme might play out once it is in operation. Climate policy is becoming a data challenge as much as a policy-design challenge. Dr Gbemi Oluleye Centre for Environmental Policy "Climate policy is becoming a data challenge as much as a policy-design challenge," says Dr Gbemi Oluleye of the Centre for Environmental Policy, who led the Imperial team. "Governments need to assess thousands of installations, firms and products while understanding implications for emissions coverage, revenues, trade exposure and regulated entities." These questions operate at different scales but are increasingly interconnected. "Digital tools can help shift policymaking from policy evidence to policy intelligence. They enable policymakers to identify exposure, compare policy configurations, test decisions under uncertainty and connect policy domains supporting the design, operationalisation and institutionalisation of market-based solutions." Emissions trading systems are among a range of market-based solutions that use prices, markets and financial incentives to encourage emission reductions, while giving businesses flexibility over how, where and when they decarbonise. Under an ETS, the government sets a limit (or cap) on the total emissions permitted from covered activities, typically reducing this cap over time. Emissions allowances are then allocated to companies, either free of charge or through auctions. Each allowance generally represents permission to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. Companies must surrender sufficient allowances to cover their verified emissions. Those that reduce their emissions below their allowance holdings can sell their surplus allowances to companies that need additional allowances, for example because reducing emissions from their activities is more technologically challenging or costly. This creates a financial incentive to reduce emissions while ensuring that total emissions remain within the cap. Some ETS regimes also allow companies to use carbon credits generated through eligible projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gases, such as afforestation or certain carbon capture and storage activities. These projects may be located domestically or internationally, depending on the rules of the scheme. Tools for policymakers The first tool that Imperial's researchers helped develop is an ETS Threshold Calculator. This enables users to explore how different emissions thresholds influence the design and coverage of an ETS, including the installations covered, emissions brought within the scheme, administrative burden and potential revenue from auctioning carbon credits. "Higher thresholds can reduce administrative burden, but may lower emissions coverage and auction revenues," Dr Oluleye explains. "Lower thresholds increase coverage but can bring more small emitters into the system for limited additional benefit. The ETS Threshold Calculator enables policymakers to explore these trade-offs by testing different thresholds and sector combinations and examining their implications for coverage, regulated entities and indicative revenues." The second tool addresses an international aspect of carbon emissions, since any national approach to the issue will also be affected by what neighbouring countries and significant trading partners have decided to do. For example, the European Union has operated an ETS since 2005, with increasingly ambitious carbon reduction targets. This has driven up the cost of emitting carbon within the bloc, giving companies an incentive to move carbon-intensive production elsewhere. To address this risk of "carbon leakage" the EU has created a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which makes importers pay a tariff on the carbon emitted during the production of goods outside the EU. Regardless of whether emissions have leaked from the EU or not, this exposes countries such as Malaysia to additional costs on their exports to Europe. So, the Imperial team developed a CBAM Viability and Liability Assessment Tool, which integrates trade information with relevant EU methodologies to help users estimate potential exposure, embedded emissions and carbon-related liabilities. It does this across all relevant product codes within the six CBAM sectors (iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity) and allows users to incorporate verified company-specific emissions data for more accurate, tailored analysis. Digital tools are not intended to replace policymaker judgement. Instead, they create an interactive policy laboratory, making the consequences of different assumptions and decisions more visible. Dr Gbemi Oluleye Centre for Environmental Policy "Our Malaysia assessment estimated approximately 2.56 million tonnes of embedded CO₂ across assessed CBAM-covered exports, with aluminium accounting for around 87%," Dr Oluleye says. Wider analysis also identified substantial exposure elsewhere, with Russia and China recording the highest estimated EU CBAM liabilities. "Exposure therefore varies considerably across countries, sectors and products. Understanding where exposure lies, why it arises and how different policy choices could change it requires moving beyond static analysis towards interactive decision-support tools." The tools were developed with Muhamad Humam Safi'i and Dr Daniel Cristiu, with broader support at Imperial from Dr Raúl Rosales and Dr Danny Pudjianto. The work

artigo.texto: Brasil disputa liderança em data centers, diz Economist O Brasil está em uma disputa acirrada para se tornar um dos principais destinos globais de investimentos em data centers, segundo reportagem da revista britânica The Economist. O país aposta em sua matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável e em um mercado digital em rápida expansão para atrair gigantes da tecnologia. A expansão mundial da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial abre uma janela de oportunidade que o governo e o setor privado tentam aproveitar. América Latina ainda tem participação modesta A América Latina reúne menos de 600 data centers, com capacidade total próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW), volume inferior ao do Reino Unido, conforme dados citados pela revista. O Brasil, sozinho, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030, um salto expressivo que reflete o potencial de crescimento do setor. Esse cenário coloca o país em posição de destaque na região, mas ainda distante dos líderes mundiais. A transição para uma economia digital mais intensiva em dados exige investimentos robustos em infraestrutura, e o Brasil busca se posicionar como alternativa competitiva. Energia limpa é trunfo brasileiro Um dos principais atrativos do Brasil é a sua matriz elétrica: cerca de 85% da eletricidade vem de fontes renováveis. Para um setor que demanda volumes enormes de energia para manter servidores em operação contínua, a disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial competitivo relevante. Além disso, o custo de construção pode favorecer países latino-americanos: um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend estima que erguer um data center no Vale do Silício custa cerca de US$ 14 por watt, enquanto na América Latina os valores variam de US$ 11,50 no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. Essa vantagem de custo, somada à energia renovável, torna o Brasil uma opção atraente para empresas que buscam reduzir despesas e cumprir metas ambientais. A combinação de fatores pode acelerar a chegada de novos empreendimentos ao território nacional. Latência impulsiona demanda por proximidade O crescimento do consumo digital na região também é um motor importante: quase 80% da população latino-americana já utiliza a internet, mas boa parte dos dados ainda é armazenada e processada nos Estados Unidos. Essa distância afeta a velocidade de acesso: uma informação hospedada no estado americano da Virgínia pode levar cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. Quando o processamento ocorre em Vinhedo, no interior paulista, o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos. A redução da latência — intervalo entre o envio de uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema — é especialmente relevante para empresas que dependem de aplicações digitais rápidas, como serviços financeiros, comércio eletrônico e plataformas de streaming. Isso cria uma demanda adicional por estruturas de processamento instaladas mais perto dos usuários, beneficiando cidades do interior paulista, como Araçatuba e região, que podem se tornar polos de infraestrutura digital. Governo reduz tarifas para atrair investidores O governo brasileiro também tenta estimular a chegada de empreendimentos por meio da redução de tarifas de importação sobre equipamentos de tecnologia. A medida visa tornar o país mais atrativo para investidores, reduzindo o custo inicial de implantação de data centers. A iniciativa é parte de uma estratégia mais ampla para posicionar o Brasil como hub regional de processamento de dados. Além disso, grandes empresas de tecnologia procuram regiões que possam funcionar como pontos estratégicos para suas redes globais de processamento, e o Brasil, com sua localização geográfica e mercado consumidor, desponta como candidato natural. A combinação de incentivos fiscais e demanda crescente pode destravar novos projetos. Desafios de infraestrutura elétrica persistem Apesar das vantagens, transformar o potencial em novos empreendimentos depende de superar obstáculos significativos. A infraestrutura elétrica é um dos principais desafios: regiões com boa conexão à internet nem sempre são aquelas com maior disponibilidade de energia. Além disso, problemas na transmissão e a demora para obter autorização de conexão à rede podem comprometer o cronograma dos projetos. Esses gargalos exigem coordenação entre governo, concessionárias de energia e investidores para garantir que a expansão dos data centers não esbarre em limitações estruturais. Para o noroeste paulista, que busca atrair investimentos em tecnologia, a melhoria da infraestrutura elétrica pode ser um fator decisivo para captar novos negócios e gerar empregos qualificados. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é a capacidade atual de data centers no Brasil e a projeção para 2030? O Brasil concentra quase metade da capacidade da América Latina, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. A expectativa é alcançar 5 gigawatts (GW) até 2030, segundo Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers. Por que a matriz elétrica renovável é um diferencial para o Brasil na atração de data centers? Cerca de 85% da eletricidade do Brasil vem de fontes renováveis, o que é um diferencial importante, pois o setor de data centers demanda grandes volumes de energia limpa para operar. Como a localização de data centers no Brasil pode reduzir a latência para usuários locais? Uma informação hospedada na Virgínia (EUA) leva cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo, enquanto se o processamento ocorrer em Vinhedo (SP), o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos, reduzindo drasticamente a latência.

artigo.texto: CATL remained China’s largest power-battery supplier by installations in October 2026, with 39.60 GWh and a 40.00% market share. CnEVPost reported the figures on November 19, attributing them to the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance (CABIA). CATL’s share fell 0.93 percentage points from September even as its installation volume increased. CATL led China’s October battery market BYD ranked second with 21.36% of China’s October power-battery installations, leaving an 18.64-percentage-point gap between the two companies. CATL’s lead narrowed from September, when the gap was 19.83 points, according to CnEVPost’s CABIA-attributed figures. Market share is a company’s portion of all installations in the market. It can fall even when a company installs more batteries, if total installations grow faster. Rising installations do not guarantee a rising market share: the total market sets the pace. Why CATL’s share fell as its installations rose CATL’s installations increased about 11.6% month over month, from 35.49 GWh in September to 39.60 GWh in October. China’s total power-battery installations grew faster, rising 14.0% month over month to 99.4 GWh. That difference in growth rates explains how CATL could add installation volume while losing 0.93 percentage points of share. CATL’s LFP and ternary shares moved in opposite directions The change varied by battery chemistry. CATL’s share of China’s LFP installations edged up, while its share of ternary-battery installations fell. The segments have separate totals, so each share describes CATL’s position within that chemistry rather than within the whole market. The reported decline extended through October On November 20, the South China Morning Post reported that October marked CATL’s sixth consecutive monthly decline in China market share. It linked the trend to domestic automakers diversifying their battery suppliers. CATL’s January–October position remained stronger than its October-only share Across January to October 2026, China’s power-battery installations totaled 675.6 GWh, up 16.9% from the same period a year earlier. CATL accounted for 293.28 GWh and a 43.55% share; its cumulative share was 0.76 percentage points higher than a year earlier. BYD recorded 127.58 GWh and an 18.94% share over the same period.

artigo.texto: The midterm elections — with data centers a key issue in many races — helped provide clarity around the environment for data center development, James Burke, Vistra president and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this month. “Before the elections, in many markets, we were seeing concerns about data centers in the way that the public was reacting to the pace of development, who had control over those decisions, what impact could it have on electric prices, water, all of that,” Burke said on the Nov. 6 call. “Moving past this election is a positive just in terms of being able to understand what's at stake, and now how do we move forward?” So far, the key messages from Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa have been “very similar to some of the key messages that Governor Abbott had expressed and … consistent with messages we've been expressing, which is there has to be some guardrails on this development,” Burke said. Vistra wants tougher requirements for data center interconnection, including higher collateral requirements and take-or-pay agreements for transmission charges, according to Burke. “As we've said for some time, load interconnect queues were overstated across the country and especially in [the Electric Reliability Council of Texas footprint], driven by speculation from developers,” Burke said. Even with the midterm elections and regulatory actions around data centers, through 2030 Vistra expects load to grow by 4% to 6% a year in ERCOT and by 2% to 3% annually in the PJM Interconnection footprint, according to Burke. Despite Vistra’s expectations for load growth in ERCOT, power prices there have been trending lower due to some crypto mining facilities coming offline so they can convert into data centers, and the state’s data center audit and permitting pause, Burke said. “We do not see this as a long-term impact,” he said, noting that ERCOT hit a 91 GW peak demand record this year. Vistra’s fleet has grown to about 50 GW with its Oct. 30 Cogentrix acquisition, Burke said. The fleet includes combined cycle and peaking power plants that are running more often, according to Burke. “As renewable penetration continues throughout the country, you're seeing these assets get called on more,” Burke said in response to an analyst question about potentially selling off parts of the fleet. “So we've been bullish on dispatchable. We've been bullish on flexibility … So as a long-term owner-operator, we like the fleet.”

artigo.texto: A Victorian homeowner paid $74,000 AUD ($49,000 USD) for an off-grid setup with 65 solar panels and 46 kilowatt-hours of battery storage, according to a 2024 report cited by Dubbo Photo News. Here's what to know Household self-sufficiency can extend beyond electricity to supplying water and managing wastewater, making owners responsible for those services. Going off-grid can involve disconnecting a home from the electric grid and other public utilities. For most properties, a grid connection remains the cheapest electricity option, the Australian Government's energy.gov.au website explained. But off-grid power can make financial sense for remote properties where connecting to the network would be expensive or impractical. Household electricity use determines the cost of a stand-alone solar installation. For homeowners comparing solar options, EasyHome is a user-friendly marketplace offering solar shoppers exclusive pricing and unique deals from trusted partners. More background Construction detritus, wildlife droppings, and other debris can contaminate collected rainwater, so owners disconnecting from public water need to manage those risks. With proper installation and maintenance, however, rainwater tanks can provide a safe supply, NSW Health noted. NSW Health emphasized cleaning gutters every three to four months for water-independent homes, as well as regularly checking water storage tanks for cleanliness. Owners must keep household sewage systems working properly and obtain council permission both to install and to operate them, the NSW Office of Local Government says. What can be done? Rooftop solar panels are the most effective solution to rising energy prices, and solar leases offer those savings with no upfront costs. Homeowners can go solar without taking on the full responsibilities of an off-grid home. Prospective buyers and builders should check local code requirements before committing, assess their home's needs, and seek expert guidance when planning such a system. For households dealing with high electric bills, EasyHome is like Groupon for home energy, negotiating exclusive offers for its large user base. It also offers special battery deals: pairing solar with storage boosts savings and provides backup electricity during outages — useful benefits for households that decide to keep their grid connection. Energy used for heating and cooling can be reduced through intentionally deployed insulation, glazing, and shading, the Australian Government's Your Home guide advised.
