artigo.texto: Data centers are physical facilities housing computers, servers, storage systems, and networking equipment used to store, process, and deliver digital information. Though the data center boom stretches back to the late 1990s, data centers have recently become highly contentious, challenging public policy decisionmakers as their size and numbers continue to grow across the US. The balance has shifted over a short period, especially with the rapid growth of hyperscale data centers with their large footprints. The public’s posture of indifference toward data centers shifted to hostility and rage against them. Several states and local jurisdictions have either placed moratoria on data centers or are asking voters whether to impose such moratoria. Opponents (who include local people and outside environmental and anti-AI groups) contend that data centers are bad for communities and the country, but many communities just don’t want them irrespective of the evidence. They have complained about, among other things, higher electricity prices, water use, the noise, congestion, climate change, and pollution. On the positive side, data centers supply the computing power behind the AI tools poised to revolutionize scientific research, automation, and cloud services. Economically, they have the potential to raise productivity, wages, and the quality of life. Data centers have the potential to spur local economic development and expand the local tax base. Three concepts in economics are pertinent for policymakers, especially local government officials, responsible for the permitting of data centers. They affect the timing for building data centers, the handling of local opposition, and the government’s role in promoting them. The last two topics present a conflict between the local population and government officials. Overall, the three concepts tell us that public policy on data centers is unlikely to lead to the best outcome from society’s perspective, if only because political forces will dominate rational economic thinking. The Precautionary Principle Those who favor a moratorium on data centers subscribe to the precautionary principle. The principle supports the “min-max” strategy, which aims to minimize the maximum harm that can result from an adverse event. The precautionary principle applies to environmental and safety policies across different industries and contexts. This principle says that even in the face of uncertainty, society should act today to avoid major problems in the future. Uncertainty refers to the lack of complete proof that the harm done by data centers to local communities and society in general is significant. The uncertainty can arise, for example, from unreliable evidence that electricity prices will appreciably rise, the availability of water will seriously decline, or AI will cause massive job losses. The precautionary principle reflects a “better safe than sorry” stance that assigns a benefit to prevention even with inconclusive risk. It acts as insurance against major future problems or catastrophic events. Measured precautionary actions might include a detailed investigation of water availability and the likely rise in electricity prices because of data centers. Advocates of moratoriums implicitly assert that the costs of delay are small compared to the risk of moving ahead to build data centers today. When the risk extends to the faster and more immediate growth of potentially precarious AI as more data centers get built, the precautionary principle becomes more persuasive. The precautionary principle is not devoid of controversy, however. Critics point to its shortcoming compared to a cost-benefit analysis that takes into account uncertainty and the risk aversion of the decisionmaker. “Safe” may have a high cost and the “sorry” may have a remote chance of happening. In this instance, delaying action would likely fail a cost-benefit test. It could, however, be justified only if society assigns an extremely high risk to data centers. What is the opportunity cost to society to avoid a possible problem tomorrow? The precautionary approach provides little guidance. When people purchase insurance, they at least implicitly compare the premiums with the expected cost from a bad event. Shouldn’t society have an idea of the costs of stopping or suspending the building of data centers today? What are the benefits from halting the building of data centers? In sum, the precautionary principle might not reflect an economically rational way to set socially desirable policy. What’s your political type? Find out right now by taking The World’s Smallest Political Quiz. Take the Political Quiz Looking at risk from a rational perspective, a relevant question is whether a cautious approach to data centers is worth paying for. Is the risk of delaying or halting the building of data centers worth the benefits? That’s what policymakers should be asking. One paradigm for a wait-and-see strategy toward data centers is real options theory. It suggests that action should proceed incrementally until we know more. Waiting may be a rational response to a slow-moving uncertain peril in an environment of fast-changing technology. On the downside, there exists the risk of a potentially high cost from irreversibility in waiting too long to avoid a “tipping point,” or the threshold at which the US loses competitiveness in the global market for AI and suffers economically. That means that preventive action by slowing down the building of data centers could cause great harm to the US economy. It also may be unrealistic that we will have available more precise information on the dangers of AI. One must ask whether a wait-and-see strategy is simply a tactic to stall the building of data centers or has merit as a rational reaction to an uncertain future with the possibility of dire consequences. artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. — The debate over how to regulate data centers is moving from unincorporated Hillsborough County to Tampa City Hall. Tampa City Council approved a resolution advancing a proposed temporary moratorium on data center development, giving city staff time to review Tampa's Comprehensive Plan, Land Development Code and City Code and recommend potential regulations. WATCH REPORT FROM JADA WILLIAMS: The council's action does not enact the moratorium itself. Instead, it moves the proposed ordinance toward the public hearing process. Susan Johnson-Velez with Tampa's Legal Department told council members that the proposal stems from a motion made in late October. "Council asked staff to bring back a resolution doing a number of things related to data centers, among them preparing an interim development control or moratorium ordinance to allow staff time to review the Comprehensive Plan, the Land Development Code, and the City Code so that we could come back to council with recommendations on regulations for data centers," Johnson-Velez said. Hillsborough County has been considering the same questions for months Tampa's action comes as Hillsborough County has spent months examining how it could regulate data centers before significant development occurs. On Aug. 5, county commissioners directed staff to evaluate a potential framework for future data center regulations, including whether to limit or prohibit the use of county drinking water for cooling. The county's subsequent November report says modern data centers associated with artificial intelligence can involve very large buildings with significant demands on power and water. Cooling and backup power equipment can also produce persistent noise, according to the report. Commissioner Harry Cohen told Tampa Bay 28 in August that the county wanted to proceed cautiously. "We're going to do some study. We are going to assess what the impacts of these centers could be, and we're going to proceed very, very cautiously before we even entertain the idea of allowing anything like this to be built," Cohen said. During that August meeting, members of the public also urged commissioners to act before projects begin moving forward. "It's clear that we need to hit the brakes on explosive growth and data center projects," one speaker told commissioners. Another urged the board to "protect our communities until thorough research and safeguards are in place." What could Hillsborough County's rules look like? By November, the county's Development Services staff had outlined several potential approaches. The framework includes requiring planned-development zoning or allowing data centers as conditional uses only in certain zoning districts. It also considers separation requirements designed to address potential noise impacts on residents, livestock and sensitive wildlife. Other possibilities include: - Enhanced screening around data center sites - Architectural requirements intended to break up large, monolithic building faces - Limits on the use of potable, or drinking, water for cooling - Requiring the use of reclaimed water Data centers are not currently listed as permitted uses within Hillsborough County's standard zoning districts, according to the county report. That means a data center development would currently need to be specifically approved through planned-development zoning. The county also identified electricity demand as a significant consideration, including possible cost impacts on other customers. However, its report does not propose regulations addressing electricity rates because those are regulated by the Florida Public Service Commission. County moratorium proposal deferred Hillsborough County has also considered a temporary moratorium of its own. On Nov. 10, commissioners had an item before them that would have declared "zoning in progress" and scheduled public hearings for consideration of an ordinance establishing a one-year temporary moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated Hillsborough County. However, commissioners deferred that item to a date to be determined. artigo.texto: que são mega data centers de Inteligência Artificial, onde estão projetos no Brasil e por que precisamos de leis rigorosas para conter as Big Techs Por Andressa Santa Cruz – Greenpeace Brasil | A era da Inteligência Artificial (IA) virou uma corrida desenfreada que exige cada vez mais territórios, recursos e dados. No Brasil, mega projetos das gigantes da tecnologia avançam em meio a isenção de impostos, enquanto comunidades e consumidores enfrentam os prejuízos. Mas dá tempo de agir antes que os danos se tornem irreversíveis. “Antes de seguir expandindo os data centers de IA que só aumentam os lucros bilionários das Big Techs, o Brasil deve saber o custo e definir as regras para que o povo brasileiro não pague a conta dos impactos” explica Julia Catão, especialista em Tecnologia do Greenpeace Brasil. O que são Mega Data Centers de IA? São centros de dados de hiperescala para desenvolver modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA), concentram milhões de servidores para processar, armazenar e transmitir enormes volumes de dados, podendo consumir energia equivalente a países inteiros e milhões de litros de água potável. A diferença está no tamanho e na capacidade: data centers tradicionais operam os serviços digitais que usamos no dia a dia (enviar mensagens, assistir a vídeos e acessar plataformas); já mega data centers de IA são instalações computacionais de escala e impactos industriais e atendem sobretudo às Big Techs. Quais os impactos dos Mega Data Centers de IA? - Aumento na conta de luz: usam a rede local e elevam os custos da energia nas residências – nos EUA, as tarifas chegaram a triplicar para mercados, custo que é repassado aos consumidores. - Consumo de água: apesar de existir “circuito fechado”, há perdas e reposição; nos EUA, o consumo anual chegou a 1 trilhão de litros d’água. - Poluição sonora: geradores fazem ruído insuportável, alto e constante, afetando a qualidade de vida das famílias vizinhas. - Emissões de gases de efeito estufa: a possibilidade de usar fontes fósseis, ampliando as emissões que agravam a crise climática. - Pressão sobre os territórios: ocupam áreas enormes que podem chegar a mais de 100 campos de futebol, disputando terras, água e energia com comunidades locais. - Concentração de poder: domínio de empresas estrangeiras sobre o mercado e as infraestruturas impede o avanço tecnológico no país. Nos EUA, onde mais tem data centers no mundo, a população fez vários protestos contra e o tema foi decisivo nas eleições. Nova York suspendeu novas instalações de hiperescala até ter leis mais rígidas e países europeus também pausaram projetos como Irlanda, Holanda e Dinamarca. Quais são os projetos de Mega Data Center no Brasil? O Brasil já possui data centers (cerca de 225 e quase metade fica no estado de São Paulo), mas os mega projetos para desenvolver IA estão começando a chegar em todo país. O mais avançado está em construção no território indígena do povo Anacé, em Caucaia (CE), região metropolitana de Fortaleza. Segundo o Governo do Ceará, abrigará as tecnologias de IA do TikTok e a previsão é começar a operar no segundo semestre de 2027. Confira abaixo projetos de mega data centers em andamento no Brasil. Lei Redata e a importância de regular data centers no Brasil No Brasil, o Redata (Lei 15.504/2026), sancionada em setembro, criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter. Na prática, concede isenções de impostos para atrair centros de dados ao país — uma renúncia fiscal estimada em R$ 7 bilhões, segundo Secretaria Especial da Receita Federal, ou seja, recursos públicos que deixam de ser arrecadados. Aprovado sem participação social ou diálogo com as comunidades atingidas, o Redata abre brechas preocupantes, como o incentivo à combustível fóssil. O desenho da lei favorece as Big Techs em detrimento do povo brasileiro e do clima global. Enquanto estados norte-americanos e países europeus discutem limites rígidos, o Brasil se torna alvo da expansão acelerada. O que são Big Techs e quem controla a corrida da Inteligência Artificial? As Big Techs são gigantes da tecnologia que estão entre as empresas mais ricas e influentes do mundo, como Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvdia, Microsoft e TikTok – seus fundadores e administradores ocupam o topo da lista de bilionários da Forbes. São exemplos de como a “inovação” acontece quando é controlada por poucos: lucros recordes, cortes de empregos e a falsa promessa de que automação trará benefícios, porém na prática acumulam infrações trabalhistas, sociais e ambientais. Por que regular Big Techs e Data Centers? Regular não é censurar ou frear o desenvolvimento tecnológico, é assegurar que a população faça parte com salvaguardas que respeitem os ciclos da natureza, o bem-comum e que tragam retorno para a sociedade. Para isso, precisamos de criar regras: - Regulação das Big Techs (ambiente digital e democracia): estabelece limites e responsabilidades para as grandes empresas de tecnologia, incluindo transparência sobre algoritmos, proteção de dados e direitos digitais. - Regulação de data centers (infraestrutura física e recursos naturais): impõe análise de riscos e leis firmes para a construção e operação desses empreendimentos, considerando os impactos socioambientais. Parem os mega data centers! Nove organizações — Instituto Terramar, Amazônia Sem Data Center, CTRL+Z, Data_Labe, Instituto Decodifica, Mulheres pelo Clima do Vale do Paraíba, Coding Rights, Filha do Sol e Greenpeace Brasil – se uniram para frear o avanço de mega data centers de IAs no Brasil até que sejam assegurados: - Consentimento e Transparência: Participação social ativa e consulta livre, prévia e informada para as comunidades tradicionais. - Licenciamento Ambiental completo: Estudo e relatório de impacto assegurando transição energética justa e proibindo instalação em áreas de importância ecológica. - Fim da isenção de impostos: Quem lucra com infraestrutura digital em larga escala deve se responsabilizar pelos custos e impactos, e investi

artigo.texto: Midea has launched its Energy Storage business in Australia expanding its local product portfolio. Already an established and trusted presence in many Australian homes across air conditioning, heating, refrigeration, laundry and other smart household appliances, Midea’s local expansion into residential energy storage comes as Australian households look for ways to take greater control of electricity use, maximise rooftop solar investments and reduce reliance on grid electricity. Leading the new Australian portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system designed to bring energy storage functionality together in a single solution. When paired with a suitable solar installation, residential batteries can store surplus electricity for use later, reducing reliance on grid purchases and reducing energy costs over time. PowerInfi also reflects Midea’s broader approach to home energy, with energy storage sitting alongside technologies such as air conditioners, heat pumps and other major household appliances in its portfolio that use energy throughout the home. Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased with a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed for flexibility, the Omni X offers installers and homeowners another option to meet differing household energy requirements. Midea Energy Storage showcased its local range for the first time at the recent All Energy Australia 2026, held in Melbourne last month. PowerInfi and Omni X were displayed alongside Midea air conditioners and heat pumps, illustrating the breadth of the company’s home energy and climate technology portfolio, and provided installers, industry partners and other stakeholders an opportunity to explore the solutions and learn about Midea’s plans for the market. Midea Australia and New Zealand general manager, Ivan Ma, said Australia is an important market for Midea Energy Storage. “There is strong rooftop solar adoption here and a growing interest in household energy independence, so it is a natural next step for us to be able to offer our residential energy storage technologies to Australian homeowners,” Ma said. "Australians already know Midea through the many appliances and climate control solutions they use every day. “We're building on that familiarity and trust in energy storage, which will increasingly become an important part of the modern connected home of the future.” Ma said choosing a residential energy storage system is a significant investment. “Consumers are making a long-term decision about how they power their homes, and they need confidence in the company standing behind that investment,” he said. “We see enormous potential to bring greater confidence and choice to this market, and to consider how energy storage, heating, cooling and appliances can work together to deliver a better experience for consumers.”

artigo.texto: A estimativa atribuída à Epoch AI coloca o data center da Huawei em Horinger, na Mongólia Interior, em cerca de 81 mil equivalentes H100 — aproximadamente 7% da capacidade computacional estimada de Colossus 2, associado à xAI. Um equivalente H100 expressa capacidade computacional em relação ao acelerador Nvidia H100. Portanto, os 81 mil equivalentes não representam uma contagem de GPUs Nvidia instaladas. Como Horinger se compara a Colossus 2 As estimativas usam a mesma unidade, o que permite comparar a escala computacional dos dois campi: A estimativa de Horinger equivale a cerca de 7% da estimativa para Colossus 2. É uma comparação entre capacidades computacionais estimadas, não entre contagens verificadas de aceleradores físicos. Para comparar a escala de data centers, use a mesma unidade: equivalentes H100 expressam capacidade computacional estimada, não o número de GPUs instaladas. Como a estimativa foi calculada O método atribuído à análise combina observações de infraestrutura com estimativas de chips. Imagens de satélite permitem identificar equipamentos de refrigeração; a partir deles, estima-se a dissipação de calor e a capacidade do campus. Para estimar a quantidade de aceleradores, o cálculo também considera as vendas de chips da Huawei e o intervalo entre a venda e a implantação. A estimativa atribui ao campus cerca de 105 mil chips Ascend 910C e 8 mil Ascend 910B. Em um relato publicado em novembro de 2026, quatro edifícios de refrigeração densa somavam uma capacidade estimada de 286 MW; três eram descritos como operacionais naquele relato. A mesma análise cita uma subestação de 304 MW e geradores de reserva de 230 MW como referências para conferir a estimativa. Esses valores se referem a infraestruturas distintas dos 286 MW atribuídos aos quatro edifícios.

artigo.texto: Energy Vault Closes $78 Million Financing for Texas Battery Storage Project The financing will support construction of the SOSA Energy Center, with commercial operations expected in Q3 2027 November 24, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Energy Vault, a utility-scale energy storage project developer, has closed $78 million in construction and bridge financing for its 150 MW/300 MWh SOSA Energy Center battery storage project in Madison County, Texas. The bridge financing will be repaid through an $80 million preferred equity investment already committed upon project completion. Energy Vault said the construction financing, preferred equity investment, and a draw on the OIC preferred facility are intended to fund the project through construction and commercial operations on a non-recourse basis. The SOSA Energy Center was the first energy storage asset formally acquired and placed into development under Asset Vault, Energy Vault’s platform for owning and operating energy storage and artificial intelligence infrastructure assets. Once completed, the project will operate on a merchant basis in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas North market. Energy Vault said the project will retain the flexibility to enter into a contracted offtake agreement as market conditions change. Construction began in the fourth quarter of 2025 after the company secured site control and reached environmental and interconnection milestones. Civil work has been completed, and a substation has been installed. Energy Vault is handling the project’s engineering, procurement, and construction. Major equipment is expected to arrive at the site in the coming months. Commercial operations are scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The company said the SOSA Energy Center represents an investment of approximately $100 million in Madison County. Energy Vault estimates that the project will generate $9.3 million in tax revenue for North Zulch Independent School District and Madison County over 10 years. Construction is also expected to create 65 local jobs. In September 2026, the company acquired more than 2.3 GW of U.S. battery energy storage development projects from Colorado-based developer and operator of utility-scale battery storage projects, Goshe Energy Storage. In the first nine months of 2026, publicly announced energy storage project funding increased by 197% year over year, compared to 9M 2025, according to Mercom’s recently released 9M 2026 Funding and M&A for Energy Storage report.

artigo.texto: Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy have agreed to develop a 380MW/1.5GWh portfolio of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Spain. The seven-project deal, involving sites in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra, is anticipated to bring new energy storage capacity online from 2027 to the first half of 2028. The transaction, said to be the largest BESS deal in Spain, establishes a long-term partnership to develop, build and operate the stand-alone BESS projects. Sungrow Renewables is a subsidiary of Sungrow Power Supply Group, while Actuate is an energy storage platform backed by private equity firm NGP. The portfolio includes stand-alone battery installations, some of which are already under construction, while others are scheduled to reach ready-to-build (RtB) status by 2027. Specific sites in the agreement include the Valencia Cluster in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón), Santiago in Lousame (A Coruña), Berja in Almería, and the Navarra Cluster in Olite and Cordovilla. Sungrow Renewables Western Europe Daniel Sánchez said: "This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain's BESS market. "With 380MW and 1.5GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution." The agreement could lead to further collaboration, as both companies aim to expand their presence in the energy storage sector and help stabilise Spain's electricity network. According to Sungrow Renewables, it has previously delivered hybrid solar photovoltaic (PV) and stand-alone battery storage projects in Spain and currently operates in over 20 countries. Actuate Energy invests in and operates energy storage assets to support renewable power and grid stability across Europe. The company has chosen Spain as its first European market, citing the country's significant renewable energy uptake and established project opportunities. Actuate Energy CEO Ben Skinner said: "Spain is a market leader in deploying renewable energy, but battery storage has not kept pace. "This portfolio marks a real step forward for the Spanish grid, adding flexible assets that respond in seconds to keep the system stable, allowing more renewables to come online." Last month, Sungrow announced plans to partner with ENGIE and Elecnor to advance the 150MW/300MWh Hazelwood BESS in Victoria, Australia. "Sungrow and Actuate sign 380MW battery storage deal in Spain" was originally created and published by Power Technology, a GlobalData owned brand.

artigo.texto: Two years after fighting off a landfill proposal, Russell County residents questioned the new set of developers hoping to build a data center campus on a different parcel of a historic former coal mine site near the town of Cleveland. The developers are still waiting for approval of a power agreement and looking to attract a company to operate three or four data centers. Ground could be broken for the project by next fall, they told a crowd in Lebanon on Wednesday. Oasis Digital Properties developers discussed their timeline for the project, shared projected economic benefits and addressed environmental and quality-of-life concerns about the project. Virginia is the state with the most data centers, most located in the northern part of the state, but in recent years more proposals have come to the coalfields in far Southwest. About 100 people turned out for the forum held by the developers. The crowd included Cleveland residents and their neighbors in nearby communities, who took notes, asked questions and pushed back on details like the amount of water that would be used and how the noise would be controlled. Oasis entered into an option agreement with the Russell County Industrial Development Authority, which owns the land, in July 2025 to explore developing the site.The partnership opened a 36-month period for the company to “prove” its project to the authority, Ross Litkenhous, co-founder of Oasis, said during the forum. Litkenhous said in an interview on Friday that the agreement allows Oasis to purchase the property until July 2028, but it is “not going to move forward unless they have a project that makes sense.” The purchase price would be just under $3 million, he said. New details and some changes have emerged since Cardinal News’ initial story on the project in September. Water and power usage Appalachian Power told the Oasis team that the utility has 300 megawatts of untapped power capacity available at its Carbo plant, Litkenhous said in a September interview. The company is still waiting on this power purchase agreement to be finalized, he said Wednesday. He said Friday that he does not know when the agreement would happen, but it’s a key step toward moving forward with the project. He said that the cost of bringing that power to the site will not fall on customers and added that while power bills are going up across the board, “it will not be because of this data center.” Residents highlighted the rate increases Appalachian Power has already initiated and questioned how Litkenhous could guarantee the buildings’ increased usage wouldn’t have trickle-down effects. Previously, Litkenhous said that water consumption would depend on the clients that would ultimately occupy the buildings. He said at the meeting that Oasis has committed to using a closed-loop system to cool the buildings. Closed-loop cooling systems would reuse water but use more power, he previously said. He added Friday that there would still be regular water use anticipated for people working in the buildings. He said Wednesday that would likely fall between 5,000 and 10,000 gallons per day, per building, and that was less than a large office building. He said the water would not come from Lake Bonaventure, a 66-acre lake nearby. Oasis has not yet reached an agreement with the county’s public service authority, which the developers hope will provide the water, he said Friday. Pollution concerns Litkenhous said that as part of the project, Oasis will sign an agreement with the authority that will outline community benefits and parameters on development. Details will be shaped by feedback from the meeting, submitted public comments and another forum planned for the spring, he said. As part of the agreement, Oasis will commit to keeping the noise at an agreed-upon level, which would typically be between 55 and 60 decibels. He compared that level of sound to an electric dryer and said it would be measured at its property line. In addition to power from the grid, the data centers would also run backup generators on site intermittently, he said, including battery storage and tier four diesel generators, the emission standard required by state law. Potential stormwater runoff during construction and operations phases would be managed by a team of engineers, he said when questioned about impact to nearby Dumps Creek, which flows into the Clinch River. Litkenhous said Oasis would pay for any independent impact study if the county or authority calls for one. Noise, air and water pollution were front of mind for several speakers, as was whether any community benefit agreement could actually be enforced with the clients who would occupy the buildings. Nick Over, the co-founder of Oasis, said the agreement would carry with the land regardless of the final client, and Litkenhous said the county would be able to enforce its provisions. Consequences of any violations are yet to be determined, he said. Jennifer Chumbley, who lives on a neighboring farm, said noise travels in the mountains and asked whether it would reach her home in the middle of the night. On the Friday evening before the forum, Chumbley was part of a smaller group of people who met in a Cleveland community center to learn more about data centers and strategize before the forum. “My main question for you is this: Can you guarantee in writing, with 100% certainty, that this data center will not harm the health or well-being of our community or even one person who lives in it?” Chumbley asked the developers. “That’s the only question I have for you guys tonight.” Oasis developers answered some questions during the meeting, but wrote down several, including Chumbley’s, they said they would respond to later. Jobs and tax revenue The financial benefit of the potential data center campus is quantified by a projected $4.6 million in tax revenue per year, Litkenhous said during the meeting, a revision from the projection of $20 million per year that he gave in Septem

artigo.texto: Infrastructure is emerging as a standout investment trend heading into 2027, as spending on energy security and artificial intelligence fuels demand. Preqin data shows infrastructure fundraising rebounded sharply in the third quarter of 2026, with $62 billion raised across 21 funds, bringing this year's total to $101 billion across 65 funds. Rene Lubianski, managing partner, infrastructure at Brookfield Asset Management, said infrastructure is a "cornerstone" of the private markets giant's business during the group's third-quarter earnings call Nov. 6. The firm has raised roughly $50 billion in capital commitments across its infrastructure strategies over the past year. Earlier this month, Brookfield said the latest vintage of its flagship infrastructure strategy had received $26 billion in commitments, with $13 billion coming after the end of the quarter. "This puts us well on track to exceed our $30 billion target in early 2027," Lubianski said. "At that size, the fund would surpass the $28 billion raised for its predecessor to become the largest closed-end infrastructure fund ever raised. "If the current momentum continues, it could also become the largest closed-end private fund ever raised in any sector." 'A challenge and an opportunity' The fundraising surge is unfolding even as investors wait longer to exit existing infrastructure holdings. Portfolio companies owned by the 50 largest infrastructure general partners had an average holding period of 7.6 years in 2025, up from 6.1 years in 2021, according to Boston Consulting Group. Exit activity improved from the prior two years, although many transactions involved continuation vehicles and open-ended infrastructure funds, according to a BCG analysis published earlier this year. Looking ahead, institutional investors appear to have room to bulk up their infrastructure allocations. Goldman Sachs' latest annual 2026 Global Alternatives Survey — which polled some 225 institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurance investors, family offices and other wealth managers between June and August — found that 43% of respondents have a more favorable outlook on infrastructure investment compared with a year ago, with 7% who were less favorable. Nearly half of investors, 49%, with a target allocation to infrastructure said they were under-allocated, compared with just 5% who were over-allocated, according to the study, published Oct. 21. "Geopolitical tensions and their effects on inflation, interest rates, and growth prospects continue to impact valuations and investors' ability to return capital. Those constraints coincide with extraordinary demand for private capital to finance the infrastructure supporting AI expansion — creating both a challenge and an opportunity," said Jeff Fine, global co-head of alternatives capital formation, Goldman Sachs Alternatives. Why infrastructure now J.P. Morgan Asset Management strategists said Nov. 12 that the sector stands to benefit from stronger government and corporate spending next year, while offering protection if that spending keeps inflation and interest rates elevated. Hugh Gimber, executive director and global market strategist at JPMAM, said infrastructure has some of the "strongest foundations" among alternative assets in the current economic environment. The sector has evolved over the past three years, Gimber noted, with data centers, communications networks, renewables and energy storage accounting for a growing share of investment alongside traditional assets such as transport and utilities, helping support returns. Power generation has been a standout, returning almost 40% a year over that period and 60% in the past year, according to JPMAM's 2027 Investment Outlook, published on Nov. 16. Defense and energy security concerns, coupled with the rise of AI, are also accelerating Europe's push for greater self-sufficiency — and the infrastructure needed to support it. "Infrastructure assets today are well geared to some of these stronger spending pushes," Gimber told media, including CNBC, at a recent macro outlook roundtable Nov. 12. "You have much more coming from digital, you have much more coming from renewables, and these tie in much better, particularly in Europe, to the self-sufficiency push that we see underway." Inflation protection JPMAM said a lasting resolution to the Middle East conflict could help ease inflationary pressures on economies next year. But if price pressures prove more persistent, infrastructure bets could also offer greater portfolio protection for investors. Karen Ward, managing director and EMEA chief market strategist at JPMAM, said renewed escalation in the conflict could push inflation higher, potentially triggering simultaneous falls in stocks and bonds. That risk strengthens the case for alternatives that can cushion portfolios against inflation shocks, she added. In an economy powered by higher spending, investors need protection against both recession and inflation — underscoring the need for a larger long-term allocation to alternatives, Ward said.

artigo.texto: In summary Some colleges are setting up their own data centers and designing AI products to rival ChatGPT. The community colleges and the UC systems are both discussing expanding these AI alternatives, even as they continue to work with commercial providers. On Thursday, the University of California announced another deal with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to students. At the same time, California’s higher education systems are considering building their own data centers and creating in-house alternatives to ChatGPT, Claude, and other commercial AI products. College administrators say they want to explore all options without limiting themselves to just one vendor. Some tech leaders say these alternatives to ChatGPT are not only possible but would save money and avoid data security risks. The California Community Colleges system — the largest higher education system in the country — is asking the state for $21 million next year to develop a more independent AI network that would, according to the proposal, be a “fraction of the cost of commercial solutions.” The University of California is considering doing something similar, though the system has yet to put forward a formal proposal. California State University spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith said the 22-campus system is having “initial conversations” with the UC and community colleges about collaboration on AI but did not share other details. While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn’t finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. “This is the model that the higher education system in the state of California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD. Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said. The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. To develop their own AI systems, colleges don’t work from scratch — they use other AI tools, known as open-weight models, including Chinese products such as Kimi or DeepSeek or American ones such as Llama and Gemma. Getting these products up and running can be costly, but once operational, they are often not only cheaper than ChatGPT or Claude but also give schools more control. The code behind these low-cost models is typically free to use or change, allowing colleges to rename and rebrand the AI or even repurpose it entirely. The second benefit is control. The Cal State contract with OpenAI specifically says that the company cannot use student data to train its models, but Hayward said these kinds of agreements still have risks and unknowns. “There’s just this concern that somehow it’s going to leak,” he said, adding that internally developed AI tools give colleges “end-to-end control” over the data. That control is helpful for research and for operations. Campuses can develop AI uses that are tailored to help with other projects that commercial models like ChatGPT or Claude aren’t necessarily built for, such as using AI to help with admissions or course enrollment. Lupo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo said these more independent AI models also allow computer science professors and students to design their own AI experiments without having to worry that a third-party might change its model in the middle of an experiment. Hayward said the last benefit is environmental. The community college system has lofty climate goals, including reducing potable water usage by 50%. He said that by adapting open-access or open-weight AI models, colleges take on more of the burden of AI computing internally, which means they can more closely track the power and water demands of these systems. “We can better monitor and know our AI footprint,” Hayward said. “It’s somewhat obscured when you use big vendors like Anthropic and Google.” Pushback to OpenAI For many UC and Cal State leaders, however, big vendors still hold a lot of sway. “OpenAI models are more ad

artigo.texto: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan will receive an US$8.5 million grant from the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) to prepare for trading carbon credits with South Korea. The documents were signed on 25 November during a meeting between Umid Abidkhodjaev, Deputy Minister of Economy and Finance, and representatives of KOICA and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), the ministry said. The grant is being provided under KOICA's technical assistance programme for a project titled "Supporting Uzbekistan's Implementation of the Paris Agreement and Joint Actions with the Republic of Korea under Article 6". The project will be implemented jointly with GGGI. The talks were attended by Kim Myung Jin, head of KOICA's office in Uzbekistan, Stella Seung Yeon Lee, head of GGGI's office in Uzbekistan, and specialists from both organisations. The parties discussed Uzbekistan's transition to a green economy and the regulatory and institutional framework for carbon credit trading. The project will involve developing rules, guidelines and a joint action plan for carbon credit trading between Uzbekistan and South Korea. The grant will also support the establishment of a training centre for specialists involved in preparing and managing carbon projects. The centre will be equipped with the necessary facilities and offer training programmes. Another component will involve pilot projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in agriculture, energy and water management. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to cooperate voluntarily in meeting their climate commitments. Under Article 6.2, one country can transfer verified emissions reductions generated by projects within its territory to another country. These transfers are known as internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs). The purchasing country can count them towards its national climate targets, while the selling country must exclude the same reductions from its own accounting to prevent double counting. Article 6.4 establishes an international carbon credit mechanism supervised by a United Nations body, while Article 6.8 covers non-market approaches to cooperation. Countries agreed on the main rules for implementing Article 6 at the COP26 climate conference in Glasgow in 2021. In 2025, GGGI, with financial support from KOICA, implemented the Green Restoration of the Aral Sea Region project in Karakalpakstan. It focused on developing climate-resilient agriculture, introducing water-saving technologies and attracting green investment. The new project continues KOICA and GGGI's cooperation in Uzbekistan on green development, climate change adaptation and sustainable finance. According to the ministry, it will expand Uzbekistan's opportunities to participate in the international carbon market and help the country achieve its climate goals.

artigo.texto: China fixes solid-state battery marketing myths From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly £42,900,000 to £53,900,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. The unified safety standards are next, and it won’t be long before China gets those rubber-stamped. artigo.texto: Em Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, a promessa de um investimento de R$ 3 bilhões em infraestrutura digital tornou-se motivo de conflito. Moradores da região do Bairro do Tanque organizaram o movimento "Fora Data Center" para barrar a instalação de um complexo de processamento de dados de hiperescala, o Data Center Alfa, previsto para operar entre 2029 e 2030. O cerne da disputa não é apenas o tamanho do empreendimento — que ocuparia uma área equivalente a 50 campos de futebol -, mas a forma como ele chega à cidade. Para a comunidade, há um abismo entre a burocracia oficial e a realidade dos fatos. A contradição é clara. De um lado, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não há pedidos de licenciamento ambiental nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente e que qualquer projeto precisará passar por rigorosos estudos da Cetesb e outros órgãos. Do outro, a infraestrutura elétrica já está sendo moldada para receber o gigante. Documentos da concessionária Isa Energia e do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) revelam que já houve autorizações para a expansão de 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de módulos de entrada de 138 kV, especificamente para atender ao Data Center Alfa. Para os moradores, isso indica que o projeto está muito mais avançado do que a administração municipal admite publicamente. Enquanto a empresa DataSpots (do Grupo ON) mantém silêncio e não responde a questionamentos, quem vive no Bairro do Tanque lida com a incerteza sobre recursos básicos. A maior preocupação é a água. Em uma região onde não há rede de abastecimento público ou saneamento básico, as famílias dependem inteiramente de poços artesianos e "caipiras". Gabriel Tonobohn, morador do bairro há mais de três anos, relata a fragilidade do sistema: "A maioria usa um poço caipira e já está ficando sem água na época de seca". A chegada de um complexo que exige volumes massivos de água para resfriamento de servidores pode, na prática, secar a única fonte de sobrevivência da comunidade. Além da água, a qualidade de vida está sob ameaça por três fatores: Para as famílias que residem no local há décadas, o risco não é a desapropriação formal com indenização, mas a desvalorização total de seus imóveis. Se o bairro se tornar barulhento, quente e sem água, as casas perdem o valor de mercado. "Se torne esse bairro inabitável… elas vão ser obrigadas a sair dali. E elas não vão conseguir vender ou alugar essa casa para ninguém", explica Gabriel. É a perspectiva de ter que recomeçar a vida do zero, sem a compensação financeira que acompanharia uma obra pública. Até o momento, o movimento "Fora Data Center" já reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas e pressiona a Câmara Municipal para alterar o Plano Diretor e o Código de Obras, tentando criar barreiras legais contra a instalação de complexos de hiperescala antes que a primeira pedra seja lançada. artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries made of a cathode, anode, electrolyte, separator, and current collectors that move sodium ions between the cathode (positive electrode) and anode (negative electrode) during charging and discharging. The movement of sodium ions changes between the cathode and anode during charging and discharging. Sodium ions move from the cathode to the anode through the electrolyte and vice-versa during the discharging state. Electric mobility conventionally uses lithium-ion batteries to provide power for the majority of electric vehicles. Lithium-ion batteries provide higher energy density, and they are lightweight and have a compact design, making the device easier to fit and move. The reason for shifting from lithium-ion batteries to sodium-ion batteries is to achieve overall improved performance of energy storage devices, which could also enhance affordability, safety, and supply chain security. As consumer demand for electric vehicles increases, manufacturers began exploring sodium-ion batteries as an alternative option to reduce reliance on costly lithium-ion batteries and replace expensive materials with abundant sodium and cheaper metals. Following is a list of the top ten companies playing an important industry role in developing sodium-ion batteries and updating existing charging solutions through advances in electrolyte chemistry, cell engineering, and existing lithium-ion production lines. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited) A Chinese manufacturing company developing a sodium-ion charging solution as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and energy storage systems. The company has shown outstanding performance in developing sodium-ion batteries by achieving a First-generation Cell Spec that reached up to 160 Wh/kg cell energy density, 15-minute charging to 80% battery charge, and overcoming challenges in extreme moisture conditions which cause rapid chemical degradation and structural collapse in sodium-ion batteries. HiNa Battery Technology The company manufactures sodium-ion batteries and battery chemical components using copper-iron-manganese layered oxide cathodes and hard/soft carbon anodes. The company’s headquarters is in Liyang, Jiangsu Province, China specialising in sodium-ion battery research, cell manufacturing and energy storage solutions. This company employs a tabless, double aluminium current collector design to lower internal resistance and improves manufacturing techniques to make sodium-ion cells more efficient and increase energy storage capacity. BYD (Build Your Dreams) BYD is globally recognized for manufacturing electric vehicles and charging solutions. In terms of material and electrochemistry, BYD uses highly stable polyanion materials and electrochemical refinements for the cathode and transition metal chemistries to stabilize layered transition metal oxides and suppress undesirable phase transitions. BYD’s sodium-ion cells operate across wide temperature ranges (-40°C to 80°C) on the 3rd-gen platform and support fast charging/discharging rates paired with its Blade cell architecture. The multi-chemistry approach implemented by BYD in its sodium-ion battery technology enhances overall battery performance and balances cost, durability, extreme-weather conditions, energy density, and cycle life across different applications. Faradion Faradion manufactures sodium-ion battery technology for electric vehicles that lowers reliance on costly metals while offering strong safety and fast charging. The charging solution is designed to run on existing lithium-ion manufacturing lines without cobalt, lithium, or copper while targeting 30% lower cost than lithium-ion. EVE Energy The company commercializes high-durability NF155L sodium-ion cells built on lithium-compatible manufacturing lines. These cells use NFPP chemistry and are designed primarily for stationary battery energy storage systems (BESS) that provide thermal and fire safety by producing less flammable gas under extreme thermal runaway. EVE Energy is also expanding its sodium-ion battery production for electric vehicles by targeting electric two-wheelers with high-durability, low-temperature cells while building a manufacturing facility in Huizhou, Guangdong Province, China, targeting 2 GWh of annual production. The platform eliminates the use of an anode as a current receiver, enabling the flow of electric current by using an anode-free structure. This reduces manufacturing costs and increases energy density. The sodium ions release from the cathode, travel through the electrolyte, and deposit directly on the negative current collector as a thin layer of metallic sodium. artigo.texto: Governor Sherrill's Ponders Data Center "Faustian Bargain' BY COLLEEN O'DEA New Jersey’s U.S. senators both voted last Thursday against a divisive bill that seeks to speed permitting for new energy projects and require data centers to pay for the power they use, while also weakening environmental protections. Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s position on the bill, which still needs to pass the House, where its future is uncertain, is less clear. Her office declined to comment on it. Energy policy has been a priority of hers since taking office 11 months ago. New Jersey needs to increase supply in order to blunt electricity increases – last year, power bills jumped by about 20%. But the state also has strong environmental laws and a population that values the clean water and open spaces in the most densely populated state in the nation. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) combines some clean energy provisions and the promise of jobs with reduced environmental protections. It has pitted the Citizens Climate Lobby and AFL-CIO against the Sierra Club and NAACP. It divided the Democratic caucus, with 14 Democrats joining the Republican majority Thursday to pass the bill 62-33 and send it to the House of Representatives. Only two Republicans opposed the bill. If sent to his desk, President Trump likely would sign it. A policy statement from the White House touted a number of provisions of the bill, saying it would “remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.” The New Jersey State Chamber of Commerce and four regional chambers signed on to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s statement of support for quick action on the bill: “Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.” But many environmental organizations disagree and oppose some or all of the bill’s provisions to weaken environmental protections. Doug O’Malley, director of Environment New Jersey, called it a “Faustian bargain” that the nation should not accept and he praised Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, for voting against the measure. “This would be a really bad deal for New Jersey and the country,” O’Malley said. “We would be sacrificing the natural environment for the promise of clean energy but there would be a ton of rollbacks of permitting protections for fossil fuel projects.” The bill would weaken a number of environmental protection laws, including the Clean Water Act, making it harder for groups to stop projects that could harm the environment. One such project is the Northeast Supply Enhancement Project or NESE, a proposed expansion of a pipeline carrying natural gas from Pennsylvania through New Jersey to New York and that would require the installation of six miles of pipeline through the Raritan Bay. The project is back before the state Department of Environmental Protection after a federal appeals court vacated state approvals for it two months ago. “It’s a false choice,” O’Malley said of the bill. “We think you don’t think you have to sacrifice environmental protections for clean energy.” While the bill would require data center developers to cover the costs of the electricity they consume, there would still be “huge environmental impacts,” including in water usage that cools the high-capacity computers needed for artificial intelligence processes, O’Malley said. In voting no, both Booker and Kim said that while they support the bill’s clean energy goals, it does not do enough to stop potential abuses of a new permitting system by Trump, including those involving new immigration detention systems. "I believe the climate crisis demands urgent action, and smart permitting reform can unleash a generation of new good-paying union jobs and new technology,” Kim said in a statement. “I voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage. Unfortunately, those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump Administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable.” Booker’s statement explaining his “no” vote went further. "I respect the work done on this bill with the goal of accelerating clean energy and building out our grid, but I do not believe it meets the mandate voters have charged us with to put a check on the corruption, chaos and cruelty of Trump's administration,” he said. “I am particularly concerned that the legislation would eliminate the courts’ authority to block the administration’s illegal projects, including ICE detention centers.” As the Senate considered the bill, Kim had proposed several amendments, including one that would allow local communities to challenge immigration facilities that skipped environmental review. One of those is in Roxbury, where federal officials recently signed a contract to advance the conversion of a warehouse to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility despite having agreed to halt work at the site until they conduct required environmental reviews in response to a lawsuit filed by the state and the township. Sherrill, who opposes the ICE plans for Roxbury, has signed legislation and taken a number of other steps meant to increase the state’s energy supply and prevent further electricity increases due to data center development, though she has not gone as far as New York Gov. artigo.texto: Squadron Energy has submitted plans for a proposed 1,000MW battery energy storage system at Cullen Bullen, 25km north of Lithgow to the NSW Department of Planning and Environment. The proposed Cullen Bullen Battery would be Australia’s biggest battery, boasting eight hours of long-duration energy storage. Related article: AER grants electricity retailer authorisation for Squadron The Waratah Super Battery in New South Wales is currently Australia’s largest operating battery storage system by output at 850MW/1,680MWh, while Western Australia’s Collie Battery Energy Storage System holds more total storage energy at 2,400MWh. The Cullen Bullen Battery is proposed to connect directly to Transgrid’s existing 500kV transmission network. It would help support a more reliable electricity system by storing clean energy when it is abundant and supplying it when needed. The project is in the early stages of development, with Squadron seeking feedback from the local community to help inform its design and development. Squadron Energy project developer Sean Cross said engaging with the community early and delivering lasting local benefits were priorities for Squadron. “We want to hear from local residents and businesses as we develop this proposal, understand what matters to them and identify opportunities for the project to benefit the wider community,” Cross said. “Squadron is committed to delivering real benefits for local families and businesses through investment in infrastructure, funding for community programs and the creation of local jobs and training opportunities. Related article: Big Canberra Battery fully commissioned and operational “We’re already investing in the local community through our sponsorship program, with funding available to support organisations delivering education and training, community development, health and wellbeing, and environmental initiatives.”

artigo.texto: Ford has started producing LFP battery cells at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility in Marshall. The US$3 billion (RM12.4 billion) factory is owned and operated by Ford, but uses technology licensed from CATL. The first batch has been shipped to the Louisville plant in Kentucky for use in prototypes of the Fathom EV pick-up truck, which is planned for launch next year. Ford also plans to begin battery pack production at the Michigan facility in 2027, before the Fathom launches. The carmaker said in a release that the cells use a prismatic design and contain no nickel nor cobalt – helping cut production costs versus nickel-based battery chemistries – and that the “assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.” Reuters quoted Ford advanced development projects VP Alan Clarke as saying that working with CATL was the fastest way to build affordable EVs in the US. “CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” he said. Reuters reported in September that US transportation secretary Sean Duffy urged Ford CEO Jim Farley in a letter to sever ties with Chinese firms including CATL, Geely and BYD, and that China committee chair John Moolenaar said: “Ford should work with our nation’s allies, not our adversaries.” Ford replied in a statement that Duffy’s letter was a “wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines”, adding that “while others continue to import Chinese batteries, Ford is investing to build batteries here in America” and that “Ford owns the plant, controls the operation and employs the workforce.”

artigo.texto: Electra AI and South Korean battery diagnostics business MinTech have announced a collaboration that aims to reduce downtime, revenue losses, and safety risks for battery-storage operators. Here's what to know Electra's Battery Fleet Analytics software can analyze operational data to identify emerging risks in real time. The collaboration combines that software with MinTech's inspection hardware, according to Interesting Engineering. MinTech uses electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and in-house diagnostic algorithms. The technology examines batteries' electrical characteristics to reveal potential issues. Operators can receive advanced warning of potential faults from Electra's software-as-a-service platform, which can recognize patterns linked to battery health. If you're facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity prices, whole-home batteries offer backup protection, while battery leases can help homeowners avoid $20,000 or more in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace offering battery shoppers unique prices and exclusive deals from trusted partners. More background The collaboration comes as battery energy storage systems become a bigger part of the grid by helping supply grids during peak times, supporting renewable energy operations, and supporting data centers. These installations may run many battery cells and modules around the clock. Meaning a developing fault can affect more than a single battery, potentially disrupting the availability of the whole facility. MinTech's diagnostic work spans production, routine operation, reuse, and recycling. Its systems include electric vehicle battery testing and storage that gives used batteries a second life. Rising energy prices make battery reliability more important. What's being done? Electra and MinTech plan to explore additional joint work on diagnosing battery issues, analyzing data, and forecasting risks. If you're not ready to install a whole-home battery, you still have options. Pila offers a plug-and-play battery backup alternative at a substantially lower price point than whole-home systems. If you're weighing storage alongside solar, EasyHome works like Groupon for home energy, negotiating special offers for its large audience to secure unique battery deals. It also offers special solar deals; pairing panels with a battery can increase savings and provide backup electricity during outages. Fabrizio Martini, CEO and co-founder of Electra AI, emphasized how the companies' technologies complement each other. "MinTech brings deep expertise at the diagnostics layer, and Electra brings the intelligence layer that turns operational data into predictive insight." artigo.texto: Sungrow launches modular commercial energy storage range Mon, 23rd Nov 2026 (Today) Sungrow has launched a modular commercial and industrial energy storage portfolio that includes the PowerKeeper system and the new PowerKeeper Lite. The products are designed for commercial and industrial applications and can be paired with Sungrow's SHCX hybrid inverter series, including the SH50/80/100/110/125CX models and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 range. The launch expands Sungrow's offering in a market where businesses are seeking storage systems that can adapt to different site layouts, connect to varied grid conditions and reduce installation complexity. Organised under the "Keeper Family" brand, the portfolio centres on modular configurations across a power range of 50 kW to 125 kW and a capacity range of 50 kWh to 1,000 kWh. Safety focus PowerKeeper is positioned as the heavier-duty product in the line-up. Sungrow says the system uses a three-layer safety structure covering "proactive detection, instant interception, and physical containment". According to Sungrow, the system has undergone more than 700 tests from cell to system level. The company also highlighted features including 50 cm water-immersion protection, fire-spread prevention, resistance to triple-height drops and explosion venting. PowerKeeper is intended to address common issues in commercial and industrial storage projects, including site adaptation, installation, operation and maintenance, and performance in demanding grid environments. Sungrow also says the product uses energy management algorithms that can deliver an additional 10% to 30% in monthly revenue, although it did not provide further detail on the assumptions behind that figure. Installer design Alongside PowerKeeper, Sungrow introduced PowerKeeper Lite for the IP20 segment. The system is also compatible with Sungrow's existing SH50/80/100/110/125CX hybrid inverters and the SH30/40/50CX-P2 series. PowerKeeper Lite is designed for easier installation and servicing. Sungrow says the unit supports both vertical and horizontal layouts, allowing it to fit different indoor spaces. It also uses plug-in connections and wall-side cabling intended to reduce wiring work during deployment. For operation and maintenance, the system links to Sungrow's iSolarCloud remote diagnostics and control platform. On-site fault-finding is supported through an inverter viewing window and LED indicators at battery-pack level. The emphasis on installation reflects a broader issue in the commercial and industrial market, where deployment costs and site constraints can weigh heavily on project economics. Suppliers have increasingly focused on modular products that can be configured to suit space limitations and varied customer load profiles. Grid scale The Keeper Family is also intended for larger projects and more difficult grid conditions. According to Sungrow, the SHCX system can support direct parallel connection of up to 10 units, with on-grid and off-grid switching. It also includes virtual synchronous generator, or VSG, grid-forming functions. In microgrid use cases, Sungrow says battery storage can operate alongside diesel generators to meet changing demand while maintaining voltage and frequency stability. The portfolio supports a DC/AC ratio of 2.0 and charging at 1.6 times rated capacity. Sungrow also says a single unit can connect to photovoltaic modules at up to twice rated power, allowing excess solar generation to be stored rather than curtailed. Commercial and industrial energy storage has become an increasingly contested segment for suppliers of batteries, inverters and energy management software. Demand has risen as businesses seek to manage electricity costs, integrate more on-site solar generation and maintain supply through weaker or unstable grids. System flexibility has become a key selling point in that market, particularly in regions where industrial sites differ widely in available floor space, grid connection standards and backup power requirements. Products that can be scaled in smaller increments or installed in multiple orientations can reduce engineering changes and shorten deployment timelines. Speaking about the new line-up, Sungrow says the portfolio was built to cover a wide range of commercial and industrial scenarios. The company describes the products as combining modular design, simplified installation and broader grid adaptability across the range. "The PowerKeeper Family delivers comprehensive energy storage solutions across diverse C&I scenarios," Sungrow said.

artigo.texto: UK and EU agree to link Emissions Trading Systems Announced at the 2026 UK-EU Summit, the agreement aims to address differences in carbon markets, regulations and allowance prices. The UK Emission Trading Scheme and EU Emission Trading System (ETS) will become more closely aligned from January 2028. From this point, ETS allowances issued in either the UK or EU can be used for compliance across either scheme. Both systems operate on a cap-and-trade basis, requiring companies covered by the schemes to hold allowances for each tonne of greenhouse gas emissions produced. The UK Government estimates that linking the systems could add up to £3.8bln to the UK economy annually by 2040. The anticipated benefits include a larger carbon market, price stability, reduced trade barriers, lower administrative costs and greater incentives for industrial investment. Linking the systems could benefit energy-intensive industries, including cement, steel and aluminium manufacturing, which face significant costs associated with their carbon emissions. A carbon price therefore creates an additional operating cost for manufacturers, making investments in lower-carbon technologies more financially viable. The ETS linking agreement could give these manufacturers access to a larger carbon market, potentially increasing trading liquidity and improving carbon pricing security. Another aim is to reduce carbon-related trade barriers by enabling exemptions from the UK and EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAMs) for eligible goods traded between the two markets.
