artigo.texto: Eight EU States Urge Early Entry of Road Carbon Market Ministers from eight member states back immediate application of CELE 2, a carbon market covering buildings and road transport fuels. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Transportation Live Poll Should the EU carbon market expand to cover home heating and road transport fuel? Ministers from Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden wrote to EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra supporting the European Emission Trading System 2 (CELE 2). Portugal and the other signatories called for its immediate entry into force, while Italy and Poland have urged delaying or easing it. Why it matters The letter frames CELE 2 as an economically efficient way to accelerate decarbonisation of road transport and buildings, and cites recent energy disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz as evidence that Europe must cut reliance on imported fossil fuels. The dispute over timing reflects a split between member states on how quickly to price carbon in these sectors. Eight member states signed the letter urging CELE 2 into force, while the system was created in 2023 with a scheduled start in 2028. The letter does not specify revenue, emissions volumes or price levels, and the outcome of the impact assessment agreed in October 2026 remains unknown. The players Wopke Hoekstra Wopke Hoekstra is the European Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth, responsible for the EU's climate policy and emissions trading framework. Italy Italy is a major EU economy in the Mediterranean whose government has joined calls to delay or ease CELE 2 before its scheduled start. Poland Poland is a Central European EU member state whose fossil-fuel-dependent economy has led it to urge a delay or easing of CELE 2. The details The ministers of Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden sent the letter, which Denmark initiated, to Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra. CELE 2 complements the original EU carbon market, which covers power, heat, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, by covering fuel use in buildings and road transport. Timeline - 2023: CELE 2 is created. - October 2026: EU leaders at the European Council summit commit to assess CELE 2's impact before entry into force. - 2028: CELE 2 is initially scheduled to enter into force. Roadmap CELE 2 extends the EU Emissions Trading System, which priced carbon only in power, heavy industry, aviation and shipping, into buildings and road transport. The split between eight member states pushing for early entry and Italy and Poland seeking delay shows how the expansion is being contested as Europe weighs energy security against its decarbonisation timetable. If CELE 2 takes effect earlier, the cost of fuel used for road transport and heating in buildings could rise sooner as carbon pricing reaches those sectors. The timing debate will determine when households and fleet operators begin to feel that cost. The takeaway The debate over CELE 2 is less about whether to price carbon in transport and buildings than about how fast Europe moves, a choice that will shape fuel costs for drivers and homeowners across the bloc. Following the Commission's impact assessment will show which timetable is adopted. What happens next The Commission is expected to carry out the impact assessment agreed at the October 2026 European Council summit before CELE 2's 2028 entry into force. With roughly 10% charge left most days, they asked whether one or two more batteries would be worthwhile. The additions would potentially bring storage to around 36 kWh. "Really happy with the system overall though obviously at the moment we're relying heavily on overnight charging," the original poster wrote. The family wanted to install an air conditioning system that heats the home in winter. They were using higher dishwasher settings and considering bathroom underfloor heating they had previously left off, encouraged by solar power and cheap overnight electricity. One commenter described doing more laundry and sometimes choosing an oil-filled radiator over gas heating while working from home. After buying a 16-kWh battery, their household's daily electricity consumption had increased to 12–13 kWh from 8–9 kWh. Running out of stored electricity during particularly cold weather had prompted another household to consider adding batteries, despite already having substantial storage and a heat pump. They questioned whether another battery would be worth buying to avoid £100 (~$131) in annual charges, based on paying an extra £2 (~$2.62) on 50 days each year. What can be done? One commenter suggested scheduling the underfloor heating to run during off-peak hours, then cycling it on battery power during peak periods. They also recommended using Home Assistant and shifting electricity-intensive activities to cheaper hours. Commenters encouraged the homeowner to spend more time understanding their household's electricity needs before investing in additional storage. Responding to advice to size storage around typical days, they wrote: "I think this gets at my issue as I'm not sure what a common day looks like now. Though I agree about good habits about using energy. Aircon will likely increase it significantly when in heating mode… gah." After clarifying their winter heating plans using the heat pump, the original poster took the community's advice to step back. "Waiting seems sensible," they conceded. artigo.texto: Moment Energy has introduced Nova, a commercial and industrial battery energy storage system rated at 200 kW and 500 kWh that runs on repurposed electric-vehicle batteries, TaiyangNews reported. Each Nova block carries UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications, and the company has opened orders with first deliveries planned for Q1 2027. Moment Energy Nova at a Glance The Moment Energy Nova is a modular storage block aimed at businesses that want to shave peak demand, firm up on-site solar, or ride out grid trouble. It is not a home battery and it is not a utility-scale container. Reports place it squarely in the commercial and industrial tier, which sits between a residential wall unit and a multi-hundred-megawatt-hour grid project. Every headline number comes from the announcement coverage. The table below lists what reports confirm for a single Nova block, plus one figure we calculated ourselves from those inputs. Note that the 2.5-hour figure is a simple division, not a tested runtime. Real duration depends on depth of discharge, temperature, inverter losses, and how the operator sets the state-of-charge window. Moment Energy has not published a round-trip efficiency figure in the coverage we reviewed. How Nova Turns Retired EV Batteries Into Storage An EV battery does not die when a car retires it. Packs usually leave vehicles once they can no longer deliver the range or acceleration drivers expect, but they still hold a large share of their original capacity. A stationary system asks far less of a cell. It does not need to be light, it does not need to deliver sudden bursts for acceleration, and it can sit in a climate-managed enclosure. That mismatch is the whole business case for second-life storage. A pack that is too tired for a car can still cycle once a day on a factory floor for years. Electrek framed Nova in exactly those terms, describing a 500 kWh system that runs on retired EV batteries. The hard part sits between the junkyard and the enclosure. Retired packs arrive with different chemistries, different ages, and different histories. Someone has to test them, sort them, and group compatible units so the finished system behaves predictably. The fact sheet confirms production at Megafactory 1 but does not describe the sorting and grading steps in detail, so we will not invent a process description here. What the reports do establish is the outcome. A buyer gets a finished, certified storage block, not a pile of salvaged modules to engineer into a system. For a facilities manager, that distinction matters more than the cell source. Few plant operators want to own the risk of integrating used packs, and a certified product moves that risk back to the manufacturer. What 200 kW and 500 kWh Mean in Practice Power and energy are different things, and the Nova numbers show why. The 200 kW rating describes how fast the block can move electricity in or out at any instant. The 500 kWh rating describes how much it can hold. Divide one by the other and you get the 2.5 hours mentioned above, a profile that suits daily peak shaving better than multi-day backup. To put 500 kWh in context, it equals the usable energy of several modern passenger-EV battery packs. That is a loose comparison, since pack sizes vary widely by model, but it explains why a stack of retired packs can be repackaged into a single industrial unit. A mid-size warehouse, a cold-storage facility, or a small manufacturing line could plausibly use one block to trim its utility demand charges. Commercial customers often pay for their single highest 15-minute spike of the month, not just total consumption. A battery that discharges during that spike can cut the bill without touching production. Reports describe the target application only as commercial and industrial energy storage, so specific customer types and tariff savings remain our reading of the product class, not a Moment Energy claim. Power-hungry sites with unreliable feeds have similar needs. Our earlier look at technologies that keep data centers running without grid overloads shows how on-site storage has moved from optional to expected for operators with tight uptime targets. Nova targets a smaller scale than a hyperscale campus, yet the logic is the same: buffer the grid and keep the load steady. UL 1973 and UL 9540: Why the Certifications Matter For stationary storage, certification is not decoration. Insurers, fire marshals, and utilities routinely ask for it before they approve an installation. Moment Energy says Nova holds both UL 1973 and UL 9540, and that pairing is the reason the launch drew attention. What the two standards cover UL 1973 addresses the battery system itself, meaning the packs, their management electronics, and their protective features. UL 9540 looks at the energy storage system as a whole, including how the battery, power conversion, and controls work together. A product that clears both has been judged at the component level and at the system level. Why used cells make this harder Certifying a system built from new, uniform cells is routine. artigo.texto: Want 24/7 clean power for data centers? Try giant heat batteries. Data center developers are scrambling to find enough electricity to power their energy-intensive facilities. Some are building their own fossil gas power plants. But that comes with tradeoffs — sky-high equipment costs, yearslong waits for backlogged turbines, and growing public backlash against their polluting plans. A new report from think tank Energy Innovation proposes a faster, cheaper, and cleaner route for powering off-grid data centers: giant heat batteries that are fueled by low-cost solar and wind. This “hybrid thermal power” approach can be cost-competitive with fossil gas in many parts of the country, said Eric Gimon, the report’s author and an Energy Innovation senior fellow. Even more important, it can deliver power within a year or two in places where renewable energy is under development, he said — much faster than the wait for a gas plant. “It’s a pretty simple solution that hyperscalers and developers can pursue,” Gimon said. “You can do off-grid that’s fast, clean, reliable, and affordable.” Nevertheless, Gimon said he’s unaware of a U.S. data center taking this approach today. That’s despite the availability of heat batteries from a number of different companies, including Antora, Brenmiller Energy, Electrified Thermal Solutions, and Rondo Energy. These energy storage systems use electricity to heat rocks, bricks, or other materials to temperatures exceeding 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit). The systems can retain that heat for hours, days, or even weeks at a time, and then dispatch it later. Most thermal storage systems installed today supply industrial process heat for everything from food processing to cement production. But they can also use that heat to boil water, spin a steam turbine, and produce electricity. Storing heat to make electricity has its drawbacks. The process recovers only about 40% of the total energy that’s been put into it, mainly because of losses in converting heat to steam and then to power, Gimon said. That’s not great, compared with the typical low-to-mid-90% “round-trip efficiency” rate for lithium-ion batteries. “But when I started modeling it, I realized TES [thermal energy storage] is cost-effective,” he said. Data centers that want to run independently of the grid and on clean energy will need to store enormous amounts of power for when solar and wind aren’t available. As long as the solar and wind power is cheap enough, and the value of the electricity being generated from the steam turbines is high enough, the efficiency losses are tolerable. In fact, thermal batteries would be cheaper than conventional lithium-ion storage over longer durations, Gimon said. Gimon also looked at how fossil-fueled boilers could run on fuel stored on-site, to give the thermal storage and gas turbines emergency backup power, much like data centers rely on emergency backup diesel generators today. This graphic shows how all the pieces fit together. All told, Gimon estimated that these “hybrid thermal power brick” systems can deliver reliable, round-the-clock power at a cost of about $120 per megawatt-hour — a figure that includes the cost of developing the renewables that deliver their primary power. Depending on where a data center is located, that can be competitive with building a dedicated gas-fired power plant. References range from about $72 per MWh for a data center in West Texas to the $140 to $165 per MWh that investment bank Jeffries estimated Meta is paying for an off-grid gas power plant in Ohio. But for large data center developers, “the issue right now isn’t so much cost, but speed to power,” Gimon said. Data center developers have proposed hundreds of gigawatts of gas-fired power plants across the country, but those plans are constrained by the gas-turbine supply chain, workforce availability, and pipeline capacity. By comparison, thermal energy storage systems are relatively new technologies whose producers are eager to scale up, he said. And while demand for steam turbines is beginning to tick up, those manufacturers are not nearly as backlogged, he said. Arpit Dwivedi, founder and CEO of thermal energy storage startup Cache Energy, agreed that the industry could scale up quickly. His company’s technology uses standard steel components and stores heat in limestone-derived pellets coated in a proprietary binder. Those components are “simple and abundant,” which makes it easier to “build things faster,” he said. The startup has enough manufacturing capacity today to build about a gigawatt-hour of its systems per year, “and we haven’t made a big deal about it,” Dwivedi said. He estimated the company could scale up to 10 GWh per year in 12 months and 100 GWh per year in 24 months without much trouble. Cache Energy has already deployed its technology to store on-site wind power for industrial heating and space heating, Dwivedi said. The company has been talking with data center developers about using its heat batteries for electricity generation, though he declined to share more information. For data center developers to adopt thermal energy storage at scale, “we need one or two real projects that show it really works” in that setting, he said. Hybrid thermal systems also open opportunities for solar and wind developers. Gimon estimated that a renewables-only project could boost its value threefold by adding a thermal battery and steam turbine that can deliver reliable “clean, firm” power. Landing an off-grid data center client could help them avoid the risk of yearslong wait times to connect to the grid, and would give them enough time to secure federal tax credits before they expire. Data center developers could also look to hybrid thermal systems to streamline their path to securing a grid interconnection, he said. artigo.texto: A new peer-reviewed study from MIT researchers estimates that the electricity powering US data centers contributed to about 650 premature deaths in a single year, and that much of the harm landed far from the buildings themselves. The paper, published November 19, 2026 in Environmental Research Letters, puts hard numbers on a question the cloud industry has mostly answered with carbon pledges: what happens to the air that people breathe when data centers pull more power from the grid? According to coverage from Technology Networks and TechRadar, the answer is that data centers worsen air quality across a wide area, including in states that host very few of them. The finding lands at an awkward moment. Cloud and AI demand is pushing grid planners to add capacity, and our earlier look at Goldman’s 52 GW projection for US data centers in 2028 showed how much of that new load analysts expect gas generation to cover. The MIT work gives that story a public-health dimension. It measures not just how much power data centers use, but where the resulting pollution drifts and who inhales it. This analysis walks through what the study reports, what it leaves unanswered, and what it means for cloud buyers, operators and regulators. We stick to the figures confirmed for the paper. Where the public record is silent, such as on specific companies, power plants or emissions tonnage, we say so plainly rather than fill the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the MIT Study Found on Data Centers and Air Quality The paper is titled “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States.” Yuang Chen and colleagues are listed as the authors, and the research comes from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It appeared in Environmental Research Letters on November 19, 2026. The geographic scope is the contiguous United States, and the analysis uses data from 2023. The headline result is an estimate of about 650 premature deaths tied to data center electricity demand. The authors split that total by pollutant. Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, accounts for an estimated 513 of those deaths. Ground-level ozone accounts for another 137. Both pollutants have well-documented links to respiratory and cardiovascular harm, which is why health researchers treat them as the standard yardsticks for air-quality damage. The second finding matters as much as the first. The study reports that pollution tied to data center demand does not stay local. Emissions from the power plants that supply the grid travel through the atmosphere and cross state lines, which means the communities that absorb the damage can sit well downwind of the data centers causing the demand. MIT co-author Noelle Selin summed up the pattern in a single line reported in coverage of the study: “The impact of data centres on air quality extends over a vast area.” The Numbers: 650 Deaths Split Between PM2.5 and Ozone The two pollutant totals add up cleanly: 513 plus 137 equals 650. Using that arithmetic, PM2.5 accounts for roughly 79 percent of the estimated deaths and ozone for roughly 21 percent. Those percentages are our own calculation from the reported figures, not numbers the authors published, so treat them as a convenience for reading the split rather than a separate finding. PM2.5 dominates because the particles are tiny enough to travel deep into the lungs and, from there, into the bloodstream. They form both directly, as soot from combustion, and indirectly, when gases from smokestacks react in the air. Ozone works differently. It forms when sunlight cooks precursor gases such as nitrogen oxides, and it tends to build over hours and distance. That difference in chemistry is one reason a pollution plume can cause harm far from its origin. A figure of 650 deaths in one year deserves context, because “premature deaths” is a statistical estimate and not a count of named individuals. Health-impact studies of this type combine modeled pollution exposure with established relationships between exposure and mortality. The result is a population-level estimate with uncertainty bands. The public summaries we reviewed report the central numbers, and we will not invent confidence intervals that the fact sheet does not confirm. How Electricity Demand Turns Into Downwind Pollution From the meter to the smokestack A data center does not burn fuel for its servers in the typical case. It draws electricity from the grid, and the grid has to generate that electricity somewhere. The study’s core mechanism follows that chain. When a data center’s demand rises, power plants supplying the grid respond, and any plants that burn fossil fuels release the associated pollutants. The data center is the cause of the demand, but the stack that emits sits elsewhere, often in a different state. This indirect link is why corporate sustainability claims and health outcomes can diverge. A company can buy renewable energy certificates that match its annual consumption and still draw hour-by-hour power from a grid that leans on fossil plants. The study does not accuse any named operator of that. It simply shows that the aggregate effect of data center load on the grid carries a measurable human cost. Why the pollution crosses state lines Once emitted, pollutants ride the wind. The paper reports that atmospheric transport carries the resulting pollution across state lines and affects downwind communities. Air does not respect jurisdictional borders, and neither do the chemical reactions that turn precursor gases into fine particles and ozone. A plume released in one state can add to the pollution burden of residents far from the source. The fact sheet for this story does not give a travel distance in miles, and we will not guess one. artigo.texto: World’s first 300 MW artificial-cavern energy storage plant connects to China’s grid China has connected a 300-megawatt compressed air energy storage plant to the power grid, using four underground chambers excavated in hard rock rather than natural salt caverns. The Yuanchu No. 1 facility in Gansu province is designed to store 1.8 gigawatt-hours of electricity, offering another option for large-scale storage in regions without suitable salt formations. The plant achieved its first grid connection on Nov. 16, according to China Energy Engineering Corporation, the project developer. The company describes it as the world's first grid-connected compressed air energy storage (CAES) facility to use purpose-built underground rock caverns, a claim CGTN reported. China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, developed Yuanchu No. 1. The project cost about $374 million (2.5 billion yuan) and is expected to generate 600 gigawatt-hours annually. Its 300-MW generating unit can discharge stored energy for six hours per cycle. Rock caverns store pressurized air underground The facility's storage system consists of four interconnected chambers excavated about 361 feet (110 meters) below ground. Together, they provide roughly 7.1 million cubic feet (200,000 cubic meters) of storage volume and are designed for pressures of up to 18 megapascals. CAES uses electricity to run compressors that force air into a storage space. When electricity is needed, the compressed air is released and expanded through turbines to generate power. The process allows energy produced at one time to be stored and used later, helping balance fluctuations in supply and demand. Yuanchu No. 1 uses an adiabatic, non-combustion design. Instead of burning natural gas to heat the air before it reaches the turbines, the plant captures heat generated during compression and stores it. During discharge, that heat is returned to the compressed air before it expands through the turbines. The thermal system combines pressurized hot water with molten salt to store heat at different temperatures, according to the project report. Water stores lower- and medium-temperature heat, while molten salt stores higher-temperature heat. Both release heat in stages during power generation. An alternative to salt-cavern storage Many underground CAES systems rely on natural salt caverns, which can provide suitable storage but are available only in certain geological settings. Excavating chambers in hard rock could make the technology viable in more locations, although geology and the cost of excavation and sealing remain important constraints. That flexibility could matter in Yumen, which sits in the Hexi Corridor, a major wind and solar development area in northwest China. The plant is intended to absorb surplus renewable electricity when supply is high and return power to the grid when demand increases. China Energy Engineering Corporation says the station has an electricity-to-electricity conversion efficiency of 72%. However, long-term operating data will be needed to establish how efficiently the plant performs in routine service. The project is part of China's wider expansion of compressed air storage. An October 2026 industry report cited by PV Magazine said 13 CAES projects, totaling 4.95 GW and 23.95 GWh, were under construction. Wider deployment will depend on whether projects can demonstrate reliable cavern performance, competitive construction costs, and sustained efficiency.

artigo.texto: From July this year, if a battery loses more than 0.5% of its mass during a vacuum bake test at {{120ºC}} for six hours, you can't legally call it an all-solid-state unit - at least not in China. That single metric matters more than any press release we've read this decade. For the last five years, automakers have put the "solid-state" label on anything with slightly less liquid sloshing around inside. China closed that marketing loophole with the rollout of GB/T 43568-2026. It establishes a formal threshold that strips away the PR fluff and forces OEMs to show actual factory readiness instead of optimistic lab charts. To secure an official all-solid-state designation, the liquid electrolyte must sit below 5% of the total cell weight. In August 2026, the International Electrotechnical Commission officially approved a China-led proposal to establish global testing and application guidelines for automotive solid-state batteries. The implications stretch into how legacy brands engineer their upcoming platforms. China is effectively shaping global markets without exporting a single battery. If you're a Chinese manufacturer already dominating the electric vehicle supply chain, aligning your export models with a domestic standard reduces compliance friction to zero. Foreign competitors face a reverse burden. European and American automakers now have a choice - they can either adapt to a framework designed without their input, or they can spend years trying to draft a new standard from scratch while the market moves on. There is no dedicated European solid-state standard published yet. Japan has advanced R&D, but lacks an equivalent national mandate to enforce it. We're already seeing the results of this regulatory clarity on the ground. Doctex spun up a manufacturing facility in Tianjin producing certified solid-state cells with an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. Far from being some fragile lab prototypes - they are going straight into production vehicles, offering a 15% to 20% bump in real-world driving range. Not everyone is moving at the same pace. Geely is working to complete full vehicle validation and pack layout integration by the third quarter of 2026. BYD has mapped its solid-state development timelines closer to 2027. Saike Power is still pouring concrete for its 0.1 GWh sulfide pilot line down in Yibin, pushing actual machine testing to the final months of 2026. It highlights the massive capital divide between battery suppliers who are fully industrialized and those still chasing the chemistry. State-backed Dongfeng Motor is prepping a 0.2 GWh plant to integrate its own oxide-polymer hybrid cells into a fleet of 100 demonstration vehicles across Hubei province. They're targeting driving ranges pushing toward the 620 miles mark, which sounds absurd until you look at the validation data. During winter testing up in Mohe - one of the coldest places in China - these cells kept 72% of their energy capacity. They also survived high-temperature {{170ºC}} oven bake evaluations without losing structural integrity. That kind of thermal stability addresses the strict thermal runaway and single-cell failure requirements laid out in the mandatory GB 38031-2025 EV safety rules that arrived this summer. The hardware needed to build these cells is also changing. Gotion High-Tech validated a pilot line using 100% locally manufactured machinery, integrating domestic slot-die coaters and high-pressure rollers into the factory floor. This cuts their reliance on international procurement entirely. When you eliminate overseas logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical tariff friction, the cost of scaling drops dramatically. Upgrading production lines with domestic equipment is projected to save the industry billions. It shifts initial factory budgets down to between RMB 400,000,000 and RMB 500,000,000 (roughly $59,000,000 to $74,000,000) per GWh. That financial insulation gives domestic brands a huge buffer against price wars. Western automakers simply don't have that localized machinery leverage yet. But having machinery readily available is only one part of this monumental shift. China is building a layered regulatory framework that scrutinizes every single component inside the pack. The new GB/Z 214-2026 guidance document issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology targets the solid electrolytes themselves. It establishes a uniform vocabulary and strict material parameters for suppliers, ensuring everyone evaluates the same physical characteristics in the exact same way. If an electrolyte material doesn't meet the baseline, it doesn't get CCC certification, and it won't be sold or imported into China. This prevents cell producers from swapping in cheaper, unverified electrolyte compounds to hit cost targets. It treats individual chemical components as distinct product categories with their own (enforceable) technical expectations. But even with this much manufacturing progress, we need to stay realistic about the timelines. CATL has openly acknowledged that widespread commercialization of true all-solid-state batteries will likely be restricted until 2030 due to anomalies in solid-interface resistance. The physics of moving ions through a solid medium at scale without degradation is still a big problem. For now, conventional liquid setups will continue to reach high-volume delivery records. That is the reality of mass manufacturing - the transition simply won't happen overnight, but the technical and safety definitions are now set in stone. By drawing a hard line with the GB/T 43568-2026 classification and pushing it through the IEC, China has ended the era of vague battery marketing. The unified safety standards are next, and it won’t be long before China gets those rubber-stamped. Automakers who want to sell a premium solid-state electric vehicle will have to build one that passes all the tests. For European and American brands, the pressure might be too much. artigo.texto: Ohio OKs gas plant for data centers despite local voter backlash Ohio regulators just greenlit construction of a big gas plant to power a data center complex, despite local residents’ overwhelming rejection of the projects in this month’s elections. The permit approval itself is not unique: Around the U.S., energy-hungry data center developers are racing ahead with controversial plans to build natural gas–fired generation. But critics of the recent Ohio ruling say it highlights the state’s leniency toward fossil-fuel projects compared with its tight restrictions on solar and wind farms, which are often denied permits due to local opposition. “There’s a huge double standard for fossil fuels and renewables in the state of Ohio,” said state Rep. Tristan Rader, a Democrat who serves as ranking minority member on the Ohio House Energy Committee and took part in the case as a nonvoting member of the Ohio Power Siting Board. The gas plant in question is an 800-megawatt facility to be built at a data center complex under development in the central Ohio village of Ashville. As of now, the plant won’t be connected to the grid at large and will serve just the computing warehouses. The project site is close to homes, as well as a playground, park, and soccer field, Rader noted. “This plant is literally going to be throwing a shadow on these communities,” while spewing health-harming pollution, Rader said during the Power Siting Board’s Nov. 19 meeting. Yet Ohio has more stringent requirements for wind and solar, which emit zero air pollution. Ashville’s Village Council passed a resolution in April to back the data center and gas plant project, after its developer, EdgeConneX, agreed to pay up to $102 million to support municipal, school, and community work. But the deal didn’t sit well with some residents, who gathered enough signatures for a referendum on whether to overturn the resolution. On Election Day, Ashville was one of dozens of U.S. communities to reject data centers, with 81% of the village’s voters opposing the local government’s agreement with EdgeConneX. Even so, the Power Siting Board’s decision OK’ing the gas plant finds that the developer met a statutory requirement that the project is in the public interest. Regulators pointed to factors like the project’s economic benefits, backing from the Village Council and local school district, and the developer’s promises to limit noise and construction hours. That’s sparked frustration from clean energy advocates in the state. The board has denied multiple solar projects on the basis that local opposition outweighs economic benefits or has proposed permit conditions aimed at addressing community concerns, said Chris Tavenor, general counsel for the Ohio Environmental Council, which was not a party to the case. “In this case, the Board does the exact opposite, using those community benefits and conditions to justify ignoring local concerns,” he said in an email. In this decision and those pertaining to renewable energy, critics take issue with the Power Siting Board’s deference to local governments, even when evidence shows they are not necessarily reflecting the wishes of the broader public. In 2025, for example, the Power Siting Board’s staff recommended against the Grange Solar project in Logan County on the basis of pushback from local governments. But a majority of individuals who submitted comments wanted the solar farm. The developer ultimately withdrew its plan and opted to pursue projects elsewhere. And earlier this year, regulators nixed the Crossroads Solar farm in Morrow County because all nearby local governments opposed the project. Although that ruling noted the “presence of strong, united opposition” among the local population, dozens of comments were apparently fake, and an analysis by the developer found that the number of verifiable individuals against the project was not overwhelming in comparison with its supporters. The board’s staff also did an about-face from supporting Crossroads Solar to opposing it after one township changed its position from neutral to opposed. “Ultimately, the Ohio Power Siting Board has demonstrated its hypocrisy,” Tavenor said, “by approving a natural gas facility for a data center where it has denied renewable energy projects with less significant opposition.” Regulators, for their part, acknowledged the Ashville vote in their decision but asserted that they have authority to issue the permit regardless of the outcome of the election. The 108-page opinion also says that conditions agreed to by the village, the developer, and the board staff were enough to deal with public concerns. The board also gave short shrift to opponents’ argument that the gas plant proposal fails to meet a separate legal requirement that projects have minimal environmental impact. Its take stems from the fact that the developer opted for reciprocating internal combustion engines and simple-cycle natural gas turbines over less-polluting combined-cycle turbines or fuel cells, which are more expensive right now. Regulatory staff argued that “minimum” doesn’t demand the lowest environmental impact but depends on a plant’s purpose, available technology, and economics. The board decided that the project meets the requirement, basically punting to the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency’s expected issuance of air permits for the facility. Project opponents have 30 days to ask for reconsideration of the ruling. Unless the Power Siting Board changes its mind, an appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court could follow. Kathiann M. Kowalski is a contributing reporter at Canary Media who covers Ohio.

artigo.texto: A Europa está resgatando suas velhas usinas desativadas para lhes dar uma segunda vida: virar data centers Com 700 MW assegurados e filas de espera que chegam a 10 anos, usinas desativadas na Europa voltam a valer verdadeiras fortunas no boom da IA A energética alemã Uniper planeja converter usinas desativadas no Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda em data centers. O negócio inicial, que prevê a transformação de uma unidade e negociações avançadas para outras duas, aproveita o espaço e o acesso garantido à transmissão elétrica. Com capacidade estimada em 700 MW, essa infraestrutura pode abastecer cerca de sete data centers de hiperescala, marcando uma nova vida para instalações históricas em resposta à crescente demanda digital europeia. A empresa de energia alemã Uniper está prestes a fechar um negócio que pode dar um verdadeiro salto aos centros de dados na Europa: o plano é converter suas usinas desativadas na infraestrutura mais disputada do momento, como revelou o Financial Times. Essas antigas instalações têm tudo o que um data center precisa: espaço de sobra, boas vias de acesso e, o mais importante, uma conexão garantida à rede de transmissão de energia elétrica. Um acordo cercado de sigilo O negócio ainda é cercado de segredo, mas dois detalhes cruciais já vieram a público. O primeiro é que a energética está a ponto de selar um contrato em uma de suas 10 propriedades paradas — distribuídas entre Reino Unido, Alemanha, Suécia e Holanda — para transformá-la em um centro de processamento de dados, além de manter conversas avançadas sobre outras duas localidades. O segundo é que seu CEO, Michael Lewis, calcula em cerca de 700 MW a capacidade de rede elétrica assegurada nesses pontos. De acordo com a Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), essa potência seria suficiente para abastecer em torno de sete data centers de hiperescala ou perto de 70 instalações de menor porte. Ainda não se sabe com certeza quais desses 10 locais serão contemplados, embora haja fortes pistas de que as primeiras opções fiquem no Reino Unido e na Alemanha, como o próprio executivo deixou escapar em meados do ano. artigo.texto: The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint. Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this” To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit. Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice). With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever. To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside. Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency. “That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event. In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found. To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation. Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” “In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports. Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. artigo.texto: Despite the recent attention on new electric demand created by data centers, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries sees greater potential for long-term growth in the utilities sector, MHI President and CEO Eisaku Ito said earlier this month. Utilities and independent power producers accounted for 94% of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ new gas turbine orders in 2024 and 2025, Ito said. Although many U.S. data center operators say they intend to install their own off-grid generation, Ito argued that these plans rely on smaller gas-fired power plants that cost more to run than the larger plants utilities and IPPs are pursuing. In the long-term, Ito said, the cost differential will push data centers to connect to the grid, ultimately supporting utilities' expansion plans. His comments, made during a call with analysts on Nov. 6, according to a translated transcript, come as fallout from the U.S. midterm elections and stock market volatility raise questions about the future of the artificial intelligence buildout in North America. Ito expressed confidence in utilities' long-term expansion plans, arguing that growing demand for electricity does not rely solely on data centers. “Electricity demand from data centers is expected to grow rapidly in the United States, but data centers still account for only around 10% of the country's total electricity demand,” Ito said. “If some of the anticipated growth in demand does not materialize, there will be some impact, but we believe the effect on our overall GTCC business would be limited.” MHI booked 8 GW in orders for large frame gas turbines in the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, compared to 16 GW of orders in all of FY 2025. Profit for the company’s Energy Systems segment rose 80% on account of increased orders and shifts in the value of the yen, according to the company's financial statements. “We are also beginning to see the benefits of improved pricing on new unit projects, lower loss-related costs and greater production efficiency,” MHI CFO Hiroshi Nishio said. Company executives said they continue to take a conservative approach to forecasting demand and expanding manufacturing capacity. The company expects global demand for gas turbines at all manufacturers and makers to average about 70 GW per year over the next five years — somewhat lower than the 100 GW MHI expects will sell across all manufactuers this year amid what Ito characterized as “exceptionally strong” demand he does not anticipate will continue. But Ito said he remains confident in MHI’s company backlog, noting that the company vets new orders carefully and hasn’t had any order cancellations in the past two years. The company plans to double its gas turbine production capacity by 2030, though most of the additional capacity will come from improved processes and automation at existing plants in the U.S. and Japan. “We are improving productivity and driving other initiatives at a pace that outstrips the growth in orders,” he said. MHI also signaled that it's exploring opportunities to expand into other infrastructure-related markets. Ito said MHI will release additional details in May, but suggested the company is interested in expanding its gas turbine service and repair capabilities, as well as investing in unmanned systems that can operate in harsh environments. At the same time, MHI plans to divest some of its aerospace business, he said. “These examples may seem quite different, but they all share a common theme: resilience,” Ito said. “We aim to identify new business opportunities in infrastructure and industrial machinery through the lens of resilience and turn them into future growth.”

artigo.texto: A new study from the University of Oklahoma puts hard numbers behind a question that planning boards across the country keep asking: what draws data centers to a community? According to the University of Oklahoma announcement, researchers examined 212 U.S. data centers run by 11 major technology companies, including Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta. Land-use diversity came out as the strongest factor, ahead of the other signals the team tested. The story is dated November 20, 2026, with an update on November 22. It lands at a moment when cloud and AI operators are hunting for sites faster than most local governments can write zoning rules. Our earlier look at an immersion-only data center pitched at under 30,000 square feet showed how much the building itself is changing. The OU work asks a different question: not how to build the hall, but why a given town gets it. This analysis walks through what the study found, what it left out, and what the findings mean for cloud planners, local officials and anyone who has watched a substation upgrade or a rezoning notice appear at the edge of town. We keep to the facts the university has published. Where the record is thin, we say so. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the OU Study Actually Measured Kijin Seong, Ph.D., is an assistant professor in the Division of Planning, Landscape Architecture and Design at OU’s Christopher C. Gibbs College of Architecture. He co-authored the research. The team did not survey executives or ask companies to explain their reasoning. Instead, it looked at where 212 existing facilities sit and tested which local characteristics tracked with those locations. The sample spans 11 major technology companies. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are named in the announcement, and the other seven are not identified in the material we reviewed. That matters for readers who want company-by-company patterns. The published summary reports aggregate findings, so we cannot say whether Meta favors different communities than Microsoft does. The analysis grouped its explanatory factors into three families: land use, infrastructure and workforce. Land use covers the mix of activities in the surrounding area. Infrastructure covers electrical substations and major roads. Workforce covers concentrations of information technology workers. Those three families gave the researchers a way to compare very different sites on the same terms. Land-Use Diversity: The Strongest Factor in Data Center Site Selection The headline result is the one that surprises people. Land-use diversity, meaning a neighborhood or district that mixes housing, commerce, industry and services, was the strongest factor the analysis identified. Many readers would have guessed that wide-open, single-purpose land wins. The OU team found the reverse pattern holds up better in the data. Why would a mixed area attract a server hall? The study summary does not offer a causal story, and we will not invent one. What we can say is that mixed-use areas tend to come with the things a large facility needs to function: established utility service, road networks, nearby workers and a local government used to permitting different kinds of buildings. A diverse land-use pattern may work as a proxy for all of that. What diversity does and does not mean Diversity here describes the surrounding community, not the data center parcel. A site can sit on a quiet lot and still score high if the district around it mixes uses. For local officials, that distinction changes the pitch. A town does not need to rezone everything for servers. It needs to look like a place where varied development already happens. Practitioners have long published checklists that treat land as a gate. A site selection criteria guide from Base Operations is one example of that genre, which lists the factors developers screen before they commit. The OU analysis adds something those checklists rarely supply: a pattern drawn from where 212 real facilities actually went. Substations, Roads and IT Workers: The Supporting Signals Three more factors helped explain where facilities landed. Proximity to electrical substations, access to major roads and concentrations of information technology workers all showed up in the analysis. None of them beat land-use diversity, but each one added explanatory power. The substation finding fits the physical logic of the business. A data hall is, at its core, a very large electrical load with cooling attached. Sitting close to a substation shortens the path between the grid and the racks. It does not guarantee capacity, and the OU summary reports no megawatt figures, so readers should not read the finding as a statement about how much power any site gets. Major roads matter for less glamorous reasons. Construction crews, generators, cooling equipment and replacement hardware all arrive by truck. Roads also bring staff to the door during shifts. The study treats road access as one measurable proxy for that logistics burden. The IT workforce signal is the most interesting for smaller communities. Facilities cluster where technology workers already live. That suggests that talent, not just land and power, shapes the map. Towns hoping to land a cloud region should ask whether they can supply or attract the people who run it. artigo.texto: As the engines of artificial intelligence, large data centers can consume as much power as medium-sized cities, straining grids and prompting expensive upgrades to U.S. energy infrastructure. New research finds that residents, and especially lower-income and rural residents, are disproportionately bearing the costs. In the study, published Nov. 9 in Nature Energy, Cornell researchers analyzed growth in energy demand and infrastructure projects for four major U.S. power grids from 2020 to 2025 and found that data centers have hiked wholesale energy prices and on average paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs linked to their growth — $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill in 2025. The remaining $5.13 billion, or 62 percent, fell largely on residents, with the lowest income households seeing extra energy costs up to 28 percent of their incomes. “We were trying to answer a very simple question: With the booming of data centers, who pays for that expansion and who benefits?” said Fengqi You, the Roxanne E. and Michael J. Zak Professor in Energy Systems Engineering in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering. “It’s not just a question of generating enough electricity but of whether the rules for paying for the grid are keeping pace with who is driving new demand.” The research is the first multi-region, long-term assessment of how data center development impacts infrastructure growth and how costs are distributed across communities. It comes amidst a boom in data center construction. The researchers found that transmission investment in energy infrastructure projects increased from $2 billion in 2020 to $34 billion in 2025, with data centers driving much of that rise. Debates are ongoing – from local communities to state governments to Congress – about who picks up the bill as growth accelerates; data centers are projected to consume between 8% and 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with 70% to 80% of that attributed to AI. With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site). “In a lot of discussions right now, people take one side or the other, completely yes on data centers or completely no,” said You, director of the Cornell AI for Sustainability Initiative. “But there are benefits and costs, and the key issue in the end is how to balance the trade-offs.” Sharing the cost of power infrastructure The team analyzed data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers, as well as power-price records, rate filings from utilities, power-line plans, and federal household and job data. The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date. State incentives for data centers have provided returns on the investments, if inconsistently, the researchers found. Some states, such as California, reaped $180 in worker income for every dollar spent, while Virginia increased income $2 for every dollar invested. The researchers determined that the presence of an existing, qualified workforce was a stronger indicator of high returns than the amount of incentive spending. Data centers also increased wholesale electricity prices, the amounts utilities pay regional power markets before delivering the electricity to homes. In the most-affected hubs, data center growth raised those prices by nearly 10 percent or more by 2025. In Virginia, the costs jumped 15 percent and in California’s southern Bay Area, 20 percent. In contrast, residents in New York and New England, where data center construction has been limited, have not seen clear price increases due to data center expansion, the researchers found. “I think that means we’re at a good starting point in New York to think about the next steps,” You said. “Economic benefits, job benefits, investment, fairly allocating the costs – these are the dimensions and trade-offs we need to consider.” A key problem is how the costs of new infrastructure projects are currently shared: The allocation is often based on previous patterns of energy consumption. “It’s kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” You said. “Because if you’re going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there’s no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they’re not using energy. So with this model of relying on past consumption, households end up taking on much of the infrastructure costs.” Many more rural and lower-income residents saw proportionally higher bills; the share of rural families shouldering a high energy burden — spending more than 6% of their incomes on energy – rose 76% more than among urban residents. The authors cite a national survey finding that rural residents are also less likely to use AI tools like ChatGPT than urban residents. The impact on energy bills also has a wide geographical reach. For example, residents in New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio help pay for grid upgrades linked to data center growth in Virginia, the researchers said. “You do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure,” You said. “The grid connects communities across states, and cost-sharing rules connect them financially.” Using insights from the data, You and Feng recommend changes to cost-sharing rules and strategies to lower burdens. In all four regions, they found that, if data centers cut back power use during 22 of the region’s peak demand hours each year, they would relieve strain on the grid and minimize the need to expand. artigo.texto: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant that the company would not own or control, according to documents reviewed by Reuters and a person with direct knowledge of the request. The company rejected the proposal, saying such a stake would likely garner public scrutiny, risk future capital-raising, and outweigh any benefit to shareholders, the documents from July and August showed. “51% is far outside precedent and invites scrutiny,” Pure Lithium’s legal counsel Skadden Arps wrote in an 22 August memorandum reviewed by Reuters that outlined Lutnick’s request. The federal government’s unsuccessful attempt to take majority control of Pure Lithium has not been previously reported. This article is based on documents that include emails between Pure Lithium and the Commerce Department discussing a meeting between Lutnick and Pure Lithium’s CEO, as well as a memorandum written by Pure Lithium’s legal counsel outlining Lutnick’s request. Lutnick’s plan marks one of the latest moves by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company, and comes as the secretary and former investment banker faces increased scrutiny over his ties to corporate executives and companies affected by decisions made by his department. The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies since Donald Trump returned to the White House, including chipmaker Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), extending its reach into the private sector in a way recent administrations have not. However, it has not taken a majority stake in any company, with its most serious effort a proposed rescue of Spirit Airlines, the low-budget airline that ceased operations in May. Thus far, the largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials (NYSE:MP), which would make it the largest shareholder. A Pure Lithium representative, when asked about the proposal, did not dispute the account. The Commerce Department did not respond to questions about the proposal posed by Reuters for this story. It is not illegal for the federal government to acquire equity stakes in a private company and the administration has defended these efforts, particularly through using funds stemming from 2022’s CHIPS Act, which was designed to boost domestic research and manufacturing of semiconductors. Lawmakers opposed to the practice, though, contend the law never authorised such ownership. No court has ruled on the question. Privately held Pure Lithium has developed a lithium metal battery that it says is far more efficient than a traditional lithium-ion battery and can be built without graphite, nickel, or cobalt. If Pure Lithium’s battery can deliver, it would be a major advancement for the energy storage industry. If mass produced, the battery could potentially shift how the US military and other federal contractors power millions of devices, analysts have said. At a 29 July meeting in Washington with Pure Lithium CEO Emilie Bodoin, Lutnick expressed interest in the battery’s capabilities, including its efficiency. He said the US government needed to control the company so the battery could be used by the US military and other agencies, according to the person and documents reviewed by Reuters. The two had been meeting to discuss a legal dispute with Japan’s Panasonic (TYO:6752) related to the battery technology, according to the person and the documents. The meeting, which lasted roughly 45 minutes, was arranged by billionaire Robert Friedland, one of Pure Lithium’s largest shareholders. A company co-founded by Friedland, I-Pulse, received US$250 million ($366.36 million) from the Commerce Department in June. Friedland attended the July meeting alongside David Shapiro, a senior adviser at the Commerce Department, according to the documents. Through a spokesperson, Friedland declined to comment for this article. The White House has repeatedly said strategic investments in the minerals and related sectors are needed because they are critical to US economic competitiveness. The White House did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Reuters has no evidence that Lutnick personally holds a stake in either I-Pulse or Pure Lithium. A Commerce Department spokesperson, speaking on behalf of Lutnick, said she did not think he is invested in either company. Both companies are privately held and do not need to disclose their ownership. US control discussed As part of his effort to persuade Bodoin to give the government the controlling stake, Lutnick said the takeover could also help with the Panasonic dispute, according to the person. Pure Lithium sued Panasonic in March, accusing the Japanese company of reverse-engineering Pure Lithium’s lithium metal battery technology, an allegation Panasonic disputes. The case is set for a January hearing to decide whether to grant Pure Lithium a preliminary injunction against Panasonic. The Commerce chief had previously helped negotiate a tariff-linked agreement last year that included a US$550 billion pledge from Tokyo to invest in the US economy. In exchange for the majority stake, Lutnick said that US$1 billion from Japan’s pledge would be set aside to build a manufacturing plant that a special-purpose investment vehicle controlled by Tokyo and Washington would own, according to an 22 August memo from Pure Lithium’s attorneys to Friedland. However, Pure Lithium would not have received any funding under the proposal, according to the documents. The company would have been contracted to operate but not own the plant, and would be granted a portion of the plant’s revenue after paying for the debt servicing costs on the invested US$1 billion. Lutnick also told Pure Lithium to send 100 of its batteries to the Energy and Defense departments for testing, according to the documents. Pure Lithium rejected Lutnick’s request

artigo.texto: St. Charles may get a battery storage system meant to reduce energy costs as part of a pilot program with its electricity provider, even while the city’s future with the Illinois Municipal Electric Agency, or IMEA, remains uncertain. The city is looking to work with IMEA, which would pay for and manage the project, on the construction of a battery storage facility that St. Charles would take over management of in the event the city does not continue to get its energy from the electricity provider past 2035. Generally speaking, a battery energy storage system, or BESS, works by storing electrical energy in batteries so it can be used later, said St. Charles Director of Public Works Peter Suhr at a meeting of the St. Charles City Council’s Committee of the Whole on Nov. 16, at which a measure expressing the city’s support for participating in the pilot program was recommended for approval. Such a system can lower utility bills by storing electrical energy when the energy is least expensive, and then discharging that stored energy when prices are at their highest, Suhr said. It can also improve electricity reliability because a system can act as a backup generator during power outages. The measure recently recommended for approval by the Committee of the Whole is essentially a preliminary step to allow St. Charles to work with IMEA on the proposed battery storage project in the city. At this point, the city is looking for council approval for initial analysis work and participation in a request for proposals with IMEA for the project, Suhr said. The project is set to be formalized in a contract around March, Suhr said. St. Charles is one of 32 municipalities across Illinois that are part of IMEA, a nonprofit joint action agency that sells electric power to municipally-owned utilities, per its website. The city began purchasing partial electric power for its electric utility with IMEA in 1999, and entered into its current contract to get all of its electric power from them in 2004. The city is among those served by PJM Interconnection, the regional grid that includes northern Illinois, 12 other states and the District of Columbia. The downstate area is part of the Midwest Independent System Operator grid, or MISO, which also serves 14 other states from Mississippi to North Dakota as well as Manitoba in Canada. As part of a sustainability plan that details its goal of reducing the power supplied to its member municipalities to net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, IMEA has been looking at the feasibility of utility-scale behind-the-meter battery storage on its member distribution systems, according to its website, and it is now looking to pursue pilot projects for this technology. Several months ago, IMEA sent out requests for proposals to all 32 municipalities, with the goal of having one battery storage pilot in the PJM market, and another in the MISO market, Suhr said. According to Suhr, IMEA received responses from both Naperville and St. Charles, but St. Charles was ultimately selected for the planned pilot. The idea behind the pilot program is to allow city staff and IMEA to “dip (their) toes into this technology,” Suhr said. If successful, it could be scaled up in the future. Being part of the pilot would give the city hands-on experience with battery storage technology and help prepare its electric utility for future power supply decisions, a city memo indicated. The program anticipates systems in the range of 1 MW to 5 MW, with a capacity of about four hours’ worth of energy, or less than 1% of St. Charles’ total peak load, Suhr said. The proposed location of the battery storage system is at a substation between Kirk Road and the East Side Sports Complex. This proposal comes as St. Charles’ long-term relationship with IMEA remains uncertain. Last year, the City Council voted against extending its contract with the electricity provider after its current agreement expires in 2035, though returning to IMEA is not necessarily out of the question for good. Among the major concerns raised about the IMEA contract was the potential environmental impact of the city getting its electricity from the cooperative electric supplier. One of IMEA’s primary suppliers is a downstate coal plant called Prairie State that was one of the top 10 biggest polluters in the country, according to 2023 data from the United States Environmental Protection Agency. How nearby Naperville, another IMEA member, will procure its electricity post-2035 is similarly still playing out. Participating in the battery storage pilot with IMEA would not lead to any direct costs to St. Charles until at least 2035, because IMEA would be handling things like construction and maintenance, Suhr said. But, if the city opts not to continue working with IMEA, St. Charles would be responsible for costs associated with the battery storage system. A system like this is expected to cost the city around $100,000 to $200,000 annually, according to Suhr. The measure recommended for approval at the Nov. 16 Committee of the Whole meeting essentially allows the city to move forward with participating in the pilot program. The measure is expected to come to the City Council for final approval on Dec. 7, per the resolution. From there, IMEA would seek vendors for the project, Suhr said, and an official contract would be expected to come back to the City Council for approval around March. mmorrow@chicagotribune.com

artigo.texto: VNET Group Q3 2026: Wholesale Data Center Capacity Surges 44% on AI Demand As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on November 23, 2026. AI demand is showing up in the capacity numbers: wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, plus a fresh 60MW order from a major cloud provider. The loss per ADS beat expectations, full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed, and the board authorized a $50 million ADS buyback against a $611 million market cap. Continue ReadingShow less VNET Group posted a GAAP loss per ADS of $0.04 for the third quarter of 2026, beating expectations. Part of that came from a fair-value gain on financial instruments that meaningfully narrowed the net loss attributable to VNET to $12.44 million, compared with $45.97 million in the same period a year earlier. VNET reported $443.66 million in total net revenues, missing expectations, though the figure still represented 15.4% growth year over year. Wholesale IDC was the strongest segment, with revenues up 27.6% year over year and reaching 41.1% of total net revenues, while retail IDC grew a more modest 5.1%. Wholesale data center capacity in service jumped 44% year over year to 1,127MW, and the quarter ended with a fresh 60MW order from a leading cloud service provider, a concrete signal that AI-driven demand is translating into contracted business. Another 548MW of wholesale capacity was under construction at quarter end. Sponsored Despite the revenue miss, management reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance, targeting revenues of $1.72 billion to $1.77 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $531.47 million to $561.41 million. The board also authorized a $50 million ADS repurchase program, a notable capital return commitment against a $611 million market cap. Risks worth watching include gross margin compression from heavier depreciation as the rapid capacity build comes online, a wholesale utilization rate that slipped to 70.7% from 74.3% a year earlier as new capacity ramps up, and a significant debt load. Regulatory scrutiny around Chinese firms accessing Nvidia computing power abroad adds an additional layer of uncertainty the guidance does not fully address. Sources Mentioned: VNET

artigo.texto: Citing concerns about its effects on the environment and residents’ health, members of the South Whitehall community on Monday pleaded with officials from the state Department of Environmental Protection to reject a massive data center across the road from Parkland High School. During a three-hour meeting at Cedar Crest College, the DEP fielded questions and listened to testimony from people who live near the proposed $8.9 billion Project Atlas site, or who have children attending the high school. Representatives from Project Atlas developer CDE Acquisitions LLC- Edged US also answered questions about the project, though few in the audience seemed satisfied with their answers. Alice Lenthe, an environmental engineer and member of the South Whitehall Civic Alliance, which is raising money to fight the project in court, urged the DEP to consider the wildlife that would disappear if wetlands on the data center site were destroyed. She noted that Edged has proposed buying wetlands in another part of the Lehigh River watershed through mitigation credits — something that is allowed under the federal Clean Water Act — to make up for the wetlands they’d destroy in South Whitehall, but said that wasn’t enough. “The loss of wetlands is a local issue. While the DEP permits the purchase of credits, those credits do nothing to alleviate the enormous harm that Project Atlas, if approved, would impose on the environment of this community,” she said. Lenthe blasted the developer’s vague answers to her questions about their plan, and said Edged did not respect the community it was trying to become part of. “In this, as with every other aspect of Project Atlas, Edged shows their contempt of local residents and the local environment,” Lenthe said. Monday’s review was a key stepping stone for the proposed 1.5 million-square-foot campus on Cedar Crest Boulevard. At stake are two permits the developer needs to begin construction near tributaries of Coplay Creek and Jordan Creek. There is no deadline for the DEP to rule on the permits. South Whitehall Township manager Tom Petrucci testified that the township is not recommending approval of the project at this time, since the township engineer has identified unresolved issues, including how stormwater would move through the site and affect neighboring properties. Logan Kreglow, another South Whitehall resident, raised concerns about waivers the developer is seeking related to stormwater management at the Mauch Chunk intersection leading into the proposed construction zone. Kreglow, a civil engineer, reminded the DEP representatives that Edged filed their waiver application on Aug. 8, 10 days before Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order mandating that all data centers go through an extended two-part DEP review. Under the order, data centers must get local officials’ approval before seeking DEP permits. “Atlas hurried their application to avoid a more thorough and appropriate permit review process,” Kreglow said. “This is exactly the type of project the executive order is meant to protect us from. Do not let them be grandfathered in.” In a statement posted online after the meeting, the South Whitehall Civic Alliance said they were disappointed that they didn’t get answers from the developer about other environmental concerns, including how soil contaminated with arsenic and lead would be addressed during construction, whether the lithium ion batteries that will be used in the data center operation were safe, as well as questions about noise and air pollution testing. “Residents should not have to ask the same questions repeatedly, only to receive vague assurances instead of substantive answers. If the applicant’s representatives cannot explain these issues at a public meeting, DEP should not consider those concerns resolved,” Alliance members wrote. Project Atlas developers will be back before the planning commission Jan. 13. That meeting will be held at Parkland High School. The deadline for the township to act on the plan is Feb. 28. The DEP will continue to collect written testimony from people affected by the data center project until Dec. 7. Comments can be emailed to pkania@pa.gov.
