artigo.texto: Os carros estão cada vez mais parecidos com smartphones sobre rodas e precisam de conectividade para melhorar a experiência dos motoristas. É de olho nessa transformação que a TIM está ampliando sua presença na indústria automotiva. A operadora acaba de fechar uma parceria com a BYD para oferecer conectividade embarcada inicialmente a cerca de 200 mil veículos da montadora chinesa nos próximos dois anos. O acordo também prevê a instalação de uma infraestrutura dedicada de redes 5G e 4G no complexo industrial da BYD em Camaçari – a maior fábrica de veículos eletrificados da América Latina. A parceria faz parte da estratégia da operadora de ampliar sua atuação no mercado corporativo, através da unidade TIM B2B Solutions, oferecendo portfólio de soluções que vão desde a conectividade a serviços de tecnologia. Detalhe: a iniciativa ganha escala em um momento de expansão da BYD no mercado brasileiro. A montadora ultrapassou a marca de 300 mil veículos em circulação no País em 2026. “Hoje, a tecnologia é um dos principais motores de transformação da indústria automotiva e da mobilidade,” disse Alberto Griselli, CEO da TIM Brasil. Nos veículos da BYD, a tecnologia utilizada será o eSIM – uma espécie de chip digital que facilita a ativação remota de serviços. A solução da TIM permitirá interações com motoristas desenvolvidas pela montadora em seu próprio aplicativo e através das mídias no carro. Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da BYD do Brasil e head de marketing e comercial da BYD Auto, diz que a ideia é que a experiência digital do consumidor continue evoluindo ao longo da vida útil do automóvel. Segundo o executivo, a parceria com a TIM vai permitir à BYD ampliar a oferta de serviços e funcionalidades e garantir que a experiência de quem escolhe a marca continue evoluindo mesmo depois que o veículo sair da concessionária. “O consumidor brasileiro está cada vez mais exigente, e não basta oferecer um carro com tecnologia de ponta se essa experiência não continuar evoluindo ao longo do tempo,” disse Baldy. A outra frente da parceria está em Camaçari, onde a BYD inaugurou sua maior operação industrial fora da China. O complexo ocupa uma área de 4,6 milhões de metros quadrados, que será atendida pela infraestrutura de conectividade da TIM. O projeto prevê a instalação de sete pontos de cobertura externa e 63 equipamentos distribuídos entre os galpões e as áreas operacionais da fábrica. A cobertura dedicada foi planejada para acompanhar o crescimento da produção e conectar não apenas os colaboradores e visitantes, mas também os sistemas operacionais e os próprios veículos ainda durante a fabricação. Com isso, diz o CEO da TIM, diferentes etapas da operação poderão trocar informações em tempo real, facilitando a integração dos processos industriais e abrindo espaço para novas aplicações digitais. A infraestrutura também foi dimensionada para acompanhar a expansão da capacidade produtiva da montadora, combinando conectividade e digitalização industrial. Para a TIM, o acordo com a BYD representa mais um avanço em um mercado que vem ganhando importância com a digitalização dos veículos e das operações industriais. A companhia já conecta mais de 670 mil veículos por meio de soluções da chamada Internet dos Veículos (Internet of Vehicles, ou IoV): uma tecnologia que permite integrar automóveis a redes e serviços digitais. “Esta parceria com a BYD une a digitalização de uma das mais importantes operações industriais em desenvolvimento no Brasil à evolução da conectividade embarcada dos veículos,” disse Griselli. Segundo Griselli, a operadora também oferece soluções de Internet das Coisas (IoT), computação em nuvem, cibersegurança e aplicações com inteligência artificial para apoiar a transformação digital de empresas de diferentes setores – que já são linhas de negócios relevantes dentro da companhia.

artigo.texto: Sellersburg updates zoning rules for data centers, solar farms Sellersburg, Indiana, has unanimously approved new zoning regulations for data centers, solar farms, and energy storage facilities, requiring developers to apply for zoning changes and go through a public approval process. Town leaders passed the ordinance to address what they described as a gray area in the previous development rules. Under the old ordinance, developers could argue that such facilities could be built in industrial zones. The new regulations establish "solar energy district" and "data center district" as specific zoning categories, though no properties are currently zoned for these uses. "Because there are no current zones of those uses, there would have to be a very public process that would have to go to where someone who wanted to potentially do that, if they ever did, they'd have to come through the town process to get something rezoned and basically so they'd have to send out letters," Town Manager Charlie Smith said. "According to state statute, there would be public hearings. They'd have to come to the zoning meeting, present to the zoning planning commission for their zoning change request, and then the planning commission would then make a recommendation to the town council, and the elected town council would have the ultimate final say on those type of uses," he added. Officials noted that only two properties within the town limits have the capacity to accommodate such developments. "I think that our biggest goal was to make sure that we just went on ahead and put it to rest and made everybody understand the fact that they were not in favor of nothing like this, nor do we want anything like this in our community, and to be able to tighten up the rules and regulations a little bit more," Sellersburg Town Council President Brad Amos said. The council president and town manager emphasized that the change ensures decisions remain with elected officials, reducing the likelihood of legal disputes. "This needs to be decided by the people that are appointed and elected by the body with the community's input, which it was. And then we could take this, put it to our standards, eliminate the gray area, and here's what it is. Here's what it's not. Here's the process. If you don't like it, maybe this isn't the community for you," Smith said. The new zoning standards also apply to large-scale energy storage facilities, with the regulation intended to protect properties within the town limits in the future.

artigo.texto: The boundaries between smart home technology, household appliances and residential energy management are becoming increasingly blurred. Midea, a name increasingly familiar to many Australian households through its air conditioners, refrigeration, laundry and other household appliances, is taking another step into that convergence with the launch of its residential energy storage business in Australia. Announced on 24 November 2026, the expansion brings Midea’s PowerInfi and Omni X energy storage solutions to the local market, following their Australian debut at All Energy Australia in Melbourne last month. Under its vision of “Energy Links All”, Midea is positioning its energy storage business around accessible residential energy solutions, drawing on its existing manufacturing capabilities and research and development across the broader household technology ecosystem. PowerInfi: An all-in-one residential energy storage system Leading Midea’s Australian energy storage portfolio is PowerInfi, an all-in-one residential energy storage system. When paired with a suitable rooftop solar installation, residential battery systems allow households to store surplus electricity generated during the day for use later, potentially reducing grid electricity purchases and improving the utilisation of existing solar investments. PowerInfi features a modular design and was recognised with a 2026 Red Dot Design Award, with judges highlighting its robust construction and user-oriented operating system. The system represents a significant expansion of Midea’s existing household technology portfolio, bringing energy storage alongside products that are among the largest consumers of electricity in Australian homes. Omni X provides another option for Australian households Midea is also introducing Omni X, a standalone energy storage solution showcased in a 7kWh battery configuration. Designed with flexibility in mind, Omni X provides installers and homeowners with another option when considering energy storage solutions suited to their household requirements. Australian pricing, available system configurations and detailed technical specifications were not provided as part of the launch announcement. From household appliances to whole-home energy management What makes Midea’s entry into this market particularly interesting to me is not simply the arrival of another residential battery manufacturer. Throughout 2026, DRN has been getting to know Midea across an increasingly diverse range of household appliances, from ice makers and benchtop dishwashers to inverter microwaves and, more recently, the Athena air conditioner. Each represents a different type of household energy demand, from refrigeration cycles and water heating to short bursts of high-power cooking and sustained climate control. In our Midea 3 Place Benchtop Mini Dishwasher Plus review, Peter measured actual electricity consumption across different wash programs, looking beyond the energy efficiency label to understand real-world running costs. Our coverage of the Midea 45L Smart Inverter Microwave explored inverter technology in a household appliance characterised by relatively short periods of high energy demand. The 12kg ice maker, meanwhile, represents another type of discretionary household load, where the timing of operation could potentially be aligned with periods of cheaper electricity or surplus solar generation. Meanwhile, my own experience with the Midea Athena has taken things a step further, integrating the air conditioner into Home Assistant and exploring how its operation can be aligned with my three-hour daily free electricity window. Rather than simply reacting to room temperature, I can begin to consider electricity pricing as part of the decision-making process for heating and cooling the home. (Full review is coming!) These are individual examples of something I have been exploring for some time: how we can move beyond evaluating household appliances in isolation and start considering their collective impact on household energy consumption. Connecting the dots with SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER Back in September, DRN covered Midea’s unveiling of its SMART MASTER whole-home AI ecosystem at IFA 2026. Among the technologies showcased in Berlin was AI ECOMASTER, Midea’s approach to coordinating household energy consumption across connected appliances, solar generation and battery storage, taking into account changing household demand and electricity prices. At the time, we identified intelligent energy management as one of the more compelling practical applications of whole-home AI. Today’s Australian residential energy storage announcement adds another important piece to that picture. With Midea now offering both energy storage and many of the appliances that consume electricity throughout the home, the potential exists to bring generation, storage and consumption together under a more coordinated energy management strategy. What remains to be established is how PowerInfi and Omni X fit into Midea’s wider SMART MASTER and AI ECOMASTER ambitions, particularly for Australian households. There are also important questions around interoperability with existing solar installations, third-party appliances, open smart home platforms such as Home Assistant and Australia’s increasingly diverse electricity tariffs. Having spent much of 2026 exploring different parts of Midea’s appliance portfolio, I am particularly interested in seeing how those pieces might eventually work together. The battery itself is only part of the story. The intelligence connecting it to the rest of the household could ultimately be just as important. artigo.texto: SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ. The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported. The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors. Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built. The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms. In Texas, a land swap puts the project past a moratorium The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported. Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it. That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.” Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported, citing Politico. The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune. Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters. The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections. In Arizona, a 6-gigawatt campus tests a rural grid The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star. It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades. SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star. The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs. Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure. On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement. She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3. Is growth paying for growth? Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. artigo.texto: The EU and UK have reached an agreement to link their Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), with the aim of going operational by 2028. Incineration of waste, excluding landfill, is included among the sectors and activities covered by the linking agreement. EU and UK leaders have committed to applying the agreement as of 1 January 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK. The intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025 and means that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel. The European Commission (EC) says the agreement will also create a ‘larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price’. As a result of the agreement, the UK will expand its ETS to include aviation and maritime, which the EC says will cover over 10 million tonnes of additional CO2 emissions as part of the system. The agreement provides the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies across the UK and the EU. The UK ETS sets an overall cap on total emissions from in-scope sectors, which is divided into allowances. It currently applies to energy-intensive industries, the power generation sector, and the aviation industry. Operators who are covered by the scheme must acquire allowances through auctions run by the UK ETS Authority, from other participants through secondary markets, or, if eligible, they can obtain UKAs from their free allocation. The scheme creates a market for carbon allowances, allowing operators who decarbonise to trade allowances with those whose operations continue to emit.

artigo.texto: A desaceleração dos data centers O lado positivo de uma pausa na alucinante corrida dos laboratórios de IA Atualizado 24/11/2026 Tenho um amigo que recentemente decidiu tirar um ano de folga de seu cargo de professor titular de matemática para estudar segurança em inteligência artificial (IA). Com a OpenAI divulgando 722 artigos que alegam soluções para 377 questões matemáticas até então não resolvidas, e com os modelos de IA ficando cada vez melhores, ele está preocupado se sua profissão tem futuro. Se um matemático brilhante pode ser substituído com tanta facilidade, por que o resto de nós não está preocupado? Parte da resposta pode ser que, embora a IA possa resolver uma variante da conjectura de Navier-Stokes, meu banco ainda não criou um chatbot confiável capaz de resolver um problema de transferência de fundos sem que eu exija, irritado, falar com um ser humano. Os laboratórios de IA estão usando técnicas recursivas de autoaperfeiçoamento para dotar seus modelos ainda não lançados de capacidades de pesquisa ainda mais milagrosas, e os primeiros a adotar a tecnologia em alguns setores já contam com bots negociando contratos e conciliando faturas com entregas. Mas a adoção por empresas tradicionais está avançando lentamente no geral, e as capacidades de IA que elas podem usar ainda são modestas. Por que, então, tantas empresas de IA estão usando tanta capacidade computacional para desenvolver modelos mais sofisticados, cujas capacidades só algumas poucas conseguem aproveitar em sua plenitude? Além da emoção de criar uma forma nova e mais rápida de inteligência, acredita-se que o primeiro laboratório a criar um modelo totalmente capaz de se autoaperfeiçoar se beneficiará de suas capacidades que melhoram exponencialmente e ficará permanentemente à frente da concorrência. No entanto, parece improvável que os concorrentes não sigam o exemplo em pouco tempo. O líder poderia ter um ou dois meses de vantagem, ainda que com um crescimento exponencial de capacidade, mas os seguidores mais ágeis podem muito bem descobrir técnicas que lhes permitam ultrapassá-lo e assumir a liderança. É exatamente isso que vem acontecendo na corrida pela capacidade de IA, com as posições de liderança dos modelos mudando com frequência. Parece improvável que qualquer vencedor domine para sempre - especialmente se puderem contratar funcionários uns dos outros - a menos que literalmente neutralizem ou destruam seus concorrentes. Esperamos que essa não seja a intenção de ninguém. Outro motivo pode ser simplesmente que nenhum dos líderes dos principais laboratórios de IA confia nos outros para lidar com o poder que vem acompanhado de capacidades extraordinárias de IA. Cada um é motivado não só pelo desejo de vencer, mas também pela sensação de que apenas ele é capaz de lidar bem com esse poder. Outra fonte de impulso é o medo de que a China alcance os EUA. Modelos chineses de IA têm se mantido apenas alguns meses atrás dos modelos líderes dos EUA. Assim como na corrida por capacidades nos EUA, é improvável que fiquem muito mais para trás, a menos que os EUA consigam montar uma campanha mais eficaz para impedir o acesso chinês aos chips mais avançados, tanto na China quanto no resto do mundo. Com os principais laboratórios de IA sob intensa pressão competitiva para continuar expandindo as fronteiras das capacidades dessa tecnologia, a resistência à ampliação dos recursos computacionais não é algo tão ruim Não importa o motivo, o enorme investimento em recursos computacionais para o treinamento de modelos pressiona os laboratórios de IA a gerar mais receita - quanto antes, melhor. Por isso que a Anthropic lançou uma joint venture, a Ode, para impulsionar o uso da IA em empresas não-tecnológicas, usando engenheiros da Anthropic integrados a essas empresas. Isso significa que alguns bancos poderão ter chatbots muito superiores em breve, pressionando todos os bancos a seguirem o exemplo. Quanto tempo levará para que os empregos de atendimento ao cliente se juntem aos de professores de matemática? É claro que há várias maneiras de implementar a IA. É possível substituir os empregos existentes ou redesenhar o trabalho e o treinamento de habilidades para que as capacidades dos funcionários atuais sejam muito ampliadas. A primeira opção gerará receitas mais depressa, mas resultará num desastre social; a segunda exigirá mais tempo e reflexão, mas preservará empregos e estabilidade. As empresas que estão sendo alvo de um aumento no uso da IA estão na melhor posição para implementar uma IA centrada nos funcionários, mas precisam assumir mais responsabilidade pelo futuro de seus funcionários, mesmo que o governo ofereça mais incentivos para que as corporações resistam aos lucros de curto prazo obtidos por meio de demissões. Há muitas ideias viáveis - como impostos sobre o uso de tokens corporativos e créditos para treinamento de funcionários -, mas poucos governos as puseram em prática. A conclusão parece inevitável: a sociedade não está pronta para uma implantação em larga escala da IA. Mas talvez estejamos vendo agora um movimento para desacelerar a enorme expansão da capacidade computacional. Muitos líderes políticos nos EUA estão exigindo uma pausa nas aprovações de novos data centers, ecoando preocupações das comunidades locais e chamando a atenção para as consequências mais amplas de uma implantação descontrolada da IA. Diante da perspectiva de que haja menos recursos computacionais disponíveis para monetizar a IA no médio prazo, investidores serão forçados a limitar a alocação de recursos onerosos para o desenvolvimento de modelos. Uma desaceleração na construção também eleva o custo do uso da IA, o que vai mudar o cálculo por trás das decisões de substituir funcionários. Isso permite que a oferta de chips e memória se equilibre, de modo que os custos não aumentem inexoravelmente no futuro. artigo.texto: Protesters demand Anne Arundel County close data center loophole in Severn expansion fight Protesters are demanding the Anne Arundel County Council close a loophole in a data center moratorium that allows the expansion of existing facilities. A crowd of protesters demonstrated Saturday on Telegraph Road in Hanover in opposition to an expansion of a data center in Severn. "Why didn't they close that loophole when they had an opportunity?" said Micheala Burgnon, with Indivisible Odenton. The County Council voted to extend a moratorium on building new data centers until 2028, but the moratorium does not apply to expanding existing facilities, including a 110,000-square-foot data center in Severn, where the owner wants add another 89,000 square feet to it. "The expansion would more or less drop a data center the same size as the existing one right next to the existing one," said Erin Sherman, with Indivisible Odenton. The plan also calls for demolishing existing paved areas on the west side of the building and installing 13 backup generators. The owners have not said what type of fuel they want to use, which, coupled with a lack of information in general about the facility, is troubling to residents. "I think of data centers as kind of a necessary evil. My problem is with a lack of transparency surrounding them as well as the unknown environmental aspects," said Kiri Shipp, a resident "We don't know enough about this data center and what's happening right in our back yard," said Starr Hood, a resident. Protest organizers with Indivisible Odenton started a petition drive to get the Anne Arundel County Council to close the loophole. Organizers canvassed neighborhoods collecting signatures. "(We're) asking them to stop the expansion. We've got over 1,000 signatures on that petition so far," Burgnon said. The petition will be delivered to the next meeting of the County Council on Dec. 7.

artigo.texto: The South Korean government said it will invest a total of 15 trillion won ($10.2 billion) by 2030 to secure 13.6 gigawatts of battery energy storage systems, a 3.4-fold increase from about 4 gigawatts of installed battery storage capacity at the end of last year. Lee Ho-hyun, vice minister of climate, energy and environment, said at the 24th Energy Strategy Forum held at the Shilla Hotel in Seoul's Jung district on the 24th that it is "now time for an energy storage revolution." He added that the government "will significantly expand policy and budget support to grow the ESS market." To that end, the ministry plans to invest 1.1 trillion won ($749 million) in 2027 alone to build 2.7 gigawatts of new storage capacity. Annual bidding volumes, set at about 0.5 gigawatt under the 11th Basic Plan for Long-Term Electricity Supply and Demand, rose to 1.08 gigawatts last year and 1.18 gigawatts this year. The push for storage reflects the growing importance of flexible power sources that can bridge the gap between electricity generation and consumption as renewables account for a larger share of the mix. "Going forward, producing a lot of energy will not be enough," the vice minister said. "The key to the success or failure of the energy transition is how reliably the electricity we generate can be delivered to the time and place where it is needed." Kim Jae-eon, a professor of electrical engineering at Chungbuk National University, said in a keynote address that the government's large-scale deployment plan must translate into competitiveness for domestic industry. "We need to build an implementation framework so that domestic procurement and demonstration projects lead to actual business," the professor said.

artigo.texto: Em 23 de novembro, a Valencia Plaza informou que a SpainDC ainda finalizava o recurso contra o Real Decreto 1032/2026 e previa apresentá-lo ao Supremo em 25 ou 26 de novembro. A associação havia anunciado em 20 de novembro que contestaria a norma e pediria sua suspensão cautelar. A declaração da SpainDC confirma a intenção da entidade; o relato de 23 de novembro registra o prazo previsto para o protocolo. O que determina o decreto espanhol O Conselho de Ministros aprovou o Real Decreto 1032/2026 em 20 de novembro. A norma foi publicada no Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) em 21 de novembro e prevê entrada em vigor no dia seguinte. O texto oficial estabelece que a maioria das obrigações se aplica a centros de dados com pelo menos 10 MW de capacidade de acesso à rede, incluindo certos agrupamentos de instalações no mesmo local e sob o mesmo proprietário. Esse limite mede o acesso à rede, não a potência de TI. O artigo 13 tem um patamar separado para obrigações de divulgação de informações: 500 kW de potência de TI. Para entender o alcance da norma, separe a capacidade de acesso à rede da potência de TI: os limites medem coisas diferentes. O decreto também separa duas regras de energia renovável. Uma exige que 80% do consumo total seja coberto por autoconsumo elegível ou contratos de energia renovável que atendam às condições da norma. Em geral, a geração associada deve ter começado a operar no máximo 36 meses antes do início das operações do centro de dados ou do primeiro uso da energia. Os contratos elegíveis precisam durar pelo menos seis anos. A outra regra é horária: em cada hora, ao menos 80% do consumo deve ter cobertura equivalente de eletricidade renovável gerada naquela mesma hora. O texto reconhece, sob condições específicas, autoconsumo, contratos renováveis e armazenamento. Há ainda uma alternativa de transição de cinco anos para instalações elegíveis que participem tecnicamente do sistema automático de redução de potência. Nesse percurso, a cobertura exigida nas horas P1 é de 60% até 31 de dezembro de 2028. A partir de 1º de janeiro de 2029, passa a 70% nas horas P1 e 60% nas P2 até o fim da transição. Antes da aplicação do sistema europeu de etiquetagem, os limites gerais de transição são PUE máximo de 1,25 e WUE máximo de 0,1. O prazo para cumprir a exigência de eficiência energética começa após dois anos de operação; para a de eficiência hídrica, após um ano, conforme o calendário de verificação do decreto. As regras de soberania digital têm escopo específico: abrangem centros de dados que hospedem sistemas do setor público classificados como de nível alto no Esquema Nacional de Segurança da Espanha. A norma prevê condições de localização e acesso na União Europeia e no Espaço Econômico Europeu, além de exceções para operações tecnicamente necessárias. Os argumentos em torno das novas regras O preâmbulo do decreto afirma que a procura por acesso à rede pelos centros de dados pode competir por capacidade limitada. A justificativa do governo é alinhar a expansão digital à rede elétrica e às metas de energia e meio ambiente, com exigências de geração renovável, eficiência e acesso à rede. A SpainDC considera impraticáveis as regras de adicionalidade renovável e de correspondência horária. A associação também argumenta que a alternativa ligada à redução automática de potência pode ameaçar a operação ininterrupta dos centros de dados e afetar investimentos. Essas são as posições da entidade sobre os efeitos da norma.

artigo.texto: Two forces are behind falling energy storage costs, which is a boon for the clean energy industry. The market features growing competition among battery manufacturers and a possible lithium surplus in 2027. Here's what to know As SolarQuarter detailed, InfoLink's Energy Storage Supply Chain Price Forecast Report projects a slight lithium surplus in 2027. Battery-grade lithium carbonate prices could fall to about 99,800–117,900 Chinese yuan ($14,945-$17,656) per U.S. ton in the first half of that year. The forecast comes after declines in storage-cell prices. In July 2026, the tax-inclusive average prices for both 280 amp-hour and 314 amp-hour lithium iron phosphate storage cells dropped 4% to 0.36 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to the outlet. Smaller, 100 amp-hour cells averaged 0.44 yuan per watt-hour, down 2.7% from June 2026. For households facing grid instability and time-of-use electricity rates, whole-home batteries can keep essentials running during outages, while leases can help protect homes without upwards of $20,000 in upfront costs. EasyHome is a marketplace connecting battery shoppers with trusted partners offering unique prices and exclusive deals — another avenue for homeowners exploring backup power as storage-cell costs decline. More background The cost of lithium iron phosphate cathode material used in storage applications declined to approximately 47,800 yuan ($7,158) per U.S. ton, bringing tax-inclusive storage-cell production costs to around 0.31 yuan (around 5 cents) per watt-hour, according to SolarQuarter. These declines can translate to savings down the road for consumers looking to tap into their storage systems. Home batteries can also help reduce energy bills by supplying stored electricity during expensive peak-pricing periods. For households seeking a smaller-scale option, Pila offers plug-and-play battery backup at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. What's being done? Intense competition among battery manufacturers as supply expands is putting additional pressure on storage-cell prices, according to SolarQuarter. Lithium carbonate prices could still rise before the projected surplus in 2027. InfoLink's September and October 2026 price forecast is about 131,500–136,100 yuan ($19,692-20,381) per U.S. ton, above the expected August 2026 average near 127,000 yuan ($19,018) per U.S. ton. The firm expects seasonal demand and restocking to support that increase. According to SolarQuarter, China will begin taxing lithium-ion battery consumption at 2% on September 1, 2026, with the rate rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Meanwhile, the estimated U.S. tariff rate for lithium-ion battery systems originating in China is around 40.9%. China's July 2026 average free-on-board export prices were $50.30 per kilowatt-hour for 280 amp-hour cells, $51 for 306 amp-hour cells, and $50 for 314 amp-hour cells, per the outlet. For shoppers exploring their options, EasyHome works like Groupon for home energy, negotiating special offers for its large audience and providing unique battery deals. It also offers special solar deals. Pairing solar with a battery can increase savings and provide backup power during outages, giving homeowners another way to put energy storage to work. artigo.texto: Stafford County residents raise concerns over massive data center project during town hall STAFFORD COUNTY, Va. (7News) — For the second time in recent days, Stafford County residents voiced concerns over a massive data center project expected to come to a vote in less than a month. The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is considering a proposal that would build 37 data centers on 9 million square feet of land along Kings Highway near I-95. More than 100 residents signed up to speak about this project during the public comment period for Thursday's planning commission meeting. SEE ALSO | Tracking potential high impact Thanksgiving Day nor'easter On Sunday, dozens of residents sounded off during a town hall meeting hosted by Board of Supervisors Chairman Deuntay Diggs. "Obviously, I'm against the data centers. I want Stafford to just be a sleepy bedroom community. What is wrong with that? Why do we have to be all this stuff? And remember, every time you put a data center on a piece of property, that's a place you can't have your magical stuff for people to do in Stafford County because now there's no land available," one resident said. Another resident added, "We just know this is too big of a project to do all at one time without knowing what the impact's going to be 15 years down the road." At both meetings, community members raised concerns about electricity use and costs, property values and health. During Sunday's town hall, residents lined up behind microphones to directly address Diggs. "I do think it's going to impact my hearing, my ability to enjoy my property peacefully, which I have a right to," one resident said. Another resident echoed this sentiment: "There is nothing to stop this grotesque health problem, this hazard. I want to know how you guys react to, 'Is it the money we need, or is it the people we're going to protect?'" Members on the board of supervisors have expressed the need for these facilities because of the tax revenue they could bring. Diggs and other officials have estimated this project could generate millions of dollars each year. "Overall, the project is going to bring in about $193 million. When you look at the general government, this is just an approximate number, we're at about $220 million to run just the general government itself," Diggs said. "We could fund our first responders, increases for salaries for our educators. It helps with a multitude of issues, in terms of our water throughout the county." 7News On Your Side asked Diggs why the board is considering this project despite the opposition heard at both of these recent meetings. "Well, the issue is we need revenue here in Stafford, and we've raised taxes for five consecutive years on our constituents. When I look at our last election, it was about affordability. We're looking at how do we fill that gap, not just with data centers, but overall economic development," Diggs said. "We're listening to our constituents, and we're put in a predicament right now where constituents are saying, 'Do not raise our taxes,' but then they're also not wanting data centers. We're trying to figure out what other economic development can fill the revenue gap." The Stafford County Board of Supervisors is expected to vote on this project on Dec. 15.

artigo.texto: US Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-NC, has introduced bipartisan legislation to prevent Chinese telecommunications companies previously identified as national security threats from accessing American data centers and cloud services. The Digital Infrastructure Security Act of 2026, House Bill 11100, introduced by Harrigan and US Rep. Dave Min, D-CA, seeks to extend existing federal telecommunications restrictions to digital infrastructure that handles sensitive American financial, medical, and military information. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) previously revoked or denied telecommunications licenses for China Telecom Americas, China Unicom Americas, and China Mobile USA over national security concerns. However, those actions did not automatically remove the companies’ equipment and connections from American data centers. According to Harrigan’s office, investigations identified more than 108,000 instances of Chinese-linked networks redirecting internet traffic between 2018 and 2025, raising concerns about foreign interference and the potential exposure of sensitive information. “China has spent years stealing American technology and targeting our communications networks, and we know they’re not going to stop,” Harrigan said in a press release announcing the legislation. Harrigan said the legislation would address gaps in existing federal restrictions by prohibiting the companies from operating domestic data centers or conducting business with Americans through cloud services, including through subsidiaries and other intermediaries. “What concerns me is that we’ve already identified these companies as national security threats, revoked their licenses, and somehow still allowed them to keep a foothold in our data centers,” he said. “When we’re talking about the systems that handle Americans’ financial information, medical records, and sensitive military data, I think that’s a pretty reasonable safeguard.” Under the legislation, the FCC would enforce the restrictions, with fines of up to $1 million per violation or per day for continuing violations. Existing operations and contracts would have 180 days following enactment to comply. It would also establish a waiver process subject to a federal national security assessment. The legislation comes as North Carolina grapples with the rapid expansion of data centers and their impact on electricity demand, water resources, and local infrastructure. More than 30 local governments across the state have enacted temporary moratoriums on data center development, while state lawmakers repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity consumed by data centers earlier this year. Broader legislation, Senate Bill 730, the Ratepayer Protection Act, remains stalled in the Senate and would establish additional ratepayer protections, water-use standards, and restrictions on data center ownership by entities tied to foreign adversaries, including China. Harrigan criticizes Nvidia CEO’s reinstatement The legislation coincides with heightened scrutiny in Washington over the relationship between American technology companies and China, including Monday’s reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected by US officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate Huang on Nov. 23 following discussions with Huang and input from senior federal government officials. The company said its board was confident that his reinstatement posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump supported Huang’s reinstatement, while several congressional Republicans, including Harrigan, criticized the decision on X. “For the past two years, I have privately said there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised,” Harrigan wrote in a post on X. “Turns out, well, we all know.” Harrigan argued that Huang’s reinstatement was premature and called for further congressional investigation into the potential national security implications. “His reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake,” he continued. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the company and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.” Harrigan called for investigations by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees. “Today, we sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law,” he said. “That is a dangerous precedent to set, and one I believe will come at a significant cost to our country in the long run.” Harrigan’s Digital Infrastructure Security Act was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on Nov. 19.

artigo.texto: Haroldo Almeida participa do PodCast AgroAmbiental para debater Caatinga, crédito de carbono e mudanças climáticas Comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, participante da COP30 e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista é o convidado do 7º episódio. O PodCast AgroAmbiental recebe, nesta terça-feira (24 de novembro), às 20h, o ambientalista Haroldo Almeida, comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, integrante do Fórum Brasileiro de Mudança do Clima e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga. O sétimo episódio traz à discussão temas de grande relevância para o futuro do Semiárido nordestino, como a preservação da Caatinga, a gestão dos recursos hídricos, o avanço da desertificação, o mercado de créditos de carbono e os resultados da 30ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP30), realizada em Belém, no Pará, em novembro de 2025. Com uma trajetória marcada pela participação em iniciativas ambientais, debates institucionais e ações de conscientização, Haroldo compartilha experiências acumuladas ao longo de sua atuação e apresenta propostas que buscam conciliar conservação ambiental, valorização dos recursos naturais e geração de oportunidades econômicas para as populações do Sertão. Trajetória ambiental e defesa dos recursos hídricos Um dos assuntos abordados durante a entrevista é a trajetória de Haroldo Almeida na defesa do meio ambiente, especialmente no Alto Sertão alagoano. Ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia e participante das discussões do Comitê de Bacia da Região Hidrográfica do Sertão do São Francisco, o ambientalista trata sobre a importância da gestão participativa das águas, os desafios enfrentados pelos municípios e a necessidade de políticas públicas voltadas à conservação dos recursos hídricos. A conversa também destaca a importância do Rio São Francisco para o desenvolvimento regional, a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a proteção da vegetação nativa e a adoção de medidas capazes de garantir maior segurança hídrica às populações sertanejas. O episódio propõe uma reflexão sobre a relação entre a preservação ambiental e o desenvolvimento econômico, especialmente em uma região que depende diretamente da disponibilidade de água para o abastecimento humano, a agricultura e a pecuária. Desertificação e os desafios da conservação da Caatinga A desertificação é outro tema importante do episódio, considerando os impactos que a degradação ambiental pode provocar sobre a produtividade do solo, a disponibilidade de água e as condições de vida das comunidades rurais. Haroldo participou de um seminário internacional sobre o combate à desertificação, realizado na Câmara dos Deputados, em Brasília, onde foram discutidas estratégias de enfrentamento da degradação das terras e a necessidade de ampliar as ações de recuperação ambiental no Semiárido. Durante a entrevista, são abordadas as diferenças entre a seca, característica natural da região, e os processos de desertificação, que podem ser agravados pelo desmatamento, pelas queimadas, pelo sobrepastoreio e pelo manejo inadequado do solo. O debate também chama a atenção para a importância da Caatinga, bioma exclusivamente brasileiro que possui significativa biodiversidade e desempenha papel fundamental no equilíbrio ambiental do Nordeste. A discussão busca demonstrar que a conservação da vegetação nativa, a recuperação de áreas degradadas e a adoção de práticas produtivas sustentáveis são fundamentais para garantir melhores condições ambientais e econômicas às futuras gerações. Crédito de carbono pode representar oportunidade de renda para agricultores do Sertão Um dos principais destaques do episódio é a proposta de Crédito de Carbono Integral Bio-Sócio-Hidro-Energético, iniciativa idealizada por Haroldo Almeida que busca desenvolver mecanismos de valorização dos serviços ambientais prestados pela Caatinga e pelas comunidades que contribuem para sua conservação. Presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista apresenta os fundamentos da proposta e discute as possibilidades de inserção dos pequenos produtores rurais em iniciativas relacionadas ao mercado de carbono. A entrevista procura esclarecer, de maneira acessível, o que são créditos de carbono, como funciona esse mercado, quais são os critérios para sua geração e de que forma a manutenção da vegetação nativa pode representar uma oportunidade econômica para os proprietários rurais. Também são discutidos os desafios relacionados à quantificação, à certificação e à comercialização desses créditos, além da importância de mecanismos que assegurem transparência, confiabilidade e participação das comunidades locais. Entre os questionamentos levantados está a possibilidade de transformar a preservação ambiental em uma atividade economicamente atrativa, contribuindo para reduzir a pressão sobre a vegetação nativa e estimular a recuperação de áreas degradadas. A discussão propõe uma questão central: será possível que, no futuro, um agricultor do Sertão consiga obter renda pela conservação da Caatinga, mantendo a vegetação em pé? Participação na COP30 e valorização da Caatinga no cenário internacional A participação de Haroldo Almeida na COP30, realizada em Belém, também ocupa espaço importante na entrevista. O ambientalista compartilha experiências de sua passagem pela conferência, considerada um dos principais encontros internacionais sobre mudanças climáticas, reunindo representantes de governos, instituições, pesquisadores e organizações da sociedade civil. Durante o evento, Haroldo participou de discussões e articulações voltadas à valorização da Caatinga, à justiça climática e ao reconhecimento das iniciativas de conservação desenvolvidas no Semiárido nordestino. artigo.texto: A new study finds U.S. hyperscale data centers use about 2% of the nation’s electricity. In Oregon, Virginia and Iowa, the share is above 10%. Data centers’ electricity use is soaring, and in some states it already makes up a large share of the power supply. That’s the finding of a Harvard-led study in Nature Sustainability. The researchers catalogued 403 hyperscale data centers in the U.S. They estimate these facilities use about 82 terawatt-hours a year, roughly 2% of the nation’s electricity and about as much as nearly 8 million homes. The facilities are also tied to about 26 million metric tons of carbon emissions a year. The national number hides big differences between states. In Oregon, the facilities in the study equal about 18.6% of 2024 retail electricity sales. Virginia comes in at about 15.5% and Iowa at about 13.1%. A utility filing suggests Virginia’s real share is closer to 28%. The researchers say their numbers are probably low. The study counts only facilities they could verify. Data centers are also increasingly building their own gas power plants on site, and about 143 GW of those plants have been proposed nationally. Power from those plants doesn’t show up in utility sales data. Better tracking could help. Federal energy surveys don’t count data centers as their own category of customer. A permitting bill now before the Senate would direct the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) to measure how much electricity data centers use. Until that happens, state and local planners won’t have a clear picture of how fast the demand is growing. artigo.texto: BASF will narrow its battery business to cathode active materials, agreeing to sell its recycling operations to cylib and seeking partners for idle plants in the US and Finland. Alongside the restructuring, it has begun delivering cathode material from Schwarzheide, Germany, to China’s CATL. The sale, signed on 20 November 2026, covers BASF’s European and North American recycling operations with their intellectual property, contracts, and the black mass and prototype recycling plants at Schwarzheide. Completion is expected in the second or third quarter of 2027, and terms were not disclosed. The Battle Creek site in Michigan and a precursor plant in Harjavalta, Finland, are both mothballed. Their status reflects a reset BASF began in 2024 as electric vehicle markets shifted, cutting investment and costs while securing long-term customer contracts. The CATL deliveries follow a global framework agreement signed in July 2025, under which the two developed a cathode product to CATL’s specification and moved it into German production. BASF also supplies CATL in China from its Changsha plant, giving it a foothold with the cell maker in both markets. Daniel Schönfelder, President of BASF’s Battery Materials division, said cathode materials are where its chemistry expertise creates most value for customers. Gideon Schwich, Co-Chief Executive of cylib, said the Schwarzheide plant extends its European network for turning end-of-life batteries into black mass. Why this matters: - Local production, Chinese value chain. German-made cathode material destined for a Chinese cell maker’s European plants shows that ‘from Europe for Europe’ supply chains still run through Chinese technology and ownership, while upstream refining of lithium and other key inputs remains heavily concentrated in China. - Local materials ease trade compliance. European-made cathode material could help CATL’s European cells meet tightening UK-EU rules of origin and EU Battery Regulation requirements, strengthening its position with automakers seeking compliant supply. - Chinese demand sustains European capacity. With European cell start-ups failing to materialise at scale, securing CATL as an anchor customer suggests Western materials suppliers increasingly depend on Chinese cell makers to keep European cathode plants viable.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - The number of data center projects cancelled in the U.S. more than doubled in the third quarter, compared to the same period last year, according to data released Tuesday from Relae, the climate solutions company formerly known as Carbon Direct. - Sixteen data center projects were stopped in the third quarter due to community opposition, Relae said in a blog post. That’s up from seven in the same quarter of 2025. - Relae, which has a data center cancellation tracker, said there were 70 data center projects “blocked, withdrawn or stalled since 2024,” representing $271 billion in estimated or announced investments. Dive Insight: The rise in cancellations came amid an election season that saw data center pushback — along with affordability and geopolitical concerns — play a role in Democrats flipping both the House of Representatives and Senate. Relae estimated that $64 billion in planned investments were stopped in Q3. Most of the projects were stopped by local governments, with seven stopped with formal denials and four being axed due to zoning bans. The other five projects were cancelled due to developer withdrawals, according to Relae. Relae said three trends have emerged as data centers have drawn an increasing share of the public ire: “more cancellations, greater intervention by local governments, and the importance of transparency (or lack thereof) to communities.” “At present, local opposition is not inherently a broad referendum on AI, although this could quickly change in the future,” Relae said in its blog. “Instead, our research shows that most community concerns are within a project team’s control.” A lack of transparency represented the top concern for communities, representing a leading or secondary theme for 34 of 44 stopped projects that Relae analyzed. Voters approved measures to restrict data center development in jurisdictions across 10 states, and an NBC exit poll found that 76% of voters opposed new data centers being built in their communities. The same exit poll found that 56% said data centers were a crucial or major factor in choosing a congressional candidate. “Data centers have moved to the center of American politics,” Relae said. “As public views of the projects have turned more negative, they have become material for stump speeches, attack ads, and ballot measures.” Of the 47 local ballot measures on data centers this past election, 46 passed that would limit or ban development, the firm said. The success of such measures “shows the growing significance of data center development as a local electoral issue,” Relae said.

artigo.texto: Goleta has begun taking steps toward banning data centers in the Good Land. In a 4-1 vote, the Goleta Planning Commission on Monday moved forward an ordinance that would permanently prohibit data centers in the city. The ordinance will now head to the City Council for review. The city currently doesn’t have regulations on data centers, according to Anne Wells, the city’s advance planning manager. Goleta has not permitted any data centers or received applications, supervising planner Andy Newkirk said. He said that while most people think of data centers as large-scale facilities, they can be the size of a “normal office building,” and it’s “certainly possible” that the city could receive a proposal. The drafted permanent ordinance is a way for Goleta to get ahead “of a potential issue” and “not get caught off-guard,” Newkirk said. While the ordinance would be permanent, the city could revisit the details of the prohibition in the future. “I do think it is a good idea to have an ordinance and to get ahead of it,” Commissioner Jennifer Fullerton said. City staff highlighted water, electricity, noise and air pollution as potential data center impacts. “We are very aware that in other jurisdictions around the country, this is becoming a really big issue, and we know that in other areas of regulation we have been caught unprepared,” said Peter Imhof, planning and environmental review director. Commissioner Rita Serotkin had similar sentiments. She referred to Goodland Guns’ relocation next to a preschool and daycare facility as sneaking “around behind.” Goleta’s proposed ordinance defines a data center as a facility that houses a group of networked computer systems used for data storage and processing, to be used for the storage, processing and/or distribution of data. The facilities may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, backup batteries, fire suppression systems, enhanced security features and other associated utility infrastructure to support operations, according to city staff. Goleta’s proposed ordinance also includes a lengthy description of what is not considered a data center. A data center is not, according to the staff report: an enclosed room, suite or other accessory space containing computer servers, data storage and processing equipment, network switching equipment, telecommunications equipment, and related supporting equipment, including cooling, electrical, backup power and security systems, that are used to support and facilitate an allowed on-site principal use that takes up no more than 20% of the floor area of the principal use. The 20% allowance considers businesses that may need data center-like facilities on site, according to the city staff report. However, that 20% allowance brought some concerns Monday night. It was later swapped in favor of an exemption that would allow for data center-like facilities that use less than 3 megawatts of energy. Some commissioners had worried about how it would affect local technology companies. “My only concern is the 20% and not having reached out to the tech companies,” Fullerton said. Commissioner Cary Penniman, who voted against the recommendation Monday night but supports preventing “hyperscale data centers” in Goleta, had similar concerns. He worried about how it would impact small startups coming out of UC Santa Barbara. “I don’t think we want to prevent that from happening,” he said. “There are some unintended consequences.” He advocated that city staff develop a tighter definition of a data center. He posted a question to staff that a public commenter had asked earlier in the night: “What are we exactly trying to prevent?” Others were concerned about the energy use from the allowance. “The primary concern for me is sort of the energy and water usage, and so that’s where I feel like the restriction should be,” Commissioner Katie Maynard said. She asked staff why they decided to go with the floor area instead of “focusing on things that are most (concerning) for data centers such as energy or water.” She advocated for the allowance to be 3 megawatts or less. Newkirk said the decision was made to provide some flexibility. “Thinking (of) it as a proxy, it would be fairly consistent over time, where I think the energy demands may be really a standard today might not make much sense tomorrow,” he said. Wells also told the commissioners that city staff looked at other jurisdictions and floor area is a typical measure. Cherie Cabral spoke Monday on behalf of the California Construction Labor Management Trust and urged the Planning Commission against supporting a “blanket ban.” She also encouraged the commission to look at possible advantages that data centers could bring to the city and other cities’ regulations. “It’s entirely doable to create regulations that would address most of the issues, and in fact, many of the issues that are under discussion at the moment are generated out of social media as opposed to something that comes out of studies,” she said. Commissioner Anne Miller acknowledged the commissioner’s concerns about local impact, but insisted that the timing of establishing an ordinance was important. “I think it’s important to get on top of this now before something really disastrous happens in the meantime,” she said. “It’s moving so quickly, and it’s scary, I think.” Monday night’s discussion comes about a month after the Earl Warren Fairgrounds’ CEO put an end to speculation that the fairgrounds were considering a data center.

artigo.texto: Centre Proposes Energy Storage Mandate for Rooftop Solar Ministry of Power has proposed state-level storage mandates for rooftop solar systems exceeding 500 kW. November 24, 2026. By EI News Network The Ministry of Power has proposed empowering State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) to mandate energy storage systems for consumers with renewable energy generation capacities exceeding 500 kW, in a move aimed at strengthening grid stability and improving renewable energy integration. The proposal seeks to address the operational challenges faced by power distribution companies amid the growing adoption of rooftop solar systems across the country. Under the proposed framework, state regulators would be authorised to prescribe energy storage requirements for prosumers, enabling them to store surplus electricity generated during solar hours and utilise it during periods of peak demand. The draft amendments also propose changes to the net-metering framework, allowing state regulators to determine applicable charges. Rooftop solar installations exceeding 5 kW could attract network-related charges, while smaller installations would remain exempt. The proposed mechanism is expected to help distribution companies recover network infrastructure and operational costs while facilitating the continued expansion of distributed renewable energy generation. The Ministry has also proposed revised timelines for implementing Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs. Commercial and industrial consumers with connected loads exceeding 10 kW would be brought under the tariff framework from April 1, 2027, followed by other consumer categories, excluding agricultural consumers, from April 1, 2028. Electricity tariffs during solar hours would be at least 20 percent lower than normal tariffs, encouraging consumers to shift electricity consumption to periods of higher renewable energy availability. The proposed amendments could drive demand for battery energy storage systems and energy management solutions, particularly among commercial and industrial consumers with large rooftop solar installations. The measures are part of the government's broader efforts to modernise India's electricity distribution network, improve renewable energy utilisation and ensure grid reliability as the country accelerates its clean energy transition. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands (PROPUBLICA) - A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. artigo.texto: Cookeville Planning Commission postponed a vote Monday on proposed data center regulations that would establish zoning restrictions based on facility size. Community Development Director Jon Ward said staff revised the original proposal after reviewing model regulations developed by UT advisors. “One of the primary conclusions from that review is that data centers can vary significantly in scale and impact,” Ward said. “A relatively small facility occupying a few thousand square feet is very different from a larger hyperscale data center campus that may consume tens or even hundreds of megawatts of electricity.” Ward said the amendment divides data centers into five categories based on building size and projected electricity demand. Smaller facilities could operate in some commercial and light manufacturing districts, while the largest facilities would require special exceptions in Heavy Manufacturing districts. “The revised standards place greater emphasis on potential impacts to adjoining properties,” Ward said. “These include measurable noise standards based upon the type of adjoining property, acoustics studies for larger facilities and certain facilities near residential property, screening of generators and mechanical equipment, limitations on routine generator testing, and additional review where exterior equipment could affect adjoining residential uses.” Ward said utility providers would have to confirm they could accommodate a facility operating at full capacity before development could be approved. “It would allow the utility to consider existing demand, previous committed capacities, future developments, planned capital improvements, our system reliabilities, peak conditions, and reasonably anticipated future utility demands elsewhere in the city,” Ward said. Ward said several commissioners expressed concerns about whether residents could face higher utility bills as a result of data center development. The proposed regulations would not obligate the city to pay for infrastructure improvements needed to serve a facility. Ward said recently enacted state legislation generally prevents municipalities and electric utilities from absorbing electrical infrastructure costs for qualifying data centers. The law applies to facilities with projected peak electrical demands of at least 50 megawatts. “We shouldn’t assume that every smaller facility contemplated by the amendment would fall within that statutory protection,” Ward said. Planning staff will consult with utility departments to address commissioners’ concerns before bringing the amendment back for consideration in December. In other business, the commission granted conditional final plat approval for Emerald Forest Estates, which includes 71 residential lots, and amended the commission’s bylaws to require meeting agendas to be posted on the city’s website at least 48 hours before regular meetings.

artigo.texto: L&T Wins 300 MW / 900 MWh BESS Order for Khavda Project L&T’s Renewables business and LTEPS jointly secures an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System at Khavda, Gujarat. November 25, 2026. By News Bureau L&T’s Renewables business and LTEPS jointly secures an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System at Khavda, Gujarat. Two L&T verticals – the Renewables business and L&T Electronic Products and Systems (LTEPS) - have jointly won an order to develop a 300 MW / 900 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at Khavda in Gujarat. The project will feature a three-hour BESS, with a power capacity of 300 MW and an energy storage capacity of 900 MWh. By storing surplus renewable energy during periods of high generation and releasing it during peak demand, it will help maximise clean-energy utilisation, strengthen grid stability and enhance the flexibility and reliability of power supply. The advanced BESS solution will incorporate liquid-cooling technology to deliver higher power density, enhanced safety and a longer operating life. The facility will play a crucial role in improving grid flexibility and enabling greater integration of renewable energy into India's power network. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: ALEXANDRIA — The city of Alexandria continues to study and discuss data center regulations. The Alexandria Planning Commission put together a data center study that includes a draft ordinance. The new zoning district was titled, “Data Center Planned Unit Development” and amended existing city code sections as necessary to accommodate the new district provisions. ADVERTISEMENT The draft was presented for commission discussion and suggested revisions. If the commission desires, the final version will be available for public hearing in either December or January. At an Alexandria Planning Commission meeting , City Planner Mike Weber presented a draft zoning ordinance framework intended to regulate the location, design, operation and approval process for future data center developments in the city. The creation of two categories of data centers were proposed: 1. Small-scale data centers (tentatively up to 2-4 MW) permitted through a conditional use permit process in I-1 "Light Industrial" and potentially B-1 "General Business" zoning districts. 2. Large-scale data centers requiring approval through a specialized data center Planned Unit Development (PUD) process. Development standards under consideration include: Minimum site area requirements. Noise impact studies and mitigation measures. Landscaping and perimeter buffering requirements. Utility and infrastructure capacity studies. Performance guarantees associated with public infrastructure improvements. Project phasing requirements. Decommissioning and site restoration standards. Weber noted that developers will have to present a preliminary proposal that meets the city requirements and utility capacity. Prior to approval of a PUD, there could be requirements for formal studies on noise or environmental concerns. Unlike a conditional use permit, which grants the use permanently and runs with the land, data center Planned Unit Developments could have a sunset date: An approved PUD could expire after five years if no construction was started. Commission members sought clarification on the potential thresholds for distinguishing small and large data center developments. They discussed utility demand and coordination with public utility providers. ADVERTISEMENT Commission members engaged in extensive discussion about the proposed standards regarding noise, visual impacts, and screening requirements. Appropriate building material and architectural standards were considered. Comparisons were drawn to existing industrial uses and how future development standards should be applied. A public hearing is anticipated at a future meeting, with the likelihood of continuing the hearing as additional information and revisions become available. In July, the council voted to place a moratorium on data centers within the city of up to one year for the construction, expansion, application for any permit, or application contemplating construction or expansion for data centers. Data centers are massive centralized hubs used to house computer networks, storage and computing infrastructure. According to information from CBS news, data centers for Artificial Intelligence use huge amounts of electricity and water, driving up costs and causing climate concerns. In other action, the Alexandria Planning Commission talked about a variance that was earlier submitted to Bill Fath on behalf of Fath Family Properties. Chairperson Deb Parrott announced applicant Bill Fath withdrew a variance application on Monday, Nov. 16. No public hearing, discussion or action was taken.
