artigo.texto: COP31 in Türkiye saw the launch of a Global Energy Storage Alliance (GESA), with 27 co-initiating organisations at the outset. The alliance was founded by the China Energy Storage Alliance, the China Renewable Energy Engineering Institute, and China Southern Power Grid Energy Storage. Co-initiators include CATL (HKG:3750), BYD Energy Storage, and other industry players. GESA brings together battery manufacturers, power utilities, state-owned enterprises, and research institutions to collaborate on six key areas. These include facilitating international dialogue, building a global storage project and standards database, advancing research and technology, improving market mechanisms, strengthening supply chains and trade, and mobilising investment, particularly in developing economies. GESA describes itself as open, technologically neutral, and market-oriented. The alliance is dominated by organisations and companies from China, though it also includes ACWA Power (TADAWUL:2082) from Saudi Arabia, among other international co-initiators. With China continuing to lead the battery and energy storage industries, GESA provides another potential path to strengthen that position. However, its influence will depend on securing broader international participation. For China, the alliance provides a way to develop international standards for energy storage products that will inevitably be exported globally. As the battery energy storage industry expands, GESA’s focus on international standards, capacity building, and climate action, alongside its goal of increasing investment in developing economies, aligns with COP’s drive for an equitable and just transition. Following its COP31 launch, GESA has invited international industry players to join the platform to help align technical standards and mobilise storage investment in emerging markets. artigo.texto: Under the new rules, installations and shipping companies must generally surrender emissions allowances by 30 September each year. The decree entered into force on 22 November, the day after its publication in the BOE. Real Decreto-ley 41/2026, dated 20 November and published in BOE No. 290 on 21 November, amends Law 1/2005, Spain’s emissions-trading statute, and transposes Directives (EU) 2023/958 and 2023/959. For shipping companies, the surrender requirement will be phased in until it covers 100% of verified emissions from 2026 onwards. Maritime coverage also depends on the voyage: 100% of emissions are covered on voyages between ports under EU member-state jurisdiction, while 50% are covered on voyages from a port outside the EU to a port under a member state’s jurisdiction. The BOE text refers to emissions verified and recorded for 2024, including allowance deliveries entered in the Union Registry. The law also lets certain shipping companies seek reimbursement from commercial operators for allowance costs. That does not remove the shipping companies’ own obligations. Until 31 December 2030, ships with ice class IA or IA Super, or an equivalent class under HELCOM Recommendation 25/7, may surrender 5% fewer allowances. The Ministry of Transport and Sustainable Mobility is responsible for the maritime system, including its monitoring and verification requirements. Repeated non-compliance can lead to orders expelling or immobilising vessels. A separate emissions-trading system covers fuels consumed in buildings, road transport and other sectors. The regulated entities are companies that release those fuels for consumption, not the final consumers. They need authorisation and must submit annual verified emissions reports by 30 April. From 2028 to 2030, they must also report the average share of allowance costs passed on to consumers. Hospitals that meet the specified conditions may qualify for financial compensation. The BOE text says the decree transposes Directives (UE) 2023/958 and 2023/959, which amend the EU emissions-trading framework established by Directive 2003/87/CE. The changes extend the system to maritime transport and establish a separate fuel scheme under the EU’s «Objetivo 55» package. Spain says transposition is needed to access the Social Climate Fund, established by Regulation (EU) 2023/955. The fund supports vulnerable households and microenterprises, as well as vulnerable transport users. It is financed mainly through a share of EU revenue from emissions-allowance auctions. To receive funding, member states must submit national Social Climate Plans that meet the regulation’s requirements. A proposed Spanish Plan Social para el Clima envisages more than €9 billion for measures and investment aimed at reducing vulnerable groups’ dependence on fossil fuels. The proposal went through public consultation and information proceedings in May and June 2026. More than half of its proposed resources are earmarked for housing, including over €4.7 billion for work in that area. The plan remains a proposal. A separate account of campaign proposals in Zaragoza appears in earlier campaign coverage. For aviation, the decree updates free allowance rules and creates a reserve for sustainable aviation fuels and other eligible non-fossil fuels covering 2024 to 2030. It also sets out rules for returning allowances received incorrectly and meeting obligations under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Operators must report annually on aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. Industrial installations face revised free-allocation rules. Certain sites subject to energy-audit requirements may receive reduced allocations if they fail to follow recommendations. Installations whose emissions exceed the 80th percentile of relevant benchmarks must submit climate-neutrality plans. Verification of targets and milestones is a condition of receiving the free allocation available under EU rules. A new chapter also makes the Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge the national authority for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (MAFC), working with customs authorities and the European Commission. Other provisions extend beyond emissions trading. The decree changes rules for data centres, including a compensation system for deviations from additionality and hourly-correlation requirements. It establishes offences for breaches involving those requirements or energy and water efficiency, as well as certain sustainability disclosures. Operators hosting public-sector information systems classified as category ALTA face digital-sovereignty duties and may be subject to corrective orders and penalties. Their responsibility is limited to matters within their direct or contractual control. For electric-vehicle charging stations, the power threshold relevant to certain permits and public-utility declarations falls from 3,000 kW to 250 kW. Some electricity-supply infrastructure can avoid administrative authorisations if it does not require environmental assessment or seek public-utility status, and if the required project documents are filed in advance. A separate amendment provides an exemption route for qualifying charging-station infrastructure of up to 3,000 kW. The decree also recognises electricity consumed from nearby storage installations associated with consumption as renewable self-consumption. The government cited the overdue transposition deadline and infringement proceedings against Spain to justify using an emergency decree. Its final provision sets 22 November 2026 as the date the decree enters into force.

artigo.texto: CSIRO Urges Australia to Build Battery Manufacturing Scientists say Australia should make battery components locally rather than export critical minerals for overseas processing. Updated on Nov. 24, 2026 in Electric Vehicles Live Poll Should Australia manufacture more batteries domestically rather than exporting raw minerals? CSIRO scientists urged Australia to build a battery manufacturing industry instead of exporting critical minerals. A CSIRO report released in early November identified local manufacturing capabilities that could produce battery components. Why it matters Australia is the world's number one lithium producer, yet it exports raw minerals and ships end-of-life batteries overseas for materials recovery. Building domestic capacity could capture more value from resources the country already holds. More than 600,000 home batteries have been installed under a federal scheme since July 2025. Electric vehicle sales have risen rapidly since March, though the report does not quantify the growth rate. The players CSIRO The Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation is Australia's national science agency, conducting research across industry and environmental fields. The details Australia has nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper and graphite, but exports them as raw materials for overseas processing. A CSIRO report released in early November found Australia could manufacture battery casings using aluminium aerosol can expertise and copper foil from scrap wire. Timeline - July 2025: Federal home battery scheme began installations. - March: Electric vehicle sales began rapid growth. - Early November: CSIRO released its battery manufacturing report. - Tuesday: CSIRO scientists delivered the battery manufacturing warning at an event. Roadmap The federal home battery scheme, operating since July 2025, has installed more than 600,000 units and created domestic demand for batteries. The CSIRO report asks whether that demand can support local manufacturing rather than continued reliance on imported finished batteries. Local battery manufacturing could affect the price and availability of home and electric vehicle batteries over time. Households already using the federal scheme may see the supply chain behind their installed batteries change as domestic capacity develops. The takeaway Australia's mineral wealth gives it a head start in battery production, but capturing that value depends on processing and manufacturing at home. Tracking the CSIRO report's proposals will show whether local industry follows. Further reading Explore more on Electric Vehicles to see how battery supply chains are shaping the market. Source note: This article includes information reported by The Singleton Argus. Live Poll Should Australia manufacture more batteries domestically rather than exporting raw minerals?

SK Broadband keeps its name and, by its own estimate, keeps more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales and roughly KRW 1.2 trillion in EBITDA. The company says the entity left behind after the spinoff will post more than KRW 4 trillion in annual sales. The 2030 goal therefore asks for growth on top of a base that has already lost its data center and submarine cable revenue. That is a harder claim than a target that counts infrastructure income. The reports do not say which year the KRW 4 trillion base refers to, and they do not break the target into segments. Readers should treat the 2030 figure as management ambition. That framing signals that management sees the old mixed structure as a distraction rather than a strength. Separation also sharpens accountability. Once SK Horizon reports on its own, its utilization, build cost and customer mix become visible in ways they were not inside a larger carrier. SK Broadband, by contrast, gets judged on subscriber economics, content costs and enterprise contracts. Neither company can hide weak results inside the other’s strong ones. artigo.texto: Residents react to Google data center pause in Botetourt County ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - A judge’s ruling has halted work at the site of a planned Google data center in Botetourt County after finding the county mishandled its agreement with the company. Crews had already begun moving dirt at the site. Under Monday’s ruling, work must stop until public hearings are held in accordance with state law. The Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance called the decision a step in the right direction. Alliance member Kathryn Hatam said she believed the county and Google were moving too quickly. “We felt specifically that Botetourt County and Google were rushing the process and that wasn’t fair to the community, it’s not fair to the environment,” Hatam said. Tim Dooley, one of the attorneys behind the lawsuit against Botetourt County, said the ruling gives him hope that changes can be made. Dooley also works closely with the alliance. “There is a degree of fatalism in the public when these these big deals come down and people are not as powerless as they sometimes imagine unfortunately,” Dooley said. Hatam said she wants county leaders to use the ruling as a reason to go back to the drawing board. “The people are watching you now. We have a government here that is supposed to be of, by, and for the people and every local official swore an oath to that effect. So are you taking that oath seriously?” she said. In a statement, Botetourt County said it is reviewing the ruling and considering its next steps. “The county respects the legal process and appreciates the attention the court gave to hearing this matter. The county is reviewing the ruling with its legal counsel and the Board Members and is evaluating its options going forward.” Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Town of Selma's planning board is set to meet on Monday evening to consider agenda items related to a proposed data center. The board will consider a conditional rezoning request and special use permit of Montana-based Advanced Manufacturing, Inc.'s application to build a 177,000-square-foot, single-story data center dubbed "Project Volt." Other WRAL Top Stories The developer's rezoning request, according to town documents, encompasses over 100 acres near I-42 and Buffalo Road. People living near the proposed site tell WRAL that they are considering selling their homes if the data center plans become reality. "There's no way you can tell me I'm not going to be able to hear that thing around the clock if I decide to stay," Ron Parrish said. His family, he said, has lived on Eason Lane in Selma for four generations. Parrish told WRAL that neighbors had conversations with the data center developers on Monday about potential property sales. Representatives for Advanced Manufacturing did not respond to WRAL's request for comment. Meanwhile, people at recent public meetings have called for more transparency from town officials, as concerns about the facility's potential water consumption, electricity use, and noise loom. "For a while, it's going to hurt. What that's going to bring, we just don't know and that's what's causing a lot of headache here," Parrish said. Planning documents said that the applicant "will fund the required power infrastructure and reclaimed water system, which will supply all process water used to cool the facility." Selma leaders last month approved new regulations for data center projects in the town. The rules address electricity, water usage and cooling, and noise levels. Mayor Byron McAllister and a town spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on resident concerns or how the new rules would impact Project Volt. A town staff report on the project said many of the items required in the data center ordinance are not required until a building design is completed. The report goes on to say that an approved electricity study must be completed prior to construction, and that noise levels would be set as a condition of the special use permit. The items would need approval from Selma's town council before becoming final. McAllister indicated a council vote could happen early next month.

artigo.texto: View the interactive full-screen On 22 acres of the old Delta View Golf Course north of the Contra Costa Canal, Pittsburg has approved a three-story data center, an electrical substation, and a yard of 37 backup diesel generators. The city signed off on the design Dec. 11, 2025, at a hearing before a single official. Amhari Perkins, who started a petition against the project in June, said many residents did not hear about it until this spring. Since then, the controversy over the old golf course has packed Pittsburg City Hall past capacity, drawn a petition with more than 28,000 signatures, and pitted neighbors against union members in the council chamber. On Oct. 26, the City Council passed a 45-day emergency moratorium on new data centers. It exempts this project and expires Dec. 10 unless the council extends it. The data center’s first phase is already approved, but it still needs a power contract from the City Council and a permit for its generators from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District. A Scot Scoop review of 154 public records found that the data center was never secret. In 2019, the City Council approved a deal for a technology park on the land that “would include one or more data centers.” But the approvals came in three steps, each in a different forum. In 2024, the City Council approved a land-use plan the developer had applied for. In December 2025 came a state exemption for the project’s 37 backup generators and a design review hearing before one city official, the zoning administrator. The city also has money riding on the outcome: it lent the developer the entire $16.8 million price of the land, a debt since cut to $10.5 million, and its own utility will sell the data center its power. The city’s main response to the backlash, an advisory committee, was set up to advise only the city manager, so that, as City Manager Darin Gale wrote in August, its meetings would not be “Brown Act meetings,” California’s open-meetings law. What the city and the developer have said since the backlash does not always match what they wrote before it. The city manager says the developer, AVAIO, expects to use 4,000 to 6,000 gallons of water a day; AVAIO’s engineers told the wastewater agency they would need about 58,000, mostly to cool its servers. AVAIO says its design “may use substantially less.” A 2019 city agreement anticipated that the full park, across all phases, would “ultimately require approximately five million gallons of water per day.” AVAIO told Scot Scoop that “no project is proposed” for the rest of the site, but its own emails and memos plan for one: In March, it asked the agency about water for its “future phases,” and in June it told the federal government it expects more than $1 billion in investment there. From Black Diamond to data hub Pittsburg arose as a coal town called Black Diamond, then around heavy industry including Dow Chemical and the Columbia Steel mill. CalEnviroScreen, the state’s screening tool, places two census tracts within 1.5 miles of the golf course in the top 10% statewide on its overall score, which weighs pollution and residents’ vulnerability to it. That is the backdrop for the data center’s 37 backup diesel generators. AVAIO’s 2024 filing put their cancer risk at up to 17 in a million; the California Energy Commission requires measures holding it to no more than six. “For over 100 years, we had dirty industrial,” Gale said, but later said “heavy” was the word he meant. Today, about 43% of residents are Hispanic or Latino, and about a third speak Spanish at home. The city’s stake The city started negotiating over the golf course in August 2017, seven months before it closed the money-losing municipal course; the timeline below traces the deal. Between 2018 and 2024, the city ran a survey and held community meetings advertised with door hangers, more outreach than what state law requires, Gale said. In April 2022, AVAIO’s Pittsburg Data Hub LLC took over the deal. That September, the city sold about 102 acres to another AVAIO company, a land company, for $16.8 million and lent it the entire price at 2% interest, with no payments due for 42 months. If the city did not approve a project within two years, the company could give the land back and cancel the debt. In March 2024, a state filing listed Pittsburg Data Hub as the applicant for the technology park plan itself, which covers about 76 acres. ‘Will be a data center’ By September 2023, on a referral from a city staff member, AVAIO’s engineers at Kimley-Horn were asking Delta Diablo, the wastewater agency for Pittsburg, Antioch and Bay Point, about the golf course’s recycled water lines. On Feb. 7, 2024, Kimley-Horn engineer Ryan Bernal told the agency the land north of the canal “will be a data center,” using recycled water “for irrigation as well as cooling.” Three weeks later, on Feb. 28, the city sent out its first formal environmental notice, titled “Pittsburg Technology Park Specific Plan.” Its third page said Phase 1 would include “a data center and corresponding substation.” Of 14 written comments, one came from an individual. By July 2024, the draft environmental report described the Pittsburg Data Hub in detail, including its 37 generators. Four of its 12 comment letters came from residents. One, from a woman identified only as Nancy, argued that a project with about 30 generators could not be “low impact” and objected that a zoning administrator, “rather than the citizens,” would have the final say over the buildings. artigo.texto: A new study co-authored by a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health researcher has found that over the course of a year, the largest data centers in the United States use four times as much power as the city of Los Angeles. Findings also indicated that such centers’ electricity consumption and carbon emissions rival those of some U.S. states. The study, published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability, examined hyperscale data centers (HDCs), the largest and most powerful class of data centers that support services such as cloud computing, large language model training and global deployment of artificial intelligence tools. The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions since the rise of AI. The authors include researchers from Harvard University and Falco Bargagli Stoffi, an assistant professor in the UCLA Fielding Department of Biostatistics. They compared their findings on power usage to electricity sales by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), which serves approximately 4 million Angelenos. “Our central estimate suggests that the 403 hyperscale data centers we studied across the United States used nearly four times as much electricity as LADWP sells to its customers in a year,” said Bargagli Stoffi, adding that the analysis attributed more than half, or 54%, of the centers’ electricity use to fossil fuels. The study was one of the first to combine fragmented data, helping to better paint a picture of the emissions of individual facilities. “Better public information on electricity use would help communities and policymakers assess the environmental consequences of this industry’s growth,” Bargagli Stoffi said. The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is heavily generated by coal-fired power plants. The study found that four states — Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa —accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied.

Horne Co-Executive Chairman Alongside Milton "Todd" Ault III Mr. Ault to Step Down as Executive Chairman After Company Energizes Initial 20 MW at Michigan AI Data Center LAS VEGAS , Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that William B. Horne, its current Chief Executive Officer, has been named Co-Executive Chairman of the Board alongside founder and current Executive Chairman Milton "Todd" Ault III. Mr. Horne will continue to serve as the Chief Executive Officer of the Company. Mr. Ault plans to step down as Co-Executive Chairman after the Company's Michigan AI data center is fully energized. Upon Mr. Ault's resignation as a Co-Executive Chairman, Mr. Horne will become Chairman of the Board and continue as CEO and Mr. Ault will remain a member of the Company's board of directors. The Company expects to energize the initial 10 megawatts ("MW") of critical AI compute capacity at its Michigan AI data center in December 2026 and is targeting the end of March 2027 for the second 10 MW. "I want to see the Michigan AI data center through to full energization," said Mr. Ault. "Will has led Hyperscale Data as CEO for nearly six years. I trust his judgment, and I want our stockholders and employees to know who will lead the Company when I leave." Additionally, Hyperscale Data is preparing to separate Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), and its portfolio businesses in 2027. Management expects that separation to advance its 2027 goal of positioning Hyperscale Data as a pure-play AI data center operator, with the Michigan AI data center as its flagship facility. The Company invites all stockholders, investors and members of the public to join its virtual earnings call and Investor Day on Monday, November 23, 2026, at 2:30 p.m. Pacific time (5:30 p.m. Eastern time). Management will review financial results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. The Investor Day discussion will follow immediately and will cover the Company's businesses, operations and strategic priorities. All stockholders, investors and other interested parties are invited to participate. Interested parties are encouraged to register using the following link: Webinar Registration. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, ACG, is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: 24 Novembro 2026 Demanda de energia elétrica foi de 82 TWh, cerca de 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade do país, com emissões de 26 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A informação é publicada por ClimaInfo, 24-11-2026. Em um ano, entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025, os 403 maiores centros de dados dos Estados Unidos emitiram mais dióxido de carbono do que a Dinamarca, que tem cerca de 6 milhões de habitantes. É o que mostra um estudo publicado na revista Nature Sustainability na semana passada. A pesquisa é uma das primeiras a estimar o consumo de eletricidade e as emissões de centros de dados hiperescaláveis (HDCs, sigla em inglês) desde o surgimento da inteligência artificial, segundo a Euronews. Em diferentes cenários de carga, esses HDCs consumiram entre 68 e 99 terawatts-hora (TWh) de eletricidade, associados a aproximadamente 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (MtCO₂). No cenário médio, a demanda de eletricidade desses data centers foi de 82 TWh, correspondendo a 1,8% do consumo total de eletricidade dos EUA, com emissões de CO₂ atribuíveis de cerca de 26 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono. Cerca de 54% da geração atribuída foi proveniente de fontes de combustíveis fósseis, principalmente gás e carvão. A estimativa de emissões é de duas a três vezes maior do que a demonstrada em estudos anteriores, afirmou a autora sênior do estudo, Francesca Dominici, professora de bioestatística de Harvard. “É o equivalente à emissão de CO₂ de um pequeno país europeu”, disse a especialista, acrescentando que os planos para mais 2 mil centros de dados tornam essa quantidade ainda mais preocupante para o futuro, destaca a AP. Os HDCs são a maior classe de centros de dados, sendo o tipo que executa serviços em nuvem e treina grandes modelos de IA. Os edifícios da amostra tinham uma capacidade elétrica média de cerca de 40 megawatts, explica a Earth.com. 🔍 Adicione o Instituto Humanitas Unisinos – IHU às suas fontes favoritas do Google Os pesquisadores começaram o estudo com 675 locais candidatos de um banco de dados comercial e mantiveram os 403 que puderam ser confirmados. Cada endereço foi associado a um telhado, e sua área foi verificada no OpenStreetMap. Em seguida, os pesquisadores analisaram imagens de satélite e aéreas em busca de indícios de um centro de dados: grandes telhados uniformes, equipamentos de refrigeração e uma subestação ao lado. Dos HDCs analisados, 142 estão localizados na Virgínia, que abriga mais estruturas desse tipo do que qualquer outro estado dos EUA, 56 no Oregon e 38 em Ohio. Nenhum data center opera em sua capacidade nominal máxima a cada hora, e as empresas não divulgam suas cargas reais. Por isso, a equipe multiplicou a capacidade de cada instalação pelas horas do ano e por um fator de carga. Os pesquisadores executaram quatro versões desse fator, desde uma carga leve até uma destinada a abranger o treinamento pesado de IA, para chegar aos resultados. Agora a equipe planeja examinar os efeitos das emissões associadas aos HDCs na saúde, conta Francesca. “As centrais elétricas movidas a combustíveis fósseis nos sistemas regionais de distribuição de energia, associadas a essa demanda, também liberam outros poluentes, como partículas finas, óxidos de nitrogênio e dióxido de enxofre, que estão diretamente ligados a doenças cardíacas e pulmonares e à morte prematura”, disse a especialista. As pessoas que respiram esses poluentes vivem perto das usinas, que podem estar longe de qualquer centro de dados.

artigo.texto: Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE), incluindo Dinamarca, Finlândia, Alemanha, Luxemburgo, Países Baixos, Portugal , Espanha e Suécia, manifestaram-se em defesa do novo Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (ETS2). Oito países da UE estão se unindo para proteger o mercado de carbono contra pressões para adiá-lo. Oito Estados-membros da União Europeia (UE) defenderam conjuntamente o sistema alargado de comércio de emissões do bloco, alertando que novos atrasos ou ajustes à sua implementação poderão comprometer a segurança energética, prolongar a dependência dos combustíveis fósseis importados e dificultar o investimento em tecnologias limpas. Em carta enviada ao Comissário Europeu para a Ação Climática, Wopke Hoekstra, em 23 de novembro, os ministros do clima argumentaram que a dependência de combustíveis fósseis importados representa riscos econômicos e de segurança significativos. O ETS2 é visto como uma ferramenta para promover a eletrificação nos transportes e na construção civil, reduzindo assim a necessidade de importação de petróleo e gás. A medida surge em meio à pressão da República Tcheca, Hungria, Polônia , Eslováquia, Itália e Grécia para flexibilizar ou adiar o sistema. Na cúpula de outubro, os líderes da UE concordaram em revisar o impacto do ETS2 antes de sua implementação a partir de janeiro de 2028. Segundo esse mecanismo, os combustíveis utilizados no transporte rodoviário e no aquecimento estariam sujeitos a um preço de carbono, o que poderia aumentar os custos para o consumidor. Este é também um ponto de discórdia, tendo em conta os já elevados custos da energia e do custo de vida na Europa. Oito ministros alertaram que ajustes ao ETS2 poderiam comprometer a estabilidade da política climática e impactar os planos de investimento das empresas. Eles também argumentaram que o Fundo Social para o Clima deveria ser mantido para apoiar famílias e empresas vulneráveis que enfrentam custos crescentes. Por outro lado, o vice-primeiro-ministro checo, Karel Havlíček, afirmou que a implementação do ETS2 no atual contexto económico e geopolítico é ilógica. Alertou que a imposição de taxas adicionais seria difícil de ser aceite pela população, uma vez que muitas famílias já enfrentam a pressão do aumento dos preços da energia e do custo de vida.

artigo.texto: Scientists have long warned of the massively growing environmental footprint of AI data centers, facilities that are often powered by gas plants and releasing a staggering amount of pollution and waste heat. In an effort to maximize the amount of available solar energy — and avoid the wrath of a public that has squarely turned against data centers — tech CEOs have become increasingly serious about launching the facilities into orbit instead. SpaceX, in particular, has taken the concept to its extreme, with CEO Elon Musk proposing the launch of up to one million orbital data centers, each significantly larger than the International Space Station, to meet the surging demands for AI computing power. But besides some glaring questions surrounding the concept’s viability and the potentially debilitating effects for astronomy research, the orbiting satellites could multiply certain forms of pollution by over 100 times, University College London chemistry professor Eloise Marais and research fellow Connor Barker argue in a new paper to be published in the journal Earth and Space Chemistry. The team found that launching such a large number of data centers could boost total emissions from rocket launches, including the release of ozone-damaging chemicals and other pollutants into the upper atmosphere, by more than 150 times compared to last year’s measurements — while generating up to 150 times more nitrogen oxides released during reentry. While scientists have long suspected that SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket is releasing copious amounts of potentially ozone layer-damaging chemicals during launch, the company’s much larger Starship rocket could exacerbate the environmental damage considerably. According to Marais and Barker’s calculations, the company would need to launch at least 5,000 Starship rockets a year to fill out its planned constellation — a huge number compared to the mere 330 orbital rockets that launched last year globally. However, the researchers had to base their paper of some major assumptions. As Scientific American points out, SpaceX has yet to disclose some basic information needed to gauge the exact environmental footprint of its lofty plans. “It became apparent [early on in our research] that the kind of information that’s needed isn’t there,” Marais told the magazine. For one, how much nitrogen oxides will be released by SpaceX’s reusable Super Heavy booster itself remains unclear at best. We also don’t know what materials the company will use for its hardware, meaning that the researchers were unable to estimate the toll that metal pollution would take on the atmosphere. Therefore, the duo is calling on companies to disclose more information about their launches. “There’s nothing here that’s perfect, but there has to be a solution to go forward that can simultaneously respect the proprietary information while also demanding that we know what is being dumped in the atmosphere,” University of British Columbia space pollution expert Aaron Boley, who was not involved in the study, told SciAm. Nonetheless, by basing their calculations on previous estimates involving NASA’s Space Shuttles, the team still found that Starships could release as much in nitrogen oxide emissions a year as an entire European country. “The unprecedented increase in anthropogenic chemicals stands to modify stratospheric aerosols, deplete ozone, alter climate, perturb mesospheric nitrogen, and degrade air quality,” the researchers concluded in their paper. “These risks should incite regulators to demand provision of information needed to calculate emissions and enable environmental impact assessments.” More on orbital data centers: Anybody Who Thinks Orbital Data Centers are a Good Idea Is Suffering from AI Psychosis, Experts Argue

artigo.texto: Parcerias B.Grimm e NTT buscam oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de IA de 400 MW na Tailândia Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Pontos-chaveO memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez… Ver mais - O memorando apenas compromete os parceiros a buscar uma oportunidade de 400 MW, em vez de confirmar a construção. - O negócio existente de geração e distribuição de energia da B.Grimm sustenta o seu papel energético no plano do data center. - O acordo separado da NTT com a Bloom Energy mostra que a disponibilidade de energia agora determina a rapidez com que a capacidade de IA pode ser entregue. A B.Grimm anunciou em 24 de novembro de 2026 que a B.Grimm Power havia assinado um memorando de entendimento com a NTT Global Data Center para buscar uma oportunidade de desenvolver um centro de dados de 400 MW na Tailândia, abrangendo infraestrutura digital, um ecossistema de IA e infraestrutura energética, com investimento estimado em aproximadamente 113 bilhões de THB. O memorando é um acordo para buscar a oportunidade, não uma confirmação de que as obras já começaram. Nopadej Karnasuta, presidente da B.Grimm Power para Tailândia, Malásia e Negócios de Soluções de Energia & Industriais, participou da visita ao Japão durante a qual o documento foi assinado. Segundo a B.Grimm, a visita, liderada pelo vice-primeiro-ministro e ministro das Finanças Ekniti Nitithanprapas, ocorreu de 17 a 21 de novembro de 2026. Conversas no Japão conectam infraestrutura de IA e energia Em um comunicado de 23 de novembro de 2026, o Conselho de Investimentos da Tailândia informa que a delegação esteve em Tóquio de 17 a 20 de novembro de 2026. O Diálogo de Investimento e Negócios Tailândia–Japão BOI–Keidanren reuniu 64 executivos japoneses do setor privado, de 38 empresas de nove setores. As discussões abordaram três cadeias de suprimentos: veículos modernos; infraestrutura de IA e eletrônica avançada; e redes elétricas modernas. Essas prioridades correspondem de perto à combinação de computação e energia prevista no MoU. A delegação também visitou o NTT Data Mitaka EAST Data Center para estudar segurança, continuidade dos sistemas e eficiência energética em infraestruturas que dão suporte à IA. Segundo o relato da B.Grimm, Ekniti destacou que as instalações da NTT no Japão são eficientes, silenciosas, respeitam o meio ambiente e conseguem coexistir com as comunidades locais. A B.Grimm Power também pretende manter essas práticas e compartilhar conhecimentos e tecnologia com a população tailandesa no longo prazo. Operações de geração de energia e digitais da B.Grimm A B.Grimm Power leva para a proposta uma operação consolidada no setor de energia. Seu perfil corporativo informa que a empresa tem capacidade instalada de 5.180 MW, fornece energia por meio de suas próprias redes de distribuição a mais de 400 clientes industriais e tem como meta garantir contratos de compra de energia que totalizem 10.000 MW até 2030. Com sede na Tailândia, a empresa desenvolve, financia, constrói e opera usinas de energia em áreas sem instalações anteriores. Essas operações são relevantes porque o MoU inclui explicitamente a infraestrutura energética, além do centro de dados e do ecossistema de IA. A B.Grimm também tem uma iniciativa de infraestrutura digital industrial. Em 18 de junho de 2026, a subsidiária B.Grimm BeyondBridge e a INET criaram a B.Grimm INET para desenvolver e operar plataformas na Tailândia voltadas à gestão de energia, a sistemas ambientais e de serviços públicos inteligentes, ao monitoramento e à gestão de gases de efeito estufa, à segurança na nuvem e a tecnologias de IA. A iniciativa anterior documenta a expansão da B.Grimm para além da geração de energia, com entrada no setor de plataformas digitais industriais, antes do acordo com a NTT. Expansão regional e estratégia energética da NTT A NTT DATA nomeou Yasuhiro Kajiki em 10 de setembro de 2026 para o cargo de diretor-geral para Japão e Ásia-Pacífico da NTT Global Data Centers, com responsabilidade pelas operações regionais e pela estratégia de crescimento. A empresa associou a ampliação das atribuições do cargo ao aumento da demanda dos clientes por infraestrutura digital preparada para IA na região da Ásia-Pacífico. Um acordo com a Bloom Energy, anunciado em 5 de novembro de 2026, prevê que a NTT instale 900 MW de capacidade de geração de energia no local em vários projetos de centros de dados no mundo todo, com os primeiros envios planejados para 2027. A NTT DATA espera que os sistemas modulares de células a combustível da Bloom permitam disponibilizar energia à medida que as obras avançam e ampliar a capacidade para atender às cargas de trabalho de IA, cada vez mais intensivas em energia. “Nossos clientes estão desenvolvendo recursos de IA em um ritmo que a rede elétrica, sozinha, nem sempre consegue acompanhar, e a rapidez para disponibilizar energia tornou-se um dos fatores decisivos para fornecer capacidade onde e quando ela é necessária”, afirmou Doug Adams, CEO da NTT Global Data Centers. Anunciado separadamente do MoU tailandês, o acordo com a Bloom mostra por que o papel da B.Grimm no setor de energia é importante: para os centros de dados de IA, garantir energia escalável é essencial para fornecer capacidade computacional. A questão em aberto é a execução: será que os parceiros conseguirão combinar a expansão dos centros de dados da NTT com as operações de energia e a experiência em infraestrutura digital da B.Grimm para oferecer a eficiência, a operação silenciosa e a convivência com as comunidades destacadas durante a visita ao Japão? Isso transformaria um memorando firmado durante uma missão de investimento na infraestrutura de IA operacional que a Tailândia busca.

artigo.texto: Key Takeaways - The top-spec Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 features a foldable steering wheel, turning a concept BYD showcased at the 2019 Shanghai Auto Show into reality. - BYD said the feature is not only a parked rest solution, but also a technology reserve for future L3 and L4 autonomous driving built on steer-by-wire. The world's first mass-produced foldable steering wheel, featured on the Tai 9 flagship SUV from BYD's (HKEX: 1211) Fang Cheng Bao brand, traces its conceptual roots back 7 years to the 2019 Shanghai Auto Show. On April 16, 2019, BYD debuted the E-SEED GT concept car at the Shanghai Auto Show, showcasing for the first time a retractable steering wheel that could fold into the dashboard in autonomous driving mode — a design widely viewed as science fiction at the time. The BYD E-SEED GT concept car showcased a retractable steering wheel design in 2019: Seven years later, that concept has reached mass production on the Tai 9, which was launched on November 19. The SUV starts at 279,900 yuan ($41,700), with the top-spec variant priced at 329,900 yuan featuring the foldable smart cockpit. The feature sparked some skepticism on the Chinese internet over whether it is necessary following its release, though such doubts have been rare in overseas communities. In a statement shared with CnEVPost on Monday, BYD said the foldable smart cockpit is not only a solution for current parked rest needs, but also a forward-looking technology reserve for future L3 and L4 autonomous driving. Videos highlight the details of the BYD Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9's foldable steering wheel. The core prerequisite for a foldable steering wheel is eliminating the mechanical steering column in favor of steer-by-wire technology. Its mass production was also enabled by regulatory relaxation in China. On July 1, 2026, China's mandatory national standard GB 17675-2025 took effect, removing the requirement for a mechanical connection in steering systems. BYD was one of the drafting units of the standard. Built on BYD's in-house steer-by-wire technology, the steering wheel uses a 180-degree hinge and high-precision motors derived from embodied AI robots, supporting folding from 0 to 180 degrees and taking about 10 seconds to stow away. Once folded, it frees up about 25 centimeters of legroom for the driver, pairing with a seat that reclines to 165 degrees to meet needs such as resting while waiting for a charge or camping. In terms of operational boundaries, the steering wheel can only be folded when the vehicle is completely stopped and shifted into Park. It cannot be operated while driving, and must be fully unfolded and locked before the vehicle is allowed to move. The steer-by-wire system features 5 layers of redundancy across power supply, communication, sensing, control, and actuation, and the folding system has obtained ASIL-D functional safety certification, according to the company. BYD said the folding mechanism has completed 96,000 durability tests across extreme temperatures ranging from -30°C (-22°F) to 85°C (185°F), with a start-stop lifespan of 80,000 cycles, and that the airbag has passed deployment verification in both folded and unfolded states. Around the foldable smart cockpit, BYD has filed a cumulative 272 patents and is positioning this top-spec technology anchor as an interface for next-generation smart cockpits, the company said. artigo.texto: AOI Announces Multi-Year Long-Term Agreement with Tier-1 Hyperscale Datacenter Customer SUGAR LAND, Texas , Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AOI (NASDAQ: AAOI), a leading provider of advanced optical and HFC networking products that power AI, today announced it has signed a multiyear long-term agreement (LTA) with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer. Under the agreement, AOI will supply the customer with 800G transceiver products as well as laser diodes over the four-year time period from December 2026 through December 2030. Other products may be added depending on future needs. The customer has agreed to purchase a minimum commitment of approximately $1.5 billion of 800G transceivers in 2027 and approximately $0.7 billion in laser diodes between 2028 and 2029. As part of the agreement, AOI will contribute a $2 million one-time expense to accelerate qualification efforts with this customer. The customer made no commitment of capital as part of this LTA. "Securing another LTA with a second hyperscale customer provides us with meaningful long-term revenue and demand visibility, and reinforces our technology leadership, differentiated capabilities in advanced optics, and important role in the AI infrastructure ecosystem," said Dr. Thompson Lin, AOI's Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer. "We believe we are well positioned with our automated manufacturing capabilities and in-house laser technology to support the next phase of AI datacenter deployment." Lin continued, "We have a long history of manufacturing lasers and have strategically curated our portfolio to provide the high-performance optical sources driving the industry's shift toward silicon photonics, near-packaged optics (NPO), and co-packaged optics (CPO). As part of this agreement, we will be supplying our laser diodes, some of which we expect will be used to power CPO architectures, starting in 2028. We believe that in the future, CPO and related technologies will continue to drive increased demand for high-power lasers and we plan to further expand our laser manufacturing capacity in Texas to support this anticipated growth." "The customer's forecast indicates significant demand beyond the purchase commitments specified in the agreement over its four-year term," said Dr. Stefan Murry, AOI's Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer. "While not guaranteed, the current level of demand based on long-term discussions with the customer exceeds $10 billion over the four years of the LTA. Expanding our production capacity would position us to serve that demand, but additional sales beyond the $2.2 billion of purchase commitments specified in the agreement will depend on our ability to bring that capacity online and secure additional purchase commitments. Under the LTA, we have committed to supplying volumes needed, including a commitment to ship an agreed-upon quantity of products made in the USA, starting in the first quarter of 2027 and ramping throughout 2027. We believe this agreement supports our ability to further increase our capacity, allocate capital, and invest in advanced technologies with greater confidence. To support this accelerating customer demand, we are continuing to expand our capacity and remain focused on executing on our expansion plans." artigo.texto: Washington wants America’s AI infrastructure to stay home. But Americans aren’t sure they want it next door, and companies are discovering that building at home is becoming increasingly difficult. The future of U.S. data center investment now depends on whether America can make home the easiest place to build, not just the most expensive place to leave. A Friday Warning With No Details On Friday, November 20, President Donald Trump issued a warning to American companies expanding data center infrastructure overseas. The message was blunt: build in the United States, or face a “tremendous tax.” “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at the White House. “If they do that, they can. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.” He framed the threat around China, arguing that overseas infrastructure could ultimately benefit America’s biggest strategic competitor. “China will take all of them,” he said, explaining why he would not allow data centers to go into other countries. The announcement sounded decisive. The policy behind it, however, remains unclear. Trump provided no tax rate, implementation timeline or legal mechanism, and acknowledged that he had not yet discussed the proposal with his own officials. Congress’s role in imposing a new federal tax also remains a significant question, because a president cannot create a federal tax by announcement alone. But the threat raises a question bigger than what Washington intends to do to companies building abroad: If America wants companies to build at home, is it making the United States more attractive, or simply threatening the alternatives? That is the central question for U.S. data center investment. Why Companies Look Beyond America Data centers are the factories of the AI economy. They house the computing capacity needed to train AI models, operate cloud services and process billions of requests. Their location matters because electricity, cooling, connectivity, land, permitting and proximity to customers determine how quickly and economically they can operate. That is why international expansion is not automatically a retreat from America. Companies build abroad to serve customers in regional markets, meet data residency requirements, reduce latency and secure favorable operating conditions. International infrastructure can strengthen an American company’s global business rather than surrender it. Finland illustrates the point. In September 2026, Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finnish digital infrastructure, its largest investment in Europe. The expansion builds on Finland’s existing data center presence and reflects the country’s energy and infrastructure advantages, including access to carbon-free electricity and a cold climate that can help reduce cooling requirements. Finland is not China. It is a U.S. ally competing for investment. Google’s decision should prompt Washington to examine what makes overseas markets attractive, not assume every foreign project weakens America. If U.S. data center investment is to stay in America, Washington must compete on the same terms: power, price, speed and permission. What Americans Actually Want Here is the contradiction Washington cannot ignore: the government wants more data centers built at home, but many Americans do not want them in their communities. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on June 11, 2026, surveying 4,531 people over six days, found that just 33 percent agreed it was mainly a good thing to build data centers at a rapid pace, while 64 percent disagreed. Some 57 percent said they would oppose a data center being built in their own community, including two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans. That finding has hardened, not softened. In a Gallup survey conducted March 2-18, 2026, among 1,000 U.S. adults, 71 percent opposed constructing an AI data center in their local area, including 48 percent who were strongly opposed. In the same survey, only 53 percent opposed a nuclear energy plant nearby, meaning data centers are now less popular than nuclear plants. By August 2026, the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center reported that 61 percent of Americans opposed new data centers in their area, up from 49 percent earlier in the year. Opposition crossed party lines, with majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents expressing resistance. An Ipsos Consumer Tracker released September 15, 2026, found 69 percent were concerned about the growth of AI data center construction in the United States, including 37 percent who were very concerned. Among those concerned, the top worries were strain on local water supplies at 50 percent, strain on the electrical grid at 41 percent, and higher residential utility bills at 35 percent. These are not simply objections to technology. Residents worry about who pays for grid upgrades, whether electricity bills will rise, how much water facilities consume, and whether communities have any meaningful say over projects that could reshape their surroundings. Washington wants America to host the AI boom. But the people expected to host the infrastructure are increasingly asking what they get in return. That question will decide the future of U.S. data center investment far more than any threat. The America That Says No The resistance is already affecting development. Data Center Watch reported that at least 75 U.S. projects valued at approximately $130 billion were blocked or delayed during the first quarter of 2026. In the second quarter, it recorded at least 45 additional project disruptions valued at nearly $68 billion. These are quarterly figures, not necessarily unique projects across the six-month period, but they show the scale of disruption. In September 2025, Google withdrew its proposed $1 billion data center development in Franklin Township, Indiana, ahead of a council vote that threatened its rezoning approval. artigo.texto: Veja o resumo da notícia O Brasil busca ampliar sua participação no mercado global de data centers, impulsionado pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial (IA) e pela demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Segundo reportagem da revista britânica The Economist, o país reúne condições favoráveis para atrair investimentos no setor. Sendo assim, entre os principais diferenciais estão a oferta de energia renovável, o crescimento do mercado digital e a localização estratégica para conexões internacionais. Além disso, o avanço da inteligência artificial tem elevado a necessidade de capacidade computacional em diferentes regiões do mundo. Nesse cenário, o Brasil tenta se consolidar como um dos principais destinos para novos empreendimentos. Brasil atrai investimentos bilionários em data centers A expansão do setor já aparece em projetos anunciados no país. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty desenvolve um complexo de data centers e planeja ampliar suas operações. De acordo com a The Economist, a companhia pretende investir US$ 1,2 bilhão na região, acompanhando o crescimento da demanda por armazenamento e processamento de dados. Desse modo, o movimento reflete o interesse de empresas em ampliar a infraestrutura necessária para sustentar serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Capacidade de data centers pode chegar a 5 GW até 2030 Apesar do potencial de crescimento, a América Latina ainda representa uma parcela pequena da infraestrutura mundial de data centers. Segundo a publicação britânica, a região possui menos de 600 instalações, com capacidade conjunta próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW). O volume é inferior ao registrado apenas no Reino Unido. O Brasil, por sua vez, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade, com aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados. A expectativa é de expansão nos próximos anos. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030. Caso a projeção se confirme, o país poderá ampliar significativamente sua presença no mercado internacional de infraestrutura digital, em meio à crescente demanda por processamento de dados e inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: Reino Unido e UE concordam em conectar sistemas de comércio de emissões até 2028 O Reino Unido e a União Europeia chegaram a um acordo para conectar seus sistemas de comércio de emissões, com data-alvo de 1º de janeiro de 2028 para que a conexão entre em operação, conforme noticiado pelo ENGINE. A medida foi concebida para se alinhar à extensão programada pelo Reino Unido da precificação de carbono ao transporte marítimo internacional, segundo um explicativo publicado em 20 de novembro pelo Departamento de Segurança Energética e Net Zero do Reino Unido. Como parte da extensão prevista, o Sistema de Comércio de Emissões do Reino Unido passará a abranger metade das emissões de viagens internacionais que conectam portos do Reino Unido e portos de fora do país, para navios de 5.000 toneladas de arqueação bruta ou mais, a partir de 1º de janeiro de 2028. Desde 1º de julho de 2026, o sistema já cobre todas as emissões de viagens domésticas e de embarcações atracadas em portos britânicos. O ETS da UE funciona em bases semelhantes, aplicando-se a 50% das emissões em viagens entre portos da UE e portos de fora do bloco, ao mesmo tempo que obriga as empresas de navegação a responder pela totalidade das emissões de viagens entre portos da UE. Após a conexão, os dois sistemas continuarão a funcionar de forma independente, mas permitirão que as empresas de navegação usem licenças de qualquer um dos mercados para cumprir suas obrigações, o que pode eliminar a necessidade de os operadores abrangidos pelos dois sistemas comprarem licenças britânicas e licenças da UE separadamente. O ETS do Reino Unido também espelhará o tratamento dado pela UE aos portos vizinhos de transbordo de contêineres. Os portos que constam da lista designada pela Comissão Europeia não serão tratados como portos de escala britânicos ao se determinar quais emissões de viagem são cobertas pelo sistema, e essa lista é revisada a cada dois anos. Cronograma de conformidade e alinhamento administrativo O arranjo também pretende tratar das obrigações de emissões relativas a 2027, com o primeiro prazo para o uso intercambiável de licenças fixado em 30 de setembro de 2028. As duas partes buscam ainda um processo administrativo compartilhado que possa permitir às empresas de navegação lidar com a conformidade nos dois sistemas em um único arcabouço. O Reino Unido também pretende eliminar seu preço mínimo de leilão para licenças de carbono assim que a conexão entrar em vigor. O acordo busca alinhar mais estreitamente as regras de navegação do ETS do Reino Unido às do ETS da UE, incluindo os requisitos de monitoramento, relato e verificação. O Reino Unido planeja descontinuar o arranjo temporário que permite às empresas de navegação entregar licenças referentes a apenas 50% das emissões em viagens entre a Grã-Bretanha e a Irlanda do Norte, e espera-se que essas viagens passem a enfrentar a exigência integral de 100% a partir de 2028, igualando outras rotas domésticas britânicas. Espera-se que navios de passageiros e ro-pax que atendem ilhas com menos de 200.000 residentes e sem ligação rodoviária ou ferroviária com o continente sejam elegíveis a uma derrogação temporária de entrega de licenças até pelo menos 31 de dezembro de 2030. Navios com classe de gelo também devem receber uma redução de 5% em suas obrigações de entrega de licenças até pelo menos a mesma data. Combustíveis de menor emissão e revisão da medida global Quanto à contabilização de combustíveis, os operadores poderiam aplicar um fator de emissão zero a biocombustíveis elegíveis, combustíveis renováveis de origem não biológica e combustíveis de carbono reciclado, desde que atendam aos critérios de sustentabilidade e de redução de gases de efeito estufa estabelecidos na Diretiva de Energias Renováveis da UE. O governo britânico também indicou que examinará como suas regras de precificação de carbono interagem com qualquer futura medida global de emissões adotada pela Organização Marítima Internacional. A revisão buscaria evitar a cobrança dupla das empresas de navegação por emissões idênticas, mantendo os requisitos de conformidade viáveis. O departamento afirmou que qualquer revisão considerará mudanças relevantes no ETS da UE, com resultados destinados a sustentar o apoio à descarbonização marítima e a manter a consistência com o net zero. Preparativos técnicos e aprovações legislativas ainda estão pendentes antes que os dois mercados de carbono possam ser unidos até janeiro de 2028.

artigo.texto: Johnson Creek board delays vote on proposed data center The Village Board president said he wants more information before the board moves forward. Johnson Creek board delays vote on proposed data center The Village Board president said he wants more information before the board moves forward. The Johnson Creek Village Board delayed a vote Monday on a proposed data center in Jefferson County, with the board president saying he wants more information before the board decides whether to move forward. The proposal, called the Johnson Creek Connectivity Hub, is a one-story, 100,000-square-foot edge data center planned for an industrially zoned site near River Drive and County Road Y. The developer, RadiusDC, says the facility would support everyday online services, including video calls, online banking, and streaming. At Monday’s meeting, residents raised concerns about potential water use, noise and environmental effects. Rosa, a community member who spoke at the meeting, asked board members to consider the project’s possible impact on her young daughter. “I will come up to you when I see you and I want you to look my daughter in the eyes and tell her that this is the best option for her,” Rosa said. “She’s 2 years old.” RadiusDC says the project could bring construction and full-time jobs and generate about $500,000 a year in property taxes. The company says construction could begin in 2027, with the facility expected to open in 2029, subject to approvals. Board President John Swisher drew cheers from the crowd when he suggested tabling the vote. He said the time will allow staff to take a closer look at any potential public health impacts and consider operations at similarly sized data centers in other communities. Trustee Rooney Freimund said tabling the vote wouldn't change public opinion. After initially being opposed to the project, he now believes it would benefit Johnson Creek, suggesting it doesn't compare to large-scale projects in other cities. "An airport is an airport, right? Watertown compared to Chicago O’Hare are two different airports," Freimund said. I’ve heard every one of you. I believe you love this community. I love the community too. I believe this project is good for Johnson Creek. We’re going to agree to disagree.” The board is expected to take up the proposal again Jan. 11, 2027.

artigo.texto: Piedmont delays two data center proposals amid utility and zoning concerns PIEDMONT, Okla. (KOKH) — Two proposed data centers in Piedmont will have to wait until December for further consideration after the City Council delayed action on both projects Monday night. Council members voted 3-2 to postpone consideration of Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky until Dec. 3. Later in the meeting, the council also voted 3-2 to bring Beltline Energy's proposal back on the same date while the city attorney reviews questions about changes previously approved by the council. Both developers are seeking to rezone agricultural land for industrial data center developments, but neither project received final approval Monday night. Cloverleaf's Project Open Sky involves a rezoning application from Cimarron ProjectCo LLC and Cimarron DevCo LLC. The developers want to change the property's zoning from A-1 General Agriculture to a Planned Unit Development, or PUD, which would establish development standards for the proposed data center. The application was scheduled for its first ordinance reading Monday night. However, the council voted to postpone further consideration until a special meeting on December 3rd. Beltline Energy is also seeking to rezone agricultural land for its proposed data center. Some Oklahomans raised concerns about whether Piedmont's infrastructure could handle the demands of the proposed developments, particularly when it comes to electricity, water, and sewer services. "The whole thing for me, being retired in utility, is the electric capacity this is gonna take, and also the water and the sewer," said Billy Parker, a Yukon resident. "There's so many questions left that are not answered about the water and the sewer, what it's gonna take for these data centers and so much of that and the electric that they're gonna use." Those concerns were echoed during the council's discussion of Beltline Energy's proposal. One council member urged the city to postpone further action until the development agreement had been fully reviewed. He argued that important details about the project's cooling system remained unresolved. The council member said Beltline previously indicated it was considering moving away from a closed-loop cooling system in favor of air cooling or another alternative. He questioned how much water the original system would hold, whether it would need to be flushed periodically, and what impact a different cooling method could have on noise and electricity demand. "After working on this issue for 10 months, these answers were very disappointing to me, to say the least," he said. He also questioned whether an air-cooled system would require additional fans and how those fans would be powered. "This is all too vague for me personally to take," he said. The council member argued Piedmont should settle the details of the development agreement before moving forward with additional land-use decisions. "First we need to agree on the development plan, then move on to annex or not," he said. The discussion also raised concerns about whether amendments approved during the council's October 26th meeting were accurately incorporated into an ordinance outlining the proposed rezoning for Beltline Energy's project. Council members questioned whether discrepancies between the approved meeting minutes and the ordinance could expose the city to a legal challenge. During the discussion, the city attorney acknowledged that inconsistencies could be challenged. The attorney also explained that the city's required second reading provides an opportunity to review the language and determine whether corrections are needed. A council member proposed directing the city attorney to compare the approved October 26th meeting minutes with the ordinance and identify any differences. His motion called for a report outlining whether the amendments had been properly incorporated and what consequences the city could face if the ordinance did not accurately reflect the council's previous actions. He also proposed preparing a corrected ordinance and holding another first reading if significant changes were necessary. However, another member argued the city could complete that review while keeping the proposal on track for a second reading December 3rd. The council ultimately voted 3-2 to amend the motion, allowing the ordinance to return for a potential second reading at the December meeting while the city attorney reviews the language. If the review identifies significant changes that need to be made, the ordinance may have to return for another first reading rather than moving directly toward final approval. Both data center proposals are expected to return to the Piedmont City Council on December 3rd, when members could take additional action depending on the outstanding reviews and discussions.

artigo.texto: Data centers: Oportunidades e controles de exportação A expansão dos data centers no Brasil ganha impulso com incentivos fiscais, mas enfrenta desafios diante das restrições dos EUA ao acesso a semicondutores. terça-feira, 24 de novembro de 2026 Atualizado em 23 de novembro de 2026 16:03 O Brasil quer atrair data centers com energia renovável e incentivos fiscais. Os Estados Unidos querem controlar quem utiliza os semicondutores que tornam esses investimentos possíveis. As duas políticas agora se encontram nos projetos de empresas que pretendem instalar servidores em território brasileiro. A localização será nacional; parte das condições para funcionamento dependerá de Washington. O REDATA, aprovado pelo Congresso e sancionado em setembro, traz vantagem concreta. Equipamentos importados representam parcela elevada do investimento, e a tributação brasileira encarecia a instalação, enquanto outros países ofereciam benefícios para receber os mesmos projetos. Reduzir esse custo melhora a posição do Brasil numa disputa em que o investidor compara energia, conectividade, impostos e previsibilidade. O REDATA prevê suspensão de tributos federais nas aquisições abrangidas, acompanhada de contrapartidas. Como regra geral, exige destinar ao mercado brasileiro ao menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo de serviços e investir no país o equivalente a 2% das compras beneficiadas, com condições diferenciadas previstas na legislação. Também estabelece requisitos energéticos e limite de consumo de água no resfriamento. Desta forma, o desenho institucional busca vincular a renúncia fiscal a benefícios locais. Como se sabe, a importância dos datacenters ultrapassa o interesse dos fornecedores de equipamentos. Capacidade computacional tornou-se infraestrutura estratégica para empresas, governos e pesquisa. Assim como portos permitem movimentar mercadorias, datacenters permitem processar informações em escala. A inteligência artificial pode parecer imaterial na tela do usuário, mas depende de instalações, cabos e muita eletricidade. O Brasil dispõe de vantagens nessa combinação. Sua matriz elétrica majoritariamente renovável interessa a empresas que precisam conciliar expansão computacional e metas de redução de emissões. A conectividade internacional e o tamanho do mercado interno também contam. Nenhuma dessas vantagens, entretanto, dispensa investimentos em transmissão, armazenamento e segurança do abastecimento. Água exige cuidado semelhante. O REDATA estabelece índice de eficiência hídrica para resfriamento de até 0,05 litro por kWh, medido anualmente. O parâmetro permite avaliar o desempenho das instalações, mas precisa ser acompanhado da análise das condições locais de abastecimento e de fiscalização durante a operação, pois a eficiência de cada unidade não resolve a pressão acumulada sobre uma bacia hidrográfica. Neste tema, a experiência norte-americana traz uma advertência. Levantamento citado pela Agência Internacional de Energia identificou 46 projetos de data centers de inteligência artificial bloqueados, retirados ou paralisados após oposição local, entre janeiro de 2024 e meados de maio de 2026. Estavam associados a mais de US$ 170 bilhões em investimentos anunciados. A esses desafios soma-se uma nova restrição. Em 19 de novembro, o BIS - Bureau of Industry and Security, do Departamento de Comércio norte-americano, publicou uma norma que combina dois controles. Um exige licença para operações abrangidas com determinados semicondutores avançados destinadas a Brasil, Indonésia, Malásia, Singapura e Tailândia. Outro alcança equipamentos utilizados em datacenters que forneçam acesso remoto, acima dos parâmetros definidos, a empresas sediadas, ou com controladora final sediada, em Macau ou nos países do grupo D:5 (China, Rússia, Irã, Coreia do Norte, Cuba e Venezuela). A distinção nesta regulamentação importa: a exigência relacionada ao destino brasileiro não depende apenas de demonstrar atendimento a clientes restritos. A norma prevê exceção condicionada para empresas sediadas nos Estados Unidos, além de obrigações de reporte e diligência. Esta nova regulamentação já entrou em vigor, e receberá comentários até 19 de janeiro de 2027, o que pode ser uma oportunidade para empresas brasileiras interessadas no tema responderem tecnicamente à consulta, buscando regras previsíveis para investimentos futuros. O investidor em datacenters no Brasil terá que atentar para esta regulamentação dos EUA, pois sua lógica é a de monitorar quem utiliza a capacidade computacional, mesmo sem receber fisicamente o chip. Para os contratos, haverá impactos com relação à concessão de licenças, risco de financiamento, contratos de serviços que identifiquem usuários, informações societárias e mudanças na operação. Para o Brasil, surge ainda uma questão concorrencial. Se as condições de acesso aos equipamentos variam conforme a sede e o controle das empresas, projetos instalados no mesmo território podem enfrentar exigências diferentes. Essa assimetria merecerá atenção diplomática, pois se o Brasil oferece incentivos à localização, os EUA consideram a identidade de quem investe e de quem será atendido. Nada disso elimina a oportunidade, para o Brasil, de exportar serviços digitais. Projetos aprovados na Zona de Processamento de Exportação do Pecém mostram que essa possibilidade já integra a agenda de investimentos. Energia, conectividade e processamento podem ser combinados para atender clientes no exterior, respeitadas as condições de cada regime. O Congresso brasileiro criou uma parte das condições para disputar esses investimentos. Agora, autoridades e empresas precisam articular infraestrutura, licenciamento ambiental, proteção de dados e acesso aos equipamentos. Ao governo cabe também tratar com os Estados Unidos das restrições que atingem o Brasil. Aos investidores, cabe incorporar essas condições à avaliação econômica, antes de comprometer capital, sempre relevante quando se trata de um datacenter. Welber Barral Sócio de Barr

artigo.texto: In a late meeting Monday night attended by dozens of people opposing the Trident Data Center, the Aurora City Council approved a ban on giving tax incentives to data center developers. It’s the latest salvo fired against data centers by the City Council. Recommended Stories The vote happened toward the end of the meeting, following the unanimous approval of a temporary data center moratorium and an announcement from Vantage Data Centers that Trident would no longer be built in its initially proposed Aurora location. The ordinance, proposed by Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman, is one effort of many in recent months by the Aurora council to regulate data centers. Aurora’s city code allows the city to use retail tax revenue and construction material use tax revenue generated by qualifying development projects to help finance public improvements and attract businesses. It also allows the city to waive sales or use taxes for certain developers. The ordinance, passed unanimously by the council, would prohibit data center incentives entirely. “There is an unprecedented amount of money behind data centers, largely driven by AI, and they do not need our tax dollars,” Coffman said about his proposed ordinance. Mayor Pro Tem Alison Coombs said she agrees with the ordinance but thinks a broader conversation about development incentives and oversight procedures needs to happen. The council already has the ability to vote on every sales and use tax incentive, including those for data centers, Coombs said, adding that if the council does not want to give incentives to a data center, it can vote against them. Coffman countered that the process, which happens in executive sessions, is not transparent to the public. “I don’t think it’s wise to bind the hand of future councils,” Councilmember Curtis Gardner said in a previous study session, adding that creating a sweeping rule for one industry “is not a good way to do governance.” Four tax incentives have been issued for data centers totaling $83 million. As of earlier this year, about $9 million had been paid out against that potential, City Manager Jason Batchelor said.
