artigo.texto: How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure 1 / 2 How data center backlash could put banks’ AI bets under pressure Claire Williams 5 min read Key insight: Local opposition to data-center construction could threaten lending and underwriting business for banks, particularly for projects still awaiting permits or approval. Forward look: Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., is pushing for greater disclosure of AI-related financing, a proposal with bipartisan support that could gain traction in the next Congress. WASHINGTON — Along with the election cycle's blue wave that's shifting power on Capitol Hill, voters also delivered a sweeping rebuke to artificial intelligence and a data center build-out that fueled many grassroots movements across the country. In Washington, this means accounting for an upswell in voter anger over AI's projected job losses and having an answer for data centers that many motivated voters do not want to live near. In local and state governments, policymakers are considering moratoriums or additional requirements for data centers that will make them more palatable to their constituents. One of the biggest flashpoints for this debate is Loudoun County, Virginia, said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., in an interview with American Banker. Loudoun County, home to "data center alley," recently paused processing new data center applications for a year. "Loudoun County actually is ground zero," Warner said. "They've got, candidly, the oldest data centers, the loudest, the most inefficient data centers in the country." Warner is not only one of the senators representing Virginia, he's also one of the leaders in the upper chamber on AI policy, particularly as it pertains to banks and other financial companies. "I've been just amazed at the concentration of capital," he said. "I've never seen anything like this. Where anything that has AI attached to it, you know, its valuation gets an extra zero." For the financiers of these data centers who are counting on a coming AI boom and want a piece of that market, a nationwide backlash to the build-out could cause some problems. "Banks should closely monitor and be very concerned about potential limits or moratoriums on AI data centers," said Peter Dugas, CEO of the advisory firm Regulatory Intelligence Group. "Fed Governor Barr recently spoke about potential bank runs due to AI circular financing, and a ban on current data center builds would only add to that stress." For banks, the immediate concern from local opposition in key areas like Loudoun County is more about future or pending business, rather than losses on already-functioning data centers. "I haven't seen anything that suggests there's a credit problem, but certainly it's a potential revenue problem for banks that have been engaged in lending to the sector… and now are questioning what their growth projections look like," said Brian Gardner, a Washington policy strategist at Stifel. The potential headwind mostly depends on the development stage of individual projects. Those that have secured permits and begun construction are less likely to be affected by local opposition than developments that are still awaiting approval. "It shouldn't be a material issue for facilities that are already under construction and are already permitted," Gardner said. "I think it's more for those projects that were on the drawing board or that were in the application phase." And while local moratoriums or other delays might be a problem for data center financiers, depending on the bank or other financial backer, the prospects for national legislation remain slim, especially as President Donald Trump retains veto power for the next two years. "This is a state and local issue, and a federal moratorium is highly unlikely," Gardner said. "I still believe that. I'm probably as confident in that view as I have been." Still, there will be "noise" around a federal moratorium, which presents headline risk for those who want to finance data centers, he said. And there are other ways lawmakers can look at the data-center issue without trying to issue a full moratorium. One of those ways comes from Warner, who late last week introduced a bill alongside Republican Sens. John Kennedy of Louisiana and Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., that would require nonfinancial companies to disclose to the Securities and Exchange Commission all debt arrangements or commitments used to finance AI infrastructure. It's the kind of narrower proposal that, especially with the level of Republican sign-off present in the co-sponsors of the legislation, could make it into law. Warner said in the interview that he's gotten buy-in from some people inside the administration, but that, of course, it's a long way from a bill's introduction to the president's desk, especially in the current political moment. "It's always easier said than done," he said. Warner specifically mentioned special purpose vehicles, or SPVs, that he said allow companies to move potentially risky financing arrangements off their balance sheets, escaping oversight from federal regulators. He said the number of companies using those structures, and the lack of standardization around them, make it harder to assess the concentration of capital flowing into AI. "I'm not accusing that there's something underhanded going on, but this is plain vanilla, 'we need more transparency,'" he said. Warner said he has discussed the proposal with major technology companies and large banks designated as systemically important financial institutions, or SIFIs. While those conversations have involved requests to adjust the language, he said the response has not been outright opposition. "I've talked to hyperscalers, I've talked to some of the big SIFI banks," he said. "They'd like maybe a paragraph slightly different, but nobody starts with 'this is a crazy idea.'"

artigo.texto: California Universities Build Campus AI Data Centers to Control Compute Costs and Data Governance California universities are building campus AI data centers to curb rising vendor cloud costs and protect sensitive student and research data governance. On November 23, 2026, California higher education systems, including the University of California, California State University, and California Community Colleges, accelerated investments in on-campus artificial intelligence data centers and localized open-weight computing clusters. The push establishes institutional digital sovereignty to control escalating commercial software licensing fees, eliminate vendor lock-in, and safeguard sensitive research and student records under strict university governance. What happened Public universities and community colleges across California are deploying on-premises hardware clusters and open-weight artificial intelligence models to counter growing dependence on commercial vendors. According to investigative reports published on November 23, 2026, by CalMatters and partner outlet LAist, institutional leaders across the University of California (UC), California State University (CSU), and the California Community Colleges system are launching on-campus AI data centers and localized computing infrastructure. The push toward local compute is grounded in physical campus deployments. At California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, university leadership unveiled an on-campus computing facility known as the AI Factory, detailed in an official announcement by California Polytechnic State University. Housed in the computer science building, the facility provides dedicated computing power for students and faculty. Simultaneously, the University of California, San Diego expanded its campus AI platform, documented by the University of California San Diego, which operates TritonGPT out of the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC). Concurrently, the California Community Colleges system—representing 116 colleges and the largest postsecondary education network in the United States—submitted a formal budget proposal seeking 21 million dollars in state funding to build an interconnected, sovereign AI compute network. The initiatives represent an institutional effort to control escalating subscription fees and protect student records, even as university systems maintain commercial enterprise agreements. Key details of campus AI deployments Campus computing architectures across California reflect diverse strategies tailored to undergraduate education, high-performance academic research, and statewide community college administration. Cal Poly’s AI Factory was funded by a 3 million dollar gift from the estate of Intel co-founder Robert N. Noyce through the School of Applied Computing. Providing 1,300 terabytes of storage and four NVIDIA DGX B200 systems, it enables faculty like Dr. Jonathan Ventura (drone ecology) and Dr. Paul Anderson (spinal cord genomics) to train models on university-controlled hardware without transmitting protected data externally. At UC San Diego, TritonGPT has evolved into TritonAI, serving administrative and research queries across campus. UCSD shares its underlying software architecture with peer campuses, supporting BearGPT at UC Berkeley and SCOUT at UC Merced. Linking these distributed facilities is the California Research and Education Network (CalREN), an 8,000-mile fiber-optic network operated by CENIC that currently connects approximately 20 community college districts, UC campuses, and CSU universities. Background and commercial cloud tensions The turn toward on-campus compute stems from mounting fiscal and governance friction between public university administrations and commercial artificial intelligence vendors. Systemwide enterprise agreements have grown increasingly expensive. The University of California negotiated enterprise terms for ChatGPT Edu starting at 10 dollars per user per month, with advanced capabilities reaching 30 dollars per user per month. The California State University system signed enterprise contracts with OpenAI extending through 2029 with commitments totaling roughly 56 million dollars. Per-seat commercial licensing creates unpredictable operational expenditures that strain departmental budgets when usage spikes beyond contract quotas. In contrast, acquiring on-premises server hardware converts variable operational costs into amortized capital investments, allowing universities to deploy open-weight models without per-query token fees. Statutory privacy compliance presents an equally critical driver. Public universities manage legally protected records under the FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) and the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Commercial vendor contracts generally stipulate that user data will not be used to train frontier models, but campus administrators remain wary of potential data leakage. On-premises clusters ensure strict data residency within university firewalls. Environmental transparency also shapes compute governance. Assessing the direct compute carbon footprint of closed cloud queries remains difficult due to commercial vendor opacity. Running localized infrastructure under sustainable HPC practices allows university facility managers to monitor power draw and cooling demands directly against institutional sustainability targets. artigo.texto: President Donald Trump has threatened to penalize US technology companies that build data centers overseas, saying they must keep their investments in the United States or face a “tremendous tax” during a White House press conference on November 20. Trump declared that companies could still build facilities abroad but would face additional taxes and he also acknowledged that he had not informed his staff about the proposal before announcing it. The proposal could affect major US technology companies, including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, which have invested in data centers overseas. These facilities allow cloud service providers to operate closer to international customers and comply with local data regulations. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story, but I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now, they’re here.” Trump told reporters at the White House after returning from his trip to Asia as reported by NBC News. “We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country, we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad but He did not explain how the proposed restrictions would be enforced or when they might take effect. Trump argued that restricting overseas construction would help the United States maintain its lead over China in artificial intelligence. His remarks followed a separate US policy announced earlier this week requiring licenses for purchases of advanced computer chips. The measure is intended to help authorities monitor where the chips are used and prevent computing resources from reaching Chinese companies as reported by CNBC. The proposed restrictions also come as data center construction faces growing opposition in the United States. A CNBC survey found that 64 percent of registered voters opposed having an AI data center within 10 miles of their homes, while only 13 percent supported one. Concerns include rising electricity demand, noise pollution and the impact of large facilities on nearby communities. Opposition to data center projects also became an issue in the November 3 midterm elections, with Democratic candidates campaigning for tighter construction regulations. The Pew Research Center estimated that the United States had about 3,000 data centers as of April, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction. According to a report by the BBC, Canada has been positioning itself as an alternative location for major technology companies looking to expand their AI infrastructure. Trump urged communities to accept the projects and negotiate financial benefits rather than oppose them. “You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don’t shut them off,” he said. No details have been provided on whether the proposed tax would apply to existing overseas facilities, future construction projects or both. It is also unclear whether the administration intends to introduce a formal ban or use tax penalties to discourage companies from investing abroad.

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – The to-do list for Democrats who will soon control lawmaking in Harrisburg is almost certain to include party staples like a minimum wage increase and reproductive rights legislation, but the biggest question may be how to respond to intense public demand for action on data centers. On Tuesday, a high-profile pollster gave The Center Square a preview of forthcoming poll data that shows Pennsylvanians want lawmakers to act. And, hotspots of public outrage continue to simmer around the state over proposals to build the giant buildings stuffed with servers. In Lackawanna County, Superintendent Patrick Sheehan of Mid Valley School District on Tuesday said his district has gone to court to intervene in a situation in which Olyphant Borough Council voted to drop its traditional "conditional use" public hearing process on a big data center proposal. In exchange for that vote, the developer has agreed to pay more than $100 million for community benefits. In Lehigh County Monday night, the state Department of Environmental Protection hosted a hearing on state permits requested for so-called 'Project Atlas'. The proposed 1.5 million-square-foot data center complex would be built in Lehigh County across the street from the state's fifth-largest high school, Parkland. The project does not yet have full local approvals. Megan McDonough, Pennsylvania director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, said Gov. Josh Shapiro and the DEP appear to be "bending over backwards to build this data center." State Senator-elect Mark Pinsley, in a press release issued Tuesday by Food & Water Watch, said he opposed Project Atlas. "A massive data center has no business going across the street from Parkland High School or next to a residential neighborhood," he said. Pinsley was one of four Democratic challengers who beat incumbent Republican senators in the Nov. 3 general election, helping bring an end to more than 30 years of Republican dominance in the Senate. Come January, his party will control the Senate, House, and governor's office. And the public is expecting substantive action on data centers, if new polling overseen by veteran Pennsylvania pollster Chris Borick is any indication. Borick ran a nationally recognized polling operation at Muhlenberg College for many years. In his new post as director of the just-created Lehigh University Opinion Observatory, Borick expects the Bethlehem research center to release data by mid-December on its first polling deep-dive, which is on data centers. The results, he said, are "unquestionable" in showing "the Pennsylvania public is highly concerned with data center development. It played a role with their election decisions this fall and they want actions from policymakers." It would be difficult for the state legislature to do less about data centers than it did in 2026. The House and Senate failed to pass any substantive legislation on the issue. Gov. Josh Shapiro, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, was a high-profile supporter of the data center industry as it mushroomed in Pennsylvania from late 2024 into early 2026. He appeared at the controversial "Project Hazelnut" site in Luzerne County in late 2024 to launch a "fast track" state permitting program that included many big data center proposals. In August, facing the barrage of public negativity, he reversed course and issued an executive order that pulled data centers from the fast track list and put up "guard rails" on the industry. Among other things, the state DEP put into its permit review processes a set of Shapiro-backed safeguards. Minimum wage and reproductive rights legislation got prominent mentions in Democratic post-election press conferences. But references to potential new data center laws were muted. "I refuse to let this be pushed aside, forgotten about, overlooked," state Sen. Katie Muth, a Montgomery County Democrat, said in an interview Tuesday. Muth has pushed unsuccessfully for a three-year moratorium on data center development. She also wants to see elimination of the sales tax break given to data center companies and a legal wall to prevent data centers from being considered public utilities, among other things. The Olyphant Borough Council votes taken on Nov. 17 triggered deep concern in some quarters. One 5-2 vote ratified a legal settlement between the borough and developer Ercor Triboro that does away with the traditional conditional use process involving a public hearing. A separate 5-2 vote approved a community benefits agreement that would dole out $100 million-plus to the community over 15 years. "Residents deserve to have a voice in these decisions and any move to foreclose on that process is wrong," said state Rep. Kyle Mullins, a Democrat whose district includes Olyphant. Mullins said the site originally was supposed to be developed with warehouses with "thousands of jobs" and the switch to data centers means public hearings are necessary. In Harrisburg, he said, "We need urgent action to change the law on data centers." The Mid Valley School District's cluster of buildings is 1.5 miles from the site but Sheehan, the school superintendent, said the location is pretty much "right behind us." Two thousand students as young as five years old and about 200 staffers are on the campus during the day, Sheehan said. The school district has an obligation to protect "the health, safety, and welfare of the students and staff," he said. It would have carried out that obligation by taking part in the public hearing process that has been scrapped, according to Sheehan. Hence, Sheehan said, the district sought to intervene in the court case. A hearing on its participation is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Lackawanna County Court. The district also is seeking proposals on noise and environmental studies to be done at the proposed data center site. artigo.texto: Energy Vault has closed $78 million in construction and bridge financing for its SOSA Energy Center, a 150 MW/300 MWh battery energy storage project in Madison County, Texas. The non-recourse financing supports construction of the project, which is expected to begin commercial operations in the third quarter of 2027. The bridge financing will be repaid using an already committed $80 million preferred equity investment when the project is completed. An additional draw on Energy Vault’s existing OIC preferred facility will provide incremental project equity. Together, those financing arrangements are intended to support SOSA through construction and into commercial operation. The bridge and preferred equity amounts represent different stages of the financing structure rather than entirely separate, additive sources of permanent capital. Construction Advances Toward 2027 Operations Construction began in the fourth quarter of 2025. Civil work is complete, a substation has been installed, and major equipment is expected to arrive in the coming months. Energy Vault is performing the engineering, procurement and construction work itself. Site control, environmental and interconnection milestones are already in place. Once operating, SOSA will provide power and ancillary services in the ERCOT North market. It will initially operate on a merchant basis, retaining flexibility to enter an offtake agreement as market conditions evolve. Asset Vault Expands Owned Infrastructure SOSA was the first storage asset acquired and placed into development through Asset Vault, Energy Vault’s platform for owning and operating energy storage and AI infrastructure assets. The company projects $250 million to more than $300 million in long-term revenue and recurring EBITDA margins of approximately 65% to 75%. Those figures are forward-looking expectations rather than contracted results. The approximately $100 million project is expected to create 65 construction jobs and generate an estimated $9.3 million in tax revenue for North Zulch Independent School District and Madison County over 10 years. O acordo amplia a parceria além da carta de intenções não vinculativa anunciada em 26 de outubro de 2026, combinando a plataforma PowerBuoy® da Ocean Power Technologies com a infraestrutura de computação de alto desempenho da Stratum, incluindo GPUs NVIDIA B300. Avaliação de Viabilidade Técnica e Comercial A Ocean Power Technologies realizará uma avaliação técnica e comercial da potencial implantação da infraestrutura de computação da Stratum em plataformas offshore alimentadas principalmente por geração de energia renovável no local. A avaliação examinará a geração de energia, o armazenamento de energia, os requisitos de refrigeração, a infraestrutura de comunicações, a integração da plataforma e os locais potenciais de implantação. As empresas também irão avaliar se a utilização do ambiente marinho circundante para refrigeração poderá reduzir o consumo de energia em comparação com os centros de dados convencionais em terra. Programa de Demonstração Potencial Offshore O acordo inicial abrange apenas as atividades de viabilidade e planejamento. A fabricação de equipamentos, a integração da GPU, a implantação em alto-mar e os testes em alto-mar exigirão um acordo separado. Após a conclusão da avaliação, as empresas pretendem analisar as conclusões e negociar os termos de um possível programa de demonstração, incluindo acordos de licenciamento para a plataforma da Ocean Power Technologies. artigo.texto: Vantage Data Centers announced Monday that it will not build Trident Data Center in the initial proposed spot near several Green Valley Ranch neighborhoods, including a 55+ community. Aurora City Attorney Pete Schulte announced the decision from Vantage early on during Monday night’s Aurora City Council meeting. The announcement was met with standing applause from the crowd of meeting attendees. Recommended Stories Shortly after the announcement, the council unanimously passed a temporary data center moratorium that will last through September of next year while the council creates regulations for such development. Data centers have been at the forefront of debate during recent Aurora council meetings. Dozens of Green Valley Ranch residents have attended meetings since late September to oppose Trident Data Center, which was proposed to go on a plot of land at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue. Trident as proposed would have been two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. The land sat across from The Reserve, a 55+ community, and other neighborhoods. In late October, Vantage officially agreed to seek alternative locations for the proposed data center in a letter to the council. Vantage officials asked the council for at least 90 days to find another location and requested that the city hold off on new data center rules until then. On Monday night, Vantage announced that it was dropping the location, but had not yet found an alternative. The company cited “recent community concerns” as the reason for moving Trident. Several hours earlier, the council moved forward with a resolution in study session to urge Vantage to move Trident. Before the resolution could go to an official vote at the regular meeting, Vantage had announced its decision. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state,” Misty Allen, Vantage’s vice president of public policy for North America, said in a statement. While many members of the public celebrated the decision, many of them also said they were opposed to any data centers coming to Aurora regardless of the proximity to neighborhoods. Following the Trident announcement, the council passed a temporary data center moratorium in a unanimous vote. It was the third time the council has voted on a data center moratorium since August, when the council voted in opposition of a temporary moratorium. In October, the council voted in opposition to an indefinite one. On Monday, Mayor Mike Coffman proposed a moratorium again, this time proposing that it last through September 2027 and exclude vacant land north of I-70 and east of Powhaton Road, which is far from residential areas, he said. Councilmember Alli Jackson said residents don’t want any data centers in their city at all, adding that she would vote in support of the temporary one because there would not be enough votes for a full data center ban. Councilmember Stephanie Hancock said data centers “are here to stay,” adding that a temporary moratorium is the best they can do. “I think Aurora is doing a good job of wrapping our arms around this as we’re learning more, as this technology changes every single day,” she said. “We really can be the gold standard for how this works. I think we should continue to be thoughtful, engaged, not get involved in hyperbolic rhetoric and really look at the facts as they are and work from that perspective.” Councilmember Alison Coombs said there is “nothing hyperbolic” about studies showing pollution from data centers is more significant than previously thought, pointing to a recent AP report. “I think we have to recognize the reasonable skepticism that is not hyperbole or hysteria coming from our community,” Coombs said.

artigo.texto: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk says the company's best data center construction workers could be former baristas or shelf-stockers. "Those are some of our best people, and they've never done data centers before," Musk said earlier this week during a remote appearance at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin. Musk said that SpaceX has assembled an internal team, which he called "ArmyX," that has broken down all the jobs needed to construct data centers into smaller tasks "that are easily trainable in a few days." "You don't need people that have, say, been doing networking cables for their whole life," he said. "You divide the tasks into things that can be where you can train someone new who may have been a Starbucks barista or stocking shelves at Target." The billionaire praised the skills and work ethic that retail and fast-food workers could bring to data center construction. Musk specifically called attention to the skills of a former In-N-Out cook. "Let me tell you, if you get some aces out of In-N-Out who've been making epic burgers all day long perfectly, they're going to do a damn good job of network cables," he said. Musk says this team is powering SpaceX's expansion of its massive Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers in Memphis. During SpaceX's most recent earnings call, Musk said that he "would be surprised" if the company added less than 13 gigawatts of compute by the end of 2027. Like the rest of the industry, SpaceX has a lot riding on the buildout. According to its latest earnings report, the company is spending more than ever on AI — and that could soon double. Business Insider previously reported that SpaceX offered employees a 20% pay increase if they volunteered to work six weeks in Memphis or Southaven, Mississippi, where another large data center is located. "These days when I go to Memphis, which I go to Memphis pretty frequently, it's becoming a well-oiled machine where it's just getting done," Musk said. "And we run a twenty-four-seven operation. So I can walk the site at one or two in the morning and see more or less the same productivity as I would the next morning at 10 AM, seven days a week."

artigo.texto: As baterias de armazenamento de energia elétrica são apontadas por especialistas, empresas e pelo próprio governo como um dos instrumentos mais importantes para dar flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico brasileiro em meio ao avanço acelerado das fontes solar e eólica. Mas uma disputa que se desenrola simultaneamente no Congresso Nacional e no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) pode transformar essa solução tecnológica em uma nova fonte de pressão sobre as tarifas de energia. Estudo da Frente Nacional dos Consumidores de Energia (FNCE) divulgado na terça-feira, 24 de novembro, calcula que o Projeto de Lei nº 3.716/26 poderá adicionar até R$ 6,26 bilhões por ano à conta de luz caso seja aprovado com a previsão de ratear entre todos os consumidores o custo das baterias que serão contratadas no leilão marcado para dezembro. Ao longo dos 15 anos previstos nos contratos, o impacto acumulado pode alcançar cerca de R$ 94 bilhões. A estimativa foi elaborada com base nos preços-teto previstos para o certame e em projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), considerando um volume potencial de até 5 gigawatts (GW) de contratação. Segundo a entidade, a despesa seria cobrada por meio do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade (ERCAP), mecanismo criado para remunerar os investimentos em armazenamento. O centro da disputa não está na necessidade das baterias — há consenso crescente de que o armazenamento é fundamental para lidar com a intermitência das fontes renováveis. O embate envolve quem deve pagar essa conta. A legislação atualmente em vigor atribui aos geradores a responsabilidade pelos custos associados às baterias. O PL 3.716/26, porém, propõe alterar essa lógica e distribuir a cobrança para todos os consumidores do País, inclusive aqueles atendidos por distribuidoras cuja carteira de energia é majoritariamente formada por hidrelétricas e térmicas. Para a FNCE, isso criaria um subsídio cruzado considerado injustificável. Presidente da entidade, Luiz Eduardo Barata afirma que a discussão não deve ser confundida com uma resistência à expansão do armazenamento. Segundo ele, as baterias são essenciais para o futuro da matriz elétrica brasileira. O problema, sustenta, é transferir para toda a sociedade um custo originado principalmente pela necessidade de acomodar a geração intermitente de determinadas fontes. “Quem causa o custo deve pagar pelo custo”, resume Barata. Na avaliação dele, as baterias não funcionam como uma reserva tradicional de capacidade, que permanece disponível para uso eventual. Diferentemente das térmicas acionadas apenas em momentos específicos, os sistemas de armazenamento operarão de forma permanente para garantir a entrega da energia produzida por usinas solares e eólicas em horários nos quais não há geração suficiente. A defesa da mudança na regra ganhou força entre agentes do setor após a aprovação da legislação que atribuiu o encargo aos geradores. Inconformados com a obrigação, grupos empresariais passaram a buscar alternativas para socializar a despesa. Uma delas foi a inclusão do tema, por parte do deputado federal Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP), no Projeto de Lei 3.716/26, que tramita em regime de urgência na Câmara dos Deputados e pode ser votado a qualquer momento. Paralelamente, para não depender da votação do PL na Câmara, a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica) ingressou no STF na semana passada questionando justamente a regra que responsabiliza os geradores pelo custeio das baterias a serem contratadas no leilão. A ação busca reverter o modelo estabelecido na legislação e ainda pede a suspensão do leilão. Retrocesso Para Barata, a pressão para alterar as regras ocorre justamente quando o País finalmente avança na estruturação de um mercado de armazenamento. O executivo afirma que suspender ou adiar o leilão representaria um retrocesso. “Atrasar o leilão pode comprometer o enfrentamento dos cortes de energia e dificultar o equilíbrio do sistema”, argumenta. A posição da FNCE é favorável à realização do certame nas datas previstas e à manutenção da legislação atual — a entidade enviou o estudo para várias autoridades, entre elas o ministro de Minas e Energia, Alexandre Silveira; o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB); e o ministro Cristiano Zanin, do STF, que está analisando a demanda da Abeeólica. Barata afirma que é legítimo que o consumidor que contrata energia de um gerador que depende de armazenamento arque com esse custo. O que considera inadequado é obrigar consumidores sem qualquer vínculo com essa contratação a pagar a mesma conta. Para explicar a lógica, o dirigente recorre a uma comparação simples – um grande evento, no qual parte do público chega de carro e utiliza estacionamento, enquanto outra parte vai a pé ou de transporte coletivo. “A cobrança do estacionamento para quem estacionou seria natural; já dividir a despesa igualmente entre todos os participantes, independentemente do uso, seria uma distorção”, diz. Na avaliação da FNCE, o mesmo princípio deveria valer para as baterias. A discussão ocorre em um momento decisivo para a transição energética brasileira. O crescimento acelerado das fontes renováveis tornou mais frequentes episódios de curtailment, quando usinas precisam reduzir ou interromper a geração por falta de capacidade do sistema para absorver toda a energia produzida. Nesse contexto, as baterias passaram a ser vistas como um instrumento estratégico para armazenar excedentes e aumentar a eficiência do sistema. Barata reconhece que a manutenção da regra atual pode elevar os custos da energia proveniente de fontes solar e eólica e reduzir parte da competitividade desses empreendimentos, especialmente no mercado livre. “Ainda assim, consideramos que o setor renovável já recebeu incentivos suficientes ao longo dos últimos anos e que a expansão das tecnologias deve ocorrer sobre bases economicamente sustentáveis”, adverte. artigo.texto: Competitive Analysis of Electric Vehicle Battery Market: FMI Tracks Cell Innovation, Gigafactory Expansion and OEM Supply Competition Future Market Insights (FMI) has published its Competitive Analysis of Electric Vehicle Battery Market, examining the competitive positioning, technology developments, manufacturing expansion and OEM supply strategies of global electric vehicle battery manufacturers. The assessment covers battery cell producers, vertically integrated EV manufacturers, regional gigafactory investments and emerging battery technologies, with a focus on developments from 2025 through 2026 and the market outlook for 2026-2036. FMI identifies CATL, BYD (FinDreams Battery), LG Energy Solution, Panasonic Energy, SK On, Samsung SDI, CALB, Gotion High-Tech, EVE Energy and Envision AESC among the companies shaping the competitive landscape. The analysis highlights the concentration of battery manufacturing capacity among leading Asian producers and the growing importance of localized production in North America and Europe. Competition is increasingly centered on cell-to-pack integration, LFP cost optimization, fast-charging capability, high-energy-density prismatic cells and solid-state battery development. Get detailed market forecasts, competitive benchmarking, and pricing trends: https://www.futuremarketinsights.com/reports/sample/rep-gb-5388 The study examines how battery suppliers compete for multi-year OEM contracts through manufacturing scale, chemistry specialization, regional supply networks, pack economics and technology roadmaps. The public competitive-analysis page provides selected company developments and operating milestones but does not publish a numerical company market-share breakdown or complete market forecast values. Detailed market sizing, supplier share estimates and forecast assessments remain proprietary FMI research where not publicly disclosed. Competitive Analysis of Electric Vehicle Battery Market: Supplier Structure and Commercial Dynamics FMI describes the electric vehicle battery market as highly consolidated among leading cell manufacturers, with Chinese suppliers dominating structural cell-to-pack LFP technologies and South Korean and Japanese manufacturers competing for OEM supply contracts through localized production capacity. Chinese battery manufacturers and vertically integrated cell-to-pack systems CATL and BYD (FinDreams Battery) are identified as major competitors in LFP battery technology and structural cell-to-pack designs. Their competitive positioning includes vertical integration across battery materials, cell manufacturing and pack engineering. CATL's Qilin and Shenxing battery platforms and BYD's Blade battery technology illustrate the importance of pack architecture, manufacturing efficiency, energy utilization and fast-charging performance. The competitive analysis also includes CALB, Gotion High-Tech and EVE Energy, which participate in LFP, NMC, LMFP and large-format cylindrical battery development. South Korean and Japanese manufacturers expanding localized production LG Energy Solution, SK On, Samsung SDI and Panasonic Energy compete for automotive OEM programmes across North America, Europe and Asia. Their strategies include expanding localized gigafactory production, converting existing facilities toward LFP manufacturing and developing high-energy-density cylindrical and prismatic cell technologies. Localized production is commercially important for OEMs seeking regional supply, reduced logistics exposure and eligibility under applicable sourcing or regional-content requirements. FMI highlights factory investments and production expansion in the United States, Canada, Poland and Hungary as part of the competitive landscape. Technology differentiation and battery procurement priorities Battery suppliers compete through multiple technical and commercial attributes: • LFP chemistry and cost efficiency: Cobalt-free battery chemistries are relevant to mass-market EV affordability and localized supply strategies. • Superfast charging: Manufacturers are developing batteries intended to support shorter charging intervals and improved charging performance under challenging temperature conditions. • High-energy-density prismatic cells: Advanced cell architecture and energy density are targeted toward long-range passenger vehicles and premium EV platforms. • Cylindrical cell development: 2170 and 46-series formats are positioned for automotive applications requiring high-power performance and manufacturing scalability. • Solid-state battery commercialization: Suppliers continue investing in next-generation battery technologies for premium and future EV platforms. • Regional manufacturing capacity: OEMs evaluate factory locations, production ramp-up, sourcing eligibility, supply continuity and multi-year contract execution. FMI's competitive assessment connects these developments with OEM purchasing requirements involving pack cost trajectories, thermal safety, fast-charging performance, battery carbon-footprint reporting and regional-content compliance. The development reflects the company's focus on regional product adaptation, fast-charging performance and battery technology commercialization. • Panasonic Energy - July 2025: The company commenced mass production at its second North American gigafactory in De Soto, Kansas, with 30 GWh capacity. artigo.texto: Baterias industriais de 47 toneladas chegam ao Brasil por navio em viagens de até 60 dias. Elas embarcam parcialmente carregadas, exigem cuidados especiais e ganham importância com os leilões brasileiros de armazenamento. Uma caixa metálica com pouco mais de seis metros de comprimento parece pequena diante de um navio de carga. Mas, quando ela abriga um sistema de armazenamento de energia elétrica, o peso pode chegar a 47 toneladas. É com equipamentos desse porte que fabricantes chineses abastecem projetos de baterias no Brasil. Em entrevista publicada pelo UOL em 24 de novembro de 2026, a Trina Storage detalhou como essas unidades chegam ao país: são 45 a 60 dias de viagem marítima, sem empilhamento a bordo e com carga elétrica limitada a 10% a 30%. O procedimento faz parte da logística adotada pela fabricante para levar sistemas de grande capacidade até o destino. O peso é apenas uma das dificuldades. Embora o formato lembre o de um contêiner de transporte, o interior reúne milhares de componentes elétricos que precisam chegar intactos ao local da instalação. A unidade já sai da fábrica com sua estrutura industrial, o que exige um planejamento diferente daquele aplicado a uma caixa comum de mercadorias. - Caminhões entram em um trem para atravessar o Canal da Mancha, com até 32 veículos seguindo por baixo do mar enquanto os motoristas viajam em outro vagão - Os trilhos chegavam ao rio Paraná e continuavam sobre uma balsa, que levava vagões de uma margem à outra antes de a ponte Francisco de Sá ligar a ferrovia - Da etiqueta lida por scanner ao avião para Manaus, Total Express reforça o caminho das encomendas da Black Friday com máquina capaz de separar 220 mil volumes por dia - BR-304 terá desvio por cerca de 40 dias em Mossoró para instalar posto que seleciona caminhões por pesagem em movimento antes de encaminhá-los à balança de fiscalização Uma bateria do tamanho de um contêiner pode pesar cerca de 47 mil quilos O modelo Elementa 3 ajuda a entender a escala desses equipamentos. A ficha técnica da Trina Storage informa dimensões de 6,058 metros de comprimento, 2,438 metros de largura e 2,896 metros de altura, equivalentes às de um contêiner marítimo High Cube de 20 pés. A capacidade nominal de cada unidade é de 6.250 quilowatts-hora (kWh). A massa declarada, de aproximadamente 47 mil quilos, inclui os componentes e a estrutura do sistema. Por isso, a escolha da embarcação, dos equipamentos de movimentação e do espaço reservado para a carga tem de considerar muito mais do que as dimensões externas. Para visualizar o tamanho de uma operação, basta imaginar cem unidades desse modelo: juntas, representariam cerca de 4.700 toneladas de equipamentos, sem contar outros materiais necessários à implantação do projeto. Esse exemplo matemático mostra por que o transporte marítimo é adequado a um mercado que trabalha com grandes volumes. Segundo a fabricante, as unidades costumam viajar em navios de carga geral, conhecidos no setor como breakbulk. Nesse tipo de operação, cada peça é movimentada individualmente, em vez de ser tratada como mais um contêiner comum de uma pilha. Mesmo quase descarregadas, as baterias continuam sendo cargas perigosas A escolha de um nível de carga reduzido durante a travessia tem relação com a segurança e a preservação das células. A energia armazenada precisa ficar dentro de uma faixa que evite tanto uma descarga profunda quanto o embarque de uma bateria totalmente carregada. Isso não elimina os cuidados exigidos para o transporte. A Organização Marítima Internacional (IMO) inclui as baterias de lítio instaladas em unidades de transporte na lista de mercadorias perigosas do Código IMDG, sob a identificação UN 3536, classe 9. Uma bateria de grande porte também reúne partes que podem sofrer danos mecânicos. Ao longo de semanas no mar, a movimentação da embarcação, a exposição à umidade e as mudanças de temperatura tornam o acondicionamento da carga importante para preservar o funcionamento dos equipamentos. A restrição de empilhamento relatada pela Trina faz parte desse cuidado. Ao contrário de uma mercadoria cujo valor está apenas no conteúdo, nesses sistemas o próprio gabinete também integra o produto. Uma deformação que prejudique suas portas, vedações ou componentes internos pode comprometer a montagem e atrasar a entrega ao empreendimento. O que existe dentro de uma bateria capaz de armazenar 6,25 MWh Em maio de 2026, a Trina Storage apresentou a nova geração do Elementa para o mercado norte-americano. O equipamento utiliza células de 587 ampères-hora e reúne sistemas de monitoramento, proteção elétrica e controle térmico no mesmo conjunto. As especificações do Elementa 3 indicam refrigeração por líquido, dispositivos de detecção de gases, calor e fumaça, além de mecanismos de combate a incêndio. Esses recursos foram desenvolvidos para acompanhar o comportamento do sistema durante sua operação e detectar situações anormais. Há uma diferença importante entre energia e potência. Os 6,25 MWh representam a quantidade nominal de energia que a bateria armazena. Se essa capacidade fosse entregue uniformemente durante duas horas, a potência média seria de 3,125 MW, em uma conta teórica que desconsidera perdas e limites operacionais. Em quatro horas, a mesma quantidade de energia corresponderia a uma média de 1,5625 MW. A configuração efetiva depende dos inversores, das características das células e dos limites definidos para cada projeto. Depois do desembarque, ainda há uma operação rodoviária pela frente A chegada ao porto brasileiro encerra apenas a etapa marítima. As unidades precisam seguir em veículos preparados para cargas especiais e ser posicionadas sobre as bases do empreendimento, onde passam por verificações antes da entrada em serviço. O comissionamento exige conferir as conexões elétricas, a comunicação entre equipamentos e o funcionamento dos dispositivos de proteção. artigo.texto: Keel Clears Final State Environmental Permit for Sharon Data Center Pennsylvania has approved a construction stormwater permit for Keel Infrastructure (NASDAQ: KEEL)'s planned data center in Sharon, clearing what the company had identified as the last outstanding state environmental permit for the campus. According to Pennsylvania's permit record on Friday, the project has 110 megawatts of secured power from FirstEnergy. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection issued permit PAD430004 to Keel subsidiary Mercer Node Property LLC. It expires Nov. 19, 2031. The state’s September public notice said the project would disturb about 14.6 acres and called for erosion and sediment controls and a post-construction stormwater plan. The development includes an electrical substation and two buildings to house data center equipment. Keel, formerly Bitfarms, stopped mining Bitcoin at Sharon on June 29 as it began converting its U.S. sites for AI and high-performance computing. The company said in August that it had secured zoning and land development approvals for Sharon. A tenant lease remains a milestone for the project. Keel said earlier this month that it was negotiating with prospective tenants at Sharon and that the date the campus could enter service depended on when it signed a lease and broke ground. The company also said it no longer expected to meet its goal of signing three leases across its portfolio by year-end. Keel shares fell 19.6% to $1.375 on Nasdaq on Nov. 20 amid a broader selloff in AI infrastructure and Bitcoin mining stocks.

artigo.texto: Sime Motors opens Singapore’s first BYD Certified showroom Singapore’s first BYD Certified showroom has officially opened at Auto Selection’s facility in Ubi, dovetailed with the launch of BYD Singapore’s new Certified Pre-Owned programme. The initiative introduces manufacturer-backed inspections, battery health checks and warranty coverage for eligible pre-owned BYD vehicles. The showroom is operated by Auto Selection under Sime Motors Singapore, which has been appointed as BYD Singapore’s preferred certified pre-owned programme partner. Located at 1 Ubi Road 4, the dedicated showroom will offer buyers a central place to view used BYD models, while also providing existing BYD owners with an established channel to trade in or upgrade their vehicles. To qualify for certification, vehicles must be no more than five years old and have clocked no more than 100,000 kilometres. Each vehicle must also pass a comprehensive 177-point inspection conducted by trained technicians. This includes battery health verification, with a minimum state of health (SOH) of 70 percent, in addition to checks on the vehicle's history. Certified vehicles will come with warranty and battery coverage, financing options, and genuine BYD parts for refurbishment where required. Owners will also have access to BYD's authorised aftersales network. The programme aims to give buyers greater confidence when purchasing a pre-owned BYD, while keeping vehicles within a manufacturer-backed ownership ecosystem beyond their first owner. To mark the opening, Auto Selection offered limited-time discounts on eligible BYD Certified pre-owned vehicles. Beyond the vehicles themselves, Auto Selection also plans to organise customer events and community activities, which include curated driving trips to Malaysia, movie screenings and dining experiences. Eligible BYD pre-owned customers can also continue to enjoy benefits under the BYD Lifestyle Membership programme as membership privileges are tied to the vehicle and can be carried over to a new owner, subject to terms and conditions. artigo.texto: Trump ameaça taxar empresas que instalarem data centers fora dos EUA Presidente quer concentrar infraestrutura de IA nos Estados Unidos, mas não detalhou como aplicaria a tributação às empresas. O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ameaçou impor uma tributação elevada às empresas norte-americanas que construírem data centers em outros países. A declaração foi feita durante entrevista coletiva na Casa Branca, após uma viagem à Ásia, e integra a intenção de seu governo para fortalecer a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) dos Estados Unidos na disputa tecnológica com a China. “Não vamos permitir que nossas empresas construam data centers fora do nosso país”, afirmou Trump. O presidente disse que aplicaria um imposto de grande magnitude às companhias que mantivessem esses investimentos no exterior, mas não apresentou alíquotas, instrumentos legais ou prazos para implementar a medida. Também não esclareceu se haveria exceções para instalações destinadas ao atendimento de mercados internacionais. Restrição atingiria empresas com operações globais A declaração envolve companhias norte-americanas que desenvolvem e operam infraestrutura digital em diferentes países, como Equinix e Digital Realty. A distribuição geográfica dos data centers atende a requisitos técnicos e comerciais. A proximidade entre os centros de processamento e seus usuários permite reduzir a latência de aplicações que exigem respostas rápidas, como sistemas de pagamentos. O transporte de grandes volumes de informações por longas distâncias também pode elevar os custos operacionais. Esses fatores influenciam a localização de instalações que oferecem capacidade computacional para serviços em nuvem e sistemas de IA. Política dos EUA busca limitar acesso chinês à tecnologia A manifestação de Trump ocorre em meio a outras iniciativas de Washington para ampliar a capacidade computacional norte-americana e restringir o acesso da China a tecnologias de IA. O governo apresentou um plano de ação para o setor e adotou medidas relacionadas ao abastecimento de energia dos grandes centros de processamento. Na área comercial, o Departamento de Comércio norte-americano avançou em restrições à exportação de chips avançados para países do Sudeste Asiático. O objetivo declarado é impedir que empresas chinesas obtenham essas tecnologias por intermédio de terceiros países. A expansão da infraestrutura digital enfrenta, entretanto, resistência em algumas regiões dos Estados Unidos. Comunidades e governos estaduais têm questionado o consumo de eletricidade dos empreendimentos, os impactos sobre as tarifas de energia e outras consequências locais. Até o momento, a ameaça anunciada pelo presidente não veio acompanhada de uma proposta tributária formal com condições de aplicação definidas.

artigo.texto: - Comprising seven advanced-stage battery energy storage (BESS) projects in A Coruña, Almería, Castellón and Navarra, the 380 MW / 1.5 GWh portfolio is expected to come online between 2027 and the first half of 2028. MADRID, November 24, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--SUNGROW RENEWABLES, part of Sungrow Power Supply Group, and ACTUATE ENERGY, an energy storage platform backed by NGP, today announced the largest BESS transaction to date in Spain, comprising 380 MW and 1.5 GWh of storage capacity. The transaction establishes a long-term strategic partnership between Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy, based on the companies' complementary expertise and capabilities and underpinned by a shared commitment to develop, build and bring into operation Spain's first large-scale BESS portfolio, comprising seven advanced-stage projects. The first assets are already under construction, while the remainder of the portfolio is expected to commence construction in the coming months, with the full portfolio expected to reach Ready-to-Build (RtB) status during 2027 and enter commercial operation between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The transaction marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables' pioneering commitment to energy storage in Spain, which it launched several years ago. The portfolio comprises seven stand-alone BESS projects totalling 380 MW / 1.5 GWh. These include the Valencia Cluster, located in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón); Santiago, in Lousame (A Coruña); Berja, in the province of Almería; and the Navarra Cluster, located in Olite and Cordovilla. The agreement also leaves the door open to further collaboration on the development of future assets, reflecting both companies' commitment to continued growth in the energy storage market, strengthening the resilience of Spain's energy system and reinforcing Spain's position as a strategic market within Europe. A landmark transaction for Spain's BESS market The transaction comes at a time when Spain's electricity market is in critical need for energy storage, which is reaching a significant level of maturity, with storage becoming the technology with the largest volume of grid connection applications in Spain, ahead of both solar PV and wind. As Daniel Sánchez, CEO of Sungrow Renewables for Western Europe, noted: "This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain's BESS market. With 380 MW and 1.5 GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution." Sánchez further emphasises: "at Sungrow Renewables, we backed this market when it was still a bet on the future and helped pave the way through the development and commissioning of Sanxenxo, Spain's first stand-alone BESS plant. Today, we are taking a decisive step towards accelerating renewable energy integration and strengthening the stability of the power system, in a transaction that reinforces our long-term commitment to the Spanish market. Energy storage is no longer a promise for Spain: it is strategic infrastructure that we are turning into reality." Ben Skinner, CEO of Actuate Energy, said: "Spain is a market leader in deploying renewable energy, but battery storage has not kept pace. This portfolio marks a real step forward for the Spanish grid, adding flexible assets that respond in seconds to keep the system stable allowing more renewables to come online. For Actuate Energy, this is a landmark transaction that establishes our presence in Spain enabling our growth into Europe. We are delighted to partner with Sungrow Renewables, and we look forward to operating these projects for the benefit of the country and the communities that host them." Sungrow Renewables' continued strategy in Spain This latest milestone marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables' commitment to Spain and to the integration of energy storage. The company was a pioneer in Spain in the development of hybrid solar PV projects from 2022 onward, moved early into stand-alone BESS with its Sanxenxo project, and currently has stand-alone BESS assets already in operation in the country. Spain remains a strategic market for the company, which operates in more than 20 countries. Actuate Energy's entry into Europe with backing from NGP Actuate Energy focuses on dynamic European energy markets and is committed to supporting an accelerated transition toward renewable energy by investing in and operating energy storage assets that provide stability to the power system. Actuate Energy is backed by NGP, a premier energy private equity firm with over $25 billion of cumulative equity commitments. With this agreement, Spain becomes the starting point for Actuate Energy's entry into Europe, driven by the country's high renewable energy penetration, the ongoing need to provide grid stability, and the growth potential of a mature project pipeline. About Sungrow Renewables Sungrow Renewables Development Co., Ltd. is the renewable energy development and investment platform of Sungrow Power Supply Co., Ltd. and a national high-tech enterprise specializing in solar PV, wind power, energy storage, electric vehicle charging and multi-energy integration (wind, solar, storage and hydrogen). It provides integrated solutions covering the full project lifecycle, from R&D and development through design, construction and operations, and positions itself as the world's largest solar PV developer. The company has received recognitions including being named among the world's Top 500 New Energy Enterprises, China's Best ESG Employer and Most Socially Responsible Enterprise. In line with its mission of "Clean power for all," the company aims to become a global leader in new energy generation technology. artigo.texto: Fábio Leite Haroldo Almeida participa do PodCast AgroAmbiental para debater Caatinga, crédito de carbono e mudanças climáticas Comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, participante da COP30 e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, ambientalista é o convidado do 7º episódio. O PodCast AgroAmbiental recebe, nesta terça-feira (24 de novembro), às 20h, o ambientalista Haroldo Almeida, comendador Guardião das Águas de Alagoas, ex-secretário municipal de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia, integrante do Fórum Brasileiro de Mudança do Clima e presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga. O sétimo episódio traz à discussão temas de grande relevância para o futuro do Semiárido nordestino, como a preservação da Caatinga, a gestão dos recursos hídricos, o avanço da desertificação, o mercado de créditos de carbono e os resultados da 30ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP30), realizada em Belém, no Pará, em novembro de 2025. Com uma trajetória marcada pela participação em iniciativas ambientais, debates institucionais e ações de conscientização, Haroldo compartilha experiências acumuladas ao longo de sua atuação e apresenta propostas que buscam conciliar conservação ambiental, valorização dos recursos naturais e geração de oportunidades econômicas para as populações do Sertão. Trajetória ambiental e defesa dos recursos hídricos Um dos assuntos abordados durante a entrevista é a trajetória de Haroldo Almeida na defesa do meio ambiente, especialmente no Alto Sertão alagoano. Ex-secretário de Meio Ambiente de Delmiro Gouveia e participante das discussões do Comitê de Bacia da Região Hidrográfica do Sertão do São Francisco, o ambientalista trata sobre a importância da gestão participativa das águas, os desafios enfrentados pelos municípios e a necessidade de políticas públicas voltadas à conservação dos recursos hídricos. A conversa também destaca a importância do Rio São Francisco para o desenvolvimento regional, a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a proteção da vegetação nativa e a adoção de medidas capazes de garantir maior segurança hídrica às populações sertanejas. O episódio propõe uma reflexão sobre a relação entre a preservação ambiental e o desenvolvimento econômico, especialmente em uma região que depende diretamente da disponibilidade de água para o abastecimento humano, a agricultura e a pecuária. Desertificação e os desafios da conservação da Caatinga A desertificação é outro tema importante do episódio, considerando os impactos que a degradação ambiental pode provocar sobre a produtividade do solo, a disponibilidade de água e as condições de vida das comunidades rurais. Haroldo participou de um seminário internacional sobre o combate à desertificação, realizado na Câmara dos Deputados, em Brasília, onde foram discutidas estratégias de enfrentamento da degradação das terras e a necessidade de ampliar as ações de recuperação ambiental no Semiárido. Durante a entrevista, são abordadas as diferenças entre a seca, característica natural da região, e os processos de desertificação, que podem ser agravados pelo desmatamento, pelas queimadas, pelo sobrepastoreio e pelo manejo inadequado do solo. O debate também chama a atenção para a importância da Caatinga, bioma exclusivamente brasileiro que possui significativa biodiversidade e desempenha papel fundamental no equilíbrio ambiental do Nordeste. A discussão busca demonstrar que a conservação da vegetação nativa, a recuperação de áreas degradadas e a adoção de práticas produtivas sustentáveis são fundamentais para garantir melhores condições ambientais e econômicas às futuras gerações. Crédito de carbono pode representar oportunidade de renda para agricultores do Sertão Um dos principais destaques do episódio é a proposta de Crédito de Carbono Integral Bio-Sócio-Hidro-Energético, iniciativa idealizada por Haroldo Almeida que busca desenvolver mecanismos de valorização dos serviços ambientais prestados pela Caatinga e pelas comunidades que contribuem para sua conservação. Presidente da Associação dos Produtores de Crédito de Carbono Social do Bioma Caatinga, o ambientalista apresenta os fundamentos da proposta e discute as possibilidades de inserção dos pequenos produtores rurais em iniciativas relacionadas ao mercado de carbono. A entrevista procura esclarecer, de maneira acessível, o que são créditos de carbono, como funciona esse mercado, quais são os critérios para sua geração e de que forma a manutenção da vegetação nativa pode representar uma oportunidade econômica para os proprietários rurais. Também são discutidos os desafios relacionados à quantificação, à certificação e à comercialização desses créditos, além da importância de mecanismos que assegurem transparência, confiabilidade e participação das comunidades locais. Entre os questionamentos levantados está a possibilidade de transformar a preservação ambiental em uma atividade economicamente atrativa, contribuindo para reduzir a pressão sobre a vegetação nativa e estimular a recuperação de áreas degradadas. A discussão propõe uma questão central: será possível que, no futuro, um agricultor do Sertão consiga obter renda pela conservação da Caatinga, mantendo a vegetação em pé? Participação na COP30 e valorização da Caatinga no cenário internacional A participação de Haroldo Almeida na COP30, realizada em Belém, também ocupa espaço importante na entrevista. O ambientalista compartilha experiências de sua passagem pela conferência, considerada um dos principais encontros internacionais sobre mudanças climáticas, reunindo representantes de governos, instituições, pesquisadores e organizações da sociedade civil. Durante o evento, Haroldo participou de discussões e articulações voltadas à valorização da Caatinga, à justiça climática e ao reconhecimento das iniciativas de conservação desenvolvidas no Semiárido nordestino. artigo.texto: A Greenline, empresa brasileira de tecnologia climática, anunciou a adoção de seguro obrigatório para todos os créditos de carbono mensurados e emitidos em suas operações. A iniciativa foi desenvolvida com a participação da corretora Marsh e da Akad Seguros e estabelece um limite inicial de cobertura de US$ 25 milhões por projeto, com o objetivo de reduzir os riscos financeiros associados à comercialização de ativos ambientais. A medida será aplicada aos créditos classificados como ex-post, emitidos após a verificação dos resultados dos projetos. Com isso, a contratação do seguro passa a ser uma condição para a emissão desses ativos nas operações da Greenline. A iniciativa ocorre em um mercado no qual a qualidade dos créditos de carbono, a permanência dos resultados ambientais e a regularidade dos projetos têm ganhado importância nas negociações com compradores corporativos. Entre as preocupações estão a possibilidade de os créditos perderem sua validade e os prejuízos decorrentes de falhas na entrega dos ativos contratados. O seguro foi estruturado para responder a quatro grupos de riscos: descumprimento da entrega dos créditos negociados, falhas estruturais nos projetos responsáveis pela geração dos ativos, perda permanente de sua utilidade e despesas adicionais para aquisição de créditos substitutos. A cobertura para perda de utilidade contempla situações como a desqualificação de metodologias utilizadas na emissão ou de autorizações governamentais. Já a proteção para substituição busca cobrir os custos adicionais enfrentados pelo comprador ou responsável pela operação quando os créditos originais são afetados por um evento previsto na apólice. O produto também prevê despesas emergenciais para mitigação de danos, incluindo custos imediatos com combate a incêndios florestais e auditorias realizadas após desastres naturais, conforme as condições contratadas. Cobertura pode alcançar US$ 25 milhões por projeto O limite inicial estabelecido para a solução é de US$ 25 milhões por projeto. Considerando um preço de referência de US$ 10 por crédito de carbono, o valor corresponde à proteção financeira equivalente a 2,5 milhões de créditos, associados a 2,5 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente. A referência, no entanto, não significa que todos os projetos terão esse volume de créditos emitidos ou que a indenização será automática. A aplicação da cobertura dependerá dos riscos previstos e das condições estabelecidas na apólice. Para Lucio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline, a exigência de seguro está relacionada à necessidade de oferecer maior previsibilidade às empresas que compram créditos de carbono. “Controvérsias sobre a qualidade dos créditos, regularidade fundiária e o risco reputacional do greenwashing tornaram-se tópicos centrais em nossas negociações com grandes compradores corporativos”, afirma. O executivo, a proteção securitária pode contribuir para a estruturação financeira das operações e para a redução das incertezas enfrentadas pelos participantes desse mercado. Além das novas emissões, a Greenline pretende estender a possibilidade de contratação do seguro a projetos que já eram mensurados pela companhia antes da parceria com a Akad Seguros. Nesses casos, a inclusão dependerá de avaliação e aceitação dos riscos pela seguradora. A possibilidade de extensão está relacionada, segundo a empresa, à padronização dos processos de mensuração e ao uso de tecnologias de sensoriamento remoto para acompanhar projetos de conservação de florestas nativas e redução do desmatamento. Embora a Greenline tenha participado da estruturação da demanda e estabelecido a obrigatoriedade do seguro em suas próprias operações, o produto também poderá ser contratado por outros agentes do mercado de ativos ambientais, conforme os critérios de subscrição da Akad. A iniciativa amplia a utilização do seguro como instrumento de transferência de riscos em operações com créditos de carbono. A cobertura financeira, entretanto, não substitui os processos de verificação ambiental nem elimina a necessidade de avaliar a integridade dos projetos e dos ativos negociados. “Estamos transformando ativos ambientais em instrumentos financeiros verdadeiramente bancáveis”, afirma Lopez.

artigo.texto: O gargalo que virou prioridade O fornecimento de energia virou o gargalo da expansão da inteligência artificial, e a G2 Venture Partners (G2VP) calcula que o investimento em data centers vai passar de US$ 4 trilhões até o fim desta década. O diagnóstico da gestora de venture capital é direto: a rede elétrica dos Estados Unidos saiu de um patamar de crescimento praticamente nulo e passou a absorver vários gigawatts por ano em pouco tempo, sem que a oferta acompanhe o ritmo. Brook Porter, sócio da G2VP, avalia que a demanda avança mais rápido do que o mercado costuma reconhecer. Na visão dele, os operadores de nuvem em escala massiva — os hyperscalers — e os desenvolvedores de data centers precisam ampliar o escopo da discussão caso queiram acelerar a entrega de capacidade. Gás natural resolve o agora; solar resolve a escala Como ampliar cadeias produtivas leva tempo, a saída imediata do setor tem sido garantir energia de qualquer maneira: compra, aluguel e instalação de usinas movidas a gás natural. A análise da G2VP aponta o teto dessa rota. A indústria global de equipamentos a gás natural entrega cerca de 60 GW a 70 GW por ano, enquanto a base solar já supera 1 terawatt. O contraste de escala tem origem industrial. Módulos fotovoltaicos e a maior parte das tecnologias de armazenamento de longa duração — sistemas desenhados para entregar energia por muitas horas seguidas, e não apenas por um intervalo curto — são equipamentos pequenos e modulares, produzidos em linha. Porter apoia o raciocínio na Lei de Wright, a constatação empírica de que o custo unitário cai uma fração fixa a cada dobrada da produção acumulada. Fabricar repetidamente o mesmo item é o que puxa o preço para baixo. Dois modelos de data center e a rota fora da rede Na leitura da G2VP, o mercado caminha para dois formatos: instalações menores, conectadas à rede e com geração própria, e complexos de grande porte movidos a solar combinada com armazenamento de longa duração. O objetivo declarado por Porter é operar off-grid, ou seja, fora da rede. Gerar com renováveis sem depender da conexão permitiria ao desenvolvedor comandar o próprio cronograma, escapar de parte das restrições de licenciamento — fila de acesso à rede e licenças de emissão atmosférica — e encurtar o prazo até a operação. A G2VP conhece essa indústria por dentro: liderou a rodada Série C da Crusoe e, de acordo com Porter, acompanhou em posição privilegiada a evolução da companhia e as diferentes ondas de data centers. Lítio caro, longa duração na fila Armazenamento de energia foi, nos últimos anos, sinônimo de bateria de íons de lítio — solução considerada cara demais para disputar com combustíveis fósseis no fornecimento contínuo. Uma nova geração de sistemas de longa duração, de empresas como Form Energy e Antora Energy (esta no portfólio da G2VP), reduziu de forma significativa o custo por megawatt-hora. A aceitação ampla por parte dos desenvolvedores de data centers ainda está a alguns anos de distância, conforme a avaliação da gestora. O argumento de Porter é que o planejamento comece antes: ele compara o momento a surfar as maiores ondas de Mavericks, no litoral da Califórnia — ondas desse tamanho exigem remada constante e reação rápida; quem fica parado é engolido. O que isso muda para quem investe - O gargalo energético ganha contorno industrial: a vantagem competitiva se desloca para quem domina produção em massa de módulos e de sistemas de armazenamento, e não apenas para quem tem contrato de energia assinado. - Restrições de rede e de licenciamento entram no cálculo de retorno, porque prazos de conexão mais curtos valem mais em um setor no qual a capacidade computacional se valoriza rapidamente. - O gás natural segue como solução de transição, com limite de fabricação bem menor que o da solar. - A tese off-grid ainda depende de tecnologia sem aceitação ampla, o que mantém a janela aberta para acompanhar a evolução do custo por megawatt-hora. A leitura vale para além dos Estados Unidos: ao definir qual infraestrutura energética destrava projetos de IA, o debate da G2VP ajuda a mapear onde a restrição de oferta pode comprimir margens e onde a capacidade de fabricar escala se transforma em vantagem de custo.

artigo.texto: PETALING JAYA: BM Greentech Bhd is expected to see stronger earnings in the second half of the financial year ending March 31, 2027 (2H27), underpinned by an improved contribution from its bioenergy segment and a ramp-up in battery energy storage system (Bess) deliveries. The group’s earnings for the 1H27 largely came in within market expectations and the estimates of RHB Research and Phillip Capital Research, with core net profit rising 2% year-on-year to RM24mil. In a note, RHB Research said prospects for bio-energy, the group’s key earnings contributor, remain positive. Potential engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) opportunities from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130MW Feed-in Tariff 2.0 programme supports its outlook, given the group’s estimated 60% to 70% market share among domestic boiler EPCC players. “Given a construction period of up to 30 months, we expect the programme to support earnings growth over the next two to three years,” the research house said, adding that the addressable market could reach RM1bil to RM2bil. ... • In 1H27 the company’s core net profit rose 2% year‑on‑year to RM24 million, meeting market expectations, while Q2 revenue increased 8% to RM177 million and core net profit jumped 17% to RM13 million, aided by bioenergy growth and a 7.4‑point lift in water‑treatment margin. • RHB Research remains bullish on the bio‑energy segment, citing the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130 MW Feed‑in Tariff 2.0 programme and BM Greentech’s estimated 60‑70% domestic boiler EPCC market share, forecasting an addressable market of RM1‑2 billion and keeping a “buy” call with a RM2.05 target price (13× FY27 EPS). • Phillip Capital also maintains a “buy” stance, projecting earnings momentum from expanding BESS deliveries; it expects BESS to represent about one‑third of solar revenue in FY27 and roughly half by FY28, and retains a sum‑of‑parts target price of RM2.20.

artigo.texto: Quincy’s data center boom offers lessons for Montana communities QUINCY, Wash. — From the air, the contrast is clear: a growing agricultural town beside a sprawling data center hub. Quincy’s population has grown from about 5,000 to more than 8,000 over the past two decades, as the data center industry has expanded. The city is now home to eight data center campuses. For Montana Tech Lance Energy Chair Robert Morris, who serves on Montana’s Energy Task Force, Quincy’s growth offers a look at both the opportunities and challenges communities in Montana could face. “One thing we worry about is, are we going to be overwhelmed with the growth?” Morris said. “And they’ve stayed ahead of it here.” State Rep. Alex Ybarra, a lifelong Quincy resident, pointed to a new police station and City Hall and high school as examples of the public facilities built as the city changed thanks to an expanded tax base. Neighborhoods and businesses have also expanded. At the local school district, Superintendent Nik Bergman said data centers have become workforce partners. Bergman said the high school offers a data center technician program that can help students move directly into family-sustaining job within data centers. Quincy’s experience also raises questions facing Montana communities considering data center development: where facilities should be located, how much electricity and water will be needed, and who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them? Ybarra said location matters because communities that host data centers can benefit from the tax revenue. He also said cities should be careful about the terms they accept. “If you do it wrong, like give away your water or whatever, ask for lower rates of electricity, then it doesn’t work,” Ybarra said. City data show Quincy’s eight data center campuses account for roughly 4% to 8% of the city’s total water use. Newer cooling technology is designed to operate without drawing additional water, but it requires more electricity. Grant County PUD reports residential electricity rates have risen 55% over the past 20 years, from 4.12 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2006 to 6.4 cents in 2026. The utility’s rate remains below the listed averages for Washington, Montana and the nation. The utility is planning major transmission upgrades to meet demand from additional data center development, along with another rate increase. On the question of infrastructure and who pays, Morris said Quincy’s data center companies paid for their own substations as they arrived, working with the community and Grant County PUD. “I think it’s important that the communities, the utility and the developers all work together,” Morris said. For Quincy, the transformation took two decades. Morris said the experience can offer Montana communities information as they weigh whether and how to pursue similar development.
