artigo.texto: CMBlu Plans 10 MW Battery System for Imperial Irrigation The German developer's SolidFlow storage project in Winterhaven, California, is set to be the utility's first flow battery deployment. Updated on Nov. 23, 2026 in Energy Live Poll Do you think electricity reliability in your area is getting better? CMBlu, a German battery developer, plans to build a 10 MW/100 MWh SolidFlow battery energy storage system for the Imperial Irrigation District. The California Energy Commission approved a $7.2 million grant this week for the project's first phase. Why it matters The grant is intended to strengthen grid resilience and the reliability of energy supplies for communities across California. The project would give the Imperial Irrigation District its first deployment of flow battery technology. The first phase covers 1 MW of power and 10 MWh of storage, while the full Echo Sands system is planned at 10 MW and 100 MWh, with the $7.2 million California Energy Commission grant funding only the initial phase. The total cost of the full project and the schedule for the second phase have not been disclosed. The players CMBlu CMBlu is a German battery developer that is developing the SolidFlow-based Echo Sands storage project. Imperial Irrigation District The Imperial Irrigation District is a public water and power utility serving California's Imperial Valley region. The details The battery will be installed at a hydroelectric power plant in Winterhaven, California, and is designed to store electricity for more than 10 hours to help supply the Quechan Tribe and surrounding communities. The grant comes from the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program, which is sourced from federal funds. Timeline - The California Energy Commission approved the $7.2 million grant this week. Energy Landscape The Echo Sands award is one of the grants issued under the Community Energy Reliability and Resilience Investment program to fund grid resilience projects across California. It extends that program's push for longer-duration storage by backing a 10-hour flow battery at a utility's hydroelectric site. For Imperial Valley residents and Quechan Tribe communities, the project aims to keep stored electricity available for more than 10 hours, which could improve power reliability during outages. The grant's first phase is limited to 1 MW and 10 MWh, so the full benefit depends on the planned second phase being completed. The takeaway Longer-duration storage projects like Echo Sands show how state grants can fund early phases of grid resilience work before full deployment. Readers tracking regional energy reliability should watch for updates on the second phase and the full 100 MWh system. Further reading For more on how states are funding grid storage, see the Energy section. Source note: This article includes information reported by pv magazine USA. artigo.texto: Ascendum Türkiye has partnered with global battery leader CATL to open Türkiye’s first NING Service Experience Center in Tuzla, Istanbul. Chinese battery giant CATL has signaled that it could make further investments in Türkiye after officially entering the country with the opening of its NING Service center in Istanbul. The facility, established in İstanbul in cooperation with Ascendum Türkiye with an investment of approximately 15 million euros, will provide services in a range of areas, from battery repair to the training of technical specialists. CATL Co-President of Sales and Marketing Bruce Li, who traveled to İstanbul for the opening, said the NING Service investment was the first step in the company’s long-term plans for Türkiye and signaled that CATL could consider larger investments in the country in the future. Commenting on the possibility of an electric vehicle battery investment in Türkiye, Li said: “As you know, one of the easiest options for us could be to find a local partner in Türkiye and work together on battery pack production. We can hold discussions.” “Battery cell production is a highly complex business. But yes, we are open to that as well. When the market grows and the conditions are right, we may also invest in battery cell production. If we find a suitable partner, we could also develop cooperation through licensing for cell production,” he added. Asked about CATL’s cooperation with Togg, Li said: “Togg is Türkiye’s domestic and largest electric vehicle manufacturer. We have advanced battery technologies. Therefore, what the two sides have, namely our technology and Togg’s needs, are aligned. We are working shoulder to shoulder to assess Türkiye’s electric vehicle market and the commercial opportunities in this field.”

artigo.texto: Bill would end sales tax exemption for qualifying Texas data centers State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby is a co-author of Senate Bill 293, which lawmakers expect to pass in January AUSTIN, Texas (KCBD) - A bill filed in the Texas Legislature would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby, a co-author of Senate Bill 293, said Texas taxpayers should not foot the bill for these projects. Cost of the exemption There have been concerns over data center growth since the sales tax exemption was put in place more than a decade ago. Ashby said that when the law took effect in 2013, the cost was estimated at about $15 million. He said the most recent estimate is that the exemption will cost $3.3 billion in the upcoming biennium. What the bill would do SB 293 would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers, such as those that are at least 100,000 square feet. Existing exemptions would end when the bill takes effect. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that are frankly some of the most capitalized companies in the United States, but in the world,” Ashby said. Economist suggests different approach Texas economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the exemption than remove it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have power worked out behind the grid, require you have water supply worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. Perryman said changing the current law could affect rural Texans especially. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away, and if one goes away, you’re talking about billions in an area, particularly rural, that doesn’t have a lot of development,” Perryman said. Ashby said he does not expect much pushback from businesses. “These companies are so well capitalized, and these data centers are very profitable,” Ashby said. Next steps Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the state Senate when members convene in January. Ashby also said he wants to look at providing counties with limited regulatory authority over data center development. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Shelby County Commission considers data center regulations MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - The Shelby County Commission is discussing its own potential data center regulations Monday, with just over 100 days left on the Memphis City Council’s data center moratorium. Monday’s discussion is the first reading in the full county commission. It passed on first reading 9 ayes and 4 noes. The proposal has two more readings to go through with the full commission. People in the community are on both sides of the issue. Many want stricter boundaries on where data centers can locate. Some in the business community do not want those limits. Commissioner Amber Huett-Garica proposed updating the Memphis and Shelby County unified development code. If passed, the proposal would change zoning options for data centers, set rules on noise from the facilities and outline water usage. Richard Massey, data center accountability manager for the environmental justice organization Young, Gifted, and Green, is pushing for the proposal to pass. He said the proposal may also include zoning for current facilities. “To ensure that at the same time, we are having community sessions for folks to provide recommendations, insight, and testimony about their experience that no hyperscale data center can get grandfathered in beneath the existing zoning laws that have permitted this awful business model to come into Shelby County and effectively run wild without any regulatory oversight,” Massey said. The proposal follows meetings at the city level on data center regulation. The regulation proposal that passed the Memphis City Council differed from what the community pushed for: community input. Massey said he and other community members expect pushback on the county proposal. He said they will continue to push for regulation. “Also, I think it is critical that we pass Commissioner Huett- Garcia’s ordinance because it includes a trove of things that we have been pushing for all along. It includes restrictions on noise, for example; it includes that ban on using the aquifer, for example,” he said. Supporters of data centers in the area see them as a vital economic engine for Memphis and the Mid-South. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! Click here to report a spelling or grammar error. artigo.texto: Peco customers will see electric supply rate increase Dec. 1 because of surge on power grid by data centers Peco said the increase is the result of supply prices set by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. Peco customers will see a supply rate increase of 10% per kilowatt-hour starting Dec. 1 to cover a strong surge in demand on the region’s power grid. The increase, which will amount to $10 a month on an average bill, is not something Peco sought but rather the result of the wholesale price it pays for power, the company said. Peco passes that onto customers and does not profit from it, the company said. “On Dec. 1, electric supply rates are set to increase as a result of growing demand outpacing available supply across the region,” the utility, which serves 1.7 million customers, said in a statement. Customers of Peco, which serves Southeastern Pennsylvania, are not alone. Customers of most utilities across the state will see increases. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) released an independent analysis in September warning about the rapidly growing demand driven by data center development. “Pennsylvania is at an energy crossroads,” wrote PUC Chairman Steve DeFrank. “Electricity demand and supply are moving out of balance, and the status quo is not sustainable.” In the study’s severe scenario, projected new data center demand across PJM between 2029 and 2030 alone exceeds the current annual electricity demand of the entire Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Rates are determined largely through wholesale power auctions conducted by PJM, the Montgomery County-based regional grid operator for 13 states and Washington, D.C. PJM does not sell power but holds auctions that attempt to match the supply of electricity with demand. The auctions result in wholesale prices utilities like Peco pay power generators, such as power plants. Peco then sends that electricity to customers. However, PJM has struggled in recent years to match the needed power of large-load, hyperscale data centers that run AI across its wide territory. When there is too little supply to meet demand at the capacity auctions, prices rise. In a capacity auction over the summer, PJM said it was short 6,800 megawatts of meeting demand and is seeking ways to increase that. » READ MORE: Where data centers are proposed in the Philadelphia region “Just like many other commodities, prices are high for electricity,” PJM said in a statement. “This is due primarily to the major influx in demand being driven by data centers without commensurate supply being added to the system.” PJM notes that utilities and state utility commissions control who ultimately pays for those costs. A chart PUC released Monday shows the fallout. Customers of 11 of 12 utilities across Pennsylvania will see increases on Dec. 1, just as winter arrives. The PUC chart shows Peco customers facing a rise from 11.76 cents a kilowatt-hour to 12.96 cents — or about 10.3%. Peco said that will translate to a rise of about $9 a month for customers using the average 700 kilowatt-hours per month, or a little more than a 5.3% increase in reality. Candice Womer, a Peco spokesperson, said the 5.3% figure is lower than the 10% in the PUC chart because it reflects the impact on a customer’s total monthly electric bill, which includes a delivery rate and other charges. So the estimated average bill will increase from $166.08 to $174.99. Peco customers pay two separate rates on their bills — one for supply and one for delivery. The supply rate is the one that’s increasing Dec. 1 and typically makes up about half a residential electric bill. Separately, the delivery rate is used to pay for infrastructure and services that bring electric into homes. In March, Peco sought a rate increase in the delivery side of customers’ bills for 2027, saying it needed to increase infrastructure to handle demand, but the request was met with stiff resistance by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Peco withdrew that request. » READ MORE: Facing backlash, Peco withdraws request for double-digit rate hike next year In the end, customers’ bills will depend on how much energy they use. If a customer buys electricity or natural gas from a competitive supplier, the supply price could be different. Separately, Peco will make rates for its 553,000 natural gas customers and the estimated impact on bills available this month.

artigo.texto: The National Wealth Fund has announced an equity investment in two battery energy storage projects in Eccles and Kilmarnock, Scotland, in partnership with Matrix Renewables UK Limited. As part of the partnership, Matrix will retain majority ownership of both projects, while the investment will support their development and implementation. Located along transmission corridors connecting Scotland and England, the projects will have a combined power capacity of 1 GW and an energy storage capacity of 2 GWh. Construction at the Eccles project is already underway, with commercial operations expected to commence in October 2027. Meanwhile, construction at the Kilmarnock project is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with commercial operations targeted for September 2028. Furthermore, once operational, the facilities are expected to provide storage capacity equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 520,000 households. In April 2026, Matrix Renewables secured £245 million in non-recourse financing for a 500 MW/1,000 MWh battery energy storage system project located in Eccles-Leitholm, Scotland. The project, being developed in partnership with EDF, commenced construction in November 2025. Commercial operations are expected to commence in the third quarter of 2027.

artigo.texto: Brasil disputa liderança na atração de data centers, diz The Economist CNN - O Brasil tenta aproveitar a expansão mundial da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial para se consolidar como um dos principais destinos de investimentos em data centers. O país aposta em oferta de energia renovável, mercado digital em crescimento e posição estratégica para conexões internacionais para atrair projetos. A movimentação já aparece em obras e anúncios de investimentos. Em Vinhedo, no interior de São Paulo, a Ascenty está ampliando um complexo de data centers e prevê novos empreendimentos. Segundo reportagem do The Economist, a empresa planeja investir US$ 1,2 bilhão na região, numa aposta no crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional. A América Latina ainda tem participação pequena na infraestrutura global de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Segundo a revista, a região reúne menos de 600 data centers, com capacidade total próxima de 1,5 gigawatt (GW), volume inferior ao do Reino Unido. Já o Brasil, sozinho, concentra quase metade dessa capacidade: são aproximadamente 700 megawatts (MW) instalados — e a perspectiva é de crescimento. Alessandro Lombardi, presidente da Elea Data Centers, estima que a capacidade brasileira possa alcançar 5 GW até 2030. Energia e mercado consumidor atraem investimentos Um dos principais trunfos brasileiros é a matriz elétrica. Isso porque cerca de 85% da eletricidade do país vem de fontes renováveis. A disponibilidade de energia limpa é um diferencial, já que o setor demanda grandes volumes de eletricidade para se manter em funcionamento. O custo de construção também pode favorecer países latino-americanos. Um estudo da consultoria Turner & Townsend estima que erguer um data center no Vale do Silício custa cerca de US$ 14 por watt. Na América Latina, os valores variam de US$ 11,50 no México a US$ 9 em Bogotá, na Colômbia. Outro fator é o crescimento do consumo digital na região: quase 80% da população latino-americana já utiliza a internet, enquanto boa parte dos dados ainda é armazenado e processado nos Estados Unidos. Essa distância pode afetar a velocidade de acesso a serviços digitais: uma informação hospedada no estado americano da Virgínia pode levar cerca de 150 milissegundos para chegar a São Paulo. Quando o processamento ocorre em Vinhedo, o tempo cai para aproximadamente dois milissegundos. A redução da latência (intervalo entre o envio de uma solicitação e a resposta do sistema) é especialmente relevante para empresas que dependem de aplicações digitais rápidas. Isso cria uma demanda adicional por estruturas de processamento instaladas mais perto dos usuários. Brasil disputa projetos de inteligência artificial A oportunidade não se limita ao armazenamento de dados de usuários locais. Grandes empresas de tecnologia procuram regiões que possam funcionar como pontos estratégicos para suas redes globais de processamento. Um dos projetos mais expressivos nesse sentido é o da ByteDance, controladora do TikTok. A companhia chinesa planeja investir até US$ 39 bilhões em data centers no Complexo do Pecém, no Ceará. A vantagem do local é a proximidade com cabos submarinos que conectam a região à Europa, à África e a outros mercados. A disputa se estende às estruturas dedicadas ao treinamento de modelos de IA. Nesse caso, a prioridade é a disponibilidade de energia, custos e condições de operação, mais do que a proximidade com o mercado consumidor. David Dias, da consultoria EY, afirmou que a América Latina terá de disputar esses investimentos com regiões como Canadá, países nórdicos, Oriente Médio e Sudeste Asiático. O governo brasileiro também tenta estimular a chegada de empreendimentos através da redução de tarifas de importação sobre equipamentos de tecnologia, em uma iniciativa para tornar o país mais atrativo para investidores. Gargalos e disputa geopolítica podem frear expansão Apesar das vantagens, transformar o potencial em novos empreendimentos depende de superar obstáculos. A infraestrutura elétrica é um dos principais desafios: regiões com boa conexão à internet nem sempre são aquelas com maior disponibilidade de energia. Além disso, problemas na transmissão e a demora para obter autorização de conexão à rede podem comprometer o cronograma dos projetos. A segurança regulatória também pesa na decisão das empresas. Investidores querem previsibilidade em temas como incentivos fiscais e proteção à propriedade intelectual. Outro ponto é a aceitação da comunidade local. Embora a resistência a data centers seja menor na América Latina do que nos Estados Unidos, já existem registros de protestos contra esses projetos nas regiões visadas para as instalações. Para Fabro Steibel, do Instituto de Tecnologia e Sociedade do Rio de Janeiro (ITS-Rio), a questão geopolítica adiciona uma camada de complexidade. Na semana passada, o Departamento de Comércio dos Estados Unidos anunciou a exigência de licença para que data centers brasileiros recebam semicondutores avançados. A medida reflete a preocupação de Washington de que empresas chinesas possam utilizar, remotamente, equipamentos instalados em outros países para desenvolver modelos de inteligência artificial e contornar restrições americanas à exportação de chips.

artigo.texto: The 2026 midterm elections that swept Democrats into power in Congress and state legislatures also delivered a stunning rebuke to the artificial intelligence industry. Ballot measures that limited the construction of data centers – from California to Kansas to North Dakota – were approved by voters in 40 of 41 instances. These measures included the Kansas prohibition on construction of a type of battery energy storage system, a 180-day moratorium on data centers in Maine, and the outright ban on data center construction in Ohio. Drawing on recent survey data, we suggest that the Democratic sweep and the nationwide rejection of data centers are related. Republicans’ connections with an unpopular AI industry may have contributed to their poor showing at the polls. We are survey researchers. Our August 2026 survey of a nationally representative sample of 1,000 American adults shows that opposition to data centers is widespread. The survey shows that 65% of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. This opposition is bipartisan, with 76% of Democrats, 67% of independents and 52% of Republicans opposed to the sites. To better understand the sources of this opposition, we asked respondents to explain it in their own words. Twenty-eight percent of respondents voiced concerns about the negative environmental impact of data centers. One respondent stated: “Draining our water reserves significantly with a data center would be catastrophic to our region.” Some respondents, 15%, also expressed concerns about data centers’ negative impact on their quality of life. For example, one respondent said: “Noise issues, energy issues and visual site are three issues that are major concerns for a AI data center to be in the area I live in.” Ten percent of respondents singled out the centers’ connection to increased utility costs. One respondent said that “ever since a data center has been built in my local area the prices of water and electricity have more than doubled.” Finally, 13% of respondents expressed a broad distrust of AI and the industry itself, with one stating, “I think that AI needs to be better regulated and a lot more developed and proven safe before any massive full scale deployment.” Despite mounting public opposition to data centers, President Donald Trump expressed strong support for data center construction before Election Day. He said that if Americans want to live in “crime-infested areas” and “squalor,” they should not have a data center. Days after the midterms, Trump threatened to penalize U.S. companies that build data centers overseas. As widespread opposition to data centers grew through 2026, Republican congressional candidates increasingly had to weigh loyalty to Trump against local backlash. As Election Day neared, many Republican candidates had distanced themselves from unrestricted data center construction. In contrast, many Democrats made opposition to data centers an important theme of their campaigns. Our poll suggests that these efforts may have resonated with voters. Among Americans who expressed opposition to data centers, 48% indicated they would support the local Democratic candidate in the U.S. House of Representatives, compared to 25% for the Republican candidate. And 47% of those living in states that held a Senate election were planning on voting for the Democratic candidate, while 28% planned to vote for the Republican Senate candidate. Even taking partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics into account, opposition to data centers was associated with an intention to support Democratic House and Senate candidates. Given widespread public concern about data center construction, Democrats have electoral incentives to make AI regulation a part of their legislative agenda in the new Congress. Whether or not they enact new legislation, popular opposition to data centers is unlikely to abate anytime soon. Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links.

artigo.texto: UK and EU aim to link emissions trading schemes by January 2028 The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, targeting 1 January 2028 for the arrangement to take effect alongside the UK's planned expansion of carbon pricing to international shipping. IMAGE: Flags of the UK and the EU. Getty Images The agreement could simplify compliance for shipping companies operating under both schemes by allowing them to use UK and EU carbon allowances interchangeably, the UK's Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer on 20 November. Under the planned expansion, the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) is set to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages between UK and non-UK ports for vessels of 5,000 GT and above from 1 January 2028. The UK ETS has already covered 100% of emissions from domestic voyages and emissions at berth in UK ports since 1 July 2026. The EU ETS similarly covers 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports, while requiring shipping companies to account for all emissions on voyages between EU ports. The UK ETS will also adopt the EU's approach to neighbouring container transhipment ports. Ports on the European Commission's designated list will not count as UK ports of call when determining which voyage emissions fall under the scheme. The list is updated every two years. Once linked, the two schemes will continue operating separately but allow shipping companies to use allowances from either market to meet their emissions obligations. This could eliminate the need for operators covered by both schemes to purchase UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately. The arrangement is also intended to cover emissions obligations for 2027, with the first deadline for using allowances interchangeably scheduled for 30 September 2028. The UK and EU are also working towards a common administrative process that could allow shipping companies to manage compliance under both schemes together. The UK also plans to remove its minimum auction price for carbon allowances when the link takes effect. Impact on shipping The agreement aims to bring UK ETS shipping rules more closely in line with those of the EU ETS, including requirements for monitoring, reporting and verifying emissions. The UK plans to end the temporary arrangement that allows shipping companies to surrender allowances for only 50% of emissions on voyages between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. These voyages are expected to face the full 100% requirement from 2028, bringing them in line with other domestic UK routes. Meanwhile, passenger and ro-pax vessels serving islands with fewer than 200,000 residents and no road or rail connection to the mainland are expected to qualify for a temporary surrender derogation until at least 31 December 2030. Ice-class vessels are also set to qualify for a 5% reduction in their allowance surrender obligations until at least the same date. The agreement also addresses how shipping companies can account for lower-emission fuels. Operators would be able to apply a zero-emission factor to eligible biofuels, renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) and recycled carbon fuels, provided they meet the sustainability and greenhouse gas savings requirements under the EU Renewable Energy Directive. The UK government has also said it will review how its carbon pricing rules interact with any future global emissions measure adopted by the IMO. The review would aim to avoid charging shipping companies twice for the same emissions while keeping compliance requirements manageable. “Any review would take into account any relevant changes to the EU ETS, and its outcomes will maintain support for maritime decarbonisation, and remain consistent with net zero,” the department said. The UK and EU are working towards bringing the two carbon markets together by January 2028, with technical preparations and legislative approvals still required. artigo.texto: Elon Musk said AI companies may soon run into serious cash shortages as they wait for revenue-generating data centers to come online. The SpaceX and Tesla CEO replied to an X post on Saturday that showed comparatively low stock valuations for semiconductor manufacturers, relative to their expected profits. This could suggest that investors are bearish on AI-powering chip companies continuing to notch soaring profits in the race for compute — a sign that data center construction may face serious headwinds in the near future. "The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year," Musk said, adding that delays in data center activations would require "hundreds of billions" in more capital for AI companies. "Where will that come from?" he asked. Tech stocks in US markets took it on the chin last week. The S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory on Friday, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from recent highs. The market carnage prompted some to speculate that the AI bubble had popped. Financial regulators in semiconductor-heavy Taiwan on Saturday said they would limit short selling — an action similar to one taken by US regulators during the 2008 housing crisis. Though leading AI and AI-adjacent companies like Meta, Microsoft, and Anthropic are reporting growing revenue, they're also spending massive sums to secure compute — powered by key hardware that enables chatbots and other AI tools. Compute is largely provided by data centers, which have faced their own series of setbacks recently, from backlash from the communities where they are being built to the blue midterm wave and construction delays. And without a reliable network of data centers, AI companies are hobbled in their ability to scale to meet investor demand. Data center operators, meanwhile, are left at the altar with their multibillion-dollar investments failing to generate revenue. "Getting this amount of compute turned on, cooled and working reliably is incredibly hard," Musk said.

artigo.texto: BOSTON — Opponents of data center development have launched a campaign to put new restrictions before Massachusetts voters in 2028, as a $16 billion project proposed in Sutton sharpens the debate. The Committee to Restrict Data Centers, which filed initial paperwork with state regulators in September, announced the campaign recently and launched sign4restrictingdatacenters.org, where residents can pledge support for a ballot petition and request a signature form by mail. The Kraft Group is pursuing a data center campus in Sutton that, if completed, would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the country. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents of the central Massachusetts town, adding to the unfolding national debate over AI development, electricity consumption, water use and potential effects on utility bills. The website urges visitors to help restrict data centers, citing concerns about increasing electric bills, water consumption and noise from equipment that can “sound like jet engines.” It also calls for local voter approval of proposed facilities. At the bottom of the site, organizers included a declaration: “No Ai was used on this site.” The committee’s proposal, designated Petition 26-08 by the attorney general’s office, would establish requirements for new data centers and expansions of existing facilities, including a two-thirds vote of approval by residents in the host community. Under the petition, a data center could not receive a municipal permit unless its electricity supplier agreed not to shift costs onto other customers and committed to providing enough electricity from 100% renewable resources to meet the facility’s needs without reducing renewable energy available to others. Operators would also have to guarantee recovery of infrastructure costs if a facility closes, reduces capacity or violates its contract. The proposal also requires water suppliers to certify that existing systems can accommodate a facility without materially affecting service to existing customers in the host or neighboring communities. Operators would need drought-related water reduction plans. Municipalities would have to publicly disclose permitting documents online, and voters would decide whether to approve a proposed facility at an election at least 180 days after the community announces its permitting decision and releases the relevant documents. The state auditor could audit data centers and their electricity and water suppliers, with municipalities authorized to require facilities to cease operating until certain violations are corrected. The committee is chaired by Jim Fleming, a political consultant who operates a signature-gathering company and said he has connections to communities that have raised concerns about data center projects, including Westfield and Holyoke. Sen. John Velis, a Westfield Democrat, is also promoting the campaign. “The completion and proposed construction of data centers around the state has caused local community groups to organize to either stop or delay new centers,” Velis said in the committee’s press release, citing concerns about electricity costs, environmental uncertainty, water usage and noise. Fleming submitted the proposal shortly before this year’s August filing deadline, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office certified it in September. The committee is not planning to collect signatures for the first available deadline this month, Fleming said. Organizers have until Nov. 18 to submit 74,574 signatures, representing 3% of the votes cast in the 2022 gubernatorial election, to qualify for the next stage of the process. Because the proposal is intended for the 2028 ballot, they can pursue the initial signature threshold next fall, when the requirement will be based on votes cast in this month’s gubernatorial election. That approach gives organizers more time to build public support and leaves them an opportunity to submit alternative versions of the proposal by next August’s filing deadline. Fleming indicated the language already approved by the attorney general may not be the version ultimately advanced. Filing early also puts lawmakers on notice as they begin a legislative session in January. If enough signatures are collected next fall, the Legislature would have until early May 2028 to act on the proposal. If lawmakers do not pass it, supporters would need to gather a smaller round of signatures by early July to secure a spot on the November ballot. Fleming said the prospect of a ballot question is intended, in part, to prompt legislative action before voters are asked to decide the issue. “If the legislature passes a law like this that is good, and not just an executive order, then we will wrap this entire process. And this will hopefully encourage them to do this,” he said. The petition would go further than Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order, signed Sept. 8, which established requirements for state agencies reviewing large data center projects. The order generally applies to facilities exceeding 25 megawatts, while the petition sets a lower threshold of 5 megawatts of peak annual demand. Healey’s order directs state agencies, including the Department of Environmental Protection and the Energy Facilities Siting Board, to develop policies addressing electricity, water, environmental impacts and community benefits. It requires developers to procure incremental clean electricity, with an alternative compliance payment available, and directs agencies to develop ratepayer protections. Unlike the proposed ballot measure, the order does not require a communitywide vote. Instead, it calls for community benefit agreements and municipal guidance. It also applies only to facilities built or expanded after it took effect. Like any executive order, it can be amended or revoked by a future governor. The campaign is emerging amid broader political resistance to data centers. Voters favored restrictions in 40 of 41 local ballot contests held

artigo.texto: Affordability and data centers were on the ballot this November. Voters made it clear that they are concerned about both issues: prices are too high and the neighborliness of data centers is in doubt. In a time of economic turbulence, cities and counties are struggling to pay for schools, roads and public safety without the tax revenue data centers generate. Where can part of the solution to affordability and concerns with data centers be found? Vacant lots. Vacant lots can host data centers that are well maintained, comply with local architectural requirements, have security and bring in much-needed cash for local projects. An eyesore and security problem can become a revenue generator and a secure property. However, some are determined to keep data centers from developing the local economy and unsightly properties at any cost. In early November, an activist helped block the development of a $5 billion data center that was set to break ground in the next year or so. The data center was supposed to be built on the site of Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. The vacant lot is now overgrown with grass and weeds, stretching across nearly 90 acres in Landover, Md. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Prince George's County, home to the former mall, is facing a $130 million budget deficit. It has lost a Six Flags amusement park, is losing the Washington Commanders to Washington, D.C., and has suffered thousands of federal job losses. Developers projected about $53.5 million a year in local tax revenue if the data center were to be built. The activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, isn't moved by those numbers or how they help her neighbors. "Money is, you know, a made-up concept," she said. "We buy into it every day, and we choose that this has value and this doesn't have value and to me the environment has the highest and utmost value and I need to honor that in any way." The rejection of a project to help revitalize a site that sorely needs it and fill the county's coffers perfectly encapsulates the political debate around data centers. Too often, proposed data centers receive automatic opposition from activists and politicians. As a result, some of America's most vulnerable and desperate communities are losing millions of dollars in tax revenue that could fund schools, fix roads, pay emergency responders and more. Landover Mall is sadly not the only example. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects across the country worth approximately $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026, which Data Center Watch describes as the largest single-quarter total on record. That's roughly as much as all of 2025, in just three months. HOW AMERICA CAN WIN THE AI RACE WITHOUT BURNING VOTERS In Virginia, Prince William County stands to miss out on as much as $400 million in projected annual tax revenue following the collapse of Digital Gateway, once billed as one of the largest data center complexes in the world. The county had approved the project, but courts invalidated its rezoning approvals. The remaining developer withdrew its legal challenge in July 2026, effectively ending the plans. On the other hand, communities that are looking to the future and allowing data centers are reaping the benefits. Virginia’s Loudoun County has embraced data centers, which have generated 38% of general fund revenue in the county’s FY2026 budget. That revenue has helped the county lower its real property tax rate every year for a decade, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026. That's real money back in homeowners' pockets. That is revenue its neighbor, Prince William County, is missing out on. HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF In Henrico County, Virginia, data center tax revenue pays for an Affordable Housing Trust Fund that helps first-time homebuyers with down payments. A single mother working toward a nursing degree said her new mortgage costs less than her old rent. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's data center expansion helped the parish pay for $50,000 teacher bonuses. THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO Data center developers have a responsibility to communities: listen to their concerns, be transparent and collaborative about their plans, design in ways their neighbors approve and work to mitigate or eliminate undesirable local impacts. They must also pay their own electric and water costs, establish noise limits and continually work with local community groups and elected officials to address concerns as they arise. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Data center development can be and often is a win-win for developers and the community. But even these efforts are not enough for some. Money may be a "made-up concept" to some, but the lower tax rates in Loudoun County, the down payment in Henrico and the teacher bonuses in Richland Parish are real. Immovable opponents are ignoring the economic benefits data centers can bring and leaving funding for community projects on the table. History shows other counties will take advantage of this lack of foresight and benefit.

artigo.texto: The Tennessee Valley Authority is set to receive $1.7 billion in aggregate payments from an unnamed data center customer under its new tariff for data centers above 5 MW, the federal utility said in a Nov. 12 U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. “Capacity commitment charges under the agreement are based on a rate of approximately $1.5 million per MW of requested capacity above 5 MW,” the filing said. “This rate reflects TVA's current cohort-based pricing methodology, which may be revised for future customer cohorts.” The new tariff took effect Oct. 1 and will be phased in through 2029, the filing said. That phase-in period will apply to existing customers to allow them to retain their existing rate structure for a period of time, the Nashville Scene reported in August. TVA CEO Mike Skaggs said during a Nov. 13 earnings call that the change to data center rates has supported the utility’s investments. Those investments include extending the lives of the utility’s existing nuclear units and “helping expand the nuclear fuel and supply hub in the East Tennessee area,” he said. The utility recently received the first small modular reactor construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission for a BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River Site in Oak Ridge, “although TVA has not yet decided whether to construct a reactor at the site,” its filing said. Skaggs came out of retirement to serve as interim CEO following the retirement of former CEO Don Moul and was instated as TVA’s permanent CEO following a Nov. 10 board meeting, TVA’s vice president of financial planning and investor relations Clifton Lowry said on the call. TVA’s filing also noted that in August, the utility’s board approved 1.5 GW of new natural gas generation, “targeted to be online in 2032.” As of Sept. 30, TVA said it “had spent $463 million on long-lead-time equipment associated with previously approved projects, which will now be utilized in connection with the project. TVA could spend up to an additional $3.1 billion on this project.” That previously approved project is TVA’s defunct Middle Tennessee Energy Solution project. In August, TVA said its approval of the new 1.5 GW gas facility “closes out” the previous project, “and all funding has been transferred to the New Gas Facility 2032.” TVA’s President and CFO Tom Rice said that the utility is in a “strong financial position” to executive its $13 billion capital investment plan over the next three years. That investment comes on top of the more than $23 billion in investments since 2020, Rice said. However, TVA’s filing notes that it “continues to experience supply chain pressures resulting from inflation, tariffs and other trade restrictions, material constraints, and labor availability.” “These factors have contributed to project delays, limited availability of critical materials, and increased costs for both materials and labor,” the utility said. “TVA anticipates that inflationary and tariff pressures will persist into 2027. Although these challenges have been managed with limited disruption to business operations thus far, continued or escalating pressures could result in more substantial operational impacts and increased pressure on power rates.”

artigo.texto: Key Points - Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann recently suggested that SpaceX could acquire stalled data centers. - The key trigger for such an acquisition would be data centers that already have power. - As pushback against AI data centers grows, electricity becomes an increasingly important factor for investors to consider. Wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies(NASDAQ:SPCX) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting. The key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so important and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy(NYSE:BE), NextEra Energy(NYSE:NEE), and Brookfield Renewable(NYSE:BEP). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » SpaceX sees the problem very clearly SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers. Image source: Getty Images. As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Bloom Energy is a high risk/high reward option Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The company's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an important inflection point for the business. But investors are well aware of the opportunity, pushing the stock higher by more than 1,200% over the past three years. With a lofty price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 100x, it is very clearly a well-loved stock. And yet, the opportunity to power AI data centers remains substantial, and perhaps only getting larger. If you are an aggressive growth investor, you should at least consider Bloom Energy, even if you only end up adding it to your wish list. NextEra Energy covers two bases NextEra Energy is one of the world's largest utilities. In fact, it is looking to get even bigger, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy(NYSE:D). Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most important data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time. But there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield. Brookfield Renewable is focused on clean energy For investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy. The key here, however, is that Brookfield Renewable largely sells power under long-term contracts outside of the regulated framework. It already has large deals with AI giants Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT) and Google. Add in the goal of at least 5% annual distribution growth, and income lovers would be remiss if they didn't at least examine Brookfield Renewable and the AI opportunity ahead of it. There's usually more than one angle to play If you think Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann is on to something, you could simply buy SpaceX. That's fine, but it isn't the only takeaway from his insight. The real story is that access to electricity is increasingly important. And you can also play that investment theme with companies like Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable. Should you buy stock in Bloom Energy right now? artigo.texto: At a bilateral summit on 20 November, EU and UK leaders announced the finalisation of negotiations on creating a joint carbon market. The agreement is set to apply from 1 January 2028, provided it is ratified in both jurisdictions. This was reported by the European Commission on its official website. According to the Commission, the link will create a larger and more liquid market with a more stable carbon price. It is expected to support both sides’ ambitions to achieve climate neutrality, as well as promote more efficient investment decisions and the sustainable development of both economies. The intention to link the systems was first announced at the first EU-UK summit in May 2025. At the same time, the EU Emissions Trading System has been linked to the Swiss system since 1 January 2020, and this link will remain in place. What will change for aviation and maritime transport The UK will extend its emissions trading system to aviation and maritime transport, adding more than 10 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions to it. According to the European Commission, this should stimulate the decarbonisation of these sectors. Both systems will also monitor the non-CO₂ climate effects of aviation. Exemption from CBAM? Linking the systems lays the groundwork for a possible future mutual exemption from each side’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). This would reduce red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel. Recently, EcoPolitic reported that the European Commission adopted rules for deducting carbon prices paid outside the EU from CBAM obligations. This allows producers to avoid paying twice for the same emissions.

artigo.texto: Residents raise concerns over Brewer’s proposed data center ordinance BREWER, Maine (WABI) — Residents and members of the Maine People’s Alliance gathered outside the Brewer Auditorium on Monday, raising concerns about proposed changes to the city’s data center regulations. “People are really upset about the idea of data centers coming to Maine,” said Megan Smith, Penobscot County community organizer for the Maine People’s Alliance. “We love our outdoors here. We don’t want it spoiled.” The proposed changes would increase the maximum capacity for data centers from 20 megawatts to 50 megawatts. Brewer Planning Board member Joy Sinclair, who attended the demonstration, said the proposal would also increase the allowable level of low-frequency noise near residential properties. The proposal also calls for noise studies and ongoing monitoring, along with closed-loop cooling for server equipment. Sinclair was the only Planning Board member to vote against the proposal. She said she is concerned about the potential impact on homes along the Orrington line and toward Holden. “The information that is available shows that what happens is that these are built. They tear up people’s lives. They make it impossible to live near them. Their property values plummet,” Sinclair said. Demonstrators also raised concerns about potential water and electricity use and said they hope to inform residents about the proposal. The city will hold an informational meeting at 6 p.m. Tuesday at the Brewer Auditorium. Public comment will also be allowed at the Dec. 8 City Council meeting. The proposed changes still need City Council approval. Brewer City Manager, Eric Glidden, provided WABI with a statement regarding the proposal and it is included in full below: “The proposed regulations are more stringent in several respects than what is currently in place. The proposed amendments are available for public review on the City’s website under the “News” section. These changes include additional requirements related to water usage, more comprehensive permitting standards, mandatory connections to the City’s wastewater system to ensure wastewater is properly treated, stricter noise controls, and restrictions limiting data center development to the Industrial 2 (IND-2) zone, which is primarily located behind the City landfill. The proposed increase in allowable capacity from 20 MW to 50 MW is largely driven by economies of scale. Based on discussions with the City’s consultant, larger facilities may be more economically feasible because the substantial upfront costs associated with data center development can be spread across a larger operation. Increasing the allowable capacity would make Brewer more competitive in attracting this type of investment, while the proposed regulations would establish stronger protections for the community. City staff have been making a concerted effort to identify opportunities for responsible economic development, particularly on industrially zoned land that has remained undeveloped for many years. Our goal is to encourage investment that can strengthen the City’s commercial tax base and potentially reduce the tax burden on residential property owners, while ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place to protect our residents and municipal infrastructure. Ultimately, these are proposed regulations, and the City Council has not yet made a decision on whether to adopt them. We recognize that residents have important questions and concerns, and we welcome their feedback as part of the public review process. All proposed data centers would be required to disclose their anticipated maximum daily water demand, how that water would be used, and any recycling or reuse systems. The developer would also be required to submit a water-use study prepared by a qualified consultant approved by the Brewer Water Department. That study would evaluate whether the City’s water system has sufficient capacity to serve the facility, whether existing infrastructure can deliver the required water, and whether any improvements would be necessary. The proposed regulations also include requirements for closed-loop cooling systems, intended to help manage water consumption. Ultimately, the purpose of these requirements is to ensure that the City has the information necessary to evaluate a proposed development’s impacts on infrastructure, municipal services, and local resources before any decisions are made. Any project would be evaluated based on its specific characteristics and anticipated demands. City staff have been working develop thoughtful and responsible regulations for data centers, with the goal of ensuring that appropriate protections are in place for our community should such development be proposed in Brewer. Our primary goal is to ensure any development is done responsibly. At the same time, we recognize that many residents have strong opinions and concerns about data centers, along with important questions and about their potential impacts. That is precisely why the City is holding a public informational meeting tomorrow evening. We genuinely want to hear from our residents, understand their concerns, answer questions, and receive feedback before the City Council begins its formal consideration of the proposed amendments. At the earliest, the City Council will consider the proposed amendments at its regularly scheduled meeting on December 8, when they are currently scheduled for a first reading. The amendments are then scheduled for a second reading at the January 12 City Council meeting. We are also open to holding additional informational meetings. These meetings will provide additional opportunities for public comment as the Council considers the proposed regulations." Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive bibliometric survey examining approximately 3,060 peer-reviewed publications published between 2015 and 2024 has established a unified electrochemical framework that explains how transition metal oxide electrodes transition between surface-dominated pseudocapacitive charge storage and bulk diffusion-controlled battery reactions. Rather than treating rechargeable batteries and electrochemical capacitors as entirely disconnected technological domains with isolated operating principles, the decadal synthesis reveals that transition metal oxides operate along a continuous charge-storage continuum governed by fundamental physicochemical descriptors. These governing descriptors include intrinsic electronic conductivity, solid-state ion diffusion kinetics, the spatial density of electrochemically accessible redox-active sites, surface adsorption energetics, defect chemistry, and crystallographic phase stability under repeated cycling. By evaluating material modifications across both device architectures simultaneously, the unified model demonstrates how structural engineering, morphologic tailoring, and chemical doping systematically shift an electrode’s charge-storage mechanism toward either rapid surface-confined power delivery or high-capacity bulk energy storage, resolving longstanding fragmentation in literature. The extensive analysis underscores that pristine transition metal oxides face an inherent performance trade-off between delivering high theoretical capacitance through multi-electron Faradaic redox transformations and suffering from severe kinetic and mechanical limitations. While conventional graphite anodes in commercial lithium-ion batteries are constrained to a theoretical capacity of 372 milliampere-hours per gram through reversible lithium intercalation, transition metal oxides undergoing multi-electron conversion mechanisms, such as hematite and cobalt oxide, boast theoretical capacities exceeding 800 to 1,000 milliampere-hours per gram. Similarly, single and mixed-valence metal oxides offer specific capacitance values that far outstrip traditional carbon-based electric double-layer capacitors, which rely exclusively on electrostatic charge separation. However, pristine oxides typically exhibit poor intrinsic electronic conductivity, sluggish solid-state ion transport kinetics, substantial volume expansion during repeated cycling, and structural degradation. These interconnected physical constraints induce rapid electrode pulverization, severe capacity fading, and high charge-transfer resistance, preventing pristine bulk oxides from realizing their full theoretical electrochemical capabilities without targeted structural modifications. Within the established framework, electrochemical energy storage systems are distinguished by the kinetic nature of their charge-transfer processes, which can be quantitatively mapped using technique-specific electroanalytical signatures. In electrical double-layer capacitors, energy is stored via electrostatic ion accumulation at the electrode-electrolyte interface without electron transfer, yielding superior cycling stability and elevated power densities but modest energy density. In contrast, battery-type materials undergo diffusion-controlled Faradaic ion intercalation or conversion reactions within the bulk crystalline lattice, producing nonlinear galvanostatic charge-discharge profiles with distinct voltage plateaus and sharp redox peaks in cyclic voltammetry. These physical mechanisms are evaluated through the power-law relationship relating current to voltage scan rate, where a power-law exponent b approaching 1.0 identifies an ideal surface-confined capacitive response, whereas an exponent near 0.5 indicates diffusion-limited bulk storage. Transition metal oxides uniquely span this boundary, frequently exhibiting intermediate exponents between 0.6 and 0.9 that reflect hybrid electrochemical behavior. To overcome the intrinsic conductivity-capacitance trade-off, material synthesis routes dictate the resulting crystal architecture, defect distribution, and electroactive surface area of transition metal oxide electrodes. Hydrothermal and solvothermal synthesis methods typically yield two-dimensional nanosheets or elongated nanorods that provide high specific surface areas and short ion diffusion paths, which facilitate rapid ion transport and elevate pseudocapacitive contributions. Template-assisted synthesis produces hollow, mesoporous structures capable of accommodating mechanical strain during cycling to enhance durability, though often at the cost of synthetic complexity. Chemical vapor deposition deposits high-purity thin films with precisely controlled thicknesses that reduce internal resistance, while electrochemical deposition enables direct electrode growth on conductive substrates to minimize interfacial contact resistance. Complementing these synthesis routes, advanced engineering strategies—such as inducing oxygen vacancies through defect engineering, incorporating conductive carbon frameworks, creating multi-component heterostructures, and introducing aliovalent dopants—alter the underlying electronic band structures, raise charge-carrier concentrations, and lower activation energy barriers. The mechanistic utility of this unified continuum is exemplified in the contrasting behavior of individual transition metal oxides, beginning with nickel oxide and cobalt oxide. Nickel oxide functions as a prototypical hybrid material in alkaline electrolytes, where charge storage is governed by reversible Faradaic redox transitions involving the divalent and trivalent nickel redox couple. At elevated scan rates or within nanostructured architectures, nickel oxide displays surface-confined pseudocapacitive kinetics with power-law exponents between 0.6 and 0.9, while at lower operating rates, deeper proton diffusion into the bulk crystalline lattice triggers battery-type storage. artigo.texto: Australia has the natural resources and know-how to create a thriving battery manufacturing industry but is missing opportunities by exporting critical minerals rather than turning them into high-value products. Scientists from the CSIRO issued the warning at an event on Tuesday, also recommending more international partnerships and a greater focus on manufacturing individual components rather than trying to make entire batteries. The call comes as Australians embrace battery technology, with more than 600,000 home batteries installed under a federal scheme since July 2025 and rapid electric vehicle sales since March. Speaking at an event called Australia's Battery Opportunity, CSIRO mineral resources principal research scientist Joanne Loh said the nation had enviable access to valuable raw materials. "We have all the minerals needed for batteries, specifically lithium-ion batteries - we're the number one producer in terms of lithium… we have nickel, cobalt, manganese, aluminium, copper, graphite, you name it," she said. "However, we export all of these as raw materials overseas so even though we might have it, we're actually sending it overseas for processing, then importing them back as batteries." The nation also shredded batteries at the end of their lives and exported the materials, Dr Loh said, rather than using them. Australia had also stopped manufacturing elements that could be used in batteries, such as aluminium foil, CSIRO senior research engineer Geoff de Looze said. The nation could re-establish that facility, he said, and target the local production of key components like aluminium casings and copper foil. "We do have some gaps in Australia's capability so when we look at them we need to rank them and work out which ones we can take on and which ones we want to leave alone," Mr de Looze said. "Any of the manufactured parts going into batteries, Australia can take on." A CSIRO report released early in November found Australia could use its expertise in manufacturing aluminium aerosol cans to produce battery casings, for example, or manufacture copper foil from scrap wire. Identifying gaps in the global battery supply chain could allow Australian companies to partner with larger manufacturing firms from the region, CSIRO senior principal research scientist Adam Best said, rather than competing with an established industry. "We need to work closely with our partners in Asia, Pacific, North America, Europe, to find where we fit in this middle part such that we can do… that manufacturing, that value-adding, to capture more value from our resources," he said. "Then Australia does have a brighter future that can lead to a future with energy security." Australian Associated Press

artigo.texto: Rowan students will work at Vineland’s massive data center under a new program Engineering students will work in six-month stints at DataOne in Cumberland County as the Vineland data center finds its footing. Engineering students at Rowan University will work at DataOne, a massive data center complex in Vineland, as soon as next year under a new agreement, Rowan announced Tuesday. The announcement comes after DataOne was hit in September with a $1 million fine for violating clean-air laws. The center has faced criticism — and a now-dismissed lawsuit — from neighbors who say it has impacted their quality of life. DataOne’s CEO, Charles-Antoine Beyney, said the program is an effort to partner with one of the state’s largest universities, teach young people about data centers, and create a local artificial intelligence workforce. “They can realize that data centers, AI factories, when they are properly built, are definitely not the enemy of mankind,” Beyney said. “On the contrary, they are beautiful assets that generate tremendous amount of value for all the local communities.” The agreement took effect on Sept. 29. Beyney, a French entrepreneur who has developed data centers around the world for nearly two decades, founded DataOne, the European data center company building the 2.4 million-square-foot, 300-megawatt plant in Cumberland County. The Vineland facility’s internal technology, operated by Nebius Group, an Amsterdam-based AI infrastructure company, will fuel Microsoft’s AI tools. The project is expected to bring about 200 long-term jobs to the city. Leaders at DataOne approached Rowan about a partnership, and Rowan agreed, said Giuseppe Palmese, the dean of the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering. Rowan has been expanding its engineering co-op programs, Palmese said, which give students the chance to work at local companies for six to eight months to gain mechanical and electrical skills. Students will have to apply and interview for the data center jobs, which will begin the summer before their senior year and carry into the fall semester. The first group of students — three or four workers — are expected to be onboarded by April, Beyney said, when most construction at Vineland’s DataOne facility, less than a half-hour drive from Rowan, will be done. Students will be paid for their work, Beyney said. No money is being exchanged between Rowan University itself and DataOne as part of the program, Palmese said. Because data centers fuel AI, Palmese said, they are likely here to stay. Thus, working at DataOne will give students the chance to get ahead in the field and experience a data center while it is still in development, he said. Palmese said some students have expressed interest in the program already, while others have criticized AI. “When we work in a place like a data center, there are issues there to deal with. You have the environmental aspects of it, noise pollution aspects of it, and what engineers do is solve those problems,” Palmese said. “So it’s an overall benefit to our students.” Rowan University likely will not be the only education partner for DataOne, Beyney said. He expressed interest in sending DataOne representatives to local high schools and colleges to teach about data centers and AI. “We could be sending some people to at least get the right information in front of the students, because they are being so disinformed and so fake-news-fed by so many different forms of medias,” Beyney said. “Sometimes it’s good to have the real truth.” A Pew Research poll from this summer shows that American opinions on data centers, including among young people, have grown more negative, at least when it comes to how the plants will affect the environment. Beyney said neighborhood complaints about noise are not his biggest concern right now, even as controversies surround AI plants across the country. “We are not building for the next six months. We are building for the next decade, or two decades. So I don’t care about the noise that can happen right now,” Beyney said, “but I do care how strong the value proposition of DataOne will be for the community.” “They will realize that everything we say was true,” Beyney said. “We were not liars. We were even under-promising and over-delivering.” Inquirer South Jersey

artigo.texto: Moment Energy has launched Nova, which integrates repurposed EV batteries from multiple vehicle platforms using an AI-powered BMS Individual battery packs can be replaced as they age, with the company targeting a system lifetime of over 20 years The system has achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A Moment Energy, a Canada-based battery energy storage system (BESS) provider that uses repurposed EV batteries, has introduced its new BESS, Nova. The 200 kW / 500 kWh BESS is designed for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications and is produced at the company’s Megafactory 1. The deliveries for this product are planned for Q1 2027. Moment Energy states that its Nova system is capable of integrating batteries sourced from multiple EV platforms and accommodating differences in battery condition and state of health. The system uses the company’s proprietary AI-powered battery management system (BMS). It continuously evaluates battery packs with different states of health and optimizes their operation to maintain system performance, efficiency, and reliability. The company emphasizes that the system comes with a swappable battery architecture that allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age, without replacing the entire system. According to Moment Energy, this architecture extends the system lifetime by over 20 years under the company’s capacity augmentation service. Multiple Nova units can also be combined to create higher-capacity storage systems. Operating at 800 V DC, each unit measures 2.94 x 1.80 x 2.54 m and uses liquid cooling for thermal management. It is designed to operate between -25°C and 50°C and at altitudes of up to 2,000 m. It also carries a high seismic rating under IEEE 693. Safety is particularly important in this scenario, as the previous operating history and varying degrees of degradation may introduce additional considerations compared to newly built batteries. The company claims the Nova achieved UL 1973 and UL 9540 certifications and has been tested to UL 9540A, which evaluates fire propagation associated with thermal runaway in battery energy storage systems. Moment Energy describes it as the first BESS made using repurposed EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification. The system uses EV batteries sourced from vehicles already operating in North America, which are subsequently reengineered for stationary storage. The company has also highlighted the system's compliance with US Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.

artigo.texto: King George County data center fight turns into a battle over water KING GEORGE COUNTY, Va. (7News) — With 685 data centers either built or planned for construction, Virginia is far and away the nation's data center leader but one of those planned projects, in King George County, has come under greater scrutiny by local leaders and the reason has everything to do with a precious natural resource: water. “Water is the new gold," King George County Administrator Matthew J. Smolnik told the 7News I-Team in a recent interview. "I remember 20 years ago sitting with DEQ [Department of Environmental Quality] and drawing a line in I-95, saying 'If you're east of this line, we're coming for you and they're coming for us.'" RELATED | Lawmakers eye data center moratorium as Virginia environmental coalition ramps up pressure As recently as September 2023, water levels on the Rappahannock River near Fredericksburg, Virginia, had reached historic lows. Back then, you could walk across parts of the Rappahannock without getting wet. The Rappahannock widens ten miles downriver as it winds through King George County. Many in the mostly rural county of just 29,000 were surprised in December 2019 when their Board of Supervisors greenlit plans for an Amazon data center project on the site of the old Birchwood coal-fired power plant. With the purchase, Amazon secured a state DEQ permit allowing it to draw up to 6.6 million gallons of water per day from the Rappahannock River. “The deal the old board struck was a bad deal for King George," state Sen. Richard Stuart, R-Westmoreland, told 7News. “Where people got really upset was, they had no information and the next thing they know, that board voted to approve it and they even gave them data center buildings on the river. I couldn't get any information from the company because they wanted me to sign an NDA and I refused to do it," Stuart added. Amazon has since agreed not to build directly on the bank of the Rappahannock but acknowledged it negotiated the data center deal out of public view, requiring county officials to sign nondisclosure agreements at the time. “Most of the negotiation was done in a closed session. So, little to no information had been brought out to the public to have input on it," David Sullins, Chair of King George County Board of Supervisors, said. In October, Amazon ended its policy of using nondisclosure agreements with local officials on data center projects, according to a company spokesperson. In 2023, Sullins successfully ran for the King George County Board of Supervisors largely because of a lack of transparency surrounding the Birchwood data center project. The board has since tasked Smolnik and Stuart, who’s also the county attorney, with fixing what the men describe as a bad backroom deal, cut by the previous board. King George County sits on the Potomac aquifer, a massive underground water supply that stretches from Fairfax to the north and south to Virginia Beach. SEE ALSO | This week: Two high-stakes data center public hearings in Spotsylvania and Stafford That water source, which is critical to Virginia communities, is declining so much so that Virginia’s Department of Environmental Quality has told King George and other communities east of I-95 they need to start looking elsewhere for water. If King George County is forced to turn to surface water for its drinking water, its only option nearby is the Rappahannock River, and it too is under stress, according to conservation groups. In April 2025, the non-profit conservation group American Rivers issued a report, which placed the Rappahannock as the sixth most endangered river in the United States. "The increasing strain on water resources, and the absence of unified water management, threaten the river’s ability to meet the needs of both people and nature," the American Rivers report read in part. At present, the county does not have its own water intake on the river. Most of the residents are on private wells. That means King George County officials find themselves in the awkward position of having to negotiate with Amazon for the future source of its water, which could flow from the intake Amazon is currently permitted to use on the Rappahannock. “It is a highly unusual situation for a county to have to be negotiating with another entity to share a water intake," Brent Hunsinger, Advocacy and Coastal Programs Director with the non-profit Friends of the Rappahannock, told 7News. Hunsinger said he's not aware of another situation like the one that exists in King George County. He pointed to a July 2026 report by the Virginia Senate, which raised alarms about the declining levels of the Potomac aquifer. “That report has realized that economic development in the future might not be possible," Hunsinger said of the corridor east of I-95. “All the capacity is used. So, there's no additional capacity unless we make adjustments somewhere. That's why so many things are being forced to the river," Stuart said. The I-Team asked Amazon how much water it will use from the Rappahannock for its Birchwood data center. While the company didn’t answer that specific question, in a statement, a spokesperson said: “Our agreement with King George County includes a binding commitment not to build data center buildings next to the Rappahannock River and a $10 million contribution to the county’s new Career and Technical Education School.
