artigo.texto: An Asset or a Liability: How Data Center Policy Will Shape ERCOT’s Future By: Joshua Loucks, Kiersten Saathoff, and Brent Bennett Key Points: - Texas is facing unprecedented electricity demand from data centers. ERCOT is tracking over 474 GW of large-load requests, nearly 90% from data centers, on a grid that currently peaks over 90 GW. - Data centers are not the cause of rising electricity bills. Renewable energy mandates and retirements of thermal generation have driven most price increases, while the states adding the most demand have seen some of the smallest rate increases. - Texas is positioned to lead the world in AI infrastructure the way it has led previous energy booms. Getting the integration right turns a decade of private capital into durable grid capacity and economic opportunity. - Data centers can strengthen the ERCOT grid by financing new reliable generation and transmission, but not without changes to current policies that socialize reliability and transmission costs. - The window for getting the design right is closing. Interconnection decisions and transmission commitments made in the next few years will lock in outcomes for decades. Executive Summary Texas is on track to host the largest concentration of data centers in the world. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is now tracking more than 474 GW of large load interconnection requests, 90% of it from data centers (ERCOT, 2026b). Only a fraction of that queue will ever be built, but the fraction under contract is already substantial: Cushman & Wakefield estimates 3,396 MW operating in Texas today with 4,730 MW under construction, and 28,763 MW planned—more than eight times what is in operation today (Cushman & Wakefield, 2026). Whether that growth becomes an asset or a liability to the ERCOT grid is not a matter of chance. It is a matter of policy design, and the window for getting the design right is now. Data center growth is increasingly being blamed for rising electric bills, but the evidence does not support that claim. California and New York have posted the largest rate increases while losing demand, while Texas and Virginia have added the most data center load in the country without steep price increases. Recent research has found that doubling data center capacity at a fixed level of residential demand lowers residential retail prices by 3.5% (Watten et al., 2026). The drivers of rising bills are elsewhere: mandated retirement of reliable generation, transmission built for distant wind and solar generation, and aging distribution infrastructure (Pyle et al., 2025). The risk to Texas consumers is not the data centers themselves but the electric grid that will serve them. Less than 20% of the 456,578 MW in ERCOT’s generation queue is reliable thermal generation (ERCOT, 2026c). In fact, Texas has not added significant firm dispatchable capacity in over a decade, and wind and solar have been overbuilt to a point that significant amounts are being curtailed (Modo Energy, 2025). Both facts point to a market design that produces a reliability deficit and promotes inefficiency, which ratepayers pay for. Meeting new load with still more intermittent generation would erode reliability and push hyperscalers off the grid—a shift already underway, with more than 40 GW of private grid development announced in Texas (Thomas, 2026a). Islanded capacity enables speed and innovation, but it does not ensure the on-grid reliability residential consumers depend on. Handled well, data centers become the anchor load that funds firm generation and spreads fixed costs across a broader base. Handled poorly, Texas adds inflexible load to an increasingly intermittent fleet. That is the choice facing Texas today, and Texas needs to make the right policy choices to responsibly accommodate data center growth to the benefit of all its citizens. Introduction Texas will likely be home to more data centers than any other state by the end of this decade. While the size and pace of the buildout may seem like a daunting reality, in practice it offers a unique opportunity to improve ERCOT’s ability to handle extreme weather and supply volatility while lowering electricity costs for Texas consumers. Throughout history, technological and industrial advancements that have drastically altered society have also impacted policy, economics, and our environment. From the invention of the cotton gin to the dawn of the internet, American society, culture, and economics have been drastically altered at each turn. Typically, advancements have been tangible or relatively narrow in scope, but artificial intelligence (AI) is bringing rapid and sweeping changes to almost every business sector as well as in our personal lives. AI, particularly the means by which it is powered, presents a historically unique intersection between industry and consumers. The power, water, and even land required to make advanced computing possible is not particularly unique to new industrial advancements . Whether it was textile mills powered through hydropower in Upstate New York in the 1800s or coal-fired steel mills in Pennsylvania, American energy and ingenuity have been the catalyst of growth and opportunity. The challenges data centers present in the 21st century may be more abstract, but in reality, are quite similar to challenges other power-intensive industries have posed in the past. These challenges, if addressed promptly and cohesively through responsible water, land, and electricity production and use agreements, can lead America and the globe into a new era of prosperity and growth. This paper will address the various power and electrical infrastructure needs to provide the computing necessary for the “AI Revolution,” in addition to the economic opportunity these facilities can bring. artigo.texto: Buscando expansão no Nordeste, Tecto anuncia data center no Recife Empreendimento de plataforma controla pelo BTG Pactual terá capacidade escalável de até seis megawatts e integra plano da companhia de investimentos de US$ 2 bilhões até 2028 A Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, anunciou nesta terça-feira (24) seu primeiro data center em Pernambuco, o segundo no Nordeste. O empreendimento, batizado de TREC1, será instalado no Recife e terá capacidade inicial de 1 MW (megawatt), com possibilidade de expansão de até 6 MW. Segundo a companhia, com a expansão, a ideia é montar uma estratégia "AI Grid", criando uma rede de data centers regionais, conectando polos do Brasil a pontos estratégicos no exterior. "A estratégia da empresa combina duas camadas: a AI Factory reúne instalações de grande porte e alta densidade, voltadas ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial e ao processamento intensivo de dados. E AI Grid distribui a infraestrutura de processamento por meio de data centers regionais interligados, aproximando-a dos locais onde os dados são gerados e consumidos", afirmou em comunicado. A operação está prevista para inicar no primeiro trimestre do ano que vem e atenderá as chamadas "hyperscales", que são operadoras, provedores de nuvem e de conteúdo e empresas do segmento enterprise, oferecendo serviços de colocation, interconexão e serviços gerenciados para operações que demandam alta disponibilidade, segurança e baixa latência. Como mostrou a CNN, com alta demanda do setor e oferta abundante de energia renovável, o Nordeste segue avançando como um forte polo de data centers no país, ampliando a presença do setor para além do eixo Rio-São Paulo. Atualmente, a Tecto opera em Fortaleza (CE) o TFOR3, que é o maior centro de dados em operação da região. Conhecido como "Mega Lobster", o empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, e foi inaugurado em outubro do ano passado. Para o CRO da companhia, Tito Costa, a região reúne a conectividade internacional e uma demanda crescente por infraestrutura digital, tendo papel estratégico na expansão da empresa. “Acreditamos que Recife está para Fortaleza, assim como o Rio de Janeiro está para São Paulo. Essa é a lógica da nossa estratégia AI Grid, que conecta data centers, levando capacidade de processamento para perto das empresas e complementando as grandes estruturas do AI Factory”, acrescentou. Com os dois polos conectados (Recife e Fortaleza), os clientes da companhia poderão distribuir suas operações entre diferentes localidades, inclusive para estratégias de recuperação de desastres e continuidade dos negócios, sem sair da região. A capacidade final é de 20 MW (megawatts), com a expansão ocorre em etapas, acompanhando a demanda dos clientes. A previsão da empresa é de aumentar a capacidade inicial de 4 MW para 8 MW até o começo de 2027. A partir da chegada do TREC1, a empresa passará a contar com oito data centers operacionais até 2027, sendo cinco no Brasil (incluindo o de Recife, três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro) outros três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Além dessas unidades, a companhia segue com o desenvolvimento do TGRU1, em Santana de Parnaíba (SP), com 200 MW, um dos maiores do país em capacidade, que será voltado para aplicações que empregam inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Há também o TPOA1, em Porto Alegre (RS), com 20 MW. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. Brasil deve dobrar capacidade até 2030 Ao todo, dos 660 MW que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. Ainda segundo a consultoria, a ocupação dos data centers brasileiros chegou a 96% no primeiro semestre deste ano. Para a colunista da CNN Infra, Joísa Dutra, o setor busca acelerar os investimentos de forma mais eficiente, buscando alianças internacionais, ao mencionar o lanlamento da AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), da qual fazem parte empresas como Emerald AI, Google e NVIDIA, além de outras quase 20 companhias. O objetivo da aliança é criar protocolos e melhores práticas os investimentos. Os esforços dessas empresas são para criar condições para que esses investimentos em data centers possam ocorrer de modo eficiente, possam ocorrer mais rápido no tempo", avaliou a colunista. A iniciativa surge em resposta a um fenômeno já observado em diferentes países, inclusive no Brasil: a resistência de comunidades locais à instalação desses empreendimentos. Joísa descreveu esse comportamento como "nimby" — expressão em inglês que significa "not in my backyard", ou seja, "aqui não, não no meu quintal". Segundo ela, esse tipo de reação, antes associado a plantas de energia ou projetos de transmissão, começa a aparecer também no segmento de data centers. Atualmente, São Paulo concentra o setor, mas a expansão deve alcançar outras regiões, como no Nordeste, impulsionado por incentivos do Redata e pela abundância de energia renovável na região. Para Tito Costa, a concentração paulista decorre da proximidade entre clientes, redes e outros data centers, mas avalia que disponibilidade de energia e terrenos levará o mercado a novos polos à medida que os atuais se saturarem.

artigo.texto: Jensen Huang Reinstated as NVIDIA CEO NVIDIA announced Monday, November 23, that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as president and CEO, effective immediately, reversing a leadership transition that began with his November 12 resignation, previously reported by Data Center Frontier. In an official statement, NVIDIA said its board voted unanimously to restore Huang to his executive position and board seat following discussions with the company's co-founder. The board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. Harvey C. Jones will remain board chair, while Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, returns to her responsibilities as chief financial officer. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in the announcement. NVIDIA emphasized that its independent investigation into reports of a possible foreign intelligence operation targeting Huang will continue. The company has also established additional national security and export-control oversight and plans to appoint a chief compliance officer. Huang's return restores the executive most closely associated with NVIDIA's transformation into the leading supplier of AI computing infrastructure, as the industry continues its rapid expansion of accelerated computing and AI data center capacity. Keep pace with the fast-moving world of data centers and cloud computing by connecting with Data Center Frontier on LinkedIn, following us on X/Twitter and Facebook, as well as on BlueSky, and signing up for our weekly newsletters using the form below. About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Data centers – A expansão da inteligência artificial (IA) deve provocar um aumento de 70% nas emissões de carbono dos data centers até 2030. A projeção é da Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE), que relaciona o crescimento à necessidade de ampliar a infraestrutura tecnológica para atender à demanda por processamento de dados, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na China. De acordo com o relatório anual da agência, o consumo de eletricidade de data centers deve dobrar até o fim da década, em comparação com os níveis atuais. A inteligência artificial será responsável por aproximadamente três quartos desse crescimento, devido à necessidade de maior capacidade computacional. LEIA: Nvidia anuncia retorno imediato de Jensen Huang ao comando da empresa A estimativa da AIE é que os data centers voltados à IA consumam 350 terawatts-hora (TWh) adicionais de eletricidade por ano até 2030. O volume supera o consumo anual de energia do Reino Unido. O avanço acontece em um cenário de mudanças no setor energético mundial, que também enfrenta pressões sobre o abastecimento e precisa atender a outras necessidades, como climatização e crescimento populacional. Combustíveis fósseis devem abastecer data centers Mesmo com os investimentos de grandes empresas de tecnologia em fontes renováveis, a geração de eletricidade por meio de combustíveis fósseis deve avançar em ritmo mais acelerado para acompanhar a expansão dos data centers. Na China, a previsão é que aproximadamente metade da eletricidade consumida por essas instalações venha de usinas a carvão até 2030. A parcela restante será fornecida principalmente por fontes renováveis, com participações menores de energia nuclear e gás. Nos Estados Unidos, o gás natural deve representar cerca de 60% da eletricidade destinada aos data centers até o fim da década. Em agosto de 2026, os projetos anunciados para novas usinas a gás vinculadas a essas estruturas somavam aproximadamente 180 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, número próximo ao de toda a geração a gás atualmente disponível na União Europeia. Infraestrutura mundial cresce com avanço da IA O levantamento da AIE também aponta uma rápida expansão da capacidade global de data centers. Nos últimos dois anos, o indicador aumentou dez vezes, chegando a 17 GW. Com os projetos que estão em construção, a expectativa é alcançar aproximadamente 50 GW. Atualmente, a capacidade instalada mundial é de 120 GW. Outros 120 GW devem ser acrescentados até 2030, sendo que três quartos dessa expansão serão destinados a instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial. O crescimento da infraestrutura reforça o desafio energético associado ao desenvolvimento da IA. Embora a tecnologia amplie a capacidade de processamento e sustente novos serviços digitais, sua expansão também aumenta a demanda por eletricidade e pode prolongar a dependência de fontes de energia responsáveis por emissões de carbono. artigo.texto: North Carolina is taking an aggressive approach to protecting electric customers from the financial risks of the data center boom, requiring technology companies to put more money on the line for power plants and other infrastructure built to serve them. While much of the attention surrounding last week's North Carolina Utilities Commission decisions focused on Duke Energy's rate increases, regulators also approved sweeping financial safeguards for data centers. Other WRAL Top Stories In interviews with WRAL, Duke Energy, the Data Center Coalition and Utilities Commissioner Floyd McKissick offered new insight into the strength of those protections and how they could affect future development. "I think that's probably one of the most substantial portions of the rate case decision that, to be honest with you, has gotten very little attention," McKissick said. How far North Carolina went Regulators nationwide are grappling with how to accommodate growing electricity demand from data centers without shifting costs onto households and small businesses. North Carolina's requirements go considerably further than a settlement negotiated by Duke Energy, major technology companies and other stakeholders. Under the new rules, qualifying data centers must: - Sign electricity service contracts lasting at least 10 years. - Pay demand charges based on at least 75% of their contracted power capacity, even if they use less. - Pay upfront for certain infrastructure built specifically to serve them. - Provide financial guarantees for transmission upgrades and penalties associated with breaking contracts. - Provide financial security against potential stranded power generation costs. That last provision is particularly significant. A power plant could have an expected lifespan of 35 years, while a data center might only commit to receiving electricity for 15 years. If the facility closes and there isn't enough demand from other customers to replace it, someone still has to pay for that investment. North Carolina is requiring financial safeguards against that possibility. "Oh my gosh, I don't know how much further we could go than what we went," McKissick said. The commission also expanded the reach of the protections by basing their applicability on when qualifying electricity service begins or expands, rather than when a contract was signed. McKissick estimated roughly 20 previously signed agreements would have fallen outside the requirements under the original settlement. Duke Energy and the data center industry respond Duke Energy says it had already incorporated financial protections into agreements with data center developers. "The Utilities Commission wanted to go a step further than the protections that we already have in our contracts," a Duke Energy representative told WRAL on Monday. Duke said it has not received feedback indicating developers plan to abandon projects because of the new requirements. The Data Center Coalition says its members support paying the full cost of the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve their facilities. Its concerns center on why manufacturers and other large electricity users aren't subject to the same requirements and how some of the additional charges will be calculated. "When you single out data centers, you're not doing anything to protect residents from other sources of large load growth on the grid," Dan Diorio, who leads the coalition's state policy efforts, told WRAL. In a written statement, the coalition also called for greater certainty about the costs companies will face. "Cost allocation should rest on what a customer costs the system, not on what kind of business it is, and companies need to know what they will pay before making long-term commitments," said Alex Cutchey, the coalition's director of state regulatory energy policy. McKissick shares one of those concerns. He said he would have preferred to extend the financial safeguards to other large electricity users, including manufacturers. What it means for your electric bill Gov. Josh Stein and Attorney General Jeff Jackson have spent months advocating for stronger ratepayer protections, holding a news conference in October calling on regulators to go beyond Duke Energy's proposed settlement. Stein also called for data centers to bring their own clean energy, a requirement the commission did not adopt. The new safeguards come as Duke Energy prepares to raise electricity rates in January and invest billions of dollars in infrastructure to meet growing demand. While the protections won't prevent electricity bills from rising, they are designed to reduce the risk of customers paying for infrastructure built to serve data centers if those companies fail to fulfill their commitments. McKissick told WRAL on Monday that the rules are already in effect. Some existing data center contracts may need to be renegotiated, and the decision could face appeals. Jackson's office said it is still reviewing the commission's decision.

artigo.texto: Conheça Maxx Morando, baterista e marido de Miley Cyrus Músicos se uniram em matrimônio em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21); eles foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em 2021 A cantora Miley Cyrus, 33, se casou com o músico Maxx Morando, 28, em uma cerimônia privada na cidade de Palm Springs, na Califórnia, no sábado (21). O artista é mais conhecido por tocar bateria e atualmente faz parte da banda de rock alternativo Liily, de Los Angeles. Segundo a revista americana People, boa parte da família de Cyrus marcou presença no casamento da cantora: sua mãe, Tish Cyrus; seu pai, Billy Ray Cyrus; e sua irmã, Noah Cyrus; além da namorada de Billy Ray, Elizabeth Hurley, e o filho dela, Damian Hurley. Neste domingo (22), ela também publicou registros da cerimônia em suas redes sociais. Conheça Maxx Morando, o marido de Miley Cyrus Nas redes sociais, o artista é mais reservado e, ao todo, realizou apenas 20 publicações em sua conta do Instagram. A última delas foi em setembro, em apoio ao lançamento de "Bass Persuades", o álbum mais recente de Miley. Para seus quase 70 mil seguidores, ele ainda compartilhou outras conquistas da amada. Segundo a People, ele trabalhou em duas faixas — "Handstand" e "Violet Chemistry" — do álbum de Cyrus, "Endless Summer Vacation". Morando também produziu várias canções e escreveu a faixa-título do nono álbum de Cyrus, "Something Beautiful". Para o último álbum de Miley Cyrus, Maxx Morando foi creditado como co-produtor, ao lado de Michael Pollack e Kid Harpoon. Antes de fazer parte do Liily, Maxx também tocou na banda The Regrettes de 2015 a 2018. Os dois mantêm um relacionamento discreto desde que foram vistos juntos pela primeira vez em novembro de 2021. Em uma entrevista concedida à Vogue britânica em junho de 2023, a vencedora do Grammy detalhou a história de como conheceu Morando. "Fomos colocados em um encontro às cegas", disse Cyrus. "Bem, foi às cegas para mim, mas não para ele", esclareceu ela à publicação. "Pensei: 'O pior que pode acontecer é eu ir embora'." Esta é a segunda vez que a cantora pop sobe ao altar; ela foi casada com o ator Liam Hemsworth entre 2018 e 2019, com o divórcio oficializado em 2020. artigo.texto: What if AI data centers could help make senior housing more affordable by turning wasted server heat into a useful community resource? Two seemingly unrelated trends are creating major infrastructure challenges in the United States. One is familiar to virtually every CIO; the other may be less so. Less familiar, America’s demand for senior living communities is rising faster than developers are building them. The oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year, and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe. According to NIC MAP’s 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030 and exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace. Much more familiar is the rapid expansion of AI data centers and their effects on surrounding communities. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. With new facilities being proposed across the country, growing electricity demand, water consumption, noise pollution and more have created widespread community concerns. What if these two challenges could help address each other? Data centers generate enormous amounts of heat that must be removed so servers can reliably operate at or near peak performance, but creative planning can turn this heat into a valuable resource for nearby residences, potentially reducing heating expenses and demand for additional energy. The underlying technology is already working in Europe, and a proposed development in Chicago offers a glimpse of how it could be adapted in the United States. I believe there’s an opportunity to take this idea further by exploring partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. In the right circumstances, these arrangements could reduce heating costs and create new revenue opportunities to help make senior housing more affordable for our most populous generation as they enter their golden years. Excess heat as a community resource Cooling is a fundamental requirement of data center operations, and historically, data centers have rejected heat into their surrounding environments, whether through air cooling, evaporative cooling or other methods. Liquid cooling is increasingly being incorporated into data center designs to accommodate the higher power requirements of AI infrastructure. In any of these scenarios, removing heat offers an opportunity to use it rather than simply discard it. In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network. As CIO has reported, the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network that supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions. Both sides receive something useful. The community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange. This approach is not always appropriate. The engineering requires more than connecting two buildings. Data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. Heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used. Still, Groningen demonstrates how data center heat capture can become part of a community’s energy infrastructure, and the United States is beginning to explore similar opportunities. In Chicago’s Bronzeville neighborhood, for example, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project’s developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. The proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents. Although still in the proposal stage, Metropolis Pointe’s design reflects an important evolution in thinking as developers begin to consider how infrastructure can support the needs of neighboring communities and buildings. If this approach can work for conventional residential developments, it can likely be applied to improve the lives of our growing senior population. A new partnership model for senior housing Senior living communities may be particularly well suited for this. They operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements. Heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses, and in colder climates, traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost. As high energy costs persist in the United States and across the world, construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets. NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. Hopefully efforts to close that gap will incorporate new approaches to development and financing, not just more of the same accepted inefficiencies. I envision at least two potential opportunities for data center developers to help. First, heat recovery can reduce operating expenses. A senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network, offsetting some of the energy otherwise purchased for heating and hot water. artigo.texto: Minneapolis Data Center Moratorium Ends With No New Rules After Veto Override Fails The Minneapolis City Council fell short Nov. 20 in its 7-5 vote to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance, leaving the city with no new rules as its six-month moratorium ends Nov. 21. The ordinance would have limited data centers to existing downtown buildings, capped their size, required energy and water disclosure and created overlay districts requiring council approval for each site. Frey said those changes amounted to a de facto ban and would create inconsistent rules. Council members including Jamal Osman warned data centers can now move in with almost no limits. Advocates cited energy and water use. Data centers now fall back under existing zoning rules. Minneapolis is set to lose its temporary limits on new data centers this weekend with no new rules in place, after the City Council failed Nov. 20 to override Mayor Jacob Frey’s veto of a data center ordinance. The override vote failed 7-5. The council needed nine votes to overturn the mayor’s action. The city’s six-month moratorium on data centers ends Nov. 21, and the city council says it can’t enact another one. After the vote, council members debated whether to try to pass new rules before the deadline. “Right now as we stand, there is no regulation on data centers,” Council Vice President Jamal Osman said during the meeting, according to CBS Minnesota. Ward 9 Council Member Jason Chavez warned that without action, “It is going to be open season everywhere else.” If no new rules pass before the moratorium expires, data centers fall back under the city’s existing zoning code, which allows them with a permit in 10 of the city’s 15 zoning districts. The council approved the ordinance 7-6 on Nov. 12, after a proposal to ban new data centers outright failed 6-7. The ordinance would have allowed data centers in existing buildings in two downtown zones while creating an overlay district and capping their size, and it required disclosure of energy and water use. The overlay district meant the council would have to approve each new data center. Frey vetoed the ordinance Nov. 19. In his veto letter, he said the staff recommendation the council started with is “one of the strictest data center regulatory frameworks in the country,” and that the council’s late amendments “result in a de facto ban.” He objected most to requiring a separate overlay district for each site, writing that it “would create inconsistent rules for everyone, including residents, and would lead to arbitrary rule making.” He also argued that downtown needs commercial development to ease the city’s “property tax crunch.” In a statement to the MSR, Frey said: “I look forward to quickly developing a thoughtful policy that supports economic development and our property tax base while addressing community concerns around noise and energy use.” In an email to media Nov. 20, Frey’s press secretary, Jennifer Lor, said the staff framework, which the council’s Committee of the Whole approved Nov. 10, would have restricted new data centers to existing downtown buildings, required them to share buildings with other uses, limited server space, encouraged renewable energy and required disclosure of energy, water and generator use. The overlay district, she said, came from an amendment by Council Member Robin Wonsley that failed in committee and was added before the final vote. Lor disputed suggestions that the staff approach would shut residents out. Data centers would still need a conditional use permit, which triggers a public hearing, she wrote. “Primary zoning is not the equivalent of ‘as of right’ development.” Minneapolis Downtown Council CEO Adam Duininck, who urged Frey to veto the ordinance, told the MSR the main concern for developers is predictability. “Capital flows toward certainty,” Duininck said. “When approval ultimately depends on a discretionary vote of a city council, uncertainty increases substantially.” Ward 8 Council Member Soren Stevenson, who voted for the ordinance, said in a Facebook post Nov. 19 that the council had turned to regulation only after a full ban failed. “When the ban didn’t pass, we voted for a regulatory framework that offers protections and ensures that community members will at least have a say in data center proposals,” Stevenson wrote. He called the veto “one of the most dangerous I have seen yet.” Osman, who represents Ward 6, also criticized the veto in a Facebook post that day. “That means data centers can move in with almost no rules. And neighbors don’t get a say,” Osman wrote. “This is exactly what I wanted to avoid.” Advocates, including Twin Cities Democratic Socialists of America, the Climate Justice Committee and Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, rallied outside City Hall on Nov. 10 for a ban or, at minimum, strict regulations, citing data centers’ energy and water use and arguing that downtown buildings could be used for housing or grocery stores instead. “Instead of building more affordable housing, we are saying our greatest imagination of how to build new buildings should go towards a data center,” Wonsley, who represents Ward 2, said at the rally. “That’s shameful.” If a ban failed, Wonsley said, the council should at minimum pass the strongest possible regulations. “We want to make the terrain as difficult as possible so that they know you don’t have a home here in Minneapolis,” she said. artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) prorrogou até esta segunda-feira, 23 de novembro, às 12h, o prazo de inscrição online nos dois leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. Originalmente, o período de inscrições terminaria na sexta-feira, 20, às 23h. A alteração foi comunicada pela Comissão Permanente de Leilões (CPL) da agência na quinta-feira, 19. As demais datas do cronograma foram mantidas, incluindo o prazo para aporte das garantias de proposta, que também termina nesta segunda-feira, às 23h. Leilões de baterias O primeiro certame, marcado para 2 de dezembro, será destinado a sistemas de armazenamento com requisitos de conteúdo nacional, enquanto o segundo, em 4 de dezembro, não terá restrição quanto à nacionalidade dos equipamentos. Os editais foram aprovados pela Aneel em 27 de outubro, com preços-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para o leilão nacional e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para o segundo certame. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de suprimento previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. A homologação dos resultados está programada para abril de 2027. Na aprovação dos editais, a agência também reduziu as garantias financeiras exigidas dos participantes e flexibilizou condições de participação, mantendo mecanismos de comprovação da capacidade financeira dos empreendedores.

artigo.texto: Por Agência Minera Brasil 23 de novembro de 2026, às 11:10 A disputa por uma nova fábrica de veículos elétricos mobilizou cidades do Norte de Minas nas redes sociais. Mas o que pesa na decisão de uma montadora? E o que o lítio da região tem a ver com isso? A notícia correu rápido. A BYD, montadora chinesa que já produz carros elétricos e híbridos em Camaçari (BA), avalia investir cerca de R$ 1 bi em uma segunda fábrica no Brasil, desta vez de vans e caminhões elétricos, com previsão de 2 mil empregos. Minas Gerais disputa o projeto com São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. O governador eleito, Cleitinho Azevedo, afirmou que pretende procurar o presidente da empresa para apresentar o estado. Nas redes sociais, a disputa ganhou contornos locais. Moradores de Araçuaí, Capelinha e outras cidades do Norte de Minas e do Vale do Jequitinhonha passaram a defender que a fábrica fique na sua cidade. Em alguns comentários, a defesa de uma cidade vem acompanhada de ataques à vizinha: uma “não tem água”, outra “não tem estrutura”. A mobilização é legítima e mostra uma região que quer crescer. Mas vale perguntar: até onde essa torcida ajuda, e a partir de que ponto ela atrapalha? O que uma montadora procura Empresas desse porte não escolhem endereço por curtidas. A decisão costuma levar em conta: • Logística: rodovias, ferrovias e acesso a portos, para receber peças e entregar veículos. • Mercado e fornecedores: proximidade dos grandes centros consumidores e das empresas que fornecem componentes. • Infraestrutura: terreno, energia elétrica em quantidade, água e saneamento. • Mão de obra: trabalhadores qualificados ou condições para formá-los. • Segurança jurídica e incentivos: regras estáveis, licenças com prazos previsíveis e condições negociadas com o governo. Camaçari é um bom exemplo. A BYD ocupou o antigo complexo da Ford, num polo industrial já estruturado. E, segundo a imprensa baiana, 86% dos trabalhadores da fábrica são da Bahia: a mão de obra local pesa, desde que esteja preparada. E o lítio? O Norte de Minas e o Jequitinhonha vivem um momento raro. Empresas como Sigma Lithium, CBL, PLS Brasil (Projeto Colina), Lithium Ionic e Atlas Lithium têm minas em operação ou projetos em desenvolvimento na região, de olho no lítio usado em baterias. É natural ligar uma coisa à outra, já que a BYD aposta nas várias etapas da produção, da bateria ao veículo. Mas o lítio sai das minas mineiras ainda como concentrado, e o país tem poucas das etapas que o transformam em bateria. Ter lítio por perto ajuda a contar uma boa história, mas não garante, sozinho, uma fábrica de veículos. Um polo tecnológico no Jequitinhonha? A oportunidade pode ser maior do que uma fábrica. O Vale do Jequitinhonha tem condições de se tornar um polo tecnológico, reunindo no mesmo território: • mineradoras, que extraem e beneficiam o lítio; • empresas de conversão química, que transformam o concentrado em carbonato e hidróxido de lítio; • indústrias que usam esses produtos, como fabricantes de baterias e de veículos; • formação de pessoas, com Senai, cursos técnicos, institutos federais e universidades; • pesquisa e tecnologia, com a academia trabalhando ao lado das empresas. Cada elo atrai o seguinte. Uma fábrica como a da BYD seria uma peça desse polo, não a única. O maior obstáculo hoje é a infraestrutura, em especial as estradas. Para que um polo funcione, a produção precisa chegar com rapidez e segurança aos centros consumidores e aos portos. Em apresentação à Câmara dos Deputados, o próprio Ministério de Minas e Energia listou trechos de rodovias, como a BR-367, entre as obras importantes para o transporte do lítio. Torcida que ajuda, rivalidade que atrapalha Uma cidade que se mobiliza mostra disposição. Mas quem investe olha a região como um todo. Quando cidades vizinhas trocam acusações sem base técnica, o recado que fica é de conflito, não de oportunidade. E a disputa real não é entre Araçuaí, Capelinha ou Salinas: é entre Minas, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. Além disso, a cidade vizinha não é concorrente. O desenvolvimento de uma ajuda as outras: trabalhadores circulam entre elas, fornecedores de um município atendem empresas do outro e o dinheiro dos salários se espalha pelo comércio de toda a região. Um grande investimento em qualquer uma delas movimenta também as do entorno. Há um risco maior: transformar cada grande investimento em disputa política ou em boato. Regiões com fama de instáveis, onde a desinformação se espalha e as regras mudam, parecem mais caras e arriscadas para quem decide onde investir. Preparar-se para o desenvolvimento A fábrica pode vir para Minas ou não. Pode vir para o Norte ou para outra região. Mas a lição vale para qualquer cenário: as cidades que se destacam são as que se preparam. Qualificam trabalhadores, organizam dados confiáveis, melhoram a infraestrutura e atuam juntas, como região. artigo.texto: I’m a momentum trader, and I’m always looking for stocks where the potential reward outweighs the risk. Today I’ve got my eye on Vertiv Holdings . I already own a position in Vertiv and I'm looking to buy more. The Ohio-based company provides essential equipment for data centers, including power management and cooling systems that keep servers running. Key points Strong third-quarter earnings and surging orders show demand is still high. Local restrictions could delay data center construction, but they haven't translated into canceled orders. Vertiv generates free cash flow without taking on the same financial risks as its customers. Vertiv shares plunged 25% in the first two trading days after the November midterms amid growing concerns that opposition to data center development could lead to construction restrictions. Shares have continued to slide and are now trading roughly 55% below their May high of $379.94. What's interesting is that while the political rhetoric is getting worse, Vertiv's underlying business is getting stronger. This creates the kind of asymmetric trade I'm looking for. Why I'm buying Business is booming despite the backlash In Vertiv's third-quarter results, revenue surged 61% from a year earlier to $4.31 billion, while adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.21, beating Wall Street's estimate of $1.82 by roughly 21%. Adjusted operating margin reached 25.2%, and organic orders more than doubled from a year earlier. Management also raised its full-year guidance. Those are impressive numbers for a company whose shares have been cut nearly in half. A delay doesn't mean a cancellation There is political opposition to data centers, but there's a key distinction between local opposition and a nationwide slowdown in data center construction. So far, restrictions have been limited to the local level, with bans in towns across six states. There are no statewide bans. I think states and communities that don't want data centers may ultimately reject them, while those that welcome the investment will attract more development. That could change where data centers get built, but it doesn't necessarily eliminate the demand for them. An overlooked advantage Vertiv sells the power and cooling infrastructure that those companies need. It doesn't carry the same construction-related debt burden as the customers financing these massive projects. The company generates positive free cash flow and receives advance payments from customers. That matters in an environment where investors are increasingly questioning the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv Holdings, YTD Management also raised its dividend by 60% on November 16, another sign of confidence in the company's cash generation. Why now? Wall Street's consensus price target for Vertiv is approximately $329, implying roughly 92% potential upside from current levels. Given the stock's recent volatility however, I would use stops to protect capital if shares continue to weaken. Bottom line The biggest risk is that the political backlash gains enough traction to produce statewide restrictions or more widespread delays in data center construction. Vertiv's stock is also trading well below its major moving averages, so the technical damage is real. But right now, the company's results aren't showing the deterioration that its stock price suggests. Steven Grasso is the CEO of Grasso Global Inc. artigo.texto: EU, UK Agree to Link Emissions Trading Systems The EU and UK have agreed to link their Emissions Trading Systems (ETS), a statement posted on the European Commission’s (EC) website recently announced. The parties committed to applying this agreement as of January 1, 2028, subject to the ratification process and entry into force in the EU and UK, a separate statement posted on the EC site noted. It highlighted that the intention to link the two systems was announced at the first EU-UK Summit in May 2025. This EC statement pointed out that the UK will expand its ETS, including for aviation and maritime. As a result, over 10 million tons of additional CO2 emissions will be included in the system, “incentivizing decarbonization,” it noted, adding that both the EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects. “This linking will provide the basis for a possible future mutual exemption from the respective carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), reducing red tape and costs for companies on both sides of the Channel,” the statement highlighted. The statement pointed out that the EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since January 1, 2020. It revealed that this link will remain in place. “Linking the EU and the UK ETS’ brings benefits for both sides,” the EC statement said. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK, creating a level playing field for businesses on both sides of the Channel,” it added. “It will also create a larger, more liquid carbon market with a more stable carbon price, supporting the EU and the UK on our paths to climate neutrality,” it continued. “A larger carbon market also enables more efficient investment decisions, supporting the sustainable development of the EU and UK economies,” it went on to state. A release posted on the UK government website on November 20 announced that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had agreed a “landmark package” with the European Union at the UK-EU Summit in Brussels and confirmed the linking of the UK and EU’s ETS. “Linking the UK and EU’s emissions trading schemes creates the world’s largest linked carbon market,” this release stated. “It will exempt GBP 6.5 billion [$8.4 billion] of British exports, including steel and aluminum, from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), removing a major post-Brexit barrier to trade,” it added. “Linking our emissions markets is expected to add up to GBP 3.8 billion [$4.9 billion] a year to the UK economy by 2040,” it continued. A policy paper explaining the EU-UK ETS linking agreement, which was published on the UK government website and pointed out “key features” of the deal, noted that the UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate but linked systems. Industry Reaction In a statement sent to Rigzone, industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said plans to link the UK and EU Emissions Trading Systems “should only be taken forward on terms that prioritize competitiveness of UK industry, reduce trade barriers, and provide investment certainty”. “Any agreement must also guard against higher UK charges for industrial carbon emitters that could disadvantage domestic operations against international competitors facing lower or no equivalent costs,” OEUK added. OEUK said in its statement that UK industrial competitiveness “must be at the core of any agreement with the EU”, noting that the UK’s oil and gas and renewable energy sectors “are critical to European energy security and are underpinned by closely connected markets, infrastructure, and supply chains”. The industry body also emphasized in the statement that cooperation on energy, carbon markets, and security “must promote increased investment across the UK and Europe”. Enrique Cornejo, OEUK Energy Policy Director, highlighted in OEUK’s statement that “the competitiveness of UK industry must be at the heart of any agreement with the EU”. “Our oil and gas and renewable energy sectors are critical to European energy security,” he added. “Any closer carbon market alignment must strengthen competitiveness, reduce trade barriers and support investment, alongside continued cooperation on energy security and resilience,” he continued. In a separate statement sent to Rigzone, an Ineos spokesperson said linking the UK and EU Emissions Trading Schemes “risks imposing yet another financial burden on British manufacturing at a time when industry is already struggling to survive”. “Linking the EU and UK ETS schemes will add further cost to businesses in addition to sky-high energy prices,” the spokesperson added. “Based on current costs, linking the Emission Trading Scheme to the EU ETS, will mean an additional 10 percent increase in carbon tax for UK businesses who are already paying a 70 percent premium due to speculation of linkage,” the spokesperson continued. This spokesperson highlighted that the EU is reviewing its emissions trading system and said “it makes little sense for Britain to commit to alignment before knowing what the future rules will be, or what influence the UK will have over them”. “This will add to uncertainty for UK industry and further undermine investment confidence,” the spokesperson noted. This spokesperson went on to state that “any agreement must protect the long-term competitiveness of British industry, maintain effective safeguards against carbon leakage and address the growing threat from cheap, high-carbon imports from China and the USA”. “The government argues that closer alignment with Europe will deliver economic growth. But if the result is higher costs, factory closures and the loss of British jobs, in practice the opposite is true,” the spokesperson warned. artigo.texto: Data centers, geopolítica e IA: a ameaça de Trump à expansão global da nuvem Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Por Alessandra Montini* – A inteligência artificial depende de uma base física: data centers, energia, água e chips avançados. Por isso, decisões políticas sobre onde essa infraestrutura pode ser construída têm efeito direto sobre quem consegue desenvolver e usar IA. Em 20 de novembro de 2026, o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou em coletiva na Casa Branca que não permitirá que empresas americanas construam data centers fora do país e ameaçou aplicar um imposto elevado e outras penalidades severas a quem descumprir a diretriz. A justificativa apresentada foi evitar que a China assuma o controle dessas estruturas no exterior. Quero analisar aqui com vocês os possíveis impactos dessa ameaça sobre a cadeia global de computação em nuvem e IA, com atenção especial às economias emergentes, como o Brasil. Vale ressaltar que, segundo a análise da revista Veja, trata-se de uma intenção política ainda sem regras detalhadas, e o próprio presidente admitiu que não havia discutido o plano formalmente com sua equipe. As consequências descritas abaixo são, portanto, cenários possíveis, e não efeitos já consolidados. Risco para o modelo de expansão das Big Techs Empresas como Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta e Oracle, além de operadoras como Equinix e Digital Realty, sustentam seus serviços em infraestruturas distribuídas globalmente. Essa distribuição serve a dois objetivos: reduzir a latência, aproximando o processamento do usuário, e cumprir leis locais que exigem o armazenamento de dados dentro do território nacional. O caso mais imediato citado pela reportagem é o plano do Google de investir cerca de US$ 15 bilhões em data centers e infraestrutura de IA na Finlândia entre 2027 e 2028, que Trump disse pretender bloquear. Além do impacto sobre projetos específicos, a ameaça de penalidades cria insegurança jurídica para contratos internacionais já firmados e obriga as empresas a reavaliar cronogramas de investimento em escala global. Geopolítica: infraestrutura como ativo de segurança nacional Ao justificar a medida pela necessidade de conter a China, Washington trata a infraestrutura física da internet como ativo estratégico de segurança nacional. Esse movimento se insere em uma disputa tecnológica mais ampla, frequentemente descrita como uma nova “Guerra Fria” e que tende a fragmentar a rede global em blocos. Há, porém, um efeito potencialmente contraditório. Se empresas americanas forem impedidas de investir fora dos Estados Unidos, países em desenvolvimento e mercados emergentes podem passar a depender mais de alternativas chinesas, como Huawei Cloud, Alibaba e Tencent, para atender à sua demanda por processamento de dados. A medida, pensada para limitar a influência chinesa, poderia assim abrir espaço para ela. Impactos sobre economias emergentes e o caso brasileiro Vários países buscavam se posicionar como polos regionais de data centers, atraindo investimentos com energia limpa e incentivos fiscais. O Brasil, com sua matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, é um exemplo. Esses países enfrentariam agora um duplo obstáculo: a possível proibição de investimentos diretos de empresas americanas e as restrições recentes à exportação de chips avançados de IA. Na mesma semana do anúncio, o Departamento de Comércio dos EUA incluiu o Brasil em uma lista que exige licença prévia para a exportação desses chips, medida que, segundo o material analisado, também atinge Singapura, Malásia, Tailândia e Indonésia. Sem infraestrutura local de ponta, empresas e governos teriam de processar dados a longa distância, o que encarece os serviços de nuvem e retarda a adoção de ferramentas avançadas de IA. Em termos acadêmicos, trata-se de um risco de ampliação da desigualdade tecnológica entre os países que concentram capacidade computacional e os que dependem dela. Gargalo energético e oposição interna nos EUA Concentrar toda a expansão global de data centers em território americano também esbarra em limites internos. De acordo com a reportagem, a resistência de comunidades locais, motivada pelo alto consumo de energia e água e pelo impacto ambiental, já levou ao cancelamento de cerca de US$ 260 bilhões em projetos em 2026. Na própria coletiva, Trump pediu que essas comunidades parem de barrar novos empreendimentos e negociem compensações financeiras com as empresas. O ponto revela uma tensão central: a política de “manter tudo em casa” exige que o país absorva os custos ambientais e energéticos de uma expansão que, até aqui, vinha sendo parcialmente distribuída pelo mundo. A ameaça de Trump evidencia que a computação em nuvem e a IA deixaram de ser apenas questões de mercado e passaram a ocupar o centro da estratégia geopolítica. Entre os efeitos possíveis estão a paralisação de investimentos bilionários, a fragmentação da infraestrutura global, o fortalecimento de concorrentes chineses em mercados emergentes e o aumento de custos e atrasos tecnológicos para países como o Brasil, além de tensões energéticas dentro dos próprios EUA. Como a medida ainda não foi detalhada, o acompanhamento de sua regulamentação é essencial. Para a área de IA, a lição é clara: o desenvolvimento da tecnologia depende de decisões sobre energia, território e soberania digital, e não apenas de avanços em algoritmos. *Alessandra Montini é Diretora do LabData, da FIA Business School

artigo.texto: The Department of the Army recently began soliciting data center proposals for Fort Rucker. The Wiregrass site is one of nine military bases listed in a request for proposals (RFP) released on Friday. “The Department of the Army (“DA”) is issuing this Request for Proposals ('RFP' or 'Solicitation') to solicit competitive proposals from private, public and/or not-for-profit entities interested in leasing non-excess DA land ('Properties') for development of commercial power generation facilities and data centers under a long-term lease agreement(s) ('Enhanced Use Lease' or 'EUL') at Blue Grass Army Depot, Pine Bluff Arsenal, Tooele Army Depot, Sierra Army Depot, Fort McCoy, Fort Bragg, Fort Hood, Fort Rucker, and Joint Base Lewis-McChord ('Installations')," the RFP states. “The EUL(s) that would result from this RFP would be for the purpose of the selected Offeror(s) designing, financing, permitting, developing, constructing, installing, owning, maintaining, operating, securing, and decommissioning a commercial power generation facility and a data center ('Project'). DA’s preference is for integrated power generation facility and commercial data center Projects, but an Offeror can elect to propose power generation only. DA may elect to award one or more EULs pursuant to this RFP.” The 1819 Newsletter Enter your email below to get our top stories delivered straight to your inbox every weekday morning. When asked about the Army's RFP, U.S. Rep. and Sen.-elect Barry Moore (R-Enterprise) told 1819 News in a statement on Tuesday, “My priority is ensuring Fort Rucker remains well-positioned to carry out its critical role in our national defense.” “As the Army moves through this process, I look forward to learning more about the potential opportunities and impacts for both the installation and the surrounding communities,” Moore said. “Any proposed development should be carefully evaluated to ensure it serves the best interests of our military and the people of Alabama.” According to the Army, “Power Generation Facility and Data Center Project” applicants may submit proposals for both power generation and a data center. Proposals are not restricted to any particular data center size or capacity. However, the Army’s preference is for the following data center frameworks: Profile 1: Hardened, physically isolated campuses built to ICD 705 standards for Top Secret/IL6 workloads. Profile 2: Large-scale hyperscale and AI/HPC facilities targeting PUE ≤ 1.15. Offerors electing to integrate commercial data centers alongside generation assets may do so within a unified campus master plan. “Proposed Projects must provide energy resilience capabilities to the DA that will be part of the lease consideration to be provided to DA by the Leassee,” the RFP states. “These capabilities must include the provision of resilient power within one (1) hour of a grid outage and fora minimum of fourteen (14) continuous days, and providing any required improvements to DA’s utility infrastructure that may be required to enable the Installation to accept delivery of the resilient power. For purposes of this RFP, a grid outage is defined as any loss of power from the grid serving the Installation. Preference will be given to Offerors whose Proposal is for the provision of contingency power in excess of fourteen (14) continuous days.” According to the RFP, “projects must avoid draws on water aquifers and must prioritize industrial greywater,treated municipal effluent, or closed-loop cooling towers. Water usage must be net-neutral or better. Offeror shall, at its sole expense, source all industrial process water from non-potable alternative sources, which may include brackish groundwater,reclaimed municipal wastewater (graywater), or treated industrial/agricultural runoff,subject to DA approval and regulatory compliance. DA expects that all power generated and data center capacity (where applicable) will be sold to third-party off-taker(s). The selected Offeror will be responsible for identifying and securing off-taker(s).” Proposals are due by January 18, according to the Army. artigo.texto: Indian solar manufacturer Kosol Energie is looking to make a bigger play in India's battery energy storage system (BESS) market through its subsidiary KoBESS, bringing a portfolio of storage solutions spanning residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and utility-scale applications to the country. The company is leveraging more than a decade of experience in battery energy storage deployments, with its solutions having been in the market since 2015, primarily catering to the US market. It is now looking to replicate that experience in India, as renewable energy integration, round-the-clock power requirements and energy cost optimisation increasingly drive demand for storage. Speaking to Saur Energy International, Kayan Kalthia, Executive Director – Business Development at KoBESS, said the company sees battery storage playing a critical role in transitioning renewable energy from an intermittent source to firm power. “Renewable energy plus BESS is what gives a firm load and RTC power, round-the-clock power,” Kalthia said, outlining the company's vision for energy storage in the Indian market. A portfolio spanning multiple segments KoBESS is positioning itself across three major market segments, with a manufacturing facility having a capacity of 6 GW, according to Kalthia. Its portfolio includes residential storage solutions ranging from 5 kW to 25 kW, C&I offerings including 250 kWh, 500 kW and 1 MWh systems, and utility-scale battery storage containers with capacities of 5 MWh and 6.2 MWh. The company is seeking to differentiate its offerings through quality assurance and reliability testing, with Kalthia stating that every product and bill of materials used has undergone reliability testing. He also pointed to the company's existing deployments and projects with more than a decade of operating experience as evidence of the technology's maturity. Indigenous EMS at the centre of its offering. A key part of KoBESS's strategy is its energy management system (EMS), which Kalthia described as the company's primary differentiator. Both the hardware and software for its energy management platform have been developed in-house in India, and the technology has been deployed for more than a decade. The EMS is designed to optimise energy consumption, power sourcing and storage utilisation based on a customer's requirements. KoBESS aims to use the software capabilities and historical deployment data to demonstrate the economics of storage to prospective customers, including potential returns on investment. Moving beyond standard BESS sizing KoBESS is also focusing on customised storage solutions rather than recommending battery capacity based on standardised configurations. Kalthia said the company first studies a customer's energy consumption and load profile through a data acquisition system installed at the facility. The data is then analysed through its software to determine the required BESS capacity, the most suitable application, potential savings and the expected payback period. The approach is intended to help customers better understand the economics of battery storage before committing to an investment. Autonomous energy optimisation and market participation The company is also pitching its storage systems as part of a broader energy optimisation platform that can factor in consumption patterns, weather forecasts and holidays to determine the most economical energy mix. Kalthia cited Kosol Energie’s own captive power plant as an example of the approach, describing a planned hybrid installation comprising approximately 12 MW of solar DC capacity and 25 MWh of BESS. The system is intended to match the factory's consumption at 15-minute intervals, moving it towards near-100% renewable power supply. He added that the platform can also support revenue stacking and autonomous energy market participation, including buying and trading electricity in the open market, depending on the applicable market framework and customer requirements. Betting on India's growing storage market KoBESS is introducing its existing international product portfolio to India rather than developing a separate range exclusively for the domestic market. Kalthia said the company sees Indian entrepreneurs and businesses becoming increasingly receptive to new technologies and believes energy storage investments can deliver meaningful returns. With its focus on residential, C&I and utility-scale systems, indigenous energy management technology, and experience in international deployments, Kosol Energie is looking to establish KoBESS as a broader player in India's evolving energy storage market. The company's pitch is that BESS is no longer merely an add-on to renewable energy installations, but increasingly a tool for firming power, optimising energy costs and enabling greater renewable energy integration. artigo.texto: The transaction establishes a long-term strategic partnership between Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy, based on the companies’ complementary expertise and capabilities and underpinned by a shared commitment to develop, build and bring into operation Spain’s first large-scale BESS portfolio, comprising seven advanced-stage projects. The first assets are already under construction, while the remainder of the portfolio is expected to commence construction in the coming months, with the full portfolio expected to reach Ready-to-Build (RtB) status during 2027 and enter commercial operation between 2027 and the first half of 2028. The transaction marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ pioneering commitment to energy storage in Spain, which it launched several years ago. The portfolio comprises seven stand-alone BESS projects totalling 380 MW / 1.5 GWh. These include the Valencia Cluster, located in La Vall d'Uixó (Castellón); Santiago, in Lousame (A Coruña); Berja, in the province of Almería; and the Navarra Cluster, located in Olite and Cordovilla. The agreement also leaves the door open to further collaboration on the development of future assets, reflecting both companies’ commitment to continued growth in the energy storage market, strengthening the resilience of Spain’s energy system and reinforcing Spain’s position as a strategic market within Europe. The transaction comes at a time when Spain’s electricity market is in critical need for energy storage, which is reaching a significant level of maturity, with storage becoming the technology with the largest volume of grid connection applications in Spain, ahead of both solar PV and wind. As Daniel Sánchez, CEO of Sungrow Renewables for Western Europe, noted, “This transaction marks a major milestone for Spain’s BESS market. With 380 MW and 1.5 GWh, it is the largest battery energy storage transaction completed to date in Spain and, crucially, is backed by an advanced-stage portfolio of projects already moving into construction. Energy storage in Spain is moving from ambition to execution. “At Sungrow Renewables, we backed this market when it was still a bet on the future and helped pave the way through the development and commissioning of Sanxenxo, Spain’s first stand-alone BESS plant. Today, we are taking a decisive step towards accelerating renewable energy integration and strengthening the stability of the power system, in a transaction that reinforces our long-term commitment to the Spanish market. Energy storage is no longer a promise for Spain: it is strategic infrastructure that we are turning into reality.” Sungrow Renewables’ continued strategy in Spain This latest milestone marks the continuation of Sungrow Renewables’ commitment to Spain and to the integration of energy storage. The company was a pioneer in Spain in the development of hybrid solar PV projects from 2022 onward, moved early into stand-alone BESS with its Sanxenxo project, and currently has stand-alone BESS assets already in operation in the country. Spain remains a strategic market for the company, which operates in more than 20 countries. Actuate Energy focuses on dynamic European energy markets and is committed to supporting an accelerated transition toward renewable energy by investing in and operating energy storage assets that provide stability to the power system. Actuate Energy is backed by NGP, a premier energy private equity firm with over $25 billion of cumulative equity commitments. With this agreement, Spain becomes the starting point for Actuate Energy’s entry into Europe, driven by the country’s high renewable energy penetration, the ongoing need to provide grid stability, and the growth potential of a mature project pipeline.

artigo.texto: Central Virginians urge Henrico leaders: ‘Don’t give water to data centers’ Data centers are popping up across several rural and suburban counties in Central Virginia, banking on one very important and finite resource: water. On Nov. 17, local activists from several Central Virginia counties held a rally along the James River in Henrico, imploring local leaders to protect the area’s limited water resources and quell data center growth in the region. In Central Virginia, water is a geopolitical issue; Henrico currently sells millions of gallons of water each day to nearby rural localities such as Hanover and Goochland. Henrico also owns Cobbs Creek Reservoir in rural Cumberland County, which could be the main water source for Cumberland’s planned natural gas power plant. And over the past year, both Goochland and Hanover have proposed multiple hyperscale data centers near their borders with Henrico – data centers that would require large amounts of water and electricity. While several of Hanover’s proposals were eventually shot down, Goochland’s plans for four data center campuses totaling nearly 3,000 megawatts – less than a mile away from some Western Henrico neighborhoods – are moving forward. Standing alongside the banks of the James River in Varina, one of the last rural areas in the now suburbanized Henrico County, local activist and Henrico resident Aileen Rivera urged Henrico’s Board of Supervisors to prevent Cobbs Creek Reservoir from being used for what will become the second largest natural gas plant in the entire country. “Henrico County has both the ethical and moral responsibility to put the health, safety, and well-being of its residents first,” Rivera said. “Our elected officials have a duty to protect the people they represent, not simply accommodate the needs of powerful industries. Economic development should never come at the expense of public health.” Rivera pointed to last year’s water crisis in Henrico – when nearly half of the county, and almost all residents in Varina, lost access to water for several days after a Richmond water plant failed – as evidence that Henrico cannot afford to sell or provide water to industrial users before ensuring that its own residents have access. “Henrico has already experienced how vulnerable its water system can be when it depends on regional water infrastructure,” she said. “Henrico County must exercise caution. Water is not an unlimited resource, nor should it be treated as a commodity that can be committed to industrial development without a thorough assessment.” At the rally, activists from across Central Virginia – Goochland, Hanover, Cumberland, Fluvanna, and elsewhere – pushed one overarching message: “our individual fights are all connected.” A natural gas plant in Cumberland would provide energy to data centers in Goochland and Hanover, which would require water sold by Henrico. “All of these problems lead back to the data center epidemic that’s plaguing Virginia,” said Jennifer Corpus, a Hanover resident and founder of the anti-data center group, Friends of Hanover. “Every group standing here is fighting a different piece of the exact same problem, and the reason why we are standing here together today is so that everyone can see the whole picture.” Henrico leaders have said that while they are locked into a long-term contract to sell water to Goochland County, there are no plans to sell additional water that could be used to support data center growth. Several Henrico supervisors also have said that although they oppose the planned data centers along the Goochland-Henrico border, it is ultimately under the jurisdiction of Goochland supervisors. Despite reigniting talks with Cumberland last November on a potential water contract that would allow Henrico to sell Cumberland water from Cobbs Creek Reservoir, Henrico officials have said that there is no current water agreement between the two counties and those talks have stalled. Dominion Energy has not yet secured a water source for the new Cumberland natural gas plant. Henrico already has dozens of data center campuses in Varina’s White Oak Technology Park. While Henrico supervisors have passed new measures that prevent data centers from being built outside of the park without a public approval process, those measures came after the rezoning of what will become a large 17-data center campus expansion for tech giant QTS in an area near the park. Rivera called the data center-filled tech park Henrico’s “big mistake” that nearby localities should learn from and avoid. “I urge everybody visiting from out of town, you’re close enough to White Oak Technology [Park] where all the data centers are, go take a look,” she said. “Go take a look and see what happens.” Liana Hardy is the Citizen’s government and education reporter.
