artigo.texto: Two communities in Texas and Arizona are holding votes next month to determine the future of SpaceX data center plans in their areas. On December 9, the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission in Arizona and the Starbase City Commission are both scheduled to vote on proposals related to the data center project. The two votes center around a special land use authorization and a tax incentive package for the data centers. SpaceX plans to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing campuses, making them two of the largest data center projects in the country. Read More on AI "These investments will expand local tax bases, generate substantial new revenue for schools and public services, and create economic opportunities that extend far beyond the facilities themselves," SpaceX said on its website. SpaceX Data Center in Texas In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a 444-acre plot in Brownsville, near its own Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. SpaceX said the project has already created more than 3,000 construction jobs, with more than 500 permanent jobs coming once its operations begin. It also pledged $200 million to expand Brownsville's water and wastewater infrastructure. The company added that the facility is designed to "stand on its own" by generating its own electricity rather than pulling from the public power grid. The City Commission of the City of Starbase will convene on December 9 to consider approval of a 10-year, 100 percent property tax abatement. Starbase City officials declined to comment to Newsweek. Last week, the Cameron County commission voted against a tax break for the SpaceX data center. The company sought a tax break in Starbase, where two of the three City Commission members are current SpaceX employees. "As Texas communities consider major supercomputing investments, careful long-term tax planning is essential," SpaceX said. "The proposed abatement was designed to address this challenge: provide the County with substantial, predictable new revenue through payments in lieu of taxes (PILOTs), incentivize continued investment and meet the County’s economic development goals." The project was granted an air pollution permit by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) after outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott directed the regulatory agency to pause all data center permits until it completes its impact evaluations. Newly-elected Governor Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, made halting data center construction a pillar of her campaign to ensure lawmakers can provide adequate protections for Texans. SpaceX Data Center in Arizona SpaceX also plans to build a $50 billion, 747-acre data center in Cochise County, Arizona, about 80 miles east of Tucson. According to the proposal, SpaceX said the plan would reduce electricity bills by up to 20 percent and create 1,000 permanent jobs. This facility would also use a dry cooling system and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, but local residents worry about the already strained aquifer. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning board will vote on the special use authorization for Tombstone Resource LCC, the company building the SpaceX data center. This vote will determine if the project is allowed to proceed under current zoning rules. On November 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the county to postpone the December 9 vote until state and federal agencies could provide a full review of the project. "The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude," Mayes said in a statement. "The company’s proposal raises serious unanswered questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts and effects on surrounding communities. Those issues must be fully examined by the appropriate state and federal agencies before any local approval moves forward." In her letter, Mayes said the project could consume up to six gigawatts of electricity, which is nearly 20 percent of the state's current power-generating capacity, and could strain the local groundwater supplies. She also highlighted concerns about traffic, strains on local emergency service resources and the impact on local wildlife. She said the company's proposal leaves a lot about the project uncertain, saying that "the sheer scale of its power demand and physical size presents exorbitant risks," and reminded the commission of its duty to ensure the development is feasible before construction is approved. Mayes will host a town hall scheduled for Thursday, December 3, for residents to voice concerns. Newsweek reached out to Cochise County officials, Attorney General Mayes and SpaceX for comment. artigo.texto: Several Indiana Cities Sour On Local Tax Breaks For Data Centers By Carson Gerber FPI News SOUTH BEND – Randy Figg has a major regret during his nearly five years serving on the St. Joseph County Council: voting to approve one of the most lucrative local tax abatement packages in the state for the more than $11 billion Amazon Web Services data center campus near New Carlisle. He said when the project was first brought to the council in 2024, economic development officials indicated AWS would walk away if it didn’t get the tax breaks that will save the company billions of dollars over more than 30 years. In retrospect, Figg said, that likely wasn’t the case. In just the first half of this year, those abatements cost the county $38 million in property tax revenue. “Can you imagine if St. Joe County had that money?” Figg said. “I’m done with taxpayers supporting these businesses.” That sentiment is growing among state and local officials as data centers continue to draw fierce opposition from residents who blame the developments for rising utility bills and are demanding the nation’s tech giants pay their fair share. Once considered a necessary tool to attract business investments, more Indiana cities and counties are questioning the use of local tax abatements for data centers that are searching for communities open to development. Out of 92 counties, 36 have moratoriums or bans on the projects. Gov. Mike Braun on Monday said even though he supports data center developments, they shouldn’t receive local tax abatements. Qualifying projects already don’t have to pay state sales taxes and can get lucrative incentive packages from the Indiana Economic Development Corp. “These are the richest companies in the world,” Braun said during the Indianapolis Business Journal’s Future of Energy Summit. “They should be enhancing the community.” Justin Ross, a public finance economist at Indiana University, said many city and county officials didn’t understand their bargaining power when data centers first started building in the state. Now, with fewer counties allowing the developments and surging demand for AI, local officials are realizing they have the upper hand in negotiating economic development deals, he said. “They’re saying, ‘Not only can we not give them a tax exemption or abatement. We can actually ask for more and get it,’” Ross said. Saying ‘No’ That’s the approach Kokomo is taking. In October, the city announced Digital Realty was pursuing a 476-acre data center campus in an industrial-focused region of the city. The caveat: the project would not receive any local tax abatements, an unusual move for an Indiana city or county considering a major project. Mayor Tyler Moore said they “rolled the dice” and put the no-tax-abatement stipulation in place because residents don’t want their tax dollars subsidizing data centers. Also, the developments don’t create enough permanent jobs to justify one, he said. Digital Realty said in a statement it accepted those terms and decided to build in Kokomo because of the city’s “skilled workforce and history of successfully delivering large-scale projects.” “We value open dialogue with residents and local leaders, and that feedback is helping guide how we invest in and grow with the community,” the company said in an email. The city anticipates the project will generate between $44 million and $55 million in annual property tax revenue once complete in 2033. Moore said a portion of those dollars would go to every school district in the county and likely allow the city to do away with its recently implemented trash fees. Moore said he “wholeheartedly” believes local tax abatements for data centers are on the way out as officials realize companies will build without getting one. “I think a lot of them are seeing the public outcry,” he said. Earlier this month, an Indianapolis City-County Council committee recommended that the full council reject about $113 million in tax breaks for DC Blox, a data center developer approved to construct two buildings on Indianapolis’ east side. The recommendation represented a stark break with a decision in September by another city development commission that approved a $240 million tax break for Sabey Data Centers located on Indy’s southwest side. Local officials across the state are questioning the use of tax abatements as they anticipate significant revenue losses from last year’s Senate Bill 1, which will cost cities and counties more than $1.4 billion in local property tax revenue by the end of 2028, according to the Indiana Legislative Services Agency. Figg said that’s a major reason he regrets voting to approve the abatements for the AWS campus in St. Joseph County, where the legislation is projected to cut $100 million from local coffers. The county estimates it will collect $1.4 million a year in taxes on the tech equipment in each data center building, but the abatement is about $7.2 million per building and lasts for over 30 years. AWS plans to build around 32 buildings in total. The county is also receiving around $1.15 million a year in property taxes on each building. Once the 50% property tax abatement expires in 2036, officials expect to receive $2.3 million from each building. Jeff Rea, president and CEO of the South Bend Regional Chamber, said in an op-ed piece that the county “played the long game” with the tax abatements in order to land the long-term economic benefits the project will bring, like over 1,000 permanent new jobs. But Figg said even though the county is getting additional tax money now, it also needs the revenue currently lost to the tax breaks to help offset losses from the Senate Bill 1. “We’ve got to come up with new revenue, and so you can’t be giving abatements away,” he said. ‘A True Commitment To Our Community’ As Indiana communities pull back on local abatements, some companies are taking matters into their own hands. artigo.texto: Tennessee Valley Authority filing references $1.7 billion data center deal It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off. What This Story Is About - A Securities and Exchange Commission filing hints at a major data center project within the Tennessee Valley Authority’s service area. Why It Matters - The deal describes a data center customer prepared to pay the utility almost $2 billion for power. What Happens Next - Many of the details of the project aren’t public, like when the project will begin. For Context - The TVA announced new rates for data centers in September. KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT) - It would appear the Tennessee Valley Authority’s new data center rates are paying off; a new Securities and Exchange Commission filing from the utility implies a large-scale data center may soon be built within the TVA’s service area, netting the country’s largest utility provider a $1.7 billion payday. An annual report form publicly available makes reference to the deal, saying the TVA would see a $31 million primary payment when the agreement is finalized, with the rest to come in 59 installments. That total payoff — $1.7 billion in “aggregate payments” — is important, since it’s the first agreement to fall under the TVA’s new rates. In September, TVA officials announced the new dollar amount data centers would pay for power: $1.5 million per megawatt over five megawatts. Breaking down the numbers — $1.7 trillion worth of megawatts that cost $1.5 million each — the new data center could have a power draw in the neighborhood of 1,100 megawatts. TVA Spokesperson Scott Brooks confirmed the math checked out, but he didn’t go so far as confirming the center’s capacity. Since the TVA is a partially private operation, not all information about the utility is publicly available. “Your understanding is correct, but we wouldn’t speculate on the capacity,” Brooks said. The TVA’s status as a public-private body also means some details of the deal are still under wraps, like which company wants to build the data center and where. Brooks wasn’t able to confirm the information either. “TVA does not disclose confidential business information regarding individual customers or prospective economic development projects,” he said. “Consistent with longstanding practice, we protect commercially sensitive information while working with customers, local power companies and economic development partners.” The filing also doesn’t say when a facility could begin construction, but it does say the TVA expects to log that first $31 million payment in November. artigo.texto: Indiana Township officials are preparing new regulations in case any data center developers come knocking. A public hearing to discuss a proposed zoning ordinance amendment setting various conditions on such developments is set for 6 p.m. Dec. 9 at Town Hall, 3710 Saxonburg Blvd. The 18-page draft is available for review at the township office and online at indianatownship.com. Supervisors may vote on the ordinance after the public hearing. “We want to have the public hearing and solicit input from the community,” Mayor Darrin Krally said. “I can’t say with certainty that it meets every single need as is today, but that’s why we have the process.” Several township officials said there have been no requests to build a data center as of mid-November, and it is important to get rules in the books before any plan submissions. “I have been fighting to keep data centers out of Indiana Township since summer 2025, when I first sent a model ordinance to our township manager (Dan Anderson),” Supervisor Jonathan Newmann said. “I would ban data centers outright, but state law currently prevents (us) from doing so. The next best thing is to pass the proposed ordinance the board is considering in December. Currently, our zoning code has no specific protections against data centers, and we saw in Springdale the disastrous consequences of not having a law in place when the developers come to town. “We need to get this ordinance on the books and keep pressure on Gov. (Josh) Shapiro to redeem his past failures on data centers by giving local municipalities like Indiana Township the power to completely ban them from our community.” Springdale’s problem Springdale residents spoke out against a proposed data center several times within the past year. Developer Allegheny DC Property Co. LLC revealed initial plans to build a hyperscale AI data center at the former site of the Cheswick Generating Station in August 2025. In December, borough council approved the conditional-use application for the project. The Allegheny County’s Economic Development (ACED) Planning Division has been reviewing the application because Springdale does not have ordinances in place establishing its jurisdiction over subdivision and land use decisions. County officials recently found nearly 100 problems with the application. However, many may easily be fixed, and two issues will have to be thoroughly addressed. The first involves noise pollution, and the second deals with soil contamination. It is unclear when or how those problems may be corrected. The ACED has until Jan. 26 to approve, approve with conditions or deny the developer’s Preliminary Land Development Plan. Indiana Township’s ordinance Indiana Township’s proposed zoning ordinance amendment would define data centers as a conditional use in the light industrial zoning district. Regulations include a minimum lot size of 15 acres and a maximum data center building height of 35 feet, plus up to an additional 10 feet for roof-mounted equipment such as cooling and ventilation systems, according to the ordinance. Data centers and data center accessory uses must be set back at least 200 feet from the lot line of any property line of a school, residence, child or adult daycare, hospital, nursing home, community center and similar developments. Other rules include a minimum setback of 150 feet from all other adjoining proper lines and road rights-of-way, and a landscape buffer must be at least 50 feet in width. Applicants also must conduct a sound study and vibration study by certified professionals, submit a water feasibility study and an energy usage plan. The energy use plan must show an annual electricity demand, energy supply sources that will be used, proposed sources of back-up power and energy storage capacity if applicable. The ordinance also would require applicants to monitor and report energy efficiency and emissions data to the township on a regular basis. An emergency response plan would be needed with detailed procedures for fire suppression, containment, ventilation and evacuation, as well as evaluation of the access roads and hydrant locations within the site to ensure suitable access for emergency equipment. Data centers also must provide at least one parking space for every employee, based upon the maximum number of employees on-site during the largest shift. The proposed ordinance was recommended for approval by the township’s planning commission in August. Krally believes the proposed regulations are strong and necessary. He also said a data center would be a benefit to the township and create jobs. “In general, data centers are definitely needed,” Krally said. “You and I are speaking on an iPhone. We use iPads. We use laptops. Everybody has their technology that they love. It definitely serves a need from a community standpoint — if you have tracks of land that are zoned accordingly and it can work with little or no disruption and whosever building it is responsible, coming in and helping the community (and) being a community partner. “A ban is ridiculous. We can’t have it anyways, but to me just banning is ignorant. You don’t say, ‘We’re never going to do it,’ without a conversation.” The mayor said he looks forward to the public hearing and finding ways to keep the community safe while helping America stay at the forefront of the technology race.

artigo.texto: Podcast: Rockford Mayor Janessa Neal outlines data center talks By Steve Summers and Kevin Haas Rock River Current Get our mobile app ROCKFORD — Mayor Janessa Neal joined Steve Summers on This Week in the Stateline to discuss where data center talks stand after the announcement that Microsoft is the company eyeing Monarch Energy-controlled land for development. This week’s episode also includes a recap on the Socktober benefit for Rock House Kids and the upcoming Holiday Home Walk in Rockton. Neal’s segment is the third in the episode, beginning around the 19:30 mark. Neal and Summers conversation came after the more than five-hour public hearing where residents gave feedback on potential data center regulations, with the vast majority saying tougher restrictions are needed. “I’m glad that people showed up to voice their concerns because that’s what this moment is about,” Neal said. She also emphasized that although Microsoft is considering the development, the tech giant still has not put forward an official proposal for consideration. “There is nothing signed. artigo.texto: Em um ano, data centers dos EUA geraram 25 milhões de toneladas de CO2 O gás liberado na geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados retém calor na atmosfera e favorece o aquecimento global A geração de eletricidade para abastecer 403 centros de dados de grande porte nos Estados Unidos esteve associada à emissão de 25,7 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO2) entre maio de 2024 e abril de 2025. A estimativa é de um estudo liderado pela Universidade Harvard e publicado em 16 de novembro na revista Nature Sustainability. O volume é de duas a três vezes maior que uma estimativa anterior para 2018. Conhecidas como centros de dados de hiperescala, as instalações analisadas abrigam servidores que sustentam serviços como o armazenamento de arquivos na nuvem e o treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). Os números englobam o consumo de eletricidade das instalações para o conjunto de serviços que elas oferecem. Consumo se aproxima de estados americanos No cenário central do estudo, os centros de dados consumiram cerca de 82 terawatts-hora em 12 meses, o equivalente a 1,8% de toda a eletricidade usada nos Estados Unidos no período. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles A estimativa variou de 68 a 99 terawatts-hora conforme o nível de atividade dos servidores. No limite superior, o consumo se aproxima do que estados como Indiana, Michigan e Tennessee usam, cada um, em um ano. A demanda também se concentrou em poucas regiões. Virgínia, Oregon, Ohio e Iowa responderam, juntos, por mais da metade da eletricidade consumida pelas instalações analisadas. De onde vem a eletricidade dos data centers ? - Gás natural: Foi a principal fonte, responsável por cerca de 38% da eletricidade usada pelos centros de dados. - Carvão: Respondeu por aproximadamente 15% do consumo. Somadas, as fontes fósseis forneceram cerca de 54% da eletricidade usada pelas instalações. - Redes elétricas regionais: Cerca de um quarto do consumo ocorreu em regiões onde a geração de eletricidade emitia mais CO2 por unidade de energia do que a média americana. Conforme o nível de atividade das instalações, as emissões associadas ao consumo de eletricidade ficaram entre 21 milhões e 31 milhões de toneladas de CO2 no período analisado. O estudo identificou diferenças entre as regiões porque a quantidade de CO2 liberada para gerar eletricidade varia conforme as fontes usadas em cada rede.

artigo.texto: Expansão dos data centers pressiona infraestrutura do setor elétrico Alta demanda amplia necessidade por energia e exige novas soluções para garantir estabilidade e segurança no fornecimento O avanço dos investimentos em inteligência artificial e a expansão dos data centers no Brasil aumentam a pressão sobre o setor elétrico e reforçam a necessidade de modernização da infraestrutura de transmissão e distribuição de energia. Segundo o PDE (Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia) 2036, elaborado pela EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), o consumo de eletricidade dessas estruturas deve saltar de 3 terawatts-hora (TWh) em 2026 para 30 TWh em 2036, um crescimento de dez vezes em uma década. Além de ampliar a oferta de energia, o desafio está em garantir estabilidade e qualidade no fornecimento. Data centers, especialmente os voltados à inteligência artificial, operam com cargas elevadas e precisam de abastecimento contínuo, o que exige redes capazes de responder rapidamente às oscilações de consumo e às variações na geração de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica. A EPE ainda afirma que a demanda do setor já faz parte do planejamento energético desde 2023. Em entrevista à CNN, Thiago Prado, presidente da empresa, afirmou que diversos lotes de transmissão relacionados à conexão de data centers já foram licitados, inclusive no estado de São Paulo. A companhia também elaborou estudos para viabilizar a conexão de projetos de data centers e hidrogênio verde na região Nordeste, com demanda estimada em aproximadamente 4 gigawatts. Outra frente de atuação envolve reforços e melhorias na infraestrutura existente. Entre as tecnologias consideradas está o DLR, sistema que utiliza sensores instalados nas linhas de transmissão para monitorar a temperatura dos cabos e identificar momentos em que é possível transportar mais energia com segurança, ampliando a capacidade de conexão de novas cargas. O monitoramento da demanda também é incorporado às revisões quadrimestrais e aos estudos do PDE. Nesse cenário, a automação ganha importância para acompanhar as variações do consumo, antecipar sobrecargas e garantir a estabilidade do sistema elétrico diante da entrada de grandes empreendimentos. Como mostrou a CNN, com alta demanda, o Brasil deve dobrar a capacidade de seu mercado de data centers até 2030, com boa parte da nova capacidade já contratada antes mesmo de ficar pronta. Ao todo, dos 660 MW (megawatts) que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados, segundo levantamento da consultoria JLL. Para Tito Costa, CRO da Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, prevê que o Brasil dobre a capacidade até o fim de 2027. E que, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplique o volume. "Eu tenho bastante segurança hoje de que é bem provável dobrar a capacidade já no ano que vem. E, nos próximos cinco anos, quadruplicar é bastante razoável", afirma Costa. Atualmente a empresa tem sete data centers em operação, sendo três em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro e três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Outros dois centros estão em construção: um em Porto Alegre e outro de 200 MW (cerca de 20% da capacidade brasileira) em Santana de Parnaíba, na Grande São Paulo. Ao todo, o plano de investimentos da companhia é estimado em US$ 2 bilhões, previstos entre 2026 e 2028, para acelerar a expansão na América Latina. Ainda segundo Vinicius Dias, CEO do Grupo Setta, conglomerado de empresas com atuação em engenharia elétrica, a capacidade de entregar energia com qualidade no ponto de conexão será determinante para a atração de investimentos. Dias explica que a automação vai definir quanto do crescimento previsto para a próxima década poderá ser atendido com a infraestrutura existente. "Novas linhas de transmissão levam anos para ficar prontas, e uma rede com esse nível de inteligência abre espaço para conectar mais carga com segurança nesse intervalo, o que pode ser decisivo para o país não perder investimentos em data centers para outros mercados”, concluiu o executivo.

artigo.texto: Legal development Democrats made broad gains nationally on November 3, 2026. For many of the Democratic winners, a key campaign talking point was a commitment to limit or restrict future data center development. Our earlier alert, “Key takeaways for data center developers from the 2026 midterm elections” addressed the national picture. This Legal Development focuses on Texas, where the change in state leadership is likely to have the most immediate consequences for projects already in the pipeline. Developers should prepare for the following: - Utility costs and affordability are likely to drive policy, and Democrats have an opening to act on voter frustration over energy costs. - Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa may inherit ERCOT's pause on energizing new large-load data centers and its delayed Batch Zero classifications and study. TCEQ has stated it has resumed normal permit review. The ambitious platform she has proposed is likely to result in a broader halt soon after inauguration. Her stated scope covers all state permits, including for projects already underway, although the legal mechanism, start date, and duration have not been defined. - Developers should prepare for slower and more searching permit review, even if a formal moratorium does not come to pass. - Grandfathering terms will likely decide which projects go forward, so priority goes to securing power, permits, and site work now. In Texas, the key questions include whether sufficiently complete local permit applications establish vested rights, how the PUCT’s large-load rule applies to projects that had not energized by October 8, 2026, and how 2027 legislation may affect projects already in ERCOT’s Batch Zero study. - Tax exemptions and abatements are at risk, and in Texas, support for repeal crosses party lines; project economics should be tested without them. - As community opposition to data centers accelerates statewide, binding commitments on water, local investment, and transparency, including limits on nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), increasingly decide whether projects move forward. Current state of play: Texas data center directives and key dates Between June and September 2026, Governor Greg Abbott issued four executive directives affecting data center development. On June 10, Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to pursue measures to protect residential ratepayers from data center-related infrastructure costs, including requiring data centers to pay costs attributable to their electric infrastructure, and directed the PUCT and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to review their existing authority. On August 3, he directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit all data centers advancing through ERCOT's interconnection process, requiring information on public financial assistance; power consumption and on-site generation; water consumption, sources, and cooling technology; noise, light, and traffic impacts; and ownership and control. The directive states that any project that fails to comply with PUCT and ERCOT requirements must be denied connection to the grid. For loads of 75 MW or more, the audit overlays ERCOT’s “Batch Zero” process, a one-time, system-wide study under rules the PUCT approved in June that classifies qualifying large-load requests as base load, studied load, or excluded load. ERCOT issued provisional, conditional classifications on September 3, 2026, subject to verification and other conditions. The audit and verification process has affected the timing of Batch Zero classifications and study completion.1 On September 14, Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to enforce water-use reporting requirements. Noncompliance may result in referral for criminal prosecution and disqualification from obtaining, amending, or renewing Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) water-rights permits under Chapter 11 of the Texas Water Code. On September 21, Abbott directed TCEQ to halt all permits sought by data centers and pause issuance of all permits related to data center projects until ERCOT completes its review. He further directed that no other state agency move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until the PUCT, ERCOT, and TWDB information is acquired. In its October 19 compliance update, TCEQ reported that it had paused issuance of all permits related to the construction or development of infrastructure directly supporting data centers, was screening pending applications, and, where possible, was suspending claimed authorizations. TCEQ temporarily shut down its STEERS e-filing portal so that agency staff could review all applications to determine whether they were related to data centers. The STEERS system has now reopened for construction, multi-sector, and concrete production general permits. According to press reports, TCEQ received notice from the governor’s office on November 13 that ERCOT had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers and started normal permit review. On November 16, 2026, TCEQ reportedly issued an air authorization for a gas-fired plant serving planned data centers. Impact of Texas results on data center development In the midterm election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott, becoming the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than three decades. Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, and Democrats won every statewide office on the ballot, including attorney general. Democrats will control the Texas House, while Republicans retain a majority in the Senate. During her campaign, Hinojosa announced a six-point platform for the next legislative session. Governor-Elect Hinojosa’s 'Texans First Data Center Priorities' Status as of November 19, 2026. Planks are campaign proposals; none has been enacted. On October 22, 2026, Hinojosa stated that, as governor, she would issue a moratorium on all data center approvals

artigo.texto: Exceção dos EUA não garante chips para data center do TikTok no Ceará Restrições já afetam financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares ligado à ByteDance na Ásia O governo dos Estados Unidos abriu uma exceção nas novas restrições à tecnologia de inteligência artificial que pode beneficiar o TikTok, mas deixou de fora uma questão decisiva para o data center de mais de 200 bilhões de reais que a chinesa ByteDance pretende instalar no Ceará: a importação de semicondutores avançados. A regulamentação americana, publicada em 19 de novembro, permite determinadas operações de computação destinadas exclusivamente a sistemas comerciais de recomendação de conteúdo, como os algoritmos utilizados por redes sociais. A exceção, entretanto, não representa uma autorização irrestrita para a compra de chips e servidores. O empreendimento brasileiro continua sujeito às exigências de licenciamento aplicáveis aos equipamentos abrangidos pela norma. A distinção aparece no texto da regulamentação do Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), órgão do Departamento de Comércio responsável pelos controles de exportação. Uma das disposições permite que empresas forneçam capacidade computacional para sistemas que classificam, filtram ou recomendam conteúdos e produtos a usuários, desde que essa seja sua finalidade exclusiva e sejam cumpridas obrigações de comunicação às autoridades americanas. A proteção não se estende a sistemas capazes de produzir textos, imagens, vídeos, softwares e outros conteúdos por meio de inteligência artificial generativa. Outro dispositivo estabelece, de forma independente, a necessidade de licença para exportar determinados semicondutores avançados para cinco países, incluindo o Brasil. Na prática, mesmo um sistema enquadrado na exceção para recomendação de conteúdo poderá depender de autorizações adicionais para receber equipamentos. A dúvida é particularmente relevante para o complexo em construção no Pecém, desenvolvido pela Omnia, do Pátria Investimentos, em parceria com a Casa dos Ventos, para atender à ByteDance. Anunciado como o primeiro data center do TikTok na América Latina, o empreendimento prevê investimentos superiores a 200 bilhões de reais ao longo de suas etapas de implantação e modernização, incluindo 108 bilhões de reais em equipamentos de alta tecnologia até 2035. A primeira fase deverá entrar em operação em 2027. Conforme revelou o Radar Econômico na sexta-feira, 20, a estrutura logística planejada contempla até 15 voos mensais com equipamentos destinados ao complexo. A possibilidade de que parte desses componentes dependa de autorizações americanas introduz uma incerteza sobre o cronograma de implantação. Os efeitos das restrições já começaram a aparecer em outro empreendimento ligado à ByteDance. Segundo reportagem da Bloomberg, bancos interromperam os trabalhos de estruturação de um financiamento de 480 milhões de dólares destinado à compra de processadores avançados da Nvidia para um data center na Malásia que atenderia à companhia chinesa. A operação estava sendo organizada pela Aolani Cloud, de Singapura. De acordo com pessoas familiarizadas com as negociações, representantes de cinco instituições financeiras passaram a discutir a possibilidade de abandonar ou deixar de participar do empréstimo diante do risco de descumprimento das novas regras americanas. O episódio não demonstra que o investimento brasileiro tenha sofrido restrições semelhantes, mas revela que a mudança regulatória já produz consequências concretas para projetos associados à empresa. O alcance das medidas vai além do transporte físico de semicondutores. Washington pretende impedir que empresas sediadas na China tenham acesso a grandes volumes de processamento americano por meio de data centers instalados em terceiros países. A regulamentação exige verificações sobre os beneficiários da capacidade computacional, incluindo estruturas de propriedade e controle indireto. Para o projeto do Ceará, isso torna relevante não apenas a origem dos equipamentos, mas também a finalidade de sua utilização, a capacidade de processamento instalada e as empresas que terão acesso aos servidores. A eventual utilização de modelos de inteligência artificial generativa poderá resultar em exigências diferentes daquelas aplicáveis exclusivamente aos algoritmos de recomendação. A ByteDance foi questionada pelo Radar Econômico sobre a finalidade específica dos sistemas previstos para o Pecém, a possibilidade de utilização da exceção americana, a necessidade de licenças para importação de chips e eventuais mudanças no calendário de implantação. A companhia também foi procurada para esclarecer se os equipamentos da primeira fase já foram contratados e se as entregas dependem de autorizações dos Estados Unidos. Até a conclusão desta versão, não havia respondido aos questionamentos. A definição será importante para determinar se o investimento brasileiro encontrará uma alternativa dentro das próprias regras americanas ou se precisará atravessar um processo adicional de aprovação para colocar seus servidores em funcionamento.

artigo.texto: A expansão das fontes fotovoltaica e eólica na última década diversificou os modais do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB), historicamente organizado em torno das hidrelétricas. Desse crescimento, porém, deriva o desafio de compatibilizar a geração de eletricidade a partir de fontes não despacháveis à flexibilidade do sistema, sem a qual a assincronia entre oferta de energia e oscilações de consumo exige cortes na geração. Chamados de curtailment, os cortes no sistema interligado nacional passaram de 18 TWh em 2024 para 58 TWh em 2025, segundo o ONS. O mesmo país que investe pesadamente na ampliação da oferta de energia restringiu cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica no ano passado. Neste cenário, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (Bess), assumem protagonismo no SEB. Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente, fornecendo-a nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham parte das funções de flexibilidade associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas. Enquanto a Lei Federal nº 15.269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento, a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 balizou as regras para os leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro deste ano, criando condições para uma grande expansão do Bess no futuro próximo. Avanços contrastam com regras ambientais ainda em fase embrionária Diante disto, muitos agentes setoriais se apegam à crença de que o licenciamento do Bess será “simples” porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos preexistentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. Mesmo admitida a possibilidade de instalação do Bess em áreas antropizadas, os critérios adotados pelas oito unidades da federação que já regularam o enquadramento ambiental da tecnologia impõem limites às expectativas de simplicidade. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil, mas classificam o potencial poluidor como médio e baixo, respectivamente, e estabelecem limites distintos de não incidência de licenciamento. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. Goiás e Rio de Janeiro incluem baterias em categorias que também abrangem subestações. Em São Paulo e Minas Gerais, como na maioria dos estados, não foram identificados critérios de enquadramento para o Bess. Não surpreende, portanto, que as primeiras licenças ambientais emitidas para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia abranjam diferentes modalidades. Na Bahia, em julho de 2025, uma licença de alteração incluiu o sistema de armazenamento no Complexo Fotovoltaico Cedro. Em novembro do mesmo ano, o Rio Grande do Sul concedeu licenças prévias e de instalação unificadas aos Bess Pontal e Lagoa, vinculados a complexos eólicos. No dia 27 daquele mês, o Piauí emitiu licença prévia ao Bess Lagoa do Barro Associado, enquadrado em tipologia específica. Esses casos, além de contrariarem a doce ilusão de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indicam que o Bess não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. Os arranjos distintos (autônomo ou integrado) ajudam a explicar essa heterogeneidade, mas a ausência de diretrizes nacionais específicas pode submeter até mesmo projetos comparáveis a exigências severamente desiguais. Normatização do licenciamento do Bess aponta para modelo híbrido Sistemas diretamente associados a usinas solares, parques eólicos ou instalações de transmissão tendem a ser licenciados de forma integrada ao empreendimento principal, enquanto projetos standalone, especialmente aqueles voltados à oferta de potência e à prestação de outros serviços ao sistema, tendem ao enquadramento autônomo. A questão se torna particularmente sensível porque a expansão do Bess e a construção das regras ambientais específicas para a tecnologia coincidem com a reformulação do próprio licenciamento pela Lei Federal nº 15.190/2025. Com dispositivos do novo marco questionados no STF, os vultosos investimentos previstos para o Bess estão à mercê de algum grau de insegurança jurídica. Há, por fim, uma dimensão material que não pode ser subestimada. Baterias de íons de lítio apresentam riscos ambientais concretos (thermal runaway, incêndio e vazamento químico) e, após sua vida útil, tornam-se resíduos que exigem logística reversa, reciclagem e reprocessamento industrial. Essa estrutura permanece frágil no Brasil. O debate setorial avançou mais na dimensão operacional que na construção de uma cadeia robusta de pós-uso para baterias de grande porte. Assim, o desafio do licenciamento alcança tanto o Bess quanto a infraestrutura necessária ao tratamento e à destinação de suas baterias.

artigo.texto: By Staff Reporter | A new data center planning to break ground in Cochise County next year is facing some resistance from Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes. Mayes asked county officials to delay their Dec. 9 vote on Tombstone Resources, the company name used to request a special use permit for Cochise SuperComputer Campus, a proposed SpaceX data center. The attorney general advised the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to provide the residents of the county with more answers on the project prior to deciding whether or not to grant SpaceX a special use permit. In a request letter to the commission, Mayes echoed the estimate that the proposed data center would consume an energy equivalent to nearly 20% of the state’s total power generating capacity. “SpaceX’s proposal raises serious questions about energy reliability, water use, emergency response capabilities, traffic impacts, and more,” said Mayes. Mayes advised the officials that the scope of these concerns warranted full examination from state and federal agencies prior to local approval. SpaceX promised to contribute $50 billion in the region’s essential local services, public education, infrastructure, and other undisclosed public goods. The company also stated that it would complete a biological and special-status species assessment before breaking ground. According to SpaceX, the data center campus was designed to not disrupt the natural migratory patterns for sandhill cranes — Cochise County is a recognized wintering area for these birds — and that their company would survey for nesting birds, raptors, and burrowing owls. In conversations with Frank Antenori, chair of the Cochise County Board of Supervisors, SpaceX reiterated their promise to spend $3.6 billion to upgrade the power grid, not rely on groundwater to run the facility, and adhere to the county’s rules on light pollution. SpaceX says the campus will rely on closed-loop cooling, a dry-cooled system with no evaporation spray. Antenori told AZ Family that SpaceX estimated the data center would bring “about 1,000 jobs,” around half only requiring a high school diploma or GED, in addition to 1,500 secondary jobs. SpaceX projects that the data center will bring up to $103 million in new annual property tax revenue, and up to $250 million in a one-time county sales tax benefit. The company also projected a 10% to 40% decrease in electricity bills for all Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative members for the life of the data center development, and an additional annual benefit to those members of approximately $260 million to be used for residential bill relief, the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative Foundation, and new capital credits for all members. If approved, the data center would become one of the largest in existence in the U.S. It would take up approximately 750 acres of land to house nine supercomputing buildings, each around 500,000 square feet. SpaceX appears confident that the county will approve its special use permit request. Their webpage reports that construction will begin in 2027. Mayes announced a town hall for residents to discuss the proposed data center, scheduled for Thursday, Dec. 3 from 5:30 to 7 p.m. AZ Free News is your #1 source for Arizona news and politics. artigo.texto: A expansão dos data centers voltados à inteligência artificial (IA) exige soluções que reduzam o tempo de conexão à rede elétrica e ampliem a capacidade de processamento sem aumentar a ocupação das instalações. Nesse contexto, uma nova plataforma de energia de média tensão foi desenvolvida para atuar diretamente no ponto de conexão com as concessionárias, reunindo proteção elétrica, estabilização de cargas e continuidade de fornecimento em um único sistema. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Vertiv propõe modelo para levar projetos de IA à produção O Vertiv PowerNexus MV UPS, apresentado pela Vertiv em 19 de novembro, foi projetado para instalações de colocation, neocloud e hiperescala. Com estrutura para instalação externa, o equipamento transfere parte da infraestrutura de energia para fora do data hall, preservando o espaço interno para servidores e sistemas de computação. A plataforma combina um sistema de alimentação ininterrupta (UPS) de média tensão com recursos de ride-through, que permitem suportar distúrbios e falhas temporárias na rede elétrica, e suavização das variações de carga provocadas pelas operações de inteligência artificial. Segundo a fabricante, o sistema alcança eficiência operacional de pico de até 98,5%. Quando integrado a baterias de longa duração, pode oferecer até quatro horas de alimentação de backup, reduzindo a dependência de geradores a diesel. Entre as funcionalidades está a proteção de cargas críticas com qualidade de tensão Classe 1, conforme a norma IEC 62040-3. A solução também foi projetada para absorver variações rápidas de demanda dos sistemas de IA antes que elas sejam transmitidas à rede elétrica, contribuindo para a estabilidade do fornecimento. A arquitetura em skid, fornecida como um conjunto integrado, busca simplificar a instalação e reduzir a necessidade de coordenação entre diferentes fornecedores de UPS, baterias e demais componentes da infraestrutura de energia. A empresa também disponibiliza um modelo de simulação PSCAD para avaliar o comportamento do sistema e sua interação com a rede elétrica antes da implantação. Testes de desempenho A plataforma passou por demonstrações de prova de conceito com a participação de QTS, SoftBank e Rosendin no Centro Global de Pesquisa e Desenvolvimento de Energia e Experiência do Cliente da Vertiv, em Bolonha, na Itália. De acordo com a fabricante, os testes demonstraram estabilidade em cargas de 0% a 100%, precisão de tensão Classe 1 durante mudanças rápidas de demanda e capacidade de suportar distúrbios elétricos. Entre as condições avaliadas estavam uma queda total de tensão por 150 milissegundos e uma sobretensão de 25% durante cinco segundos. A Vertiv também anunciou a criação de um laboratório dedicado a sistemas de média tensão em Bolonha, com previsão de entrada em operação em 2027. A instalação será utilizada para pesquisa e desenvolvimento, testes em tensão plena, treinamento e validação de arquiteturas de energia, incluindo sistemas de média tensão, conversão para 800 VDC e armazenamento em baterias. artigo.texto: The transaction secures capital against contracted, insured delivery of durable removals, proof that high-integrity projects can now access scalable debt beyond equity. State of Sao Paulo, Brazil--(Newsfile Corp. - November 24, 2026) - InPlanet and Idemitsu Americas Holdings (IAH), a wholly owned subsidiary of Idemitsu Kosan (Idemitsu), today announced the closing of one of the first non-recourse project financings in the Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) sector. InPlanet and Idemitsu Americas Holdings Close Non-Recourse Debt Facility, Setting a New Standard for Financing ERW Carbon Removal. To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit: https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/8814/324893_f9020ca7c4c68ba6_002full.jpg The debt facility will fund the delivery of more than 28,500 tonnes of contracted Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) and is structured to be repeatable, providing a template for how institutional capital can finance verified CDR at scale. Financing Carbon Removal at Scale Gigaton-scale carbon removal requires financing that can scale deployment beyond equity alone. This agreement was designed to do that, with downside protection backed by an existing carbon removal agreement to remove more than 28,500 tonnes of CO₂ between 2026 and 2028. The financing also includes carbon delivery insurance provided by CFC, covering specified project delivery risks for a defined portion of the delivery. CFC is a specialist insurance provider supporting high-quality carbon market transactions, and the Howden Broking Group provided broking service to InPlanet for this transaction. The financing decision was supported by InPlanet's operating track record, including more than 200,000 tonnes of silicate rock applied across Brazilian farmland. This delivery is enabled by Bedrock OS, InPlanet's AI-powered operating infrastructure, which supports project execution across its portfolio and consolidates logistics, farm, and laboratory data into auditable records for reporting. Each project strengthens the underlying dataset and AI models used to optimize delivery and scale ERW. To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit: https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/8814/324893_f9020ca7c4c68ba6_003full.jpg By linking capital to contracted demand, insured delivery, and the operational infrastructure required to execute at scale, the structure demonstrates how high-integrity carbon removal can be financed like infrastructure and replicated across projects, regions, and buyers as the market matures. For Idemitsu, the partnership forms part of a broader strategy to expand its role in carbon markets as it works toward a carbon-neutral society by 2050. As global demand grows for permanent, measurable, and verifiable removal solutions, Idemitsu is deepening its engagement with durable CDR pathways, with ERW emerging as an area of focus due to its potential for scale. "InPlanet's work in Brazil combines scientific rigor with real operating scale, which is what durable carbon removal needs in order to move beyond pilots,"said Masanori Abe, President of Idemitsu Americas Holdings Corporation." By linking capital to contracted demand and insured delivery, this agreement demonstrates a financing approach we expect to be repeatable. IAH looks forward to building on it as we expand our CDR business." Today, InPlanet operates Brazil's largest ERW program by farmland treated, with access to more than 100,000 hectares through its partners. Working with farmers nationwide, InPlanet applies finely ground silicate rock to agricultural land, accelerating a natural process that permanently captures atmospheric carbon while restoring soil fertility, reducing chemical input costs, and strengthening long-term farm profitability. In December 2024, InPlanet delivered the world's first independently verified ERW carbon removal credits, which subsequently received a post-issuance "A" rating from BeZero Carbon. "In just two years, we went from delivering the world's first independently verified enhanced rock weathering credits to operating the largest ERW program in Brazil. This financing with Idemitsu takes that work to its next level, it shows that carbon removal grounded in solid science can also be financed like real infrastructure," said Felix Harteneck, Founder & CEO of InPlanet. "For us, this is about more than capital. Japan is continuing to develop its carbon market and standards for high-integrity carbon removal, and we look forward to contributing to that dialogue." Compliance Demand in Japan and Brazil Idemitsu and InPlanet will focus on markets where climate ambition and carbon market infrastructure are advancing in step. Japan is continuing to develop its carbon market framework and policies supporting high-integrity carbon removal. Any future use of ERW credits would remain subject to applicable methodologies, regulations, and eligibility requirements. In Brazil, Law 15.042/2024 established the SBCE (Brazilian Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading System), putting removals on the same legal footing as avoided emissions. Both markets are opening compliance pathways for durable carbon removal, creating long-term, regulated demand for credits that have until now relied almost entirely on voluntary buyers. In Japan, the carbon market framework and policies for high-integrity carbon removal continue to evolve, although any future use of ERW credits will remain subject to applicable methodologies, regulations, and eligibility requirements. artigo.texto: CHAMPAIGN — A proposed development just east of the Interstate 57/74 interchange that includes a solar farm, battery storage systems and two small data centers has attracted the concern of a nearby business owner. “It’s an eyesore for one thing, but it’s also a danger,” said Judy Parkinson, co-owner of Research Press Publishers. “The data centers and the batteries are my big concern. Those are not the kind of thing you should have in such a close-to-the-city area. If they did it out in the countryside, it wouldn’t bother me.” She fears that the battery energy storage systems could be a fire hazard that might impact her business if a blaze breaks out. IAG Investments — Champaign Mattis LLC, which is managed by Anthony Donato, seeks to develop approximately 30 acres of vacant land at 2703 N. Mattis Ave. into an industrial site that includes “flex warehouses and a solar farm with accessory battery energy storage systems,” said city of Champaign Associate Planner Mia Trevino. As previously reported by The News-Gazette’s Kathy Reiser, Anthony Donato and Donato Solar have developed several other solar arrays with data farms in and around Champaign-Urbana in recent years. The solar farms are run by Donato Solar and the data centers are operated by Gail Technology. Anthony Donato founded the former company and is the owner of the latter. “The proposed site plan includes five commercial flex warehouses with 3,000 square feet of data centers in proposed Buildings 1 and 5 that are 1.2 (megawatts), approximately 60 percent of the respective buildings’ area,” Trevino wrote in a report to the plan commission. “The performance standards for data centers require a minimum 200-foot setback from residential zone property and are maintained in the proposed site plan. Given that the property is primarily surrounded by interstate right-of-way, and adjacent to industrial and commercial use, a power generation facility would be appropriate at this site.” Peyton Childress, who spoke on behalf of the applicant at a recent plan commission meeting, said that the proposed development is a “behind-the-meter” solar project, with the power generated being used by the buildings on-site. “It will cover all of the energy needed for those five buildings, especially with the batteries on-site, because then during times where the sun is not out, then all of the stored energy from that solar array will be housed in the units of the battery and then can still power the facility itself,” she said. “So any excess energy we’re going to be storing in the battery containers and then we’ll use on-site. So no, I don’t foresee that we will be needing excess energy.” The five battery containers will be located behind the warehouses and out of sight of any potential tenants, she noted. “They do all have fire-suppression systems built in,” Childress said. “There’s a multitude of sensors that send warnings if any element of the container gets too hot, things like that.” According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, there have been lithium battery fires at some battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities. Such fires are very hard to put out and may reignite “hours or days later,” EPA officials said. These blazes can also release harmful gases. “Communities should also note that despite some high-profile incidents, improvements in BESS quality and design have led to a decrease in the number of failure incidents per gigawatt hour deployed,” the agency said. Planning and Development Director Bruce Knight said that fire safety is evaluated as part of the building permit review process. The fire department “has already looked at this development proposal and signed off on it with the assumption that it’ll comply with all building and fire codes,” he added. The subject property is located west of and across the street from 2612 N. Mattis Ave., where Research Press is based. Parkinson co-owns the book-publishing business with her brother and sister; the land on which the business sits is also owned by the family. In addition to fire safety, her other concerns include the facility’s proximity to residences east of her business and potential noise pollution. “They say that sometimes the data centers get noisy because of the cooling,” Parkinson said. Childress told the plan commission that the buildings will be “temperature-controlled.” “A lot of people are worried about water consumption as well, if that’s how we cool any of the server pods — none of that will be taking place here,” she said. “Any water on site would be bathroom or kitchen at inside of the commercial space. So these (data centers) would all be cooled by the temperature-controlled building.” She also noted that the developer will put in the vegetation screening that is required by the city. The proposed project comes as larger data-center developments have come under scrutiny. For instance, an advisory question on the April 6 ballot will ask Champaign County residents if the county should “support the development of large and/or hyperscale data centers, defined as larger than 10 megawatts of total power, within Champaign County.” The county currently has a moratorium on the development of data centers with “at least 10,000 square feet of processing area”; the ban is set to end in April. “They’re only 1.2 megawatts,” Trevino said of the data centers in the proposed project. “People usually consider a normal-size data center to be between 5 to 10 megawatts. Hyperscale’s more like starting at 100 megawatts. So really, this (project) could be seen more as a server room than what we think of as a data center.” Knight later added that the city is looking to impose a one-year moratorium on data centers over 10 megawatts so that staff can research the issue and develop ordinances. He expects the city council to vote on the one-year moratorium on Dec. 15. “Over 10 megawatts, based on our research, is where they start to have any kind of external impacts,” he said. artigo.texto: Virginia stands at a crossroads on data center development. The choice need not be simply between unrestricted growth and a statewide moratorium. A more prudent path is to approve projects when their risks are understood and safeguards can be enforced, while allowing targeted, conditional pauses where essential questions remain unanswered and the government has authority to act. Localities are already taking different approaches. Loudoun County now requires special exceptions in several districts where data centers had been allowed by right. Fairfax County strengthened setbacks and noise protections while retaining some by-right development. These differences matter because every project affects a particular community. But electricity, water, transportation and environmental impacts do not necessarily stop at local boundaries. That leaves Virginia with a larger question: Should development continue under existing rules, be broadly halted or be evaluated project by project using evidence and enforceable conditions? Policy and law makers should consider taking a more comprehensive approach in developing the state’s regulatory framework. The commonwealth’s own research demonstrates why careful evaluation is warranted. The Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission’s 2024 study, “Data Centers in Virginia,” found substantial economic benefits, especially from construction, and significant local tax revenues. It also projected immense growth in electricity demand and identified risks involving infrastructure costs, water use and residential impacts. A subsequent JLARC report released this month estimated that the state received 22 cents in tax revenue for each dollar of the data center sales tax exemption during fiscal years 2021 through 2025, reflecting revised assumptions about how strongly exemptions influence location decisions. Statewide findings, however, cannot determine whether a particular facility belongs on a particular site. That requires examining projected electricity demand, water supply, cooling technology, backup generation, noise, traffic and proximity to homes and schools. A cooling-system label alone cannot establish total resource demands. Virginia has also begun strengthening its regulatory framework. The State Corporation Commission approved Dominion Energy’s GS-5 rate class, effective Jan. 1, for large-load customers meeting specified thresholds. Minimum-demand provisions can reduce risks to other ratepayers, but they cannot eliminate every possibility of cost shifting. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s Executive Order 22, issued Sept. 18, directs work on community planning, noise protections, cooling-water scarcity, backup-generation impacts, energy affordability and grid reliability. But a directive to develop a regulation or evaluate a problem is not the same as a completed, enforceable safeguard. That distinction matters when communities are deciding whether a project should proceed. Responsible oversight should therefore cover a data center’s entire life cycle. Before approval, officials should evaluate the site, design and cumulative demands on electricity, water, roads and public services. During construction and operation, measurable standards should be backed by reporting, enforcement and corrective action. Planning should also address future expansion, upgrades, closure and potential long-term public liabilities. This is especially important in regions such as western Tidewater and Hampton Roads, where communities share natural resources and infrastructure. Local decisions can have regional consequences. Virginia does not have to choose between technological investment and responsible governance. It can welcome development while insisting on credible evidence, fair allocation of costs, regional coordination and enforceable protections. When critical information is missing, pausing long enough to get the answers is not opposition to progress. It is responsible public policy. Charles W. “Bill” Robinson of Carrollton is a retired U.S. Army officer and civilian employee for the Department of Defense. He has experience with artificial intelligence, data architectures and operational implications.

artigo.texto: Google to use geothermal energy from Oregon volcano to power data centers Quaise Energy has signed a purchase agreement with Google to develop superhot geothermal energy near Bend, with electricity expected to begin flowing as early as 2030. The agreement marks big step for Project Obsidian, which Quaise is developing on Bureau of Land Management land south of Newberry National Volcanic Monument, 20 miles south of Bend. The project aims to tap deep underground heat to generate electricity for Google’s data center operations in The Dalles. The agreement also provides a major customer for the project’s initial phase, which Quaise has been developing around a planned 50-megawatt power plant. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the agreement. Harry Kelso, a spokesperson for Quaise, said a power plant will bring economic benefit to Central Oregon. “To date, we’ve injected more than $6 million into Deschutes County businesses as part of Project Obsidian, and we expect that local impact to continue as the project advances,” Kelso said. The project is expected to support 200 to 400 construction jobs and create more than 50 permanent positions in engineering and operations, according to Quaise. Earlier this year, Quaise drilled its first well at the site, a confirmation well expected to reach a depth of about 15,000 feet. The company is using conventional drilling methods for initial development, with plans to introduce its experimental drilling technology in a later phase. The technology uses concentrated electromagnetic energy to break through hard rock and is designed to reach extreme underground temperatures that could make geothermal power more viable. Quaise estimates superhot systems could produce up to 10 times more electricity per well than traditional geothermal systems. Google has operated in The Dalles since 2006 and now has three data centers in the area. The company said its Oregon data centers use 83% carbon-free energy and that the new agreement will expand its investment in clean energy. Google also said it has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon over the past 20 years. Data centers have come under fire in recent months amid public backlash against their massive energy and water needs. Around 75% of Americans now say they oppose data center construction near them. Deschutes County Commissioner-elect Jamie Collins, a climate scientist and former environmental emergency response official, said in a statement on Tuesday that “transparent and deep engagement with our community” is needed. Collins is calling on Obsidian for public outreach and engagement with tribal nations and community organizations. He also wants to learn if some of the energy will be available for residents and businesses in Central Oregon. I’m excited that Central Oregon could become a net exporter of clean energy, but right now our county doesn’t have enough energy of any kind — or enough of the basic infrastructure like power lines — to meet our own needs over the next five years,” Collins said. Project Obsidian is separate from the geothermal development being pursued by Mazama Energy in another part of the Newberry area. Both companies are pursuing enhanced geothermal systems, which use engineered underground reservoirs to extract heat from rock rather than relying on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs. Quaise announced a $180 million Series B financing round in August, including a $35 million investment from drilling contractor Nabors Industries. The company ultimately hopes to expand Project Obsidian beyond its initial 50-megawatt capacity, potentially reaching 250 megawatts or more if the geothermal resource supports further development.

artigo.texto: Forest Grove considers new restrictions on data centers near schools and homes How close should a data center be allowed to operate near a school or someone's home? That's one of the questions Forest Grove city leaders will consider Monday night as they work toward new restrictions on future developments. The Forest Grove City Council and Planning Commission will hold a joint work session at 6 p.m. Monday, Nov. 23, to discuss proposed changes to the city's development code. Among the ideas under consideration are requiring greater distances between data centers and nearby neighborhoods, restricting where the facilities can be built and placing additional limits on their operations. The discussion comes more than a month after the city temporarily stopped accepting applications for new data center developments, giving officials time to examine potential impacts on residents, infrastructure and industrial land. While the proposed regulations could change where future data centers are allowed, they also raise another question: What happens to projects that have already received approval? City considers 1,000-foot buffer around schools During an earlier work session on Nov. 9, city planners presented possible restrictions that included a 1,000-foot buffer between data centers and schools and a 250-foot separation from residential areas. City councilors also asked staff to examine larger residential buffers, including 500 feet, and provide maps showing how those distances would affect where data centers could be built. Other options discussed included restricting standalone data centers in certain industrial zones and examining building size, utility demands and backup power systems. No final decisions have been made on those proposals. The discussion reflects growing questions about the impact of large data centers on surrounding communities. Although these facilities support everything from cloud computing to artificial intelligence, they can also require substantial electricity and infrastructure. For families living near proposed developments, concerns include the noise generated by cooling equipment, emissions from backup generators and how industrial facilities might affect nearby schools and neighborhoods. A data center already approved near a middle school One development at the center of the local debate is Crane Data Centers' project on Heather Street, near Neil Armstrong Middle School. The company's planned campus includes multiple phases and more than 100 megawatts of capacity, according to information published by Crane Data Centers. The project has already received land-use approval from the city, meaning the temporary moratorium does not automatically stop it. Crane has described its development as using air-based cooling and biodiesel-fueled backup generators. Those features have become part of the discussion over the facility's potential environmental impacts. Matt Knight, a Forest Grove community advocate and former City Council candidate who has researched the project, has raised questions about the generators' potential emissions, the amount of electricity required and the financial incentives provided for the development. In research published Oct. 16, Knight acknowledged that some of his earlier concerns had been addressed, including questions about water use and noise mitigation. However, he said more information is needed about the project's backup generators, emissions controls and any health-risk assessments. Knight has not claimed that the project has been proven to pose a health hazard. His research also points to the broader question facing city leaders: whether Forest Grove's existing regulations adequately protect surrounding neighborhoods and how those protections should be strengthened for future developments. Forest Grove temporarily pauses new data centers On Oct. 12, the Forest Grove City Council voted to adopt a 120-day moratorium on new data center development. The pause also applies to expansions of existing data centers of 20% or more. According to the city, the moratorium was adopted to give officials time to review the potential impacts of data centers and consider changes to the development code. However, the restrictions are not retroactive to projects that have already received land-use approval. That distinction is significant for the Crane development. Even if Forest Grove ultimately adopts stricter school and residential setbacks, those rules would not automatically overturn the project's existing approval. Whether future modifications or additional phases would require new approvals subject to updated regulations remains a question for city planning officials. The city's temporary moratorium is scheduled to expire Feb. 9, 2027, unless officials take further action. Why Forest Grove temporarily banned new data center development Forest Grove's temporary moratorium goes beyond concerns about data centers being built near schools and homes. City officials say the facilities could also threaten future housing development, strain the electrical grid and limit opportunities for other businesses. In Resolution No. 2026-47, adopted Oct. 12, the City Council outlined several concerns that prompted its decision to temporarily halt new data center development. According to the resolution, Forest Grove's development code currently allows data centers in all industrial zones without regulations specifically designed for those facilities. City officials also raised concerns about the amount of land data centers occupy compared with the relatively small number of permanent jobs they typically create. The resolution warns that allowing too many data centers could consume industrial land needed by other businesses, potentially harming the city's long-term economic health. Another concern involves housing. Forest Grove anticipates that an ongoing housing capacity study will find the city lacks enough buildable residential land to meet demand over the next 20 yea

artigo.texto: The Wilson County Planning Commission unanimously approved on Nov. 20 a resolution that, if approved by the county commission, will set regulations for data centers in the county regarding location, water use, sound levels and power usage. The Planning and Zoning committee approved the resolution on Sept. 28. The next county commission meeting is scheduled for Monday, Dec. 21. In June, the commission approved a six-month moratorium on data centers. The moratorium ends Dec. 22. The county commission created the Data Center Advisory Committee when it voted for the moratorium. The advisory committee held four meetings and proposed where the centers can be located (Light Industrial Zones), what type of water systems will be allowed, sound level monitoring and megawatt capacity for the different sizes of the centers. Data centers in the county will be required to have a “closed loop (water) system” that will reuse and recirculate water without using water from a municipal water system. If the commission approves the resolution, the county will hire a sound engineer for “noise assessment, monitoring and mitigation.” Data centers must also monitor the sound which is to be collected constantly. Those reports must be submitted quarterly to the county. Two wattages of data centers will be allowed: those less than 100 megawatts and those greater than 100 megawatts. Size limits are broken down into those less than 300,000 square feet and those greater than 300,000 square feet. The buildings on the site should be at least 100 feet from a street and 1,000 feet from all areas which are agricultural, residential or commercially zoned districts. All data center buildings must be at least 2,000 feet from schools, daycares, medical facilities or any place of public assembly. A buffer consisting of an earthen berm of at least 40 percent of building height is required. It must be topped with state-allowed landscaping. Data center applications must have verification from utility providers that centers will not cause utility rate increases.
