artigo.texto: A coalition of six Central Massachusetts legislators is pressing state agencies and utility providers for strict public oversight before issuing permits for the Kraft Group’s proposed $16 billion Unified Parkway Data Center in Sutton. Spanning 10 buildings and requiring 900 megawatts of power, the project would rank as the fourth-largest data center in the U.S., according to one of the lawmakers, if fully built out on property off Boston and Providence roads in Sutton. The state lawmakers representing Sutton and surrounding communities are urging energy, environmental and utility regulators to slow down and answer key infrastructure questions before permits are issued for the data center. The lawmakers sent letters to state agencies, regional planners, National Grid and Aquarion Water Co. The letters call for a transparent review process aligned with Gov. Maura T. Healey’s data center executive order signed in September. Sens. Michael O. Moore and Ryan Fattman, along with Reps. Joseph McKenna, Paul Frost, David Muradian, and Michael Soter representing Sutton and surrounding communities, in letters to the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs and the Central Massachusetts Regional Planning Commission – as well as the utility companies – urge a public approval process that aligns with the framework laid out in Healey’s data center executive order and request that a slate of important questions be answered before permits are issued. The letters say that Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft’s proposal, if completed as envisioned, is projected to demand the same amount of power as a sizable city and could consume the same amount of water as roughly 23,400 households in an estimate extrapolated from the International Energy Agency’s estimate of typical data center water usage. Though the Kraft Group says it’s in discussions to independently source electricity and is exploring reclaimed water for the project, the letters say critical questions remain unanswered about whether the company will follow through on these promises. The letters sent by lawmakers emphasize the uncertainties and raise additional questions about protections for air and water quality, impacts on utility rates, how the project will change Sutton and neighboring communities, and each organization’s role in the approval process. “Horror stories and broken promises plague hyperscale data centers built by companies like xAI and Meta across the United States,” they stated. “If Robert Kraft wishes to build his data center in our communities, he must make extensive commitments that the Unified Parkway Data Center will not increase electricity rates, affect the local water supply, or disrupt the peaceful neighborhoods we call home,” Moore, D-Millbury, said in a statement. “A government that represents the best interests of its people must ensure a proposal of this scale leaves no questions unanswered. It is our job to make sure that members of the community have ample opportunities to weigh in at every step of the process – and, if the company goes back on its promises, that we have a system set up to hold the Kraft Group accountable.” “While I recognize the potential tax benefits this project could bring, those benefits must be weighed against crucial questions surrounding energy demand, water resources, and quality of life for residents,” Fattman, R-Sutton, said. “A project of this scope deserves an extensive and transparent review, including opportunities for residents to have their voices heard before any decisions are made. As both a Sutton resident and its state senator, I look forward to being fully engaged in that process and guaranteeing these concerns receive the thorough attention they deserve.” While the project is proposed to be built on land owned by the Kraft Group’s Unified Global Packaging Group in Sutton, the data center would border the towns of Millbury and Grafton, with impacts expected to extend to nearby Northbridge, Auburn, Upton, Douglas, Uxbridge, Oxford and Webster. The letters emphasize that constituent concerns in these communities include energy costs, air quality impacts, light and noise pollution, and the disruption of surrounding ponds, rivers and the aquifer it would sit atop. At the time the letters were sent, the Unified Parkway Data Center proposal remained very high-level with scarce details on how the project would affect the region and noncommittal statements on how the company may mitigate energy and water concerns, according to the legislators. “Our constituents deserve to have a full understanding of the potential impacts that this data center complex would have on their cost of living, their communities, and the environment,” the legislators write. “Equally, our regulatory process needs to ensure that if this project moves forward, our constituents are fully protected against those impacts.” Still in preliminary review The data center proposal is still in preliminary review, with no formal applications filed and no agreements negotiated. At a press conference Nov. 17, the governor did not weigh in on the controversial concept, but outlined more of her thinking around local control over the proposal. “It’s a hot topic right now. I’m going to leave it to the people of Sutton,” Healey said at the time. Guardrails of her executive order, which include expectations for securing tax breaks, stipulate that new data centers should directly procure or develop the energy resources to support their operations — without raising energy costs for ratepayers and straining the electric grid. Data centers should also be situated where sufficient water supplies, wastewater and infrastructure exist, and they must minimize air emissions. Communities should also play a “meaningful role” in project planning and development, the Healey administration said. artigo.texto: Ação popular pede liminar para barrar obras de data center em Atibaia Ação popular foi resultado de reportagens publicadas pelo Metrópoles. Entre as exigências está a suspensão de possíveis licenças concedidas São Paulo — Após reportagem do Metrópoles revelar, nesse domingo (22/11), que o projeto de um data center estimado em R$ 3 bilhões de reais está com previsão de ser instalado em Atibaia, interior de São Paulo, uma ação popular apresentada o Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) nesta segunda-feira (23/11) pede a suspensão liminar de eventuais licenças do empreendimento sem a devida avaliação de impacto ambiental. A ação contra o município apresenta uma série de exigências e requerimentos, divididos entre medidas liminares de urgência, obrigações de transparência documental e pedidos definitivos de mérito. Dentro das medidas liminares de urgência, está o pedido de suspensão imediata dos efeitos de eventuais licenças, alvarás ou aprovações municipais concedidas para a implantação do data center, sem a demonstração prévia do cumprimento da legislação ambiental e urbanística e a exigência de que o município se abstenha de permitir qualquer início de obras, supressão de vegetação, movimentação de terra ou intervenção ambiental relacionada ao empreendimento até a comprovação da regularidade dos atos. No âmbito da transparência e exibição de documentos, a pasta exige a apresentação, por parte da prefeitura, de todos os expedientes administrativos existentes sobre o projeto, incluindo consultas preliminares, estudos, pareceres e certidões, a identificação de todas as pessoas físicas e jurídicas envolvidas no projeto, bem como os agentes públicos responsáveis por suas análises e aprovações, e a apresentação de uma declaração administrativa detalhada explicando a situação e informando os registros preliminares existentes, caso a prefeitura confirme a inexistência de processo formal de licenciamento. Entre no canal de WhatsApp do Metrópoles SP O processo ainda solicita: - Anulação definitiva de todos os atos administrativos municipais vinculados ao Data Center Alfa cuja ilegalidade ou lesividade ao meio ambiente, aos recursos hídricos e ao patrimônio local seja comprovada - Extensão da declaração de invalidação a todas as autorizações subsequentes que dependam de atos considerados nulos - Exigência de que o Município observe integralmente, antes de qualquer nova autorização material, os estudos ambientais, a proteção ao uso do solo, o impacto hídrico e a realização de audiências e participação popular quando exigido pela legislação Em nota enviada ao Metrópoles, a Prefeitura de Atibaia afirma que não foi citada, notificada ou tem conhecimento de demanda judicial relacionada à implantação de data center no município. Ademais, como já informado a este veículo em outra oportunidade, não existe pedido de autorização para implantação de empreendimento “data center” no município. Moradores se mobilizam contra instalação de data center O Metrópoles noticiou, neste domingo, que Atibaia, no interior paulista, entrou na mira das grandes empresas de tecnologia e deverá ser a futura sede de um data center de R$ 3 bilhões, em uma região de divisa entre área rural e área urbana da cidade. Temendo possíveis consequências ambientais, os moradores da cidade passaram a se mobilizar contra o projeto, redigindo uma petição que solicita à prefeitura a proibição de data centers de hiperescala no município. O requerimento do movimento popular Fora Data Center pede o envio à Câmara de Vereadores de um projeto de lei complementar para alterar o código de obras e o plano diretor municipal. Um abaixo-assinado do coletivo reuniu, até meados de novembro de 2026, mais de 4 mil assinaturas. A conexão foi autorizada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) em outubro de 2025. O documento, ao qual o Metrópoles teve acesso, permite a expansão em 15 quilômetros da linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois novos módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV, com a premissa de atender o Data Center Alfa. A Prefeitura de Atibaia, por sua vez, afirmou à reportagem que não identificou nos registros da Secretaria do Meio Ambiente, pedido de licenciamento ambiental vinculado ao projeto. O movimento Fora Data Center alerta para o risco da retirada de vegetação nativa da Mata Atlântica e de contaminação irreversível do lençol freático, em razão dos reservatórios de óleo diesel no subsolo, utilizados por data centers de hiperescala para alimentar centenas de geradores de emergência (UPS).Os moradores do Bairro do Tanque também temem um estresse hídrico, que pode gerar falta de água, já que o bairro é atendido parcialmente pelo sistema de abastecimento de água encanada e não dispõe de atendimento por rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto.

artigo.texto: The residents of Michigan's Ypsilanti Township are continuing to fight back against what they're calling a proposed "data center" after the University of Michigan's Board of Regents approved funding for a new research computing center last week. The board voted 7-1 on the $785 million construction costs for the $1.25 billion high-performances computing center intended for medical, science, clean energy, engineering and national security research. It's planned for a 124-acre site zoned for industrial use, with an additional 20 acres designated for a DTE electrical substation. The university said this project is not a data center or manufacturing site, but rather a "computing and research hub designed to advance science and education." University Promises Before the vote, University President Domenico Grasso said this project is "a critical step towards realizing one of the University of Michigan's most innovative and needed research initiatives." Read More on AI The university is partnering with Los Alamos National Laboratory and the state to deliver 50 megawatts of power initially, possibly expanding to 100 at full build-out, and is expected to "put Michigan at the forefront of the next generation of scientific discovery, which is where we always want to be." Grasso promised to work closely with the surrounding community to protect the environment, monitor utility usage and preserve the Huron River. He also said the board will commit $5 million over the next five years to the greater Ypsilanti area through its Community Partnership Program. "Leadership is not about pretending we know everything or have the perfect solutions; It is about listening and learning, recognizing where we can improve, and adjusting as appropriate," he said. "We want the people who live and work here to understand our motives and plans, and see the benefits of this partnership." In a letter to Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, Grasso said the university signed a Memorandum of Understanding in late 2024/2025 and said the Los Alamos has made no commitment of funds. “All activities require a separate agreement that will govern specific terms, conditions, funding and any other contractual obligations between U-M [the University of Michigan] and LANL [Los Alamos National Lab]," a spokesperson for Los Alamos told Newsweek. "There is no additional obligation between U-M and LANL. The classified computing center is not currently in the out years' NNSA [National Nuclear Security Administration] budget profile.” According to the Michigan Daily, Los Alamos confirmed that the facility would be used to research nuclear weapons. Community Backlash Critics of the project call it another data center that is set to disrupt the community and local environment. Residents and groups like Stop the Data Center have been protesting this facility for months. Reporting from Planet Detroit highlights outrage from residents, and promises from a local attorney to "use every legal means necessary to stop the data center." “U of M has gone far afield when it comes to the constitutional autonomy which they have enjoyed by virtue of being a university,” attorney Doug Winters said at a Thursday panel discussion. The United Tribes of Michigan (UTM) has also pushed back against the proposal, expressing its desire to preserve Native American cultural and heritage sites in the region and raised concerns about land use, noise levels, water consumption and electrical power needs. It also asked to be included in consultation about the facility's development. "Ypsilanti Township is along the Huron River in Southeastern Michigan and is located in an area that was used by Indian tribes for river and trail travel throughout history," UTM said in a resolution. "The area includes many sites of burials and other locations indicating indigenous usage and Ypsilanti Township is strongly concerned about a proposed data center within its boundaries, particularly about the potential impact on tribal cultural resources." In October, the university released a statement that it is conducting the appropriate due diligence and that a preliminary background search found "no evidence of archeological artifacts or culturally-sensitive materials found at the project site." Regent member Paul Brown, the only no vote, has joined community members protesting the facility. In August, he released a statement calling to stop the super computer site due to a lack of adequate community engagement. "When our development affects communities, we have to take responsibility to involve the people who live there," he said. "The university has failed to engage in an adequate conversation with those most affected and I cannot stand by and support this project being shoved down their throats, in a way that looks like environmental racism." The university is exempt from local building and zoning laws and does not pay property taxes. Michigan House Democrats introduced legislation in June to revoke the school's unilateral authority to circumvent zoning laws and town ordinances to buy land. “My community has been shaken by the university’s decision to quietly buy up land for the massive Los Alamos Data Center,” state Representative Jimmie Wilson of Ypsilanti said in a statement. “Every decision they’ve made was without consultation with local leaders or residents, and when the township board stood up and formally opposed it, U-M just ignored us and bulldozed ahead. "We are the ones who live here, pay taxes here and raise our kids here, but a multi-billion-dollar institution can just decide to drop a massive project in our backyard and expect us to deal with it," he said. "That is a complete betrayal of the public trust, and we’re putting a stop to it.” Local Community Impacts The university said the plan will not draw from or discharge into the Huron River or local groundwater and intends to protect local wildlife around the river. artigo.texto: PETALING JAYA: BM Greentech Bhd is expected to see stronger earnings in the second half of the financial year ending March 31, 2027 (2H27), underpinned by an improved contribution from its bioenergy segment and a ramp-up in battery energy storage system (Bess) deliveries. The group’s earnings for the 1H27 largely came in within market expectations and the estimates of RHB Research and Phillip Capital Research, with core net profit rising 2% year-on-year to RM24mil. In a note, RHB Research said prospects for bio-energy, the group’s key earnings contributor, remain positive. Potential engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning (EPCC) opportunities from the Sustainable Energy Development Authority’s 130MW Feed-in Tariff 2.0 programme supports its outlook, given the group’s estimated 60% to 70% market share among domestic boiler EPCC players. “Given a construction period of up to 30 months, we expect the programme to support earnings growth over the next two to three years,” the research house said, adding that the addressable market could reach RM1bil to RM2bil. “Looking ahead, we think that its bio-energy business remains a multiyear growth catalyst,” it said. RHB Research maintained its “buy” call on BM Greentech, with an unchanged target price (TP) of RM2.05. The brokerage continued to view the stock’s valuation as attractive at 13 times financial year 2027 (FY27) forecast price-to-earnings, one standard deviation below its five-year mean. Meanwhile, Phillip Capital Research saw the group’s earnings momentum picking up in 2H27 as Bess deliveries ramp up. In its second quarter, the company’s revenue and core net profit grew by 8% and 17% respectively, from the preceding quarter to RM177mil and RM13mil, mainly supported by stronger bioenergy deliveries and a 7.4-percentage-point increase in the water treatment segment’s pre-tax profit margin to 10.7%. Solar pre-tax profit, however, remained marginal at RM0.3mil due to a lower-margin utility-scale project mix and slower progress in the commercial and industrial segment. Phillip Capital Research expects the solar segment to benefit from increased Bess deliveries, with management guiding that Bess could account for about a third of solar revenue in FY27, rising to about 50% by FY28. The research house reiterated its “buy” recommendation with an unchanged sum-of-parts derived TP of RM2.20.

artigo.texto: Proposed Colleton County data center raises questions amid moratorium COLLETON COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — A proposed data center development in Colleton County is raising questions about the county’s moratorium and drawing continued opposition from some residents. The first data center development was proposed in the county about a year ago, triggering a lawsuit and a moratorium. The lawsuit was settled last month, establishing restrictions on where data centers can be built. Two more developments have since been proposed. Lighthouse DC plans to purchase approximately 315 acres from Coastal Electric Cooperative near Interstate 95 Exit 62. The property includes the 99-acre site of the former Pomega Battery Systems project and adjacent land. Construction on the first phase is planned for 2027, with delivery targeted for 2028. “Wait, which one? Because there’s so many different things going on at all times and you want to claim that we have a moratorium, then why are we having these conversations right now?” Colleton County resident Alice Banwart said. The county says its moratorium does not affect the two developers considering data centers because both have expressed interest in areas excluded from the moratorium. The moratorium remains in place until the county’s comprehensive plan is updated to reflect areas where digital infrastructure will not be allowed. Under the lawsuit settlement, a new overlay district bans data centers across most of the county’s portion of the ACE Basin and directs development toward industrial areas. Some residents remain concerned about the potential effects on their homes. “It’s still a data center which, you know, none of us really want, but if it’s going to happen, the county is doing the right things and putting it in the right locations,” said Jennifer Singleton, a Colleton County resident and plaintiff in the settled lawsuit. “I would hate to see a situation where we can’t raise our animals, our kids are having problems sleeping and it forces us to the point that we couldn’t even live at the place that we want to call home and if I could be buried there, I would,” Banwart said. Proposed investment, jobs and taxes The county is considering a fee-in-lieu-of-tax agreement, or FILOT, for the redevelopment of the Colleton Industrial Campus. County officials say the project would bring more than $600 million in combined investment, making it the largest capital investment in county history. Lighthouse plans to make at least $400 million in qualifying investment to develop the digital infrastructure campus. The company estimates the initial 20-megawatt phase will include more than $200 million in infrastructure and $400 million in customer equipment. The county estimates the first phase will support approximately 16 direct jobs with an average annual wage of $85,000, 45 indirect permanent jobs in the community and approximately 200 construction workers. It projects employment will grow to more than 200 full-time permanent positions as the campus expands. The county also projects that, at full energization, the project will pay more than $600 million in taxes over the course of the agreement, including more than $288 million to the Colleton County School District. “If we can’t afford the basics of, you know, fire protection, 911, like that’s pretty bad, right? And there’s no industry that’s really breaking down the door saying we want to move to Colleton County,” Singleton said. Colleton County Council Chairman Scott Biering said the project’s industrial location and projected revenue would benefit the county. “This is a landmark investment for Colleton County,” Biering said. “The project is appropriately sited in an existing industrial area, and the revenue generated will assist the county in stabilizing and improving public services, while protecting our existing tax base. The project charts a brighter future for our citizens. It will provide high-quality, long-term employment opportunities for our workforce and fund vital services such as public education, sanitation, law enforcement and emergency services.” Steve Murdaugh, a county council member and chairman of the SouthernCarolina Alliance, also praised the project and the partnerships behind it. “I am excited about the investment by LightHouse DC in Colleton County, both as Chairman of the SouthernCarolina Alliance and as a member of Colleton County Council,” Murdaugh said. “This project represents the largest capital investment in the history of Colleton County and is a tremendous milestone for our community and our region. Beyond the significant investment itself, this project will create new employment opportunities for our citizens and generate substantial revenues for both the County government and our School District, providing additional resources to enhance public services, strengthen our schools, and improve the quality of life for our citizens. I want to commend the Colleton County Economic Alliance staff and thank our partners at Coastal Electric Cooperative, Inc. for their continued commitment, hard work, and partnership in advancing economic development opportunities in Colleton County. Projects of this magnitude are the result of strong partnerships, a shared vision, and a continued commitment to moving our community forward.” Utilities, water and noise Coastal Electric Cooperative CEO Mark Walling said the project would benefit the cooperative and its members. “We expect Lighthouse to have an immediate, positive impact on our community and our cooperative,” Walling said. “The presence of a large, stable user on our system will support the fixed costs to deliver electricity to our members, improve grid reliability and protect our ratepayers.” The proposed utility service framework would require large users to: - Sign contracts of at least 15 years with early termination penalties. - Prepay for necessary electric infrastructure upgrades. - Lower electricity use during potential energy outages or

artigo.texto: Report: Lutnick asked battery startup Pure Lithium to accept US takeover US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, the Reuters report says. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asked Pure Lithium in July to give Washington a 51% controlling stake in exchange for funds to build a manufacturing plant, which would neither be owned nor controlled by the US battery startup, according to a report by Reuters. Lutnick’s plan marks another attempt by the Trump administration to acquire a stake in an American company. Pure Lithium, however, rejected the proposal, saying such a stake could lead to public scrutiny and risked future capital-raising activities, the Reuters report says, citing documents from July and August. The Trump administration has taken stakes in several companies including Intel, but it has not yet taken a majority stake in any company. The largest equity stake the Trump administration has agreed to would give it a 15% stake in rare earths company MP Materials, the report said. According to Pure Lithium’s website, lithium metal batteries will replace the incumbent lithium-ion battery. The company’s “patented, vertically integrated production process delivers the highest quality Lithium metal anode, contributing to exceptional battery performance.”

artigo.texto: Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) alertou para o risco de déficit de potência no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional) já em 2027 caso a Justiça suspenda o leilão de baterias, previsto para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Esse risco existe mesmo após a realização do LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) de março e reforça a necessidade da contratação de baterias, segundo manifestação. O documento, ao qual a Agência iNFRA teve acesso, teve por objetivo subsidiar a defesa da União na ADI (Ação Direta de Inconstitucionalidade) movida pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica) no STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal). A entidade questiona a regra de custeio do certame e pediu, cautelarmente, a suspensão da realização. Na manifestação, assinada no último dia 17, a consultoria jurídica do MME defendeu a legalidade dos certames de baterias e a importância de continuidade do cronograma. A pasta afirmou ainda que não há necessidade de regulamentação prévia sobre o custeio que remunerará as baterias, uma vez que a cobrança só seria iniciada em agosto de 2028. Esse mesmo entendimento foi levado pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) no outro processo movido pela Abeeólica, este na Justiça Federal em Brasília. A reguladora também disse que não há necessidade de urgência para definir o encargo e afirmou que uma suspensão do certame atrasaria a entrada das baterias e afetaria os mais de 5 mil projetos cadastrados.

artigo.texto: Aurora neighbors hope new data center moratorium passes city council Aurora residents who have been pushing for restrictions on new data centers are hopeful as a new moratorium is scheduled to be introduced to the city council. Michael and Linda Trimble know what it's like to live next to a data center. They used to live in Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the world's largest concentration of data centers. In fact, one was right across the street from their home, which they found problematic. "It was like they really did not think about the community where they were building the data centers," said Linda Trimble. "It was noisy. It was warmer. It took up a lot of space. They tried to put trees between to block off some of the noise, but it really didn't work," said Michael Trimble. They moved to Aurora to retire and get away from it, but a few months ago they learned that a new data center will be built nearby. "This is a big déjà vu for us," said Michael Trimble. "Here we are again, another data center." They learned the Trident data center will be built in their neighborhood in northeast Aurora. The couple is worried because Michael Trimble's health is now once again in jeopardy. He got pulmonary fibrosis after decades of working at Rocky Flats and says that a nearby data center can cause dangerous complications for him. "The particulate matter in the air is going to cause me problems, hospitalization and a higher mortality rate," he explained. The Trimbles' neighbor Shane O'Neil also has experience with data centers. "I was a data center manager, and those things generate a lot of noise," said O'Neil. He says he's worried about Michael Trimble and his other neighbors. "We have a huge, heavy, heavy presence of veterans in this community, and a little bit of noise like that, it's going to set them off," said O'Neil. That's why they are hoping Aurora City Council does something to protect them. The council has considered moratoriums recently and voted them down. The Trimbles and O'Neil say they felt betrayed by that decision. "Corruption. Pure. Plain and simple," O'Neil said. "It's all about money. It's about making people richer," said Michael Trimble. Now another moratorium is going to be introduced at Monday's city council meeting. This one would last until September 2027 and would prevent new data center construction west and south of the intersection of the proposed Aerotropolis Parkway and I-70. Council member Curtis Gardner, who has been against a moratorium, posted on Facebook that this time he is on board and thinks they have the votes to pass it. O'Neil and the Trimbles are hoping he is right "I hope the people on the city council have clear heads and realize that there are people here," said O'Neil. That city council meeting will be held on Nov. 23 at 6 p.m. at the Aurora Municipal Center.

artigo.texto: East Texas lawmaker co-authors bill ending data center sales tax exemption Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago. TYLER, Texas (KLTV) - State Sen.-elect Trent Ashby (R-Lufkin) co-authored a bill that would remove the sales tax exemption for qualifying data centers. Senate Bill 293 would rescind the sales tax exemption passed over a decade ago and would apply to data centers such as those with a footprint of at least 100,000 square feet. The bill’s filing comes amid concerns from Texans about the growth of data centers, as well as their use of water and electricity. “It just doesn’t make sense to continue to subsidize these data center companies that, frankly, are some of the most capitalized companies not just in the United States but in the world,” Ashby said. “When the law took effect in 2013, at that time the comptroller estimated that the cost of this bill would be about $15 million,” he continued. “The most recent estimate that we have for the comptroller is that in the upcoming biennium for our state, that this sales tax exemption will cost $3.3 billion.” Existing exemptions would expire when the bill takes effect. Economist Dr. Ray Perryman said he would rather see additional requirements for data centers to qualify for the sales tax exemption rather than removing it entirely. “Maybe requiring that you have your power worked out behind the grid, requiring that you have your water supplies worked out, those kinds of things,” Perryman said. “I’d prefer to see us do something like that that improves the overall structure but allows this development to happen.” Perryman mentioned changing the current law could impact rural Texans in particular. “It’s enough of an incentive that some of these data centers would go away and every time one goes away, you’re really talking about billions of dollars in spending, again quite often in a rural area that doesn’t have a lot of economic development,” added Perryman. In contrast, Ashby said he does not expect significant opposition from businesses. “I don’t think that we’re likely to see a large pushback from the data center community,” said Ashby. “These companies are so well capitalized and these data centers… are very profitable.” Enough lawmakers have signed onto the bill for it to pass the Texas Senate when they convene in January. artigo.texto: Malaysia has stopped waiting for Washington to police its server halls. If you run or rent AI compute in Southeast Asia, one more route to Nvidia's chips for blacklisted buyers just got harder to use. Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, will advise data center operators not to host, lease space to or provide services for seven companies the US added to its trade blacklist this week, according to Bloomberg and Free Malaysia Today on Tuesday, November 24. The seven were put on the Commerce Department's Entity List in a final rule dated November 23, and they are tied to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer at the center of the chip diversion scandal. Three of the listed names are Malaysia-linked: Speedmatrix, MSFusion and PT Megaspeed International. The parent, Megaspeed International Pte Ltd in Singapore, is also listed, along with other affiliates in Singapore and Thailand. MITI says the Malaysian Investment Development Authority will pass the warning to operators. The ministry's line is that Malaysia won't allow itself to be used as a channel to get around export controls, and that it will act against anyone found breaking the law. Notice the word is advise, not ban. No deadline has been set, and the operators who will receive the notice have not been named. MITI also pushed back on the framing. It says PT Megaspeed International is not a Malaysian entity and is neither a data center operator nor a tenant in the country, going by investment agency records, and that Speedmatrix is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Singapore company. Eleven days earlier, on November 13, the ministry had said it never cleared Megaspeed or Speedmatrix of anything, and that Speedmatrix was a tenant at data centers in Malaysia. That's a narrow answer to a broad question: the firms may not be Malaysian by incorporation, but the racks they used sit in Malaysian buildings. Alice Huang, a Chinese national who has since left Megaspeed, was watched by US agencies for about a year after being photographed at dinners with Jensen Huang in Singapore. Nvidia says the contacts were routine and that no chips were diverted. - china recruited megaspeed executive to spy on nvidia - who did china recruit to spy on nvidia Not all Malaysian data centers face the new US chip curb. The one that matters is a separate US rule published on November 19, which requires licenses for data centers supplying large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China. Colocation operators feel that rule most, because they rent out the physical space and often can't see who ends up using the compute. Frankly, that blind spot is the whole problem, and it's why a warning letter from MIDA will matter less than whether operators start asking tenants harder questions. Singapore first, now Johor This follows Singapore's own line. Its prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said the city-state won't allow circumvention of export controls and is ready to facilitate US checks on AI chip use. Malaysia is the bigger physical test. Johor, across the causeway, has been the overflow site for Singapore's data center demand, and operators there have built fast on the promise of AI tenants. The scale of what Washington is chasing is large. Bloomberg has reported that Megaspeed imported at least $4.6 billion of Nvidia hardware, based on Malaysian and Indonesian customs data. For Chinese AI developers, the effect is direct. Renting GPU capacity in a neighboring country has been the workaround for the US ban on shipping top chips to China, and every operator that screens tenants more closely narrows it. Nvidia isn't named in the rule, but its customers' customers are now the ones being checked, and a listed buyer can't easily take delivery of new systems. Malaysia has its own money at stake. Tighter US chip rules already cloud the country's data center push, so Kuala Lumpur is balancing Washington's goodwill against an industry it has courted with incentives and a national investment framework. Listing doesn't automatically cover affiliates, one analysis of the rule notes, so operators must screen counterparties themselves rather than wait for a longer list. MITI has not said what happens to existing contracts with the seven firms. Neither Nvidia nor Megaspeed's affiliates had publicly responded to the Malaysian advisory at the time of writing. artigo.texto: AURORA | Audience members of Monday’s city council meeting broke into applause when lawmakers passed a data center moratorium that will prevent construction of new facilities in a majority of the city through September 2027, following months of back and forth. Council voted unanimously for the temporary pause, although Councilmember Curtis Gardner was excused from the meeting. Additionally, the developer behind the controversial Trident data center announced it will relocate the facility. Mayor Mike Coffman congratulated the neighbors of the Trident facility for organizing successfully. “I’m just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed,” Coffman said. Under the moratorium, data centers would be prohibited from locating west and south of the intersection of Powhaton Road and Interstate 70 until after Sept. 30, 2027, or until city council determines appropriate land use regulations are in place. The moratorium, like the previous proposals, would not impact data centers that have already had development applications accepted, which includes Trident. The Trident data center has drawn significant backlash from neighbors in the Windler, Green Valley Ranch and Reserve communities over concerns with the potential environmental and health impacts. However, a statement from Vantage Data Centers, which is developing Trident, said it is no longer pursuing the original site on East 48th Avenue, but is continuing to look for an alternative location. It also said Vantage will continue to engage the city on their proposed campus. “In response to the recent community concerns, Vantage voluntarily initiated a review of alternative sites, and the examination of viable alternatives continues,” Misty Allen, vice president of public policy in North America for Vantage, said. “While we will no longer pursue the current site for our proposed campus, Vantage remains committed to being a responsible long-term partner in the state.” While previous iterations of moratoriums failed, council members supported this compromise. Mayor Mike Coffman said he feels it’s a good compromise by exempting the vacant land on the east side of the city while protecting residential communities and allowing the city to continue to draft rules. Councilmember Stephanie Hancock, who opposed past moratoriums, said she thinks Aurora is leading the way on data center regulations, adding “data centers are here to stay.” “I’m not in favor of the word moratorium, that really bothers me and I think it sends a weird message to businesses,” Hancock said. “But we want to keep in mind that our communities want safety, they want to make sure we’re building efficiently and effectively, and I think Aurora is doing a good job of wrapping our arms around this as we’re learning more.” Meanwhile, Councilmember Alli Jackson took issue with the moratorium not going far enough, noting the potential impact of pollution is not limited to nearby communities. She advocated for a total moratorium. “I do have a hard time voting on this because when I listen to the community, and what I hear them say, is that they don’t want data centers in Aurora, period,” Jackson said. “I understand … the votes aren’t going to change for that type of verbiage, so I will vote for this, but when we talk about the safety of our constituents, pollution doesn’t care about (zoning).” The moratorium doesn’t have to last until September 2027, but could end earlier, whenever council decides appropriate rules are in place. The council is already working on changes to the city’s development code regarding data centers, including residential setbacks and a requirement for a noise study. The residential setback would prohibit data centers within 750 feet of residentially-zoned areas and make data centers a conditional use when they’re located between 750 feet and a half-mile from residential areas. Councilmember Amy Wiles said she is exploring other regulations related to vibrations, low frequency noise and community benefit agreements. Councilmember Angela Lawson also noted the state legislature will likely have several bills targeting data centers. Several public commenters spoke in support of the moratorium during the meeting and asked the council to go further and do more to protect neighbors from the potential impacts. A few speakers opposed the moratorium. Chaz Tedesco, representing a local labor union, commented in favor of data centers and against the pause, citing the jobs they provide for local construction workers. “Aurora should not have to choose between protecting neighborhoods and supporting jobs,” Tedesco said. In addition to the moratorium, the council had planned to vote on a resolution stating its support for Trident to move to another location and directing the city manager to facilitate the relocation. However, since Trident announced its plans to move locations, the resolution was pulled from the agenda. Council also voted unanimously on a prohibition on tax incentives for data centers. “I think it’s important to send the message to data center developers that these incentives don’t exist and they can make their decisions accordingly,” Coffman said. Coombs called the ban “performative” because she said the council should have a more general discussion on tax incentives. However, she voted for the prohibition, citing community support for it. The prohibition will end the practices of tax revenue sharing or remitting sales or use tax back to data centers in exchange for jobs, however it would not apply to existing agreements, according to the draft policy. The city has already committed to four incentive agreements, with a maximum total rebate of about $83 million. One of the incentive agreements is for the Trident data center, which could receive up to $39 million in tax rebates. The ban will need one more vote before taking effect.

While they discuss designing their own AI, the UC, Cal State and community college systems continue to use commercial providers. UC spokesperson Stett Holbrook told CalMatters the purchasing amendment of the new OpenAI agreement isn't finalized yet, even though the university has already announced the deal. That disclosure emerged after reporters for CalMatters repeatedly asked for a copy of the purchase agreement. The previous OpenAI contract requires the UC to pay a minimum of $10 per user per month for ChatGPT EDU licenses and a minimum of $30 per user per month for another advanced ChatGPT platform. The Cal State system signed contracts with OpenAI that extend through 2029 for roughly $56 million. The community colleges’ chancellor’s office has AI cooperation agreements with Google, Microsoft, Adobe and IBM but no systemwide financial arrangement with any AI company. University-designed AI models are cheaper and ensure more privacy, but they’re “not quite necessarily as intuitive,” said Craig Hayward, a strategic advisor to the community college chancellor’s office on AI. “Your prompting game needs to be more on point to get the value out of them.” Locally, individual universities are already moving forward with their own AI plans. This month, Cal Poly San Luis Obispo announced the creation of its AI data center, which is intended to serve the whole campus, according to Chris Lupo, the director of the university’s school of applied computing. The most advanced, university-controlled AI platform is at UC San Diego, where university IT services collaborated with its supercomputing center to create TritonGPT, a nod to the campus mascot and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. The San Diego platform has licensed or shared aspects of its AI development with other UC campuses to help them develop their own chatbots, including BearGPT at Berkeley and SCOUT at Merced. UCSD was also cited as a partner in the community college system’s AI proposal. “This is the model that the higher education system in the state of California is trying to expand,” said Zachary Johnson, the senior director of AI strategy for UCSD. Why sovereign AI is gaining popularity For the community college system, developing an independent or sovereign AI system comes with three main benefits, Hayward said. The first is cost. While tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are the most popular examples of AI, they’re expensive, with individual plans reaching $200 per month and incurring further costs to go beyond usage limits. artigo.texto: For nearly 35 years, the railroad to Port MacKenzie has existed mostly as cleared ground. The idea dates to 1992, when the Cook Inlet port itself did not yet exist. Work came in fits and starts after that. A right-of-way was cleared, and much of the bed was built, but the rails themselves never went down, according to the Alaska Beacon. Now the 32-mile line has money. The railroad's board signed off on the $311 million project this past week, and a federal grant announced in October covers most of the bill. The railroad's chief executive, Bill O'Leary, told the Beacon that construction could begin next summer. In public, the line has been pitched as a freight corridor for minerals, natural gas pipeline materials and national security. Documents filed near its two ends tell a more complicated story. At the port, a coal power developer is pursuing plans for an "Advanced Manufacturing & Compute Campus." Near Houston, where the spur would meet the railroad's main line, the state's development authority has won approval for state land for what its application calls "a behind-the-meter data park." Read More on News Neither data center has been built, and no public record shows a committed tenant for either. But taken together, the records show a railroad being revived at the same moment, and in the same places, that Alaska is deciding whether to welcome a power-hungry industry. Why It Matters Across the U.S., the race to build data centers for artificial intelligence has collided with questions about where the power will come from and who pays for it. In Alaska, one answer on the table is coal. In March, the Interior Department announced that Terra Energy Center had reached a $1 billion agreement in principle with Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems. The deal covers boilers for a 1.25-gigawatt coal power plant in Alaska. The department called it "the first order of utility-scale coal power plant boilers in the United States since approximately 2006." A Korean private equity firm, KOREIT, pledged $500 million. The project also lands in the middle of a political transition. The incoming governor, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, has said he would seek a temporary ban on new data centers. What To Know The port end. In March, the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly adopted a resolution backing a joint marketing effort with Terra Energy Center Corp. to court "large power consumers." The resolution lists its first priority as "Attraction of data center and advanced computing facilities." It promises "firm baseload power supply from TECC's planned generation facility" and says land near Port MacKenzie offers "exceptional access to tidewater." Neither the resolution nor the staff memo attached to it uses the word coal. The Interior Department's announcement does. The memo says Terra holds a land-use permit for about 1,058 acres near Lake Lorraine, in the port district. The permit lets Terra test the feasibility of "an Advanced Manufacturing and Computing Campus." A draft term sheet in a September 2025 Port Commission packet targets "approximately 30 MW initial load" for that campus. The developer would have to pour a slab by December 31, 2028, or the borough could take the land back. Mayor Edna DeVries vetoed the resolution in a message dated March 5, citing "the risk that Mat-Su Borough has placed themselves in." She noted that data centers "often require conditional use permits," a subject "the assembly has not discussed." The Assembly overrode her 6-1 on March 17, the Anchorage Daily News reported. The resolution says nothing in it obligates the borough to sell or lease land. Port backers are already planning around the tracks. The Alaska Beacon counted a coal-powered computing project among the developments lining up at the port ahead of the line. The mine. One industrial project already tied to the port is not a data center. In October 2025, the Department of War awarded $43.4 million under the Defense Production Act to Nova Minerals' subsidiary, Alaska Range Resources. The money is for military-grade antimony trisulfide. According to Nova, the plan pairs a mine with a refinery at Port MacKenzie. The mine and refinery are planned projects, not operating facilities. Critical minerals, a category that includes antimony, were among the reasons federal officials gave for funding the railroad. The grant announcement does not mention coal power or computing. The Houston end. In its application to the state Department of Natural Resources, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA) describes plans for about 20,000 acres near Houston. They include "secure, scalable data centers," "a behind-the-meter data park" and a "data / energy campus." The application also mentions utility corridors for electricity, natural gas and fiber, and land "adjacent to the Alaska Railroad centerline." It does not mention the Port MacKenzie line. AIDEA's fact sheet puts the land about 2 miles north of Houston and says AIDEA would not pay for the land's value, only related costs such as surveying. In a July 30 letter to Mat-Su legislators, Executive Director Randy Ruaro wrote: "There is no committed data-center tenant." On November 10, the Department of Natural Resources approved a smaller transfer of about 6,800 acres. DNR cited 2,306 public comments and "substantial public concern" over the transfer, including "the prospect of scalable data center facilities," in its final decision. Days later, borough officials asked the state to reconsider. They wrote that "Point Mackenzie and portions of West Susitna offer more appropriate locations for these uses," the Anchorage Daily News reported. That would move the development to the port end of the line. What the grant announcement leaves out. artigo.texto: In Depth: Why Oklahomans should prepare to see more data center proposals As part of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's campaign, she promised a crackdown and more regulations on data centers that she and many others who won earlier this month said they were behind skyrocketing power bills and taking up too much of the state’s water. “We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans and right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans and [they] are being taken advantage of,” said Hinojosa. “So, the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections. We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure as governor, I lead to ensure that happens.” The State of Texas has seen its number of data centers soar in just the last few years. Some of these are hyperscalers, others are more in the traditional sense of data centers and server farms. In 2021, there were 83 operating by the end of the year. At the end of 2025, that number jumped to 145. We don’t have the 2026 numbers yet, but more projects were both built and proposed. Texas and other states have now elected officials that intend to crackdown and regulate data centers. Oklahoma has elected leaders who said we are open for business, and it's time to consider some of these investments. Tulsa Democratic State Representative Amanda Clinton, one of the main lawmakers in Oklahoma City trying to regulate data centers, speaks unedited about why Oklahomans need to be prepared for more data center proposals as these companies and developers look to leave Texas and other states.

artigo.texto: 247 – Moradores de Atibaia, no interior de São Paulo, estão se mobilizando contra a possível instalação de um data center avaliado em R$ 3 bilhões no município. O empreendimento, previsto para uma região próxima ao Bairro do Tanque, desperta preocupações relacionadas ao abastecimento de água, à preservação ambiental e aos impactos sobre a qualidade de vida da população. Organizados no movimento Fora Data Center, os habitantes cobram transparência das autoridades e defendem mudanças na legislação municipal para impedir a construção de grandes complexos de processamento de dados. Segundo reportagem do Metrópoles, o movimento reuniu mais de 4 mil assinaturas em um abaixo-assinado até meados de novembro. A mobilização ocorre em meio a questionamentos sobre a ausência de consultas públicas específicas para discutir o empreendimento, embora documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica indiquem preparativos para atender à futura instalação. Com pouco mais de 160 mil habitantes, Atibaia passou a integrar os planos de expansão de empresas de infraestrutura digital. O projeto em discussão, denominado Data Center Alfa, é apresentado pela DataSpots, empresa do Grupo ON, com previsão de início das operações entre 2029 e 2030. A iniciativa prevê a construção de um complexo de grande porte em uma área de transição entre zonas urbanas e rurais. O terreno inicialmente considerado para a instalação possui extensão equivalente a aproximadamente 50 campos de futebol. Moradores cobram participação nas decisões sobre o empreendimento O movimento Fora Data Center elaborou uma petição destinada à Prefeitura de Atibaia solicitando medidas para impedir a implantação de data centers de hiperescala no município. O documento também reivindica o encaminhamento de um projeto de lei complementar à Câmara Municipal para modificar o Código de Obras e o Plano Diretor. Uma das principais reclamações dos moradores é a falta de informações detalhadas sobre o empreendimento e seus possíveis efeitos sobre a região. A comunidade afirma que não foi previamente informada sobre os planos de instalação do complexo nem convocada para participar de audiências públicas específicas sobre os impactos ambientais e sociais da atividade. A situação ganhou novos contornos após a divulgação de documentos e comunicados relacionados à ampliação da infraestrutura energética local. Documentos indicam planejamento de infraestrutura elétrica Em 17 de junho de 2026, a concessionária Isa Energia apresentou, durante audiência pública, um estudo de impacto de vizinhança referente à implantação de ramais destinados à conexão da linha de transmissão de 440 kV Bom Jardim–Água Azul à subestação de transmissão Fernão Dias, de 440/500 kV. De acordo com o movimento de moradores, a apresentação concentrou-se na necessidade de reforçar o sistema elétrico regional, sem detalhar suficientemente a relação da obra com os projetos de data centers. Entretanto, um comunicado divulgado pela própria concessionária indicava que a ampliação da rede também tinha como finalidade viabilizar empreendimentos de infraestrutura digital, incluindo o Data Center Alfa, com previsão de conexão à Subestação Atibaia 2. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) autorizou, em outubro de 2025, uma conexão destinada ao atendimento do projeto. Conforme documento obtido pelo Metrópoles, a autorização contempla a expansão de aproximadamente 15 quilômetros de linha de transmissão e a implantação de dois módulos de entrada de linha em 138 kV. A existência dessa autorização alimentou os questionamentos dos moradores sobre o estágio de desenvolvimento do empreendimento e o acesso da população às informações sobre sua implantação. Prefeitura afirma não ter recebido pedido de licenciamento Apesar dos documentos relacionados à infraestrutura elétrica, a Prefeitura de Atibaia informou que não encontrou, nos registros da Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente, solicitação de licenciamento ambiental vinculada ao data center. Em manifestação encaminhada ao Metrópoles, a administração municipal afirmou que qualquer proposta formal deverá cumprir as exigências legais pertinentes. “Caso seja formalizada proposta de implantação de data center, serão exigidos todos os estudos, licenças e autorizações legalmente aplicáveis, observadas as competências do município, da Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb) e dos demais órgãos responsáveis”, declarou a prefeitura. A posição do governo municipal contrasta com as informações disponibilizadas pela DataSpots, que apresenta o Data Center Alfa em seu portfólio como um empreendimento aprovado e estruturado. Publicações especializadas também mencionaram o projeto entre os investimentos planejados pela empresa no Brasil. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo portal Datlaz, a DataSpots prevê investimentos de R$ 39 bilhões no país, incluindo a unidade projetada para Atibaia. Embora esses registros indiquem avanços no planejamento empresarial e energético, a autorização de conexão à rede elétrica não equivale, por si só, à concessão das licenças ambientais e urbanísticas necessárias para a construção. Consumo de água preocupa famílias que dependem de poços Entre os principais temores da população está a possibilidade de agravamento da escassez hídrica no Bairro do Tanque, onde parte dos moradores depende de poços para obter água. A região não dispõe de cobertura integral dos serviços de abastecimento e também enfrenta limitações na infraestrutura de coleta e tratamento de esgoto. O morador Gabriel Tonobohn, que vive no bairro há três anos e meio, relatou que a disponibilidade de água já representa uma dificuldade para diversas famílias, sobretudo durante os períodos de estiagem. “A gente mora em um bairro que não tem saneamento, não tem água encanada, não tem esgoto. artigo.texto: The nation’s largest data centers used at least as much energy in one year as the entire state of Michigan, and were responsible for more carbon emissions than some entire countries, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The researchers focused on 403 large facilities and found that the climate pollution driven by these “hyperscale” data centers is three times greater than previously estimated. Energy use across the country’s thousand-plus data centers is likely much higher than the study captures, said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctorate researcher at Harvard. “This paper is just providing a floor estimate,” he said. Data centers contain the servers and computer chips that enable artificial intelligence, online commerce and cloud storage. They require a constant supply of energy to run and cool internal hardware. Communities near data centers have raised concerns about air pollution, and electricity and water use — issues that some political observers believe moved the needle toward Democrats in this month’s midterm elections. Scientists had previously taken a stab at projecting the amount of energy used by data centers, but the Harvard research team said few focused on the large facilities that power AI. Their servers process enormous amounts of data and need enormous amounts of electricity to operate. The average data center in the study consumed as much power as 30,000 homes. The precise amount of electricity used by data centers is difficult to determine because their operators rarely release this information. In this case, the researchers relied on satellite imagery and data from a private company about the facilities’ square footage and their maximum permitted energy use between 2024 and 2025. Then, the researchers used maps to determine which power plants the data centers likely draw electricity from. Based on the types of fuels those facilities burn, the researchers estimated the climate-warming emissions linked to the data centers. “We just wanted to find independent numbers,” said Guidi, “and not just companies’ sustainability claims.” The Harvard team found that the data centers in their sample consumed about 2% of all of the electricity used in the country during the period they studied. And more than half of that energy came from burning fossil fuels. Can Hankendi, a data center researcher at Boston University who was not involved with the study, called the research “very well built.” He said the lack of transparency around data centers’ energy use is a common challenge for researchers in the field. In an email to WBUR, Hankendi said the researchers had to make some assumptions, which he called “reasonable.” “Even though there will be some accuracy issues, they still give us some ballpark numbers to start from,” he wrote. “These estimations are important not only for researchers, but also for policymakers and the public.” The study also suggests that certain parts of the country are more burdened than others by climate pollution driven by data centers. Fossil fuel-burning power plants were more common in Virginia — the state with the most data centers — and Ohio, whereas other states like Oregon have greener electric grids, so data centers there were potentially responsible for less climate-warming gases. The data center industry is evolving so quickly that the numbers in the study “are already outdated in a way,” said Guidi. According to the independent market tracking company Clearview, last year there were 1,163 data centers in operation. That number is expected to skyrocket this year, with 578 new data centers under construction and more proposed. As companies look to build quickly, they are increasingly turning to on-site power generators, said study co-author Francesca Dominici, professor of biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Some developers have managed to power data centers without connecting to the grid, she said. But the generators they use often rely on fossil fuels like natural gas or diesel, and they may be less efficient and more polluting than traditional power plants. In the coming years, Dominici said she hopes that will change. Some energy experts have suggested the power needs of data centers could spur clean energy development. “In some of the industry the big cloud providers are indeed trying to move into a renewable source of energy,” she said, “but we are not seeing that yet.” “Data center development could become actually a positive thing for the community if it’s done responsibly,” she said. This article was originally published on WBUR.org.

artigo.texto: Introducing a microstructured egg-box topography at the interface between metallic lithium and a Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte increases the discharge current density at which interfacial voiding commences by a factor of ten. When the operating temperature is elevated to 60 degrees Celsius, the same contoured interfacial configuration successfully accommodates pulsed currents reaching 8 milliamperes per square centimeter while maintaining continuous ionic transport. To evaluate performance under dynamic conditions representative of practical automotive applications, researchers subjected the contoured cells to discharge current profiles derived directly from the Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure. Current and voltage time series from battery testing of a Hyundai Ioniq, sourced from Argonne National Laboratory electric vehicle evaluation datasets, were converted into equivalent cell-level areal current densities based on a 77.4-kilowatt-hour total pack energy capacity and an assumed cell areal capacity of 5 milliampere-hours per square centimeter, with regenerative charging currents excluded. Tested at 2 megapascals of stack pressure and 60 degrees Celsius, the egg-box contoured interface successfully sustained the full demanding WLTP discharge profile, which involves peak discharge currents reaching 9 milliamperes per square centimeter. The geometric profile of the microstructured interface was designed as a continuous three-dimensional egg-box pattern generated by sweeping a mathematical cosine function along the trajectory of an identical, perpendicular cosine function. The interfacial surface topography is formally defined by the mathematical expression where the surface elevation f(x,y) equals H multiplied by the cosine of 2 pi x divided by S plus H multiplied by the cosine of 2 pi y divided by S. In this formulation, H represents the peak height or amplitude, fixed at 5 micrometers, while S defines the peak separation or spatial wavelength, set to 30 micrometers. Print trajectories were compiled with NanoWrite software on a commercial Nanoscribe Photonic Professional GT system operating in a dip-in laser lithography configuration, utilizing a 25-times magnification lens with a numerical aperture of 0.8 and liquid IP-S resin. The circular templates, measuring 5 millimeters in diameter with a contoured face opposite a flat baseline face, were built in a layer-by-layer sequence using a slicing distance of 1 micrometer, a hatching spacing of 0.5 micrometers, and a lateral writing block size of 300 micrometers by 300 micrometers. Following optical polymerization, the templates were washed in propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate of at least 99.5 percent purity to dissolve unpolymerized precursor resin, rinsed with isopropanol of at least 99.5 percent purity, dried under vacuum overnight, and transferred directly into an argon-filled glovebox environment maintained below 1 part per million of oxygen and moisture. Solid electrolyte pellets were fabricated by loading 30 milligrams of Li6PS5Cl argyrodite powder, possessing an average particle diameter of 1 micrometer, together with the microstructured polymer template into a 5-millimeter die set. Applying a uniaxial compaction pressure of 400 megapascals imprinted the egg-box surface topography directly onto the ceramic powder while consolidating the electrolyte disc to an overall thickness of approximately 1 millimeter. After mechanical pressing, the polymeric template was detached from the shaped electrolyte pellet. Both contoured and flat comparative Li6PS5Cl discs subsequently underwent thermal sintering in a muffle furnace at 300 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes to optimize bulk ionic conductivity. Electrochemical validation of interfacial stripping behavior was performed within specialized three-electrode pouch cells assembled inside the inert argon glovebox. Metallic lithium discs measuring 1 millimeter, 0.5 millimeters, and 5 millimeters in diameter served as the working, reference, and counter electrodes, respectively, with an insulating polymer layer isolating the working and reference elements on one face of the electrolyte pellet while the counter electrode resided on the reverse side. The critical current density for stripping was quantitatively tracked using a Gamry 1010E potentiostat via a stepped chronopotentiometry protocol. Cells were initially cycled by electrochemically plating lithium at 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter and stripping at 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter to a fixed areal capacity of 0.2 milliampere-hours per square centimeter. In subsequent cycles, the plating current was maintained at a constant 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter while the stripping current density was increased incrementally by 0.2 milliamperes per square centimeter per cycle. To evaluate the architectural concept under complete electrochemical device conditions, solid-state full cells were assembled by coupling the contoured lithium anode with a composite transition-metal oxide cathode. The cathode composite was formulated by mortar-and-pestle blending of LiNi0.83Mn0.06Co0.11O2 powder, Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte, and conductive carbon nanofibres in a weight ratio of 75 to 22 to 3. For standard full cells, 5.2 milligrams of this composite powder were co-pressed with 30 milligrams of Li6PS5Cl and the polymer template at 400 megapascals, after which a 5-millimeter lithium disc was affixed to the anode side. artigo.texto: AI data centers drive up demand at Britain’s factories The building of artificial intelligence data centers has lifted the UK’s manufacturing output to a 27-month high, according to survey data that shows the economy as a whole continuing to grow. S&P Global’s overall purchasing managers’ index, measuring the health of the UK economy, came in at 52.3 for November in its initial estimate published on Monday. That was down slightly from October’s final reading of 52.9 but still above the 50-mark that indicates economic expansion. Growth in the UK’s dominant services sector slowed to a five-month low, yet this was partly offset by the highest sub-index score for factory output since July 2024 — the same month in which the current Labour government came to power. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being helped by a surprisingly resilient UK economy, which has outpaced its major European peers so far this year. While surging energy bills are expected to dent consumer confidence over the winter, surveys such as the PMI still show strong business activity — helped by AI. Factory managers “noted stronger sales pipelines, as well as forthcoming investment spending and planned growth in overseas markets,” the S&P report said. “A number of goods producers cited a recent surge in orders related to data center build-outs.” However, there were other causes for concern in the PMI data. Employment shrank again in November, reversing October’s index score — which had been the first increase in more than two years. The UK’s growth this year has failed to drive more hiring, and the survey showed some firms shedding jobs in an effort to boost productivity. Input prices climbed at a slower pace than the previous month but remain elevated at 68.3, while the sub-index for output price growth slid modestly from 57.3 to 56.6. “The combination of resilient output growth and stubbornly elevated inflation meanwhile makes another rate hike by the Bank of England at its December meeting a near certainty, and raises the likelihood of another hike in February,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. (By Julian Harris)

artigo.texto: US company to invest $117 mln in battery storage project in central Vietnam U.S.-based Arbin Energy LLC will invest $117 million in a factory producing battery energy storage systems and battery testing equipment at the Danang Hi-Tech Park in Danang city, central Vietnam. The Danang Hi-Tech Park and Industrial Zones Authority (DSEZA) has approved the investment policy and Arbin Energy LLC as the investor for the Arbin Energy Danang Factory project. The project will cover 5.34 hectares at the Danang Hi-Tech Park, with total investment exceeding VND3.05 trillion ($117 million). The factory will focus on manufacturing battery energy storage systems (BESS), battery testing equipment and machinery used in battery production. Its BESS production line will have a designed capacity of 5,000 containers per year, equivalent to 5 GWh annually. The project will add energy storage equipment manufacturing to the hi-tech park's industrial portfolio and create opportunities to connect with supply chains involving companies in power electronics, measurement and automation. Construction is scheduled to begin in December 2026, with production expected to start in the third quarter of 2028. With the latest project, the Danang Hi-Tech Park has attracted a total of 14 foreign direct investment (FDI) projects, with combined registered capital of $830.5 million. In September 2026, during a working visit to the United States, Chairman of the Danang People's Committee Nguyen Manh Hung held a meeting with Arbin Instruments, chaired by its chairman, Chaojiong Zhang. The two sides discussed and updated the company's investment plans in Danang, focusing on project scale, technology, products, infrastructure requirements and implementation timelines. In addition to manufacturing operations, the discussions covered potential cooperation in research and development (R&D), technical training and partnerships with universities and technology companies in the city. The two sides also reviewed investment procedures and agreed on the next steps for implementation. Founded in 1991, Arbin Instruments is headquartered and operates its manufacturing facilities in College Station, Texas, in the United States. Over its 35 years of operations, the company has grown into one of the world's leading manufacturers of battery testing equipment and energy storage system testing solutions. Its core business focuses on researching, designing and manufacturing high-precision battery testing equipment, electric vehicle battery pack testing systems, solutions for industrial-scale battery production, and software systems for data management and analysis. According to the company, its equipment systems are currently used in more than 55 countries. In addition to its approximately 6,000-square-meter headquarters and manufacturing complex in Texas, Arbin Instruments has expanded its operations to Germany, China, India, South Korea, Vietnam and other markets. Its customers include electric vehicle manufacturers, battery producers, consumer electronics companies, universities and research institutes worldwide. In Vietnam, Arbin Energy LLC was established in August 2026, with its registered office at Lot A10, Danang Hi-Tech Park, Lien Chieu ward. The company has initial charter capital of VND52.14 billion ($2 million), and is wholly owned by Chaojiong Zhang, a U.S. citizen born in 1945, who also serves as its chairman. As of August 2026, the United States was one of Danang's key investment partners, with 87 FDI projects worth more than $346 million, ranking seventh among more than 70 countries and territories investing in the city. With support from U.S. diplomatic missions and investment promotion programs, Da Nang has gradually established ties with several leading global technology corporations, including Synopsys, Marvell, Nvidia and Qualcomm. artigo.texto: Trending The cost of state and local state tax breaks for data centers in Ohio is skyrocketing, according to one non-profit group, and has cost the state's public schools $374 million annually. Ohio started granting the state and local sales tax exemptions in 2013 for data center purchases of equipment and construction materials, according to the study by Policy Matters Ohio, a progressive think operating in Cleveland and Columbus. Other groups, however, support the limited use of sales tax incentives with negotiated community benefits. When the tax exemptions were first enacted, "they were designed for an earlier era of smaller data centers and are ill-equipped for the explosion of hyperscale facilities across the state," according to the study. "Since then, the state has signed agreements with the largest technology companies - Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft." Amazon's exemption, according to the study, was signed in 2014 and lasts for the next 40 years. "When the contract was signed, the state agreed to provide Amazon with an estimated $77 million in sales tax breaks in exchange for $1.1 billion in investment," the study states. "In late 2024, the company announced an additional $10 billion investment and said it would invest a total of $23 billion by 2029." But with increased investment comes higher tax breaks. Policy Matters Ohio estimated the actual Amazon subsidy might be 20 times more expensive than originally estimated. Earlier this year, Gov. Mike DeWine directed the Ohio Tax Credit Authority to suspend any new data center tax exemptions. “I fully support the Ohio General Assembly’s work to study the issue and bring forward facts about data centers, including the local benefits to communities when tax exemptions are granted,” DeWine said in a statement. In its study, Policy Matters Ohio calls for making the governor's temporary pause permanent. Ohio currently has 262 data centers, according to the website DataCenterMap. The Buckeye Institute, a conservative think tank in Columbus, supports the sales tax exemptions for goods used in manufacturing, Greg Lawson, institute senior research fellow, told The Center Square. "This is because a sales tax should only be applied at the point of sale of the final good or service," Lawson said. "If you apply it to intermediate goods used to make a final good or service you effectively raise the price of that good or service. This applies to data centers as well because servers and other equipment used inside are not the final good or service, data storage or AI training is. Thus, the sales tax would increase these costs." But he added the tax breaks "deserve hard scrutiny" because they shift costs onto residents. "They should be used sparingly and if they are used, they should be limited in size and length, and communities should negotiate direct benefits, such as payments to the community, before construction begins," Lawson said.
