artigo.texto: City Council locks out data centers for 90 days to craft a plan to deal with them QUINCY — The Quincy City Council on Monday put up a temporary “closed for business” sign for any data center companies that might be eying the city. Mayor Linda Moore said as of Monday, the city has not received any applications for a data center, but she noted that she has heard about conversations that have been happening with landowners. In an effort to get ahead of any inevitable applications, the council passed a 90-day moratorium on the applications to give the council a chance to put plans in place requirements that the city would have before a center could even be considered. Moore noted that with solar farms, the city was behind the curve and had to fight after the fact to make changes in city ordinances while trying to meet the requirements put forth by state regulators. One takeaway from the discussion was the belief that data centers are inevitable. Moore noted that any data center built anywhere in the country between Washington D.C. and Quincy will impact the power grid that feeds this region, and so Quincy needs to consider what benefits can be gained in exchange for the inevitable costs. “They’re going to suck our power off the grid,” Moore said. “We’re all on the same grid, so if they’re going to suck the power and raise our rates, why not at least get the economic benefits of them?” Moore said her administration has already been working behind the scenes to try and determine what requirements the city could impose, including zoning requirements, setbacks from neighbors, sound-level controls, and landscaping to name a few. With the 90-day moratorium imposed, Moore anticipates having enough time to get additional information collected such as power-usage information from Ameren Illinois and reviews of other municipalities regulations to see what can be applied to Quincy. Aldermen will have a chance to weigh in before any ordinance is submitted to the city’s Plan Commission. If approved by the Plan Commission, the council will then have three readings of a new ordinance to make final adjustments. The moratorium was on the agenda for the first of three readings on Monday, but aldermen voted to waive the requirement for three readings and passed the moratorium on a vote of 13-0 with Ald. Mike Adkins, R-3, being absent. The council also approved a bid from Leander Construction of Canton, Ill. for the addition of two more pumps into the system at the city’s water treatment plant. At a cost of just over $1.53 million, Director of Public Works Jeffrey Conte said the pumps will reduce the city’s electric bill at the treatment plant by as much as 35% because the pumps being installed are more efficient, though they are also more vulnerable to flooding inside the facility caused by high rain volumes or other events. Conte said the newer pumps that are able to withstand flooding better have proven to be robust in those situations, but he noted they’re not as efficient in their power usage. This new project should provide the plant with strong redundancies while reducing power usage in ordinary operation. A new ordinance up for consideration Monday would see changes put in place in regard to the city’s garbage collection. The changes would eliminate the garbage sticker programs effective as of March 1 and would increase rates for the standard tote from $12.99 per month to $15 per month while the smaller totes offered would have a cost of $10 per month. Conte told the council at the new rates, the city would still subsidize the garbage operations at a rate of around $450,000 in the next fiscal year. He said the break-even point that would eliminate a need for a subsidy right now would be $20 per month for the full-size totes and around $16.50 for the smaller totes, both costs that would still be lower than private-hauler costs. The new ordinance, if passed, would also require private contractors to adjust their pick-up schedules to match the city’s schedules so that residents aren’t dealing with garbage collections from different companies nearly every day of the week.

artigo.texto: If you've spent any time in Statesboro lately, you've probably heard somebody talking about the proposed data center on Burkhalter Road. Depending on who you ask, it's either the best thing that could happen to our community or the worst. One side sees jobs, investment, tax revenue, and a seat at the table in a rapidly changing economy. The other sees questions about water use, power consumption, noise, property values, and whether an industrial-scale operation belongs so close to residential neighborhoods. [wjcl.com], [griceconnect.com] Before I go any further, let me say something that may disappoint everyone. I don't have a horse in this race. I'm not a developer. I'm not a politician. I'm not a spokesperson for the project. I'm not carrying a protest sign against it. I'm just a citizen watching neighbors argue with neighbors about what kind of town Statesboro wants to become. And frankly, that's the part of this discussion that interests me most. Because long after the lawyers finish their work, long after the engineers submit their reports, and long after the council casts its votes, we'll still be neighbors. We'll still sit beside one another in church. We'll still meet in the grocery store. We'll still cheer for the Blue Devils and the Eagles. We'll still call Statesboro home. What strikes me is how quickly modern debates force us into opposing camps. You're either "for growth" or "against growth." You're either "pro-business" or "anti-business." You're either protecting the future or standing in its way. Life is rarely that simple. A person can welcome economic development and still have legitimate concerns. A person can oppose this project without opposing progress. A person can believe the developers are sincere and still ask hard questions. That's not obstruction. That's citizenship. And maybe that's what is getting lost. The real issue isn't whether a data center is good or bad. The real issue is whether we can have an honest conversation about it. Can residents ask questions without being dismissed as alarmists? Can supporters discuss potential benefits without being treated as villains? Can we disagree without assuming the worst about one another? I hope so. Because the future of Statesboro won't be determined solely by a data center. It will be determined by whether we can remain a community when difficult decisions come along. Every growing city eventually faces moments like this. A new industry. A new subdivision. A new highway. A new opportunity. A new risk. Reasonable people look at the same facts and come to different conclusions. That's nothing new. What would be new is forgetting how to listen. I've read enough history to know that today's controversy becomes tomorrow's memory. But the character we display during the controversy lasts much longer. So where do I stand on the Burkhalter Road data center? I stand with the people who are asking questions. I stand with the people who are trying to answer them. I stand with the belief that a community deserves both opportunity and accountability. And beyond that? I don't have a horse in this race. I just happen to live in the town where it's being run. Dr. Charles Cravey has a Bachelor of Science in sociology from Georgia Southern, a master's degree in sacred literature from Trinity Theological Seminary and a doctoral degree in theology from Trinity. In addition to being a retired pastor, Cravey is a writer, photographer, recording artist, songwriter, singer and producer.

artigo.texto: Aurora passes partial data center moratorium as Trident data center cancels site plan Aurora community members advocating for an end to data centers saw major wins during Monday night's Aurora City Council meeting, with the passage of a partial temporary moratorium and the cancellation of plans for one controversial facility. It was another Aurora City Council meeting where data centers took center stage. "We all need clean water to drink, we all need clean air to breathe, how can AI possibly be more important than that? It isn't," one community member said during public comment. "Trident mega data center must not be built in our neighborhood," another community member said. But as passionate neighbors spoke, a major announcement came. "Trident just announced they have abandoned the site next to your neighborhood for the data center," said Peter Schulte, city attorney for Aurora. Cheers erupted from an audience full of neighbors there to speak out against the Trident data center. A City of Aurora spokesperson told CBS Colorado, "Neither City Manager Jason Batchelor, City Attorney Pete Schulte nor other members of the city team were aware of that news until it was reported by various outlets near the start of the meeting." "I'm just grateful that the nightmare is over with and that you prevailed, congratulations," Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman said. "Wow, what an announcement, you know," one community member said during public comment, ripping up their printed speech to cheers and laughs from the audience. But many neighbors still want to see a full data center moratorium. "A moratorium gives us all time to reflect, research and hear from those impacted," one community member said at the meeting. Council took a step in that direction, unanimously passing a moratorium on data centers located west and south of the intersection of I-70 and Powhaton Road, covering much of the city. Only a few attendees spoke against that moratorium. One community member responded to the news, saying, "We ask you to consider the full impact of this decision, including the working families whose livelihoods depend on these opportunities." Councilmembers attribute the moratorium passing and Trident data center reversal to the community members who spoke out. "These people right here are proof that you can make a difference if you use your voice," said Aurora Councilmember Amy Wiles. "Thank you for everyone who voted for this. We have a long road to go, but thank you," one community member said during public comment. That moratorium on new data centers in the south and west parts of Aurora goes into effect immediately and will last through September 2027, or until city council takes further action. Monday night, the council also discussed a proposed ordinance to prohibit future sales tax incentives for data centers.

artigo.texto: Monday public hearing to allow comment on proposed data center ordinance MONDAY PUBLIC HEARING TO ALLOW COMMENT ON PROPOSED DATA CENTER ORDINANCE Planning Commission to consider recommending regulations that would require special use permits for all data centers and establish standards for location, utilities, noise and other impacts. The Dalton-Varnell-Whitfield County Planning Commission will hold a public hearing Monday, Nov. 23, to consider proposed amendments to the Unified Zoning Ordinance establishing regulations for data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities. Whitfield County posted an initial draft of the proposed ordinance on October 12 and invited public comment. The Dalton Daily Citizen has reviewed the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration Monday, including changes from the original draft. The following is a detailed examination of the proposed regulations, what they would require of data center developers and operators, and how the proposal has changed since it was first made available for public review. THE ORDINANCE AT A GLANCE Nine things to know about the proposed data center regulations - No automatic approvals. Every new data center would require a Special Use Permit from the applicable elected governing authority. - Industrial areas only. Small data centers could locate in M-1 or M-2 districts. Large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would be limited to M-2. - Distance requirements. Data centers would have to be separated from homes and other protected locations by 1,000 to 2,000 feet, depending on facility size, with additional property setbacks and landscaping requirements. - Water and electricity. The proposal would limit certain cooling systems, require detailed utility capacity reviews and address who pays for infrastructure improvements. - Noise and construction. Facilities would face noise, vibration, lighting and construction restrictions, including shutdown requirements for uncorrected noise violations. - Public notification. Developers of large, hyperscale and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have to hold community meetings and notify property owners within 2,500 feet. - Emergency planning and reporting. Facilities would need emergency response plans. Larger operations would also have to submit annual reports on water use, electricity demand, generator operations and complaints. - Cleanup guarantees. Developers would have to plan for eventual closure. Larger facilities would need financial guarantees of at least $1 million or 125% of estimated cleanup costs, whichever is greater. - Penalties for violations. Continuing violations could result in fines of up to $1,000 per day, with additional enforcement options. NOTE: These are proposed regulations, not adopted law. The Planning Commission’s Nov. 23 hearing is part of the review process. Elected governing bodies would have to adopt the ordinance before it takes effect. Every data center would require special approval Under the revised ordinance scheduled for consideration at the Nov. 23 Planning Commission meeting, all data centers would require a Special Use Permit and would be allowed only in designated industrial zoning districts. Data centers would not be permitted in residential, agricultural, commercial or other zoning districts. Under the original draft posted on the city website Oct. 12, small data centers would have been permitted by right in M-1 (Light Manufacturing) and M-2 (Heavy Manufacturing) districts, while large data centers would have been permitted by right in M-2 districts. Hyperscale data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities would have required Special Use Permits. The revised proposal eliminates those by-right allowances. Small data centers would still be eligible for consideration in M-1 and M-2 districts, while large and hyperscale facilities and cryptocurrency mining operations would be limited to M-2 districts. However, all would require Special Use approval. The ordinance would not permit data centers in other zoning districts, including residential, agricultural, commercial, Planned Unit Development (PUD), Urban Planned Unit Development (UPUD) and Mixed Use (MU) districts. A Special Use Permit would require review through the Planning Commission and approval by the applicable governing authority, rather than allowing a qualifying facility to proceed solely on the basis of its zoning classification. How data centers would be classified The proposed ordinance establishes three categories of data centers based on building size and electrical demand. Small data centers would have no more than 20,000 square feet of gross floor area and peak electrical demand of no more than 10 megawatts (MW). Both limits would have to be met for a facility to qualify as small. Large data centers would be those that meet neither the definition of a small data center nor that of a hyperscale data center. The revised draft replaces the original definition, which specified facilities with 20,000 to 100,000 square feet of floor area or electrical demand between 10 MW and 50 MW. Hyperscale data centers would be facilities exceeding 100,000 square feet of gross floor area or having peak electrical demand of at least 100 MW. Meeting either threshold would qualify a facility as hyperscale. The original draft established the hyperscale electrical threshold at 50 MW. The revised proposal doubles that threshold to 100 MW while retaining the floor-area threshold of more than 100,000 square feet. The ordinance also defines a data center campus, requiring the aggregate floor area and peak electrical demand of buildings and phases within a common campus to be considered when determining classification. The provisions are intended to prevent developers from avoiding applicable requirements by dividing projects into smaller buildings, parcels or phases. Understanding size and electrical demand Both building size and electrical demand are commonly used to classify data centers

artigo.texto: Após ações judiciais, setor de baterias defende manutenção de leilão Associação de Soluções de Armazenamento afirma que contratações são urgentes e disputas devem ser mantidas nas datas marcadas A Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) defendeu nesta 2ª feira (23.nov.2026) a manutenção dos leilões de baterias em 2 e 4 de dezembro, datas marcadas inicialmente no cronograma de contratações do governo. A manifestação vem em reação a duas ações judiciais contra o certame apresentadas na última semana à Justiça Federal e ao Supremo Tribunal Federal. Ambos os processos foram protocolados pela Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), que pede que a disputa não seja realizada antes da definição das regras sobre o rateio dos custos de contratação das tecnologias. A entidade também questiona a constitucionalidade de um trecho da Lei 15.269 de 2025, que determina que os custos de contratação de reserva de capacidade por meio de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias sejam rateados exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia. Segundo a Absae, a contratação de baterias para o Sistema Interligado Nacional é “urgente” e não pode ser adiada. A associação avalia que as ações judiciais “fazem parte do processo e não alteram essa necessidade” e, portanto, podem ser resolvidas no “campo político” depois de já realizados os leilões. A discussão ocorre enquanto tramita na Câmara o PL 3.716 de 2026, que revoga o trecho da lei questionado pelas eólicas e aplica para as baterias a regra geral de divisão de custo entre todos os consumidores, conforme as demais contratações de reserva de capacidade do sistema elétrico. Caso o texto seja aprovado antes do leilão, a Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) pode ter de rever as regras da disputa, o que pode levar ao adiamento do certame. “Os leilões precisam acontecer nas datas previstas. A contratação é urgente para reforçar a segurança do fornecimento, são apenas 18 meses do certame à operação em agosto de 2028. A discussão sobre os encargos deve avançar, mas não pode impedir os certames”, afirma Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae. A posição vai na contramão do que defendeu a Abeeólica ao pedir o adiamento de todas as etapas do certame, incluindo disputa, adjudicação, homologação e assinatura dos contratos. Segundo a associação, seria impossível para os agentes de geração calcular os riscos e impactos econômicos antes de as regras estarem definidas. ABSAE DEFENDE PROJETO DE LEI Fabio Lima defende que eventuais efeitos do PL 3.716 de 2026 podem ser aplicados mesmo se o texto for aprovado depois do leilão, com as demais etapas da contratação já em andamento. Com isso, a correção alcançaria os contratos da disputa de dezembro e resolveria a controvérsia “na origem”, sem interromper o calendário de contratação, afirma a associação. “A judicialização faz parte do processo, mas não pode adiar uma contratação de que o sistema precisa. Adiar o leilão não elimina a necessidade de potência, só reduz o tempo para atendê-la. A questão do custeio é real e deve ser resolvida no Congresso, e isso pode ser concluído após as sessões públicas, sem prejuízo”, disse Lima. artigo.texto: Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Reset no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O carbono passou a ter preço. Já são 87 impostos e sistemas de comércio de emissões em vigor no mundo, cobrindo 29% das emissões globais. A Europa começou a cobrar pelo carbono embutido nas importações. E o Brasil está regulamentando o seu próprio mercado, o SBCE, que deve estar em plena operação em 2031. O tema se tornou pauta econômica. Hoje influencia decisões de investimento, financiamento e competitividade. Mas, quanto mais ele avança, mais difícil fica entender como as peças se encaixam. - Por que, exatamente, colocar um preço no carbono? - Qual a diferença entre o mercado regulado e o voluntário, e onde eles se cruzam? - Quem será obrigado a reduzir emissões no SBCE, e a partir de quando? - O que são CBE e CRVE? - Como o CBAM europeu e o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris afetam as empresas brasileiras? - Por que um crédito jurisdicional pode valer três vezes mais que um crédito de projeto? O Guia Reset de Mercados de Carbono responde a essas e outras perguntas de forma didática, mas com a profundidade de quem precisa entender esses mercados na prática. Em quatro capítulos, o guia passa pelos sistemas internacionais, pelo mercado regulado brasileiro e pelo mercado voluntário. No fim, mapeia as oportunidades em sete frentes, do Corsia ao setor financeiro. Muitas dessas oportunidades têm prazo. A aviação internacional entra na fase obrigatória do Corsia em 2027. Os créditos florestais brasileiros têm vantagem enquanto as tecnologias de remoção não ganham escala. E as regras do SBCE ainda estão sendo escritas. Quem se posicionar agora tende a influenciar as regras e os preços do que vem depois. O planeta tem pressa, os negócios também. Clique aqui para baixar.

artigo.texto: A weekly roundup of public health news Data center boom could hurt progress fighting air pollution Fifteen years of progress combating climate change in the U.S. could be wiped out in three years as new gas-fired plants are built to power data centers, a new report from the Sierra Club warns. The U.S. has made substantial progress in reducing pollution from electricity generation in recent years, largely by closing coal-fired power plants and expanding renewable energy, according to the Nov. 16 report. Between 2015 and 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from power plants serving the electrical grid fell 22%, for example. That progress is now threatened as large data centers are being built to support artificial intelligence. While some facilities draw electricity from the existing grid, others are developing their own generating stations. More than 550 gas-fired power plants are planned or under construction nationwide, representing a nearly 40% increase in generating capacity, the report said. At least one-third of that new capacity is expected to serve data centers. Just a dozen data center projects with on-site gas plants could annually release nearly 180 million tons of carbon dioxide — a major driver of climate change — along with fine-particle air pollution linked to asthma, heart attacks and strokes. Many data centers operate under permits that limit public review and require little pollution reporting. A bill now making its way through Congress, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, would further weaken review requirements so data centers and their energy sources can be built faster, a move that has been condemned by health advocates. A new poll by the Environmental Protection Network found 88% of U.S. adults support equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers and believe their expansion should not cost Americans their health. High heat linked to premature births, dementia, traffic crashes As climate change increases temperatures across the U.S., new research shows heat is posing risks to health throughout the lifespan. The dangers of heat to human health come even before birth, a Nov. 18 study in JAMA Network Open finds. Exposure to high temperatures during pregnancy was linked with an increased risk of premature birth. Researchers examined more than 12 million births in Brazil between 2015 and 2019, finding high temperatures during the week before delivery were associated with a 14% higher risk of premature birth. Heat exposure earlier in pregnancy also was linked to premature delivery. Researchers suggested that high temperatures may trigger processes involved in labor or interfere with early fetal and placental development. High temperatures also can pose risks to health later in life, an October analysis in Alzheimer’s & Dementia shows. Researchers examined two decades of data on U.S. older adults, finding people who were exposed to more days of dangerously high heat had a 23% higher risk of developing dementia than those with little exposure. People who experienced an average of seven or more days annually in which the heat index reached at least 103 degrees faced the highest risk. The link between extreme heat and dementia was stronger among people in communities with greater socioeconomic disadvantage and less access to central air conditioning. Socioeconomic disadvantage also can play a role in whether people exposed to high heat die from cardiovascular disease, Nov. 18 research in PLOS Climate says. People with heart-related conditions face a greater risk of death when exposed to hotter summers and repeated heat waves, according to an analysis of nearly 64,000 people in the U.K. Risks were greater among people without college degrees and those living in poorer neighborhoods or areas with less green space. For every 1-degree Celsius increase in average summer temperature, the risk of death rose 15%. People exposed to four or more heat waves annually had a 24% higher risk of death than those experiencing two or fewer. Higher temperatures also can influence whether someone dies in a car crash, a new study in the Journal of Urban Health finds. Researchers examined 10 years of data from California, linking extreme heat with increases in the number of crashes and injuries. The most intense heat events were linked to about 180 additional crashes and 100 injuries annually statewide, they estimated. Policies could have long-term consequences for U.S. health Recent federal policy changes could cause lasting damage to the health of the nation, weakening public health agencies and worsening health disparities, a recent study warns. Cuts to healthcare, research, food assistance and public health programs under the Trump administration are impacting U.S. health, with further harms ahead, according to the study in The Lancet Regional Health–Americas. Vulnerable Americans are at highest risk. People with low incomes, rural residents, people of color, immigrants and people with disabilities are expected to face the greatest impacts, researchers said. The policy changes could lead to more illness and preventable deaths, long-term losses in public health capacity and damage to science. Among the most significant recent changes are cuts to Medicaid and new eligibility requirements that could leave millions of Americans without health insurance. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program changes could increase the number of uninsured people by 7.5 million by 2034. Medicaid enrollment had already fallen by 4.8 million people between April 2025 and April 2026, before most of the new requirements took effect. Meanwhile, the expiration of federal subsidies that allowed people to afford health insurance has increased costs and fueled declining enrollment. Rural communities face particular risks as Medicaid funding reductions threaten hospitals and healthcare providers already struggling with financial pressure

artigo.texto: Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has invited bids for the supply of renewable energy from an Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS)-connected generating plant comprising a solar photovoltaic (PV) system and a co-located Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The procurement will be conducted through competitive bidding, followed by an e-reverse auction. The last date for online bid submission is December 10, 2026, at 3 PM. DMRC will open the technical bids on December 11, 2026, at 3 PM. The date for opening financial bids and conducting the e-reverse auction will be announced after the technical evaluation. According to the Request for Selection (RfS) document dated November 19, 2026, the tender carries an earnest money deposit (EMD) of ₹23.9 crore. Selected bidders will have 15 months from the issuance of the Letter of Award (LOA) to complete the work. Bidding Schedule And Requirements DMRC has scheduled the pre-bid meeting for November 26, 2026, at 11 AM at Metro Bhawan, New Delhi. Prospective bidders can submit their queries and seek clarifications until November 27, 2026, at 5 PM. The tender document carries a non-refundable fee of ₹20,000, excluding applicable GST. Bidders must submit their technical and financial proposals through the Central Public Procurement (CPP) portal. The tender security can be submitted through bank guarantee, fixed deposit receipt or electronic payment modes, subject to the conditions specified in the tender document. The bid validity period is 120 days from the last date of submission. Solar And Storage-Based Renewable Power Procurement The tender covers renewable power procurement from an ISTS-connected solar PV generating plant integrated with a co-located BESS. The selection process will involve technical and financial bid evaluations, followed by an e-reverse auction. The procurement brings solar generation and battery storage together under a single renewable power supply arrangement. However, the available bid information sheet does not specify the proposed solar generation capacity, BESS capacity or the contracted power supply duration. The detailed scope of work, qualification requirements, bid evaluation framework and Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) provisions are referenced in the complete RfS documentation.

artigo.texto: Após repercussões em redes sociais e questionamentos levantados por moradores e veículos de comunicação sobre possíveis impactos ambientais e urbanos, a Prefeitura da Estância de Atibaia comunicou oficialmente que não existe nenhum projeto de instalação de data center protocolado na administração municipal para avaliação ou liberação. Ausência de processos técnicos e ambientais Conforme os esclarecimentos do Poder Executivo local, a ausência de pedidos formais significa que não há análises técnicas em andamento nem procedimentos de licenciamento ambiental abertos para contemplar esse perfil de estrutura tecnológica na cidade. A gestão municipal destacou que, no passado, houve apenas uma aproximação informal e de caráter consultivo por parte de interessados no segmento. O contato preliminar, no entanto, não gerou compromissos, tratativas oficiais ou abertura de expedientes administrativos, uma vez que nenhuma documentação foi submetida aos setores competentes. Atratividade logística e exigências legais Situada no entroncamento de duas rodovias estratégicas do Estado de São Paulo, Atibaia registra frequente interesse de empresas dos setores industrial e de tecnologia que buscam expansão. A administração reforçou que eventuais propostas que venham a ser formalizadas no futuro passarão por um rigoroso escrutínio legal. Caso qualquer projeto do gênero venha a ser apresentado, o trâmite exigirá: - Avaliação minuciosa de acordo com a legislação e os ritos administrativos vigentes; - Apreciação técnica pelo Conselho Municipal de Defesa do Meio Ambiente de Atibaia (COMDEMA); - Aprovação e emissão de licenças junto aos órgãos fiscalizadores nas esferas municipal, estadual e federal.

artigo.texto: ZE Energy, a European electricity flexibility provider, has announced the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi battery energy storage system (BESS) project, in the Piedmont region in Italy, from ReFeel New Energy. Fully permitted and ready to build, the 59 MW project will have a storage capacity of up to nearly 480 MWh, equivalent to a duration of up to eight hours. Located in Magliano Alpi, in Piedmont, the project is a standalone BESS connected to the 132 kV high-voltage grid via an existing Terna substation. It will provide the northern Italian grid with long-duration flexibility capacity, able to absorb electricity when generation is abundant and release it during periods of high demand or system stress. In an Italian power system where demand exceeded 300 TWh in 2025, with 15% met by net imports, the accelerated rollout of renewables is increasing the need to connect flexibility systems to the grid. With more than 44 TWh generated in 2025, up 25% y/y, solar PV illustrates this trend: battery storage absorbs surplus energy during production peaks and then releases it to the grid when generation can no longer cover demand. With 59 MW of power and 472 MWh of storage capacity, Magliano Alpi will help balance supply and demand, manage consumption peaks, and keep the northern Italian grid stable. After Sessa Aurunca, in Central-Southern Italy, and Elena, in the South, ZE Energy is expanding and diversifying its Italian portfolio with the acquisition of the Magliano Alpi project, located in the North and sized to meet complementary flexibility needs and markets. This transaction illustrates the company’s ability to source and execute acquisitions of permitted, ready-to-build projects, to which it brings its industrial expertise by integrating the entire value chain (development, engineering, construction, operation). ZE Energy is thus continuing its rollout across Europe, with the goal of reaching 1.5 GW of installed capacity by 2030. Rocco Mauro, Head of M&A and Business Development Italy at ZE Energy, said: “With Magliano Alpi, we are strengthening our presence in Italy through a project that can bring flexibility to the power system, as close as possible to the needs of consumers in the north of the country. “We are delighted to have acquired this project from ReFeel New Energy and would like to commend the quality and constructive spirit of our collaboration throughout this transaction. “Magliano Alpi once again illustrates our ability to grow our portfolio through a strategy of targeted acquisitions, favouring high-quality assets that complement our existing projects and help diversify our geographic footprint. We intend to continue our development in Italy on the basis of this same approach.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. The EU and the UK have finalized negotiations to link their respective emissions trading systems (ETS) effective Jan. 1, 2028. Following Brexit, UK ETS was created in 2021, but there were immediate calls from businesses for the EU ETS and UK ETS to be linked. Negotiations began in late 2025, and a deal was announced at the EU-UK summit on Nov. 20, 2026, in Brussels. “The agreement will ensure that the same set of climate rules related to emissions trading will apply in the EU and the UK,” the European Commission’s Directorate General for Climate Action said on Nov. 20. If the deal is ratified on both sides of the English Channel, it will simplify airline compliance and create a larger market with more stable carbon pricing. The UK will also introduce a “one-stop shop,” so airlines will deal with a single authority for both schemes rather than separate UK and EU regulators. Work is underway to operationalize the agreement, passing any necessary legislation in 2027, with a view to enacting procedures in January 2028. “From this date [Jan. 1, 2028], UK and EU allowances can be used interchangeably across both schemes. The first surrender deadline where UK and EU allowances will be accepted across both schemes will be Sept. 30, 2028, with respect to operators’ obligations for the 2027 compliance year,” the UK government said. The UK ETS and EU ETS will continue to operate as two separate systems, with “dynamic alignment,” and the UK government said it will have an early “decision-shaping role” when the EU develops new EU ETS policies. In July 2026, the European Commission announced plans to extend the EU ETS to cover flights between the EU and non-EU countries within a 5,000 km (3,100 mi.) radius. This drew strong opposition from aviation stakeholders, who see the move as extraterritorial, undermining global efforts through Corsia, the International Civil Aviation Organization’s program to stabilize net CO2 emissions from international flights. The UK Department for Transport acknowledged the draft EU proposal and said it is aligning with “elements” of the EU ETS, including the scope of aviation coverage, to maintain a level playing field. “Both EU and UK ETSs will apply monitoring for aviation’s non-CO2 climate effects,” the European Commission said. The EU ETS has been linked with Switzerland’s ETS since Jan. 1, 2020. This link will remain in place.

artigo.texto: A computational study evaluating multi-carrier microgrids has revealed that integrating battery storage into a hybridized renewable infrastructure can reduce daily operating expenditures by approximately 92.97 percent. The investigation, conducted by researchers Dedacus N. Ohaegbuchi, Oliver Dzobo, and Eniafe Festus Ayetiran and published in the journal Sustainable Energy Research, demonstrates how intelligent scheduling can coordinate electricity, thermal energy, and gas networks under volatile market conditions. Focusing on the complex, continuous operational demands of an abattoir facility, the team modeled an integrated framework uniting solar photovoltaics, combined heat and power cogeneration, a biomass-fueled boiler, absorption chilling, and energy storage systems. Using a stochastic optimization framework based on the nature-inspired Firefly Algorithm, the researchers addressed the severe operational challenges caused by solar intermittency and fluctuating time-of-use electricity tariffs. Their simulation outcomes indicate that coordinated scheduling not only curbs reliance on the conventional power grid but also establishes an economically viable pathway for rural and semi-industrial multi-energy hubs. The core research motivation stems from the operational vulnerabilities of conventional centralized power systems when confronted with expanding multi-carrier energy requirements in rural and semi-industrial sectors. Facilities such as commercial abattoirs require simultaneous and dependable supplies of electrical power, high-temperature thermal energy, and active refrigeration. In conventional setups, meeting these disparate loads independently leads to elevated operational expenses, severe fuel dependency, and heightened carbon footprints, particularly under dynamic utility pricing structures. Combined heat and power systems substantially elevate overall energy efficiency through the simultaneous generation of electricity and usable heat, yet their rigid operating envelopes create significant scheduling bottlenecks when deployed in isolation. Coupling cogeneration machinery with intermittent renewable sources, such as solar photovoltaic panels, further complicates dispatch decisions due to weather-induced generation fluctuations. The researchers recognized that managing these cross-carrier dependencies requires an integrated multi-energy system capable of dynamically routing energy vectors, absorbing surplus generation, and shielding rural commercial operations from peak utility electricity tariffs. To evaluate this multi-energy architecture under rigorous conditions, the authors designed a comprehensive technical model reflecting an industrial abattoir facility. The generation and conversion infrastructure incorporates a 3.5-kilowatt solar photovoltaic array covering a surface area of 25 square meters with an operational efficiency of 18.6 percent. Base thermal and electrical baseloads are supported by a 700-kilowatt combined heat and power unit operating with an electrical conversion efficiency of 35 percent and a thermal efficiency of 40 percent. Supplementary heating is provided by an auxiliary biomass-fired boiler rated at 1000 kilowatts with an efficiency of 90 percent, accompanied by a dedicated gasification unit operating at 80 percent efficiency. To address cooling demands, the system incorporates a 200-kilowatt absorption chiller exhibiting a performance efficiency of 90 percent. Thermal management is handled by a 1000-kilowatt heat exchanger operating at 95 percent efficiency with 5-kilowatt charge and discharge capabilities, while electrical flexibility is governed by a 500-kilowatt-hour battery energy storage system with an initial state of charge of 400 kilowatt-hours, a 50-kilowatt-hour lower limit, and 95 percent round-trip efficiency. The daily economic scheduling problem is formulated as a single-objective mathematical optimization over a twenty-four-hour planning horizon divided into hourly time steps. The objective function minimizes total operational expenditure by aggregating electricity procurement costs from the conventional distribution grid, offsetting them with export revenues from surplus electricity sold back to the utility, and factoring in the fuel costs of natural gas and biomass gas consumption. Specifically, the formulation tracks seven hourly decision variables: power imported from the grid, power exported to the grid, photovoltaic generation utilized, fuel inputs to the combined heat and power unit, fuel consumed by the boiler, biomass-derived gas generation, and battery discharge power. Electricity export tariffs are fixed at 0.29 dollars per kilowatt-hour, while operational maintenance for the solar photovoltaic array and battery discharge degradation are each parameterized at 0.01 dollars per kilowatt-hour. Fuel prices reflect long-term contracts, pricing network natural gas at 0.157 dollars per unit and biomass gas at 4.00 dollars, contrasted against hourly dynamic time-of-use tariffs. Enforcing physical feasibility requires a comprehensive suite of equality and inequality constraints governing energy balances, conversion boundaries, and operational logic across all subsystems. The electrical balance equality constraint mandates that total hourly generation—comprising imported utility electricity, efficiency-adjusted solar generation, electrical cogeneration output, and battery discharging—must precisely match the facility electrical demand of 250 kilowatts plus battery charging and grid export quantities. Similarly, the thermal balance equality ensures that total heat supplied by the cogeneration unit and the boiler matches demand, accounting for heat exchanger power, absorption chiller needs, and thermal energy storage flows. A third equality constraint regulates the gas supply balance between network imports and biomass gasification output. artigo.texto: As Bulgaria sets world records in battery energy storage penetration, the government plans to introduce a tax on revenues generated by battery systems. Although the 5% levy, proposed through the 2027 budget bill, aims to bring in additional funding to shield businesses from high electricity prices, it could also discourage investment in the energy storage sector. The government’s proposal, added just before the 2027 budget bill was submitted to parliament, stipulates that the tax would apply only to standalone battery energy storage systems and remain in force throughout 2027, according to a report by Capital. The revenues would replenish Bulgaria’s Electricity System Security Fund (ESS), which compensates businesses for high electricity prices. The government plans a EUR 2 billion package to help households, businesses, and energy-intensive industries cope with high energy prices, with EUR 1.5 billion coming from the fund and the remaining EUR 500 million from the Bulgarian Development Bank. The 5% levy could bring in tens of millions of euros annually Based on recent output and prices, Capital calculated that the 5% levy on standalone batteries would bring in between EUR 28 million and EUR 30 million annually. However, new battery projects are expected to increase average daily output by 20% in 2027, boosting the amount to between EUR 34 million and EUR 36 million. In October, the overall operating power of battery systems in Bulgaria reached 6.23 GW, compared to 5.41 GW in mid-August and 3.43 GW before the end of May, according to data from the Electricity System Operator (ESO). Strong pushback from the sector Although the government’s proposal has yet to be debated in parliament, it is already facing strong opposition from the sector. Dimitar Beleliev, chairman of the Bulgarian Association of Electrical Engineering and Electronics (BASEL), said the group “categorically opposes” the idea, noting that “batteries do not produce electricity, but help balance it and use it more efficiently.” The tax could put the brakes on projects planned for 2027 Investors in some of the largest battery portfolios have told Capital that the new levy could lead to an outflow of projects scheduled for the end of 2027. According to them, the fact that it would be charged on revenues rather than profits is even more worrying. The Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity (APSTE) also strongly opposes the proposal, pointing out that about EUR 3 billion has been invested in battery systems in Bulgaria in the last two years alone.

artigo.texto: Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh BESS capacity pipeline Key highlights - Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. - Six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, led by a 900 MW/1,800 MWh Maharashtra project. - Four named hybrid projects disclose a combined 450 MWh of storage capacity. - Oriana Power reports more than 1.8 GW of solar energy assets alongside its BESS portfolio. powered by IRIS Oriana Power Limited reports over 2.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity, including commissioned, under-construction and allocated projects. Its six named BESS awards total 2.45 GWh, while four named hybrid projects disclose a further 450 megawatt-hours (MWh) of storage whose inclusion in the headline total is not specified. Know Oriana Power inside out Results, valuation, peers and who's buying, in one view. What BESS capacity does Oriana Power report? Oriana Power reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity on its storage page. The presentation states that this figure includes commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but does not split the total between those project stages. One GWh equals 1,000 MWh, so the stated portfolio is above 2,700 MWh. Oriana Power describes BESS as a system that stores surplus solar and wind energy and releases it during periods of peak demand or grid fluctuation. The company says this time-shifting mechanism supports grid stabilisation, system reliability, asset utilisation and continuity of supply for industrial and commercial users. These are intended functions of the storage product rather than reported operating results. The 2.7-GWh figure is expressed as energy capacity, whereas power capacity is stated in megawatts (MW). This distinction matters because the presentation lists the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited BESS award as 900 MW and 1,800 MWh, showing both the rate at which a system can discharge and the amount of energy it can store. How large are Oriana Power's named BESS awards? Oriana Power's six named BESS awards total 2,450 MWh, or 2.45 GWh, based on the capacities shown for each project. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited accounts for 1,800 MWh, while the other five listed awards range from 100 MWh to 250 MWh. Oriana Power's Maharashtra award represents about 73% of the 2,450 MWh total across the six named awards. The four 50 MW projects for Rajasthan, Telangana, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu each provide 100 MWh, or two hours of storage at their stated power rating, and together account for 400 MWh. The NTPC Vidyut Vyapar award is also specified as a two-hour system, at 125 MW and 250 MWh. The 2.45-GWh sum of the named awards is at least 250 MWh below Oriana Power's over-2.7-GWh BESS headline. The presentation does not identify the projects or stages accounting for that difference, and does not state contract values, ownership structures, commissioning dates or revenue terms for these awards. Got a follow-up? Ask IRIS Which Oriana Power hybrid projects include battery storage? Oriana Power lists four hybrid projects with 450 MWh of explicitly stated storage capacity: 300 MWh for SECI, 100 MWh for Wonder Cement Limited, 20 MWh for JKCL Gottan and 30 MWh for JKCL Gujarat. The presentation presents these as individual hybrid project entries rather than as a separate aggregate storage portfolio figure. The SECI entry combines 100 MW with 50 MW/300 MWh, making its 300 MWh storage component the largest among the four disclosed hybrid projects. Wonder Cement is listed as 65.5 MW plus 100 MWh, without a separate battery power rating. JKCL Gottan is listed at 27 MW plus 10 MW/20 MWh, while JKCL Gujarat is listed at 50 MW plus 15 MW/30 MWh. Oriana Power defines its hybrid offering as Solar+Wind, Solar+BESS and Wind+BESS configurations. The company says combining complementary generation profiles with storage where applicable is intended to raise annual energy yield, smooth output relative to single-technology plants, and use land, transmission infrastructure and common balance-of-plant more efficiently. The presentation does not say whether the 450 MWh in named hybrid projects is included in the over-2.7-GWh BESS figure, so the two amounts should not be added together. How does BESS fit within Oriana Power's project portfolio? Oriana Power places its over-2.7-GWh BESS capacity alongside more than 1.8 gigawatts (GW) of solar energy assets. Both figures include commissioned, under-construction and allocated capacity, but they measure different things: the solar figure is generating power capacity in GW, while the BESS figure is stored energy capacity in GWh. The solar project list includes 234 MW for Damodar Valley Corporation, 128 MW for Dalmia Cement, 100 MW for Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited and 52 MW for Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited therefore appears in both portfolios, with a 100 MW solar project and the 900 MW/1,800 MWh BESS award. Oriana Power says it creates a separate special-purpose vehicle (SPV) for every project because customers, states, lenders and contract terms can differ. The company says each SPV has its own approvals, grid connectivity, lender security and cash flows, while different commercial operation dates, loan tenors and repayment schedules can be tracked over 15 to 25 years. The presentation does not identify which SPVs hold the reported BESS or hybrid capacities. Conclusion Oriana Power's presentation shows storage as a substantial disclosed business line alongside more than 1.8 GW of solar assets. The company reports over 2.7 GWh of BESS capacity, while the six named BESS awards add to 2.45 GWh and four named hybrid projects specify 450 MWh. artigo.texto: To give Borough staff time to look into what potential impact data centers could have on Petersburg, the Assembly has been considering a moratorium on issuing permits for the facilities. Last week, assembly members voted 5–2 to broaden the proposed moratorium, so it would apply to “all” data center development. Originally, the temporary freeze was aimed at “certain” projects — data centers that would use uncontained cooling systems, require more power than allowed, or rely on generators instead of Petersburg’s power grid. The Petersburg community has mixed feelings about data centers. The moratorium’s authors are especially concerned about the potential for off-grid operation. Utility Director Steve Harbour, who helped author the ordinance, testified at a public hearing for the moratorium in mid-November. “I don’t know the right answer. I don’t know how we all feel morally on the data center issue. But I do know none of us wants generators running 24/7, and that’s the purpose of this ordinance, and keeping our water clean,” he said. Harbour said the Borough can work on addressing big picture questions, but needs the moratorium in the meantime. “It’s not perfect, and I agree that there’s a lot of mixed emotions and feelings in town. I’ve talked to people that think [a data center could] be good to help with rates. I’ve talked to many that think it’s bad,” he added. “We can have all sorts of public meetings and all that to decide. But we should do that after we pass this ordinance.” Now, that measure is being revised so that the moratorium would apply to “all” data center development, regardless of whether a project runs off or on the local power grid, or what kind of cooling system it uses. Assembly Member Jeff Meucci pitched the amendment. “I think if we’re going to take a moratorium, we’re going to take a real moratorium, and stop any kind of additional building permits for any kind of data center,” Meucci said. Meucci said he didn’t think the moratorium as-written would be broad enough. “I’m afraid that by having a moratorium with leaving a door open, it kind of leaves us exposed,” he said. “I think it’s the Assembly’s responsibility to pass good policy, not to do policy based on a looming threat that is out there.” Meucci proposed the change in previous meetings; it didn’t get enough Assembly support, until now. “I like it. It gives us time, and I will be voting yes,” said Assembly Member James Valentine. Even before the amendment was on the table, Valentine said he wanted the moratorium because there has been a lot of talk, without much clarity to act upon. “I want to add all these protections for us, but we haven’t seen anything in front of us to actually, like, work with,” Valentine said. “At least one moratorium, to start, gives us a breath … so we can actually work on something instead of just talk.” “This has gotten tougher and tougher as time goes on,” said Assembly Member Bob Martin. “I’m becoming more open to the full moratorium. But I still think the biggest open door here, as Member Meucci referenced, is diesel generation.” Martin said he was concerned that broadening the moratorium at this point in the process would be a “big change” without a lot of time to vet the legality. “But, I have noticed public sentiment is heading in the direction of a full moratorium. So I think I’m going to vote for the amendment,” Martin added. But not all assembly members support the change. The Borough Utility has guardrails, like power sale agreements, that protect Petersburg’s grid; but an off-grid facility that runs on diesel generators could technically bypass those protections. Vice Mayor Jeigh Stanton Gregor proposed the original moratorium, focusing on “certain” projects like that, to address the community’s “biggest vulnerabilities.” Weighing in on whether to broaden the moratorium, Stanton Gregor said the change would be unnecessary. “I think the amendment is a solution in search of a problem. I won’t be supporting it,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a necessary thing, given the protections we already have in place. My biggest concern was insulating ourselves from off-grid threats to our community.” Mayor Bob Lynn was also against the amendment. He is the board chair of Southeast Alaska Power Agency, the wholesale hydropower supplier that specifically feeds three communities in the region. As each community has authority to make decisions about proposed projects concerning the town’s power grid, Lynn said he, too, didn’t see the point of broadening the moratorium to apply to on-grid projects. “I’m gonna vote against [the amendment], but there’s still a lot of work to be done, and it’s not going to stop because I know that, from both Ketchikan and Wrangell’s perspective, they’re looking at large loads,” Lynn said. “All of us are going to be looking for power, and all of us are going to be looking to the future of what we can do. So I’m going to vote no, but … we have a lot of work ahead of us, no matter which way it goes.” The Assembly approved the amendment, with Lynn and Stanton Gregor voting against. But the Assembly agreed that there’s still more work to be done. “I think this [amendment] kind of closes the gap. Now, there’s still going to be a ton of work to do until the moratorium expires. We can’t just put this to bed and say we’re good,” said Assembly Member Donna Marsh. “We’ve got to examine every possible scenario, so that we can respect public testimony and public opinion.” The overall ordinance passed unanimously, 7–0, in its second reading. The measure will require one more round of Assembly approval before it can take effect. For now, it’s too early to tell exactly what the updated moratorium will look like, as Borough staff work on a revised version before it is considered once again at the next assembly meeting, which happens Nov. 30 at 6:00 p.m. There will be another public hearing for the proposed moratorium, as amended, during that meeting.

artigo.texto: SiTime Targets Data Center Bandwidth Upgrades with Two New Clock Families The company’s new FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families are aimed at surging AI data center bandwidth demands following its strategic acquisition of Renesas timing business. SiTime has announced the the launch of its FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 product families, targeting the surging demand for high-bandwidth clocking solutions in artificial intelligence (AI) and data center networks. The launch follows SiTime’s strategic acquisition of Renesas’s timing business, positioning the company to address a serviceable addressable market (SAM) estimated at $2 billion. These new clock generators and jitter attenuators are designed to meet the rigorous demands of next-generation networking equipment, including 224G SerDes and PCIe Gen7 architectures. To learn more about the news, we spoke with Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime. Jeff Child, All About Circuits’s Editor-in-Chief and Piyush Sevalia, Executive Vice President, Chief Business Officer at SiTime at Electronica 2026. The Bandwidth Challenge in AI Data Centers The explosive growth of AI workloads is driving an insatiable need for bandwidth within data centers. As GPUs become increasingly powerful and expensive, minimizing their idle time is critical for economic efficiency. “You’ve got to keep the GPUs busy because they are so expensive,” said Sevalia. “And so there is a major upgrade happening in networking both on the Ethernet side as well as on the interconnect side.” This constant pressure for faster data movement is forcing a doubling of bandwidth every two years. Current top-of-rack switches and smart NICs are transitioning to 224G SerDes per lane for Ethernet connectivity, while server motherboards and accelerator interconnects are moving to PCIe Gen7, which doubles the bandwidth of Gen6 to 128 GT/s. These high-speed standards demand extremely low-jitter clocking sources to ensure signal integrity, prevent bit-error rates from climbing, and avoid costly retransmits that degrade system performance. Where the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 (VC9) clock devices fit in in AI data center designs. FemtoClock 4: Targeting 224G SerDes Top-of-Rack Switches The FemtoClock 4 family (which includes the RC38616, RC38412, RC32418, and RC32412 variants) is aimed squarely at the demanding top-of-rack and spine switch market. According to SiTime, a modern Ethernet switch ASIC can require more than 40 clocks, a number that is only expected to grow. To address this density, the FemtoClock 4 architecture is highly integrated. The flagship RC38616 model, packaged in a compact 10 mm x 10 mm 144-BGA, features: - Up to six independent frequency domains: This allows a single device to synchronize multiple distinct domains within a complex system. - 18 differential output pairs: These outputs can be configured for various signaling standards (CML, LVDS, HCSL, or LVCMOS). - Ultra-low phase jitter: The device delivers an impressive 19 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (measured from 12 kHz to 20 MHz with a 4 MHz high-pass filter) in clock generator mode. The challenge of packing this much functionality into a single die is managing internal crosstalk. “When you have so many different PLLs, there’s a lot of noise in the system. You’ve got to make sure that the noise is isolated,” said Sevalia. “Otherwise, it’s going to creep into the outputs as jitter. And when you’re trying to meet the jitter spec sub 50cond jitter spec for 224G that’s not easy.” The FemtoClock 4 leverages four generations of architectural refinement to isolate internal noise, ensuring solid performance even under noisy power supply conditions typical of dense server environments. FemtoClock 4 (left), VersaClock 8 (right) VersaClock 8: PCIe Gen7 Clocking for Computing and Interconnects Complementing the FemtoClock 4 is the VersaClock 8 family (including the RC31312A, RC31309A, and RC31305A), which is designed for motherboard interconnects, smart NICs, network accelerators, and storage applications relying on PCIe. VersaClock 8 devices are highly flexible, programmable clock generators that offer: - PCIe Gen7 Compliance: They deliver an outstanding 10 fs reference clock jitter, well below the requirements for PCIe Gen7, providing significant timing margin for designers. - Low Phase Jitter: The devices achieve 30 fs RMS phase jitter at 312.5 MHz (12 kHz to 20 MHz, 4 MHz high-pass filter). - Compact Footprint: Available in 5-, 9-, and 12-output variants in QFN packages as small as 4x4 mm. SiTime claims the 12-output variant is roughly 40% smaller than comparable solutions. - High-Temperature Operation: The low-power architecture reduces self-heating, allowing operation up to 105°C board temperature, a crucial feature for densely packed computing boards. The architecture includes a single PLL and fractional output dividers, allowing the generation of up to three distinct frequency domains from a single chip. It supports both Common Clock (CC) and Independent Reference (IR) PCIe clock architectures and can store up to 18 configurations in its internal One-Time Programmable (OTP) memory. A Unified Timing Portfolio With the integration of the Renesas timing business, SiTime is pitching itself as a comprehensive "one-stop-shop" for data center timing. While the FemtoClock 4 and VersaClock 8 handle the complex clock generation and distribution, SiTime’s core MEMS oscillators (such as its TCXOs) provide the fundamental, ultra-stable synchronization pulses required across the network. “Nobody else has that kind of diversity of portfolio,” said Sevalia. “And so it simplifies the customer's job to just buy from us and get everything in place and then move on to the next big problem they have to solve.” Looking ahead, SiTime plans to further integrate these technologies. artigo.texto: Sri Lanka has launched its first comprehensive national facility dedicated to testing modern battery technologies, providing specialised testing services for local manufacturers, importers and technology developers through an investment of approximately Rs. 161.5 million. The Centre for E-Mobility and Battery Technology was officially inaugurated on Monday (23) at the National Engineering Research and Development Centre of Sri Lanka (NERDC), under the patronage of Science and Technology Minister Prof. Chrishantha Abeysena, the Department of Government Information (DGI) said. The facility is expected to improve access to specialised testing services for local manufacturers, importers, researchers and technology developers, while supporting domestic product development and increasing local value addition. According to the DGI, the centre was established to expand Sri Lanka’s testing capabilities beyond conventional battery assessments to cover modern battery technologies. Its services include evaluating the performance, capacity, durability and safety of different battery types and battery systems. The facility will also conduct assessments of battery performance under varying environmental conditions and tests on electric vehicle charging equipment, among other specialised services. Of the total investment of Rs. 161.5 million, Rs. 118 million has been provided through the Government’s National Quality Infrastructure (NQI) Strengthening Project, while NERDC has contributed the remaining Rs. 43.5 million from its own funds. The DGI said the initiative represents a step towards strengthening the country’s quality infrastructure and supporting Sri Lanka’s transition to electric mobility and renewable energy technologies.

artigo.texto: A New York City-based developer formalized its plans for the “Project Valley View” data center campus this month in Archbald. PNK Group submitted a conditional use application for two nearly 300,000-square-foot data centers on Archbald Heights Road in the borough’s portion of the Valley View Business Park, officially raising Archbald’s total proposed data centers to 53, though 32 of those data centers — Project Scott and Wildcat Ridge — are tied up in appeals. The borough marked the application as received Nov. 17 on its website. Out of the 53 data centers proposed throughout the borough, PNK Group’s is the first campus slated for the business park in Archbald’s general industrial zoning district, known as an I-2 zone. Project Valley View will be roughly across the street and southeast of Chewy’s warehouse in the business park. The developer also announced on its dedicated project website and through social media ads that it will hold an open house Dec. 8 from 5 to 7 p.m. inside one of the warehouses it developed in the Jessup portion of the Valley View Business Park at 21 Alberigi Drive. The open house will include site plans, renderings and information on the approval process. The developer will have engineers and specialists available to discuss power, noise, water, emergency planning and construction, according to the website, which encourages residents to ask questions and leave comments. “Some details are settled, and others, including acoustic modeling and final site design, are still being studied,” PNK Group wrote on its website. “We’ll be clear about which is which. If we can’t answer a question that night, we’ll follow up, and we’ll post a summary of what we heard at valleyview.pnk.group.” About the application In a conditional use application prepared by engineering firm Kimley-Horn, PNK Group describes two one-story data centers referred to as Building 1 and Building 2. The first data center is approximately 282,471 square feet; the second is approximately 269,691 square feet. An attached will-serve letter from PPL Electric Utilities confirms the utility has the capacity to power Project Valley View with about 300 megawatts of electricity slated for the third quarter of 2029. The campus will have a total of 144 emergency backup diesel generators and 144 chillers to cool its computer hardware, divided into 72 per building, according to PNK Group’s application and accompanying sound study. The campus will also have a roughly 146,360-square-foot substation, two approximately 35,000-square-foot storage buildings and a 1,200-square-foot command center building. There will be two secured entrances and two emergency entrances for first responders, with access coming off Archbald Heights Road. “The Project will not substantially negatively change the character of any surrounding residential neighborhood,” PNK wrote in its application. “The Project is located within the industrial and commercial setting of the Valley View Business Park, which includes high-intensity operations such as Amazon and Chewy, and is expected to generate fewer employee trips and less routine heavy-truck traffic than logistics and distribution uses.” The sound study modeled noise at 12 different receptors throughout the borough, with the nearest residence being more than a mile away at the end of Pike Street. Noise at the residence would be 35.8 dBA during normal operations and 40.3 dBA during an emergency with all 144 generators running, according to the study. The preliminary study also notes that it will consider neighboring Jessup’s noise restrictions. Jefferson Twp. also borders the site to the south, but the township does not have applicable noise standards, according to the sound study. As PNK Group selects its actual equipment, it will “confirm consistency, evaluate whether tonal or pulsating components are present, and determine whether low-frequency noise would be readily distinguishable above measured background conditions,” according to the application. Throughout conditional use hearings for other projects, residents have raised concerns over the impacts of low-frequency and tonal noises from data centers. “If final equipment sound levels exceed the modeled assumptions, the analysis should be updated, and reasonable and feasible mitigation may need to be incorporated as necessary,” PNK Group wrote. Zoning background PNK Group’s site falls into one of four overlay districts that former council members approved in November 2025 to permit data centers as conditional uses. The other overlays span the Wildcat Ridge, Project Scott and Project Green Mountain data center campuses. Residents have advocated for council to limit data centers to industrial land east of the Casey Highway, which would include the site of PNK’s proposed 125.29-acre campus. Archbald is in the midst of further restricting data centers with an amended zoning ordinance that would remove the majority of those overlays, limiting proposals exclusively to land within the Valley View Business Park. PNK Group previously developed two warehouses in the Jessup portion of the business park: a 255,776-square-foot warehouse on Valley View Drive and the 162,907-square-foot warehouse on Alberigi Drive where it will hold its open house. PNK also purchased land in Moosic in July for a 460,000-square-foot warehouse on Davis Street. PNK owns its data center properties under the limited liability companies DC VV and DC VV1. Earlier this month, the developer transferred a 44.47-acre lot it owns in the business park from its PNK P1 LLC to DC VV1 for $4 million. PNK P1 acquired its first Lackawanna County property — the property it transferred to DC VV1 — in February 2024 from the Scranton Lackawanna Industrial Building Company, or SLIBCO, for $3.3 million, according to a property transaction recorded Feb. 8, 2024. Cancel anytime. - Exclusive access to training across business and policy topics - Direct access to industry leaders at Eco-Business events - A seat among the decision makers shaping the region's sustainable development The country endorsed the Antalya Statement on Mobilising Private Finance for Climate Action and joined the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The statement backs a policy playbook to help governments increase demand for high-integrity carbon credits and attract private investment into climate action. It stresses that companies should use credits alongside – not instead of, or to delay – sustained emissions cuts. The commitments follow President Ferdinand Marcos Jr’s order to develop the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework through Executive Order No. 127, signed on 13 October 2026. The order directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to develop national rules for voluntary carbon markets and international trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. John Leo Algo, National Coordinator of Aksyon Klima, described the commitments as signals of the government’s determination to complete its carbon market framework and attract private investment. At a press briefing after the climate conference, he linked the search for alternative funding to what he described as a “stalemate” in climate finance negotiations at COP31. The talks ended without substantive agreement on delivering public climate finance, leaving key funding disputes unresolved. “[The Philippine government] is really keen on tapping into all possible sources of finance and other means of support, so that’s why they’re really going into the private sector investments [for carbon markets],” said Algo, also the lead coordinator for all Philippine civil society organisation delegates at the UN climate conference. The endorsements also offer opportunities to build international partnerships and strengthen the institutions needed to implement carbon markets, he added. “ ‘[The Philippine government] is really keen on tapping into all possible sources of finance and other means of support, so that’s why they’re really going into the private sector investments [for carbon markets].’ John Leo Algo, National Coordinator, Aksyon Klima Carbon credit projects already operate in the Philippines through independent voluntary standards. Singapore-based KenEco’s MinTrees programme in Mindanao, for instance, has secured credits under Verra’s standards rather than a Philippine national crediting system. Algo argued that the domestic framework must clarify what “high integrity” means in the Philippine context. “The release of the carbon market policy framework would be very critical to really defining what high integrity means,” he said. Cheng Pagulayan, Climate Justice Portfolio Manager at Oxfam Pilipinas, said attracting investment must not overshadow the rights of communities affected by carbon projects. “Any investments or involvement in carbon markets must be anchored on equity, on justice, and safeguarding of communities,” he said in the same press briefing, adding that civil society would continue pressing those demands as it examines the new commitments. Pagulayan criticised the prominence given to carbon markets at COP31, arguing that they distracted from climate justice and the responsibility of developed countries to provide climate finance. He pointed to Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which requires developed countries to provide financial resources to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt to climate change.

artigo.texto: A Anatel aprovou R$ 375 milhões para um data center de inteligência artificial que a Telebras vai operar, em acórdão publicado em 18 de novembro. A agência exigiu que a fonte do dinheiro para manter o equipamento seja definida antes de qualquer contrato. O Acórdão 325/2026 foi aprovado pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel em 4 de novembro. A decisão foi publicada 14 dias depois, liberando o valor para um data center com carga elétrica inicial de 2 megawatts e consumo teórico de até 17.520 megawatts-hora por ano. A EAF, Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz, banca a obra com o saldo do 5G. Depois, ela transfere a estrutura à União e fica proibida de explorar o data center, prestar serviço de IA a terceiros ou ceder capacidade a empresas privadas. À Telebras cabem, depois de pronto, as despesas de energia, manutenção, atualização tecnológica, segurança e suporte. A estatal fechou os primeiros nove meses de 2026 com prejuízo de R$ 90,7 milhões. Recebeu também R$ 169,9 milhões em subvenções do governo no mesmo período. Sem as subvenções, o Ebitda ajustado da Telebras seria negativo em R$ 32,9 milhões no período, segundo o balanço da empresa. Pelos mesmos números, a estatal passa a arcar com os custos permanentes do data center em um período em que ainda depende de subvenção federal para apresentar resultado positivo. O governo vem reduzindo o apoio ano a ano, dentro de um plano de sustentabilidade de cinco anos assinado com o Ministério das Comunicações em 2025. A subvenção cai de R$ 256,3 milhões em 2026 para R$ 86,3 milhões em 2029. Publicidade Só com essa trajetória de corte a Telebras projeta Ebitda positivo sem ajuda federal, e apenas em 2029 ou 2030. A conta de luz do novo data center pode variar de R$ 10,5 milhões a R$ 17,5 milhões por ano, conforme o consumo máximo teórico de 17,52 mil MWh. O valor não inclui manutenção, refrigeração nem a substituição dos aceleradores de IA mais adiante. O investimento acompanha uma corrida mais ampla: o Brasil pode atrair US$ 60 bilhões por ano em data centers até 2050, segundo projeções do setor. O apetite elétrico da inteligência artificial já preocupa em outros projetos: data centers de IA em São Paulo consomem 16,1 bilhões de litros de água por ano para resfriamento. Quando o data center entra em operação? A Telebras estima iniciar a operação até o fim de 2027, mas o local da obra ainda não está definido. O presidente da estatal, Hermano Studart Lins de Albuquerque, já citou Brasília como uma das possibilidades. O projeto prevê um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, com 20 racks de 42U, rede de alta velocidade, seis servidores com 48 GPUs e armazenamento all-flash para rodar modelos de inteligência artificial soberanos. O que acontece agora Antes de contratar qualquer etapa, a Telebras precisa confirmar o terreno e a conexão elétrica, validar os projetos de engenharia e cumprir requisitos térmicos, segundo o acórdão da Anatel. Cada fase aprovada não garante automaticamente a seguinte. Faltam ainda o orçamento anual de despesas operacionais, os contratos de prestação de serviço e a definição de como o data center vai se integrar à infraestrutura do Serpro, que já trabalha em IA soberana com a MeetKai, e da Dataprev.
