artigo.texto: A SpaceX treina bartenders, varejistas e instaladores de data centers com IA em apenas alguns dias. Na TomorrowX Summit, Elon Musk afirmou que a equipe da ArmyX detalhou o processo para que pessoas com experiência em preparação e venda de bebidas pudessem participar da expansão das unidades Colossus 1 e Colossus 2 em Memphis, EUA. A SpaceX está contratando trabalhadores sem experiência prévia no setor de tecnologia, como bartenders, repositores de supermercado ou cozinheiros de fast-food, para construir seus grandes data centers. A empresa divide o trabalho em etapas simples para que os novos funcionários possam ser treinados em poucos dias. Essa abordagem foi compartilhada pelo bilionário Elon Musk na TomorrowX Summit em Austin, EUA, no último fim de semana. Segundo ele, alguns dos melhores funcionários da equipe de construção de data centers da empresa nunca haviam trabalhado nessa área antes. Eles vinham de profissões menos relacionadas à infraestrutura de tecnologia. ArmyX: Simplificando o processo para ajudar os novos funcionários a começarem rapidamente. Para integrar mão de obra não qualificada em projetos de tecnologia, a SpaceX criou uma equipe interna chamada ArmyX. Essa equipe analisa todo o processo de construção de data centers e o divide em tarefas mais simples. Isso permite que os recém-chegados sejam treinados e concluam o trabalho em poucos dias. Segundo Musk, as empresas não precisam necessariamente contratar pessoas que tenham passado a vida inteira trabalhando com sistemas de cabeamento. Em vez disso, podem criar processos que permitam que funcionários que antes trabalhavam no Starbucks ou repunham prateleiras no Target se adaptem rapidamente a novas funções. Ele também valoriza as habilidades e a ética de trabalho de funcionários dos setores de varejo e alimentação. Ele deu o exemplo dos funcionários da rede de fast-food In-N-Out. Segundo Musk, pessoas acostumadas a fazer hambúrgueres o dia todo conseguem, sem problemas, instalar cabos de rede após o treinamento. Essa estrutura organizacional permite que a SpaceX expanda sua equipe de construção sem depender exclusivamente de pessoal com vasta experiência em data centers. Você também pode gostar Colossus 1 e Colossus 2: A escala das GPUs por trás da demanda da força de trabalho Novos funcionários estão dando suporte à expansão das instalações Colossus 1 e Colossus 2 em Memphis, EUA. Anteriormente, o Business Insider noticiou que a SpaceX ofereceu um aumento salarial de 20% para voluntários que trabalhassem seis semanas em Memphis ou Southaven, Mississippi, cidade que também possui um grande centro de dados. Uma GPU é um processador gráfico, também utilizado em sistemas computacionais para inteligência artificial devido à sua capacidade de processar grandes quantidades de dados em paralelo. Abaixo, seguem informações sobre duas dessas unidades, de acordo com a fonte: Essa escala impõe demandas significativas tanto em mão de obra quanto em cronogramas de construção. Segundo Musk, as operações em Memphis estão se tornando cada vez mais estáveis, com equipes de trabalhadores atuando 24 horas por dia. Ele afirma que pode inspecionar o local à 1h ou 2h da manhã e constatar uma produtividade quase equivalente à das 10h da manhã do dia seguinte. O cronograma de trabalho é mantido continuamente, sete dias por semana. No relatório financeiro de outubro, Musk também mencionou planos para expandir a capacidade de computação. Ele disse que não ficaria surpreso se a empresa adicionasse menos de 13 gigawatts até o final de 2027. Terafab e data centers espaciais: planos ambiciosos Além de Memphis, Musk está investindo em projetos de infraestrutura de maior escala. Segundo a Reuters, ele está construindo duas fábricas no Texas, conhecidas coletivamente como Terafab. Uma das instalações é voltada para os setores automotivo e de robótica humanoide, enquanto a outra atende à sua ambição de desenvolver um centro de dados de IA no espaço. Musk idealiza esses complexos como fábricas avançadas de chips de IA, visando uma capacidade computacional de um terawatt por ano. Esse número é o dobro do meio terawatt que, segundo algumas fontes, é a maior capacidade de uma fábrica nos EUA atualmente. Você também pode gostar No início de 2026, ele fundiu a xAI à SpaceX para apoiar o desenvolvimento de um data center espacial. De acordo com a SpaceX, a instalação de sistemas de computação fora da Terra poderia utilizar energia solar quase contínua, reduzindo assim os custos de operação e manutenção em comparação com instalações terrestres. A empresa também afirma que esse modelo poderia reduzir o impacto ambiental, pois não requer água de resfriamento nem eletricidade da rede elétrica nacional. Nota: Estes são benefícios apresentados pela empresa e não são resultados de operações verificadas de forma independente. A principal lição a ser aprendida com a abordagem de gestão de recursos da SpaceX. Desde o treinamento de ex-bartenders e funcionários do varejo para instalar infraestrutura tecnológica até planos para construir data centers no espaço, as ideias de Musk revelam como ele organiza recursos para projetos de IA em larga escala. O foco dessa abordagem é redesenhar processos para dimensionar a força de trabalho, em vez de simplesmente buscar indivíduos com experiência preexistente.

artigo.texto: Data centers have a reputation for being massive water hogs, fueling plenty of worry over Cheyenne’s recent building boom. Actual usage, however, tells a different story. Frank Strong, engineering and water resource division manager for Cheyenne’s Board of Public Utilities, told Cowboy State Daily that data centers accounted for about 2% of the city’s water sales in 2025. "We sold about 3.5 billion gallons of water in 2025, and 93 million went to data centers,” Strong said. ‘Significantly Less’ Strong said the 93 million gallons was lower than the water usage laid out in the data centers' initial proposals to the city. The difference, he said, comes down to chips, the small processors inside the servers that run the data center's computing. When developers first proposed data center projects to the Cheyenne City Council, the chips they were using needed more water-based cooling to run. “New chip technology can run at higher temperatures,” Strong said. “Newer technology has allowed them to consume less water than they had planned.” Strong did not have the exact difference in gallons between the proposed water usage and what the data centers are using now, but he said it is not a marginal one. “I would say it’s in the significantly less range,” Strong said. Almonds, Golf and AI Cheyenne’s numbers line up with a new report comparing AI water use against everyday habits. The analysis from Enverus Intelligence Research, a Calgary-based energy analytics subsidiary of Enverus, modeled water use per $25 spent across cooling scenarios and consumer benchmarks, finding AI inference uses far less water than golf or almond milk. “The research finds that skipping one almond latte saves more water than spending $100 on AI inference,” the analysis states. “Skipping one round of golf saves more than $16,000 of it.” Ryan Luther, EIR’s director of Energy Transition Research, told Cowboy State Daily that the analysis isn't a pitch for data center developers. It’s just looking at the numbers, he said. "Our reputation lives and dies on our ability to do science-based research,” Luther said. “We have clients on both sides of everything, so we're not trying to pick a side here.” Luther said the analysis was built around four different cooling methods, which he said cover just about every data center operating today. He said it also counted the water used at the power plants that generate the electricity to run those facilities, not only the water used inside the data center itself. About 90% of the water the analysis attributed to AI use was consumed at those power plants. Even with all of it counted, the total water usage still came out low. ”The amount of power used for $25 of compute is pretty low compared to $25 of power,” Luther said. ‘Different Type of Cooling’ The biggest swing in the analysis came down to how a data center is cooled. In the earliest cooling systems, $25 a month of AI use corresponded to about 21 gallons of water. Now that same usage corresponds to about a quarter of a gallon of water, which Luther said is due to modern, closed-loop systems. "There's been a huge improvement on the efficiency,” Luther said. "They still need a lot of cooling, but it's a different type of cooling. It’s not necessarily just pulling in water and evaporating it. It's more like a radiator.” As closed-loop systems become the norm, Luther said, data centers' water use will approach zero, though he said it will take a while for the whole industry to get there. Golf courses and almond farms are widely known as heavy water users. But the analysis found that AI also uses less than household electricity on an all-natural-gas grid. That same $25 a month in household electricity on a grid powered entirely by natural gas corresponded to about 31 gallons of water, compared with about 1.9 gallons for AI use in the base case, according to the analysis. Everyone Hates Infrastructure Still, Luther said some communities have reason to be concerned. As little water as a data center uses, some areas with a low water table don't have any to spare. "In places like Nevada and Utah, you have very real water constraints,” Luther said. Luther started his career in oil and gas at Enverus and has spent years studying energy projects ranging from pipelines and transmission lines to power plants and data centers. Across all of them, he said, community pushback is something he has come to expect. “Generally, the community seems to hate all infrastructure,” Luther said. “No matter what it is, if it's in your backyard or in your community, they'll find reasons to tear it down.” Though the analysis is titled "Setting the Record Straight,” on data center water usage, Luther said he doesn't necessarily expect it to change anyone's minds. But among the concerns people typically have about a new data center in their neighborhood, Luther said water use should rank low on the list. As for the others, like noise and air pollution, he said it could always be worse. “They do have noise, but they're not very loud compared to a power plant," Luther said. “A lot of the communities want the data center to invest in green spaces around them, or sound barrier walls, which I think almost all developers are more than happy to do.” Emma Jane Jackson can be reached at emma@cowboystatedaily.com.

artigo.texto: A comprehensive scientific review in Applied Physics A evaluates the critical materials science strategies required to engineer high-performance polyvinylidene fluoride nanocomposites capable of simultaneously delivering electromagnetic interference shielding and electrostatic energy storage. Modern technologies, spanning fifth- and sixth-generation telecommunications, electric vehicles, flexible wearables, and aerospace engineering, generate intense electromagnetic radiation that threatens sensitive circuitry while escalating demand for lightweight, flexible charge-storage platforms. Polyvinylidene fluoride, known as PVDF, represents an exceptionally promising thermoplastic for these dual functional roles due to its mechanical flexibility, chemical resistance, thermal stability, and high dielectric breakdown strength. However, practical implementation remains hindered by severe thermodynamic incompatibility between non-polar carbonaceous nanofillers and the polar fluoropolymer matrix, causing severe agglomeration, void formation, and deficient interfacial stress transfer. To resolve these limitations, researchers established a dual-modification paradigm coupling silane surface treatments on carbon fibers with maleic anhydride compatibilizers, forming a robust interfacial bridge that optimizes nanofiller dispersion, charge-carrier dynamics, and macroscopic multifunctional performance. The functional performance of PVDF stems directly from its semi-crystalline molecular architecture and polymorphic crystallization behavior. Composed of alternating carbon-hydrogen and carbon-fluorine bonds arranged as (CH2–CF2)n, the polymer possesses permanent microscopic dipoles arising from the vast electronegativity difference between fluorine and hydrogen atoms. Depending on processing conditions, PVDF crystallizes into alpha, beta, gamma, or delta phases. While the non-polar alpha phase adopts a trans-gauche-trans-gauche conformation, the polar electroactive beta phase exhibits an all-trans planar zigzag structure where dipoles align along the crystallographic axis. This spontaneous polarization imparts superior piezoelectric, ferroelectric, and dielectric properties essential for sensing and energy storage devices. Neat PVDF exhibits a melting point of 177 degrees Celsius, a glass transition temperature of minus 35 degrees Celsius, a density of 1.77 grams per cubic centimeter, and 50 to 60 percent crystallinity. Although pure PVDF displays impressive dielectric breakdown strength near 500 megavolts per meter, its low electrical conductivity and modest dielectric constant of approximately 10 necessitate functional filler incorporation. To overcome these dielectric and conductive constraints, researchers have incorporated diverse conductive carbonaceous fillers, including carbon nanotubes, carbon nanofibers, graphene nanoplatelets, and reduced graphene oxide. These allotropes possess outstanding intrinsic electrical conductivities and high thermal conductivities, reaching 2000 to 6000 watts per meter-kelvin for carbon nanotubes and 5000 watts per meter-kelvin for graphene. When uniformly distributed within the PVDF matrix, these high-aspect-ratio fillers construct continuous three-dimensional percolating electrical networks that facilitate Ohmic conduction and interfacial polarization. Studies show that multi-walled carbon nanotubes can elevate electrical conductivity to 0.06 siemens per centimeter, yielding electromagnetic shielding effectiveness of 30.89 decibels across the microwave X-band from 8 to 12 gigahertz at 7 weight percent loading. Furthermore, hybrid combinations of carbon nanotubes and graphene sheets promote three-dimensional networks, lowering percolation thresholds. Nevertheless, pristine carbon nanomaterials exhibit chemically inert surfaces and strong van der Waals attractions that induce severe agglomeration during melt blending, generating interfacial microvoids that degrade composite mechanical toughness and electrical reliability. Surface engineering via organosilane coupling agents provides an effective chemical pathway to tailor the surface energy and chemical reactivity of carbonaceous reinforcements. Organosilanes generally possess the molecular formula R(4-n)-Si-(R’X)n, where hydrolyzable alkoxy groups react with moisture to produce reactive silanol intermediates. When applied to electrochemically oxidized carbon fibers bearing surface hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, these silanols undergo condensation reactions to construct a durable crosslinked siloxane network linked by silicon-oxygen-silicon bonds. Concurrently, organofunctional groups, such as primary amines derived from gamma-aminopropyltriethoxysilane or epoxide moieties from gamma-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane, graft directly onto the fiber surface. Experimental characterizations confirm that surface oxidation and amino-silane deposition increase fiber surface roughness, chemical wettability, and interfacial adhesion. Quantitative mechanical evaluations reveal that incorporating silane-treated carbon fibers yields notable improvements, including a 20.0 percent increase in tensile strength, a 25.11 percent rise in flexural strength, and a 24.88 percent improvement in interlaminar shear strength compared to untreated fiber composites, establishing an active interphase for subsequent compatibilization. Complementing fiber functionalization, maleic anhydride compatibilizers play a pivotal role in modulating the rheological, crystalline, and interfacial characteristics of the PVDF continuous phase. Maleic anhydride compounds, used as molecular additives or grafted onto polyolefins like polypropylene-graft-maleic anhydride, feature reactive polar anhydride rings that exhibit strong intermolecular affinity toward polar polymer segments. Within PVDF blends, physical dipole-dipole interactions occur between electronegative carbonyl oxygen atoms of maleic anhydride and partially positive hydrogen atoms on PVDF methylene group

artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou na sexta-feira (20 de novembro) que empresas americanas serão proibidas de construir data centers em outros países, sob pena de um "imposto enorme". A ameaça mira o plano do Brasil de virar polo de IA. Em coletiva na Casa Branca, Trump disse que não vai permitir que "os data centers vão para outros países, porque a China vai ficar com todos eles". Ele admitiu não ter avisado a própria equipe antes do anúncio. Trump não informou alíquota, data de início nem o mecanismo legal da penalidade. O governo brasileiro sancionou em setembro a Lei nº 15.504, que criou o Redata. O regime isenta e reduz impostos para a instalação e a expansão de data centers no país. Segundo o governo, o incentivo representa R$ 5,2 bilhões em receita tributária perdida só em 2026. A aposta é recuperar esse valor com o investimento atraído ao setor. O que muda para o Brasil Para o Brasil, a ameaça de Trump encarece o plano de atrair data centers justamente agora. O país atraiu US$ 8 bilhões em investimentos de data centers em 2026 e concentra 49% da capacidade instalada da América Latina. É o maior polo da região, e também o mais exposto à decisão de Washington. Estimativas oficiais projetam entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em novos investimentos no setor nos próximos quatro anos. A conta depende de empresas americanas dispostas a construir fora dos Estados Unidos. Publicidade É justamente esse movimento que Trump quer taxar. A ameaça se soma a outra restrição anunciada pelos EUA na segunda-feira (16 de novembro de 2026). Uma norma passou a exigir licença para exportar chips de inteligência artificial a data centers no exterior. O Brasil entrou na lista de destinos sujeitos à exigência, ao lado de Indonésia, Malásia, Cingapura e Tailândia. Um data center médio, de 100 megawatts, acrescenta cerca de R$ 1,5 bilhão ao PIB e gera 13 mil empregos na fase de construção. É esse tipo de projeto que o Redata tenta atrair com a renúncia fiscal. O que acontece agora Trump não disse se vai buscar aprovação do Congresso americano ou usar poderes executivos para aplicar a taxação. Também não deu prazo para a medida passar a valer. Até a publicação desta reportagem, o Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) não havia divulgado nota pública respondendo à ameaça. Enquanto isso, o projeto brasileiro de política nacional de data centers segue em tramitação no Congresso. O governo tenta destravar outras frentes do setor, como o aporte de R$ 375 milhões aprovado pela Anatel para um data center de IA da Telebras. O impasse ocorre num momento em que o governo já apostava no Redata para competir nesse mercado. O cenário se soma à disputa comercial mais ampla entre Brasília e Washington. As sobretaxas de até 37,5% sobre exportações brasileiras seguem em vigor, sem acordo à vista. O ponto em aberto Trump prometeu a penalidade sem citar nenhuma empresa, nenhum valor e nenhum prazo. Isso deixa em aberto se ela sairá do papel antes dos quatro anos em que o Brasil projeta atrair até R$ 100 bilhões em novos projetos. A combinação entre a ameaça de taxação e a exigência de licença para chips de IA, anunciadas com 11 dias de diferença, é o que mais pesa sobre quem já decidiu investir no país.

artigo.texto: Synthesized through microbial fermentation by non-toxic bacteria such as Acetobacter xylinum, bacterial cellulose consists of an interconnected three-dimensional nanofiber network featuring remarkable mechanical robustness, high porosity, exceptional electrolyte wettability, and thermal stability. While conventional petroleum-based battery separators and inactive electrode scaffolds face severe limitations under rigorous operating conditions, biomass-derived bacterial cellulose has emerged as an adaptable platform capable of functioning as an active electrochemical regulator. The investigation combined quantitative bibliometric mapping with traditional literature review methodologies to analyze 97 peer-reviewed documents across 54 journals published between 2002 and 2025. The bibliometric assessment revealed a highly interdisciplinary and collaborative research landscape characterized by 411 authors and an average of 6.77 co-authors per publication. There were no single-authored papers identified in the analyzed dataset, reflecting the intricate convergence of microbial biosynthesis, nanostructure engineering, materials chemistry, and electrochemistry required to advance functional bio-nanocomposites. The literature is relatively young, possessing an average document age of 5.4 years and an average citation rate of 39.27 per paper, with peak publication volumes occurring in 2022 and 2023. Geographic analysis established that research productivity is heavily centralized, with China contributing 493 author affiliations, followed by the United States with 44 and India with 39. Collaborative network mapping indicated that the strongest bilateral partnership exists between institutions in China and the United States, accounting for eight joint publications, while emerging North-South and South-South research exchanges were observed among teams in Germany, Australia, Canada, Indonesia, and Japan. Respected interdisciplinary journals such as Chemical Engineering Journal, Journal of Materials Chemistry A, and ACS Applied Materials and Interfaces served as primary outlets for these scientific findings. By conducting author keyword co-occurrence analysis and factorial mapping, the study identified key clusters detailing the developmental shift of bacterial cellulose from a passive separator substrate into complex, multifunctional electrochemical architectures. In early research spanning 2002 to 2020, studies focused predominantly on fundamental cellulose properties and rudimentary lithium-sulfur cells. In contrast, publications from 2021 to 2025 diversified into specialized structural designs, including binder-free anodes, 3D conductive carbon networks, silicon hybrid electrodes, polymer electrolytes, and redox-active separators. The conceptual framework organized these efforts into distinct functional categories, highlighting that researchers are engineering bacterial cellulose at the molecular and nano scales to overcome persistent electrochemical hurdles. These challenges include the violent polysulfide shuttle effect, catastrophic lithium dendrite proliferation, sluggish charge-transfer kinetics, mechanical pulverization of high-capacity alloying elements, and severe thermal instability in conventional polyolefin battery membranes. In the domain of separator engineering, functionalized bacterial cellulose membranes have consistently outperformed conventional microporous polyolefin separators like Celgard. For example, Zhang and colleagues fabricated an alkali-treated, hot-pressed bilayer separator integrating nickel sulfide and conductive carbon into bacterial cellulose, which produced a 20-micrometer-thick membrane delivering an ionic conductivity of 1.34 millisiemens per centimeter and a discharge capacity of 117 milliampere-hours per gram at 2C. Similarly, Cheng and associates developed an oil-based composite separator through periodate oxidation and chitosan grafting, designated OBCS-200, which exhibited 65.8 percent porosity, 358 percent electrolyte uptake, and a lithium-ion transference number of 0.56, enabling 90 percent capacity retention across 100 cycles. Addressing severe thermal risks, another investigated composite combined nano-hydroxyapatite and melamine polyphosphate within bacterial cellulose aerogels, known as BHM/5. This separator demonstrated dimensional integrity at 200 degrees Celsius, self-extinguishing flame-retardant properties, 74 percent porosity, and an ionic conductivity of 1.44 millisiemens per centimeter, sustaining 95.4 percent capacity retention after 150 cycles at a 1C discharge rate. Beyond serving as uncarbonized porous barriers, bacterial cellulose pellicles provide exceptional precursors for synthesizing carbon nanofiber aerogels through freeze-drying and high-temperature thermal pyrolysis. These lightweight aerogels feature abundant micro-, meso-, and macroporous channels that facilitate rapid lithium-ion diffusion while providing continuous electrical pathways. Meng and colleagues demonstrated that nitrogen-doped carbon nanofiber aerogels synthesized at 900 degrees Celsius under ammonia exposure produced hierarchically porous networks rich in pyridinic, pyrrolic, and quaternary nitrogen, exhibiting oxygen reduction electrocatalytic activity comparable to commercial platinum-carbon catalysts. In energy storage contexts, Li and collaborators pyrolyzed bacterial cellulose at 800 degrees Celsius to generate carbon nanofiber aerogels specifically for lithium-sulfur cathodes, achieving an initial capacity of 1360 milliampere-hours per gram at 0.2C with 76 percent retention over 200 cycles under a sulfur content of 75 to 80 percent. Additionally, catalytic graphitization using 0.1 weight percent ferrous acetate during bacterial cellulose synthesis followed by graphitization at 1800 degrees Celsius achieved a reversible lithium-ion battery anode capacity of 529 milliampere-hours per gram after 100 cycles. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Daily presents a selection of the latest developments from China's automotive industry. Here are the key stories in this edition. Xiaomi Q3 Revenue Tops RMB 100 Billion as EV Business Grows Xiaomi Group reported revenue of RMB 107.2 billion ($15 billion) in the third quarter of 2026, maintaining its quarterly revenue above the RMB 100 billion mark. The group's gross margin also improved from the previous quarter, while its overall operating performance continued to strengthen. The automotive business remained a key growth area. Revenue from electric vehicles and other innovative businesses reached RMB 23.9 billion, while Xiaomi delivered 100,975 vehicles during the quarter. Monthly deliveries exceeded 50,000 units in October, marking a new high for the year. Xiaomi also gained ground in the higher-end vehicle segment. Its models ranked among the top three best-selling vehicles priced above RMB 200,000 in China in October. The Xiaomi Pengcheng N70 led the extended-range vehicle and midsize-to-large SUV categories, while the Pengcheng N90 topped the large SUV segment. Beyond vehicle sales, Xiaomi continued to invest heavily in technology, with quarterly R&D spending reaching RMB 9.2 billion. The company is also advancing its robotics efforts: its humanoid robots completed an eight-hour operation trial at an automotive factory, marking an initial step toward production-line deployment. XPENG Opens Public NGP Test Rides in Europe XPENG has opened its Paris showroom to the public for test rides featuring its NGP advanced driver-assistance system, becoming the first Chinese automaker to offer public urban ADAS experiences through a retail location in Europe. The move brings the company's intelligent-driving technology beyond industry demonstrations and onto real city roads, giving European consumers an opportunity to experience it firsthand. Powered by XPENG's second-generation VLA architecture, NGP is designed to handle complex urban driving scenarios. The public test rides allow local users to experience the system in familiar traffic conditions, including busy streets and intersections. XPENG and Tesla are currently the only two automakers offering comparable public ADAS experiences in Europe, according to the company. The initiative comes as XPENG steps up efforts to adapt NGP to European roads and regulations. Since July, the second-generation VLA model underpinning the system has been tested in Germany, the Netherlands and France. The company said it completed localization validation across the three markets in roughly four months, assessing the system's ability to adapt to different traffic rules, road layouts and driving environments. XPENG is targeting the first half of 2027 for its initial European vehicle deliveries, while its planned international rollout of NGP in 2027 remains subject to regulatory approval and market readiness. The public test rides offer the company an opportunity to gather feedback from local users as it prepares to bring its advanced driver-assistance technology to more European markets. CATL Opens First Battery Service Center in Türkiye CATL has opened its first NING SERVICE Experience Center in Türkiye, expanding its overseas presence beyond battery supply into after-sales support and lifecycle services. Located in Istanbul's Tuzla district, the facility was launched on November 19 in partnership with local company Ascendum Türkiye. Covering more than 1,200 square meters, the center provides battery testing, diagnostics, repair, maintenance and refurbishment services for passenger and commercial vehicles, as well as energy storage systems. It also includes exhibition and retail areas, training rooms and a customer lounge, making it an integrated service hub rather than a conventional repair workshop. A key part of the initiative is building local technical capabilities. The center will train and certify Turkish technicians under CATL's service standards, while the partnership will combine CATL's battery expertise with Ascendum Türkiye's local service infrastructure. The companies also plan to gradually expand the service network nationwide, bringing trained personnel and replacement parts closer to customers. The move reflects CATL's broader effort to build an overseas battery aftermarket ecosystem as electric-vehicle and energy-storage deployment grows. CATL said NING SERVICE currently operates 1,429 service locations across more than 80 countries and regions, supported by over 9,900 service engineers and more than 10,000 certified technicians. The network aims to reach 100 countries and regions by 2027 and 10,000 service locations globally by 2030.

artigo.texto: Court filing links Marion property to battery storage developer amid data center rumors MARION, Va. (WCYB) — A court document identifies a company with ties to a battery energy storage developer as the entity seeking to purchase more than 200 acres of Marion-owned property near Interstate 81’s Exit 47, adding new details to a development proposal that has fueled concerns among residents. An 'option agreement' filed in Smyth County Circuit Court links the Marion Economic Development Authority property to Honeycomb Power LLC, which lists an address associated with Plus Power, a company that develops utility-scale battery energy storage facilities across the country. The agreement gives Honeycomb Power the option to purchase four tracts totaling more than 200 acres. The land was transferred from the Town of Marion to its economic development authority in August. The connection has added to speculation about whether the property could be developed into a battery storage facility or a data center. Town officials have not publicly confirmed the developer's intended use for the site. Marion Mayor Avery Cornett said he believes the proposed development could be related to battery storage but declined to discuss details. “My personal assumption is that it is something related but without breaking the confidentiality of closed session and without hurting the developers chances of developing the property, I really can't comment on that disposition at this time,” Cornett said. Cornett said he did not sign a nondisclosure agreement with the developer and added they were never approached to sign one. "This is just our standard policy and how we proceed with any developer and that is to keep it confidential," Cornett said. The property on I-81 is surrounded by homes and farm land. Dennis Burton and his wife have lived next to the property since 2009. Burton said the couple considers the home their dream house and hopes to remain there but said, he'd consider moving if a data center takes over his quiet backyard. “This is our dream home. This is what we come for — to live, raise our kids, our grandkids, and we love it here. We'd hate to have to move, but you never know,” Burton said. Burton said he, like other neighbors, has heard rumors about a possible data center on the property. Residents have raised questions about transparency and the potential impact of a large-scale development on the surrounding community. Plus Power already operates a battery energy storage facility near Saltville and is pursuing another project in Smyth County. According to a technology expert News 5 spoke with from Texas, battery storage facilities are used to bolster grid reliability and have recently become paired with data centers to aid in their energy usage. Because the property is outside Marion's corporate limits, any future development would fall under Smyth County's zoning and permitting process. Burton said he hopes town leaders and developers will consider the impact a project could have on people living nearby before making a decision. “The only thing I would ask them to do is come up here and go up on this hill and look around and look at everything you're going to affect before they make their decision,” Burton said.

artigo.texto: Paris Marx questions how far transparency pledges can ease data-center opposition In a new TechCrunch interview, the Hyperscale author welcomes easier access to project details but argues that electricity, water and noise concerns run deeper. Loading page… Listen to this story In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book *Hyperscale*, Paris Marx argued that public disclosure can help residents scrutinize data-center proposals but is unlikely to resolve opposition rooted in local resource costs. He said companies’ commitments to end nondisclosure agreements do not address concerns over electricity bills, water access and noise, and questioned whether the buildout’s promised gains justify its cumulative costs. For developers, transparency may reduce suspicion, but securing community support also means addressing the infrastructure burdens directly. Marx said data centers consume more than 20% of Ireland’s electricity, and Dublin-area grid connections for new facilities have faced a moratorium. In The Dalles, Oregon, Google disclosed that its data centers used 29% of the city’s water as it sought more for expansion. Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI have committed to ending nondisclosure agreements in local-government negotiations, according to the interview. Technology companies are promising more openness around data-center projects. Journalist Paris Marx argues that disclosure alone will do little to settle the underlying disputes. In a November 22 TechCrunch interview about his book Hyperscale, he welcomed easier access to information but said community resistance reflects concerns about electricity bills, water and noise—not simply secrecy. His criticism reaches beyond how companies negotiate individual developments. Marx described the scale of construction as “fundamentally unsustainable,” arguing that its demands on host communities and cumulative environmental costs are too large. He also challenged the industry’s promised returns, saying benefits in productivity, healthcare and education had not materialized as advertised. Those are his assessments of the buildout, not findings from a new impact study. Marx’s explanation for opposition across political lines starts with proximity. An online service can feel abstract; a large facility proposed nearby brings questions about household expenses and daily life. He pointed to potential effects on water access, power bills and neighborhood noise from rooftop cooling equipment. In his view, those concerns give people with otherwise different politics a shared reason to object. His book examines data centers and generative AI, including the infrastructure behind services that users encounter through screens. Researching it required getting past the perimeter. After visiting the outsides of facilities in northern Virginia and Ireland, Marx traveled to New Zealand to tour one. He described advance passport checks, key-card-controlled doors and a warm server room filled with piercing fan noise and air conditioning. Two earlier resource disputes helped persuade him that data centers deserved a book-length investigation. Both examples, he said, showed communities confronting infrastructure demands before generative AI drove a further construction surge: You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? Paris Marx, speaking to TechCrunch TechCrunch’s interviewer cited commitments by Microsoft, Amazon and OpenAI to stop using nondisclosure agreements in negotiations with local governments. These agreements restrict what participants can share publicly. Microsoft’s commitment predates the interview: a September 30 House Judiciary Democrats announcement identified it as a change announced in March 2026. Asked how much difference those commitments would make, Marx answered, “Not a huge difference.” He nevertheless welcomed making project information easier to obtain. He described other company responses as more directly tied to resource concerns: proposals to pay for more electricity infrastructure to reduce pressure on ratepayers, and promises to use different water-based cooling systems to lower electricity consumption. Marx sees the transparency shift as a response to opposition, rather than evidence that the conflict has been resolved. With residents more familiar with data centers, he argued, unanswered questions can strengthen resistance. Keeping negotiations secret can therefore work against the companies seeking permission to build. Loading discussion... artigo.texto: POWER STRUGGLE: Inside the fight over Georgia’s growing data center industry Atlanta News First Investigates examines water use, alleged pollution and the debate over who pays as data centers expand across Georgia. ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) - Data centers are expanding across Georgia, bringing the promise of tax revenue and investment — and growing concerns about water, electricity and the impact on nearby communities. Atlanta News First Investigates identified about 160 operating or planned sites across the state. The investigation found residents and environmental advocates raising questions about the resources needed to build and power the facilities, as well as the role communities have in deciding where they go. Water use and a potential lawsuit In Fayetteville, county records show the water system has billed QTS for a total of 109 million gallons of water used at its massive data center site since meters began coming online in 2024. The company said the water was used for construction activities, including dust control, concrete work and site preparation. QTS says a closed-loop cooling system planned for the completed facility will recirculate water and substantially reduce consumption. Fayette County says the site uses less than 1% of the county’s monthly water supply. Meanwhile, the Flint Riverkeeper and local homeowners have sent a notice of intent to sue, alleging that muddy, contaminated runoff from construction has reached a creek feeding the Flint River. A notice is a step before a lawsuit can be filed; it is not itself a lawsuit. The Riverkeeper said QTS had reached out to discuss a possible resolution. The company did not respond to requests for comment on the legal allegations. A coal plant stays open In Juliette, some residents have long alleged that coal ash from Georgia Power’s Plant Scherer contaminated their well water. Georgia Power denies wrongdoing, and a judge dismissed a lawsuit against the company in 2024, finding no material facts supporting claims that the plant’s operations caused or contributed to personal injuries. Georgia Power once planned to retire the coal plant in 2028 but later changed course as electricity demand grew from industries including data centers. State regulators approved a plan to keep the plant operating. Georgia Power says it monitors water quality and is closing the ash pond in compliance with state and federal requirements. Questions about future development In Peachtree City, residents have questioned whether recently purchased land near Lake McIntosh could become a data center site. Mayor Kim Lerner said there is no proposal, no zoning for one and no interest from the city council. QTS said it had not held meetings about bringing a data center to the city. The debate extends beyond individual projects: Residents want to know how much power and water the industry will require — and whether households could ultimately share in the cost. Georgia Power has announced a three-year rate freeze and says data centers will pay their own costs, though some residents remain skeptical. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) are gaining importance in India’s power sector as utilities seek to integrate renewable energy, manage peak demand and improve grid reliability. Rooftop solar adoption, electricity banking regulations and changing demand patterns are also influencing storage requirements and procurement strategies. These issues were discussed in detail during a panel discussion among Manish Dwivedi, Chief Engineer – PPA, Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited; H.C. Sharma, Chief, Power Management, Power System Control, Quality Assurance, Technical Services and BD, Tata Limited, Power Delhi Distribution Limited; and Sunil K. Sharma, General Manager, Sustainability and Clean Technology, BSES Yamuna Power, at the second edition of Renewable Watch’s Battery Energy Storage Systems for Utilities conference. Edited excerpts… Realistic utilisation must guide project economics One of the key challenges in BESS deployment is the gap between assumed and actual battery utilisation. Project economics may be calculated on the basis of two charge and discharge cycles per day, but achieving this consistently depends on weather conditions, electricity demand and the availability of charging power. Surplus renewable energy is particularly important in determining utilisation. Batteries can store excess solar generation during the day and supply electricity during evening peak hours. However, a second daily cycle may not be feasible if sufficient renewable power is unavailable for charging. Procuring electricity from the market offers an alternative, but its commercial viability depends on the price difference between charging and discharging periods. These factors have direct implications for tariffs and contract design. If a project is priced on the assumption of more cycles than it can realistically achieve, the expected economic benefits may not materialise. Utilities therefore need to assess load profiles, renewable energy availability and peak demand before determining storage capacity and operating requirements. The duration of power purchase agreements (PPAs) also influences project economics, and utilities are preferring contract terms of around 15 years for standalone BESS projects. For developers, this means that the initial investment must be recovered over fewer years, even if the installation remains operational beyond the agreement period, thus increasing investment risk. Contract duration must also account for battery degradation, component replacement and operating life. Utilities need clarity on whether developers are required to maintain a fixed level of capacity throughout the contract or whether performance requirements can be adjusted as batteries age. Clear provisions on these aspects can help distribute risks more equitably between developers and utilities. Equipment reliability and maintenance need greater attention The operational challenges of BESSs extend beyond the batteries themselves. Inverters, energy management systems (EMSs) and other electronic components are essential to plant performance, but their maintenance and replacement requirements need to be considered during procurement. Equipment suppliers may discontinue operations in particular markets or become unable to provide convenient repair services. In one instance, a utility encountered a situation where an inverter manufacturer had discontinued its operations in Asia, requiring equipment to be sent to the US for repairs under warranty. This created logistical difficulties despite the availability of warranty support. Such risks can arise when project developers or aggregators procure equipment from multiple suppliers. The company delivering the installation may not manufacture every component, leaving the utility dependent on other firms for technical assistance and replacement parts. If a supplier exits the market or discontinues support, equipment failures can result in prolonged downtime and additional costs. Software integration presents another challenge. Utilities may require storage systems to communicate with supervisory control and data acquisition systems and respond automatically to changing grid conditions. However, the supplied EMS may not support all the required functions, while restricted software access can make modifications difficult. These risks underline the need for contractual provisions covering maintenance, software updates, component replacement and technical support. Utilities should assess the availability of spare parts and the long-term viability of equipment suppliers before awarding projects. Developing domestic repair facilities and skilled personnel will also become important as storage deployment expands. Battery degradation should not automatically lead to the retirement of an installation if maintenance and component replacement can extend its useful life. The emphasis needs to be on sustaining performance over time rather than relying solely on standard assumptions about capacity decline. Storage offers multiple applications for utilities For utilities, BESS offers benefits beyond shifting renewable electricity between different periods of the day. Storage can help manage local network constraints, address peak demand and improve supply reliability. Utilities are exploring different ownership models to expand their storage portfolios. Under the capex model, the utility owns the asset and assumes responsibility for its operations and maintenance. This approach allows utilities to build direct experience of equipment performance and operating requirements. Under the opex model, developers can undertake the investment and provide storage services under a contractual arrangement. The choice between these models depends on a utility’s investment capacity, technical capabilities and operational priorities. artigo.texto: NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Limited (NVVN) has issued a tender to select developers to supply energy from a 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The project comprises two separate projects of 93.75 MW/375 MWh each. It has sought bids till December 21. 2026. The BESS projects, with a combined capacity of 750 MWh (187.5 MW x 4 hours), would operate under a single-cycle charging and discharging arrangement. The systems can be set up anywhere in India, provided they are connected to the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) network. The tender carries a minimum bid size of 375 MWh, equivalent to 93.75 MW x 4 hours. The BESS projects would be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model, with usage determined on an "on-demand" basis. The tender document costs Rs. 15 lakh, plus 18% GST, while the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) is set at Rs. 9,24,75,000, to be submitted in the form of a bank guarantee. Previously, NVVN has awarded BESS tender to Sunsure Energy capacity at ₹6.64/kWh, and to awarded 125 MW to EnerGrid at ₹6.65/kWh. Scope Of Work A bidder, including its parent, affiliate, ultimate parent or any group company, shall submit a single bid offering a project capacity of 93.75 MW/375 MWh in the prescribed formats. The project capacity must be quoted in the form of "x MW/4x MWh", meaning that the BESS system must be rated for four hours of charging and four hours of discharging in one cycle. The BESS Developer (BESSD) must guarantee a minimum system availability of 95% on a monthly basis. In the event of any shortfall, the BESSD will be liable to pay liquidated damages to the BIA. The amount of such damages will be calculated at 1.5 times the discharge energy tariff for the discharge energy not made available during the month. The tender also offers Viability Gap Funding (VGF) to each developer for setting up the BESS projects. The funding will be limited to Rs. 18,00,000/MWh or 30% of the capital cost of the awarded project capacity, whichever is lower.

artigo.texto: Ximena Rincón, ministra de Energia do Chile, ao lado de Candela Macchi, da Moody’s Ratings: painel discutiu o potencial da América Latina para a instalação de data centers (COA/Divulgação) Editora de Projetos Especiais Publicado em 24 de novembro de 2026 às 19h45. A corrida global pela infraestrutura necessária à expansão da inteligência artificial pode abrir uma janela de oportunidade para a América Latina. Enquanto os Estados Unidos enfrentam dificuldades para atender à crescente demanda por energia dos data centers, países como Brasil, Chile e México despontam como alternativas para receber parte desses investimentos. A combinação de energia renovável abundante, custos competitivos de construção, disponibilidade de terrenos e demanda crescente por serviços digitais coloca, segundo especialistas, a região em uma posição favorável em um dos maiores ciclos de investimentos em infraestrutura das últimas décadas. O tema foi discutido durante o 2026 Council of the Americas Symposium, realizado em 19 de novembro, em Miami, nos Estados Unidos. Sob a mediação de Candela Macchi, responsável pela área de ratings e pesquisa para América Latina da Moody’s Ratings, o painel reuniu executivos dos setores de energia e tecnologia e a ministra de Energia do Chile para discutir o que falta à região para ganhar protagonismo nesse mercado. “As medidas que tomarmos hoje definirão se a América Latina será apenas uma participante dessa revolução da inteligência artificial ou se será a região que fornecerá a energia para impulsioná-la” Candela Macchi, da Moody’s Ratings Somente no primeiro semestre de 2026, cerca de 125 projetos de data centers foram cancelados ou adiados nos Estados Unidos, o equivalente a aproximadamente US$ 200 bilhões em investimentos, segundo Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy. Na avaliação do executivo, as dificuldades de acesso à energia no mercado americano abrem espaço para que a América Latina atraia não apenas estruturas destinadas a atender à demanda local, mas também grandes projetos voltados ao processamento e ao treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial. Brasil e Chile, na visão de Barrera, apresentam condições especialmente favoráveis, tanto pela disponibilidade de energia renovável quanto pelo histórico de investimentos estrangeiros em infraestrutura. “Precisamos desmistificar um pouco o risco da América Latina”, afirmou o executivo, ressaltando que os países da região apresentam diferentes níveis de maturidade e segurança para os investidores. Ricardo Alário, CEO e cofundador da ODATA, também considera a disponibilidade de energia o principal diferencial competitivo da região, seguido pela capacidade de financiar projetos de grande escala. Segundo o executivo, Brasil, Chile e México desenvolveram, ao longo da última década, um ecossistema capaz de construir e operar data centers, mas ainda precisam comunicar melhor essas vantagens ao mercado internacional. “Temos um problema de marketing, um problema de percepção. Precisamos dizer ao mundo que temos energia limpa disponível agora, a preços muito competitivos, e que somos capazes de construir e operar essa infraestrutura”, afirmou Alário. Para Sean Ludick, presidente e COO da Voltron Technology, esse movimento abre oportunidades tanto para grandes data centers quanto para estruturas de processamento distribuídas, mais próximas dos usuários e necessárias a aplicações como robótica, serviços financeiros, segurança e saúde. “À medida que as empresas deixam de experimentar a IA e passam a depender dela, cria-se uma enorme demanda recorrente por capacidade computacional”, afirmou. Para Ludick, cuja empresa já estabeleceu parcerias na Colômbia, no Chile, no Brasil e no México, o principal desafio da América Latina está na capacidade de execução dos projetos, o que exigiria integrar energia, licenciamento, conectividade por fibra óptica, equipamentos, sistemas de refrigeração e financiamento. Do ponto de vista do setor público, Ximena Rincón, ministra de Energia do Chile, defendeu políticas que ofereçam segurança aos investidores, agilidade no licenciamento e garantias de que os empreendimentos também gerem benefícios para os países que os recebem. “A América Latina pode aproveitar sua riqueza em termos de geração de energia renovável, gás e até diesel, transformando a região em uma oportunidade para o mundo e também para seus próprios habitantes”, afirmou. O crescimento do setor, entretanto, também exige atenção aos impactos ambientais e sociais. Barrera defendeu que os projetos sejam discutidos com as comunidades desde as primeiras etapas e que não comprometam a disponibilidade de recursos como água e energia para a população local. Ao encerrar o painel, Candela Macchi ressaltou que o aproveitamento dessa oportunidade dependerá da capacidade de articulação entre governos, empresas de energia, operadores de data centers e companhias de tecnologia. “As medidas que tomarmos hoje definirão se a América Latina será apenas uma participante dessa revolução da inteligência artificial ou se será a região que fornecerá a energia para impulsioná-la”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: 'Struggling communities don’t need more struggles": Prichard residents oppose data centers Prichard, AL (NBC 15) — Prichard City Council voted unanimously Monday to extend its data center moratorium for a year. The pause gives the city more time to write rules for future projects, but it will not stop Edged Energy’s proposed data center on Telegraph Road. Mayor Carletta Davis said the Telegraph Road project is not covered by the moratorium because it was already moving through the city’s approval process. She said the company still needs a city business license, and the city can use the moratorium period to write an ordinance governing how the company will operate in Prichard. “The data center that is currently proposed for the city does not fall under the moratorium,” Davis said. “But it gives us time to create an ordinance as to how they will do business here in the city of Prichard.” Councilwoman Stephani Johnson-Norwood said the city needs time to study possible regulations and how to limit the project’s potential effects. “One of the reasons we need this moratorium, because it does take a lot of studying, a lot of research, and that’s what we’ve been doing at our ordinance committee,” Johnson-Norwood said. Council members discussed possible taxes on expensive equipment, a community fund, power and water use, noise limits and zoning. Those ideas are still under review and have not been adopted as requirements. Councilman Roy Smith said he wants the city to receive a direct benefit from the project. He proposed annual contributions for two schools, saying, “I wanted a million dollars for Blount, a million dollars for Ryder each year, give it to the city for us to give out.” The council did not approve that proposal Monday. Most speakers at the hearing opposed data centers, with about three dozen speaking against them compared with three in support, according to the count at the meeting. Michael Woodard was among those who supported the project. He said data centers are becoming increasingly important and argued that the company should pay for any utility upgrades it needs. Cynthia Trainor said residents need a say in any agreement between the company and the city. “If it’s going to come to my neighborhood, then I need to be vested,” Trainor said. “I need to know everything about it. I need to have ownership of it. And I need to be aware of the accountability of that data center to me and to my fellow citizens.” Trainor said she has noticed power surges affecting her home. “Those power surges affect everything—my appliances, my livelihood, everything I do in my home,” she said. She also questioned why the company chose Prichard. “Why didn’t you go to Chickasaw first? Why didn’t you go Saraland? Why didn’t you go Mobile? Why Prichard?” How the project moved forward

artigo.texto: O debate sobre a possível instalação de um data center em Atibaia mobilizou o Executivo municipal, moradores e o sistema de Justiça nos últimos dias. Em nota oficial, a Prefeitura de Atibaia esclareceu que, até o momento, não existe nenhum projeto de implantação desse tipo de empreendimento formalmente protocolado na Administração Municipal. Por outro lado, representantes da sociedade civil organizaram um abaixo-assinado que já ultrapassou 6.500 adesões e protocolaram, nesta segunda-feira (23 de novembro), uma ação popular na Justiça além de representações ao Ministério Público de São Paulo (MPSP) pedindo medidas preventivas de controle ambiental e urbanístico. Veja mais notícias de Atibaia e região. Moradores que desejam participar do debate sobre o consumo hídrico, a preservação ambiental e as regras de zoneamento na região podem acessar e assinar gratuitamente o abaixo-assinado Atibaia não será quintal para Data Centers, aberto à comunidade. O que diz a Prefeitura de Atibaia sobre o projeto? De acordo com o comunicado oficial da Administração Municipal, como não houve protocolo formal para análise e aprovação, também não há processo administrativo, estudo técnico em andamento ou licenciamento ambiental municipal aberto para um data center na cidade. O Executivo informou que, no passado, chegou a ser procurado em caráter estritamente informal e consultivo para tratar de uma possível iniciativa do setor. Segundo a Prefeitura, o encontro não gerou qualquer compromisso, tratativa formal ou abertura de processo de autorização. A nota ressalta ainda que Atibaia, localizada no entroncamento estratégico das rodovias Fernão Dias e Dom Pedro I, recebe sondagens frequentes de diferentes segmentos econômicos. Caso uma proposta formal venha a ser apresentada no futuro, o pedido passará pelos ritos legais aplicáveis, incluindo: - Análise colegiada: Apreciação obrigatória pelo Conselho Municipal de Defesa do Meio Ambiente de Atibaia (COMDEMA) dentro de suas atribuições legais; - Licenciamento multinível: Cumprimento integral das exigências de autorização e licenciamento ambiental junto aos órgãos municipais, estaduais e federais competentes. O que pedem o abaixo-assinado e a ação popular? Enquanto a Prefeitura reforça a inexistência de trâmite formal, grupos de moradores e coletivos ambientais articulam iniciativas para ampliar a transparência e exigir regulamentação prévia antes que projetos de grande porte — estimados pelo movimento em até R$ 3 bilhões — avancem no município. Veja também: Data Center em Atibaia: avanço tecnológico ou risco ambiental? Na internet, a petição pública intitulada Atibaia não será quintal para Data Centers, vinculada ao movimento "Fora Data Center Atibaia!", contabiliza mais de 6.500 assinaturas verificadas. O documento defende a participação popular e a criação de regras municipais que impeçam a instalação de empreendimentos dessa natureza sem avaliação técnica e ambiental prévia. Entre os principais pontos de alerta levantados pelo movimento estão: - Estresse hídrico: Receio de desabastecimento no Bairro do Tanque, região que conta apenas com atendimento parcial de água encanada e não dispõe de rede coletora e tratamento de esgoto; - Vegetação nativa: Risco de supressão de áreas remanescentes de Mata Atlântica na divisa urbano-rural; - Lençol freático: Preocupação com o armazenamento subterrâneo de óleo diesel utilizado para abastecer geradores de emergência (UPS) em estruturas de grande porte. Já a ação popular apresentada nesta segunda-feira (23), reúne pedidos divididos entre medidas liminares de urgência, obrigações de transparência documental e requerimentos definitivos de mérito: - Suspensão preventiva de atos: Pedido de suspensão liminar imediata dos efeitos de eventuais licenças, alvarás ou aprovações municipais concedidas sem comprovação prévia de conformidade ambiental e urbanística; - Impedimento de intervenções: Solicitação para que o município se abstenha de autorizar início de obras, supressão de vegetação, movimentação de terra ou qualquer intervenção ambiental relacionada ao tema até que haja comprovação regular dos atos. Perguntas Frequentes sobre a discussão de Data Center em Atibaia (FAQ) 1. Existe algum projeto de data center aprovado ou em análise na Prefeitura de Atibaia? Não. Segundo nota oficial da Prefeitura de Atibaia, não há nenhum projeto protocolado na Administração Municipal, tampouco processo de análise técnica ou licenciamento ambiental em andamento para esse tipo de empreendimento. 2. Qual é o objetivo do abaixo-assinado que ultrapassou 6 mil assinaturas em Atibaia? A petição "Atibaia não será quintal para Data Centers", que reúne 6.518 assinaturas verificadas, busca garantir participação popular e defender uma regulamentação municipal que proíba a implantação de empreendimentos desse porte sem avaliação ambiental adequada. 3. O que pede a ação popular apresentada nesta segunda-feira (23)? A ação pede transparência documental e medida liminar para suspender eventuais licenças ou alvarás sem estudo prévio, além de impedir qualquer início de obras, movimentação de terra ou supressão de vegetação relacionada ao empreendimento até a comprovação de regularidade legal. artigo.texto: Impacto de custo de data centers ainda é dúvida, diz analista Pesquisa do Bank of America mostra redução da exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte em 20 anos Uma pesquisa do BofA (Bank of America) revelou que os investidores diminuíram sua exposição em ações de tecnologia no ritmo mais forte dos últimos 20 anos. O movimento ocorre em meio ao receio de uma possível desaceleração nos gastos com data centers e ao risco de uma bolha de inteligência artificial. Felipe Cima, analista de renda variável da Manchester, avalia que a pesquisa é um importante indicador do posicionamento dos grandes investidores institucionais. Segundo ele, o mercado estaria atribuindo grande importância ao valor do equity das empresas de inteligência artificial justamente no momento em que o foco se volta para o crédito. "A grande questão que se levanta é qual o retorno sobre os investimentos que têm sido feitos, até quando esses investimentos trilionários vão continuar e qual é a possibilidade de estimar um retorno sobre eles", afirmou. Juros e custo de capital no centro das preocupações O analista destacou que o cenário de juros nos Estados Unidos mudou significativamente. O ano começou com expectativas de cortes nas taxas, mas a perspectiva atual aponta para uma possível nova elevação, sem previsão de queda para o ano seguinte. "Tudo isso impacta o custo de capital dessas empresas no momento em que fica muito difícil para que elas tirem o pé do acelerador", explicou Felipe Cima. Para ele, o risco que chega ao radar é justamente se o capital necessário para financiar investimentos na casa das centenas de bilhões de dólares continuará disponível. IPO da Anthropic e a janela de oportunidade Ao ser questionado sobre o aparente paradoxo entre a apreensão com a inteligência artificial e a expectativa gerada pelo IPO da Anthropic, Felipe Cima afirmou que o movimento faz sentido estratégico. S egundo ele, empresas como Google, Micron e Amazon já investiram na Anthropic via fundos de private equity, o que dispensou a necessidade de uma abertura de capital anterior. "Talvez ela escolher esse momento seja justamente a ideia de que a janela pode se encerrar logo, caso a taxa de juros americana continue subindo", disse. O analista ainda ressaltou que, considerando apenas SpaceX e Anthropic, o volume de arrecadação em IPOs neste ano já deve superar a média anual dos últimos dez anos, que girava em torno de 50 bilhões de dólares. Data centers, política e oportunidades para o Brasil Felipe Cima também comentou sobre a resistência política à construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos, apontando que ainda há incompreensão sobre o impacto desses empreendimentos no custo de energia e no uso da água nas localidades afetadas. "Acho que houve, de certa forma, um exagero por parte dos políticos", avaliou. Para ele, essa resistência pode abrir oportunidades para outros países, incluindo o Brasil, que dispõe de energia e água abundantes. "O Brasil poderia, de uma certa forma ou de outra, acabar se beneficiando dessa diversificação", afirmou. Bolha ou não? Analista descarta comparação com a crise das pontocom Sobre a possibilidade de uma bolha de inteligência artificial semelhante à crise das empresas pontocom dos anos 2000, Felipe Cima foi cauteloso. Ele lembrou que, na época da bolha pontocom, havia empresas negociando a duas mil vezes o preço-lucro, enquanto a Nvidia, por exemplo, apresenta múltiplos bem mais modestos para os próximos anos. "Não é múltiplo de bolha, não é múltiplo de cenário de euforia", afirmou. O analista também ponderou que 90% da economia americana cresce entre 1% e 1,5% ao ano, enquanto os 10% ligados à inteligência artificial crescem entre 25% e 30%. Com base nisso, ele concluiu que é difícil falar em recessão na economia americana nos próximos 18 meses, especialmente se os Estados Unidos conseguirem acomodar a taxa de juros.

artigo.texto: Known as “Project Flyer,” the proposed 300 megawatt data center would be located just north of the Dayton Airport on Montgomery County Line Road between Peters and Dog Leg Roads. UNION — On Monday night, the City of Union announced a preliminary plan for a large data center campus, and representatives of the developer, Panattoni Data Centers, presented it at the Union City Council meeting. More than 50 people packed the meeting room, and more than 50 more stood outside in the cold waiting for updates. The meeting was streamed live on YouTube, and a recording is available on the City of Union's YouTube channel, youtube.com/@CityofUnionOhio. The project website, marketing.panattoni.com/project-flyer, has FAQs, updates and a form for submitting questions and comments. Residents will get a chance to ask their own questions next week. Panattoni will hold an informational open house from 5 to 9 p.m. Monday, Nov. 30, at 201 W. Martindale Road in Union, where project representatives will meet one-on-one with interested residents. There will be no formal presentation. Residents, interested subcontractors and scholarship applicants can stop in anytime to visit tables and review materials. Other Data Centers in Ohio By comparison, at 300 MW on 200 acres, this proposed data center would be much smaller than two other data centers proposed in Ohio. In Piqua, developer J5 LLC (doing business as Shaytura LLC) has requested about 1,400 megawatts for a campus on about 608 acres at Farrington and Washington roads, with Meta reported as the operator. That's nearly five times Union's size. / In Pike County, SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, plans the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus at 10 gigawatts, or 10,000 megawatts, with OpenAI as the tenant, on less than 500 acres of private land in its current permit application. The planned 10 gigawatts, or 10,000 MW, is more than 30 times Union's size. Project Flyer Called "Project Flyer," the proposed campus would sit on about 201 acres in the city, according to Panattoni's presentation and project website. It calls for four data center buildings, three of 320,000 square feet and one of 288,000 square feet, plus one administrative building. At full buildout, the campus would have about 300 megawatts of electrical capacity, and the developer expects to build it in phases. The land is already zoned L1 light industrial, which allows data centers, so no rezoning is required, according to the developer. A conceptual aerial rendering shown at the meeting, labeled "for illustrative purposes only," places the campus among farm fields next to an existing electrical substation. The city has been negotiating with Panattoni for some time, though it hasn't said for how long. Union City Council is led by Mayor Michael O'Callaghan and Vice Mayor John Bruns. The other council members are Robert Bennett, Linda Black, Stephen Brookover, Josh Rarick and Lynne Thomas-Roth. The meeting also included public comments, and the Gazette will report on community reaction in a follow-up story. Power, water and neighbors On its project website, Panattoni says it will pay 100% of the costs of all power, substation and other infrastructure the campus needs, which it says ensures that Ohio families' electric rates won't go up because of the development. The company says it is working with the city to evaluate using treated, recycled water from the local water treatment facility. It also says enough water and sewer capacity is available to serve the campus, and that the development will pay for any infrastructure extensions. To limit the effect on nearby properties, Panattoni says it will plan building placement, setbacks, landscaping, lighting, screening and sound-reduction measures, and that its construction plans will address traffic and site activity during each phase. Jobs and taxes The company says construction will need electrical, mechanical, civil and general construction trades, and that once it's running, the campus is expected to support permanent jobs in facility operations and related services. Panattoni says it will prioritize hiring qualified local contractors, suppliers and businesses. It hasn't released estimates of the number of jobs or of tax revenue, saying "project-specific estimates will be shared once available and validated." About the developer Panattoni Data Centers is part of the family-owned Panattoni organization, founded in 1986, which says it has developed more than 700 million square feet of real estate. The company says it has 20 years of experience building in the City of Union and is a member of the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. Its data center team reports delivering about 9.2 gigawatts of data center capacity over their careers, including 16 campuses of more than 100 megawatts each. The project website, marketing.panattoni.com/project-flyer, has FAQs, updates and a form for submitting questions and comments. The Gazette will continue to follow this story. Please feel free to reach out to the Gazette on Facebook. We are looking for community feedback through “Letters to the Editor” - please email those to editor@tippgazette.com

artigo.texto: The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) has approved tariffs for the Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (MSEDCL) to procure 2,000 MW/4,000 MWh of battery energy storage capacity for a period of 15 years. In its order dated November 23, 2026, in Case No. 218 of 2026, the commission approved a monthly tariff of Rs. 2,40,000 per MW for Part-A and Rs. 2,38,000 per MW for Part-B. The procurement will be supported through Viability Gap Funding (VGF) under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF). The approved projects will operate on a one-cycle-per-day basis, with a two-hour discharge duration. The tender was divided into two parts under a Request for Selection issued on June 30, 2026. Part-A covers 500 MW/1,000 MWh of battery storage capacity at MSEDCL substations and is exclusively reserved for eligible developers under the Mukhyamantri Saur Krushi Vahini Yojana (MSKVY) 2.0. Part-B covers 1,500 MW/3,000 MWh across Maharashtra State Electricity Transmission Company Limited (MSETCL) substations and locations co-located with existing solar projects contracted with MSEDCL. The tender received 45 bids, which were opened in August 2026. Reverse auctions conducted on August 31, 2026, determined the final tariffs after the highest bidders were disqualified in accordance with the tender conditions. MSEDCL subsequently issued Letters of Award (LoAs) to the selected developers on September 18, 2026. In Part-A, five developers were selected, with Oriana Power Limited securing the largest allocation of 400 MW. In Part-B, seven developers received awards. Oriana Power Limited secured 500 MW, followed by BSL Engineering Service Limited with 300 MW and ArMee Infotech Limited with 250 MW. All selected developers have committed to maintaining a minimum round-trip efficiency of 85%. The latest procurement process follows an earlier 2,000 MW/4,000 MWh battery storage tender for which MERC had approved a tariff of Rs. 1,65,998 per MW per month on March 6, 2026. However, the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity set aside that approval on June 5, 2026. The Supreme Court subsequently stayed the tribunal’s decision on September 9, 2026. In an affidavit submitted on November 5, 2026, MSEDCL clarified that the new procurement exercise is separate from the ongoing legal proceedings. It also stated that approval of the new tender does not depend on the Supreme Court’s interim order. VGF support of up to Rs. 18 lakh per MWh has been reserved exclusively for developers selected under the new bidding process. MERC observed that the procurement process was transparent and that the discovered tariffs were reasonable compared with recent battery storage tenders conducted by other utilities, considering the available VGF support. The commission also permitted the approved storage capacity to count towards MSEDCL’s Energy Storage Obligation, as applicable regulatory targets increase to 4% by FY 2029-30. The projects are expected to be commissioned during FY 2027-28. MERC has directed MSEDCL to execute Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreements with all selected developers within 15 days of the order and submit copies of the signed agreements to the commission for its records.
