artigo.texto: CATL leads the global EV battery market with a 39.1% share, followed by BYD at 15.2%. Solid-state, sodium-ion and silicon-anode batteries represent major areas of next-generation battery research. Energy storage demand offers new growth opportunities as global battery shipments reach 461.3 GWh in H1 2026. Batteries have quietly become the most contested part of the electric future. They decide what an EV costs, how far it goes, how fast it charges and whether it catches fire. They also decide whether a solar farm can keep running after sunset. China dominates the business, with South Korea, Japan and the United States holding on to real pockets of strength. CATL and BYD are far ahead of other competitors in EV batteries, followed by LG Energy Solution, Panasonic Energy and Samsung SDI vying to keep their place. These are the ten companies shaping the market, and what sets each one apart. CATL, based in Ningde, is the biggest name in EV batteries by a wide margin. From January to September 2026 it supplied 39.1% of the market, or 389.2 GWh of installed capacity. That is roughly two and a half times BYD’s share. Most of its batteries use LFP or NMC chemistry, and it is also pushing into sodium-ion cells, battery swapping and ultra-fast charging. A three-year, 60 GWh storage deal with HyperStrong shows that cars are no longer its only big customer. BYD, in Shenzhen, took 15.2% of EV battery installations in the first nine months of 2026. Its Blade Battery is an LFP design built around safety and low cost. BYD also builds the cars those batteries go into, which means no supplier negotiations and no waiting on anyone else’s schedule. Solid-state is the next target, with first vehicle use aimed at 2027 and mass production around 2030. That control over the whole chain is the main reason rivals struggle to match its costs. LG Energy Solution holds 8.2% of the EV market and is the strongest South Korean player. It makes NMC, NCMA and LFP cells in both cylindrical and pouch formats, and its supply deals with carmakers are spread across the world. Energy storage has been a bright spot, with shipments climbing fast in the first half of 2026, mostly in North America. The company’s next moves are LFP, new chemistries and big storage systems. Gotion, from Hefei, sits fourth with 5.1%. It makes LFP and NMC batteries and has a research team working on solid-state cells. Its roots in battery materials give it more control over its supply than most. Overseas factories and high-energy-density cells are what it is betting on for the next stage. CALB, short for China Aviation Lithium Battery, took 5.0% from January to September 2026. The Changzhou company makes LFP and ternary lithium-ion cells for cars and for energy storage. It is good at producing cells in volume and designing packs for carmakers. With EV and stationary storage demand both rising, CALB is working to build a foothold outside China. Also Read - Ford Enters Battery Manufacturing with First U.S.-Made LFP Cells EVE Energy, based in Huizhou, holds 3.6% of EV installations, but its reach is wider than that figure suggests. Its cells go into cars, consumer electronics and large storage projects, and it ranked second worldwide in energy storage battery shipments in the first half of 2026. Large-format cells and plans for factories abroad are the areas to follow. Panasonic Energy, from Japan, also holds 3.6%. Its name is tied to Tesla, which it has supplied for years with some of the best-regarded cylindrical cells around. Research now covers nickel-rich cathodes, silicon anodes and the 4680 format. Packing more energy into each cell while making it cheaper to build is the company’s primary goal. SK On, from Seoul, has 2.8% of the market. It leans on high-nickel NMC chemistry and advanced cell design. Deals with carmakers and a global network of factories keep it close to the biggest vehicle markets. Cost cutting, solid-state research and better performance drive its long-term plans. Svolt Energy, in Changzhou, held 2.6% in the first nine months of 2026. It makes LFP, high-nickel ternary and cobalt-free batteries. Cobalt is expensive and ethically messy to source, so a good cobalt-free cell is a real prize. Svolt’s European plans give it a route to markets beyond China. REPT BATTERO, based in Wenzhou, took 2.4% of EV installations. Its batteries are mainly LFP and go into cars and big energy storage projects. It focuses on large-format cells and utility-scale storage, the kind of equipment that sits beside a solar farm or substation. Growing overseas and improving cell design are its next priorities. Why this Matters Cleaner energy, electric transport and a stable grid all hang on better batteries. Cheaper cells bring down energy costs and make renewable power easier to rely on, which means less dependence on fossil fuels. The companies on this list will decide how quickly that happens and who profits from it. The next shake-up is likely to come from solid-state cells, sodium-ion chemistry, silicon anodes and recycling. CATL and BYD are far ahead on scale today, but Samsung SDI, Toyota, QuantumScape and Solid Power are attracting attention for their solid-state work. Storage may turn out to be the bigger story. Global energy storage battery shipments hit 461.3 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 71% on a year earlier, with CATL holding 27.1% of that market. Winning EV contracts is no longer enough. Power grids, renewable projects, data centres and advanced electronics all want batteries now. The companies that come out on top will be the ones that get cell performance, cost, safety and factory output right at once, and that can turn lab results into products that work reliably at scale. 1. However, it is unclear how much of TSL’s package remains unfinished. When was McAlpine Appointed for the Project? McAlpine was appointed as delivery partner for Building One in July 2024. The building and ancillary development together spanned 244,710 square metres. Additionally, the provider Glenigan valued the contract at £214.4m. Additionally, a spokesperson for the contractor said in June that its work was complete. Agratas Somerset Facility to Initially Supply Jaguar and Land Rover Agratas, part of Indian multinational Tata, plans to initially supply Jaguar Land Rover from the Somerset facility. McAlpine’s work included building an energy centre and other ancillary and support buildings. The steel frame of Building One was completed in January. In the summer, roofing and cladding were expected to continue into the third quarter of 2026. Others involved in delivering the facilities so far include design consultants Stantec, planners Turner & Townsend and steel contractor Severfield. Currently, Agratas and TSL have been contacted for comment. Lastly, when McAlpine exited in June, an Agratas spokesperson said: “As the project has progressed, we have determined that a different construction delivery model is needed to support the next phase of our development. “Following a review of the project’s requirements, we have decided to transition to a new construction partner. We thank our existing construction partner for their support to date. “This change reflects the evolving needs of the project, positioning us to deliver the next phase with the capability and focus required to meet our objectives safely, efficiently and on schedule.”

artigo.texto: A Vaisala, fabricante finlandesa de tecnologias de medição e monitoramento, completa 90 anos e inaugura operação local no Brasil, com a transferência da sede sul-americana do Rio de Janeiro para São Paulo. Fundada em 1936, na Finlândia, a companhia construiu sua trajetória a partir da meteorologia e hoje está presente nas 50 maiores farmacêuticas do mundo. Com representação no país desde 2018, ela passa a atuar como Vaisala do Brasil, e a nova sede, na Vila Olímpia, também funciona como hub para os países da América do Sul. Setores prioritários puxam a expansão Para o gerente regional da Vaisala na América do Sul, Bruno Albuquerque, o país ganhou relevância na estratégia global da companhia. Além de representar sozinho cerca de metade da economia da América Latina, o Brasil reúne setores industriais considerados prioritários para a empresa. Ele resume o cenário: “O Brasil possui um mercado interno extremamente relevante e concentra investimentos importantes em segmentos como farmacêutico, energia, mineração, healthcare, alimentos e infraestrutura digital.” América Latina volta ao centro da estratégia O cenário econômico internacional reforçou a importância da diversificação geográfica das operações globais, e a região voltou a ocupar o centro das discussões estratégicas. O avanço do acordo comercial entre União Europeia e Mercosul contribui para esse movimento. Desde 2018, a companhia amplia a atuação regional com reforço da equipe local, expansão da rede de distribuidores e desenvolvimento de novos mercados no país. Operação própria e novo escritório em SP Desde o segundo semestre deste ano, a empresa passou a operar oficialmente como Vaisala do Brasil, com estrutura própria de importação, logística, armazenamento, suporte comercial e serviços. A abertura do novo escritório em São Paulo, na última semana, marca uma nova fase no país. Sobre o efeito dessa mudança para os clientes, o executivo aponta o ganho esperado: “Essa proximidade permitirá maior agilidade operacional, suporte técnico local e melhor experiência para os clientes, especialmente em projetos de maior complexidade tecnológica.” Data centers, energia e farmacêutico lideram potencial Entre os segmentos com maior potencial de crescimento no país estão data centers, energia e farmacêutico. A demanda por inteligência artificial, processamento de dados e eletrificação da economia acelera investimentos em infraestrutura crítica. A indústria alimentícia também aparece como mercado promissor, diante das novas oportunidades comerciais entre Mercosul e União Europeia. Pesquisa e desenvolvimento acima da média do setor Com faturamento superior a € 500 milhões (cerca de R$ 2,9 bilhões), a companhia destina mais de 10% desse montante à pesquisa e desenvolvimento, percentual acima da média do setor de instrumentação industrial. O investimento sustenta tecnologias proprietárias de medição, produzidas em sala limpa na Finlândia. Entre elas estão Humicap®, Drycap®, Barocap®, Carbocap® e Peroxcap®, usadas como base para diferentes linhas de produtos. Essas tecnologias permitem medições de alta precisão e estabilidade, importantes em operações que exigem controle rigoroso de variáveis ambientais e de processo. Da meteorologia à medição industrial Segundo o gerente, a trajetória da companhia combina ciência, inovação e desenvolvimento tecnológico, com a ampliação de atuação para além da meteorologia: “Ao longo de décadas, a Vaisala expandiu sua atuação além da meteorologia e consolidou sua divisão de Medições Industriais, responsável por soluções aplicadas em processos críticos ao redor do mundo.” A fabricante se especializou em medições de gases e líquidos, com foco em temperatura, umidade, pressão e CO₂. Hoje, essas soluções são amplamente aplicadas nas indústrias de ciências da vida, que respondem por uma fatia relevante da receita da área de medições industriais. Sobre a companhia Com mais de 90 anos de atuação e cerca de 2.500 especialistas, a companhia tem ações da série A negociadas na Nasdaq Helsinki.

artigo.texto: A Quercus contestou esta terça-feira a instalação de um centro de dados destinado ao treino de inteligência artificial em Coruche, estimando que a infraestrutura possa consumir o equivalente a 40% a 50% da eletricidade utilizada anualmente no concelho. Num comunicado enviado à Lusa, a Quercus junta-se à oposição ao projeto da Associação de Defesa do Património de Coruche, alertando para as necessidades energéticas e para os potenciais impactos sobre os “recursos hídricos, a paisagem e as populações”. Segundo a associação ambientalista, o centro de dados, com uma potência de 6,4 megawatts (MW), deverá ocupar uma parcela de 7.209 metros quadrados no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia e entrar em funcionamento no final de 2027. Promovido pelo fundo de investimento Aura Capital, através da Aura Technologies, o projeto prevê a criação de 30 postos de trabalho, sem especificar se serão diretos ou indiretos, ainda de acordo com a Quercus. Na nota, a associação destaca que a venda do terreno recebeu uma pronúncia favorável da Câmara de Coruche, no distrito de Santarém, que atribuiu “uma bonificação de 40% associada ao alegado contributo para a economia local”, além de incentivos fiscais, nomeadamente isenções do Imposto Municipal sobre as Transmissões Onerosas de Imóveis (IMT) e do Imposto Municipal sobre Imóveis (IMI). De acordo com os cálculos apresentados pela associação ambientalista, a infraestrutura poderá consumir cerca de 44,9 gigawatts-hora (GWh) por ano, considerando uma taxa média de utilização de 80%. Ou seja, indica a Quercus, esse consumo corresponderia a cerca de 42% dos 107,9 GWh de eletricidade consumidos no concelho de Coruche em 2024, com base em dados da Pordata. “Caso venha a funcionar continuamente à potência máxima, poderá atingir os 56,1 GWh/ano, cerca de 52% do consumo elétrico anual do concelho”, refere a associação, ressalvando que não é ainda conhecido se os 6,4 MW anunciados correspondem à potência elétrica total do centro ou apenas à capacidade computacional instalada. Neste último caso, advertiu, poderão “faltar os consumos dos sistemas de refrigeração, alimentação elétrica e restantes infraestruturas de suporte”, elevando as necessidades energéticas da instalação. A associação critica igualmente “a ausência de informação sobre o sistema de arrefecimento previsto”, considerando que a utilização de mecanismos baseados na evaporação poderá aumentar a pressão sobre os recursos hídricos da região. Entre os possíveis impactos, a Quercus aponta riscos para o abastecimento público e para a Paisagem Protegida Local do Açude do Monte da Barca e defende a adoção de medidas que garantam o cumprimento dos limites legais de ruído. A Quercus adianta que já pediu à Comunidade Intermunicipal da Lezíria do Tejo, da qual Coruche faz parte, que se pronuncie publicamente contra o projeto, alegando existir uma acumulação excessiva de infraestruturas desta natureza na região. A associação defende ainda que o diploma anunciado pelo Governo para regular a instalação de centros de dados em Portugal deve impor restrições concretas ao consumo de energia e água e sujeitar os novos projetos a uma declaração de impacto ambiental favorável. “Temos sérias dúvidas de que os ganhos socioeconómicos justifiquem o consumo intensivo de energia e de água, a descaracterização da paisagem, a emissão de CO2 ou o ruído causado por estas infraestruturas”, afirma Mariana Garanhão, responsável pelo acompanhamento das políticas públicas na Quercus, citada no comunicado. Segundo a Quercus, a Aura Technologies planeia instalar pelo menos outros dois centros de dados em Portugal. [Duarte Lima é detido em Portugal no âmbito do caso BPN. Nas buscas que antecedem a prisão, em 2011, as autoridades descobrem uma sala secreta na casa do advogado. Enquanto isso, no Brasil, a investigação à morte de Rosalina Ribeiro continua e, desta vez, Duarte Lima presta declarações. O processo acaba por ser transferido para Portugal. E, 17 anos depois do homicídio, o julgamento vai finalmente acontecer. Já pode ouvir o sexto e último episódio de “As Sombras de Duarte Lima”, o novo Podcast Plus do Observador. Está disponível no site do Observador, na Apple Podcasts, no Spotify e no Youtube.]

artigo.texto: Empreendimento de R$ 250 milhões, com potencial de expansão para 100 MW, já é alvo de investigação do Ministério Público do Pará. Sessão será realizada nesta quinta-feira (26), no auditório da Sudam. Foto: Reprodução/Internet A vereadora Marinor Brito convocou uma sessão especial para discutir os possíveis impactos ambientais e sociais do data center BEL1, empreendimento da empresa Elea Data Centers, em parceria com a AXIA Energia, antiga Eletrobras, previsto para a área portuária de Miramar, no bairro do Barreiro, em Belém. O debate será realizado nesta quinta-feira, 26 de novembro, às 9h, no auditório da Superintendência do Desenvolvimento da Amazônia (Sudam). O projeto prevê capacidade elétrica de 7,5 megawatts (MW), com possibilidade de expansão para até 100 MW. A Elea será responsável pela operação do centro de processamento de dados, enquanto a AXIA fornecerá a infraestrutura energética. “O BEL1 vem com a promessa de modernidade. Mas quanto de água e de energia ele vai consumir? Que impacto terá sobre o meio ambiente e sobre as comunidades do entorno? O que Belém e o povo daqui ganham com isso?”, questiona Marinor Brito. Ministério Público já investiga o empreendimento O data center já é alvo de um inquérito civil instaurado em julho de 2026 pela 1ª Promotoria de Justiça de Barcarena, do Ministério Público do Estado do Pará (MPPA), sob responsabilidade do promotor Márcio Silva Maués de Faria. O procedimento investiga a legalidade da implantação do BEL1 e seus possíveis impactos ambientais, climáticos e sociais, especialmente sobre comunidades ribeirinhas e tradicionais das ilhas das Onças e Arapiranga, em Barcarena, localizadas nas proximidades da área prevista para a instalação. Entre as preocupações levantadas pelo MPPA estão a elevada demanda energética, a possibilidade de formação de ilhas de calor, a emissão contínua de ruídos e os impactos sobre os recursos naturais e as comunidades. Em agosto, a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente de Belém e a Secretaria de Estado de Meio Ambiente, Clima e Sustentabilidade informaram que não havia processos de licenciamento ambiental do empreendimento em análise. O Ministério Público também cobrou esclarecimentos da empresa sobre estudos técnicos e consultas às populações potencialmente afetadas. Em setembro, a Elea informou que o empreendimento permanecia em fase de planejamento e estudos, com implantação projetada para o fim de 2028, prazo posterior à previsão inicial de operação no segundo trimestre de 2027. Para Marinor Brito, a implantação de uma infraestrutura tecnológica dessa dimensão precisa ser acompanhada de transparência e participação popular, especialmente diante das dificuldades de acesso a serviços básicos enfrentadas por parte da população. “Decisões que mexem com o nosso território, nossos rios e nosso futuro não podem ser tomadas sem debate público, sem transparência e sem ouvir quem vive aqui”, afirma a parlamentar. artigo.texto: Quincy mayor reveals conversations have happened between landowners and data center companies QUINCY (WGEM) - Mayor Linda Moore said at Monday’s city council meeting that she has heard about private landowners in Quincy potentially nearing deals with data center developers. Moore discussed the talks at a city council meeting before the council voted to pass a moratorium on data centers. She said no official proposals have been submitted to the city, but she believes some of the discussions could soon lead to projects. “All I know is they’re getting serious and specific property owners have had conversations with the developers, so when it gets to the point where developers and property owners are talking, then a deal could be imminent,” Moore said. Moore said she learned about the conversations Thursday and that one or two began three to four months ago. The mayor said a restrictive ordinance is in the works and could go before the Quincy Plan Commission as early as January. She said it would set requirements for data centers rather than automatically prohibit them, similar to the city’s approach to solar farms. “I think we would limit them to industrial only. We do have to have to address the R1A, the rural areas within that mile and a half where a data center might want to be, so we’ll look at that as well. The other thing is to restrict is when they test their backup generators because they can be very noisy,” Moore said. Moore said the city could also extend the moratorium, ban data centers outright or make development requirements stringent enough that a developer would choose not to build in Quincy. Also at the meeting, Adams County Emergency Management Director John Simon spoke to the council about Wednesday’s proposed army detonation in Iowa. “Those are all parts of the unknowns that we don’t know of how much [lead azide] is going to be released,” he said. The date of the detonation has been up in the air over the last week. Simon said no one can assume what is going to happen until it does. “Until those things are known at and after the time of detonation, one man’s guess is one man’s guess,” he explained. artigo.texto: Em um País que investe na ampliação da oferta de energia, os cortes de geração no Sistema Interligado Nacional escancaram uma contradição na lógica de expansão do setor elétrico brasileiro (SEB): cerca de 20% da geração potencial solar e eólica deixou de ser aproveitada em 2025, segundo levantamento da Volt Robotics. Tais cortes, conhecidos como “curtailment”, ocorrem quando o sistema não consegue absorver toda a energia que as usinas poderiam produzir. Uma das principais explicações da produção excedente é a recente expansão das fontes eólica e solar, modais inseridos na classe das energias limpas. Diferentemente das grandes hidrelétricas, cuja variação dos reservatórios ajusta a geração de eletricidade às oscilações do consumo, usinas solares e eólicas não armazenam o recurso energético primário para utilização posterior, sendo dependentes, portanto, da disponibilidade instantânea de sol e vento, que nem sempre acompanha a demanda. De acordo com Marcelo Rocha, gestor ambiental com 16 anos de atuação no setor elétrico e diretor da étiK Ambiental, consultoria especializada nesse segmento, é neste cenário que os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia por Baterias (Battery Energy Storage Systems, “BESS”) se projetam como uma tecnologia chave para o futuro do SEB. “Eles guardam energia nos períodos de excedente e as entregam nos horários de maior demanda. Desempenham, neste sentido, parte das funções de flexibilidade historicamente associadas aos reservatórios hidrelétricos e às termelétricas”, explica Marcelo. A Lei Federal nº 15.269/2025 garantiu reconhecimento institucional aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia, e a Portaria MME nº 136/2026 estabeleceu as diretrizes dos leilões de reserva de capacidade previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro, questionados pela Abeeólica, que ajuizou ação civil pública no último dia 16, na 17ª Vara Federal Cível do Distrito Federal, para contestar as regras de custeio e pedir a suspensão dos certames. Em 19 de novembro, a entidade também propôs, no STF, ação direta de inconstitucionalidade contra a regra que atribui exclusivamente aos geradores os custos da contratação. A perspectiva de expansão do BESS em larga escala convive, porém, com uma indefinição ainda mais ampla no licenciamento ambiental, cujas regras específicas para a tecnologia ainda estão em construção. O mito do licenciamento ambiental descomplicado Para Marcelo, muitos agentes setoriais se apegaram à crença de que o licenciamento ambiental do BESS será “simples”, porquanto sua potencial associação a empreendimentos pré-existentes reduziria a extensão das intervenções necessárias à implantação da nova tecnologia. “O precedente do SEB, porém, revela os limites desta perspectiva”, observa. Em 1995, no âmbito das reformas do setor elétrico, a Lei Federal nº 9.074 dispensou de concessão ou autorização junto ao poder concedente os aproveitamentos hidrelétricos limitados à potência de 1 MW, a partir de então denominados “centrais geradoras hidrelétricas” (CGH). Segundo o diretor da étiK Bioengenharia, esta desburocratização, somada à reduzida intervenção para implantação das CGHs, alimentou a expectativa de que o licenciamento ambiental seria “simples”. Não obstante, a identificação de impactos cumulativos antes subestimados culminou em condicionantes às CGH’s que, em muitos casos, se igualam às aplicadas a grandes hidrelétricas. “A lição deixada pelas CGH’s não impediu que, na recente expansão das fontes eólica e fotovoltaica, os agentes setoriais reproduzissem o mesmo paradigma e, ato contínuo, obtivessem os mesmos resultados”, avalia Marcelo. O reconhecimento de impactos cumulativos e sinérgicos deu causa a exigências de avaliações cada vez mais amplas, reduzindo a utilidade do fracionamento artificial dos projetos. A depender do porte e localização da área, o licenciamento pode inclusive atingir ritos complexos. “O histórico setorial é inequívoco: pequeno porte ou baixo impacto não asseguram licenciamento simples, ainda que nominalmente simplificado”, ressalta Marcelo Rocha. Cada estado, uma régua Na avaliação de Marcelo, provavelmente o BESS não repetirá, em termos estritos, a trajetória das CGHs, fotovoltaicas e eólicas, mas tampouco escapará da lógica brasileira segundo a qual “a promessa inicial de simplicidade é tensionada pelo ‘amadurecimento’ dos órgãos ambientais e pela heterogeneidade federativa do licenciamento”, já perceptível nos critérios estabelecidos nos oito estados que, até o momento, regulamentaram o enquadramento ambiental do BESS. Piauí e Rio Grande do Sul adotam a área útil como parâmetro de enquadramento, enquanto Goiás considera a área total ocupada. Bahia e Pará utilizam a potência; Ceará e Rio Grande do Norte, a capacidade de armazenamento. No Rio de Janeiro, embora o BESS já conste entre as atividades sujeitas a licenciamento, ainda não estão claros os parâmetros quantitativos para seu enquadramento. Nos demais estados não se verifica, até o momento, normas ambientais específicas para a tecnologia. Não surpreende, à luz destes critérios, que projetos tecnicamente equivalentes possam se sujeitar a exigências distintas, ainda que em condições locacionais comparáveis. A título de exemplo, um BESS com 200 m² de área útil se enquadra na faixa de não incidência do licenciamento estadual no Piauí e no porte mínimo sujeito a licenciamento no Rio Grande do Sul. Já um sistema de 600 MWh recebe classificação de porte e potencial poluidor médios tanto no Ceará quanto no Rio Grande do Norte. Mesmo assim, enquanto as normas cearenses preveem duas etapas de licenciamento, as potiguares estabelecem três, com estudos ambientais distintos entre os estados. Na avaliação de Marcelo, este arcabouço normativo existente, além de contrariar as expectativas de que a instalação das baterias em áreas intervindas afastaria automaticamente a incidência do rito ordinário, indica que o BESS não será absorvido de modo homogêneo pelos órgãos licenciadores brasileiros. artigo.texto: Construction at the Google data center project in Botetourt County must stop, a circuit judge ordered Monday, after ruling that the county’s board of supervisors violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act when it approved a key agreement with the tech giant. All actions the county has taken since the June 24, 2025, meeting that greenlit the project are rescinded, and the county must hold a public hearing on the matter that “conforms to” the state law regarding open meetings and open records, substitute Judge Michael Doucette wrote. In other words, county residents who didn’t have the opportunity to weigh in on this issue may speak out before the board once again votes. Robert Dallas filed the suit on Nov. 2, alleging that the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing in closed session a performance agreement with Google’s developer, Helio Capital LLC, or a resolution to enact the agreement. [Disclosure: Google is one of our donors through its Google News Initiative, which helped support our expansion in the New River Valley. Donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy.] After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve the agreement, but only after it had added the item to its agenda during the meeting, Dallas alleged. It only publicized what it had voted on hours later. A lawyer for the county did not dispute those facts but argued that the county did enough to satisfy state law. During arguments in Botetourt County Circuit Court on Nov. 10, Julian Harf — representing the county, the board and the economic development authority — “stated on a number of occasions that the alleged violations … were ‘technical violations’ and on one occasion stated that ‘magic words’ were not used,” Doucette wrote to parties in the case. “Such concessions are precisely the point” that Dallas raised, the judge added. The state’s Freedom of Information Act “is a technical and strictly procedural act adopted by the General Assembly. ‘Magic words’ must be used and ‘technical violations’ are not excused.” A board failing to identify what it is voting on is a clear violation, said Megan Rhyne, executive director of the Williamsburg-based Virginia Coalition for Open Government. “FOIA is written in a way that you’re supposed to at least let the public know what you’re voting on, and so I was really heartened by that part of the ruling, because it is an acknowledgment that the public gets to know what these final votes are that their public body is taking and what it impacts.” Dallas’ legal team, led by Roanoke-based attorney John Fishwick, said in a prepared statement that it is pleased with the decision. “We believe this result sends a clear message to public bodies throughout the commonwealth, that the rule of law and the public’s right to witness and participate in government must be respected,” the statement said. Fishwick said in an email that the team would not comment beyond its press statement. Botetourt County spokesman Brent Watts said in an email to media that county leaders would review that ruling with staff and the board and will not do interviews but will “share updates as appropriate” on the matter, which remains in litigation. “The county respects the legal process and appreciates the attention the court gave to hearing this matter,” said a statement that Watts emailed. “The county … is evaluating its options going forward.” Work continued at the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site at least 40 minutes after the county issued its 3:36 p.m. statement. Opposition to the data center grew quickly The performance agreement vote was one of multiple agenda items added on during the June 24, 2025, meeting, with no prior notice. The supervisors also announced that day a reworked agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, related to the Google project. Soon after, a groundswell of opposition developed, with multiple speakers in subsequent meetings decrying what they said was the board’s secrecy, the nondisclosure agreements that the supervisors signed, and concerns about the data center’s future electricity and water use, set against the backdrop of a drought that has affected a key regional water source, Carvins Cove Reservoir. An activist group, Southwest Virginia Data Center Transparency Alliance, quickly coalesced, with its membership making its presence felt at Botetourt County supervisors meetings as well as water authority meetings. Alliance member Julie Bivins, in a text message exchange on Monday, said that the ruling is “a major win” for Virginia communities facing the prospects of “back-door deals in local government.” “At a time when environmental protections are being stripped away, this case shows how important FOIA procedures are in keeping an open and transparent government,” Bivins said. “It’s really sad that we have to force our government officials to allow the public to even have accurate and timely information on massive projects like this that have significant community impacts.” The alliance, on its website, credited a member of Dallas’ legal team, Tim Dooley, with developing the case. “Botetourt County citizens have always known that this process wasn’t done ethically or correctly,” the alliance’s Kathryn Hatam said in a news release on the website. “We just needed Tim Dooley to find the specific statutes.” Dooley, in the alliance news release, said that he hoped it is a step toward transparency and accountability from public officials in Botetourt County and the Roanoke Valley. “This is, however, only one aspect of the clandestine dealings between Google, municipal governments, and economic development entities, which demand further scrutiny,” Dooley said in the release. artigo.texto: East County News Service Photo courtesy County of San Diego (San Diego County) — In Campo, a solar-powered microgrid with battery storage can keep the local fire station, health center and library running when wildfire weather forces a power shutoff. In Otay Mesa, a 2024 fire at a lithium-ion battery storage plant flared up on and off for nearly two weeks. Both experiences lead to a question the County of San Diego is taking to residents in December: Where should large battery systems be built, and what safeguards should neighbors expect? County planners will hold two free Zoom meetings, at noon Thursday, Dec. 3, and 6 p.m. Tuesday, Dec. 8, to explain proposed zoning rules for battery energy storage systems in unincorporated communities. Both sessions will cover the same material. Residents can ask questions and hear what staff changed after a public review in August and September. Registration is optional but you can register here. A closer look at BESS On a hot evening, air conditioners can still be running well after solar panels stop producing electricity. Batteries can store surplus solar power during the day and send it back to the grid after sunset, reducing the need to fire up natural gas plants. How long a battery can help depends on how much energy it holds and how quickly that energy is used. Battery capacity serving California grew from less than 700 megawatts in early 2019 to more than 23,000 megawatts by October 2026, according to state figures. That total includes home batteries as well as large installations, some of them across state lines. San Diego Gas & Electric already operates two battery storage facilities in East County. Its 7.5-megawatt El Cajon facility went into service in March 2017 and a 10-megawatt facility in Santee began operating earlier this year. During the county’s earlier public outreach, residents raised questions about evacuation routes, how firefighters would reach a site and what particles and pollutants nearby communities might breathe during a fire. Cleanup is another concern. After the Gateway Energy Storage fire in Otay Mesa, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency required the operator to monitor conditions while workers handled damaged batteries and to pay for their removal and disposal. Residents were able to review the county’s first public draft of its proposed battery storage zoning rules from Aug. 13 through Sept. 27. In its August draft, the county proposed barring battery storage facilities larger than 600 kilowatt-hours from residential zones. Developers could apply to build them in commercial, industrial, agricultural and special-purpose zones, but the batteries would have to sit at least 100 feet from every property line. At the December meetings, county planners will explain how they revised the proposal after hearing from residents. The county expects to post the revised proposal in late November and present it to the San Diego County Planning Commission in early 2027. Staff will summarize webinar comments for the commission. Residents can also comment directly at the hearing. How to participate – Thursday, Dec. 3, at noon. Join the Zoom meeting here: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/83936915487 – Tuesday, Dec. 8, at 6 p.m. Join the Zoom meeting here: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/84201924854 To request an interpreter for either meeting, call (858) 505-6677 before 11:59 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 25 or send an email to [email protected]. Residents can register, read project updates and sign up for notices on the county’s battery storage project page. The county has also posted the presentation slides and recordings from the August and September meetings here.

artigo.texto: Click here to read highlights from the story - Wisconsin once gave the Public Service Commission broad authority to guide utilities’ long-term energy planning, but lawmakers scrapped that system in 1998, shifting more control to utilities. - Ratepayer advocates argue the hands-off approach incentivizes power plant construction over investments in energy efficiency and demand reduction. - A surge in electricity demand from data centers is driving a multibillion-dollar buildout and renewing calls for regulators to take a greater role in planning for future needs. - Regulators say current law limits their ability to compare competing proposals and assess major projects as a package, prompting calls for lawmakers to reconsider the state’s approach. Wisconsin’s electricity needs are on track to skyrocket. Utilities plan to spend billions of dollars to keep up, and ratepayers — residents, businesses and data center operators — will pick up the bill. The three-member Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, is responsible for guarding ratepayers’ wallets from unreasonable spending, but Wisconsin law gives it relatively little sway over how utilities plan for the future. The commission can review proposed power plants on a case-by-case basis, but not as part of a broader blueprint for keeping the lights on as affordably as possible. That hasn’t always been the case. Bureaucratic gridlock and a near-blackout prompted Wisconsin lawmakers to scrap a more hands-on approach to energy planning three decades ago. Utilities don’t mourn its loss. Ratepayer advocates, however, argue the hands-off approach that followed caused Wisconsin’s electricity prices to climb faster than necessary. A flurry of new power plant projects spurred in part by the data center boom is pushing that once-arcane disagreement into the public eye, and regulators themselves are now taking a side. Wisconsin once gave regulators broad planning power Investor-owned utilities generally operate as regulated monopolies: State and federal commissions grant them exclusive rights to sell electricity to consumers within a defined territory in exchange for government oversight of their rates and infrastructure projects. That basic model dates back more than a century in Wisconsin, which formed its Public Service Commission — among the nation’s first utility regulators — in 1907. The mass adoption of air conditioning and the rise of nuclear power complicated the picture in the mid-20th century. Wisconsin lawmakers responded in the 1970s by empowering the Public Service Commission to take the lead on energy planning, hoping to steer utilities toward the most cost-effective path to meeting skyrocketing electricity demand. Those powers took shape as the “Advanced Plan”: 20-year road maps for utilities to meet electricity needs. Working in two-year cycles alongside consumer advocates and other players, the commission could revise the road map to fit its priorities, and especially to save ratepayers money. “This approach requires that the utilities focus on the most cost effective means of meeting customers’ energy service needs,” the commissioners explained in a 1987 biannual report. Utilities have a strong incentive to build new power plants. Ratepayers pay for newly built plants, along with a commission-approved “rate of return” on every dollar spent on the projects, passed along to the utility’s shareholders. The commission could use the Advanced Plan to reconfigure utilities’ construction plans in search of savings. Later iterations embraced demand-side fixes, trimming future energy needs by incentivizing customers to switch to energy-efficient appliances or run factories at off-peak hours. The PSC used its planning power to chip away at utility monopolies in 1989 by beginning to open utility-owned transmission lines to other power producers. Wisconsin was an early adopter of an open transmission system, hoping to keep prices in check by encouraging competition in the electricity market. State lawmakers later directed utilities to pass control of their transmission infrastructure to a new, independent company to protect other power producers’ access to the grid. That company, now called the American Transmission Company, was the country’s first multi-state, transmission-only utility. The PSC went further in 1993, inviting third-party developers to bid for power plant projects outlined in utilities’ long-term plans. Commissioners awarded a natural gas plant in Whitewater to a New York-based developer later that year, saving We Energies’ customers an estimated $66 million. Other states deregulated their electricity markets entirely. Chaos ensued, most notably in California, where flawed execution, price gouging and a drought caused regional blackouts, a major utility bankruptcy filing and billions of dollars in economic losses. Lawmakers let utilities take the lead Wisconsin didn’t copy California’s experiment. It did, however, scrap the Advanced Plan. Utilities argued comprehensive planning was cumbersome and prone to gridlock, blaming it for a slowdown in power plant and transmission construction in the mid-1990s. Some commission staff also recognized the Advanced Plan’s deficiencies. “It became an anti-utility regulatory mechanism that put electric reliability at risk,” recalled Randel Pilo, the PSC’s chief energy economist through much of the 1990s. A close call in the summer of 1997 pushed Wisconsin’s political and business leaders, and even some ratepayer advocacy groups, to rethink the state’s approach. With nuclear power plants in Wisconsin and Illinois unexpectedly offline for repairs, utilities warned that summertime air conditioning use might stretch the state’s supply past its limits and trigger widespread blackouts. State lawmakers abolished the Advanced Plan the following year. They replaced it with what Pilo called a “regulation-lite” approach, leaving planning for Wisconsin’s energy future mostly in utilities’ hand

artigo.texto: Projeto do data center que será instalado em Belém do Pará. Foto: Reprodução A implantação do mega data center BEL1 em Belém e seus possíveis impactos ambientais serão tema de uma sessão especial proposta pela vereadora Marinor Brito. O debate será realizado nesta quinta-feira (26), às 9h, no auditório da Superintendência do Desenvolvimento da Amazônia (Sudam), com o objetivo de ampliar a discussão pública sobre os efeitos da instalação de um empreendimento dessa dimensão na capital paraense. Entre as principais questões que serão discutidas estão o volume de água e energia necessário para o funcionamento da estrutura, os possíveis impactos sobre o meio ambiente e as comunidades do entorno, além dos benefícios econômicos e sociais que o empreendimento poderá trazer para Belém e sua população. Para a vereadora Marinor Brito, a chegada de um empreendimento dessa dimensão exige transparência e participação popular. “Não somos contra a tecnologia ou o desenvolvimento. O que queremos saber é quais são os custos ambientais e sociais de um projeto desse porte para Belém. Quanto de água e energia será consumido? Quais impactos poderão atingir o nosso território e as comunidades do entorno? E, principalmente, o que a população paraense vai ganhar o que ela vai perder com esse empreendimento? Essas perguntas precisam ser respondidas com clareza”, afirma. A iniciativa também busca garantir que a implantação de grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos na Amazônia seja acompanhada de informações acessíveis e debate público. “A Amazônia não pode ser tratada apenas como um território de exploração de recursos. O desenvolvimento precisa respeitar nossos rios, nossas florestas e as pessoas que vivem aqui. Não podemos aceitar que decisões com consequências para toda a cidade sejam tomadas sem transparência e sem ouvir a população”, destaca a vereadora. A sessão será aberta ao público e contará com espaço para perguntas, manifestações e esclarecimentos. A expectativa é reunir representantes da empresa, da sociedade, especialistas e pessoas interessadas em discutir os impactos e as responsabilidades socioambientais relacionados à implantação do BEL1 em Belém.

artigo.texto: Por: Ana Paula De Raeffray e Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray O Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) da União Europeia alterou em definitivo a segurança jurídica e a dogmática do comércio internacional, alçando a intensidade de carbono à condição de elemento tributário e regulatório decisivo para o acesso de bens ao mercado comunitário. Com a consolidação de sua fase plena, a carga de emissões incorporada aos produtos deixa de figurar como mero parâmetro socioambiental para assumir a natureza de encargo financeiro cogente na aduana europeia. Essa exigência regulatória gera impactos diretos sobre setores fundamentais da indústria de transformação nacional, como o siderúrgico, de alumínio, cimento, fertilizantes e hidrogênio. A principal complexidade jurídica dessa transição reside na assimetria das metodologias de mensuração e valoração das emissões perante o mercado europeu (EU ETS). Produtos com especificações técnicas idênticas sofrerão valoração tributária desequilibrada na Europa a depender da higidez das provas documentais, do rigor das auditorias do processo fabril e da capacidade de comprovar o tributo ou preço de carbono já recolhido no país de origem. É sob a ótica dessa assimetria que a regulamentação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, adquire centralidade jurídica. A consulta pública aberta pelo Ministério da Fazenda em julho de 2026 — destinada a regulamentar as regras de Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação (MRV) — evidenciou a urgência do alinhamento normativo. Embora a legislação comunitária europeia preveja o abatimento dos valores de carbono quitados no Brasil, o exercício dessa compensação condiciona-se à estrita equivalência metodológica e à validação documental perante as autoridades em Bruxelas. A ausência de uma célere interoperabilidade regulatória entre os padrões brasileiros e europeus expõe o setor produtivo ao risco iminente de dupla oneração econômica. Trata-se de um gargalo em que a indústria nacional arrisca suportar o encargo doméstico de carbono sem a devida dedutibilidade nas exportações para a Europa, sofrendo nítida perda de competitividade no cenário global. A relevância da matéria ultrapassou o âmbito normativo interno e ingressou na esfera do contencioso internacional. Em setembro de 2026, o Órgão de Solução de Controvérsias da Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC) acolheu a abertura de painel para aferir a conformidade do CBAM e do EU ETS com os acordos multilaterais. A participação do Brasil como terceiro interessado — ao lado de jurisdições como China, Índia, Estados Unidos e Japão — evidencia que a compatibilidade do mecanismo europeu com o princípio da não discriminação é objeto de profunda controvérsia jurídica internacional. No âmbito privado, o avanço desse regramento redefine os parâmetros da elaboração contratual em operações de exportação. Cláusulas de fornecimento que se limitavam a disciplinar tarifas aduaneiras e Incoterms passam a exigir disciplinas expressas sobre a alocação do risco tributário do carbono, deveres de transparência probatória e garantias de auditoria. A estruturação de instrumentos contratuais juridicamente blindados contra contenciosos internacionais — seja na arbitragem comercial exterior ou perante jurisdições estrangeiras — tornou-se pressuposto indispensável à higidez das operações. O cenário exige atuação institucional e corporativa diligente. O Brasil detém uma matriz energética de matriz limpa, mas arrisca sofrer restrições de mercado por assimetrias de integração regulatória. Cumpre acelerar a consolidação normativa do SBCE com foco no direito diplomático e comercial, cabendo às bancas e aos departamentos jurídicos tratar a contabilidade de carbono e a gestão de prova documental como matéria prioritária de governança e compliance. Sob a perspectiva da advocacia de negócios, essa adequação pode ser convertida em vantagem competitiva. Diante de uma matriz altamente descarbonizada, a indústria brasileira reúne condições para transformar o rigor probatório em diferencial de mercado em relação a concorrentes de matrizes fósseis, desde que assegurada a validade jurídica dos certificados perante os organismos internacionais. A carga de emissões incorporou-se de forma definitiva ao cálculo do custo de exportação, alinhando-se aos encargos freteiros, cambiais e alfandegários. Para o exportador nacional, o cumprimento rigoroso e autônomo dessas exigências não constitui tema prospectivo, mas condição imperativa de segurança jurídica e sobrevivência comercial. Ana Paula De Raeffray Doutora em Direito pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo (PUC-SP). Professora dos cursos de pós-graduação da PUC-SP. Sócia do escritório Raeffray Brugioni Advogados. Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray Graduado em Business Administration pela IE University. Atuante na área de Relações Governamentais perante o Parlamento Europeu. Consultor do escritório Raeffray Brugioni Advogados.

artigo.texto: Why Liquid Cooling Could Help Solve AI’s Growing Water Problem Utah is one of six states in the United States currently experiencing water shortages. In fact, the Beehive State has faced drought conditions for 22 of the last 25 years. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise that thousands of Utah residents lodged complaints when the state approved the construction of one of the largest data centers in the world. The $100 billion Stratos Project, twice the size of Manhattan, will consume more energy than the entire state, which, naturally, raises concerns about water usage. This recent example is a microcosm of a broader concern about AI and its associated water consumption. While it’s true that AI’s computational demands generate a lot of heat that requires intense cooling, it’s important to note that the environmental impact of different approaches to cooling can vary widely. Two types of cooling: air and liquid Most legacy data centers use air cooling solutions that tap fans and air conditioning, which consume a lot of water. But these traditional cooling systems can’t keep up with the cooling needs of AI factories and hyperscalers like the Stratos Project. Beyond 40 to 50 kilowatts (kW) per server rack, air cooling is no longer reliable. Server racks earmarked for AI workloads need anywhere from 50 kW to 250kW. Soon, these racks will eclipse one megawatt (MW). In other words, while air cooling systems can use a lot of water, they can’t be used for AI factories. Data centers will need to tap more efficient cooling solutions. Big data centers supporting AI, like Stratos, will need liquid cooling solutions, which are much more efficient than traditional cooling systems, since liquids are superior heat conductors, in order to effectively and reliably cool their facilities. As a result, the electricity consumed when cooling a data center drops by almost a third (30%), according to a recent study. There are several liquid cooling options in varying stages of development, but direct-to-chip (DTC) cooling is emerging as an industry standard for AI factories because it is an efficient, reliable method, circulating liquid coolant directly on the surfaces of computer ships via cold plates. It’s the difference between refrigerating soft drinks by putting them in a large cold storage room or putting them in a small portable cooler. Often used together with DTC cooling, coolant distribution units (CDU) pumps coolant in a closed-loop system and carries away the heat removed by DTC, rejecting it outside the system. This is a sustainable combination and is an excellent option for AI infrastructure. Some common questions and misconceptions about liquid cooling Why can’t data centers use other liquids besides water? They can and they do. Liquid cooling solutions often use dielectric fluids, which are electrically non-conductive liquids made of mineral oils, petroleum distillates, silicone fluids and more. Why can’t data centers use water from the ocean? There are a few major problems with seawater. Transportation alone makes it untenable, even if you’re close to a coast. The larger problem is that ocean water is corrosive, leaving behind salt and other mineral deposits that would build up, damaging and clogging pumps, pipes, cooling systems, etc. You could in theory use seawater in a closed-loop system, but the pump and pipe equipment for saltwater is way more expensive. Plus, saltwater is more conductive than freshwater. Leakage would be a persistent concern. Other ways to make data center cooling more sustainable Even with a closed-loop system, the water demands of AI factories are great, but there are other sustainable pathways that data center designers can pursue in the years to come. Heat reuse is an effective way of harnessing the heat generated by a data center to heat nearby buildings and structures. The problem with heat reuse is that the farther a data center is from buildings, the more logistically challenging it becomes to capitalize on waste heat. This approach is more practical in Europe, since they have district heating and their data centers tend to be closer to urban areas. About half of the electricity used by data centers come from fossil fuel power plants, which consume enormous amounts of water. Renewable energy can reduce their reliance on fossil fuels. Solar and wind may appear to be insufficient energy sources, given the surging energy demands of AI data centers, but a recent large-scale renewable energy deployment in China may be a blueprint. The construction in Ningxia expects 500 megawatts in solar capacity and 1.5 gigawatts of wind power by the end of the year. Building with sustainability in mind The demand for AI shows no signs of slowing, and the heat these server racks are producing continues to grow. The amount of water needed to cool hotter racks in bigger facilities will become a problem if data centers don’t pivot, especially given the looming water crisis around the world. DTC cooling and CDUs are a great foundation for this transitional period, but data center operators need to plan with the industry’s rapid growth rate in mind. How else can they simultaneously tackle extreme heat with expanding water consumption? District heating is not an option in the U.S., but maybe renewable energy deserves a closer look. Perhaps different types of on-site generation are worth investigating. The industry may need to be more mindful of data center locations moving forward. All of which is to say, the data center industry needs to keep its options open in such a rapidly changing field. We may not yet have all the answers for tomorrow’s questions, but maybe we have the answers for today’s questions. What we don’t want is for today’s answers to die on the vine for lack of forethought. artigo.texto: Sioux City Planning & Zoning Commission advances rules governing future data center projects SIOUX CITY (KTIV) - Sioux City is moving forward with an ordinance governing projects like data centers and cryptocurrency mining farms. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, the city’s Planning and Zoning commission voted 5-0 to approve the language of a new ordinance setting out rules for those kinds of projects. Two members of the commission abstained from the vote. The city’s planning manager says it addresses what the city would require from any future projects, like noise limits, property setbacks and water use rules. It also gives the public opportunities to weigh in on any possible projects. “The Planning and Zoning Commission did put in their recommendation of a site plan requirement, so that site plan would have to go through Planning and Zoning Commission and City Council, if City Council decide they also want to keep that requirement, and so there would be that public notification with what was approved tonight,” said Chris Madsen, Planning Manager for the City of Sioux City. artigo.texto: Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition and Carbon Market opportunities: How Can the Private Sector Get Involved? November 23, 2026 Category 3 November 2026 – The shift to clean energy infrastructure that is fair for workers, communities, and the economy requires significant investment. As Indonesia advances its Just Energy Transition (JET), carbon markets can provide an additional source of financing for credible and well-designed projects, as well as benefiting the communities involved. Through the Redirecting Investments for an Inclusive Just Energy Transition (REDI4JET) project, the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), together with its consortium partners Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) and Perspectives Climate Research (PCR), brought together private sector stakeholders for a webinar exploring how private stakeholders can take part in just energy transition projects and carbon market opportunities. The discussion focused on opportunities to align Indonesia’s JET initiatives with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets, as well as ways for the private sector to participate in REDI4JET’s inception phase focused on capacity needs assessment and other activities in 2027. Indonesia’s carbon market framework is taking shape with the issuance of Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on carbon pricing. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement adds another route, allowing countries to cooperate on carbon markets through the international transfer of mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) and a Paris Agreement crediting mechanism (PACM). The voluntary carbon market continues alongside it, with growing attention to credit integrity. The opportunity for Indonesia is to align these mechanisms with just energy transition activities, such as clean energy projects that create jobs and benefit local communities, so that carbon market finance supports the transition. “In recent years, Indonesia’s carbon market framework has developed rapidly, including the start of international carbon trading through the Indonesia Carbon Exchange and stronger cooperation under Article 6. These developments open up new opportunities, but also require technical and institutional readiness from all market participants. The private sector has a key role to play in this process.” Retno Setianingsih, Energy Lead, GGGI Indonesia Within REDI4JET, carbon markets are a tool to support the just energy transition, not an end in themselves. The project’s carbon markets work includes an assessment of Article 6, voluntary and domestic carbon markets, policy recommendations, the identification and prioritization of a pipeline of mitigation activities, and the development of two pilot Mitigation Activity Design Documents (MADDs) together with the private sector. A just transition also means that projects respect workers and communities, which is why civil society organizations are part of the survey, including on safeguards, free, prior and informed consent, grievance mechanisms and benefit sharing. So, how can the private sector contribute to Indonesia’s just energy transition? The private sector is at the forefront of markets and production and can therefore help shape the policies and projects needed to advance the transition. Project developers and financial institutions, for example, can share insights on technology costs, grid constraints, and buyer preferences. Private sector involvement can help ensure that proposed projects are technically sound and commercially viable. They can also help validate potential projects and explore co-investment opportunities, supporting efforts to move projects from design towards implementation. Under REDI4JET, private sector stakeholders will have opportunities to contribute to policy recommendations that encourage investment in the energy sector, provide input into approaches such as de-risking instruments, receive technical assistance to improve the transaction readiness of energy projects, and participate in training on carbon finance and project development. This includes learning how to develop bankable projects, reach financial close, and access financing. “Private sector stakeholders can actively contribute to policy recommendations and help shape approaches that improve the investment environment, including de-risking instruments. With REDI4JET, the private sector can also benefit from technical assistance, for example, training on carbon finance and developing bankable projects, and reaching financial close,” Ardian Candraputra, Senior Energy Officer and REDI4JET Project Manager, GGGI. Building the capacity to participate in carbon markets is another important part of Indonesia’s JET. “We want to make sure that the support we develop responds to actual needs. The feedback from participants gives us a useful starting point for identifying where further training and capacity building are needed. We are keen to develop activities that address these gaps and make the process as participatory as possible.” Debi Nathalia, Investment Unit Lead, GGGI REDI4JET’s training program is planned to run over the next two to three years. The program will also bring public and private sector participants together, rather than having them learn separately, creating opportunities to exchange knowledge and clarify regulatory requirements while building the capacity needed for effective participation. For private sector stakeholders, this is an opportunity to contribute to investment, sector expertise, feedback, and participation in developing projects and strengthening the wider investment environment. Early engagement can help ensure that REDI4JET’s activities reflect market realities and that future carbon market initiatives have the support needed to progress. “We aim to bring just energy transition activities and carbon markets together, so that the transition creates more jobs and supports sustainable development across the country. We can only do that by working hand in hand with the private sec

artigo.texto: Virginia has two serious problems that ought to be considered together. We need enormous amounts of new electricity to meet growing demand, and much of rural Virginia desperately needs new industry and jobs. Data centers offer an opportunity to address both. Yet instead of figuring out how to take advantage of that opportunity, we seem increasingly focused on making it harder for them to locate here. I’ve spent much of my career in the coal industry and later worked on redeveloping former mining properties for new industrial uses in Southwest Virginia. I’ve seen what happens when communities lose the industries that supported them, and I know how difficult it is to attract new investment. Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and place demands on local infrastructure. Developers should address those concerns and pay their own way. But these facilities support everything from banking and medical research to manufacturing and national security. With artificial intelligence expanding rapidly, demand isn’t going away. The question is whether Virginia intends to benefit from that investment or watch it go somewhere else. Two proposed projects illustrate what’s at stake. STACK Infrastructure is planning a large data center campus in Pittsylvania County, near Danville. At full buildout, it could require 3,000 megawatts of electricity. According to its permit application reported by Cardinal News, the developer expects to generate most of that power on-site, likely using substantial amounts of natural gas. The final generating technology has not been determined. Separately, Dominion Energy is proposing a 3,000-megawatt natural gas power plant in Cumberland County. That plant would supply Dominion’s utility customers, not the STACK project. Think about that. One proposed data center campus could require as much generating capacity as Dominion’s entire new power plant. That’s an extraordinary amount of electricity. It’s also an extraordinary economic opportunity. Virginia needs dependable electricity Virginia already imports a substantial portion of its electricity. In 2023, net imports accounted for 36% of our electricity supply. Meanwhile, PJM, the regional grid operator, projects that peak electricity demand in Dominion’s service territory could more than double by 2046. There’s nothing inherently wrong with importing electricity. But depending heavily on other states becomes a concern when severe weather strains the entire region. There’s an economic cost as well. When Virginia imports electricity, much of the economic benefit of producing it goes somewhere else. Other states get the construction jobs, permanent employment, supporting businesses and tax revenue. Virginia’s energy policies make it harder to change that. The Virginia Clean Economy Act requires major utilities to move toward carbon-free electricity and retire certain fossil-fuel plants, subject to reliability protections. The Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative also adds a cost to emissions from covered power plants. Reducing emissions is a legitimate objective. But so are affordable electricity, a reliable grid and economic development. We can’t pursue one while ignoring the others. Wind and solar have a role, but neither can be counted on whenever electricity is needed. Batteries help for shorter periods, but several days of severe weather require dependable generation. Modern natural gas combined-cycle plants are highly efficient and can operate around the clock. Nuclear power should also play a much larger role in our long-term energy plans. After a career in energy production, one thing I know is that reliable electricity isn’t optional. Factories, hospitals and businesses need power regardless of the weather. With demand growing so rapidly, why make it harder to build the generating capacity we need? Make data centers part of the solution Data centers need dependable electricity around the clock. Developers should help finance the generation and infrastructure they require, rather than leaving existing utility customers with the bill. But we should go further. Large data centers should also contribute to grid reliability during emergencies. Depending on their design, they could provide surplus generation, use backup power where feasible or temporarily reduce demand. Some AI computing can be delayed or shifted elsewhere, reducing demand during a grid emergency. Consider what happens to electricity prices during severe conditions. Wholesale electricity might ordinarily cost $40 to $60 per megawatt-hour. During extreme demand, prices can exceed $1,000 or even $2,500. The last few megawatts needed to keep the system operating can become extraordinarily expensive. If data centers could reliably reduce demand during those critical hours, they could help avoid some of those costs. These arrangements would require firm commitments, proper engineering and reasonable compensation. But the principle is simple: establish the reliability requirements and let developers find the most economical way to meet them. That’s better than dictating the technology they must use. Rural Virginia cannot afford to miss this opportunity Consider the economic potential. Dominion’s proposed Cumberland County power plant would occupy about 150 acres. A developer-sponsored study projects approximately $502 million in local tax revenue over 36 years, along with construction and permanent jobs. STACK’s proposed Pittsylvania County development is much larger. At full buildout, projections suggest as much as $100 billion in investment, more than 2,500 jobs and up to $48 million annually in property taxes. Those are projections, not guarantees. But even a fraction of that investment could change the future of a rural community. Southside Virginia knows this story all too well. Communities around Danville and Martinsville lost thousands of jobs as tobacco, textiles and furniture manufacturing declined, leaving economic wounds that have taken decad

artigo.texto: Madison moves toward hyperscale data center ban as advocates call for statewide protections MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Madison is looking to ban hyperscale data centers within city limits as its temporary moratorium on larger facilities nears its expiration. A proposed ordinance on Tuesday’s Common Council agenda would establish long-term restrictions on the size, location and operation of data centers following months of research and public feedback. While the proposed regulations aim to protect Madison residents, environmental advocacy group Clean Wisconsin says addressing the broader impacts of large-scale data centers will require action at the state level. According to the city, there are currently no active proposals or applications for new data centers in Madison. What is Madison proposing? In January, the Common Council approved a temporary moratorium on zoning approvals for new data centers larger than 10,000 square feet as a property’s primary use, giving city staff time to study potential impacts and develop regulations. Without new regulations in place when the moratorium expires, the city says its existing zoning code would not adequately regulate the size or location of modern data centers. The proposed ordinance, sponsored by Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and Alder Derek Field, would replace that moratorium with new zoning regulations. According to a Nov. 19 Planning Division staff report, public feedback prompted several changes to the initial proposal, including reducing the maximum allowable size from 100,000 to 75,000 square feet. Under the proposed ordinance: - Data centers would be capped at 75,000 square feet per zoning lot, with no exceptions to exceed that limit. - Data centers would be prohibited in residential zoning districts. - Facilities between 50,000 and 75,000 square feet would only be allowed in designated industrial and airport zoning districts. - The largest permitted facilities would require a 500-foot buffer from areas zoned for housing and a 300-foot buffer from certain other nonindustrial districts. - Data centers 10,000 square feet or larger would require noise mitigation plans, solid walls surrounding mechanical equipment and emergency generators, and at least 1,000 feet of separation from parcels occupied by another data center of that size or larger. The combination of size and separation requirements would also effectively ban large data center campuses. A separate proposed ordinance would increase fines for violations of the city’s existing noise control ordinance. The city says all existing data centers in Madison would be permitted under the proposed regulations. In a statement Friday, Rhodes-Conway said the proposal would protect residents from potential negative impacts while continuing to allow responsible and legitimate uses of computing power. “With this proposal, the City is effectively exercising its authority, and I strongly urge State lawmakers to enact sensible data center regulation so local communities have additional tools to protect residents,” Rhodes-Conway said. Environmental advocates call for statewide action Clean Wisconsin Communications Director Amy Barrilleaux said Madison’s proposed regulations could help protect nearby residents, but the environmental impacts of large-scale artificial intelligence data centers extend beyond city limits. According to the city, Wisconsin municipalities have authority over land use and zoning but cannot regulate water consumption, energy use, energy sources or utility rates. Barrilleaux said three AI data center projects in Wisconsin are expected to collectively use more energy than four million homes. “Our energy utilities are racing to meet that need by building a large number of new gas plants,” Barrilleaux said. “This appears to be easily one of the largest, if not the largest, increases in fossil fuel energy generation in the history of Wisconsin.” She said the growing demand for electricity raises concerns about air pollution, public health, water use and potentially higher utility bills. “We can’t have Madison or Sun Prairie or Middleton all racing to figure this out,” Barrilleaux said. “There need to be statewide protections that protect every community in Wisconsin because this sort of like piecemeal approach isn’t working for the whole state.” Clean Wisconsin is calling for a statewide pause on AI data center development until additional protections are in place. The organization is advocating for greater energy efficiency, the use of clean energy, increased transparency surrounding water use and pollution, and measures to ensure technology companies cover the cost of energy infrastructure built to meet their needs. Barrilleaux said the organization has been working with state lawmakers and other advocates in hopes of seeing legislative action in the new year. “Local lawmakers do their work at the local level. That’s what they do. And so, if they feel like an ordinance is needed to protect their community, then that’s what their job is,” Barrilleaux said. “State lawmakers have that job too. It’s on the state level. And we can’t expect every community to in the next six months be able to fully protect communities as these huge projects roll out.” What comes next? A City of Madison spokesperson told WMTV Tuesday’s introduction is the first step in the legislative process. The Common Council does not discuss ordinances when they are first introduced. Several city committees will review the proposal and gather public feedback before making recommendations to the Common Council. The proposed timeline includes: - Nov. 30: Plan Commission - Dec. 16: Business and Economic Resources Committee - Dec. 21: Sustainable Madison Committee - Jan. 11: Plan Commission public hearing - Jan. 12: Common Council discussion and anticipated vote Jan. 12 is the last scheduled Common Council meeting before the city’s temporary moratorium expires on Jan. 24, 2027. artigo.texto: Two recent reports by India Ratings and Research (Ind-Ra) and CareEdge highlight widening credit divergence among domestic solar module manufacturers amid an increasing shift towards BESS manufacturing and rising operational capacity. Demand for BESS is rising as renewable energy additions outpace transmission infrastructure development. A recent ICRA report emphasises that execution is a key monitorable in building Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity amid growing storage demand and with enlarging tender pipeline. This trend is particularly acute in resource-rich states such as Rajasthan and Gujarat. This, in turn, is creating grid congestion and a growing need for storage to absorb surplus generation, shift supply to non-solar hours, and ease network constraints. India Rating and Research (IndiRa) special report, “Policy Access, Integration, and ROCE Will Drive Credit for Solar Module Manufacturers”, examines domestic manufacturing economics, ALMM-II and DCR implications, margin migration, technology and execution risks, BESS diversification, and the likely rating outlook for the sector. Emphasising on the impact on the BESS project, the research noted, a shift in Indian BESS market from tendering to execution, backed by policy support and a large tender pipeline. However, the rebound in battery prices, rupee depreciation and aggressive bids make timely battery procurement, robust LTSAs and offtake tie-ups critical for project viability. Credit Divergence & Solar Cell Import Dependence Affect the Indian Market Another key element is credit considerations, which are now emerging as an important factor requiring attention. Credit divergence across domestic solar module manufacturers is emerging in FY27, even as strong solar power demand continues, indicating widening differences in manufacturers' credit profiles. However, import dependence continues, with imported-cell modules being 3-4 US cents/W cheaper than domestic-content-requirement modules, even after basic customs duty. Consequently, the implementation of the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II will be central to absorbing domestic cell capacity. The divergence is unfolding against a backdrop of stable module capacity at 228 GW, which is more than three times the estimated annual requirement of 65-70 GW. This makes capacity utilisation, technology relevance, customer access, liquidity, and returns on capital more important than announced capacity alone. Solar to Push for Further Upstream Manufacturing From Modules to Cells and Ingots Ind-Ra marks the shift in Indian solar sector with the change in its margin pool from modules to cells. With margins likely to move further upstream towards ingots and wafers as backward integration gathers pace, its expected to favour well-capitalised integrated manufacturers. However, substantially higher capex, technology, commissioning, power, and refinancing risks will increase rating sensitivity. Therefore, the winners according to the report would be those who can provider low-debt module manufacturers with strong channels and high asset turns. This may remain viable at lower margins, while leveraged greenfield projects and standalone assemblers dependent on spot cells will be more exposed as domestic cell spreads normalise. “Policy access and integration will increasingly determine market position, but neither guarantees stronger credit quality. As manufacturers move upstream, the ability to preserve return on capital, manage technology transitions, and fund expansion without weakening liquidity will separate sustainable business models from capacity-led growth,” says Bhanu Patni, Director, Corporate Ratings, Ind-Ra. BESS Pack Costs Remain Central to Assessment At a battery pack cost of USD 70/kWh, a cumulative DSCR of 1.17-1.27 times is expected at tariffs of Rs. 2.60-2.80 lakh/MW/month. Competitive procurement and protection against cost escalation remain central to the assessment. Operational BESS capacity is also rising, signalling progress from tendering to deployment. Policy support, including the Government of India’s VGF schemes announced in 2023, 2025, and 2026, covering 135.8 GWh, provides a significant source of capital support. Battery procurement costs and currency movements remain critical to the viability of aggressively bid projects. ICRA’s sensitivity analysis highlights limited coverage headroom at lower capacity tariffs. Merchant BESS Viability: Arbitrage Margins Need Adequate Utilisation Sustained arbitrage margins and adequate utilisation are critical to merchant BESS viability. ICRA’s analysis indicates a cumulative DSCR of 1.35-1.52 times at a charging cost of Rs. 2/unit and discharge realisation of Rs. 6.0-6.5/unit, under the stated assumptions. Narrowing peak-off-peak spreads, fewer viable trading cycles, lower efficiency, and availability shortfalls remain key risks to cash flows and debt coverage, necessitating adequate liquidity buffers. Lower upfront funding and supplier guarantees do not eliminate future costs and operating risks. The report reccomends project assessments to take into account eventual duty payments under Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations (MOOWR) and check whether supplier guarantees adequately cover commitments to the power buyer. Costs not covered by the supplier, including performance penalties, additional batteries, and post-warranty maintenance, remain important risks for the developer.
